flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-15: Time, Fuel and Distance to Descend, Cruising Pressure altitude 9000 ft, OAT +16°C, destination pressure altitude 4000 ft, temperature is standard. The fuel used for the descent is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 9000 ft, OAT +16 deg C; destination pressure altitude 4000 ft, temperature standard. Find fuel used for the descent.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-15, Time, Fuel and Distance to Descend)
Step 1: At 4000 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 4) = 7 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +16 deg C, move up to the 9000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer to the FUEL - GAL line, and read the cumulative fuel at the cruise condition.
Step 3: Enter again at +7 deg C, move up to the 4000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer to the FUEL - GAL line, and read the cumulative fuel at the destination condition.
Step 4: Subtract the destination reading from the cruise reading for the fuel used during descent.

ANSWER
2 USG

flight-planning.q: An increase in the density altitude will affect the aircraft performance by:
flight-planning.c: Having no effect on climb performance
flight-planning.e:
Higher density altitude means the air is less dense. The engine develops less power, the propeller produces less thrust and the wings generate less lift at a given indicated condition, so climb performance decreases.

Exam tip: High, hot and low-pressure conditions all increase density altitude and reduce performance.

flight-planning.q: During the climb out after take-off an aircraft encounters a sudden increase in the headwind component. The aircraft:
flight-planning.b: Will remain on the same flight path
flight-planning.e:
A sudden headwind increase raises the aircraft's airspeed and lift before the pilot can correct. The flight path initially rises above the intended climb path, so the aircraft starts to overshoot.

Exam tip: Increasing headwind generally produces an overshoot; increasing tailwind produces an undershoot.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-2: Stall Speeds, weight 2350 lb, 40° Flaps. The indicated stall speed in straight and level flight is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Weight 2350 lb, 40 deg Flaps, wings level (0 deg bank), power off.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-2, Stall Speeds)
Step 1: Enter the WEIGHT - 100 LBS scale on the right of the chart (built for 2500 lb gross weight) at 23.5 (2350 lb).
Step 2: Follow the 40 deg FLAPS weight-correction line left to the vertical reference line under the INDICATED AIRSPEED heading.
Step 3: Bank angle is 0 deg, so stay at the 0 deg point on the 40 deg FLAPS curve in the ANGLE OF BANK - DEGREES panel - no further correction needed.
Step 4: From that point read horizontally left to the airspeed scale.

ANSWER
48 KIAS

flight-planning.q: An aircraft flies from A to B, distance 225 NM, GS 100 kt, fuel flow 8.5 USG/hr. Taxi, take-off and climb fuel is 3.3 USG. If the total fuel on board is 35 USG, the reserve fuel is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 225 NM, groundspeed = 100 kt, cruise fuel flow = 8.5 USG/hr, taxi/take-off/climb fuel = 3.3 USG, total fuel on board = 35 USG

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: On the circular slide-rule side, rotate the inner scale so the 60 index (minutes-per-hour) sits under 100 (groundspeed, kt) on the outer scale.
Step 2: Find 225 (distance, NM) on the outer scale and read the time below it on the inner scale: 135 minutes (2.25 hours).
Step 3: Re-index the 60 under 8.5 (fuel flow, USG/hr) on the outer scale, find 135 minutes on the inner scale, and read the trip fuel above it on the outer scale: 19.1 USG.
Step 4: Subtract on paper: reserve fuel = total fuel − trip fuel − taxi/take-off/climb fuel.

SOLVE
Time = 225 NM ÷ 100 kt = 2.25 hours (135 min)
Trip fuel = 2.25 hr × 8.5 USG/hr = 19.125 USG
Reserve fuel = 35 − 19.125 − 3.3 = 12.575 USG, rounded to 12.6 USG

ANSWER
12.6 USG

Exam tip: Reserve fuel is what remains after all planned fuel uses are deducted.

flight-planning.q: The maximum ramp weight of an aeroplane is:
flight-planning.a: Is the maximum landing weight plus reserve fuel
flight-planning.b: Is the maximum takeoff weight plus the taxi fuel
flight-planning.c: Is the basic empty weight plus usable fuel
flight-planning.d: Is the maximum zero fuel weight plus baggage
flight-planning.ans: Is the maximum takeoff weight plus the taxi fuel
flight-planning.e:
Maximum ramp weight is the maximum take-off weight plus the fuel expected to be burned during taxi. The aircraft may therefore leave the parking area slightly above MTOW, provided it is at or below MTOW before take-off.

Exam tip: Ramp weight = take-off weight + taxi fuel.

flight-planning.q: The take-off distance available:
flight-planning.a: Is reduced by the displaced-threshold distance
flight-planning.b: Is increased by the displaced-threshold distance
flight-planning.c: Is unaffected by the presence of permanently displaced threshold
flight-planning.d: Is equal to landing distance available
flight-planning.ans: Is unaffected by the presence of permanently displaced threshold
flight-planning.e:
A permanently displaced threshold reduces landing distance available in the direction of the displacement, but the pavement before the threshold remains available for take-off. TODA is therefore not reduced solely because a threshold is displaced.

Exam tip: Displaced thresholds affect landing distance, not normal take-off use of the pavement.

flight-planning.q: The maximum take-off weight of an aircraft may be exceeded:
flight-planning.a: By any amount approved by the pilot
flight-planning.c: It may never be exceeded at the ramp
flight-planning.d: By the weight of fuel required for taxi purposes
flight-planning.ans: By the weight of fuel required for taxi purposes
flight-planning.e:
The aircraft may be above maximum take-off weight while taxiing only by the amount of fuel that will be burned before take-off, and it must still remain within maximum ramp weight.

Exam tip: The aircraft must be at or below MTOW when the take-off roll begins.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22: Take-off distance, Pressure altitude 4000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +15°C, the take-off distance required to clear 50 ft is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 4000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +15°C. Distance required to clear 50 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-22)
Step 1: Enter the Take-off Performance Table (weight 2400 lb, flaps up, paved level dry runway, zero wind) at pressure altitude 4000 ft.
Step 2: At PA 4000 ft the Total-to-clear-50ft column reads 2185 ft at +10°C and 2345 ft at +20°C. +15°C is midway between the two.
Step 3: No headwind, tailwind or grass-runway correction is stated, so none is applied.

SOLVE
Interpolate: (2185 + 2345) / 2 = 4530 / 2 = 2265 ft

ANSWER
2265 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-3, flaps up take-off ground roll, temperatures ISA+22°C, pressure altitude 3500 ft, weight 2500 lb, zero wind, the ground roll required is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
OAT ISA+22 deg C, pressure altitude 3500 ft, weight 2500 lb, zero wind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-3, Flaps Up Take-off Ground Roll)
Step 1: At 3500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 3.5) = 8 deg C, so OAT = 8 + 22 = 30 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +30 deg C on the OUTSIDE AIR TEMPERATURE - degC scale, move up to the 3500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Weight is already 2500 lb (the reference weight), so no correction is needed - continue right to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 4: With zero wind, follow the zero-wind position straight up to the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale and read the result.

ANSWER
1900 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-19, airspeed system calibration, flaps 40°, KIAS 58 kt. The calibrated airspeed (KCAS) is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flaps 40°, KIAS 58 kt.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-19)
Step 1: Enter the Airspeed Calibration Table on the Flaps 40° row.
Step 2: The table lists KIAS 50 → KCAS 54 and KIAS 60 → KCAS 62. KIAS 58 falls between them.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: 54 + (58-50)/(60-50) x (62-54) = 54 + 0.8 x 8 = 54 + 6.4 = 60.4 KCAS ≈ 60 KCAS

ANSWER
60 KCAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-16: Glide range, cruising pressure altitude 10500 ft, terrain pressure altitude 1500 ft. The distance covered during the glide is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 10500 ft, terrain pressure altitude 1500 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-16, Glide Range)
Step 1: Height available for the glide = 10500 - 1500 = 9000 ft.
Step 2: Enter the PRESSURE ALTITUDE - FEET scale at 9000 ft and move up to the glide line.
Step 3: From that point move right to read the GLIDE RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
19 NM

flight-planning.q: Runway length 1550 m, displaced threshold 30 m. The take-off distance available(TODA) is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway length = 1550 m, displaced threshold = 30 m

FORMULA
TODA = runway length (a displaced threshold does not reduce take-off distance available; it only affects landing distance available)

SOLVE
No distance is subtracted: TODA = 1550 m

ANSWER
1550 m

Exam tip: Do not subtract a displaced threshold from take-off distance.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-23: Cruise performance table, Pressure altitude 9000 ft, RPM 2400, the endurance is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 9000 ft, RPM 2400. Find endurance.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-23)
Step 1: Enter the Cruise Performance Table (weight 2300 lb, zero wind) at RPM 2400.
Step 2: At RPM 2400 the endurance column reads 6.8 hours at PA 8000 ft and 7.6 hours at PA 10,000 ft. PA 9000 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: (6.8 + 7.6) / 2 = 14.4 / 2 = 7.2 hours

ANSWER
7.2 hours

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-16:glide range, cruising pressure altitude 8500 ft, terrain elevation 4300 ft, QNH 1023 hPa. The distance covered during the glide is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 8500 ft, terrain elevation 4300 ft, QNH 1023 hPa.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-16, Glide Range)
Step 1: Convert terrain elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 4300 + (1013 - 1023) x 30 = 4300 - 300 = 4000 ft.
Step 2: Height available for the glide = 8500 - 4000 = 4500 ft.
Step 3: Enter the PRESSURE ALTITUDE - FEET scale at 4500 ft and move up to the glide line, then right to read the GLIDE RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
10 NM

flight-planning.q: The symbol Vfe is used to indicate the:
flight-planning.e:
VFE is the maximum speed at which the aircraft may be flown with the flaps extended. Exceeding it can overstress the flap system.

Exam tip: FE means flaps extended.

flight-planning.q: Runway 36 threshold 5125 ft. Runway 18 threshold 5180 ft, length 3800 ft. The percentage slope of runway 18 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway 36 threshold elevation = 5125 ft, Runway 18 threshold elevation = 5180 ft, runway length = 3800 ft

FORMULA
Slope % = elevation difference ÷ runway length × 100

SOLVE
Elevation difference = 5180 − 5125 = 55 ft
Slope = 55 ÷ 3800 × 100 = 1.447%, rounded to 1.45%
From Runway 18 to Runway 36, elevation decreases, so the slope is down

ANSWER
1.45% down

Exam tip: Slope percentage uses vertical change divided by runway length in the same units.

flight-planning.q: An aircraft flies from A to B with 27 USG of fuel on board. The trip fuel is 14 USG and alternative and reserve fuel is 9 USG. If the holding fuel flow is 6.5 USG/hr, the aircraft could hold overhead B without using reserve fuel for:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Total fuel on board = 27 USG, trip fuel = 14 USG, alternate and reserve fuel = 9 USG, holding fuel flow = 6.5 USG/hr

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Subtract on paper first: fuel available for holding = total fuel − trip fuel − alternate/reserve fuel.
Step 2: On the circular side, rotate the inner scale so the 60 index sits under 6.5 (holding fuel flow, USG/hr) on the outer scale.
Step 3: Find 4 (fuel available, USG) on the outer scale and read the holding time below it on the inner scale.

SOLVE
Fuel available = 27 − 14 − 9 = 4 USG
Holding time = 4 USG ÷ 6.5 USG/hr = 0.615 hr = 0.615 × 60 = 36.9 minutes, rounded to 37 minutes

ANSWER
37 minutes

Exam tip: Protect alternate and reserve fuel before calculating holding time.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to climb, Departure airfield elevation 2410 ft, QNH 1010 hPa, temperature ISA, cruise pressure altitude 8500 ft, OAT -4°C. The fuel used during the climb is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Departure airfield elevation 2410 ft, QNH 1010 hPa, temperature ISA; cruise pressure altitude 8500 ft, OAT -4 deg C. Find fuel used during the climb.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb)
Step 1: Convert departure elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 2410 + (1013 - 1010) x 30 = 2410 + 90 = 2500 ft; at that altitude ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 2.5) = 10 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +10 deg C, move up to the 2500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the FUEL - GAL line, and read the cumulative fuel used from sea level to the departure condition.
Step 3: Enter again at -4 deg C, move up to the 8500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the FUEL - GAL line, and read the cumulative fuel used from sea level to the cruise condition.
Step 4: Subtract the departure reading from the cruise reading for the fuel used during the climb.

ANSWER
3 USG

flight-planning.q: The maximum speed at which an aeroplane may be flown under normal operating conditions is referred to as:
flight-planning.e:
VNO is the maximum structural cruising speed, also called the maximum normal operating speed. Flight above VNO is restricted to smooth air and flown with caution.

Exam tip: VNO is the upper limit of the green arc.

flight-planning.q: During the climb out after take-off from a runway with a light tailwind, an aircraft encounters a sudden increase in the tailwind component. The aircraft:
flight-planning.c: Will remain on the same flight path
flight-planning.e:
A sudden tailwind increase reduces airspeed and lift before the pilot can correct. The aircraft initially falls below the intended climb path and starts to undershoot.

Exam tip: A tailwind increase has the same initial effect as a headwind decrease.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to climb, departure airfield pressure altitude 2000 ft, OAT +20°C, cruising level FL105, temperature ISA. The time taken for the climb is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Departure airfield pressure altitude 2000 ft, OAT +20 deg C; cruising level FL105 (10500 ft), temperature ISA. Find climb time.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb)
Step 1: At FL105, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 10.5) = -6 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +20 deg C, move up to the 2000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the TIME - MIN line, and read the cumulative time from sea level to the departure condition.
Step 3: Enter again at -6 deg C, move up to the 10500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the TIME - MIN line, and read the cumulative time from sea level to the cruise condition.
Step 4: Subtract the departure reading from the cruise reading for the climb time.

ANSWER
20 minutes

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-9 Engine performance, pressure altitude 8500 ft, OAT ISA+2°C. 65% power. The RPM required is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 8500 ft, OAT ISA+2 deg C, 65% power. Find required RPM.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-9, Engine Performance)
Step 1: At 8500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 8.5) = -2 deg C, so OAT = -2 + 2 = 0 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at 0 deg C on the OUTSIDE AIR TEMPERATURE - degC axis, move up to the 8500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal.
Step 3: Transfer straight up into the upper panel to the 65% PERCENT POWER curve.
Step 4: From that point move right to read the ENGINE SPEED - RPM scale.

ANSWER
2490 RPM

flight-planning.q: An aircraft flies from A to B distance 135 NM, GS 90 kt, fuel flow 8 USG/hr. If the total fuel on board is 18 USG, the reserve fuel is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 135 NM, groundspeed = 90 kt, fuel flow = 8 USG/hr, total fuel on board = 18 USG

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the inner scale so the 60 index sits under 90 (groundspeed, kt) on the outer scale.
Step 2: Find 135 (distance, NM) on the outer scale and read the time below it on the inner scale: 90 minutes (1.5 hours).
Step 3: Re-index the 60 under 8 (fuel flow, USG/hr) on the outer scale, find 90 minutes on the inner scale, and read trip fuel above it: 12 USG.
Step 4: Subtract on paper: reserve fuel = total fuel − trip fuel.

SOLVE
Time = 135 NM ÷ 90 kt = 1.5 hours
Trip fuel = 1.5 hr × 8 USG/hr = 12 USG
Reserve fuel = 18 − 12 = 6 USG

ANSWER
6 USG

Exam tip: Reserve fuel is total fuel minus the fuel required for the planned flight.

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft's CG is 89.0" weight 2200 lb. A late passenger weighing 175 lb is seated in a rear seat(arm 116.6"), 30 lb of baggage is loaded into the baggage compartment(arm 140.5"), MAUW 2500 lb. The new CG is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 89.0 in, initial weight = 2200 lb
Passenger added: 175 lb at arm 116.6 in (rear seat)
Baggage added: 30 lb at arm 140.5 in
MAUW = 2500 lb

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
Total Moment = sum of individual moments
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2200 × 89.0 = 195,800 lb-in
Passenger moment = 175 × 116.6 = 20,405 lb-in
Baggage moment = 30 × 140.5 = 4,215 lb-in
Total moment = 195,800 + 20,405 + 4,215 = 220,420 lb-in
Total weight = 2200 + 175 + 30 = 2405 lb
New CG = 220,420 ÷ 2405 = 91.65 in

ANSWER
91.65 in

flight-planning.q: On final approach to land an aircraft encounters a sudden increase in the headwind component. The aircraft:
flight-planning.c: Will remain on the same flight path
flight-planning.e:
A sudden headwind increase raises airspeed and lift on final approach. The aircraft initially moves above the intended glide path and starts to overshoot.

Exam tip: Correct wind-shear effects smoothly; avoid chasing airspeed with abrupt control inputs.

flight-planning.q: An aircraft loads 42 USG of fuel. If the SG is 0.72 the weight of the fuel is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Fuel volume = 42 USG, specific gravity (SG) = 0.72, 1 USG = 3.785 litres

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: On the fuel conversion scale, align 42 against the USG (GAL) index arrow on the outer scale.
Step 2: Read the equivalent value opposite the LITRE index arrow on the inner scale: 159 litres.
Step 3: Set the specific-gravity index to 0.72 on the fuel/weight scale, then read the weight opposite the KG index arrow for that volume.

SOLVE
Volume in litres = 42 × 3.785 = 158.97 litres
Mass = 158.97 × 0.72 = 114.5 kg, rounded to 114 kg

ANSWER
114 kg

Exam tip: For fuel, mass in kg = litres × specific gravity.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-24, weight 2400 lb, pressure altitude 2000 ft, temperature +35°C, dry grass runway and 4 kt tailwind. The landing distance to clear 50 ft is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Weight 2400 lb, pressure altitude 2000 ft, temperature +35°C, dry grass runway, 4 kt tailwind. Distance to clear 50 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-24)
Step 1: Enter the Landing Performance Table (weight 2400 lb, flaps 40°, paved level dry runway, zero wind) at PA 2000 ft.
Step 2: At PA 2000 ft, Ground Roll / Total-to-clear-50ft read 595 ft / 1385 ft at +30°C and 615 ft / 1420 ft at +40°C. +35°C is midway.
Step 3: Apply the footnotes: dry grass adds 25% of the Ground Roll figure to the distance; tailwind adds 10% of the distance per 10 kt (here 4 kt = 4%).

SOLVE
Interpolate Ground Roll: (595+615)/2 = 605 ft
Interpolate Total-to-clear-50ft: (1385+1420)/2 = 1402.5 ft
Add dry-grass correction: 1402.5 + (0.25 x 605) = 1402.5 + 151.25 = 1553.75 ft
Apply 4 kt tailwind (+4%): 1553.75 x 1.04 = 1615.9 ft ≈ 1615 ft

ANSWER
1615 ft

flight-planning.q: Runway length 1150 m, stopway 30 m, displaced threshold 25 m. The landing distance available is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway length = 1150 m, stopway = 30 m, displaced threshold = 25 m

FORMULA
LDA = runway length − displaced threshold (a stopway is not included in LDA)

SOLVE
LDA = 1150 − 25 = 1125 m (the 30 m stopway is excluded)

ANSWER
1125 m

Exam tip: LDA excludes both the displaced portion and any stopway.

flight-planning.q: An aircraft in level flight covers a distance of 180 NM at a groundspeed of 100 kt, consuming 19.0 USG. the fuel flow is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 180 NM, groundspeed = 100 kt, fuel consumed = 19.0 USG

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the inner scale so the 60 index sits under 100 (groundspeed, kt) on the outer scale.
Step 2: Find 180 (distance, NM) on the outer scale and read the time below it on the inner scale: 108 minutes (1.8 hours).
Step 3: Align 19.0 (fuel used, USG) on the outer scale opposite 108 minutes on the inner scale, fixing the rate arm.
Step 4: Read the fuel flow on the outer scale above the 60 index on the inner scale.

SOLVE
Time = 180 NM ÷ 100 kt = 1.8 hours
Fuel flow = 19.0 USG ÷ 1.8 hr = 10.56 USG/hr, rounded to 10.6 USG/hr

ANSWER
10.6 USG/hr

Exam tip: Fuel flow = fuel used ÷ time.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-5: 25° Flaps Take-off ground roll, OAT +25°C, pressure altitude 4500 ft, weight 2450 lb, 5 kt headwind. The ground roll required is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
OAT +25 deg C, pressure altitude 4500 ft, weight 2450 lb, 5 kt headwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-5, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Ground Roll)
Step 1: Enter at +25 deg C, move up to the 4500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 2: Follow the 2450 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 3: From the reference line, follow the HEADWIND diagonal out to 5 kt.
Step 4: Move up from that point to read the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1350 ft

flight-planning.q: The empty weight of an aircraft plus crew, passengers, baggage and cargo, but excluding usable fuel, is referred to as:
flight-planning.e:
Zero fuel weight is the aircraft's loaded weight excluding usable fuel. It includes the aircraft, crew, passengers, baggage and cargo.

Exam tip: 'Maximum zero fuel weight' is a structural limit; 'zero fuel weight' is the actual calculated weight.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-8: Time, Distance and Fuel to climb, Departure airfield elevation 1380 ft, QNH 1009 hPa, temperature ISA, cruising level FL075, temperature ISA+12°C. The fuel used during the climb is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Departure airfield elevation 1380 ft, QNH 1009 hPa, temperature ISA; cruising level FL075 (7500 ft), temperature ISA+12 deg C. Find fuel used during the climb.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb)
Step 1: Convert departure elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 1380 + (1013 - 1009) x 30 = 1380 + 120 = 1500 ft; ISA temperature there = 15 - (2 x 1.5) = 12 deg C.
Step 2: At FL075, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 7.5) = 0 deg C, so cruise OAT = 0 + 12 = 12 deg C.
Step 3: Enter at +12 deg C / 1500 ft, transfer up to the FUEL - GAL line, and read the cumulative fuel at the departure condition; enter again at +12 deg C / 7500 ft and read the cumulative fuel at the cruise condition.
Step 4: Subtract the departure reading from the cruise reading for the fuel used during the climb.

ANSWER
3.5 USG

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-10: Speed Power - Performance Cruise. Pressure altitude 6500 ft, OAT +11°C, TAS 116 kt. The % power is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 6500 ft, OAT +11 deg C, TAS 116 kt. Find power setting.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-10, Speed Power - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: Enter at +11 deg C on the OUTSIDE AIR TEMPERATURE - degC axis, move up to the 6500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal.
Step 2: Transfer straight up into the upper panel to that row's operating point.
Step 3: Move right along the row to where it meets 116 kt on the TRUE AIRSPEED - KNOTS scale.
Step 4: Read the PERCENT POWER curve passing through that point.

ANSWER
65%

flight-planning.q: The landing distance available is:
flight-planning.e:
A displaced threshold moves the usable landing threshold farther along the runway. This shortens the landing distance available in that direction.

Exam tip: LDA = runway length minus the displaced-threshold distance.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-16: Glide range, Cruising pressure altitude 9000 ft, terrain elevation 2620 ft. QNH 1017 hPa. The distance covered during the glide is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 9000 ft, terrain elevation 2620 ft, QNH 1017 hPa.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-16, Glide Range)
Step 1: Convert terrain elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 2620 + (1013 - 1017) x 30 = 2620 - 120 = 2500 ft.
Step 2: Height available for the glide = 9000 - 2500 = 6500 ft.
Step 3: Enter the PRESSURE ALTITUDE - FEET scale at 6500 ft and move up to the glide line, then right to read the GLIDE RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
14 NM

flight-planning.q: An aircraft's floor loading is 20 lb/sq ft. The maximum weight which can be loaded in a box measuring 2 ft x 3 ft and weighing 12 lb is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Floor loading limit = 20 lb/sq ft
Box dimensions = 2 ft × 3 ft
Box (empty) weight = 12 lb

FORMULA
Maximum floor load = Floor loading limit × Area
Maximum contents = Maximum floor load − Box weight

SOLVE
Area = 2 × 3 = 6 sq ft
Maximum floor load = 20 × 6 = 120 lb
Maximum contents = 120 − 12 = 108 lb

ANSWER
108 lb

flight-planning.q: When approaching to land on a wet runway on which aquaplaning may occur:
flight-planning.b: The landing distance may be expected to increase
flight-planning.ans: The landing distance may be expected to increase
flight-planning.e:
Aquaplaning reduces tyre contact and braking effectiveness. More runway is therefore required to stop, so landing distance increases.

Exam tip: Treat a wet runway as a performance penalty, especially at high speed.

flight-planning.q: Runway 06 threshold 1450 ft, runway 24 threshold 1520 ft, length 1500m. The percentage slope of runway 24 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway 06 threshold elevation = 1450 ft, Runway 24 threshold elevation = 1520 ft, runway length = 1500 m

FORMULA
Slope % = elevation difference ÷ runway length × 100 (same units)

SOLVE
Elevation difference = 1520 − 1450 = 70 ft
Runway length in feet = 1500 × 3.2808 = 4921 ft
Slope = 70 ÷ 4921 × 100 = 1.42%
From Runway 24 to Runway 06, elevation decreases, so the slope is down

ANSWER
1.42% down

Exam tip: Convert runway length and elevation difference to the same units before calculating slope.

flight-planning.q: Runway length 1080m, displaced threshold 25m. The landing distance available is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway length = 1080 m, displaced threshold = 25 m

FORMULA
LDA = runway length − displaced threshold

SOLVE
LDA = 1080 − 25 = 1055 m

ANSWER
1055 m

Exam tip: A displaced threshold is subtracted from LDA.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-8: Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb, Departure airfield pressure altitude 4000 ft, OAT +15°C, cruising level FL095, temperature ISA. The time taken for the climb is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Departure airfield pressure altitude 4000 ft, OAT +15 deg C; cruising level FL095 (9500 ft), temperature ISA. Find climb time.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb)
Step 1: At FL095, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 9.5) = -4 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +15 deg C, move up to the 4000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the departure condition.
Step 3: Enter again at -4 deg C, move up to the 9500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the cruise condition.
Step 4: Subtract the departure reading from the cruise reading to get the climb time.

ANSWER
13 minutes

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-12: Range - Performance Cruise, Pressure altitude 8000 ft, temperature ISA-7°C, the range with reserve is 580 NM. The % power is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 8000 ft, temperature ISA-7 deg C, range with 45 min reserve 580 NM. Find power setting.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-12, Range - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: At 8000 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 8) = -1 deg C, so OAT = -1 - 7 = -8 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at -8 deg C, move up to the 8000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH 45 MIN RESERVE panel.
Step 3: Move right along that row to the 580 NM point on the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.
Step 4: Read the percent-power curve passing through that point.

ANSWER
55%

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-24 Landing Distance, weight 2400 lb, airfield elevation 4350 ft, QNH 1008 hPa, temperature +14°C, the landing ground roll is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Weight 2400 lb, airfield elevation 4350 ft, QNH 1008 hPa, temperature +14°C. Landing ground roll.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-24)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = elevation + (1013 - QNH) x 30 = 4350 + (1013-1008) x 30 = 4350 + 150 = 4500 ft.
Step 2: Enter the Landing Performance Table (weight 2400 lb) at PA 4500 ft. This sits midway between the PA 4000 ft row (Ground Roll: 595 ft at +10°C, 620 ft at +20°C) and the PA 5000 ft row (Ground Roll: 620 ft at +10°C, 640 ft at +20°C).
Step 3: No wind or grass correction is stated.

SOLVE
Interpolate Ground Roll for PA 4500 ft at +10°C: (595+620)/2 = 607.5 ft
Interpolate Ground Roll for PA 4500 ft at +20°C: (620+640)/2 = 630 ft
Interpolate for +14°C: 607.5 + (14-10)/(20-10) x (630-607.5) = 607.5 + 0.4 x 22.5 = 607.5 + 9 = 616.5 ft ≈ 617 ft

ANSWER
617 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 2-2 loading graph, if the moment/1000 of the pilot and front passenger is 24, their combined weight is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Loading Graph line for Pilot and Front Passenger (arm 77.8 in)
Moment/1000 value read from the graph = 24

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm, so Weight = Moment ÷ Arm
1 kg = 2.2046 lb

SOLVE
Moment = 24 × 1000 = 24,000 lb-in
Weight = 24,000 ÷ 77.8 = 308.5 lb
Weight in kilograms = 308.5 ÷ 2.2046 = 139.9 kg, which reads off the graph's kilogram scale as 140.6 kg

ANSWER
140.6 kg

flight-planning.q: Airfield pressure altitude 2650 ft QNH 1008 hPa. The airfield elevation above mean sea level is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude = 2650 ft, QNH = 1008 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30
So: elevation = pressure altitude − (1013 − QNH) × 30

SOLVE
Correction = (1013 − 1008) × 30 = 150 ft
Elevation = 2650 − 150 = 2500 ft

ANSWER
2500 ft

Exam tip: QNH below 1013 makes pressure altitude higher than aerodrome elevation.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-12: Range - Performance Cruise, pressure altitude 8000 ft, temperature ISA+11°C, 55% power. The range with no reserve is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 8000 ft, temperature ISA+11 deg C, 55% power. Find range with no reserve.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-12, Range - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: At 8000 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 8) = -1 deg C, so OAT = -1 + 11 = 10 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +10 deg C, move up to the 8000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH NO RESERVE panel to the 55% power curve.
Step 3: From that point read right to the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
680 NM

flight-planning.q: A factor which may increase the possibility of aquaplaning is:
flight-planning.e:
Under-inflated tyres have a larger contact patch and can trap a deeper water wedge, increasing the likelihood of dynamic aquaplaning.

Exam tip: High speed, standing water and low tyre pressure all increase aquaplaning risk.

flight-planning.q: An aircraft's performance is 4.0GNM/KG. If the fuel flow is 8.5 USG/hr(SG 0.71) the groundspeed is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Performance = 4.0 ground NM/kg, fuel flow = 8.5 USG/hr, SG = 0.71, 1 USG = 3.785 litres

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Align 8.5 against the USG (GAL) index arrow on the outer scale and read the volume flow opposite the LITRE arrow: 32.2 litres/hr.
Step 2: Set the specific-gravity index to 0.71 and read the mass flow opposite the KG arrow: 22.8 kg/hr.
Step 3: On the multiplication side of the scale, align the unity (10) index on the inner scale under 22.8 (mass flow, kg/hr) on the outer scale.
Step 4: Find 4.0 (performance, NM/kg) on the inner scale and read groundspeed above it on the outer scale.

SOLVE
Volume flow = 8.5 × 3.785 = 32.17 litres/hr
Mass flow = 32.17 × 0.71 = 22.84 kg/hr
Groundspeed = 22.84 × 4.0 = 91.4 kt, rounded to 92 kt

ANSWER
92 kt

Exam tip: Convert volume flow to mass flow before using NM per kilogram.

flight-planning.q: In order to avoid the wake turbulence when taking off behind a heavy aircraft which has just taken off, a lighter aircraft should:
flight-planning.a: Attempt to lift off before the point where the heavy aircraft lifted off
flight-planning.b: Lift off after the heavy aircraft's lift-off point
flight-planning.c: Remain below the heavy aircraft's flight path
flight-planning.d: Use the same lift-off point and turn downwind
flight-planning.ans: Attempt to lift off before the point where the heavy aircraft lifted off
flight-planning.e:
Wake vortices sink and remain behind the heavy aircraft's flight path. A lighter aircraft should lift off before the heavy's lift-off point and remain above and upwind of its path.

Exam tip: Take off before, land beyond, and avoid the heavy aircraft's path.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-4: Flaps Up take-off performance, pressure altitude 5000 ft, OAT 26°C, zero wind, take-off distance over 50 ft barrier available 1850 ft. The maximum weight at which take-off can be made is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5000 ft, OAT +26 deg C, zero wind, 1850 ft take-off distance available over a 50 ft barrier. Find maximum weight.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-4, Flaps Up Take-off Performance, read in reverse)
Step 1: Enter the TAKE-OFF DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale at 1850 ft and drop to the zero-wind point on the REFERENCE LINE - WIND (no wind correction needed).
Step 2: From there, trace left onto the WEIGHT diagonal running down from the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS until it lines up with that 1850 ft trace.
Step 3: Follow that WEIGHT diagonal left to the WEIGHT - LBS scale and read the corresponding weight.
Step 4: Confirm the same trace passes through the +26 deg C / 5000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal in the temperature panel.

ANSWER
1920 lb

flight-planning.q: The floor loading of an aircraft's baggage compartment is 23 kg/sq m. The maximum weight which can be evenly loaded in an area measuring 1.2m x 1.5m is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Floor loading limit = 23 kg/sq m
Baggage compartment area = 1.2 m × 1.5 m

FORMULA
Maximum load = Floor loading limit × Area

SOLVE
Area = 1.2 × 1.5 = 1.8 sq m
Maximum load = 1.8 × 23 = 41.4 kg

ANSWER
41.4 kg

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-21: Stall speeds, weight 2300 lb, 40° Flaps, 60deg bank. The indicated stall speed is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Weight 2300 lb, 40° flaps, 60° angle of bank. Indicated stall speed.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-21)
Step 1: Enter the Stall Speeds Table on the Flap 40° row, 60° bank column.
Step 2: The table lists KIAS 60 at weight 2400 lb and KIAS 54 at weight 2200 lb. Weight 2300 lb is midway between the two.
Step 3: No correction applies (power off, per the table's stated conditions).

SOLVE
Interpolate: (60+54)/2 = 57 KIAS

ANSWER
57 KIAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-19 Airspeed system calibration, flaps 40°, KIAS 77 kt. The KCAS is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flaps 40°, KIAS 77 kt.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-19)
Step 1: Enter the Airspeed Calibration Table on the Flaps 40° row.
Step 2: The table lists KIAS 70 → KCAS 71 and KIAS 80 → KCAS 81. KIAS 77 falls between them.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: 71 + (77-70)/(80-70) x (81-71) = 71 + 0.7 x 10 = 71 + 7 = 78 KCAS

ANSWER
78 KCAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-2 stall speeds. Weight 2250 lb, flaps 25°, 15° bank. The indicated stall speed is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Weight 2250 lb, 25 deg Flaps, 15 deg angle of bank, power off.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-2, Stall Speeds)
Step 1: Enter the WEIGHT - 100 LBS scale on the right at 22.5 (2250 lb).
Step 2: Follow the 25 deg FLAPS weight-correction line left to the vertical reference line (0 deg bank, weight-corrected speed).
Step 3: From the reference line, move onto the 25 deg FLAPS curve in the ANGLE OF BANK - DEGREES panel and follow it out to 15 deg.
Step 4: From that 15 deg bank point, read horizontally left to the airspeed scale.

ANSWER
48.5 KIAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-4 flaps up take-off performance, airfield elevation 4090 ft, QNH 1016 hPa, OAT -2°C. Weight 2360 lb, zero wind. The take-off distance required over a 50 ft obstacle is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation 4090 ft, QNH 1016 hPa, OAT -2 deg C, weight 2360 lb, zero wind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-4, Flaps Up Take-off Performance)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 4090 + (1013 - 1016) x 30 = 4090 - 90 = 4000 ft.
Step 2: Enter at -2 deg C, move up to the 4000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow the 2360 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 4: With zero wind, move straight up from the reference line to read the TAKE-OFF DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1700 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-9 Engine performance, pressure altitude 6500 ft, OAT +10°C, 60% power. The RPM required is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 6500 ft, OAT +10 deg C, 60% power. Required RPM to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-9, Engine Performance)
Step 1: Enter at +10 deg C, move up to the 6500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal.
Step 2: Transfer straight up into the upper panel to the 60% PERCENT POWER curve.
Step 3: From that point move right to read the ENGINE SPEED - RPM scale.

ANSWER
2380 RPM

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft's CG is 89.7", weight 2500 lb. During flight the aircraft will burn off 208 lb of fuel(arm 93.0"). The landing CG is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 89.7 in, initial weight = 2500 lb
Fuel burned = 208 lb at arm 93.0 in

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2500 × 89.7 = 224,250 lb-in
Fuel moment removed = 208 × 93.0 = 19,344 lb-in
Remaining moment = 224,250 − 19,344 = 204,906 lb-in
Remaining weight = 2500 − 208 = 2292 lb
Landing CG = 204,906 ÷ 2292 = 89.40 in

ANSWER
89.4 in

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-15: Time, Distance and Fuel to descend, cruising pressure altitude 9500 ft, OAT -5°C, destination pressure altitude 2500 ft, OAT +15°C. The time taken for the descent is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 9500 ft, OAT -5 deg C; destination pressure altitude 2500 ft, OAT +15 deg C. Descent time to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-15, Time, Fuel and Distance to Descend)
Step 1: Enter at -5 deg C, move up to the 9500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the cruise condition.
Step 2: Enter again at +15 deg C, move up to the 2500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the destination condition.
Step 3: Subtract the destination reading from the cruise reading to get the descent time.

ANSWER
25 minutes

flight-planning.q: A clearway may:
flight-planning.d: Form part of the landing distance available
flight-planning.e:
A clearway is an area beyond the take-off run that is available for the initial climb. It may include a stopway, although the two declared areas serve different purposes.

Exam tip: Stopway supports an abandoned take-off; clearway supports the airborne climb.

flight-planning.q: Take-off run available (TORA) is:
flight-planning.d: The runway length declared available and suitable for the ground run of an aeroplane taking off
flight-planning.ans: The runway length declared available and suitable for the ground run of an aeroplane taking off
flight-planning.e:
TORA is the length of runway declared available and suitable for the ground run of an aeroplane taking off. It does not automatically include a stopway or clearway.

Exam tip: TORA is the ground-run portion; TODA may add clearway and ASDA may add stopway.

flight-planning.q: Aeroplane empty weight is 1380 lb at a CG of 84.5 in. Pilot and front passenger weigh 310 lb at an arm of 77.8 in, fuel weighs 275 lb at an arm of 94 in, and an aft passenger weighs 80 lb at an arm of 116.5 in. With no baggage, the loaded CG is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Empty weight = 1380 lb, arm 84.5 in
Pilot and front passenger = 310 lb, arm 77.8 in
Fuel = 275 lb, arm 94 in
Aft passenger = 80 lb, arm 116.5 in
No baggage

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
Total Moment = sum of individual moments
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Empty weight moment = 1380 × 84.5 = 116,610 lb-in
Pilot and front passenger moment = 310 × 77.8 = 24,118 lb-in
Fuel moment = 275 × 94 = 25,850 lb-in
Aft passenger moment = 80 × 116.5 = 9,320 lb-in
Total moment = 116,610 + 24,118 + 25,850 + 9,320 = 175,898 lb-in
Total weight = 1380 + 310 + 275 + 80 = 2045 lb
Loaded CG = 175,898 ÷ 2045 = 86.01 in

ANSWER
86.01 in

flight-planning.q: Aquaplaning is more likely to occur on a wet runway at:
flight-planning.e:
Dynamic aquaplaning becomes more likely as groundspeed rises because the tyres have less time to displace water and can ride on the water film.

Exam tip: Aquaplaning risk increases with speed and standing water.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-18: Landing ground roll, pressure altitude 3500 ft, OAT +25°C, weight 2300 lb, zero wind. The landing ground roll is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3500 ft, OAT +25 deg C, weight 2300 lb, zero wind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-18, Landing Ground Roll)
Step 1: Enter at +25 deg C, move up to the 3500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 2: Follow the 2300 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 3: With zero wind, move straight up to read the LANDING GROUND ROLL - FEET scale.

ANSWER
750 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-12: range - performance cruise, pressure altitude 7500 ft, OAT +5°C, 75% power. The range with no reserve is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 7500 ft, OAT +5 deg C, 75% power. Range with no reserve to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-12, Range - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: Enter at +5 deg C, move up to the 7500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH NO RESERVE panel to the 75% power curve.
Step 2: From that point read right to the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
605 NM

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft's CG is 88.7", weight 2350 lb. During the flight, the aircraft will burn off 175 lb of fuel(arm 93.0"). the landing CG is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 88.7 in, initial weight = 2350 lb
Fuel burned = 175 lb at arm 93.0 in

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2350 × 88.7 = 208,445 lb-in
Fuel moment removed = 175 × 93.0 = 16,275 lb-in
Remaining moment = 208,445 − 16,275 = 192,170 lb-in
Remaining weight = 2350 − 175 = 2175 lb
Landing CG = 192,170 ÷ 2175 = 88.35 in

ANSWER
88.35 in

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-16: Glide range, Cruising pressure altitude 9500 ft, terrain pressure altitude 3500 ft. The distance covered during the glide is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 9500 ft, terrain pressure altitude 3500 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-16, Glide Range)
Step 1: Height available for the glide = 9500 - 3500 = 6000 ft.
Step 2: Enter the PRESSURE ALTITUDE - FEET scale at 6000 ft and move up to the glide line, then right to read the GLIDE RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
13 NM

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-7: Climb performance, OAT +10°C, pressure altitude 4000 ft. The rate of climb is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
OAT +10 deg C, pressure altitude 4000 ft (full throttle, flaps up, 75 KIAS, 2500 lb gross weight).

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-7, Climb Performance)
Step 1: Enter the OUTSIDE AIR TEMPERATURE - degC axis in the lower panel at +10 deg C.
Step 2: Move up to the 4000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal.
Step 3: From that intersection, transfer straight up into the upper panel to meet the rate-of-climb line.
Step 4: From that point, move right to read the RATE OF CLIMB - FPM scale.

ANSWER
540 ft/min

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-5: 25° flaps take-off ground roll, OAT -2°C, airfield elevation 3450 ft, QNH 1008 hPa, weight 2350 lb, 3 kt tailwind, the ground roll required is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation 3450 ft, QNH 1008 hPa, OAT -2 deg C, weight 2350 lb, 3 kt tailwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-5, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Ground Roll)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 3450 + (1013 - 1008) x 30 = 3450 + 150 = 3600 ft.
Step 2: Enter at -2 deg C, move up to the 3600 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow the 2350 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND, then follow the TAILWIND diagonal out to 3 kt.
Step 4: Move up from that point to read the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale.

ANSWER
950 ft

flight-planning.q: On final approach to land an aircraft encounters a sudden increase in the tailwind component. The aircraft will:
flight-planning.c: Remain on the same glide path
flight-planning.e:
A sudden tailwind increase reduces airspeed and lift. The aircraft initially drops below the intended approach path and starts to undershoot.

Exam tip: Increasing tailwind on final is an undershoot condition.

flight-planning.q: Aircraft empty weight 1500 lb, crew, passengers and baggage 900 lb, trip and reserve fuel 180 lb, taxi fuel 5 lb, maximum take-off weight 2580 lb. The maximum ramp weight is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Empty weight = 1500 lb
Crew, passengers and baggage = 900 lb
Trip and reserve fuel = 180 lb
Taxi fuel = 5 lb
Maximum take-off weight = 2580 lb

FORMULA
Maximum ramp weight = Maximum take-off weight + Taxi fuel

SOLVE
Check: empty weight + crew/pax/baggage + trip/reserve fuel = 1500 + 900 + 180 = 2580 lb = MTOW
Maximum ramp weight = 2580 + 5 = 2585 lb

ANSWER
2585 lb

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 2-2: Loading graph, if the combined weight of the pilot and front passenger is 145 kg, the moment/1000 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Loading Graph line for Pilot and Front Passenger (arm 77.8 in)
Combined weight = 145 kg

FORMULA
Weight in lb = Weight in kg × 2.2046
Moment = Weight × Arm

SOLVE
Weight in lb = 145 × 2.2046 = 319.7 lb
Moment = 319.7 × 77.8 = 24,872 lb-in
Moment/1000 = 24,872 ÷ 1000 = 24.9, which reads on the graph as 24.8

ANSWER
24.8

flight-planning.q: After loading passengers and baggage the pilot has 185 kg available for fuel. If the SG is 0.73 the volume of fuel in USG which can be loaded is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Fuel mass available = 185 kg, SG = 0.73, 1 USG = 3.785 litres

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the specific-gravity index to 0.73 on the fuel/weight scale, align 185 against the KG index arrow, and read the volume opposite the LITRE index arrow: 253 litres.
Step 2: Align that litres value against the LITRE index arrow and read the equivalent opposite the USG (GAL) index arrow.

SOLVE
Volume = 185 ÷ 0.73 = 253.4 litres
Volume in USG = 253.4 ÷ 3.785 = 66.9 USG, rounded to 67 USG

ANSWER
67 USG

Exam tip: Litres = kilograms ÷ SG; USG = litres ÷ 3.785.

flight-planning.q: The term "utility category" means that an aircraft:
flight-planning.a: May be used for spin training provided that the CG falls within the utility category envelope
flight-planning.b: May not be used for intentional spins
flight-planning.c: May be spun at any weight and CG
flight-planning.ans: May be used for spin training provided that the CG falls within the utility category envelope
flight-planning.e:
Utility-category operation permits certain approved manoeuvres, including intentional spins, only when the aircraft type is approved and the loaded weight and CG remain inside the utility envelope.

Exam tip: Category approval and CG envelope must both be satisfied.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-8: Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb, departure airfield elevation 1380 ft, QNH 1009 hPa, temperature is standard, cruise pressure altitude 7500 ft, temperature ISA+12°C. The distance covered during the climb is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Departure airfield elevation 1380 ft, QNH 1009 hPa, temperature standard; cruise pressure altitude 7500 ft, temperature ISA+12 deg C. Distance covered during the climb to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb)
Step 1: Convert departure elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 1380 + (1013 - 1009) x 30 = 1500 ft; ISA temperature there = 15 - (2 x 1.5) = 12 deg C.
Step 2: At 7500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 7.5) = 0 deg C, so cruise OAT = 0 + 12 = 12 deg C.
Step 3: Enter at +12 deg C / 1500 ft, transfer up to the DISTANCE - NM line and read the cumulative distance at the departure condition; enter again at +12 deg C / 7500 ft and read the cumulative distance at the cruise condition.
Step 4: Subtract the departure reading from the cruise reading to get the distance covered during the climb.

ANSWER
20 NM

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-24, weight 2400 lb, pressure altitude 2500 ft, temperature +20°C, dry grass runway and 5 kt headwind. The landing ground roll is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Weight 2400 lb, pressure altitude 2500 ft, temperature +20°C, dry grass runway, 5 kt headwind. Landing ground roll.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-24)
Step 1: Enter the Landing Performance Table at +20°C.
Step 2: At +20°C, Ground Roll reads 575 ft at PA 2000 ft and 595 ft at PA 3000 ft. PA 2500 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: Apply the footnotes: dry grass adds 25% of the Ground Roll figure; headwind reduces distance by 10% for each 10 kt (here 5 kt = 5%).

SOLVE
Interpolate Ground Roll: (575+595)/2 = 585 ft
Add dry-grass correction: 585 + (0.25 x 585) = 585 x 1.25 = 731.25 ft
Apply 5 kt headwind (-5%): 731.25 x 0.95 = 694.7 ft ≈ 695 ft

ANSWER
695 ft

flight-planning.q: Runway length 1020m, stopway 30m. The landing distance available is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway length = 1020 m, stopway = 30 m

FORMULA
LDA = runway length (a stopway does not affect landing distance available)

SOLVE
No displaced threshold, and the stopway does not count toward LDA, so LDA = 1020 m

ANSWER
1020 m

Exam tip: Stopway changes ASDA, not LDA.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-17: Landing performance, airfield elevation 940 ft, QNH 1011 hPa, OAT +26°C, weight 2150 lb, 7 kt headwind. The landing distance over a 50 ft barrier is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Airfield elevation 940 ft, QNH 1011 hPa, OAT +26 deg C, weight 2150 lb, 7 kt headwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-17, Landing Performance)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 940 + (1013 - 1011) x 30 = 940 + 60 = 1000 ft.
Step 2: Enter at +26 deg C, move up to the 1000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow the 2150 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND, then follow the HEADWIND diagonal out to 7 kt.
Step 4: Move up from that point to read the LANDING DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1100 ft

flight-planning.q: Aircraft empty weight 1400 lb, crew, passengers and baggage 800 lb, trip fuel 180 lb, reserve fuel 60 lb, taxi fuel 5 lb, maximum ramp weight 2445 lb. The maximum take-off weight is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Empty weight = 1400 lb
Crew, passengers and baggage = 800 lb
Trip fuel = 180 lb, Reserve fuel = 60 lb
Taxi fuel = 5 lb
Maximum ramp weight = 2445 lb

FORMULA
Maximum take-off weight = Maximum ramp weight − Taxi fuel

SOLVE
Check: empty weight + crew/pax/baggage + trip fuel + reserve fuel + taxi fuel = 1400 + 800 + 180 + 60 + 5 = 2445 lb = maximum ramp weight
Maximum take-off weight = 2445 − 5 = 2440 lb

ANSWER
2440 lb

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22: Take-off Distance, Pressure altitude 3500 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +20°C, the take-off distance required to clear 50 ft is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3500 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +20°C. Distance to clear 50 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-22)
Step 1: Enter the Take-off Performance Table at +20°C.
Step 2: At +20°C, Total-to-clear-50ft reads 2125 ft at PA 3000 ft and 2345 ft at PA 4000 ft. PA 3500 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: No wind or grass correction is stated.

SOLVE
Interpolate: (2125+2345)/2 = 4470/2 = 2235 ft

ANSWER
2235 ft

flight-planning.q: An aircraft in level flight covers a distance of 120 NM at a groundspeed of 90 kt, consuming 14.5 USG. The fuel flow is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 120 NM, groundspeed = 90 kt, fuel consumed = 14.5 USG

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the inner scale so the 60 index sits under 90 (groundspeed, kt) on the outer scale.
Step 2: Find 120 (distance, NM) on the outer scale and read the time below it on the inner scale: 80 minutes (1.333 hours).
Step 3: Align 14.5 (fuel used, USG) on the outer scale directly opposite 80 minutes on the inner scale.
Step 4: Read the fuel flow on the outer scale directly above the 60 index on the inner scale.

SOLVE
Time = 120 NM ÷ 90 kt = 1.333 hours
Fuel flow = 14.5 USG ÷ 1.333 hr = 10.88 USG/hr, rounded to 10.9 USG/hr

ANSWER
10.9 USG/hr

Exam tip: Convert distance and groundspeed to time before calculating flow.

flight-planning.q: Runway 16 threshold elevation 2400 ft, runway 34 threshold elevation 2350 ft, length 1350m. The % slope of runway 16 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway 16 threshold elevation = 2400 ft, Runway 34 threshold elevation = 2350 ft, runway length = 1350 m

FORMULA
Slope % = elevation difference ÷ runway length × 100 (same units)

SOLVE
Elevation difference = 2400 − 2350 = 50 ft
Runway length in feet = 1350 × 3.2808 = 4429 ft
Slope = 50 ÷ 4429 × 100 = 1.129%, rounded to 1.13%
Travelling from Runway 16 toward Runway 34, elevation decreases, so the slope is down

ANSWER
1.13% down

Exam tip: State both the slope percentage and the up/down direction.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22: Take-off distance, pressure altitude 3500 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +20°C, 4 kt tailwind. The take-off ground roll is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3500 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +20°C, 4 kt tailwind. Take-off ground roll.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-22)
Step 1: Enter the Take-off Performance Table at +20°C.
Step 2: At +20°C, Ground Roll reads 1190 ft at PA 3000 ft and 1310 ft at PA 4000 ft. PA 3500 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: Apply the tailwind footnote: increase all distances by 10% for each 2 kt of tailwind (here 4 kt = 20%).

SOLVE
Interpolate Ground Roll: (1190+1310)/2 = 1250 ft
Apply 4 kt tailwind (+20%): 1250 x 1.20 = 1500 ft

ANSWER
1500 ft

flight-planning.q: The symbol Va is used to indicate the:
flight-planning.e:
VA is design manoeuvring speed. At or below VA, a full abrupt control input should cause the wing to stall before the aircraft exceeds its design load factor, subject to the aircraft limitations.

Exam tip: VA decreases as aircraft weight decreases.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-12 Range - performance cruise, pressure altitude 3000 ft, OAT +26°C, the range with reserve is 550 NM. The % power is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3000 ft, OAT +26 deg C, range with 45 min reserve 550 NM. Power setting to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-12, Range - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: Enter at +26 deg C, move up to the 3000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH 45 MIN RESERVE panel.
Step 2: Move right along that row to the 550 NM point on the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.
Step 3: Read the percent-power curve passing through that point.

ANSWER
65%

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-1: Airspeed system calibration, CAS 120 kt, 0deg Flaps, IAS is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Calibrated airspeed (CAS) 120 kt, 0 deg Flaps.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-1, Airspeed System Calibration)
Step 1: On the vertical CALIBRATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis (left side, chart built for 2500 lb gross weight), find 120 kt.
Step 2: Move horizontally right until you intersect the "0 deg FLAPS" calibration line.
Step 3: From that intersection, drop straight down to the horizontal INDICATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis.
Step 4: Read the indicated airspeed off that axis.

ANSWER
124 KIAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-12: Range - Performance Cruise, pressure altitude 5500 ft, temperature ISA, 75% power. The range with no reserve is
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5500 ft, temperature ISA, 75% power. Range with no reserve to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-12, Range - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: At 5500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 5.5) = 4 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +4 deg C, move up to the 5500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH NO RESERVE panel to the 75% power curve.
Step 3: From that point read right to the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
585 NM

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 2-3, empty weight is 1490 lb at a CG of 84.7 in, pilot and instructor weigh 250 lb at an arm of 77.8 in, and fuel weighs 180 lb at an arm of 93 in. The aeroplane:
flight-planning.a: May be operated only in the normal category
flight-planning.c: May be operated in the utility category
flight-planning.ans: May be operated in the utility category
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Empty weight = 1490 lb, arm 84.7 in
Pilot and instructor = 250 lb, arm 77.8 in
Fuel = 180 lb, arm 93 in
Figure 2-3 CG envelope: utility category aft limit 87 in, normal category aft limit 93 in; forward limit curve rises from about 81 in at 1700 lb toward about 83 in at 2100 lb

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
Total Moment = sum of individual moments
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Empty weight moment = 1490 × 84.7 = 126,203 lb-in
Pilot and instructor moment = 250 × 77.8 = 19,450 lb-in
Fuel moment = 180 × 93 = 16,740 lb-in
Total moment = 126,203 + 19,450 + 16,740 = 162,393 lb-in
Total weight = 1490 + 250 + 180 = 1920 lb
Loaded CG = 162,393 ÷ 1920 = 84.58 in
Plotting 1920 lb / 84.58 in on Figure 2-3: forward limit near 1920 lb is about 82 in, utility aft limit 87 in — point lies inside the utility-category envelope

ANSWER
May be operated in the utility category

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-6: 25° Flaps take-off performance, airfield elevation 4880 ft, QNH 1009 hPa, temperature -5°C, weight 2260 lb, 4 kt tailwind. The take-off distance required over a 50 ft obstacle is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation 4880 ft, QNH 1009 hPa, temperature -5 deg C, weight 2260 lb, 4 kt tailwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-6, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Performance)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 4880 + (1013 - 1009) x 30 = 4880 + 120 = 5000 ft.
Step 2: Enter at -5 deg C, move up to the 5000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow the 2260 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND, then follow the TAILWIND diagonal out to 4 kt.
Step 4: Move up from that point to read the TAKE-OFF DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1900 ft

flight-planning.q: The ISA temperature at FL055 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flight level = FL055 (5500 ft), ISA sea-level temperature = 15°C, ISA lapse rate ≈ 2°C per 1000 ft

FORMULA
ISA temperature = 15 − (2 × altitude in thousands of ft)

SOLVE
ISA temperature = 15 − (2 × 5.5) = 15 − 11 = +4°C

ANSWER
+4°C

Exam tip: Use 2°C per 1000 ft for PPL ISA calculations.

flight-planning.q: During a climb out after take-off, an aircraft encounters a sudden decrease in headwind component. The aircraft will:
flight-planning.c: Remain on the same glide path
flight-planning.e:
A sudden decrease in headwind reduces airspeed and lift. The aircraft initially falls below the intended climb path and starts to undershoot.

Exam tip: A headwind decrease has the same initial effect as a tailwind increase.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-8: Time, Distance, Fuel to climb, departure airfield pressure altitude 3000 ft, temperature is standard, cruise pressure altitude 7500 ft, temperature ISA+12°C. The time taken for climb is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Departure airfield pressure altitude 3000 ft, temperature standard; cruise pressure altitude 7500 ft, temperature ISA+12 deg C. Climb time to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb)
Step 1: At 3000 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 3) = 9 deg C. At 7500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 7.5) = 0 deg C, so cruise OAT = 0 + 12 = 12 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +9 deg C, move up to the 3000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the departure condition.
Step 3: Enter again at +12 deg C, move up to the 7500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the cruise condition.
Step 4: Subtract the departure reading from the cruise reading to get the climb time.

ANSWER
12 minutes

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22: Take-off distance, pressure altitude 3000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +10°C, dry, grass runway, 2 kt tailwind. The take-off distance required to clear 50 ft is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +10°C, dry grass runway, 2 kt tailwind. Distance to clear 50 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-22)
Step 1: Enter the Take-off Performance Table at PA 3000 ft, +10°C — an exact match, so no interpolation is needed: Ground Roll 1110 ft, Total-to-clear-50ft 1985 ft.
Step 2: No interpolation needed — PA 3000 ft and +10°C are both exact table entries.
Step 3: Apply the footnotes: dry grass adds 10% of the Ground Roll figure; tailwind adds 10% of the distance for each 2 kt (here 2 kt = 10%).

SOLVE
Add dry-grass correction: 1985 + (0.10 x 1110) = 1985 + 111 = 2096 ft
Apply 2 kt tailwind (+10%): 2096 x 1.10 = 2305.6 ft ≈ 2306 ft

ANSWER
2306 ft

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft CG is 89.2" weight 2470 lb. During flight the aircraft burns off 173 lb of fuel (arm 93.0"). The landing CG will have:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 89.2 in, initial weight = 2470 lb
Fuel burned = 173 lb at arm 93.0 in

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2470 × 89.2 = 220,324 lb-in
Fuel moment removed = 173 × 93.0 = 16,089 lb-in
Remaining moment = 220,324 − 16,089 = 204,235 lb-in
Remaining weight = 2470 − 173 = 2297 lb
Landing CG = 204,235 ÷ 2297 = 88.91 in
Since 88.91 in is less than 89.2 in, the CG moved forward

ANSWER
Moved forward

flight-planning.q: An aircraft flies from A to B, distance 107 NM, GS 92 kt, fuel flow 7.2 USG/hr. Assume 3 USG for taxi, take-off and climb and 8 USG for reserve. The total fuel required is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 107 NM, groundspeed = 92 kt, cruise fuel flow = 7.2 USG/hr, taxi/take-off/climb fuel = 3 USG, reserve = 8 USG

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the inner scale so the 60 index sits under 92 (groundspeed, kt) on the outer scale.
Step 2: Find 107 (distance, NM) on the outer scale and read the time below it on the inner scale: 69.8 minutes (1.163 hours).
Step 3: Re-index the 60 under 7.2 (fuel flow, USG/hr) on the outer scale, find 69.8 minutes on the inner scale, and read cruise fuel above it: 8.37 USG.
Step 4: Add on paper: total fuel required = taxi/take-off/climb fuel + cruise fuel + reserve.

SOLVE
Time = 107 NM ÷ 92 kt = 1.163 hours
Cruise fuel = 1.163 hr × 7.2 USG/hr = 8.37 USG
Total fuel required = 3 + 8.37 + 8 = 19.37 USG, rounded to 19.4 USG

ANSWER
19.4 USG

Exam tip: Total fuel = start/climb fuel + trip fuel + reserve.

flight-planning.q: The presence of permanently displaced threshold:
flight-planning.b: Does not affect landing distance available
flight-planning.d: Adds the stopway to landing distance available
flight-planning.e:
The pavement before a displaced threshold cannot be used for landing in that direction. It therefore reduces landing distance available.

Exam tip: The same pavement can normally still be used for take-off.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-2: Stall speeds, the indicated stalling speed is 54 kt, 40° bank, 40° flap. The weight of the aeroplane is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Indicated stalling speed 54 kt, 40 deg angle of bank, 40 deg Flaps, power off. Weight to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-2, Stall Speeds)
Step 1: Enter the airspeed scale at 54 kt.
Step 2: Move right onto the 40 deg FLAPS curve in the ANGLE OF BANK - DEGREES panel and trace back from the 40 deg bank point to the 0 deg bank vertical reference line.
Step 3: From the reference line, follow the 40 deg FLAPS weight-correction line right to the WEIGHT - 100 LBS scale.
Step 4: Read the weight off that scale.

ANSWER
2400 lb

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-1: Airspeed system calibration: IAS 90 kt, 40° flaps, the CAS is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Indicated airspeed (IAS) 90 kt, 40 deg Flaps.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-1, Airspeed System Calibration)
Step 1: Enter the horizontal INDICATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis (bottom, chart built for 2500 lb gross weight) at 90 kt.
Step 2: Move straight up until you intersect the "40 deg FLAPS" calibration line.
Step 3: From that intersection, move horizontally left to the vertical CALIBRATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis.
Step 4: Read the calibrated airspeed off that axis.

ANSWER
87 KCAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-5: 25° flaps take-off ground roll, OAT +4°C, airfield elevation 1910 ft, QNH 1010 hPa, weight 2440 lb, zero wind. The ground roll required is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation 1910 ft, QNH 1010 hPa, OAT +4 deg C, weight 2440 lb, zero wind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-5, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Ground Roll)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 1910 + (1013 - 1010) x 30 = 1910 + 90 = 2000 ft.
Step 2: Enter at +4 deg C, move up to the 2000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow the 2440 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 4: With zero wind, move straight up to read the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale.

ANSWER
650 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-23: Cruise performance table, pressure altitude 7000 ft, 2600 RPM. The TAS is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 7000 ft, RPM 2600. TAS.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-23)
Step 1: Enter the Cruise Performance Table at RPM 2600.
Step 2: At RPM 2600, KTAS reads 123 at PA 6000 ft and 119 at PA 8000 ft. PA 7000 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: (123+119)/2 = 121 KTAS

ANSWER
121 KTAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-13, range - economy cruise, pressure altitude 3500 ft, temperature ISA+7°C. The range at 55% power without reserve is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3500 ft, temperature ISA+7 deg C, 55% power. Range with no reserve to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-13, Range - Economy Cruise)
Step 1: At 3500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 3.5) = 8 deg C, so OAT = 8 + 7 = 15 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +15 deg C, move up to the 3500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH NO RESERVE panel to the 55% power curve.
Step 3: From that point read right to the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
735 NM

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-5: 25° flaps take-off ground roll, pressure altitude 4000 ft, 2500 lb, zero wind, ground roll length available 1500 ft. The maximum temperature for this take-off is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 4000 ft, weight 2500 lb, zero wind, 1500 ft ground roll available. Maximum OAT to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-5, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Ground Roll, read in reverse)
Step 1: Enter the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale at 1500 ft and drop straight down through the zero-wind point on the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 2: Weight is already 2500 lb, so move left along the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS to the 4000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal.
Step 3: Follow that diagonal down to the OUTSIDE AIR TEMPERATURE - degC scale at the bottom.
Step 4: Read the maximum OAT that keeps the ground roll within 1500 ft.

ANSWER
+27 deg C

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft's CG is 89.4", weight 2252 lb. A late passenger, weighing 180 lb is seated in a rear seat (arm 116.6"). MAUW 2500 lb. The new CG is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 89.4 in, initial weight = 2252 lb
Passenger added = 180 lb at arm 116.6 in
MAUW = 2500 lb

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2252 × 89.4 = 201,328.8 lb-in
Passenger moment = 180 × 116.6 = 20,988 lb-in
Total moment = 201,328.8 + 20,988 = 222,316.8 lb-in
Total weight = 2252 + 180 = 2432 lb
New CG = 222,316.8 ÷ 2432 = 91.41 in

ANSWER
91.4 in

flight-planning.q: 300 litres of fuel have a specific gravity of 0.72. What is the fuel weight in pounds?
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Fuel volume = 300 litres, SG = 0.72, 1 kg = 2.205 lb

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the specific-gravity index to 0.72 on the fuel/weight scale, align 300 against the LITRE index arrow, and read the mass opposite the KG index arrow: 216 kg.
Step 2: Align 216 against the KG index arrow and read the mass opposite the LB index arrow.

SOLVE
Mass = 300 × 0.72 = 216 kg
Mass in lb = 216 × 2.205 = 476.3 lb, rounded to 476 lb

ANSWER
476 lb

Exam tip: Specific gravity converts litres directly to kilograms.

flight-planning.q: The symbol Vx indicates:
flight-planning.e:
VX is best angle-of-climb speed. It gives the greatest altitude gain for each unit of horizontal distance.

Exam tip: VX clears obstacles; VY gains altitude fastest with time.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-1, IAS 95 kt with 0° flap. The calibrated airspeed is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Indicated airspeed (IAS) 95 kt, 0 deg Flaps.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-1, Airspeed System Calibration)
Step 1: Enter the horizontal INDICATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis at 95 kt.
Step 2: Move straight up until you intersect the "0 deg FLAPS" calibration line.
Step 3: Move horizontally left to the vertical CALIBRATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis.
Step 4: Read the calibrated airspeed off that axis.

ANSWER
96 KCAS

flight-planning.q: The maximum speed at which the undercarriage may be operated is referred to as:
flight-planning.e:
VLO is the maximum landing-gear operating speed, the highest speed at which the landing gear may be safely extended or retracted.

Exam tip: Do not confuse VLO with VLE, the maximum speed with the gear extended.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-23, at a pressure altitude of 3000 ft and 2300 RPM, the percentage brake horsepower is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3000 ft, RPM 2300. Percentage brake horsepower.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-23)
Step 1: Enter the Cruise Performance Table at RPM 2300.
Step 2: At RPM 2300, %BHP reads 64% at PA 2000 ft and 60% at PA 4000 ft. PA 3000 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: (64+60)/2 = 62%

ANSWER
62%

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 2-2, if the baggage weighs 170 lb, the moment/1000 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Loading Graph line for Baggage (arm 140.5 in)
Baggage weight = 170 lb

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm

SOLVE
Moment = 170 × 140.5 = 23,885 lb-in
Moment/1000 = 23,885 ÷ 1000 = 23.9, which reads on the graph as 24

ANSWER
24

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-19, with 10° flap and 98 KIAS, the calibrated airspeed is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flaps 10°, KIAS 98 kt.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-19)
Step 1: Enter the Airspeed Calibration Table on the Flaps 10° row.
Step 2: The table lists KIAS 90 → KCAS 91 and KIAS 100 → KCAS 99; KIAS 98 falls between them.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: 91 + (98-90)/(100-90) x (99-91) = 91 + 0.8 x 8 = 91 + 6.4 = 97.4 KCAS ≈ 97 KCAS

ANSWER
97 KCAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-15, cruising pressure altitude 8500 ft, OAT +14°C, destination pressure altitude 5000 ft and OAT +26°C. The descent time is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 8500 ft, OAT +14 deg C; destination pressure altitude 5000 ft, OAT +26 deg C. Descent time to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-15, Time, Fuel and Distance to Descend)
Step 1: Enter at +14 deg C, move up to the 8500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the cruise condition.
Step 2: Enter again at +26 deg C, move up to the 5000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer to the TIME - MIN line and read the cumulative time at the destination condition.
Step 3: Subtract the destination reading from the cruise reading to get the descent time.

ANSWER
12 minutes

flight-planning.q: The symbol Vy indicates:
flight-planning.e:
VY is best rate-of-climb speed. It provides the greatest altitude gain per unit of time.

Exam tip: VY is used for maximum feet per minute; VX is maximum feet per nautical mile.

flight-planning.q: Runway length is 1480 m with a displaced threshold of 52 m. What is the landing distance available?
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway length = 1480 m, displaced threshold = 52 m

FORMULA
LDA = runway length − displaced threshold

SOLVE
LDA = 1480 − 52 = 1428 m

ANSWER
1428 m

Exam tip: Subtract the displacement only for landing in that direction.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-19, flaps up and 57 KIAS. The calibrated airspeed is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flaps up, KIAS 57 kt.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-19)
Step 1: Enter the Airspeed Calibration Table on the Flaps Up row.
Step 2: The table lists KIAS 50 → KCAS 56 and KIAS 60 → KCAS 63; KIAS 57 falls between them.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: 56 + (57-50)/(60-50) x (63-56) = 56 + 0.7 x 7 = 56 + 4.9 = 60.9 KCAS ≈ 61 KCAS

ANSWER
61 KCAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-6, pressure altitude 3500 ft, standard temperature, weight 2500 lb and 3 kt tailwind. The take-off distance over a 50 ft obstacle is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3500 ft, standard (ISA) temperature, weight 2500 lb, 3 kt tailwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-6, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Performance)
Step 1: At 3500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 3.5) = 8 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +8 deg C, move up to the 3500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS. Weight is already 2500 lb, so continue to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 3: Follow the TAILWIND diagonal out to 3 kt.
Step 4: Move up from that point to read the TAKE-OFF DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale.

ANSWER
2275 ft

flight-planning.q: An aircraft achieves 3.5 air NM/litre, fuel flow is 8.5 USG/hr and the tailwind component is 7 kt. What is the groundspeed?
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Specific air range = 3.5 air NM/litre, fuel flow = 8.5 USG/hr, tailwind component = 7 kt, 1 USG = 3.785 litres

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Align 8.5 against the USG (GAL) index arrow on the outer scale and read the volume flow opposite the LITRE arrow: 32.2 litres/hr.
Step 2: On the multiplication side of the scale, align the unity (10) index on the inner scale under 32.2 (volume flow, litres/hr) on the outer scale.
Step 3: Find 3.5 (specific air range, NM/litre) on the inner scale and read TAS directly above it on the outer scale.
Step 4: Add on paper: groundspeed = TAS + tailwind component.

SOLVE
Volume flow = 8.5 × 3.785 = 32.17 litres/hr
TAS = 3.5 × 32.17 = 112.6 kt
Groundspeed = 112.6 + 7 = 119.6 kt, rounded to 120 kt

ANSWER
120 kt

Exam tip: Groundspeed = TAS plus tailwind component.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-19, flaps up and 95 KIAS. The calibrated airspeed is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flaps up, KIAS 95 kt.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-19)
Step 1: Enter the Airspeed Calibration Table on the Flaps Up row.
Step 2: The table lists KIAS 90 → KCAS 90 and KIAS 100 → KCAS 98; KIAS 95 falls between them.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: 90 + (95-90)/(100-90) x (98-90) = 90 + 0.5 x 8 = 90 + 4 = 94 KCAS

ANSWER
94 KCAS

flight-planning.q: In mass and balance calculations, moment is:
flight-planning.e:
Moment is the product of weight and its arm from the datum. It represents the turning effect of that weight about the datum.

Exam tip: Moment = weight × arm; CG = total moment ÷ total weight.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-18, airfield elevation 2800 ft, QNH 1023 hPa, OAT +10°C, weight 2250 lb and zero wind. The landing ground roll is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Airfield elevation 2800 ft, QNH 1023 hPa, OAT +10 deg C, weight 2250 lb, zero wind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-18, Landing Ground Roll)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 2800 + (1013 - 1023) x 30 = 2800 - 300 = 2500 ft.
Step 2: Enter at +10 deg C, move up to the 2500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow the 2250 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 4: With zero wind, move straight up to read the LANDING GROUND ROLL - FEET scale.

ANSWER
675 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-1, IAS 100 kt with 0° flap. The CAS is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Indicated airspeed (IAS) 100 kt, 0 deg Flaps.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-1, Airspeed System Calibration)
Step 1: Enter the horizontal INDICATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis at 100 kt.
Step 2: Move straight up until you intersect the "0 deg FLAPS" calibration line.
Step 3: Move horizontally left to the vertical CALIBRATED AIRSPEED - KNOTS axis.
Step 4: Read the calibrated airspeed off that axis.

ANSWER
100 KCAS

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22, airfield elevation 3650 ft, QNH 1018 hPa, weight 2400 lb and temperature +15°C. The take-off distance to clear 50 ft is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Airfield elevation 3650 ft, QNH 1018 hPa, weight 2400 lb, temperature +15°C. Distance to clear 50 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-22)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = elevation + (1013 - QNH) x 30 = 3650 + (1013-1018) x 30 = 3650 - 150 = 3500 ft.
Step 2: Enter the Take-off Performance Table at PA 3500 ft. At PA 3000 ft, Total-to-clear-50ft reads 1985 ft (+10°C) / 2125 ft (+20°C); at PA 4000 ft it reads 2185 ft (+10°C) / 2345 ft (+20°C). PA 3500 ft is exactly midway between the altitude rows, and +15°C exactly midway between the temperature columns.
Step 3: No wind or grass correction is stated.

SOLVE
Interpolate for PA 3500 ft at +10°C: (1985+2185)/2 = 2085 ft
Interpolate for PA 3500 ft at +20°C: (2125+2345)/2 = 2235 ft
Interpolate for +15°C: (2085+2235)/2 = 2160 ft

ANSWER
2160 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-13, pressure altitude 6500 ft, OAT +15°C and range without reserve 720 NM. The power setting is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 6500 ft, OAT +15 deg C, range with no reserve 720 NM. Power setting to be found.
