METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-13, Range - Economy Cruise)
Step 1: Enter at +15 deg C, move up to the 6500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH NO RESERVE panel.
Step 2: Move right along that row to the 720 NM point on the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.
Step 3: Read the percent-power curve passing through that point.

ANSWER
65%

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-16, cruising pressure altitude 11500 ft, terrain elevation 440 ft and QNH 1011 hPa. The glide distance is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Cruising pressure altitude 11500 ft, terrain elevation 440 ft, QNH 1011 hPa.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-16, Glide Range)
Step 1: Convert terrain elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 440 + (1013 - 1011) x 30 = 440 + 60 = 500 ft.
Step 2: Height available for the glide = 11500 - 500 = 11000 ft.
Step 3: Enter the PRESSURE ALTITUDE - FEET scale at 11000 ft and move up to the glide line, then right to read the GLIDE RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.

ANSWER
22.5 NM

flight-planning.q: With regard to windshear on final approach, a sudden decrease in the headwind component will initially cause the aircraft to:
flight-planning.c: Remain exactly on the same glide path
flight-planning.d: Climb above the intended glide path
flight-planning.e:
A sudden decrease in headwind reduces the aircraft's airspeed and lift before the pilot can correct. The aircraft therefore drops below the intended approach path and starts to undershoot.

Exam tip: A headwind decrease has the same initial effect as a tailwind increase.

flight-planning.q: To avoid wake turbulence while following a heavy aircraft on approach, a lighter aircraft should:
flight-planning.a: Remain below the heavy aircraft's flight path
flight-planning.b: Remain above the heavy aircraft's flight path
flight-planning.c: Fly directly through the heavy aircraft's touchdown path
flight-planning.ans: Remain above the heavy aircraft's flight path
flight-planning.e:
Wake vortices sink below and behind the generating aircraft. Remaining above the heavy aircraft's flight path reduces the risk of flying into the descending vortices.

Exam tip: Stay above the heavy aircraft's path and plan to touch down beyond its touchdown point.

flight-planning.q: When landing behind a heavy aircraft that has just landed, a lighter aircraft should:
flight-planning.a: Touch down before the heavy aircraft's touchdown point
flight-planning.b: Use the same touchdown point as the heavy aircraft
flight-planning.c: Touch down beyond the heavy aircraft's touchdown point
flight-planning.d: Remain below the heavy aircraft's approach path
flight-planning.ans: Touch down beyond the heavy aircraft's touchdown point
flight-planning.e:
Wake vortices are generated until the heavy aircraft's weight is firmly supported by the runway. Touching down beyond the heavy aircraft's touchdown point helps the lighter aircraft avoid the area where the vortices were produced.

Exam tip: When landing behind a heavy aircraft that landed, land beyond its touchdown point.

flight-planning.q: When landing behind a heavy aircraft that has just taken off, the lighter aircraft should:
flight-planning.a: Land beyond the heavy aircraft's lift-off point
flight-planning.b: Follow below the heavy aircraft's climb path
flight-planning.c: Touch down at the heavy aircraft's lift-off point
flight-planning.d: Touch down before the heavy aircraft's lift-off point
flight-planning.ans: Touch down before the heavy aircraft's lift-off point
flight-planning.e:
A departing heavy aircraft starts generating strong wake vortices during the take-off roll and continues after lift-off. Landing before its lift-off point keeps the lighter aircraft away from the airborne wake path.

Exam tip: Behind a departing heavy aircraft, land before its lift-off point.

flight-planning.q: The speed VNE is:
flight-planning.a: The speed that must never be exceeded in any operation
flight-planning.b: The maximum speed with flaps extended
flight-planning.ans: The speed that must never be exceeded in any operation
flight-planning.e:
VNE is the never-exceed speed. Flight above VNE can cause structural damage or loss of control and is prohibited in normal operation.

Exam tip: VNE is marked by the red radial line on the airspeed indicator.

flight-planning.q: A runway has a threshold permanently displaced by 50 metres. For take-off in that direction, the pilot may normally:
flight-planning.a: Begin the take-off only from the displaced threshold
flight-planning.b: Begin the take-off from the physical start of the runway if the pavement is suitable
flight-planning.c: Use only the landing distance available
flight-planning.d: Add the displaced distance to the stopway
flight-planning.ans: Begin the take-off from the physical start of the runway if the pavement is suitable
flight-planning.e:
A displaced threshold restricts landing use in that direction, but the pavement before it normally remains available for take-off when it is marked and suitable.

Exam tip: A displaced threshold reduces LDA, not the usable take-off run.

flight-planning.q: When landing on a wet runway where aquaplaning may occur, the recommended touchdown technique is to:
flight-planning.a: Hold the aircraft off for as long as possible
flight-planning.b: Touch down very softly and allow repeated skips
flight-planning.c: Make a firm, positive touchdown without bouncing
flight-planning.d: Land with the brakes already fully applied
flight-planning.ans: Make a firm, positive touchdown without bouncing
flight-planning.e:
A firm, positive touchdown in the correct landing attitude helps the tyres break through the water film and establish runway contact. Floating or bouncing delays effective braking and can increase aquaplaning risk.

Exam tip: Positive does not mean excessively hard; avoid prolonged float and avoid bouncing.

flight-planning.q: In mass and balance calculations, weight is equal to:
flight-planning.e:
Since moment = weight × arm, rearranging the formula gives weight = moment ÷ arm.

Exam tip: Write the triangle relationship: Moment = Weight × Arm.

flight-planning.q: In mass and balance calculations, arm is equal to:
flight-planning.e:
Since moment = weight × arm, rearranging gives arm = moment ÷ weight.

Exam tip: CG arm = total moment ÷ total weight.

flight-planning.q: The empty weight of an aircraft including unusable fuel, full operating fluids and fixed equipment is called:
flight-planning.e:
Basic empty weight includes the aircraft, fixed equipment, unusable fuel and the required operating fluids. It excludes crew, passengers, baggage, cargo and usable fuel.

Exam tip: Basic empty weight is the starting point for a loading calculation.

flight-planning.q: An aerodrome elevation is 1200 ft and QNH is 1003 hPa. The pressure altitude is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation = 1200 ft, QNH = 1003 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30

SOLVE
Correction = (1013 − 1003) × 30 = 300 ft
Pressure altitude = 1200 + 300 = 1500 ft

ANSWER
1500 ft

Exam tip: QNH below 1013 makes pressure altitude higher than aerodrome elevation.

flight-planning.q: At FL085 the temperature is ISA +7°C. The outside air temperature is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flight level = FL085 (8500 ft), ISA deviation = +7°C, ISA sea-level temperature = 15°C, ISA lapse rate ≈ 2°C per 1000 ft

FORMULA
ISA temperature = 15 − (2 × altitude in thousands of ft)
OAT = ISA temperature + ISA deviation

SOLVE
ISA temperature at 8500 ft = 15 − (2 × 8.5) = 15 − 17 = −2°C
OAT = −2 + 7 = +5°C

ANSWER
+5°C

Exam tip: First calculate the ISA temperature at the level, then apply the deviation.

flight-planning.q: An aircraft is flying at FL095 with an OAT of +5°C. The temperature deviation from ISA is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Flight level = FL095 (9500 ft), OAT = +5°C, ISA sea-level temperature = 15°C, ISA lapse rate ≈ 2°C per 1000 ft

FORMULA
ISA temperature = 15 − (2 × altitude in thousands of ft)
ISA deviation = OAT − ISA temperature

SOLVE
ISA temperature at 9500 ft = 15 − (2 × 9.5) = 15 − 19 = −4°C
ISA deviation = 5 − (−4) = +9°C

ANSWER
+9°C

Exam tip: ISA deviation = actual temperature − ISA temperature.

flight-planning.q: Aerodrome elevation is 3210 ft, QNH 1020 hPa and OAT +22°C. The density altitude is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation = 3210 ft, QNH = 1020 hPa, OAT = +22°C, ISA sea-level temperature = 15°C, ISA lapse rate ≈ 2°C per 1000 ft

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30
ISA temperature = 15 − (2 × altitude in thousands of ft)
ISA deviation = OAT − ISA temperature
Density altitude ≈ pressure altitude + 120 × ISA deviation

SOLVE
Pressure altitude = 3210 + (1013 − 1020) × 30 = 3210 − 210 = 3000 ft
ISA temperature at 3000 ft = 15 − (2 × 3) = +9°C
ISA deviation = 22 − 9 = +13°C
Density altitude = 3000 + (120 × 13) = 3000 + 1560 = 4560 ft

ANSWER
4560 ft

Exam tip: Density altitude ≈ pressure altitude + 120 × ISA temperature deviation.

flight-planning.q: An increase in temperature at a particular aerodrome will normally:
flight-planning.e:
Warmer air is less dense. For the same pressure altitude, an increase in temperature raises density altitude and reduces aircraft performance.

Exam tip: Hotter, higher and lower-pressure conditions all increase density altitude.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-10: Speed Power - Performance Cruise, pressure altitude 7500 ft, OAT +5°C and 65% power. The TAS is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 7500 ft, OAT +5 deg C, 65% power. TAS to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-10, Speed Power - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: Enter at +5 deg C, move up to the 7500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal.
Step 2: Transfer straight up into the upper panel and follow across to the 65% PERCENT POWER curve.
Step 3: From that point read down to the TRUE AIRSPEED - KNOTS scale.

ANSWER
117 kt

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-10, pressure altitude 2500 ft, temperature ISA +4°C, groundspeed 111 kt and headwind 9 kt. The power setting is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 2500 ft, temperature ISA+4 deg C, groundspeed 111 kt, 9 kt headwind. Power setting to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-10, Speed Power - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: Convert groundspeed to TAS: with a 9 kt headwind, TAS = 111 + 9 = 120 kt.
Step 2: At 2500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 2.5) = 10 deg C, so OAT = 10 + 4 = 14 deg C.
Step 3: Enter at +14 deg C, move up to the 2500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer straight up into the upper panel, then move right to the 120 kt point on the TRUE AIRSPEED - KNOTS scale.
Step 4: Read the PERCENT POWER curve passing through that point.

ANSWER
75%

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-11: Speed Power - Economy Cruise, pressure altitude 10500 ft, OAT 0°C and 55% power. The TAS is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 10500 ft, OAT 0 deg C, 55% power. TAS to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-11, Speed Power - Economy Cruise)
Step 1: Enter at 0 deg C on the OUTSIDE AIR TEMPERATURE - degC axis, move up to the 10500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal.
Step 2: Transfer straight up into the upper panel and follow across to the 55% PERCENT POWER curve.
Step 3: From that point read down to the TRUE AIRSPEED - KNOTS scale.

ANSWER
103 kt

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-11, pressure altitude 4000 ft, standard temperature and TAS 110 kt. The power setting is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 4000 ft, standard temperature, TAS 110 kt. Power setting to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-11, Speed Power - Economy Cruise)
Step 1: At 4000 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 4) = 7 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +7 deg C, move up to the 4000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer straight up into the upper panel.
Step 3: Move right along that row to the 110 kt point on the TRUE AIRSPEED - KNOTS scale.
Step 4: Read the PERCENT POWER curve passing through that point.

ANSWER
65%

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-17: Landing Performance, pressure altitude 5000 ft, OAT +32°C, weight 2500 lb and 13 kt headwind. The landing distance over a 50 ft obstacle is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5000 ft, OAT +32 deg C, weight 2500 lb, 13 kt headwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-17, Landing Performance)
Step 1: Enter at +32 deg C, move up to the 5000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS. Weight is already 2500 lb, so continue right to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 2: Follow the HEADWIND diagonal out to 13 kt.
Step 3: Move up from that point to read the LANDING DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1290 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22, pressure altitude 5000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +15°C, dry grass runway and 10 kt headwind. The required ground roll is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +15°C, dry grass runway, 10 kt headwind. Required ground roll.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-22)
Step 1: Enter the Take-off Performance Table at PA 5000 ft.
Step 2: At PA 5000 ft, Ground Roll reads 1340 ft at +10°C and 1440 ft at +20°C. +15°C is exactly midway.
Step 3: Apply the footnotes: dry grass adds 10% of the Ground Roll figure; headwind reduces distance by 10% for each 5 kt (here 10 kt = 20%).

SOLVE
Interpolate Ground Roll: (1340+1440)/2 = 1390 ft
Add dry-grass correction: 1390 + (0.10 x 1390) = 1390 x 1.10 = 1529 ft
Apply 10 kt headwind (-20%): 1529 x 0.80 = 1223.2 ft ≈ 1223 ft

ANSWER
1223 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22, pressure altitude 5000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +30°C, dry grass runway and 5 kt headwind. The take-off distance required to clear 50 ft is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
At 5000 ft and +30°C the table gives 2790 ft total and 1550 ft ground roll. A 5 kt headwind reduces the corrected distance by 10%, and dry grass adds 10% of the corrected ground-roll figure. The result is approximately 2650 ft.

Exam tip: The grass correction is based on the ground-roll figure, even when total distance is requested.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22, pressure altitude 4500 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +10°C, dry grass runway and zero wind. The take-off distance required to clear 50 ft is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 4500 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +10°C, dry grass runway, zero wind. Distance to clear 50 ft.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-22)
Step 1: Enter the Take-off Performance Table at +10°C.
Step 2: At +10°C, Ground Roll / Total-to-clear-50ft read 1220 ft / 2185 ft at PA 4000 ft and 1340 ft / 2415 ft at PA 5000 ft. PA 4500 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: Apply the dry-grass footnote: add 10% of the Ground Roll figure. No wind correction (zero wind stated).

SOLVE
Interpolate Ground Roll: (1220+1340)/2 = 1280 ft
Interpolate Total-to-clear-50ft: (2185+2415)/2 = 2300 ft
Add dry-grass correction: 2300 + (0.10 x 1280) = 2300 + 128 = 2428 ft

ANSWER
2428 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22, pressure altitude 1000 ft, weight 2400 lb, temperature +10°C and 5 kt headwind. The take-off distance required to clear 50 ft is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
At 1000 ft and +10°C the table gives 1655 ft to clear 50 ft. A 5 kt headwind reduces all distances by 10%, so 1655 × 0.90 = approximately 1490 ft.

Exam tip: Apply the headwind percentage to the complete table distance.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-22, pressure altitude 500 ft, weight 2400 lb and temperature +10°C. The required ground roll is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
Interpolate halfway between sea level, where ground roll is 845 ft, and 1000 ft, where it is 925 ft. The result is approximately 885 ft.

Exam tip: Linear interpolation is acceptable between adjacent table rows.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-23, pressure altitude 5000 ft and 2400 RPM. The range is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5000 ft, RPM 2400. Range.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-23)
Step 1: Enter the Cruise Performance Table at RPM 2400.
Step 2: At RPM 2400, Range reads 780 nm at PA 4000 ft and 790 nm at PA 6000 ft. PA 5000 ft is exactly midway.
Step 3: No correction applies.

SOLVE
Interpolate: (780+790)/2 = 785 NM

ANSWER
785 NM

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-23, pressure altitude 3000 ft and 2400 RPM. The fuel flow is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
At 2000 ft and 2400 RPM the table shows 7.7 GPH; at 4000 ft it shows 7.3 GPH. Interpolating to 3000 ft gives approximately 7.5 GPH.

Exam tip: Read the correct RPM row before interpolating between altitude rows.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-23, pressure altitude 5000 ft and 2500 RPM. The percentage brake horsepower is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
At 4000 ft and 2500 RPM the table shows 74% BHP, while at 6000 ft it shows 70% BHP. Interpolating to 5000 ft gives approximately 72% BHP.

Exam tip: Interpolate halfway when the required altitude is midway between two table rows.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-24, weight 2400 lb, aerodrome elevation 2650 ft, QNH 1018 hPa and temperature +24°C. The landing distance required to clear 50 ft is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
Convert elevation to pressure altitude: 2650 + (1013 - 1018) × 30 ≈ 2500 ft. Interpolate Figure 1-24 between 2000 and 3000 ft and between +20°C and +30°C. The resulting total distance is approximately 1372 ft.

Exam tip: Convert elevation to pressure altitude before entering a performance table.

flight-planning.q: The speed that provides the greatest gain in altitude over the shortest horizontal distance is:
flight-planning.e:
VX is the best angle-of-climb speed. It produces the greatest altitude gain for each unit of horizontal distance, which is why it is used when obstacle clearance is the priority.

Exam tip: VX is altitude per distance; VY is altitude per time.

flight-planning.q: A stopway is:
flight-planning.a: An area used to increase landing distance available
flight-planning.b: The airborne portion of a clearway
flight-planning.c: The runway area before a displaced threshold
flight-planning.d: A prepared area beyond the take-off run where an aeroplane can be stopped during an abandoned take-off
flight-planning.ans: A prepared area beyond the take-off run where an aeroplane can be stopped during an abandoned take-off
flight-planning.e:
A stopway is a prepared rectangular area beyond the take-off run available. It is intended to support an aeroplane during an abandoned take-off and is included in ASDA, not in landing distance available.

Exam tip: Stopway is for stopping after a rejected take-off; clearway is for the initial airborne climb.

flight-planning.q: Maximum zero fuel weight is:
flight-planning.a: The actual loaded weight excluding usable fuel
flight-planning.b: The maximum permissible aircraft weight with no usable fuel aboard
flight-planning.c: Maximum take-off weight less taxi fuel
flight-planning.d: Basic empty weight plus unusable fuel only
flight-planning.ans: The maximum permissible aircraft weight with no usable fuel aboard
flight-planning.e:
Maximum zero fuel weight is the structural limit for the aircraft's weight when no usable fuel is carried. It protects the airframe from excessive wing-root bending loads caused by payload in the fuselage.

Exam tip: Zero fuel weight is an actual calculated weight; maximum zero fuel weight is the limit it must not exceed.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-3: Flaps Up Take-off Ground Roll, OAT +20°C, pressure altitude 5000 ft, weight 2400 lb and 10 kt headwind. The ground roll required is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
OAT +20 deg C, pressure altitude 5000 ft, weight 2400 lb, 10 kt headwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-3, Flaps Up Take-off Ground Roll)
Step 1: Enter at +20 deg C on the OUTSIDE AIR TEMPERATURE - degC scale, move up to the 5000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 2: Follow the 2400 lb WEIGHT diagonal (lighter than the 2500 lb reference) down-left to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 3: From the reference line, follow the HEADWIND diagonal out to 10 kt.
Step 4: From the 10 kt headwind point, move straight up to read the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1475 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-3: Flaps Up Take-off Ground Roll, OAT +30°C, pressure altitude 2500 ft, 10 kt headwind and 1200 ft of ground roll available. The maximum take-off weight is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
OAT +30 deg C, pressure altitude 2500 ft, 10 kt headwind, 1200 ft of ground roll available. Maximum take-off weight to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-3, Flaps Up Take-off Ground Roll, read in reverse)
Step 1: Enter the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale at 1200 ft and move down to the HEADWIND diagonal at 10 kt.
Step 2: From that point, move left to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND, then trace back onto the WEIGHT diagonal.
Step 3: Because the ground roll needed at +30 deg C and 2500 ft stays within 1200 ft even at the chart's heaviest weight line, follow the WEIGHT diagonal up to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS, the top of the chart's weight range.
Step 4: Confirm the reference line meets the 2500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal at +30 deg C; the chart's maximum weight for this take-off is therefore the 2500 lb reference weight itself.

ANSWER
2500 lb

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-3: Flaps Up Take-off Ground Roll, aerodrome elevation 650 ft, QNH 1018 hPa, OAT +25°C, weight 2500 lb and 5 kt tailwind. The ground roll required is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation 650 ft, QNH 1018 hPa, OAT +25 deg C, weight 2500 lb, 5 kt tailwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-3, Flaps Up Take-off Ground Roll)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 650 + (1013 - 1018) x 30 = 650 - 150 = 500 ft.
Step 2: Enter at +25 deg C, move up to the 500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS. Weight is already 2500 lb, so continue right to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND.
Step 3: From the reference line, follow the TAILWIND diagonal (the opposite side of the wind panel from headwind) out to 5 kt.
Step 4: From the 5 kt tailwind point, move up to read the TAKE-OFF GROUND ROLL - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1350 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-6: 25° Flaps Take-off Performance, pressure altitude 4000 ft, temperature +20°C, 5 kt headwind and 1650 ft take-off distance available to clear 50 ft. The maximum take-off weight is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 4000 ft, temperature +20 deg C, 5 kt headwind, 1650 ft take-off distance available to clear 50 ft. Maximum take-off weight to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-6, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Performance, read in reverse)
Step 1: Enter the TAKE-OFF DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale at 1650 ft and drop to the HEADWIND diagonal at 5 kt.
Step 2: Move left to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND, then trace back onto the WEIGHT diagonal running down from the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow that WEIGHT diagonal left to the WEIGHT - LBS scale, confirming it aligns with the +20 deg C / 4000 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal.
Step 4: Read the corresponding weight.

ANSWER
2300 lb

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-6: 25° Flaps Take-off Performance, aerodrome elevation 1410 ft, QNH 1010 hPa, temperature +24°C, weight 2340 lb and 7 kt headwind. The take-off distance required to clear 50 ft is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Aerodrome elevation 1410 ft, QNH 1010 hPa, temperature +24 deg C, weight 2340 lb, 7 kt headwind.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-6, 25 deg Flaps Take-off Performance)
Step 1: Convert elevation to pressure altitude: PA = 1410 + (1013 - 1010) x 30 = 1410 + 90 = 1500 ft.
Step 2: Enter at +24 deg C, move up to the 1500 ft PRESSURE ALT diagonal, then right to the REFERENCE LINE - 2500 LBS.
Step 3: Follow the 2340 lb WEIGHT diagonal to the REFERENCE LINE - WIND, then follow the HEADWIND diagonal out to 7 kt.
Step 4: Move up from that point to read the TAKE-OFF DISTANCE OVER 50 FT BARRIER - FEET scale.

ANSWER
1125 ft

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-8: Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb, departure pressure altitude 3000 ft with OAT +30°C, cruising level FL095 with OAT 0°C. The distance covered during the climb is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Departure pressure altitude 3000 ft, OAT +30 deg C; cruising level FL095 (9500 ft), OAT 0 deg C. Distance covered during the climb to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-8, Time, Distance and Fuel to Climb)
Step 1: Enter at +30 deg C, move up to the 3000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer straight up to the DISTANCE - NM line and read the cumulative distance at the departure condition (approximately 9 NM).
Step 2: Enter again at 0 deg C, move up to the 9500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, transfer up to the DISTANCE - NM line and read the cumulative distance at the cruise condition (approximately 22 NM).
Step 3: Subtract the departure reading from the cruise reading: 22 - 9 = 13 NM.

ANSWER
13 NM

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-9: Engine Performance, pressure altitude 4500 ft, standard temperature and 70% power. The required engine speed is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 4500 ft, standard temperature, 70% power. Required RPM to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-9, Engine Performance)
Step 1: At 4500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 4.5) = 6 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +6 deg C, move up to the 4500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal.
Step 3: Transfer straight up into the upper panel to the 70% PERCENT POWER curve.
Step 4: From that point move right to read the ENGINE SPEED - RPM scale.

ANSWER
2480 RPM

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-13: Range - Economy Cruise, pressure altitude 10500 ft, standard temperature and 55% power. The range with no reserve is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 10500 ft, standard temperature, 55% power. Range with no reserve to be found.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-13, Range - Economy Cruise)
Step 1: At 10500 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 10.5) = -6 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at -6 deg C, move up to the 10500 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then transfer straight up into the RANGE WITH NO RESERVE panel to the 55% power curve.
Step 3: From that point read right to the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale (not the separate 45-minute-reserve scale).

ANSWER
765 NM

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft's CG is 88.8 in, weight 2300 lb, MAUW 2500 lb. The pilot adds 22 USG of fuel with a specific weight of 6 lb/USG at an arm of 93.0 in. The new CG is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 88.8 in, initial weight = 2300 lb, MAUW = 2500 lb
Fuel added = 22 USG at 6 lb/USG, arm 93.0 in

FORMULA
Fuel weight = Volume (USG) × 6 lb/USG
Moment = Weight × Arm
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2300 × 88.8 = 204,240 lb-in
Fuel weight = 22 × 6 = 132 lb
Fuel moment = 132 × 93.0 = 12,276 lb-in
Total moment = 204,240 + 12,276 = 216,516 lb-in
Total weight = 2300 + 132 = 2432 lb
New CG = 216,516 ÷ 2432 = 89.03 in

ANSWER
89.0 in

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft's CG is 88.3 in and its weight is 2450 lb. During flight the aircraft burns 280 lb of fuel from an arm of 93.0 in. The landing CG is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 88.3 in, initial weight = 2450 lb
Fuel burned = 280 lb at arm 93.0 in

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2450 × 88.3 = 216,335 lb-in
Fuel moment removed = 280 × 93.0 = 26,040 lb-in
Remaining moment = 216,335 − 26,040 = 190,295 lb-in
Remaining weight = 2450 − 280 = 2170 lb
Landing CG = 190,295 ÷ 2170 = 87.69 in

ANSWER
87.7 in

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-2: Stall Speeds, at gross weight with 25° flap and 30° bank, the indicated stall speed is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Gross weight (2500 lb, the chart's reference weight), 25 deg Flaps, 30 deg angle of bank, power off.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-2, Stall Speeds)
Step 1: Weight is already 2500 lb (the chart's reference weight), so no correction is needed - enter directly at the vertical reference line for the 25 deg FLAPS curve.
Step 2: From the reference line, follow the 25 deg FLAPS curve in the ANGLE OF BANK - DEGREES panel out to 30 deg.
Step 3: From the 30 deg bank point, read horizontally left to the airspeed scale.

ANSWER
54 KIAS

flight-planning.q: Fuel has a specific gravity of 0.73 and weighs 108 kg. Its volume is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Fuel mass = 108 kg, SG = 0.73

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the specific-gravity index to 0.73 on the fuel/weight scale.
Step 2: Align 108 against the KG index arrow and read the volume directly opposite the LITRE index arrow.

SOLVE
Volume = 108 ÷ 0.73 = 147.95 litres, rounded to 148 litres

ANSWER
148 litres

Exam tip: For fuel calculations, volume = mass ÷ specific gravity.

flight-planning.q: An aircraft's performance is 2.0 ground nautical miles per pound of fuel. Fuel flow is 8.5 USG/hr at SG 0.71, and the headwind component is 8 kt. The TAS is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Performance = 2.0 ground NM/lb, fuel flow = 8.5 USG/hr, SG = 0.71, headwind component = 8 kt, 1 USG = 3.785 litres, 1 kg = 2.205 lb

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Align 8.5 with the USG (GAL) index arrow on the outer scale; read volume flow opposite the LITRE arrow: 32.2 litres/hr.
Step 2: Set the specific-gravity index to 0.71; read mass flow opposite the KG arrow: 22.8 kg/hr.
Step 3: Align 22.8 with the KG index arrow; read mass flow opposite the LB index arrow: 50.4 lb/hr.
Step 4: On the multiplication side, align the unity (10) index under 50.4 (mass flow, lb/hr) on the outer scale; find 2.0 (performance, NM/lb) on the inner scale and read groundspeed above it on the outer scale.
Step 5: TAS = groundspeed + headwind component.

SOLVE
Volume flow = 8.5 × 3.785 = 32.17 litres/hr
Mass flow = 32.17 × 0.71 = 22.84 kg/hr
Mass flow in lb = 22.84 × 2.205 = 50.4 lb/hr
Groundspeed = 2.0 × 50.4 = 100.8 kt
TAS = 100.8 + 8 = 108.8 kt, rounded to 109 kt

ANSWER
109 kt

Exam tip: With a headwind, TAS is greater than groundspeed.

flight-planning.q: The maximum zero fuel weight of an aircraft is the empty weight of the aircraft:
flight-planning.c: Plus crew, passengers, baggage and cargo
flight-planning.ans: Plus crew, passengers, baggage and cargo
flight-planning.e:
Zero fuel weight is the aircraft's weight with no usable fuel aboard. It includes the aircraft, crew, passengers, baggage and cargo, as well as items already included in empty weight such as unusable fuel.

Exam tip: Maximum zero fuel weight limits structural loading before usable fuel is added.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 2-2: Loading Graph, if the total fuel loaded is 35 USG, the moment/1000 is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Fuel loaded = 35 USG, fuel density = 6 lb per US gallon, arm 93.0 in

FORMULA
Fuel weight = Volume (USG) × 6 lb/USG
Moment = Weight × Arm

SOLVE
Fuel weight = 35 × 6 = 210 lb
Moment = 210 × 93.0 = 19,530 lb-in
Moment/1000 = 19,530 ÷ 1000 = 19.5

ANSWER
19.5

flight-planning.q: An aircraft in level flight covers 158 NM at a groundspeed of 95 kt while consuming 12.5 USG. The fuel flow is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 158 NM, groundspeed = 95 kt, fuel consumed = 12.5 USG

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the inner scale so the 60 index sits under 95 (groundspeed, kt) on the outer scale.
Step 2: Find 158 (distance, NM) on the outer scale; read time below it on the inner scale: 99.8 minutes (1.663 hours).
Step 3: Align 12.5 (fuel used, USG) on the outer scale opposite 99.8 minutes on the inner scale.
Step 4: Read fuel flow on the outer scale above the 60 index on the inner scale.

SOLVE
Time = 158 NM ÷ 95 kt = 1.663 hours
Fuel flow = 12.5 USG ÷ 1.663 hr = 7.52 USG/hr, rounded to 7.5 USG/hr

ANSWER
7.5 USG/hr

Exam tip: Find time from distance and groundspeed before calculating fuel flow.

flight-planning.q: Runway 09 threshold elevation is 2250 ft, Runway 27 threshold elevation is 2200 ft, and runway length is 4300 ft. The percentage slope of Runway 27 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway 09 threshold elevation = 2250 ft, Runway 27 threshold elevation = 2200 ft, runway length = 4300 ft

FORMULA
Slope % = elevation difference ÷ runway length × 100

SOLVE
Elevation difference = 2250 − 2200 = 50 ft
Slope = 50 ÷ 4300 × 100 = 1.163%, rounded to 1.16%
From Runway 27 toward Runway 09, elevation increases, so the slope is up

ANSWER
1.16% up

Exam tip: Determine up or down in the direction of the runway named in the question.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 2-3: CG Range and Weight, empty weight is 1490 lb at a CG of 84.7 in, pilot and instructor weigh 350 lb at 77.8 in, and fuel weighs 180 lb at 93 in. The aeroplane:
flight-planning.a: May be operated in the utility category
flight-planning.b: May only be operated in the normal category
flight-planning.c: Is outside the forward CG limit
flight-planning.ans: May be operated in the utility category
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Empty weight = 1490 lb, arm 84.7 in
Pilot and instructor = 350 lb, arm 77.8 in
Fuel = 180 lb, arm 93 in
Figure 2-3 CG envelope: utility category aft limit 87 in, normal category aft limit 93 in

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
Total Moment = sum of individual moments
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Empty weight moment = 1490 × 84.7 = 126,203 lb-in
Pilot and instructor moment = 350 × 77.8 = 27,230 lb-in
Fuel moment = 180 × 93 = 16,740 lb-in
Total moment = 126,203 + 27,230 + 16,740 = 170,173 lb-in
Total weight = 1490 + 350 + 180 = 2020 lb
Loaded CG = 170,173 ÷ 2020 = 84.24 in
On Figure 2-3, 2020 lb and 84.24 in plot inside the utility-category envelope: forward limit near 2020 lb is about 83 in, utility aft limit is 87 in

ANSWER
May be operated in the utility category

flight-planning.q: An aeroplane has an empty weight of 1490 lb at a CG of 84.7 in. Pilot and front passenger weigh 350 lb at 77.8 in, fuel weighs 210 lb at 93 in, and an aft passenger weighs 100 lb at 116.6 in. With no baggage, the loaded CG is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Empty weight = 1490 lb, arm 84.7 in
Pilot and front passenger = 350 lb, arm 77.8 in
Fuel = 210 lb, arm 93 in
Aft passenger = 100 lb, arm 116.6 in
No baggage

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
Total Moment = sum of individual moments
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Empty weight moment = 1490 × 84.7 = 126,203 lb-in
Pilot and front passenger moment = 350 × 77.8 = 27,230 lb-in
Fuel moment = 210 × 93 = 19,530 lb-in
Aft passenger moment = 100 × 116.6 = 11,660 lb-in
Total moment = 126,203 + 27,230 + 19,530 + 11,660 = 184,623 lb-in
Total weight = 1490 + 350 + 210 + 100 = 2150 lb
Loaded CG = 184,623 ÷ 2150 = 85.87 in

ANSWER
85.87 in

flight-planning.q: The presence of a stopway:
flight-planning.c: Does not affect the landing distance available
flight-planning.d: Makes the stopway part of the landing runway
flight-planning.ans: Does not affect the landing distance available
flight-planning.e:
A stopway is provided for stopping an aircraft during an abandoned take-off and contributes to accelerate-stop distance available. It is not part of the landing distance available.

Exam tip: Stopway affects ASDA, not LDA.

flight-planning.q: Runway 31 threshold elevation is 725 ft, Runway 13 threshold elevation is 800 ft, and runway length is 3400 ft. The percentage slope of Runway 13 is:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Runway 31 threshold elevation = 725 ft, Runway 13 threshold elevation = 800 ft, runway length = 3400 ft

FORMULA
Slope % = elevation difference ÷ runway length × 100

SOLVE
Elevation difference = 800 − 725 = 75 ft
Slope = 75 ÷ 3400 × 100 = 2.206%, rounded to 2.2%
From Runway 13 toward Runway 31, elevation decreases, so the slope is down

ANSWER
2.2% down

Exam tip: Divide elevation change by runway length, using the same units.

flight-planning.q: With reference to Figure 1-12: Range – Performance Cruise, at pressure altitude 4000 ft and ISA +5°C, the range with no reserve is 620 NM. The power setting is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 4000 ft, temperature ISA+5 deg C, range with no reserve 620 NM. Find the power setting.

METHOD (SACAA-01 Figure 1-12, Range - Performance Cruise)
Step 1: At 4000 ft, ISA temperature = 15 - (2 x 4) = 7 deg C, so OAT = 7 + 5 = 12 deg C.
Step 2: Enter at +12 deg C, move up to the 4000 ft PRESSURE ALTITUDE diagonal, then straight up into the RANGE WITH NO RESERVE panel.
Step 3: Move right along that row to 620 NM on the RANGE - NAUTICAL MILES scale.
Step 4: Read the percent-power curve through that point.

ANSWER
65%

flight-planning.q: The basic empty weight of an aircraft is:
flight-planning.a: The empty weight including unusable fuel, full oil and fixed equipment
flight-planning.b: The maximum weight with no usable fuel aboard
flight-planning.d: The empty weight plus crew and baggage
flight-planning.ans: The empty weight including unusable fuel, full oil and fixed equipment
flight-planning.e:
Basic empty weight includes the airframe, engines, permanently installed equipment, unusable fuel and full operating fluids such as oil. It excludes usable fuel, occupants and baggage.

Exam tip: Do not confuse basic empty weight with zero fuel weight.

flight-planning.q: An aircraft achieves a performance of 3.8 air nautical miles per litre. If the fuel flow is 7.8 USG/hr, the TAS is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Performance = 3.8 air NM/litre, fuel flow = 7.8 USG/hr, 1 USG = 3.785 litres

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Align 7.8 with the USG (GAL) index arrow on the outer scale; read volume flow opposite the LITRE arrow: 29.5 litres/hr.
Step 2: On the multiplication side, align the unity (10) index under 29.5 (volume flow, litres/hr) on the outer scale.
Step 3: Find 3.8 (performance, NM/litre) on the inner scale; read TAS above it on the outer scale.

SOLVE
Volume flow = 7.8 × 3.785 = 29.52 litres/hr
TAS = 3.8 × 29.52 = 112.2 kt, rounded to 112 kt

ANSWER
112 kt

Exam tip: Air NM per unit of fuel × fuel used per hour = air NM per hour = TAS.

flight-planning.q: A loaded aircraft has a CG of 91.0 in and weighs 2400 lb. A 160 lb front-seat passenger at 77.8 in swaps places with a 100 lb rear-seat passenger at 116.6 in, and 50 lb of fuel is added at an arm of 93.0 in. The new CG is approximately:
flight-planning.e:
GIVEN
Initial CG = 91.0 in, initial weight = 2400 lb
Front-seat passenger (160 lb, arm 77.8 in) swaps with rear-seat passenger (100 lb, arm 116.6 in)
Fuel added = 50 lb at arm 93.0 in

FORMULA
Moment = Weight × Arm
CG = Total Moment ÷ Total Weight

SOLVE
Initial moment = 2400 × 91.0 = 218,400 lb-in
Swap moves 60 lb from the front-seat arm to the rear-seat arm: change in arm = 116.6 − 77.8 = 38.8 in
Moment added by the swap = 60 × 38.8 = 2,328 lb-in
Fuel moment added = 50 × 93.0 = 4,650 lb-in
Total moment = 218,400 + 2,328 + 4,650 = 225,378 lb-in
Total weight = 2400 + 50 = 2450 lb
New CG = 225,378 ÷ 2450 = 91.99 in

ANSWER
92.00 in

radio-telephony.q: What does “FA” IN Designator stand for?
radio-telephony.e: FA is the ICAO two-letter country designator assigned to South Africa, part of the global system that lets every FIR, aerodrome and beacon be identified by nationality. That's why South African FIRs (FACA, FAJA, FAJO) and aerodrome codes (e.g. FAOR, FACT) all start with FA.

radio-telephony.q: South Africa is divided into various regions in which Air Traffic Service is provided. These regions are termed?
radio-telephony.e: South Africa's airspace is divided into FIRs so that flight information, alerting and area control services can each be handled by a dedicated Flight Information Centre with a manageable workload. The three FIRs -- Cape Town (FACA), Johannesburg (FAJA) and Johannesburg Oceanic (FAJO) -- are further split into sectors (e.g. FAJA North, South-West, East) for the same reason.

radio-telephony.q: What is the abbreviation for a Control Area?
radio-telephony.e: CTA (Control Area) is controlled airspace that begins at a specified altitude or flight level rather than the ground. It is normally established above one or more TMAs, at the confluence of several air routes, to give aircraft continuous ATC protection as they climb away from or descend into the terminal environment.

radio-telephony.q: Control Area?
radio-telephony.a: Airspace of defined dimension which extend upward from the surface to an upper limit, usually as altitude.
radio-telephony.b: An airspace of defined dimensions established around an aerodrome for the protection of aerodrome traffic.
radio-telephony.c: Airspace of defined dimension which extend upward from a specified altitude or flight level to an upper limit, usually a flight level.
radio-telephony.ans: Airspace of defined dimension which extend upward from a specified altitude or flight level to an upper limit, usually a flight level.
radio-telephony.e: A CTA normally starts above the surface and extends upward to a specified upper limit. This separates it from a CTR which starts at the surface.

radio-telephony.q: Where is the most likely place a CTA (Control Area) would be established?
radio-telephony.e: A CTA typically picks up where the TMA below it ends -- existing CTA lower limits in South Africa run from about FL105 to FL145, with an upper limit usually at FL195 or FL200. Exam tip: think of CTR-TMA-CTA as stacked layers of Class C protection, each one further from the ground.

radio-telephony.q: Terminal manoeuvring area?
radio-telephony.a: A control airspace surrounding a major airport with a high volume of traffic.
radio-telephony.b: An uncontrolled airspace surrounding a major airport with a high volume of traffic.
radio-telephony.c: A control airspace surrounding a major airport with a low volume of traffic.
radio-telephony.ans: A control airspace surrounding a major airport with a high volume of traffic.
radio-telephony.e: A TMA exists because traffic converging on a busy airport from several routes needs protection while climbing or descending, and is managed by Approach Control Service, often using radar. All TMAs in South Africa are Class C, and where terrain forces different lower limits in different sectors they're subdivided into "TMA A", "TMA B" etc. -- still one TMA, like a staggered, upside-down wedding cake.

radio-telephony.q: Select the correct abbreviation for the following airspace which extend from a specified limit to a specified upper limit and is normally established at the confluence of ATIS routes in the vicinity of one or more major aerodromes?
radio-telephony.e: TMAs are positioned above one or more CTRs and/or ATZs specifically to protect aircraft climbing out from or descending into a busy airfield along converging routes. Since a TMA must start at least 700 ft above the ground, its lower limit is often stepped between sectors to follow the terrain.

radio-telephony.q: Which of the following best describes an airspace where the ATC may make use of radar to provide position?
radio-telephony.e: A TMA is controlled airspace where Approach Control Service manages IFR and VFR traffic, often using radar (call sign 'Approach' or 'Radar') to vector aircraft and provide separation, especially at busy centres like Johannesburg and Cape Town.

radio-telephony.q: When may you begin your descent for an airfield while within a TMA?
radio-telephony.a: After passing the 'top of descent' point on your flight plan
radio-telephony.b: Once the destination aerodrome is in sight
radio-telephony.c: After you have told ATC your intentions
radio-telephony.d: After clearance has been requested and obtained
radio-telephony.ans: After clearance has been requested and obtained
radio-telephony.e: Inside controlled airspace like a TMA, ATC is actively separating traffic, so any unco-ordinated altitude or heading change could cause a conflict -- this is why a pilot must always request and receive a clearance before descending, even with the destination in sight.

radio-telephony.q: What is “CTR”?
radio-telephony.e: CTR (Control Zone) airspace is established around larger airfields specifically to protect IFR traffic during approach and departure, extending from the ground up to a published upper limit. All CTRs in South Africa are currently Class C.

radio-telephony.q: Where CTR’s are established?
radio-telephony.e: A CTR sits within the lateral boundaries of a TMA, since a TMA is normally positioned above one or more CTRs and/or ATZs to protect traffic climbing out of or descending into a busy aerodrome.

radio-telephony.q: What is "Controlled airspace extending from the surface of the earth upwards to a specified upper limit"?
radio-telephony.e: A CTR starts at the surface and extends upward to a published upper limit. This is different from a CTA which normally starts above the surface.

radio-telephony.q: What is “ATZ”?
radio-telephony.e: An ATZ protects traffic taking off, landing and flying the circuit at an aerodrome, extending from the ground to at least 700 ft AGL (often 1000-1500 ft). Depending on the airfield it can be Class C, D or G -- Class G ATZs are serviced by AFIS rather than full ATC.

radio-telephony.q: Where control zones are normally established?
radio-telephony.e: Control zones protect IFR traffic in the vicinity of larger airfields, and since a CTR extends from the surface upward, it may encompass one or more ATZs (Class C or D) sitting inside it.

radio-telephony.q: Aerodrome traffic zone?
radio-telephony.a: A control airspace surrounding a major airport with a high volume of traffic.
radio-telephony.b: Airspace of defined dimension which extend upward from a specified altitude or flight level to an upper limit, usually a flight level.
radio-telephony.c: An airspace of defined dimensions established around an aerodrome for the protection of aerodrome traffic.
radio-telephony.ans: An airspace of defined dimensions established around an aerodrome for the protection of aerodrome traffic.
radio-telephony.e: An ATZ protects traffic in the immediate vicinity of an aerodrome -- typically a smaller field -- and, unlike a CTR (always Class C), an ATZ can be Class C, D or even G, in which case it's serviced by AFIS instead of full ATC.

radio-telephony.q: Which of the following airspaces require clearance prior to entering? CTR, CTA, TMA, FAD, FAR
radio-telephony.e: CTR, CTA and TMA are all controlled (Class C) airspace requiring an ATC clearance before entry. FAD (Danger Area) and FAR (Restricted Area) are Class G airspace -- a FAD needs no permission (just vigilance), and a FAR needs permission from the appropriate authority, not an ATC clearance.

radio-telephony.q: Aerodrome control shall be responsible for issuing information and instructions to aircraft under its control in order to achieve:
radio-telephony.a: An advisory service to VFR, IFR and SVFR flights
radio-telephony.b: An advisory service only for IFR flights
radio-telephony.c: A safe, orderly and expeditious flow of air traffic
radio-telephony.d: A SVFR service by day and by night
radio-telephony.ans: A safe, orderly and expeditious flow of air traffic
radio-telephony.e: Aerodrome Control Service is one of the three Control Services (alongside Area and Approach Control), and its stated objective, per the Air Traffic Services regulations, is exactly this: a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of traffic -- achieved through issuing clearances and instructions that pilots must follow.

radio-telephony.q: Which of the follow does not refer to controlled airspace?
radio-telephony.e: ATA (Aerodrome Traffic Area) is a legacy term -- it no longer officially exists and has been replaced by ATZ Class G, which is uncontrolled. TMA, CTR and a Class C/D ATZ, by contrast, are all controlled airspace requiring an ATC clearance to enter.

radio-telephony.q: Which airspace only allows IFR flights?
radio-telephony.e: Class A airspace in South Africa comprises the busiest, highest-level airspace -- FL200 to FL460 in the continental FIRs (FL245-460 oceanic), plus some busy air routes between FL145 and FL200 -- where mixing VFR traffic with fast IFR traffic at those speeds and altitudes would be unsafe, so VFR is excluded entirely.

radio-telephony.q: Which of these is a controlled area go for A?
radio-telephony.e: Class A airspace generally starts at FL200 because that's also the ceiling for VFR flight (max FL195) -- above it, only IFR traffic operates, fully separated by ATC, since visual separation becomes impractical at higher speeds and altitudes.

radio-telephony.q: Which of the following would be classified as class C airspace?
radio-telephony.e: Since Class A occupies FL200 and above, virtually all the remaining controlled airspace below that level -- CTRs, ATZs, TMAs and CTAs -- is classified as Class C, where both IFR and VFR are permitted but IFR traffic still receives full separation.

radio-telephony.q: What is the highest level available for a VFR flight?
radio-telephony.e: FL195 is the ceiling for VFR flight because Class A airspace (IFR only) begins at FL200. Exam tip: FL195 also happens to be the top of the odd-flight-level-plus-500 VFR table (eastbound), so it doubles as the highest legal VFR cruising level under the semi-circular rule.

radio-telephony.q: Which airspace has the following separation rules?
radio-telephony.e: Class C reflects the busiest mix of controlled traffic: IFR aircraft need full separation from everyone because of their speed and reliance on instruments, while VFR pilots -- who can see and avoid each other -- only need to be told where other VFR traffic is.

radio-telephony.q: What class of airspace are TMA's classified as?
radio-telephony.e: TMAs sit directly above the CTRs/ATZs of a busy aerodrome, protecting converging IFR and VFR traffic during climb-out and descent -- which is why, like CTRs and CTAs, all South African TMAs are classified as Class C rather than the less-controlled Class D or uncontrolled Class F/G.

radio-telephony.q: Which type of airspace do the following rules apply to? IFR and VFR flights are permitted. All flights are subject to ATC service. IFR flights are separated from both IFR and VFR flights. VFR flights are separated from IFR flights and receive traffic information regarding other VFR flights.
radio-telephony.e: These are standard Class C separation rules. The common SACAA trap is confusing Class C and Class D separation services.

radio-telephony.q: What type of airspace has the following description? Air traffic airspace where both IFR and VFR flights are permitted, all flights are subject to ATC and all flights are separated from each other except VFR to VFR flights where ATC provides traffic information.
radio-telephony.e: This describes Class C exactly: IFR traffic gets full separation because it can't rely on "see and avoid", while VFR-to-VFR only gets traffic information because visual pilots are expected to maintain their own separation by keeping a good lookout.

radio-telephony.q: What class of airspace has the following definition: an air traffic control service is provided to all aircraft, IFR flights are separated from each other and receive traffic information on VFR flights while VFR flights receive traffic information on all other traffic.
radio-telephony.e: In South Africa, Class D at present only exists at the Grand Central ATZ -- a smaller, less busy environment than the major Class C TMAs/CTAs, which is why VFR traffic there gets only information rather than full ATC separation.

radio-telephony.q: Which airspace has the following separation rules: IFR flights are separated from IFR flights and receive traffic information on VFR flights while VFR flights receive traffic information on all other traffic?
radio-telephony.e: Grand Central ATZ is currently the only Class D airspace in South Africa. Because traffic volumes are lower than in Class C, ATC only needs to fully separate IFR from IFR, passing VFR aircraft traffic information rather than actively separating them.

radio-telephony.q: What class of airspace permits IFR and VFR flights where all traffic receives traffic information only?
radio-telephony.e: Class G is uncontrolled airspace -- the remainder of airspace not declared as any other class, plus everything above FL460. There's no ATC service here, only Flight Information Service (FIS) on request; pilots keep their own separation, which is why broadcasting position (and listening to TIBA calls) matters so much in Class G.

radio-telephony.q: What class of airspace provides advisory services to IFR flights and traffic information to all flights?
radio-telephony.e: There's no permanent Class F airspace in South Africa -- it's declared only temporarily, for example over an air show, and published by NOTAM or AIP Supplement. While active, IFR traffic gets an advisory service and VFR gets traffic information, both requiring two-way radio.

radio-telephony.q: What does FAD stand for?
radio-telephony.e: FAD areas are usually military ranges or General Flying Areas (GFAs) used for training -- Class G airspace that pilots may enter, but should do so vigilantly since hazardous activity (low flying, parachuting, weapons testing) may be underway.

radio-telephony.q: What does FAR stand for?
radio-telephony.e: A Restricted Area (FAR) is Class G airspace that may only be entered with permission from the responsible authority -- usually military, as published in AIP ENR 5. Example: FAR23 near Upington, a military shooting range extending from the ground to FL195.

radio-telephony.q: Who is responsible for traffic separation in uncontrolled airspace?
radio-telephony.e: In Class F/G uncontrolled airspace there's no ATC to separate traffic -- only Flight Information Service (FIS), which passes on known traffic but doesn't issue instructions -- so pilots must rely on their own lookout and radio position reports to stay clear of other aircraft.

radio-telephony.q: What does FAD 127 stand for?
radio-telephony.e: FAD (Danger Area) airspace marks hazardous activity such as a military range or a General Flying Area. Unlike a Prohibited or Restricted Area, a pilot may enter a Danger Area without permission, provided they stay vigilant and keep a good lookout.

radio-telephony.q: What does FAD129 7500ALT represent?
radio-telephony.e: "ALT" on a chart means altitude -- height above mean sea level using the local QNH -- rather than a flight level (a standard-pressure reference, 1013.2 hPa). Low-level danger/restricted-area limits close to the ground are given as ALT so the boundary stays tied to actual terrain, regardless of the day's altimeter setting.

radio-telephony.q: What must you do when entering a general flying area?
radio-telephony.a: Listen out for broadcasts from other traffic
radio-telephony.c: Listen out for broadcasts, then when clear, broadcast your intentions
radio-telephony.d: Ask for permission for your intentions
radio-telephony.ans: Listen out for broadcasts, then when clear, broadcast your intentions
radio-telephony.e: Listening out before broadcasting matters most in a General Flying Area, where several training aircraft may share one frequency -- transmitting over someone else without listening first can garble both messages, so pilots wait for a gap, then give their position and intentions.

radio-telephony.q: Referring to the picture below FAD 129 has an upper limit of?
radio-telephony.e: The chart label uses ALT, meaning altitude above mean sea level. Therefore the upper limit is 7500 feet AMSL.

radio-telephony.q: The designator FAR23 found on an aeronautical chart indicates?
radio-telephony.e: FAR23, for example, is Bottelduim Military Shooting Range near Upington -- a circle of 14 nm radius from the ground to FL195. Like all Restricted Areas, FAR-designated airspace needs permission from the responsible (usually military) authority before entry.

radio-telephony.q: Permission to enter a restricted area must be obtained from?
radio-telephony.e: Restricted Areas are typically military ranges, so the "appropriate authority" is usually the military unit responsible for that airspace (as published in AIP ENR 5) -- not ATC, which has no jurisdiction over Restricted Area access.

radio-telephony.q: What type of airspace may only be entered with special permission?
radio-telephony.e: Exam tip: remember the hierarchy -- Prohibited (FAP) may never be entered, Restricted (FAR) needs permission from the responsible authority, and Danger (FAD) needs no permission at all, just vigilance.

radio-telephony.q: Referring to the picture below, FAR 86 has an upper limit of?
radio-telephony.e: The chart label for FAR 86 indicates FL120 as the upper limit. FL means flight level based on the standard pressure setting.

radio-telephony.q: Which South African airspace designator identifies a prohibited area?
radio-telephony.e: The letters after the South African prefix FA identify the type of special-use airspace: P means prohibited, R means restricted, and D means danger. Therefore FAP identifies a prohibited area.

radio-telephony.q: What type of activity is most likely to be associated with a danger area?
radio-telephony.e: Danger areas contain activities that may be hazardous to aircraft such as military exercises, blasting or aerial activities.

radio-telephony.q: Can a pilot enter a danger area without permission?
radio-telephony.d: Yes if the area is inactive
radio-telephony.e:
Danger Areas (FAD) may be entered by pilots without needing permission -- unlike Restricted Areas (FAR), which require permission from the appropriate authority. Pilots should stay vigilant and keep a good lookout for the hazardous activity the area warns of.

Exam tip: FAD = enter with caution, no permission needed; FAR = permission required; FAP = never enter.

radio-telephony.q: What is the main purpose of prohibited areas?
radio-telephony.e: Example: FAP68 in Johannesburg protects the Modderfontein Explosives Factory -- a 1 nm-radius circle from the ground to 1000 ft. Prohibited areas are usually small and cover sites where an aircraft incident, or overflight itself, would pose a serious safety or security risk.

radio-telephony.q: Who is responsible for ensuring that restricted area conditions are met before entry?
radio-telephony.e: This is the same principle that runs through the whole RT syllabus: the pilot-in-command, not ATC or any ground authority, carries ultimate responsibility for confirming that all conditions for entering special-use airspace (Restricted, Danger, or controlled) have been met before the flight proceeds.

radio-telephony.q: What does the upper limit FL145 indicate?
radio-telephony.e: Flight levels are used instead of altitudes at higher levels because all aircraft then reference the same standard-pressure datum (1013.2 hPa), guaranteeing consistent vertical separation regardless of the actual sea-level pressure at any one place -- unlike an altitude, which depends on the local QNH.

radio-telephony.q: When operating near special use airspace a pilot should:
radio-telephony.e: Special-use airspace (Restricted, Danger, Prohibited) each has its own published lateral/vertical limits and conditions in the AIP (ENR 5) -- for a Restricted Area specifically, that includes who to contact for permission -- so pilots should check the current AIP entry before flying near any of them.

radio-telephony.q: The lower limit SFC on a chart means:
radio-telephony.e: SFC means surface. When SFC is shown as the lower limit of airspace, that airspace begins at ground or water level and extends upward to its published upper limit.

radio-telephony.q: Referring to the picture below, FAR 82 has an upper limit of?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: FL105. FAR means Restricted Area South Africa, and the charted upper limit for FAR 82 is given as a flight level. 10500 AGL is wrong because it refers to height above ground level, and 10500 ALT is wrong because the published limit is expressed as a flight level, not altitude.

radio-telephony.q: What does the South African airspace designator FAP identify?
radio-telephony.e:
FAP identifies a prohibited area in South African airspace. FAD identifies a danger area and FAR identifies a restricted area.

Exam tip: FAP = prohibited, FAR = restricted, FAD = danger.

radio-telephony.q: FAP is airspace of defined dimensions within which?
radio-telephony.a: No civilian aircraft is permitted to fly at any time under any circumstances
radio-telephony.b: Flying in this area is permitted with permission
radio-telephony.c: Flying in this area sometimes is permitted.
radio-telephony.ans: No civilian aircraft is permitted to fly at any time under any circumstances
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: No civilian aircraft is permitted to fly at any time under any circumstances. A prohibited area is established to protect sensitive or hazardous locations where civil flight is not allowed. Permission-based entry applies more to restricted areas, not prohibited areas.

radio-telephony.q: What type of airspace may never be entered?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Prohibited. Prohibited airspace is airspace that civilian aircraft may not enter. Restricted airspace may be entered only with special permission, and controlled airspace may be entered after receiving the required clearance.

radio-telephony.q: May aircraft fly in a prohibited area?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: No. Prohibited areas are not available for normal civil aircraft operations. Yes with permission is more appropriate for restricted areas, while prohibited areas are established where entry is not permitted.

radio-telephony.q: What is AFIS?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Aerodrome Flight Information Service. AFIS provides useful aerodrome traffic and flight information to pilots. It is not aerodrome flight control and it is not an organization; it is an information service.

radio-telephony.q: What is the function of an AFIS?
radio-telephony.a: To give information and advice, they cannot issue clearance, decisions are made by the pilot in command.
radio-telephony.b: To give information and advice, they can issue clearance, decisions are made by the pilot in command.
radio-telephony.c: Its control airspace and they can issue clearance.
radio-telephony.ans: To give information and advice, they cannot issue clearance, decisions are made by the pilot in command.
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: AFIS gives information and advice but cannot issue clearances. The pilot-in-command remains responsible for decisions and separation. The options saying AFIS can issue clearances are wrong because that is an ATC function.

radio-telephony.q: What does a Flight Information Service located at an Aerodrome (AFIS) provide?
radio-telephony.a: Information useful for all aircraft within 50 nm of the station.
radio-telephony.b: Instructions to aircraft flying in the ATZ.
radio-telephony.c: Control of all aircraft in the ATZ and information useful for all other aircraft outside the ATZ.
radio-telephony.d: Information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flights in the ATZ.
radio-telephony.ans: Information useful for the safe and efficient conduct of flights in the ATZ.
radio-telephony.e: AFIS callsigns are the airfield name plus "Radio" (e.g. "Port Alfred Radio") to distinguish them from a controlled Tower -- a deliberate phraseology difference (e.g. "the runway is clear" instead of "cleared to land") that reminds both AFIS and the pilot that no clearance is being given, only information.

radio-telephony.q: What is the name of the airspace that AFIS operates in?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: ATA. Aerodrome Traffic Areas (ATA) no longer officially exist -- they have been replaced by ATZ Class G -- but the term is still used in the RT exam syllabus for the uncontrolled airspace where AFIS operates. CTRs and TMAs are controlled airspace served by ATC, not AFIS.

radio-telephony.q: What type of information does AFIS provide?
radio-telephony.e: AFIS (Aerodrome Flight Information Service) issues information and advice only — it never gives clearances, instructions or separation, unlike Control Service. Of these options, Advisory best captures that non-controlling, advice-only role. Note: there is also a specifically-named "Advisory Service", defined as FIS provided to IFR traffic in Class F airspace, which is a different, narrower thing from AFIS — don't confuse the two. AFIS itself falls under the general "Information Service" category, alongside FIS.

radio-telephony.q: Advisory services can give?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Information on other traffic. Advisory services help pilots maintain awareness by passing traffic information. Radar separation is a control service, and weather forecasts are not the main purpose of an advisory service.

radio-telephony.q: The route designator R987D found on an aeronautical chart indicates an?
radio-telephony.e: The suffix "D" marks an ADR (Advisory Route) -- an older classification for Class F airspace that the current AIP glossary lists as "not in use anymore" in South Africa, though it's still tested in the RT syllabus. Exam tip: don't confuse it with "R987F", the suffix for a genuine, currently active Information Route (Class G).

radio-telephony.q: When flying outside of Special Rules and below 1500 feet in uncontrolled airspace, what frequency must be used to give position reports?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 124.8 MHz. This is the common South African TIBA frequency used for position reports in uncontrolled airspace outside Special Rules Areas below 1500 ft. The other frequencies are used for different purposes or areas and would not be the standard choice here.

radio-telephony.q: The abbreviation "PIB" stands for?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Pre-flight Information Bulletin. A PIB is the compiled aeronautical information — NOTAMs, weather, airspace changes — that a pilot must review before flight, which is why AIS makes it available on request: without it a pilot could depart unaware of a closed runway, new restricted area or hazardous weather along the route. The other options are not recognised aviation terminology.

radio-telephony.q: What does AIP SUP stand for?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Aeronautical Information Publication Supplement. An AIP SUP is used for information that is important enough to need wide, timely publicity but is only temporary or supplementary to what's already in the AIP — for example a major, planned airspace change — which is why it's issued separately rather than waiting for the next full AIP amendment. An AIC, by contrast, is used for explanatory or advisory material rather than operational essentials.

radio-telephony.q: What does the code 'QDR' mean?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Magnetic bearing from a station. QDR is the magnetic bearing from a radio station. QDM is the magnetic heading to a station (in no wind), and QTE is the true bearing from a station.

radio-telephony.q: What does 'QTE' mean?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: True bearing from a station. QTE is referenced to true north and gives the true bearing from the station. QDR is the magnetic bearing from the station, while QDM is the magnetic heading to the station.

radio-telephony.q: What are the two types of flight rules?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: VFR and IFR. These are the two sets of flight rules a pilot chooses between: VFR relies on the pilot seeing and avoiding terrain and other traffic, while IFR allows flight by reference to instruments with ATC providing separation, which is why IFR needs extra licensing, equipment and fuel-reserve requirements. VMC and IMC describe the weather, not which rules are being flown — an IFR flight can be conducted in either.

radio-telephony.q: The abbreviation "VFR" stands for?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Visual Flight Rules. VFR flight depends on the pilot maintaining visual contact with the ground (or identifiable objects at night) and staying within the VMC minima for cloud clearance and visibility — which is why it's only permitted when those minima are met, and never in Class A airspace. The other options are not recognised aviation terms.

radio-telephony.q: Which one of the following is correct?
radio-telephony.a: You can use VFR in both VMC and IMC
radio-telephony.b: You can use IMC in both VFR and IFR
radio-telephony.c: You can use IFR in both VMC and IMC
radio-telephony.d: You can use VMC in VFR
radio-telephony.ans: You can use IFR in both VMC and IMC
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: You can use IFR in both VMC and IMC. IFR flight relies on ATC separation and instrument navigation rather than what the pilot can see outside, so it works equally in good weather or in cloud — indeed IFR is compulsory in Class A airspace regardless of the weather. VFR, however, depends on the pilot's own visual reference and is only legal in VMC.

radio-telephony.q: Which directional reference is used when applying the semi-circular cruising-level rule?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Question asks which directional reference the semi-circular cruising-level rule uses.

RULE
The semi-circular rule (Ch 5, CAR 91.06.33 / AIP ENR 1.7.11) splits cruising levels by magnetic track — 000° to 179° (roughly easterly) and 180° to 359° (roughly westerly) — not by heading, because wind drift can make heading differ from track.

ANSWER
Magnetic track

radio-telephony.q: The semi-circular rule shall apply when flying at?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Question asks the height at or above which the semi-circular rule applies to cruising flight.

RULE
Chapter 5 states: all aircraft cruising (flying level in cruising flight) at or above 1500' AGL in uncontrolled airspace have to adhere to the semi-circular rule.

ANSWER
1500ft AGL or above.

radio-telephony.q: In which of the following instances does the semi-circular rule not apply?
radio-telephony.a: Traffic flying VFR at a height of more than 1500 FT AGL.
radio-telephony.b: Traffic flying IFR at a height of more than 1500 FT AGL.
radio-telephony.c: Traffic flying VFR at a height of less than 1500 FT AGL.
radio-telephony.ans: Traffic flying VFR at a height of less than 1500 FT AGL.
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Question asks in which case the semi-circular rule does not apply.

RULE
The rule applies to cruising flight at or above 1500 ft AGL in uncontrolled airspace. Cruising VFR traffic below that height falls outside the rule.

ANSWER
Traffic flying VFR at a height of less than 1500 FT AGL.

radio-telephony.q: Below FL 195 according to semi-circle rules IFR and VFR magnetic track is 250 have the minimum vertical?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Magnetic track 250° (falls in the 180°–359° westbound sector), below FL195.

RULE
The Table of Flight Levels (5.3) shows IFR and VFR levels alternating by 500 ft within each track sector below FL195 — e.g. westbound IFR FL080 sits next to VFR FL085 — so the minimum vertical separation between an IFR level and its neighbouring VFR level is 500 ft.

ANSWER
500

radio-telephony.q: Which statement correctly applies the VFR semi-circular rule to a magnetic track of 090°?
radio-telephony.b: FL075 always means 7 500 ft above ground level
radio-telephony.c: The pilot must use an even-thousand flight level
radio-telephony.d: The rule is based on compass heading rather than magnetic track
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Magnetic track 090° (falls in the 000°–179° eastbound sector), VFR cruising above 1500 ft AGL.

RULE
Eastbound VFR cruising levels are odd flight levels plus 500 ft: FL035, FL055, FL075 ... up to FL195.

ANSWER
The pilot may use FL075

radio-telephony.q: At which of the following flight levels could an aircraft flying VFR on a magnetic track 270 fly according to semi-circular rule?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Magnetic track 270° (falls in the 180°–359° westbound sector), VFR cruising above 1500 ft AGL.

RULE
Westbound VFR cruising levels are even flight levels plus 500 ft: FL045, FL065, FL085 ... up to FL185.

ANSWER
FL 085

radio-telephony.q: Which of the following is a VFR flight level?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Question asks which of the listed levels is a valid VFR flight level.

RULE
VFR cruising levels always carry the +500 ft offset — odd+500 eastbound (FL035, FL055, FL075...) or even+500 westbound (FL045, FL065, FL085...). A plain flight level such as FL070, or an altitude written as 5500 ft rather than as a flight level, is not a VFR cruising level in this system.

ANSWER
FL075

radio-telephony.q: The semi-circular rule is based on an aircraft flying a?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Question asks what directional element the semi-circular rule is based on.

RULE
Both the VFR and IFR cruising-level tables (Ch 5) group aircraft by magnetic track — the path over the ground — not by heading, since heading is only where the nose points and can differ from track in wind.

ANSWER
Magnetic track

radio-telephony.q: What is the ceiling defined as?
radio-telephony.a: Height above ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 20000, covering more than 4 octs.
radio-telephony.b: Height above ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of cloud above 20000, covering more than 4 octs.
radio-telephony.c: Height above ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 2000, covering less than 4 octs.
radio-telephony.ans: Height above ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 20000, covering more than 4 octs.
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Height above ground or water of the base of the lowest layer of cloud below 20,000 ft, covering more than 4 oktas. The reference is above ground/water (not sea level) because it's the pilot's view of the sky from where they actually are that matters, and 'more than half the sky' (more than 4 of 8 oktas) is the threshold because a lesser amount of cloud doesn't meaningfully block the pilot's visual reference needed for VFR.

radio-telephony.q: The minimum visibility required for a VFR flight between 1000ft AGL and FL100 by day?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 5000 m. Between 1000 ft AGL/3000 ft AMSL and FL100, normal VFR requires 5 km visibility and 1500 m horizontal/1000 ft vertical cloud clearance, giving a VFR pilot enough distance to see and avoid other traffic and terrain in time. 1500 m is a Special VFR figure, not the normal VFR minimum in this band.

radio-telephony.q: What is the minimum ceiling for the VFR in a CTR?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 1500 ft. In a CTR, VFR traffic needs a 1500 ft ceiling so aircraft joining or leaving the circuit, and those in the pattern, have enough vertical room to manoeuvre visually and stay clear of cloud. Lower figures (600 ft, 500 ft) belong to the reduced Special VFR minima, which apply only under an ATC clearance in IMC conditions.

radio-telephony.q: What is the minimum visibility required for special VFR in an aeroplane?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 1500 m. Special VFR trades some of the normal VFR visual margin for ATC-provided separation, so the minimum visibility drops from the normal 5000 m to 1500 m — but the pilot must still be able to see well enough to remain clear of cloud and within sight of the ground. 5000 m is the ordinary VFR figure, not the SVFR one.

radio-telephony.q: Special VFR can only be requested?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: During day. Special VFR depends entirely on the pilot's own ability to stay clear of cloud and within sight of the ground, which is far harder to guarantee at night — so SVFR (for both aeroplanes and helicopters) is restricted to daytime only. Night operations require the extra rating and equipment that come with instrument or dedicated night-VFR procedures instead.

radio-telephony.q: What is the minimum ceiling for SVFR in an aeroplane?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 600 feet AGL. Because ATC is providing separation for an SVFR flight, the ceiling can be lower than the 1500 ft required for normal VFR in a CTR — but 600 ft is still needed so the pilot can remain clear of cloud and keep the ground in sight as required. This is well below the 1500 ft normal-VFR ceiling figure given elsewhere in this chapter.

radio-telephony.q: Special VFR is only allowed within a/an?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: CTR. Special VFR is an ATC clearance, and only a Control Zone has the approach/aerodrome control service able to apply the stricter IFR-style separation standards SVFR requires; an ATZ does not have this level of control, so SVFR cannot be granted there (though paragraph 3.1's exceptions cover some ATZ departures/arrivals in poor weather). A TMA and ATA are different airspace types not associated with this clearance at all.

radio-telephony.q: How much visibility do you require for VFR in a CTR / ATZ / ATA?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 5 km. The 5000 m visibility requirement for VFR in a CTR/ATZ/ATA gives pilots enough distance to see and avoid other traffic converging near an aerodrome, where traffic density is highest. 1 km is far too low for safe visual operations, while 10 km and 25 km are more than the minimum actually required.

radio-telephony.q: When flying 1500 ft. or higher, how will you indicate your intended height on a flight plan?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Flight level. Once a flight is cruising at 1500 ft AGL or higher, the semi-circular rule applies, and item 15 of the flight plan records the planned cruising level as a Flight Level (e.g. F095) rather than as an altitude or height, since flight levels are what the semi-circular rule and ATC separation are built around.

radio-telephony.q: What will a runway that has extensive patches of standing water that are visible be described as?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Flooded. A runway is reported as flooded when standing water is visible over extensive areas — the most severe of the moisture-related conditions — because at that point braking action and the risk of aquaplaning are significantly worse than on a runway with only limited water patches or a merely wet surface. This is why ATC passes on this specific wording rather than a general 'wet' report: it directly affects a pilot's landing distance and directional control planning.

radio-telephony.q: What will a runway that has significant patches of visible water be described as?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Water patches. This describes significant, visible patches of water that don't yet cover the runway extensively enough to be called flooded — an intermediate stage between a wet runway (surface moisture, no visible pooling) and a flooded one, again reported because it affects expected braking performance on landing or take-off.

radio-telephony.q: What does it mean if a runway reported to be damp?
radio-telephony.a: The surface shows a change of colour due to dry surface.
radio-telephony.b: The runway has extensive patches of water that are visible.
radio-telephony.c: The surface shows a change of colour due to moisture.
radio-telephony.ans: The surface shows a change of colour due to moisture.
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: The surface shows a change of colour due to moisture. 'Damp' is the mildest of the moisture reports — a colour change with no visible standing water at all — as distinct from wet (visible surface moisture), water patches, or flooded (visible pooling). Exam tip: remember the escalation dry → damp → wet → water patches → flooded, each step meaning progressively more water on the surface and more caution needed on landing.

radio-telephony.q: 1 hPa is roughly equivalent to?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 30 ft.
