Atmospheric pressure falls by about 1 hPa for every 30 ft of climb (true up to roughly 10,000 ft), which is exactly why the altimeter can be calibrated to read altitude instead of raw pressure. Exam tip: this rule of thumb also lets you quickly estimate altimeter error — e.g. flying on a QNH that is 10 hPa out will put you about 300 ft off your indicated altitude.

radio-telephony.q: The ISA standard atmospheric pressure is?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 1013.25 hPa. This is the sea-level pressure of the International Standard Atmosphere, chosen as a single fixed reference (rather than any day's actual pressure) so that every aircraft flying at a given Flight Level, regardless of the weather below, is using the same datum and can be vertically separated from other traffic. 1003.25 hPa and 1000 hPa are not recognised standard pressure values.

radio-telephony.q: Where is flight level zero?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 1013.25 hPa pressure level. Flight levels are based on the standard pressure datum of 1013.25 hPa, not actual mean sea level or ground level. This is why flight levels maintain standard vertical references between aircraft.

radio-telephony.q: What will the altimeter show when QNE is set?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Pressure Altitude. QNE is the standard setting of 1013.25 hPa, used once an aircraft is above the Transition Altitude so that all traffic — no matter what the actual sea-level pressure is at any given moment — shares one common reference, expressed as a Flight Level. QNH instead gives altitude above mean sea level, and QFE gives height above the aerodrome, both of which vary from place to place.

radio-telephony.q: An aircraft with the standard altimeter setting set in the subscale window, will have its vertical position indicated as?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Flight level. With 1013.25 hPa set, the altimeter reads pressure altitude, which is expressed as a Flight Level (e.g. FL75) precisely because it is not tied to any particular place's sea-level pressure — this is what allows the semi-circular rule to give consistent vertical separation across an entire route. Height AGL uses the ground as its reference, altitude uses QNH, and 'height AMSL' is not the term used for standard-pressure operation.

radio-telephony.q: Select the correct definition which refers to the standard setting of 1013.25 hPa?
radio-telephony.a: The altimeter subscale setting in hectopascals to obtain flight levels
radio-telephony.b: The altimeter subscale setting in inches to obtain flight level
radio-telephony.c: The altimeter subscale setting in hectopascals to obtain altitude
radio-telephony.d: The altimeter subscale setting in metres to obtain altitude
radio-telephony.ans: The altimeter subscale setting in hectopascals to obtain flight levels
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: The altimeter subscale setting in hectopascals to obtain flight levels. 1013.25 hPa is dialled into the subscale specifically so cruising traffic is referenced to a common, unvarying datum instead of the fluctuating actual pressure at any one place — which is what QNH (in hPa, for altitude) would give. Metres and inches are not the units used for pressure settings in South African operations.

radio-telephony.q: What does setting QFE indicate?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Height above airfield elevation. QFE uses the actual pressure at the aerodrome itself as the datum, so the altimeter reads zero on that runway — useful for circuit and local flying where a pilot mainly needs height above the airfield rather than sea level. QNH, by contrast, always references mean sea level and would show the field's elevation rather than zero.

radio-telephony.q: While on the ground at an unmanned aerodrome, another aircraft requests the QNH. How could you find this out and give it to the aircraft?
radio-telephony.a: Set your altimeter to the airfield elevation and read QNE on the subscale.
radio-telephony.b: Set your altimeter to the airfield elevation and read QNH on the subscale.
radio-telephony.c: Set your altimeter to the airfield elevation and read QFE on the subscale.
radio-telephony.ans: Set your altimeter to the airfield elevation and read QNH on the subscale.
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Set your altimeter to the known airfield elevation and read the QNH in the subscale window. QNH is the pressure setting that makes the altimeter indicate aerodrome elevation on the ground. QNE is fixed at 1013.25 hPa, and QFE would make the altimeter read zero.

radio-telephony.q: An aircraft with QNH setting set in the altimeter, will have its vertical position indicated as?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Altitude above mean sea level. QNH corrects the local pressure to sea level, so once it's set the altimeter shows altitude — the pilot's height above terrain and obstacles wherever they are, which is why QNH is used for take-off, low-level flight and landing. QFE, in contrast, only ever gives height above one specific airfield.

radio-telephony.q: The vertical position of an aircraft, flying at 6000 ft above MSL with the QNH set in the subscale window of the altimeter, is referred to as:
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Altitude. With QNH set, vertical position is always measured above mean sea level and called altitude — the figure pilots need to judge clearance above terrain and obstacles on a low-level or approach/departure phase. Elevation describes a fixed point on the ground, flight levels need the standard 1013.25 hPa setting, and height is only shown when QFE is set.

radio-telephony.q: A student forgets to change from QNH to QNE. What will be broadcast to the SSR?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Flight level. The transponder altitude encoder transmits pressure altitude based on the standard pressure reference, regardless of what the pilot has set on the cockpit altimeter. Therefore SSR altitude reporting is still based on flight level information.

radio-telephony.q: On what altimeter setting will you fly when at or below the transition altitude?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: QNH. Below the transition altitude a pilot needs to know actual height above terrain and obstacles, especially close to the ground during departure or arrival, so QNH (referenced to sea level) is used and vertical position is expressed as altitude. Above the transition level, everyone instead uses the standard setting (QNE) so that traffic is vertically separated on a common datum.

radio-telephony.q: On what altimeter setting will you fly at on or above the transition level?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: QNE. At or above the transition level all aircraft use the fixed 1013.25 hPa datum instead of their own local QNH, so pilots flying between regions with different pressure settings are still reliably separated from each other on Flight Levels. QNH is used below the transition altitude, QFE gives height above one aerodrome, and QDR is a bearing, not an altimeter setting.

radio-telephony.q: The transition level at an aerodrome is always?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Higher than the transition altitude. Between the transition altitude and transition level lies the transition layer, a buffer that must exist so no aircraft is ever cruising level while its altimeter reference is ambiguous — this is only possible if the transition level sits above the transition altitude, never below or at it.

radio-telephony.q: How high is the transition level above the transition altitude?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: At least 1000 ft. AIC 20.2 requires this gap so that the transition layer is thick enough to separate climbing and descending traffic changing between QNH and the standard setting — no aircraft may fly level inside this layer at all. Exam tip: because the transition level depends on the day's QNH, it isn't a fixed figure like the transition altitude — it moves to preserve that 1000 ft minimum.

radio-telephony.q: When should you change from standard setting to QNH?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Descending through the transition level. A descending aircraft keeps using the standard 1013.25 hPa setting (and reports Flight Levels) until it passes through the transition level, at which point it swaps to the local QNH to get an accurate altitude for the approach and landing. Climbing aircraft make the opposite change, but at the transition altitude, not the transition level.

radio-telephony.q: When should a pilot change the altimeter setting from local QNH to 1013.25?
radio-telephony.a: On the climbing passing through the transition level for that area.
radio-telephony.b: On the climbing passing through the transition altitude for that area.
radio-telephony.c: On the descending passing through the transition altitude for that area.
radio-telephony.ans: On the climbing passing through the transition altitude for that area.
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: On the climb passing through the transition altitude. Below the transition altitude a climbing aircraft stays on QNH for an accurate altitude near terrain, then swaps to the standard 1013.25 hPa setting once through it so it is now vertically referenced the same way as all other cruising traffic. The equivalent change for a descending aircraft happens later, at the transition level.

radio-telephony.q: In VMC, flights intending to land at a point beyond 25nm from any aerodrome with a published transition altitude must observe a height of?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 2000 ft as the transition altitude. Where an airfield has no published transition altitude and is more than 25 nm from any listed aerodrome, AIC 20.2 gives pilots a standard fallback of 2000 ft AGL (in VMC) so there is still a defined point to change from QNH to the standard setting, rather than leaving it to guesswork. The other options describe the transition level, not the transition altitude, for this same case.

radio-telephony.q: What is the transition altitude if it is not published and further than 25NM from control airspace?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 2000ft AGL. When no transition altitude is published and the aircraft is more than 25 nm from a listed aerodrome, AIC 20.2 sets 2000 ft AGL as the default in VMC, giving the pilot a clear point at which to change from QNH to the standard 1013.25 hPa setting. (In IMC the equivalent default is instead the lowest safe cruising altitude, since terrain clearance is the priority when visual reference isn't available.)

radio-telephony.q: Transition level in VMC is?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 3000 ft above aerodrome elevation. AIC 20.2 states that for airfields without a published Transition Level (more than 25 nm from a listed aerodrome), the VMC transition level is the nearest flight level above 3000' AGL. This differs from the IMC case, where the transition level is instead the nearest flight level 500 ft above the lowest safe altitude.

radio-telephony.q: How may a flight plan be filed?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Telephone, fax or internet. A flight plan can be filed in person or by telephone with the nearest Air Traffic Service Unit, by telephone with the AIM Service Centre in Johannesburg (0860 FLY NOW), or online via the file2fly system on the ATNS website, which is the preferred method since it reduces transcription errors and time-stamps the filing automatically. It cannot be filed through the post office or informally via family members. Exam tip: whichever method you use, always get a reference number afterwards — flight plans occasionally get lost in the system, and the reference makes it easy to trace.

radio-telephony.q: When should a flight plan be closed at an uncontrolled aerodrome?
radio-telephony.a: When you notify ATC after landing
radio-telephony.ans: When you notify ATC after landing
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: When you notify ATC after landing. At an uncontrolled aerodrome, ATC has no automatic way of knowing the aircraft has landed, so if Search and Rescue was requested the pilot must specifically close the flight plan with ATC, either by radio just before landing (e.g. "field in sight, landing in 5 minutes, please close my flight plan") or by telephone afterwards. It is not closed automatically at touchdown, and there is no fixed 5-minute grace period.

radio-telephony.q: How is a flight plan closed at a controlled aerodrome?
radio-telephony.b: It is normally closed automatically after landing
radio-telephony.ans: It is normally closed automatically after landing
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: It is normally closed automatically after landing. A flight plan is closed automatically when the aircraft lands at a controlled aerodrome, since ATC observes the arrival. Waiting 20 minutes or 2 hours is not the procedure here — those delay figures relate to Search and Rescue timing options used at uncontrolled aerodromes, not to closure at a controlled one.

radio-telephony.q: What does ETA mean?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Estimated time of arrival. ETA matters beyond just informing the destination — it is the reference time against which ATC judges a flight overdue, so if the actual arrival slips well past the filed ETA without a report, Search and Rescue action can begin. Estimated elapsed time is EET, and estimated time of departure is ETD.

radio-telephony.q: Is a flight plan required for a local flight?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: No. A purely local flight is one of the specific exceptions to the mandatory flight plan requirement. A flight plan may still be filed voluntarily for a local flight, for example to obtain Search and Rescue/alerting protection.

radio-telephony.q: How do you convert South African local time to UTC?
radio-telephony.a: Subtract 2 hours from UTC to obtain local time
radio-telephony.b: Subtract 2 hours from local time to obtain UTC
radio-telephony.ans: Subtract 2 hours from local time to obtain UTC
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Subtract 2 hours from local time to obtain UTC. South African Standard Time is UTC+2, so UTC is two hours behind South African local time. For example, 17:00 local is 15:00 UTC.

radio-telephony.q: Convert the following South African local times to UTC: 17:00, 18:00, 04:00, 13:00, 12:30.
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 15:00, 16:00, 02:00, 11:00, 10:30. South African local time is UTC+2, so subtract 2 hours from each time. 18:00 becomes 16:00 UTC, 04:00 becomes 02:00 UTC, and 12:30 becomes 10:30 UTC.

radio-telephony.q: Which mandatory item must be included in an ATS flight plan filed before departure?
radio-telephony.b: The type of VHF radio in the equipment listing
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: The route to be followed. Item 15 of the flight plan must show the planned route so that ATS can understand where the aircraft intends to fly and provide traffic and alerting services. Indicated airspeed and a co-pilot's name are not items entered on the form, and equipment is recorded using standard letter codes in item 10, not by naming a specific radio type.

radio-telephony.q: What does the transponder base its altitude information on?
radio-telephony.d: What is indicated on the altimeter
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Pressure altitude. A Mode C transponder reports altitude based on pressure altitude referenced to 1013.25 hPa, not the pilot selected QNH or what the cockpit altimeter happens to display. This ensures ATC receives a standard altitude reference from all aircraft.

radio-telephony.q: How soon must a flight plan be filed when filed in flight?
radio-telephony.a: 30 minutes before entering controlled or advisory airspace
radio-telephony.b: 1 hour before entering controlled or advisory airspace
radio-telephony.c: 10 minutes before entering controlled or advisory airspace
radio-telephony.ans: 10 minutes before entering controlled or advisory airspace
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 10 minutes before entering controlled or advisory airspace. Filing a flight plan in flight is only permitted in exceptional circumstances, such as no communication facilities at the departure point or a change of plan during the flight. The pilot must pass the flight plan details to ATS on first contact, at least 10 minutes before entering the controlled or advisory airspace.

radio-telephony.q: An ATS flight plan needs to be amended in flight when?
radio-telephony.d: ETA changes by 3 minutes or more
radio-telephony.ans: ETA changes by 3 minutes or more
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: ETA changes by 3 minutes or more. If the estimated time at the next reporting point or destination changes by 3 minutes or more, ATC must be told, which is the threshold given in AIP ENR 1.10 and AIC D003/2022. (CAR 91.03.4 and current ICAO guidance actually specify 2 minutes as the more up-to-date figure, but 3 minutes remains the value most commonly used for exam purposes.)

radio-telephony.q: Any flight plan should be activated within?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 1 hour of departure time. A filed flight plan is only a notification of intent and will simply be deleted if not activated — by making first radio contact with an Air Traffic Service Unit — within 60 minutes of the planned departure time. If the flight is delayed beyond that, the pilot must amend the old flight plan or file a new one.

radio-telephony.q: An X in Type of flight on the flight plan form means?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Mercy flight. In item 8 (type of flight), X covers any flight that is not General Aviation, Non-scheduled, Scheduled or Military — for example a medical/mercy flight, a fire-fighting flight, or a drone flight — and the nature of the flight is then specified in item 18 under STS/ or RMK/.

radio-telephony.q: Item 9 of an ATS flight plan requires the wake turbulence category of the aircraft to be completed. Select the appropriate character for an aircraft weighing 5701 kg?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Aircraft maximum all-up weight 5701 kg.

RULE
Per the wake turbulence category table: L (Light) applies up to and including 7,000 kg; M (Medium) applies above 7,000 kg but less than 136,000 kg; H (Heavy) applies at 136,000 kg or more.

ANSWER
5701 kg is at or below the 7,000 kg threshold, so the correct wake turbulence category is L (Light).

radio-telephony.q: When is it mandatory to file an ATS flight plan?
radio-telephony.a: For a flight from an uncontrolled to a controlled aerodrome, remaining below 1500 feet AGL en-route
radio-telephony.b: For a flight for which alerting action is required
radio-telephony.c: When conducting circuit training at a controlled aerodrome equipped with radar
radio-telephony.d: For a solo student flying from a controlled aerodrome to the general flying area and back
radio-telephony.ans: For a flight for which alerting action is required
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: For a flight for which alerting action is required. An ATS flight plan must be filed for a specific list of cases, and "a flight for which alerting action (Search and Rescue) is required" is explicitly one of them. A short VFR flight below 1500 ft AGL that stays within its own CTR/ATZ, or ordinary circuit training, does not by itself trigger a mandatory flight plan.

radio-telephony.q: When completing an ATS flight plan, Item 15 requires the cruising speed to be completed. To indicate this speed in knots, which character must be inserted?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: N. Item 15 needs the units to be unambiguous, so a fixed letter code precedes the figures: N + four digits for knots (e.g. N0115 = 115 kt), or M + three digits for a Mach number (e.g. M082) once an aircraft is fast enough for Mach to be the more meaningful figure. K and O are not used as speed-unit indicators on the ICAO flight plan.

radio-telephony.q: What do you enter on the flight plan form in field 9 for aircraft if the aircraft you are flying does not have a type indicator?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: ZZZZ. ZZZZ is used whenever no ICAO type designator has been assigned — typically for drones or a mixed formation — so that ATC still knows to look elsewhere on the form (item 18, under TYP/) rather than assuming the aircraft type is simply unknown or unspecified. TBN and SAR are used for entirely different purposes on the form.

radio-telephony.q: For which of the following must an ATS flight plan be filed?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: All international flights. Every international flight must have an ATS flight plan filed, regardless of flight rules. Not every domestic IFR or VFR flight, and not every training flight, automatically requires one — filing depends on the specific circumstances set out in the mandatory-filing list, such as alerting action, commercial operations, or entering controlled airspace.

radio-telephony.q: Inform ATC if there are changes in the flight plan during the flight regarding time?
radio-telephony.c: The time changes by 3 min or more
radio-telephony.ans: The time changes by 3 min or more
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: The time changes by 3 min or more. If the estimated time at the next reporting point or destination changes by 3 minutes or more, ATC must be advised, which is the threshold given in AIP ENR 1.10 and AIC D003/2022. (CAR 91.03.4 and current ICAO guidance specify 2 minutes as the more up-to-date figure, but 3 minutes is the value most commonly used for exam purposes.)

radio-telephony.q: If the aircraft is flying from an uncontrolled airfield into a controlled airfield with no other controlled airspace being flown through, must a flight plan be filed for the flight?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: No. Flying from an uncontrolled aerodrome into a controlled one, without entering any other controlled or advisory airspace en route, is one of the specific exemptions from the mandatory flight plan requirement. A flight plan may still be filed voluntarily, for example to obtain Search and Rescue cover.

radio-telephony.q: Prior to departure, an un-activated ATS flight plan will remain valid?
radio-telephony.a: For 30 mins after the estimated time of departure
radio-telephony.b: Indefinitely from the time of filing
radio-telephony.c: Until the estimated time of departure
radio-telephony.d: For 60 mins after the estimated time of departure
radio-telephony.ans: For 60 mins after the estimated time of departure
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: For 60 mins after the estimated time of departure. An un-activated flight plan is only a notification of intent and will be deleted if the pilot has not activated it — by making first contact with an Air Traffic Service Unit — within 60 minutes of the estimated departure time.

radio-telephony.q: In flight plan item 8, a student pilot flying solo should enter?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: G. Item 8 asks for the type of flight as a single letter; G stands for General Aviation, which covers ordinary private and training flights, including a solo student navigation exercise — this classification affects how ATC prioritises and handles the flight, unlike N (charter) or S (scheduled) traffic.

radio-telephony.q: While on a flight plan, upon arriving at a checkpoint you realize that you are 5 minutes before your ETA, what should you do?
radio-telephony.a: Increase power to reach the next check point on time
radio-telephony.d: Reduce power to reach the next check point on time
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Advise ATC. Being 5 minutes ahead of your filed ETA is more than the reportable threshold, so the pilot must pass ATC a revised estimate rather than silently speeding up or slowing down to force the original time to hold.

radio-telephony.q: What must be entered into item 13 (departure aerodrome and time) of an ICAO flight plan form?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Off-block time in UTC. Item 13 records the estimated off-block time — the time the aircraft starts taxiing to the holding point — expressed in UTC, not local time. Only helicopters and drones enter their take-off time here instead of an off-block time.

radio-telephony.q: The equipment on board is VHF, RT/F, VOR, ILS and mode C transponder. What would you put on the flight plan under equipment?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: S/C. VHF voice, VOR and ILS together make up the bundled 'Standard' code S in item 10a, because that combination is the baseline equipment fit assumed for ordinary IFR-capable flying — listing S avoids having to spell out V, O and L individually. A Mode C (altitude-encoding) transponder is then entered separately as C in item 10b, giving S/C.

radio-telephony.q: Your aircraft is equipped with a VHF radio and mode C transponder but no VOR. Select the correct option of how this should be entered into the equipment field (item 10) of the ATS flight plan?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: V/C. Without VOR (or ILS) on board the aircraft doesn't qualify for the bundled 'Standard' code S, so each piece of equipment must be listed on its own — V for VHF voice in item 10a — followed by C in item 10b for the Mode C transponder. This shows why item 10a is a flexible letter set rather than a single tick-box: it must describe exactly what's fitted, not a rounded-up category.

radio-telephony.q: When the number of passengers for your flight is not yet known at the time of filing an ATS flight plan, which designator should you place in Item 19 (persons on board)?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: TBN. TBN ('to be notified') is entered in item 19 when the passenger count isn't finalised at filing time, so ATC still has a complete flight plan on file — this matters because item 19's headcount is exactly what Search and Rescue would need if the aircraft went missing, so it should be updated once known rather than left blank.

radio-telephony.q: A flight plan is compulsory when?
radio-telephony.a: Search and rescue is not required
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Search and rescue is required. A flight plan is mandatory whenever Search and Rescue/alerting protection is required for the flight — this is one of the explicit triggers for mandatory filing, independent of flight duration.

radio-telephony.q: In flight plan item 15, the cruising airspeed used is?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: TAS. Item 15's cruising speed is always given as True Airspeed, not indicated or calibrated airspeed, because TAS is what actually determines the aircraft's speed over the ground and is used for ATC's time and fuel calculations.

radio-telephony.q: How long before start must a flight plan be filed?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 30 minutes. A flight plan must reach the ATSU at least 30 minutes before departure (60 minutes for an international flight) to give them time to process it and make it available to other units before the aircraft is airborne — though it may be filed up to 5 days in advance if convenient. Filing right on departure, or only 10 minutes before, doesn't leave enough lead time.

radio-telephony.q: Standard equipment S as entered in Item 10 of an ATS flight plan represents which of the following?
radio-telephony.a: VHF radio, transponder, ATZ and VOR
radio-telephony.b: VHF radio, ILS, DME and VOR
radio-telephony.e:
RULE
Standard equipment "S" in Item 10a of the flight plan specifically means VHF voice (V), VOR (O) and ILS (L) — no more, no less — because that trio was chosen as the common baseline fit for an aircraft capable of a basic instrument approach. Any other equipment (such as ADF or DME) must be listed individually using its own letter instead of, or in addition to, S.

ANSWER
VHF radio, ILS and VOR

radio-telephony.q: How soon must a domestic flight plan be filed when filed before departure?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 30 minutes before departure. Domestic flight plans need at least 30 minutes' notice so the ATSU has time to process and distribute the information before the aircraft departs; an international flight needs double that, 60 minutes, reflecting the extra coordination across borders. Filing further in advance (up to 5 days) is also permitted.

radio-telephony.q: The letter G entered into item 8 (type of flight) of an ATS flight plan means?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: General navigation. Item 8's type-of-flight letter tells ATC what kind of operation they're dealing with — G (General Aviation) covers ordinary private, training and navigation flights, as opposed to N (charter), S (scheduled airline), M (military) or X (anything else, such as a medical or drone flight), which may carry different priority or handling.

radio-telephony.q: Item 13 of an ATS flight plan requires the ETD (estimated time of departure) to be completed. The value entered in this field is based on?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: UTC. Every time on an ICAO flight plan, including the ETD in item 13, is given in UTC rather than local time specifically so that pilots and ATS units in different time zones — or on a flight crossing several — are all working from one unambiguous reference. Mixing local and UTC times on the form would risk serious misunderstanding about actual departure or arrival timing.

radio-telephony.q: Inform ATC if there are changes in the flight plan during the flight regarding airspeed?
radio-telephony.c: TAS changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach
radio-telephony.ans: TAS changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
An aircraft in flight with a filed Flight Plan.

RULE
ATC must be notified by radio if the True Airspeed (TAS) changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach from the TAS nominated in the flight plan, or if the estimated time at the next reporting point or destination changes by more than 2 minutes.

ANSWER
TAS changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach

radio-telephony.q: What is the call-sign for the Area Control Centre unit or service?
radio-telephony.e: The Area Control Centre's callsign is CONTROL (also heard as AREA), named after the control centre, e.g. "Johannesburg Control". It provides area control service to aircraft in a CTA, airway, or other part of the FIR.

radio-telephony.q: What does strength 2 in response to a radio check mean?
radio-telephony.e: Readability 2 means readable now and then. The five-point readability scale runs from 1, unreadable, to 5, perfectly readable, so a report of 2 indicates only intermittent understanding.

radio-telephony.q: Select the correct transmission by a pilot when establishing initial contact with ATC to request their joining instructions:
radio-telephony.d: Tower, this is ABC, good day
radio-telephony.e: Initial contact follows the standard format: name the station being called first, then your own callsign - e.g. "Tower, ZS-ABC" - so the correct station knows the call is meant for them before you say anything else. On a busy shared frequency, several stations may hear you, so naming the addressee first prevents confusion about who should reply.

radio-telephony.q: Under what condition may a pilot abbreviate his or her call sign when speaking to a controller?
radio-telephony.a: If the controller has last call sign and there is no ambiguity with another call sign.
radio-telephony.b: If the controller has first call sign and there is ambiguity with another call sign.
radio-telephony.c: If the controller has first call sign and there is no ambiguity with another call sign.
radio-telephony.ans: If the controller has first call sign and there is no ambiguity with another call sign.
radio-telephony.e: A callsign may be abbreviated only once ATC has used the abbreviated version and there is no risk of confusion.

radio-telephony.q: How would a frequency of 127.75 be pronounced?
radio-telephony.a: WUN TWO SEVEN POINT SEVEN FIFE
radio-telephony.c: WUN TWO SEVEN DAYSEEMAL SEVEN FIFE
radio-telephony.d: ONE TWO SEVEN DECIMAL SEVEN FIVE
radio-telephony.ans: WUN TWO SEVEN DAYSEEMAL SEVEN FIFE
radio-telephony.e: Frequencies are always spoken digit-by-digit, with as many decimals as are specified, and the decimal point is pronounced DAYSEEMAL (not "point"). This precise pronunciation, along with words like NINER and TREE for similar-sounding digits, exists to prevent frequencies being misheard over a noisy or weak signal.

radio-telephony.q: In the phonetic alphabet Q and U stand for?
radio-telephony.e: The ICAO phonetic alphabet spells out letters as Quebec (Q) and Uniform (U) rather than saying the bare letter, because single letters like Q and U can sound alike or get lost in radio static. Every pilot must learn the full alphabet by heart, since it is used for callsigns, location indicators, and any letter group that is not unmistakable in normal speech.

radio-telephony.q: How should the frequency of 125.8 MHz be pronounced?
radio-telephony.e: Radio frequencies are spoken digit by digit using standard ICAO pronunciation, and the decimal is spoken as DAY-SEE-MAL. Therefore 125.8 is transmitted as WON TOO FIFE DAY-SEE-MAL AIT.

radio-telephony.q: How should the following numbers be pronounced when transmitted over the radio: 2001 11346?
radio-telephony.a: Too zero zero wun, elevent thousand tree hundred and fower six
radio-telephony.b: Too thousand and wun, wun wun tree fower six
radio-telephony.c: Too double zero wun, wun wun tree fower six
radio-telephony.d: Too zero zero wun, wun wun tree fower six
radio-telephony.ans: Too zero zero wun, wun wun tree fower six
radio-telephony.e: Numbers are transmitted digit-by-digit (2001 becomes "too zero zero wun"), except for whole hundreds or thousands of altitude, transponder codes, or QNH, which use the words "hundred"/"thousand" instead. Since 2001 is not a whole thousand, it must be spoken as individual digits rather than "two thousand and one", to avoid ambiguity.

radio-telephony.q: What is the correct phraseology to use when making a radio transmission for test purposes?
radio-telephony.e: RADIO CHECK is the standard opening phrase used to test whether equipment is working, followed by the frequency in use. The other station replies with "reading you" plus a number from the 1 (unreadable) to 5 (perfectly readable) scale, giving both parties an objective measure of signal quality instead of a vague "yes I hear you".

radio-telephony.q: What quality would a strength 1 transmission be?
radio-telephony.e: Readability 1 means unreadable. On the standard one-to-five radio-check scale, no useful part of the transmission can be understood at level 1.

radio-telephony.q: How would a QNH of 989 hPa be used over the radio?
radio-telephony.e: QNH values are spoken digit-by-digit (NINER AIT NINER for 989), not as "nine eighty-nine", because 989 is not a whole hundred or thousand. Precise digit-by-digit pronunciation matters especially here, since a misheard QNH directly affects an altimeter setting and therefore terrain clearance.

radio-telephony.q: What quality would a strength 5 transmission be?
radio-telephony.e: Readability 5 means perfectly readable. It is the highest value on the radio-check scale and indicates that the entire transmission is clear without difficulty.

radio-telephony.q: What quality would a strength 3 transmission be?
radio-telephony.e: Readability 3 means readable with difficulty. The message can be understood, but interference, weakness, or distortion makes reception unreliable.

radio-telephony.q: How would you pronounce 3900 over the radio?
radio-telephony.e: Altitudes that are a whole hundred or thousand are spoken using the words HUNDRED/THOUSAND rather than as individual digits, so 3900 becomes TREE TOUSAND NINER HUNDRED. This shorthand is used only for round figures - a value like 3950 would have to be spoken digit-by-digit instead.

radio-telephony.q: An aeroplane with the call sign ZS-ABC is at the holding point and wants to tell ATC that he is ready to take off. What would the correct radio call be?
radio-telephony.a: Zulu Sierra Alpha Bravo Charlie, ready.
radio-telephony.b: Ready, Zulu Sierra Alpha Bravo Charlie, Tower.
radio-telephony.c: Tower, Zulu Sierra Alpha Bravo Charlie, ready.
radio-telephony.ans: Tower, Zulu Sierra Alpha Bravo Charlie, ready.
radio-telephony.e: The standard call format is: station addressed, own callsign, then the message - "Tower, Zulu Sierra Alpha Bravo Charlie, ready." Naming Tower first ensures the right unit picks up the call, and the full callsign must be used until ATC has used an abbreviated version back to you.

radio-telephony.q: What is the time given in an ATIS broadcast?
radio-telephony.e: The time included in an ATIS broadcast is stated in UTC. This lets every pilot interpret the observation time consistently regardless of local time.

radio-telephony.q: When an aircraft has been cleared to backtrack, it means that the aircraft is cleared to?
radio-telephony.a: Taxi on the active runway in the opposite direction to that used for landing and taking-off
radio-telephony.b: Reverse track and return to the point of departure
radio-telephony.c: Fly the ILS back-course beam approach
radio-telephony.d: Turn around and return to the starting area at the aerodrome
radio-telephony.ans: Taxi on the active runway in the opposite direction to that used for landing and taking-off
radio-telephony.e: BACKTRACK RUNWAY means entering the runway and taxiing along it against the landing/take-off direction - used, for example, when there is no full-length parallel taxiway to reach the threshold. Because this puts you on the active runway, the clearance must be followed exactly and you must vacate before conflicting traffic.

radio-telephony.q: What abbreviation is given to the automated recording that provides aerodrome operational information and meteorological information for departing and arriving traffic?
radio-telephony.e: ATIS (Automatic Terminal Information Service) is a continuously recorded broadcast of routine aerodrome and weather information (runway in use, QNH, wind, etc.), which pilots listen to before contacting ATC to reduce frequency congestion.

radio-telephony.q: The term CONFIRM used in radiotelephony is best described as meaning that?
radio-telephony.b: I require the transmitting party to repeat part of their last transmission
radio-telephony.c: I wish to verify the last transmission or instruction from the transmitting party
radio-telephony.d: I am in agreement with the transmitting party
radio-telephony.ans: I wish to verify the last transmission or instruction from the transmitting party
radio-telephony.e: CONFIRM asks the other station to verify whether information has been received or understood correctly. It is a request for checking information, not another word for yes.

radio-telephony.q: What does expedite mean?
radio-telephony.e: EXPEDITE means act without delay or increase the rate of movement where safe. It is not permission to ignore limitations, clearances, or safe operating procedures.

radio-telephony.q: What is the standard phraseology used when you fix an error in a transmission?
radio-telephony.e: Say CORRECTION immediately after making an error in your own transmission, then repeat the corrected part. This prevents the incorrect information from remaining unchallenged on the frequency.

radio-telephony.q: What is the meaning of the phrase Stand By?
radio-telephony.b: Wait and I will call you
radio-telephony.ans: Wait and I will call you
radio-telephony.e: STAND BY means wait and the station will call you again. It is not an approval, clearance, or instruction to continue with the message.

radio-telephony.q: What should you do if you are told to change frequency and monitor 120.4?
radio-telephony.b: Tune into 120.4 and report your position
radio-telephony.c: Stay on the frequency you are.
radio-telephony.e: MONITOR means change to the stated frequency and listen out. Do not make an initial call unless instructed or unless operationally necessary.

radio-telephony.q: What is an ATIS?
radio-telephony.a: An air traffic control unit that operates at busier aerodromes
radio-telephony.c: A continuous broadcast of recorded non-control aeronautical information
radio-telephony.d: The standard name for broadcasts by aircraft in uncontrolled airspace
radio-telephony.ans: A continuous broadcast of recorded non-control aeronautical information
radio-telephony.e: ATIS is a continuous recorded broadcast of routine non-control aerodrome information. It reduces frequency congestion, but it does not replace clearances from ATC.

radio-telephony.q: What is the meaning of the phrase Confirm?
radio-telephony.a: Let me know that you have received and understood this message.
radio-telephony.c: Have I correctly received the following...? Or did you correctly receive the message?
radio-telephony.ans: Have I correctly received the following...? Or did you correctly receive the message?
radio-telephony.e: CONFIRM is used to check whether information has been correctly received or understood. The expected reply normally confirms the information or corrects it.

radio-telephony.q: The word AFFIRM means?
radio-telephony.a: I am in agreement with the requesting transmission
radio-telephony.c: I am correcting an error in my own transmission
radio-telephony.ans: I am in agreement with the requesting transmission
radio-telephony.e: AFFIRM means yes or correct. It is used instead of the ordinary word yes because the standard word is clearer and less likely to be confused over a noisy frequency.

radio-telephony.q: What does HOLD YOUR POSITION mean?
radio-telephony.c: Stop before reaching a certain point
radio-telephony.e: HOLD YOUR POSITION means stop and remain exactly where you are. It must not be confused with HOLD SHORT, which requires stopping before a specified runway or point.

radio-telephony.q: What does Line up and wait mean?
radio-telephony.a: Start the take-off roll but do not lift off
radio-telephony.b: Take off and wait for further instructions before take off
radio-telephony.c: Taxi onto the runway and wait for further instructions
radio-telephony.ans: Taxi onto the runway and wait for further instructions
radio-telephony.e: LINE UP AND WAIT authorises the aircraft to enter the runway, align with the centreline, and wait. It is not a take-off clearance, so the take-off roll must not begin.

radio-telephony.q: What is the difference between confirm and affirm?
radio-telephony.b: Confirm means no and affirm means yes
radio-telephony.c: Affirm is asking a yes or no question, confirm means yes
radio-telephony.d: Confirm is asking a yes or no question, affirm means yes
radio-telephony.ans: Confirm is asking a yes or no question, affirm means yes
radio-telephony.e: CONFIRM asks for verification and usually requires a yes-or-no or corrective response. AFFIRM is the standard radiotelephony word meaning yes.

radio-telephony.q: What is the meaning of the phrase Go Ahead?
radio-telephony.e: GO AHEAD means proceed with your radio message. It does not authorise an aircraft to taxi, take off, or continue along a route.

radio-telephony.q: The term CORRECTION used in radiotelephony is best described as meaning that?
radio-telephony.a: I am correcting an error in my own transmission
radio-telephony.b: I am correcting an error in my filed ATS flight plan
radio-telephony.c: I am correcting an error in my previous transmission
radio-telephony.d: I am correcting an error in the transmitting party's last transmission
radio-telephony.ans: I am correcting an error in my own transmission
radio-telephony.e: CORRECTION tells listeners that the speaker is fixing an error in the speaker’s own previous transmission. The corrected information should follow immediately.

radio-telephony.q: What does it mean if ATC asks you to monitor a frequency?
radio-telephony.c: Change the frequency and report your position.
radio-telephony.e: MONITOR means listen on the specified frequency. It normally does not require an initial transmission after changing frequency.

radio-telephony.q: The reporting points or mandatory reporting points in the circuit at a controlled aerodrome are?
radio-telephony.d: Upwind, downwind, base and final approach
radio-telephony.e: At a controlled aerodrome the only compulsory circuit reports are downwind and final, e.g. ATC saying "cleared for take-off, report downwind". Other reports (base, upwind) are only required if ATC specifically asks for them.

radio-telephony.q: What is the standard phraseology to indicate that your message should be ignored?
radio-telephony.e: DISREGARD tells the receiving station to ignore the previous transmission or specified part of it. The word prevents incorrect or no-longer-valid information from being acted on.

radio-telephony.q: Why should a student pilot prefix their radio calls with the words student?
radio-telephony.a: To alert ATC and other aircraft that the aircraft making the call is on an instruction flight.
radio-telephony.b: To alert ATC and other aircraft that the aircraft making the call could perform manoeuvres not normally required for normal flying for training purposes.
radio-telephony.c: To alert ATC and other aircraft that the person making the call is a student pilot flying solo.
radio-telephony.ans: To alert ATC and other aircraft that the person making the call is a student pilot flying solo.
radio-telephony.e: The prefix STUDENT alerts ATC that the aircraft is being flown solo by a student pilot. Controllers can then allow for limited experience when workload and traffic permit.

radio-telephony.q: What should the pilot-in-command do if air traffic control gives an instruction or clearance that he or she feels is inappropriate?
radio-telephony.a: Follow the instruction or clearance, but file a report after landing.
radio-telephony.c: Accept that air traffic control are in charge, and follow the instruction or clearance.
radio-telephony.d: Request an amended instruction or clearance
radio-telephony.ans: Request an amended instruction or clearance
radio-telephony.e: The pilot-in-command remains responsible for safety and should request an amended clearance when unable or unwilling to comply safely. The pilot should not silently deviate from an ATC instruction unless immediate safety requires it.

radio-telephony.q: If you do not hear a radio call properly, what should you say?
radio-telephony.e: SAY AGAIN is the standard request for a transmission, or part of it, to be repeated. Avoid the word repeat because it can have a specialised meaning in other radio services.

radio-telephony.q: What does it mean to orbit?
radio-telephony.e: ORBIT means make a complete 360-degree turn, normally in the direction stated by ATC. The pilot must maintain safe separation and remain within any assigned area.

radio-telephony.q: At what height should you overfly an uncontrolled aerodrome when executing a standard overhead join?
radio-telephony.e: A standard overhead join at an uncontrolled aerodrome is normally flown at 2 000 ft AGL in the procedure tested here. This allows the pilot to inspect the signal area, runway, wind, and circuit traffic before descending to circuit height on the dead side.

radio-telephony.q: What is the frequency range for a VHF radio?
radio-telephony.e: VHF means the radio-frequency band from 30 MHz to 300 MHz. Aeronautical voice communication uses only part of this wider VHF band, beginning at approximately 118 MHz.

radio-telephony.q: What transponder code is used for interference?
radio-telephony.e: Code 7500 indicates unlawful interference, such as a hijacking. It is one of three internationally reserved transponder codes that can be remembered with the mnemonic ICE, from lowest to highest: 7500 = Interference, 7600 = Communications failure, 7700 = Emergency.

radio-telephony.q: If you have a radio failure in the general flying area, which of the following options would you do?
radio-telephony.a: Broadcast blind, squawk 7600, return to the field from where you took off, enter the circuit and land
radio-telephony.b: Broadcast blind, squawk 7600, route to the nearest airfield, enter the circuit and land
radio-telephony.c: Leave controlled airspace, broadcast blind, squawk 7600, and land at a suitable airfield
radio-telephony.ans: Broadcast blind, squawk 7600, return to the field from where you took off, enter the circuit and land
radio-telephony.e: Squawking 7600 alerts ATC to a communications failure even though you cannot hear or respond to them, while broadcasting blind gives any listening traffic your position and intentions. Returning to the field you departed from is the simplest option because it is a known, familiar traffic pattern that needs no further instructions from ATC.

radio-telephony.q: When you are setting a new squawk code, you should first?
radio-telephony.e: When changing squawk codes, first select STANDBY, then dial in the new code, then switch back to ALT. This prevents spurious/incorrect codes from being transmitted momentarily while cycling through the numbers.

radio-telephony.q: What is direction of a standard circuit?
radio-telephony.e: The standard circuit is always flown to the left unless ATC specifically instructs otherwise - for example "report right downwind" calls for a non-standard right-hand pattern instead. Knowing this default means a plain "report downwind" clearance always implies a left-hand circuit.

radio-telephony.q: What is the range of a VHF radio signal?
radio-telephony.e: VHF signals travel mainly by line of sight, so terrain and the curvature of the Earth limit range. Increasing aircraft or antenna height generally increases the distance over which contact is possible.

radio-telephony.q: What does TIBA stand for?
radio-telephony.b: Traffic information broadcast by the tower.
radio-telephony.e: TIBA means Traffic Information Broadcast by Aircraft. Pilots use it to exchange position and intention information in designated airspace where normal ATC separation is not being provided.

radio-telephony.q: What is the civil aeronautical VHF voice communication frequency band?
radio-telephony.e:
Civil aeronautical VHF voice communication uses frequencies from 118.000 to 136.975 MHz. The wider technical VHF spectrum is 30 to 300 MHz, but that is not the dedicated civil aviation voice band.

Exam tip: aviation voice starts at 118 MHz.

radio-telephony.q: Choose the correct order?
radio-telephony.e: ANC - Aviate, Navigate, Communicate - is a golden rule for handling any in-flight difficulty: fly the aircraft first, work out where you are going second, and only then talk to ATC. Getting this order backwards, such as fumbling with the radio while the aircraft is mishandled, is a classic way an otherwise-survivable problem turns into an accident.

radio-telephony.q: Radar identified means?
radio-telephony.a: You are no longer provided with radar control service
radio-telephony.b: Dial given code into transponder and switch it on.
radio-telephony.c: You are identified on their screen
radio-telephony.ans: You are identified on their screen
radio-telephony.e: Radar identified means ATC has positively confirmed your aircraft's position on their radar display. Once identified, the aircraft can be given a radar service (monitoring, traffic information, or vectors).

radio-telephony.q: Do you have to read back wind speed and direction when replying to an ATC clearance?
radio-telephony.e: Wind speed and direction are informational and do not need to be read back. Only instructions, clearances, and the QNH must be read back exactly as received.

radio-telephony.q: What SSR transponder code should be set if an emergency arises and you are not in communication with an ATSU?
radio-telephony.e: Squawk 7700 is the general emergency code when no more specific code applies. It alerts radar controllers that the aircraft requires priority attention and assistance.

radio-telephony.q: A VHF radio signal range will?
radio-telephony.e: Because VHF propagates by direct line-of-sight waves, the radio horizon expands the higher you climb - similar to being able to see further from a hilltop. This is why aircraft flying low or behind terrain often lose contact even when not actually far from the ground station.

radio-telephony.q: What does the IDENT function of the transponder do?
radio-telephony.a: Make the aircraft blip on the radar screen brighter for a long time.
radio-telephony.b: Make the aircraft blip on the radar screen brighter for a short time.
radio-telephony.ans: Make the aircraft blip on the radar screen brighter for a short time.
radio-telephony.e: Pressing IDENT makes the aircraft's return brighten on the controller's screen for a short time, letting the controller pick out one specific aircraft among many blips on a busy radar display. It should only be pressed when asked to, since pressing it unprompted just adds unexplained clutter to the screen.

radio-telephony.q: Select the correct statement regarding VHF propagation?
radio-telephony.a: VHF range is better over the ocean than over land
radio-telephony.b: VHF range is limited by line of sight
radio-telephony.c: The range of a VHF transmission increases at night
radio-telephony.d: The frequency used for a VHF transmission during the night should be half of the frequency used during the day
radio-telephony.ans: VHF range is limited by line of sight
radio-telephony.e: VHF propagation is mainly line of sight. Mountains, buildings, and the Earth’s curvature can block the signal, while greater altitude usually increases radio range.

radio-telephony.q: Whilst flying in controlled airspace, all aircraft must?
radio-telephony.a: Turn the radio volume down to decrease background noise when other aircraft communicate with ATC
radio-telephony.b: Not transmit unless permission is obtained
radio-telephony.d: Exchange readability checks with ATC at 30 minute intervals
radio-telephony.e: Aircraft in controlled airspace must keep a continuous listening watch on the designated frequency at all times, alongside not entering without clearance, following ATC instructions, and navigating accurately. Missing a call because you were not listening could mean missing a critical traffic or separation instruction.

radio-telephony.q: In what direction is the wind related to when its direction is given from the tower?
radio-telephony.e: Surface wind given by the tower for take-off and landing is always in degrees magnetic, matching runway numbering. All other wind information (e.g. winds aloft for navigation) is given in degrees true.

radio-telephony.q: Which factor affects the range of VHF?
radio-telephony.e: Altitude is the main practical control a pilot has over VHF range, since the signal travels line-of-sight - climbing pushes the radio horizon further away, while flying low or behind high ground can cut off a normally-working radio, even close to a station.

radio-telephony.q: A common mistake made by pilots when assuming radio failure is that?
radio-telephony.a: They do not check if the speaker or headset volume is turned up
radio-telephony.b: The incorrect beacon is selected for VHF communication
radio-telephony.c: They climb to a higher altitude
radio-telephony.d: They believe their cell phones are blocking the frequency
radio-telephony.ans: They do not check if the speaker or headset volume is turned up
radio-telephony.e: Before assuming a genuine radio failure, check the simple things first: volume, headset connections, and audio panel selection. As a rule of thumb, if the frequency is totally silent in a normally busy environment, the fault is most likely on the receiving side (e.g. volume down); if you can hear others but they cannot hear you, it is more likely a transmitter problem.

radio-telephony.q: In an attempt to correct a suspected radio failure, a pilot should check?
radio-telephony.a: The pitot/static system, POH and that the ignition switch is ON
radio-telephony.b: The volume control, selected frequency and aircraft electrical system
radio-telephony.c: For interference from cellular phones and GPS
radio-telephony.d: The appropriate frequency charts, POH and that the ignition switch is ON
radio-telephony.ans: The volume control, selected frequency and aircraft electrical system
radio-telephony.e: A systematic check follows the receive/transmit split: if you hear nothing at all, suspect the receiver side (volume, headset, frequency selected); if you can hear other stations but get no reply, suspect the transmitter or the aircraft's electrical system. This quick diagnosis tells you which kind of failure you are dealing with before committing to the full radio-failure procedure.

radio-telephony.q: What is the direction of a non-standard circuit?
radio-telephony.b: It depends on the airfield surroundings
radio-telephony.e: A right-hand circuit is 'non-standard' precisely because left-hand is the default; ATC must explicitly instruct it (e.g. "report right downwind") or it must be published for that aerodrome. This mirrors the standard-circuit rule - if nothing is said, always assume left.

radio-telephony.q: What does VHF stand for?
radio-telephony.e: VHF stands for Very High Frequency, covering 30 MHz to 300 MHz. Aviation communication frequencies occupy a smaller section within that overall band.

radio-telephony.q: A pilot on a VFR cross country flight to a controlled aerodrome experiences radio failure outside of controlled airspace. Unless otherwise published in AIP, the pilot should?
radio-telephony.a: Remain clear of controlled airspace and land at a manned aerodrome
radio-telephony.b: Broadcast blind, squawk 7700, and land at a suitable airfield.
radio-telephony.c: Remain clear of controlled airspace and land at an unmanned aerodrome
radio-telephony.ans: Remain clear of controlled airspace and land at an unmanned aerodrome
radio-telephony.e: Without a working radio you cannot request or receive a clearance into controlled airspace, so the pilot must stay outside it and land at an unmanned aerodrome where no clearance is needed - unless the AIP publishes a different procedure for that route. This follows the same logic as squawking 7600: assume nobody can talk to you, and pick the option that needs no further communication.

radio-telephony.q: What is the squawk if the radio fails?
radio-telephony.e: 7600 is the middle code of the ICE mnemonic (7500 Interference, 7600 Communications failure, 7700 Emergency) and tells ATC you have a communications failure even though you cannot hear or respond to them. Once controllers see it, they can fall back on light signals or predictable standard procedures to work with you.

radio-telephony.q: According to the AIP, when shall a pilot report position?
radio-telephony.a: At 5 minute intervals on all flights
radio-telephony.c: When flying in controlled, advisory airspace or on a flight for which alerting action is being provided
radio-telephony.d: At 30 nm intervals along any route
radio-telephony.ans: When flying in controlled, advisory airspace or on a flight for which alerting action is being provided
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: When flying in controlled, advisory airspace or on a flight for which alerting action is being provided. Position reports are required so ATC or FIS can track progress and, if necessary, initiate Search and Rescue. Outside controlled or advisory airspace, and without alerting action requested, routine fixed-interval reporting is not mandated.

radio-telephony.q: With RMK/SARNML filed, when can preliminary search-and-rescue action begin after a missed position report in controlled airspace?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: 5 minutes overdue. Where RMK/SARNML has been filed, Search and Rescue action begins once the aircraft is 5 minutes overdue at a reporting point in controlled airspace, or fails to arrive at the destination. SARNML only provides this reporting-point protection while the aircraft is in controlled airspace.

radio-telephony.q: What does the emergency ground symbol V mean?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Need assistance. This is part of the ground-to-air signal code laid out using signal strips, designed for exactly the situation where a search aircraft overflies a forced-landing site but radio contact isn't possible — V for 'require assistance', alongside X (medical assistance), N (no/negative) and Y (yes/affirm). Exam tip: every flight of more than 20 nm from base must carry a set of these strips.

radio-telephony.q: When may RMK/SARNML be entered in Field 18 of a South African flight plan?
radio-telephony.a: For every flight, regardless of destination
radio-telephony.b: When the destination aerodrome has an ATSU in operation
radio-telephony.c: Only when an ELT is carried
radio-telephony.ans: When the destination aerodrome has an ATSU in operation
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: When the destination aerodrome has an ATSU in operation. RMK/SARNML ("SAR normal") can only be requested when the destination is a manned aerodrome, i.e. one with an Air Traffic Service Unit in operation. It gives automatic SAR protection for a missed reporting point in controlled airspace or non-arrival at the destination.

radio-telephony.q: What is a distress condition?
radio-telephony.a: A condition concerning the safety of an aircraft, vessel, vehicle, or person on board or within sight, but which does not require immediate assistance.
radio-telephony.b: A condition of high stress and possible danger due to being uncertain of your position or lost.
radio-telephony.c: A condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and/or requiring immediate assistance
radio-telephony.ans: A condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and/or requiring immediate assistance
radio-telephony.e: Distress is defined by two features together: serious or imminent danger AND the need for immediate assistance - for example an engine fire or an engine failure in a single-engine aircraft. It is this need for immediate help that puts distress (MAYDAY) above urgency (PAN-PAN) in the priority-of-messages list, giving it absolute priority over all other radio traffic.

radio-telephony.q: In what order should the information in an emergency message be transmitted?
radio-telephony.a: Call-sign Type of aircraft Nature of emergency Intentions Position
radio-telephony.b: Nature of emergency Intentions Type of aircraft Position
radio-telephony.c: Flight level or altitude and heading Nature of emergency any other useful information.
radio-telephony.ans: Call-sign Type of aircraft Nature of emergency Intentions Position
radio-telephony.e: The message builds a complete picture in the order most useful to whoever is helping you: who you are, what you are flying, what is wrong, what you intend to do, and where you are - matching the standard MAYDAY structure (station addressed, aircraft ID, nature of distress, intentions, position/altitude/heading, other useful information). Giving as much of this as possible in the first transmission avoids wasting time if contact is lost partway through.

radio-telephony.q: When can SAR/NIL be indicated in Item 18 (other information) of an ATS flight plan?
radio-telephony.b: Only when the destination is an uncontrolled aerodrome
radio-telephony.c: Only when the destination is a controlled aerodrome
radio-telephony.ans: Only when the destination is an uncontrolled aerodrome
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Only when the destination is an uncontrolled aerodrome. RMK/SARNIL may only be entered when the destination has no ATSU in operation (an unmanned aerodrome). The aircraft is still subject to automatic SAR if it becomes 5 minutes overdue at a reporting point while still in controlled airspace.

radio-telephony.q: If an aircraft is already in the circuit and suffers from a radio failure, may it land?
radio-telephony.e: An aircraft already established in the circuit can continue and land, following the same core radio-failure principle used everywhere else: prefix all calls with "transmitting blind", keep a careful lookout for other traffic since they may not know your radio has failed, and follow normal circuit and joining procedures.

radio-telephony.q: What is the distress signal?
radio-telephony.e: MAYDAY, spoken three times, is the radiotelephony distress signal - repeated three times so it is unmistakable even on a poor-quality or interrupted transmission. Exam tip: the word has nothing to do with the 1st of May; it comes from the French "m'aidez", meaning "help me".

radio-telephony.q: What actions should you take if you experience an emergency after having already established radio contact with an air traffic service unit?
radio-telephony.a: Make a distress call on the frequency and set the transponder code of 7500
radio-telephony.b: Make a distress call on 121.5 MHz and maintain your assigned transponder code.
radio-telephony.c: Make an urgency call on the frequency and maintain your assigned transponder code.
radio-telephony.d: Make a distress call on the frequency and maintain your assigned transponder code.
radio-telephony.ans: Make a distress call on the frequency and maintain your assigned transponder code.
radio-telephony.e: If already in contact with an ATSU, make the distress call on the frequency in use and maintain the assigned transponder code unless instructed otherwise.

radio-telephony.q: Can you get search and rescue without a flight plan?
radio-telephony.a: Only if you ask ATC beforehand
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Yes. Search and Rescue/alerting protection is not only available through a filed flight plan: it is automatic for a flight that fails to report within 5 minutes of being expected to after departing a manned aerodrome, for any flight 5 minutes overdue at a reporting point in controlled airspace, and for a flight to a manned aerodrome that fails to arrive.

radio-telephony.q: What does the ground-to-air emergency symbol X mean?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Require medical assistance. X is part of the same ground-to-air signalling code as V (general assistance), N (no/negative) and Y (yes/affirm) — laid out with signal strips when a search aircraft is overhead but radio contact has failed, so survivors on the ground can still communicate their most urgent need. Every flight beyond 20 nm from base is required to carry the strips needed to form these signals.

radio-telephony.q: Alerting service is provided by ATSU to all aircraft requiring?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Search and rescue. Alerting Service is one of the three broad categories of Air Traffic Service (alongside Control Service and Information Service) and is provided to any aircraft that needs SAR assistance, in any airspace — which is why SAR protection can apply even to a flight with no flight plan filed at all, provided one of the automatic triggers (e.g. failing to report after departure) is met.

radio-telephony.q: Select the 3 official Search and Rescue phases?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Uncertainty, Alert and Distress phase. These are declared in that order — INCERFA, ALERFA, DETRESFA — as concern about a missing aircraft escalates from 'we're not sure everything's fine' through 'we believe something is wrong' to 'we're reasonably certain the aircraft and occupants are in grave danger', which lets the response (from a phone call to a full search) scale appropriately at each stage.

radio-telephony.q: When may RMK/SARNIL be entered in Field 18 of a South African flight plan?
radio-telephony.a: Only when the destination aerodrome has an ATSU in operation
radio-telephony.b: When the destination aerodrome has no ATSU in operation and SAR is not required
radio-telephony.c: Whenever the aircraft carries an ELT
radio-telephony.ans: When the destination aerodrome has no ATSU in operation and SAR is not required
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: When the destination aerodrome has no ATSU in operation and SAR is not required. RMK/SARNIL can only be used when the destination is unmanned. The aircraft still gets automatic SAR protection for a missed reporting point while it remains in controlled airspace, but that protection ends once the aircraft reports leaving controlled airspace, unless an emergency exists.

radio-telephony.q: If you lose radio communications, how many times must you transmit blind transmissions?
radio-telephony.e: Because a pilot with a silent radio cannot tell whether it is a receiver failure or a total failure, the standard procedure is to assume the transmitter still works and transmit blind anyway - sending each message twice to give any listening station the best chance of catching it despite the uncertain link.

radio-telephony.q: If you required assistance, what letter would you lay your signal strips to look like?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: V. Signal strips laid out as a V are the internationally recognised ground-to-air symbol for 'require assistance', used after a forced landing when the aircraft can be seen by a search aircraft but radio contact isn't possible. Exam tip: pair this with X (medical assistance), N (no) and Y (yes) from the same signalling code.

radio-telephony.q: While on a cross country flight, you notice that the oil pressure is dropping and the oil temperature is rising and elect to do a precautionary landing. What would you precede your radio call with?
radio-telephony.e: A developing problem like dropping oil pressure and rising oil temperature threatens the safety of the flight but does not yet require immediate assistance - this is the definition of an urgency condition - so it is prefixed with PAN-PAN-PAN rather than MAYDAY. If the engine actually failed or caught fire, that would escalate to a genuine distress call instead.

radio-telephony.q: Which frequencies are associated with a modern 406 MHz emergency locator transmitter (ELT)?
radio-telephony.a: 406 MHz for alerting, normally with 121.5 MHz for homing
radio-telephony.ans: 406 MHz for alerting, normally with 121.5 MHz for homing
radio-telephony.e:
A modern ELT transmits a digital distress alert on 406 MHz. It normally also includes a low-power 121.5 MHz signal that search crews can use for close-range homing.

Exam tip: 406 MHz alerts; 121.5 MHz helps rescuers home in.

radio-telephony.q: How should an urgency message be initiated?
radio-telephony.e: An urgency transmission begins with PAN PAN spoken three times. Urgency concerns the safety of an aircraft or person but does not yet require the immediate assistance associated with MAYDAY.

radio-telephony.q: Select the appropriate content of an urgency message from the list below: 1. The word MAYDAY spoken 3 times 2. The word PAN spoken 3 times 3. The station addressed 4. The identification of the aircraft 5. The nature of the urgency condition 6. The intention of the pilot 7. Present position, altitude and heading 8. Any other useful information
radio-telephony.e: An urgency message follows the same structure as a distress message, just with PAN-PAN-PAN instead of MAYDAY: station addressed, aircraft ID, nature of the urgency, intentions, position/altitude/heading, then other useful information. Giving this in order means ATC has everything needed to help even if the transmission gets cut short.

radio-telephony.q: What is an urgency condition?
radio-telephony.a: A condition concerning the safety of an aircraft, vessel, vehicle, or person on board or within sight, but which does not require immediate assistance.
radio-telephony.b: A condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and/or requiring immediate assistance.
radio-telephony.c: A condition of high stress and possible danger due to being uncertain of your position or lost.
radio-telephony.ans: A condition concerning the safety of an aircraft, vessel, vehicle, or person on board or within sight, but which does not require immediate assistance.
radio-telephony.e: Urgency covers situations that concern safety but do not yet need immediate assistance - typical examples are a low oil pressure indication or a passenger medical emergency. This is the key difference from distress: urgency traffic has priority over all routine calls, but must still give way to any distress (MAYDAY) traffic.

radio-telephony.q: A white dumbbell displayed in a signal area at an airfield means?
radio-telephony.a: Aircraft may only use the taxiways
radio-telephony.b: Aircraft may only use the runways and taxiways
radio-telephony.c: Aircraft may only use the runways
radio-telephony.ans: Aircraft may only use the runways and taxiways
radio-telephony.e: A white dumbbell in the signal area means aircraft must stay on runways and taxiways - i.e. no using the grass or unprepared surfaces. Exam tip: a dumbbell WITH black stripes reverses this - take-off and land on runways only, but taxi anywhere, including the grass.

radio-telephony.q: What does a horizontal white or orange T indicate?
radio-telephony.b: The direction of the wind, which is along the bar towards the crossbar
radio-telephony.c: The take-off and landing direction, which is along the bar towards the crossbar
radio-telephony.ans: The take-off and landing direction, which is along the bar towards the crossbar
radio-telephony.e: A horizontal white or orange T indicates the runway direction to use for take-off and landing: land or depart along the shaft, heading towards the crossbar. It is a fallback direction indicator for aerodromes without other means of showing which way traffic is landing, alongside things like the windsock and L-shaped circuit-direction markers.

radio-telephony.q: A white cross at the threshold of a runway means?
radio-telephony.c: Aircraft may only use the runways
radio-telephony.e: White or yellow crosses are placed at both ends of a runway or taxiway section that is unsafe to use - for example a waterlogged runway or ground undermined by moles - and aircraft may not land, take off, or taxi in the marked area between them. At night the same unserviceable area is marked with red lights instead.

radio-telephony.q: No aircraft shall fly under FL100 at a speed?
radio-telephony.e: The 250kt speed limit below FL100 exists to give pilots enough time to see and avoid other traffic in the busiest, most crowded layer of airspace, where aircraft of very different speeds and experience levels mix. A higher airspeed leaves far less reaction time for a visual collision-avoidance scan at low level.

radio-telephony.q: What does a series of red flashes to an aircraft in the air mean?
radio-telephony.a: Continue circling, landing clearance will be given shortly
radio-telephony.c: Do not land for the time being
radio-telephony.e: A series of red flashes from the ground to an aircraft in flight means the aerodrome is unsafe - do not land; the same signal to an aircraft on the ground means taxi clear of the landing area in use. These light signals are the fallback system for radio failure, still part of the regulations even though almost no South African airport still carries flare guns to fire them.

radio-telephony.q: An intercepting aircraft positions ahead, rocks its wings, and begins a slow level turn. What is the instruction?
radio-telephony.a: Land immediately at the present position
radio-telephony.e:
Rocking the wings from a position ahead is the standard interception signal meaning that the intercepted aircraft must follow. The intercepting aircraft then turns slowly onto the required heading.

The intercepted pilot should acknowledge and follow unless unable to comply.

radio-telephony.q: Select the correct order of priority (most to least) for the categories of messages below? 1. Flight regularity messages 2. Meteorological messages 3. Flight safety messages 4. Direction finding communication 5. Urgency messages 6. Distress messages
radio-telephony.e: The six-category priority list exists so that when ATC is busy, the most safety-critical traffic is never held up behind routine calls: distress (MAYDAY) first, then urgency (PAN-PAN), then direction finding, then normal flight-safety messages, then meteorological, then flight-regularity/admin traffic last. Exam tip: remember it as "life-threatening first, paperwork last".

radio-telephony.q: Which of the following answers are correct with regards to the order of priority for aeronautical messages?
radio-telephony.a: Flight safety messages take precedence over urgency messages.
radio-telephony.b: Flight regulatory messages take precedence over urgency messages.
radio-telephony.c: Messages relating to direction finding take precedence over meteorological messages.
radio-telephony.ans: Messages relating to direction finding take precedence over meteorological messages.
radio-telephony.e: Direction-finding communications - helping a lost or disoriented pilot fix their position - rank above ordinary flight-safety, meteorological, and flight-regularity messages in the priority list, second only to distress and urgency. This reflects that DF assistance is usually requested by a pilot already in some difficulty, even if it has not been declared as an urgency or distress.

radio-telephony.q: What does a series of white flashes to an aircraft in the air mean?
radio-telephony.c: Return to the starting point of the aerodrome.
radio-telephony.e:
A flashing white signal to an aircraft in flight instructs it to land at the aerodrome and proceed to the apron. The actual landing and taxi clearances are given separately as the aircraft approaches and lands.

Exam tip: flashing white in flight = land here and proceed to the apron.

radio-telephony.q: If a marshaller has his arms above his head in a vertical position, it means?
radio-telephony.e: Both arms held vertically above the head indicate the parking bay or position. The pilot continues to follow the marshaller until a separate stop signal is shown.

radio-telephony.q: What is the order of priority for radio telephone messages?
radio-telephony.a: Distress, Urgency, Direction finding and Flight safety
radio-telephony.b: Distress, Flight safety, Urgency and Direction finding
radio-telephony.c: Urgency, Distress, Flight safety and Direction finding
radio-telephony.d: Flight safety, Distress, Urgency and Direction finding
radio-telephony.ans: Distress, Urgency, Direction finding and Flight safety
radio-telephony.e: Distress, urgency, direction finding, and flight safety are, in that order, the four highest-priority categories of radiotelephony message, each one bumping ahead of the ones below it whenever the frequency is busy. Exam tip: distress and urgency are declared emergencies; direction finding and flight safety are still 'normal' ATC business, just ranked by how safety-critical they are.

radio-telephony.q: If a marshaller has his arms extended, bent at the elbows and is moving them up and down from chest height to head height, it means?
radio-telephony.e: Moving both bent arms repeatedly upward and downward from chest to head height signals the aircraft to move straight ahead. The pilot should continue slowly while watching for the next instruction.

radio-telephony.q: How should an intercepted aircraft acknowledge an intercepting aircraft that rocks its wings and turns away?
radio-telephony.a: Switch off all lights and continue straight ahead
radio-telephony.b: Rock its wings and follow the intercepting aircraft
radio-telephony.c: Follow me to a landing terrain.
radio-telephony.ans: Rock its wings and follow the intercepting aircraft
radio-telephony.e: This describes the First Series interception signal: the interceptor rocks its wings then makes a slow level turn onto a new heading, meaning "follow me". The intercepted aircraft acknowledges by rocking its own wings (steady landing lights at night) and following the interceptor. Exam tip: at night, replace the wing rock with steady landing lights.

radio-telephony.q: The definitions of “classes of airspace” within the republic can be found in?
radio-telephony.e: South African airspace classifications and their application are published in the AIP and supported by the Civil Aviation Regulations. These are the authoritative sources rather than informal notes or charts alone.
