radio-telephony.q: Info the ATC if there are changes in the flight plan during the flight?
radio-telephony.c: TAS changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach
radio-telephony.ans: TAS changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
An aircraft in flight with a filed Flight Plan.

RULE
ATC must be notified by radio if the True Airspeed (TAS) changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach from the TAS nominated in the flight plan, or if the estimated time at the next reporting point or destination changes by more than 2 minutes.

ANSWER
TAS changes by more than 10 kt or 0.02 Mach

radio-telephony.q: Flight plan may be filled in by?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Telephone, fax or internet (File 2 fly .co.za). A flight plan can be filed in person or by telephone with the nearest ATSU, by telephone with the AIM Service Centre, or online via the file2fly system, which is the preferred method since it is faster and less error-prone than a verbal filing. It cannot be filed through the post office or informally via family members. Exam tip: always obtain a reference number after filing — it's what you use to trace a flight plan that has gone missing in the system.

radio-telephony.q: What would a general flying area be declared as?
radio-telephony.e: A General Flying Area (GFA) is published as a Danger Area on the VFR chart, so it carries a FAD designator (for example Johannesburg GFA is FAD182). Pilots operating inside a GFA must listen out and broadcast their position, altitude and intentions on the published frequency for that area.

radio-telephony.q: How do you get UTC time from South African local time?
radio-telephony.a: Subtract 2 hours from local time to obtain UTC
radio-telephony.b: Subtract 2 hours from UTC to obtain LMT.
radio-telephony.ans: Subtract 2 hours from local time to obtain UTC
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Subtract 2 hours from local time to obtain UTC. South African Standard Time (SAST) is UTC+2, so UTC is always two hours behind local time. Exam tip: e.g. 14:00 SAST is 12:00 UTC.

radio-telephony.q: In which of the following airspace will the ATC only provide information service?
radio-telephony.e: Classes F and G are uncontrolled airspace. Here the Flight Information Service (FIS) -- not ATC -- gives pilots traffic and other information, but does not issue clearances or provide separation; pilots remain responsible for their own separation.

radio-telephony.q: A marshaller holds both arms vertically above the head. What does this signal mean?
radio-telephony.e:
Both arms held vertically above the head identify the parking position or bay. The pilot should continue under the marshaller’s guidance and stop in the indicated bay.

Exam tip: arms overhead = this parking bay.

radio-telephony.q: Which ICAO airspace class is listed as not in use in South Africa?
radio-telephony.e:
The current South African AIP lists Class E as not in use. It describes uses for Classes A, B, C, D, F and G.

Exam tip: in the current RSA classification table, Class E is the class marked not in use.

radio-telephony.q: Which mandatory item must be included in an ATS flight plan which is filed prior to departure?
radio-telephony.b: The type of VHF radio in the equipment listing
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: The route to be followed. The planned route is mandatory content in a flight plan, since ATS needs to know the intended flight path to provide traffic and alerting services. The type of VHF radio, the aircraft's indicated airspeed and the co-pilot's name are not required items on the form.

radio-telephony.q: A requirement to fly through Class F airspace (e.g. an advisory route) is?
radio-telephony.a: the airspace may only be used by night and the aircraft must be equipped accordingly
radio-telephony.b: the aircraft must be equipped with a radio capable of maintaining two way communication
radio-telephony.c: the aircraft must have a SELCAL unit installed
radio-telephony.d: the aircraft may only navigate with the use of an approved GPS
radio-telephony.ans: the aircraft must be equipped with a radio capable of maintaining two way communication
radio-telephony.e: There's no permanent Class F airspace in South Africa, but whenever it's declared, both IFR and VFR aircraft must maintain two-way radio contact with the responsible ATSU -- and if out of range, broadcast their position instead, since Class F relies on pilots reporting themselves for the advisory/information service to work.

radio-telephony.q: The flight plan closed in uncontrolled airdrome when?
radio-telephony.c: When you notify the ATC after landing
radio-telephony.ans: When you notify the ATC after landing
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: When you notify the ATC after landing. At an uncontrolled aerodrome, ATC has no automatic way of knowing the aircraft has landed, so the pilot must notify ATS after landing to close the flight plan. It is not closed automatically at touchdown, and there is no fixed 5-minute grace period.

radio-telephony.q: A prohibited area is airspace of defined dimensions within which:
radio-telephony.a: Flight is permitted after receiving an ATC clearance
radio-telephony.e:
A prohibited area is established where civil aircraft flight is not permitted. A restricted area may be entered only under specified conditions, while a danger area warns that hazardous activity may occur.

Exam tip: prohibited means no civil flight; restricted means conditions apply.

radio-telephony.q: How is an ATS flight plan normally closed after landing at a controlled aerodrome?
radio-telephony.a: It is normally closed automatically through ATS after landing
radio-telephony.b: The pilot must wait 20 minutes before closing it
radio-telephony.c: It closes two hours after the estimated arrival time
radio-telephony.d: It can be closed only by the aircraft owner
radio-telephony.ans: It is normally closed automatically through ATS after landing
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: It is normally closed automatically through ATS after landing. At a controlled aerodrome, ATS is aware of the aircraft's arrival and the flight plan is normally closed through the system without any pilot action. At an uncontrolled aerodrome, by contrast, the pilot must notify ATS after landing to close it.

radio-telephony.q: Which of the following would be classified as Class F airspace?
radio-telephony.b: All controlled airspace FL200 and above
radio-telephony.e: Class F is "Advisory Airspace" -- IFR traffic gets an advisory service and VFR gets traffic information, both needing two-way radio. There's no permanent Class F airspace in South Africa today (the old Advisory Routes, abbreviated ADR, are no longer in use) -- Class F only appears when temporarily declared, e.g. for an air show, and published by NOTAM or AIP Supplement.

radio-telephony.q: IF a marshalled has his arms extended, bent at the elbows and is moving them up and down from chest height to head height it means?
radio-telephony.e: This marshalling motion instructs the pilot to move straight ahead. The pilot should use minimum safe speed and remain focused on the marshaller until another signal is given.

radio-telephony.q: When are the altimeter setting procedures found in AIC 20-2 applicable?
radio-telephony.a: Only IFR flights operating above FL100
radio-telephony.d: All flights 1500 ft AGL and above
radio-telephony.ans: All flights 1500 ft AGL and above
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: All flights 1500 ft AGL and above. Per AIC 20.2, a pilot stays on QNH below 1500 ft AGL on a low-level flight; once cruising above 1500 ft AGL on a cross-country flight, the altimeter setting procedures (transition altitude/level and the semi-circular rule) apply, so the pilot must change to the Standard Setting on climbing through the Transition Altitude.

radio-telephony.q: An aircraft has DME, VOR and VHF RT/F. What must be filled into flight plan item 10?
radio-telephony.e:
GIVEN
Aircraft equipped with DME, VOR and VHF voice radio, no transponder.

RULE
Item 10a uses individual letters for each capability: D = DME, O = VOR, V = VHF voice. Item 10b (surveillance) uses N when no transponder is carried at all.

ANSWER
DOV/N

radio-telephony.q: When must the IDENT button be used?
radio-telephony.b: When instructed to do so by ATC
radio-telephony.d: Only after landing at a controlled aerodrome
radio-telephony.ans: When instructed to do so by ATC
radio-telephony.e: The IDENT function should be used only when requested by ATC so the controller can identify the aircraft return on radar.

radio-telephony.q: What is the meaning of the phrase “acknowledge”?
radio-telephony.a: Repeat the last transmission exactly as received
radio-telephony.b: I agree with your last transmission
radio-telephony.c: Let me know that you have received and understood this message
radio-telephony.ans: Let me know that you have received and understood this message
radio-telephony.e: ACKNOWLEDGE asks the receiving station to confirm the message was received and understood, and the standard reply should read the message back more or less word for word - not just a casual "roger" or "okay". This makes sure both parties are certain the exact information, not just the general idea, got through.

radio-telephony.q: If SAR was requested on an ATC flight plan to an uncontrolled aerodrome, when will the search and rescue be cancelled?
radio-telephony.c: Only after the aircraft is refuelled
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: When the pilot notifies ATC. At an uncontrolled aerodrome, Search and Rescue linked to a flight plan is cancelled only once the pilot closes the flight plan — normally by notifying ATC/ATSU by radio or telephone after landing. It is not cancelled automatically at touchdown, and it is not tied to refuelling.

radio-telephony.q: The VHF navigation band is?
radio-telephony.e: The VHF navigation band spans roughly 108 to 118 MHz, combining the ILS localiser sub-band (108.1-111.9 MHz) and the VOR sub-band (112.0-117.95 MHz). This is separate from the 118.0-136.975 MHz VHF voice communication band.

radio-telephony.q: FIR is?
radio-telephony.e: South Africa's three FIRs -- Cape Town (FACA), Johannesburg (FAJA) and Johannesburg Oceanic (FAJO) -- extend from the surface all the way up to FL650, with individual sectors capped at FL460. Dividing the country this way lets each Flight Information Centre (Cape Town or Johannesburg) manage information and alerting services for a defined, manageable area.

radio-telephony.q: What is the call sign for the “aerodrome flight information service” unit/service?
radio-telephony.e: RADIO is the callsign used by an Aerodrome Flight Information Service (AFIS) unit, which operates at uncontrolled aerodromes in Class G ATZs, e.g. "Port Alfred Radio".

radio-telephony.q: What is the call sign for the “aerodrome control” unit/service?
radio-telephony.e: The radiotelephony call sign for aerodrome control is TOWER. It is used when contacting the unit responsible for runway and circuit traffic.

radio-telephony.q: What does QNH refer to?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Height above mean sea level. QNH is the actual pressure at a place corrected to sea level, so setting it in the altimeter subscale makes the instrument read altitude, i.e. height above mean sea level (and airfield elevation when on the ground). This differs from QFE, which references ground level at that specific place.

radio-telephony.q: For which airports may SAR/Normal be filed?
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Controlled airports. RMK/SARNML ("SAR normal") may only be requested when the destination aerodrome is a manned aerodrome — one with an Air Traffic Service Unit in operation — which in practice means a controlled airport. Search and Rescue then starts if the aircraft is 5 minutes overdue at a reporting point in controlled airspace, or fails to arrive.

radio-telephony.q: If a marshaller has his arms extended sideways and is slowly moving them up to his head until they cross, it means?
radio-telephony.e: Arms fully extended sideways and slowly moved above the head until they cross means STOP. (A different gesture — one arm drawn across the throat — means cut engine(s).)

radio-telephony.q: What does QNE refer to?
radio-telephony.c: The local QNH setting for the aerodrome
radio-telephony.d: Height above the 1013.2 hPa pressure level
radio-telephony.ans: Height above the 1013.2 hPa pressure level
radio-telephony.e: Correct answer: Height above the 1013.2 hPa pressure level. QNE uses a fixed, arbitrary datum rather than any local sea-level pressure, which is exactly why it is used at altitude — an aircraft over Cape Town and one over Johannesburg are both referenced to the same pressure level, so ATC can maintain vertical separation without needing everyone's local QNH. This vertical distance is what's reported as pressure altitude, normally expressed as a Flight Level.

radio-telephony.q: What does it mean if a runway is reported as wet?
radio-telephony.a: Less than 25% of the surface is covered by water, slush or loose snow — enough moisture to make the surface appear reflective, but without significant areas of standing water
radio-telephony.b: More than 25% of the surface is covered by standing water deeper than 3mm
radio-telephony.c: The surface shows a change of colour due to moisture, with no visible wetness
radio-telephony.d: The runway has extensive patches of standing water that are visible
radio-telephony.ans: Less than 25% of the surface is covered by water, slush or loose snow — enough moisture to make the surface appear reflective, but without significant areas of standing water
radio-telephony.e: Wet sits between damp and water patches on the escalation scale (dry → damp → wet → water patches → flooded): the surface is visibly wet and reflective, but standing water still covers less than 25% of it. Cross the 25% threshold and it's reclassified as contaminated instead, which is a separate, stricter category used for landing-performance calculations rather than just describing the surface.

radio-telephony.q: What does it mean if a runway is reported as contaminated?
radio-telephony.a: More than 25% of the runway surface is covered by standing water deeper than 3mm, slush, snow or ice
radio-telephony.b: The surface shows a change of colour due to moisture
radio-telephony.c: The runway has significant patches of visible water, but less than 25% of the surface
radio-telephony.d: The runway is unfit for movement of aircraft and marked with crosses
radio-telephony.ans: More than 25% of the runway surface is covered by standing water deeper than 3mm, slush, snow or ice
radio-telephony.e: Contaminated is not just a more severe step on the dry-damp-wet-flooded wording scale — it's a distinct, threshold-based classification (more than 25% of the surface covered by water deeper than 3mm, slush, snow or ice) that pilots and operators use to look up landing and take-off performance figures, since a contaminated surface changes braking action and aquaplaning risk enough to require its own performance data rather than just extra caution.

radio-telephony.q: What does it mean if a runway is reported as dry?
radio-telephony.a: The runway is neither wet nor contaminated, and maintains effective dry braking action
radio-telephony.b: The surface shows a slight change of colour due to residual moisture
radio-telephony.c: Less than 25% of the surface is covered by water or slush
radio-telephony.d: The runway has been treated to remove all surface friction risk
radio-telephony.ans: The runway is neither wet nor contaminated, and maintains effective dry braking action
radio-telephony.e: Dry is the baseline at the start of the escalation scale (dry → damp → wet → water patches → flooded) — it simply means neither of the other two formal categories (wet or contaminated) applies, so full, unreduced braking action can be expected. Landing and take-off performance figures published for "dry" assume no correction for surface moisture at all.

radio-telephony.q: How does VHF Direction Finding (VDF) give a pilot their bearing from a ground station?
radio-telephony.a: The pilot presses the push-to-talk button, and the ground station reads the aircraft's magnetic bearing off its own equipment
radio-telephony.b: The aircraft's VOR receiver automatically displays the bearing without any transmission
radio-telephony.c: The pilot reads the bearing directly off a cockpit-mounted direction-finding needle
radio-telephony.d: ATC calculates the bearing from the aircraft's transponder squawk code
radio-telephony.ans: The pilot presses the push-to-talk button, and the ground station reads the aircraft's magnetic bearing off its own equipment
radio-telephony.e: VDF works on the ordinary VHF communications radio: transmitting (keying the PTT) is what triggers a bearing readout at the ground station's DF equipment, not the aircraft's own instruments. Since it uses VHF, it's limited to line of sight, just like normal VHF voice range.

radio-telephony.q: A pilot uncertain of their position asks a VDF station for a magnetic heading to steer directly to that station. What phrase should they use, and what does the resulting heading represent?
radio-telephony.a: "Please provide me with a VDF heading" - the heading given is a QDM
radio-telephony.b: "Request VDF steer" - the heading given is a QDR
radio-telephony.c: "Confirm my position" - the heading given is a QTE
radio-telephony.d: "Say my bearing" - the heading given is a QNH
radio-telephony.ans: "Please provide me with a VDF heading" - the heading given is a QDM
radio-telephony.e: QDM is the magnetic heading TO the station - exactly what a lost pilot needs to fly straight to it. Since wind drift isn't accounted for automatically, this heading should be requested again periodically rather than flown once and forgotten.

radio-telephony.q: Why is the VDF steer becoming obsolete in South Africa?
radio-telephony.a: Most of South Africa now has radar coverage, which provides the same positional help more directly
radio-telephony.b: VDF equipment has been withdrawn from service due to age
radio-telephony.c: GNSS accuracy requirements have made VDF illegal to use
radio-telephony.d: VDF only works at night and is therefore rarely useful
radio-telephony.ans: Most of South Africa now has radar coverage, which provides the same positional help more directly
radio-telephony.e: VDF was originally a way for ATC to help a lost or disoriented pilot without radar - once a controller can simply see an aircraft's position on a radar screen, requesting a magnetic heading via VDF becomes unnecessary in most of the country.

cpl-air-law.q: Which of these is not a licence issued under Part 61?
cpl-air-law.e: The National Pilot Licence is dealt with under Part 62, not Part 61.

cpl-air-law.q: Which of the following is not a listed class rating for aeroplanes under Part 61?
cpl-air-law.e: A single-engine autogyro is not an aeroplane class rating because an autogyro belongs to a different aircraft category. Aeroplane class ratings cover groups such as single-engine and multi-engine aeroplanes.

cpl-air-law.q: Part 61 applies to which of the following?
cpl-air-law.c: Issuing, revalidating, reissuing licences and ratings, examiner designation, foreign licence validation or conversion, FSTD approval, and related matters
cpl-air-law.ans: Issuing, revalidating, reissuing licences and ratings, examiner designation, foreign licence validation or conversion, FSTD approval, and related matters
cpl-air-law.e: Part 61 covers the issue and maintenance of pilot licences and ratings, examiner designation, foreign licence validation or conversion, FSTD approval and related matters.

cpl-air-law.q: Who may act as PIC of a South African registered aircraft without holding a valid licence?
cpl-air-law.a: Any foreign pilot with an ICAO licence
cpl-air-law.b: Any pilot under 25 years of age
cpl-air-law.d: A student receiving dual instruction from a rated flight instructor
cpl-air-law.ans: A student receiving dual instruction from a rated flight instructor
cpl-air-law.e: A student receiving dual instruction from a rated flight instructor may act as PIC in this specific training context without holding a full valid pilot licence.

cpl-air-law.q: Which licence may be issued without a class or type rating?
cpl-air-law.e: A Student Pilot Licence may be issued without a class or type rating.

cpl-air-law.q: What must a Part 61 licence holder do to fly a conventionally controlled microlight without an NPL?
cpl-air-law.b: Complete differences or familiarisation training and meet Part 62 requirements, endorsed in the logbook by a suitably rated instructor
cpl-air-law.d: Pass a full PPL(A) skills test again
cpl-air-law.ans: Complete differences or familiarisation training and meet Part 62 requirements, endorsed in the logbook by a suitably rated instructor
cpl-air-law.e: A Part 61 licence holder must complete the required differences or familiarisation training, meet Part 62 requirements and have the endorsement entered by a suitably rated instructor.

cpl-air-law.q: Which of these is considered a rating for special purposes?
cpl-air-law.e: An aerobatics rating is a special-purpose rating because it authorises a specialised form of operation beyond ordinary licence privileges. It requires specific training and demonstrated competence.

cpl-air-law.q: Which category ratings exist for pilots under Part 61?
cpl-air-law.e: The category ratings listed under Part 61 include aeroplane and helicopter.

cpl-air-law.q: Who determines if differences or familiarisation training is required for variants within a class rating?
cpl-air-law.e: The requirement is determined as prescribed in regulation 61.09.7(2).

cpl-air-law.q: A type rating is required for which of the following?
cpl-air-law.b: Aeroplanes certified for operation with a minimum crew of more than one pilot
cpl-air-law.ans: Aeroplanes certified for operation with a minimum crew of more than one pilot
cpl-air-law.e: A type rating is required for aeroplanes certified for operation with a minimum crew of more than one pilot.

cpl-air-law.q: Annually, a pilot must submit what?
cpl-air-law.c: A certified summary of logbook and licence currency fees
cpl-air-law.ans: A certified summary of logbook and licence currency fees
cpl-air-law.e: An annual certified logbook summary and licence currency fees must be submitted.

cpl-air-law.q: Conducting a revalidation check within 90 days of expiry has what effect on the new expiry?
cpl-air-law.d: Sets the new expiry from the last day of the original expiry month
cpl-air-law.ans: Sets the new expiry from the last day of the original expiry month
cpl-air-law.e: If revalidated within 90 days of expiry, the new expiry is calculated from the last day of the original expiry month.

cpl-air-law.q: A holder of a Part 61 licence flying a light sport aeroplane must do what?
cpl-air-law.a: Comply with Part 62 requirements for the type or class and have it endorsed in the logbook
cpl-air-law.ans: Comply with Part 62 requirements for the type or class and have it endorsed in the logbook
cpl-air-law.e: A Part 61 licence holder flying a light sport aeroplane must meet the Part 62 requirements for that aircraft and have the endorsement entered in the logbook.

cpl-air-law.q: After a failed skills test, the earliest a re-test can be conducted is when?
cpl-air-law.e: After a failed skills test, a re-test may not be conducted earlier than 72 hours later.

cpl-air-law.q: A skills test cannot be conducted until what has been completed?
cpl-air-law.a: The flight examiner has approved the flight plan
cpl-air-law.b: The ATO has issued a temporary licence
cpl-air-law.c: The candidate has successfully completed the applicable ground evaluation
cpl-air-law.ans: The candidate has successfully completed the applicable ground evaluation
cpl-air-law.e: The applicable ground evaluation must be completed successfully before the skills test is conducted.

cpl-air-law.q: Which licence types exist for helicopters under Part 61?
cpl-air-law.e: Helicopter licences under Part 61 include PPL(H), CPL(H) and ATPL(H).

cpl-air-law.q: Skills tests and competency checks may be conducted with fare-paying passengers or cargo under what condition?
cpl-air-law.a: Never; fare-paying passengers or cargo are prohibited
cpl-air-law.ans: Never; fare-paying passengers or cargo are prohibited
cpl-air-law.e: Skills tests and competency checks may not be conducted with fare-paying passengers or cargo on board.

cpl-air-law.q: The navigation element of a PPL or CPL skills test may be done how?
cpl-air-law.a: Must be flown on the same day as other elements
cpl-air-law.b: Can be done as a separate flight within 14 days
cpl-air-law.c: Can be deferred up to 30 days
cpl-air-law.d: May be replaced by simulator time
cpl-air-law.ans: Can be done as a separate flight within 14 days
cpl-air-law.e: The navigation element may be completed as a separate flight within 14 days.

cpl-air-law.q: The Director can extend a rating’s expiry for how long upon application citing exceptional circumstances?
cpl-air-law.d: Only after a new test is passed
cpl-air-law.e: The Director may extend a rating expiry by up to 30 days in exceptional circumstances.

cpl-air-law.q: A licence cancelled for failure to meet standards cannot be reissued for how long?
cpl-air-law.c: At the discretion of the ATO
cpl-air-law.e: A licence cancelled for failure to meet standards cannot be reissued for 24 months from the cancellation date.

cpl-air-law.q: A skills test for a night rating after the first PPL revalidation check has what effect?
cpl-air-law.a: Also revalidates the maintenance of competency in the same aircraft category
cpl-air-law.c: Requires an extra examiner signature from the Director
cpl-air-law.d: Counts only for the night rating, not for PPL competency
cpl-air-law.ans: Also revalidates the maintenance of competency in the same aircraft category
cpl-air-law.e: A night rating skills test after the first PPL revalidation check can also revalidate maintenance of competency in the same aircraft category.

cpl-air-law.q: If a ground evaluation and practical test are done separately, what is the maximum gap allowed?
cpl-air-law.e: The maximum gap between separate ground evaluation and practical test is 14 days.

cpl-air-law.q: A licence holder may not exercise the privileges of a licence unless what condition is met?
cpl-air-law.a: They have flown in the last 90 days
cpl-air-law.c: They comply with the validity and revalidation requirements in Part 61
cpl-air-law.d: They have logged at least 100 hours
cpl-air-law.ans: They comply with the validity and revalidation requirements in Part 61
cpl-air-law.e: A licence holder must comply with the applicable validity and revalidation requirements before exercising licence privileges.

cpl-air-law.q: Who issues, reissues, validates, or revalidates South African pilot licences?
cpl-air-law.d: The Director or appropriate authority in terms of Part 61 or Part 62
cpl-air-law.ans: The Director or appropriate authority in terms of Part 61 or Part 62
cpl-air-law.e: South African pilot licences are issued, reissued, validated or revalidated by the Director or appropriate authority in terms of Part 61 or Part 62.

cpl-air-law.q: If a licence holder fails to demonstrate required skills and knowledge, what must they do?
cpl-air-law.a: Complete remedial training and pass a new skills test
cpl-air-law.ans: Complete remedial training and pass a new skills test
cpl-air-law.e: Failure to demonstrate required skills and knowledge requires remedial training and a new skills test.

cpl-air-law.q: Before a skills test for a licence issue, what must the ATO issue?
cpl-air-law.b: A letter of recommendation to the examiner
cpl-air-law.d: An endorsement on the pilot’s licence
cpl-air-law.ans: A letter of recommendation to the examiner
cpl-air-law.e: Before the skills test, the ATO must issue a letter of recommendation to the examiner.

cpl-air-law.q: Conducting a revalidation check more than 90 days before expiry has what effect?
cpl-air-law.a: Sets a new expiry from the date of the check
cpl-air-law.c: Sets a new expiry from the last day of the month of the check
cpl-air-law.ans: Sets a new expiry from the last day of the month of the check
cpl-air-law.e: If revalidation is done more than 90 days before expiry, the new expiry is from the last day of the month of the check.

cpl-air-law.q: If a test cannot be completed in one flight due to unforeseen reasons, what may happen?
cpl-air-law.a: The candidate must restart the process
cpl-air-law.b: It can be postponed up to 30 days without note
cpl-air-law.d: It may be completed within 14 days, with reasons recorded by the examiner
cpl-air-law.ans: It may be completed within 14 days, with reasons recorded by the examiner
cpl-air-law.e: If a test cannot be completed in one flight for unforeseen reasons, it may be completed within 14 days with reasons recorded.

cpl-air-law.q: Before a re-test following failure, what must the candidate do?
cpl-air-law.a: Complete remedial training at an approved ATO and obtain a letter of recommendation
cpl-air-law.ans: Complete remedial training at an approved ATO and obtain a letter of recommendation
cpl-air-law.e: Before a re-test, the candidate must complete remedial training at an approved ATO and obtain a recommendation letter.

cpl-air-law.q: Which is not a special purpose rating listed under Part 61?
cpl-air-law.e: Balloon pilot is not listed as one of the special purpose ratings in this context.

cpl-air-law.q: Submitting an application after 30 days requires what?
cpl-air-law.c: A condonation application to the Director
cpl-air-law.d: No extra process if within 90 days
cpl-air-law.ans: A condonation application to the Director
cpl-air-law.e: Late submission after 30 days requires a condonation application to the Director.

cpl-air-law.q: The type ratings for helicopters under Part 61 are issued how?
cpl-air-law.d: By name for each type of helicopter
cpl-air-law.ans: By name for each type of helicopter
cpl-air-law.e: Under Part 61, helicopter type ratings are issued by name for each type of helicopter.

cpl-air-law.q: For initial licence issue, the application must normally be submitted within what period of the skills test?
cpl-air-law.a: Within 30 days, or 90 days for the ATPL(A) integrated course CPL/IR case
cpl-air-law.ans: Within 30 days, or 90 days for the ATPL(A) integrated course CPL/IR case
cpl-air-law.e: Initial licence issue applications must generally be submitted within 30 days of the skills test, with a 90-day case for ATPL(A) integrated course CPL/IR.

cpl-air-law.q: Who must oversee a skills test for the issuance of a licence or rating?
cpl-air-law.b: The ATO which completed the applicant’s training
cpl-air-law.ans: The ATO which completed the applicant’s training
cpl-air-law.e: The skills test for licence or rating issue must be overseen by the ATO that completed the applicant’s training.

cpl-air-law.q: For international commercial air transport operations, logbook entries must be completed within what period?
cpl-air-law.e: International commercial air transport logbook entries must be completed within 14 days.

cpl-air-law.q: A CPL holder can credit PIC time towards what?
cpl-air-law.d: A rating or ATPL in the same category
cpl-air-law.ans: A rating or ATPL in the same category
cpl-air-law.e: A CPL holder may credit PIC time towards a rating or ATPL in the same category.

cpl-air-law.q: A PPL holder may be credited in full with solo, dual, and PIC time towards what?
cpl-air-law.a: Ratings or CPL in the same aircraft category
cpl-air-law.ans: Ratings or CPL in the same aircraft category
cpl-air-law.e: A PPL holder may receive full credit for solo, dual, and PIC time towards ratings or CPL in the same category.

cpl-air-law.q: From a microlight weight-shift or gyroplane licence to PPL(A) or PPL(H), maximum credit is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: From a microlight weight-shift or gyroplane licence to PPL(A) or PPL(H), maximum credit is 10 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: Safety pilot time must be logged how?
cpl-air-law.a: As PIC if in the left seat
cpl-air-law.c: As co-pilot and marked SAFETY PILOT
cpl-air-law.ans: As co-pilot and marked SAFETY PILOT
cpl-air-law.e: Safety pilot time must be logged as co-pilot time and clearly marked SAFETY PILOT.

cpl-air-law.q: When administering a test from a non-pilot seat, an examiner may log what?
cpl-air-law.e: When administering a test from a non-pilot seat, an examiner may log co-pilot time.

cpl-air-law.q: Co-pilot time on an aircraft certified for single-pilot operation but operated under Parts 121, 127 or 135 requiring two pilots can be credited at what rate?
cpl-air-law.e: Only 50% of this co-pilot time may be credited because the aircraft is normally certificated for single-pilot operation. The reduced credit recognises useful experience while distinguishing it from full required co-pilot time.

cpl-air-law.q: A student pilot may be credited in full for what time towards initial licence issue?
cpl-air-law.b: All solo and dual instruction time
cpl-air-law.ans: All solo and dual instruction time
cpl-air-law.e: A student pilot may be credited in full for all solo and dual instruction time toward initial licence issue.

cpl-air-law.q: The Director may accept logbook entries for crediting if the original logbook was lost only if what applies?
cpl-air-law.a: The pilot provides a sworn statement only
cpl-air-law.c: The entries are substantiated by means acceptable to the Director
cpl-air-law.d: The pilot submits a police report only
cpl-air-law.ans: The entries are substantiated by means acceptable to the Director
cpl-air-law.e: Lost logbook entries may be accepted for credit only if substantiated by means acceptable to the Director.

cpl-air-law.q: A CPL holder with MCC may credit supervised co-pilot time as PIC towards ATPL up to how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A CPL holder with MCC may credit supervised co-pilot time as PIC towards ATPL up to 500 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: Flight time obtained while not complying with Part 61 requirements is treated how?
cpl-air-law.a: Cannot be credited for any purpose
cpl-air-law.b: Can be credited if completed safely
cpl-air-law.c: Can be credited if signed by an instructor
cpl-air-law.d: Can be credited if the pilot pays a fine
cpl-air-law.ans: Cannot be credited for any purpose
cpl-air-law.e: Flight time obtained while not complying with Part 61 cannot be credited for any purpose.

cpl-air-law.q: A flight examiner occupying a pilot seat may log what time?
cpl-air-law.b: PIC time, and instructor time if holding a valid instructor rating
cpl-air-law.ans: PIC time, and instructor time if holding a valid instructor rating
cpl-air-law.e: A flight examiner occupying a pilot seat may log PIC time and, if appropriately rated as an instructor, instructor time.

cpl-air-law.q: When acting as co-pilot on an aircraft certified for two pilots, what credit is allowed towards a higher licence?
cpl-air-law.e: Co-pilot time on an aircraft certified for two pilots may be credited at 100% towards a higher licence.

cpl-air-law.q: Co-pilot time must be logged when what condition applies?
cpl-air-law.b: You are in training for PIC
cpl-air-law.c: You occupy any seat in the cockpit
cpl-air-law.d: The aircraft requires more than one pilot by type certification or regulation
cpl-air-law.ans: The aircraft requires more than one pilot by type certification or regulation
cpl-air-law.e: Co-pilot time is logged when the aircraft requires more than one pilot by type certification or by regulation.

cpl-air-law.q: An instructor conducting instrument training in actual IMC must log what?
cpl-air-law.e: An instructor conducting instrument training in actual IMC logs instrument flight time.

cpl-air-law.q: Flight simulation time on an approved FSTD for instrument training must be logged how?
cpl-air-law.b: As instrument time and clearly marked as FSTD time
cpl-air-law.ans: As instrument time and clearly marked as FSTD time
cpl-air-law.e: Approved FSTD instrument training must be logged as instrument time and clearly marked as FSTD time.

cpl-air-law.q: Instructors and examiners logging FSTD time must hold what?
cpl-air-law.e: Instructors and examiners logging FSTD time must hold a valid FSTD instructor authorisation.

cpl-air-law.q: In an integrated course, PIC instrument time under supervision can be credited up to how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: In an integrated course, PIC instrument time under supervision may be credited up to 50 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: Maximum FSTD instructor time credited towards Grade II upgrade is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: Up to 100 hours of FSTD instructor time may be credited towards a Grade II upgrade.

cpl-air-law.q: From a light sport aeroplane to PPL(A), maximum credit is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A light sport aeroplane pilot converting to PPL(A) may receive a maximum credit of 30 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: For a national pilot licence, light sport aeroplane, converting to PPL(A), the maximum credit is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A light sport aeroplane NPL holder converting to PPL(A) may receive a maximum credit of 30 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: From a conventionally controlled microlight to PPL(A), maximum credit is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A conventionally controlled microlight pilot converting to PPL(A) may receive a maximum credit of 25 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: Maximum approved full-size simulator instructor time credited towards Grade I upgrade is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: Up to 1,000 hours of approved full-size simulator instructor time may be credited towards Grade I upgrade.

cpl-air-law.q: For a glider pilot converting to PPL(A), the additional 25 hours must include at least what?
cpl-air-law.a: 15 dual and 5 solo with two 100 NM cross-country flights
cpl-air-law.b: 10 dual and 5 solo with a triangular 150 NM cross-country meeting ATSU and landing rules
cpl-air-law.c: 5 dual and 20 solo with a 75 NM route
cpl-air-law.ans: 10 dual and 5 solo with a triangular 150 NM cross-country meeting ATSU and landing rules
cpl-air-law.e: The additional requirement includes at least 10 dual and 5 solo with the triangular 150 NM cross-country requirements.

cpl-air-law.q: The 150 NM triangular cross-country requirement means what?
cpl-air-law.a: The total distance is exactly 150 NM
cpl-air-law.b: The route must always include an international flight
cpl-air-law.c: The route must be three legs forming a triangle, with one point at least 50 NM from base
cpl-air-law.d: The route must be approved by the Director
cpl-air-law.ans: The route must be three legs forming a triangle, with one point at least 50 NM from base
cpl-air-law.e: The triangular cross-country route must form a triangle and include one point at least 50 NM from base.

cpl-air-law.q: A PIC supervising another pilot in actual IMC may credit what?
cpl-air-law.d: Instrument flight time towards currency requirements
cpl-air-law.ans: Instrument flight time towards currency requirements
cpl-air-law.e: A PIC supervising another pilot in actual IMC may credit instrument flight time for currency requirements.

cpl-air-law.q: Foreign military-trained pilots with certified proof of hours may be credited what percentage of hours?
cpl-air-law.e: Foreign military-trained pilots may be credited 100% of certified proof of hours.

cpl-air-law.q: A holder of a national pilot licence, weight-shift microlight, converting to PPL(A) may be credited with a maximum of how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A weight-shift microlight NPL holder converting to PPL(A) may be credited with a maximum of 25 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: From a touring motor glider to PPL(A), maximum credit is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A touring motor glider pilot converting to PPL(A) may receive a maximum credit of 30 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: For CPL(H) or ATPL(H) applicants with an aeroplane licence, aeroplane hours count as what?
cpl-air-law.d: Half-value, two aeroplane hours equal one helicopter hour
cpl-air-law.ans: Half-value, two aeroplane hours equal one helicopter hour
cpl-air-law.e: For helicopter licences, aeroplane hours are credited at half value: two aeroplane hours equal one helicopter hour.

cpl-air-law.q: A glider pilot converting to PPL(A) may be credited with how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A glider pilot converting to PPL(A) may be credited with 20 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: The additional 15 hours required for light sport aeroplane to PPL(A) conversion must include what?
cpl-air-law.a: Minimum 15 dual with no solo requirement
cpl-air-law.b: Minimum 10 dual and 5 solo with a 150 NM triangular route meeting ATSU and landing conditions
cpl-air-law.c: Minimum 5 dual and 10 solo with a 100 NM cross-country
cpl-air-law.d: No solo required if 30 hours credit granted
cpl-air-law.ans: Minimum 10 dual and 5 solo with a 150 NM triangular route meeting ATSU and landing conditions
cpl-air-law.e: The additional training must include at least 10 hours dual and 5 hours solo, including the required 150 NM triangular route.

cpl-air-law.q: Maximum total in-flight relief pilot credit towards ATPL hours is what?
cpl-air-law.e: In-flight relief pilot credit towards ATPL hours is limited to 500 hours, including a maximum of 40 hours night.

cpl-air-law.q: For CPL(A) or ATPL(A) applicants with a helicopter licence, at least how much time must be in aeroplanes?
cpl-air-law.e: For CPL(A) or ATPL(A) applicants with a helicopter licence, at least 50% of the required time must be in aeroplanes.

cpl-air-law.q: From a glider pilot licence to PPL(A), maximum credit is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A glider pilot converting to PPL(A) may receive a maximum credit of 20 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: The additional 15 hours required for touring motor glider to PPL(A) conversion must include what?
cpl-air-law.b: Minimum 10 dual and 5 solo, including one triangular 150 NM route with ATSU and landings at two different aerodromes away from base
cpl-air-law.c: Minimum 5 dual and 10 solo with a 100 NM cross-country
cpl-air-law.ans: Minimum 10 dual and 5 solo, including one triangular 150 NM route with ATSU and landings at two different aerodromes away from base
cpl-air-law.e: The additional requirement includes minimum 10 dual and 5 solo with the specified triangular 150 NM route and landings.

cpl-air-law.q: An ATPL integrated course student who passed ATPL theory is deemed to have passed theory for what?
cpl-air-law.e: An ATPL integrated course student who passed ATPL theory is deemed to have passed theory for PPL, CPL and Part 96 authorisation.

cpl-air-law.q: In-flight relief pilot time that may be credited towards ATPL total time is what percentage?
cpl-air-law.e: In-flight relief pilot time may be credited towards ATPL total time at 50%.

cpl-air-law.q: For a touring motor glider pilot converting to PPL(A), the maximum credit is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: A touring motor glider pilot converting to PPL(A) may be credited with a maximum of 30 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: For a weight-shift microlight conversion to PPL(A), the additional dual and solo time must include what cross-country requirement?
cpl-air-law.a: Two cross-country flights of at least 100 NM each
cpl-air-law.b: One triangular cross-country of at least 150 NM with one point at least 50 NM from base and full-stop landings at two different aerodromes away from base
cpl-air-law.c: One cross-country of 75 NM with one landing at an uncontrolled aerodrome
cpl-air-law.d: 5 hours instrument time and one cross-country of 150 NM
cpl-air-law.ans: One triangular cross-country of at least 150 NM with one point at least 50 NM from base and full-stop landings at two different aerodromes away from base
cpl-air-law.e: The conversion route requires a triangular 150 NM cross-country with one point at least 50 NM from base and two full-stop landings away from base.

cpl-air-law.q: Dual instruction time counts towards higher licences at what rate?
cpl-air-law.e: Dual instruction time counts at 100% towards higher licence requirements.

cpl-air-law.q: For the triangular 150 NM cross-country, at least one aerodrome of departure must have what?
cpl-air-law.d: Have an ATSU in operation and require a filed flight plan
cpl-air-law.ans: Have an ATSU in operation and require a filed flight plan
cpl-air-law.e: The requirement includes an aerodrome with an ATSU in operation and a filed flight plan.

cpl-air-law.q: Maximum FSTD instructor time credited towards Grade I upgrade is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: Up to 500 hours of FSTD instructor time may be credited towards a Grade I upgrade.

cpl-air-law.q: The 150 NM triangular route distance refers to what?
cpl-air-law.b: Total sum of the three legs
cpl-air-law.c: The distance from base to furthest point only
cpl-air-law.ans: Total sum of the three legs
cpl-air-law.e: The 150 NM triangular route distance refers to the total distance of the three legs.

cpl-air-law.q: For a multi-engine class qualification, the prerequisite is how many hours PIC of aeroplanes?
cpl-air-law.e: A multi-engine class qualification requires 70 hours PIC of aeroplanes.

cpl-air-law.q: For single-pilot helicopter operations under Part 127, a night-rated pilot must do what?
cpl-air-law.b: Fly with a co-pilot at all times
cpl-air-law.d: Meet additional experience requirements under Part 127
cpl-air-law.ans: Meet additional experience requirements under Part 127
cpl-air-law.e: For single-pilot helicopter operations under Part 127, additional experience requirements apply.

cpl-air-law.q: Which pilot licence requires a Class 1 fitness certificate?
cpl-air-law.e: An airline transport pilot licence requires a Class 1 medical certificate. Class 1 is the higher medical standard used for professional commercial and airline flight crew privileges.

cpl-air-law.q: A person under 60 years old can obtain a Class 5 fitness certificate by doing what?
cpl-air-law.b: Submitting a self-declaration to the Director
cpl-air-law.ans: Submitting a self-declaration to the Director
cpl-air-law.e: A person under 60 may obtain a Class 5 certificate by submitting a self-declaration to the Director.

cpl-air-law.q: Which licence falls under Class 3 fitness certification?
cpl-air-law.e: An air traffic controller licence falls under Class 3 fitness certification.

cpl-air-law.q: Upon expiry of a Class 1 fitness certificate, if not renewed, it can be substituted for which other classes for the remainder of its validity period?
cpl-air-law.e: An expired Class 1 certificate may be substituted by Class 2, 3, or 4 for the remaining validity period if not renewed.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 4 fitness certificate holder flying above 12 000 ft must meet what standard?
cpl-air-law.a: Meet Class 2 respiratory and lung function test standards
cpl-air-law.ans: Meet Class 2 respiratory and lung function test standards
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 4 holder flying above 12 000 ft must meet Class 2 respiratory and lung function standards.

cpl-air-law.q: Upon expiry of a Class 2 fitness certificate, if not renewed, it may be substituted by which class?
cpl-air-law.e: An expired Class 2 certificate may be substituted by a Class 4 certificate if not renewed.

cpl-air-law.q: A paraglider licence falls under which class of fitness certificate?
cpl-air-law.e: A paraglider licence falls under Class 5 fitness certification.

cpl-air-law.q: A valid Class 1 fitness certificate also deems the holder to hold which other classes?
cpl-air-law.e: A valid Class 1 certificate also deems the holder to hold Class 3 and Class 4.

cpl-air-law.q: A valid Class 2 fitness certificate also deems the holder to hold what?
cpl-air-law.e: A valid Class 2 certificate also deems the holder to hold Class 3 and Class 4.

cpl-air-law.q: Which fitness certificate class applies to a tandem paraglider pilot licence?
cpl-air-law.e: A tandem paraglider pilot licence requires a Class 4 fitness certificate.

cpl-air-law.q: Which fitness certificate class is required for a powered parachute pilot licence?
cpl-air-law.e: A powered parachute pilot licence requires a Class 4 fitness certificate.

cpl-air-law.q: A person aged 60 or older can obtain a Class 5 fitness certificate by doing what?
cpl-air-law.d: Submitting a self-declaration signed by a registered practitioner
cpl-air-law.ans: Submitting a self-declaration signed by a registered practitioner
cpl-air-law.e: A person aged 60 or older requires a self-declaration signed by a registered practitioner.

cpl-air-law.q: An ATS personnel member holding a valid Class 3 fitness certificate is also deemed to hold what?
cpl-air-law.e: A valid Class 3 certificate also deems the holder to hold Class 4.

cpl-air-law.q: A cabin crew member licence requires which fitness certificate class?
cpl-air-law.e: A cabin crew member licence requires a Class 4 fitness certificate.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 1 fitness certificate for a pilot younger than forty is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 1 certificate for this age group is valid for 12 months.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 1 fitness certificate for a CPL aeroplane holder aged sixty-two is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 1 certificate for this holder is valid for 6 months.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 3 fitness certificate for an ATC aged thirty is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 3 certificate for this age group is valid for 48 months.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 4 fitness certificate for a pilot aged forty or more is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 4 certificate for this age group is valid for 36 months.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 2 or Class 3 fitness certificate for someone aged forty-five is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 2 or Class 3 certificate for this age group is valid for 24 months.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 1 fitness certificate for a CPL aeroplane holder aged forty-five is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 1 certificate for this holder is valid for 12 months.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 1 fitness certificate for an airline transport pilot in multi-crew operations, aged fifty, is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: For the operation and age stated in the question, the Class 1 medical certificate remains valid for 12 months. Medical validity can change with age, operating role, and any limitation imposed by the medical examiner.

cpl-air-law.q: A Class 4 fitness certificate for a microlight pilot aged thirty-eight is valid for how long?
cpl-air-law.e: A Class 4 certificate for this age group is valid for 60 months.

cpl-air-law.q: An ATPL aeroplane pilot in single-crew commercial air transport, aged forty-five, gets a Class 1 fitness certificate. What is the validity?
cpl-air-law.e: For this operation and age group, Class 1 validity is 6 months.

cpl-air-law.q: Who may reduce the period of validity of a fitness certificate?
cpl-air-law.e: A designated aviation medical examiner or authorised medical assessor may shorten the normal validity period when closer medical follow-up is necessary. The reduced period becomes the pilot’s actual certificate validity.

cpl-air-law.q: For the purpose of the 10-hour limit in 24 hours, each hour spent instructing in ab initio training counts as how much?
cpl-air-law.e: Each hour of ab initio instruction counts as 1.5 hours for this limit.

cpl-air-law.q: What is the maximum total flight time for a pilot over the preceding 90 days for all flying?
cpl-air-law.e: The maximum total flight time over the preceding 90 days is 400 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: If a planned flight would cause a pilot to exceed any flight time aggregate, what is the legal position?
cpl-air-law.a: May proceed if the PIC approves
cpl-air-law.b: May proceed if the flight is under VFR
cpl-air-law.d: May proceed if duty time is not exceeded
cpl-air-law.e: The pilot may not legally operate if the planned flight would exceed the aggregate limits.

cpl-air-law.q: A flight instructor giving ab initio training towards an initial rating or licence is limited to how many hours per day?
cpl-air-law.e: An instructor giving ab initio training is limited to 6 hours in one calendar day.

cpl-air-law.q: The maximum total IFR time as part of a multi-pilot crew in the preceding 90 days is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: The maximum IFR time in this case over the preceding 90 days is 300 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: As part of a multi-pilot crew for a flight wholly or partly under IFR, the maximum total flight time in the preceding 30 days is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: The maximum for this situation in the preceding 30 days is 120 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: Under Part 91, a pilot not subject to an approved flight time and duty scheme may not fly more than how many hours in any 24-hour period?
cpl-air-law.e: The Part 91 limit is 10 flight hours in any consecutive 24-hour period for a pilot who is not operating under an approved flight-time and duty scheme. The purpose is to control fatigue exposure.

cpl-air-law.q: The annual 12-month limit for total flight time for a pilot is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: The accumulated flight-time limit is 1000 hours during the preceding 12 months. The pilot must include the proposed flight when checking whether the legal limit would be exceeded.

cpl-air-law.q: Over the preceding 6 months, a pilot’s total flight time may not exceed how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: The maximum total flight time over the preceding 6 months is 700 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: As the sole pilot for a flight wholly or partly under IFR, the maximum total IFR time in the preceding 30 days is how many hours?
cpl-air-law.e: The maximum IFR time in this case over the preceding 30 days is 100 hours.

cpl-air-law.q: If take-off and landing recency is met in a multi-engine aircraft, what does it count for?
cpl-air-law.e: Multi-engine take-off and landing recency also counts for single-engine aircraft.

cpl-air-law.q: To act as PIC or SIC on an instrument approach in IMC, within the last 90 days the pilot must have done what?
cpl-air-law.d: 2 approaches in aircraft or approved FSTD, or an appropriate skill test
cpl-air-law.ans: 2 approaches in aircraft or approved FSTD, or an appropriate skill test
cpl-air-law.e: Instrument approach recency requires at least 2 approaches in aircraft or approved FSTD, or an appropriate skill test.

cpl-air-law.q: To carry passengers by day as PIC, or SIC of an aircraft requiring more than one pilot, what must a pilot have completed within the last 90 days?
cpl-air-law.a: 3 take-offs and landings in the same class, type, or variant
cpl-air-law.b: 1 take-off and landing in the same aircraft type
cpl-air-law.c: 3 take-offs and landings in any aircraft
cpl-air-law.d: 5 take-offs and landings in the same class or type
cpl-air-law.ans: 3 take-offs and landings in the same class, type, or variant
cpl-air-law.e: Day passenger recency requires 3 take-offs and 3 landings in the same class, type, or variant within the last 90 days.

cpl-air-law.q: An aeroplane with maximum certificated mass exceeding 5700 kg is an example of what type of rating?
cpl-air-law.e: Large or complex aircraft such as aeroplanes exceeding 5700 kg normally require a type rating.

cpl-air-law.q: Except with approval, flight crew of a large aeroplane must use boom or throat microphones during which phase?
cpl-air-law.a: Only while cruising above transition level
cpl-air-law.c: Below transition altitude or transition level when on the flight deck
cpl-air-law.ans: Below transition altitude or transition level when on the flight deck
cpl-air-law.e: The requirement improves clear crew communication during the lower, higher-workload phases of flight.

cpl-air-law.q: On a pressurised aircraft, oxygen reserve must cover the period when cabin pressure altitude is greater than what?
cpl-air-law.e: For pressurised aircraft, oxygen planning considers time above 10 000 ft cabin pressure altitude after depressurisation.

cpl-air-law.q: For instrument approach recency in IMC, the minimum requirement is what?
cpl-air-law.a: 2 approaches in an aircraft or approved FSTD with reference to flight instruments only
cpl-air-law.b: 3 approaches in any aircraft by visual reference only
cpl-air-law.ans: 2 approaches in an aircraft or approved FSTD with reference to flight instruments only
cpl-air-law.e: 2 instrument approaches in an aircraft or approved FSTD, flown with reference to flight instruments only, are required for IMC approach recency.

cpl-air-law.q: For an IFR flight from controlled into or through uncontrolled airspace, the flight level selected under the semi-circular rule depends on what?
cpl-air-law.d: Only whether the flight is in VMC or IMC
cpl-air-law.e:
RULE
Under the semi-circular cruising-level rule, the flight level an IFR aircraft must select depends only on magnetic track: odd flight levels for tracks 000-179 deg, even flight levels for tracks 180-359 deg. VMC/IMC conditions play no part in selecting the level under this rule.

ANSWER
Magnetic track only

principles-of-flight.q: The best angle of attack on the wing polar diagram is marked as: (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-2.)
principles-of-flight.e:
• The vertical axis shows lift coefficient (CL).
• The horizontal axis shows drag coefficient (CD).
• The best angle of attack is the point where the lift-to-drag ratio is greatest.
• On the polar, this is found where a straight line drawn from the origin just touches the curve.
• That tangent point is labelled 4.

FINAL ANSWER
Point 4.

principles-of-flight.q: The critical angle of attack on the wing polar diagram is marked as: (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-2.)
principles-of-flight.e:
• The critical angle of attack occurs at the maximum lift coefficient.
• On the polar, this is the highest point reached before the curve begins to fall.
• That point is labelled 6.

FINAL ANSWER
Point 6.

principles-of-flight.q: The angle of attack for a minimum drag on the wing polar diagram is marked as: (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-2.)
principles-of-flight.e:
• Minimum drag occurs at the lowest drag coefficient.
• On the polar, this is the point furthest to the left on the curve.
• That point is labelled 3.

FINAL ANSWER
Point 3.

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane weighs 4,600 lb. What approximate load must the structure support in a level 50° banked turn? (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-1.)
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Aircraft weight 4,600 lb, bank angle 50 deg, level coordinated turn.

FORMULA
Load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle)
Structural load = weight x n

SOLVE
n = 1 / cos(50 deg) = 1 / 0.643 = 1.556 G
Structural load = 4,600 lb x 1.556 = 7,158 lb, rounded to 7,160 lb

ANSWER
7,160 lb

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane weighs 3,000 lb. What approximate load must the structure support in a level 20° banked turn? (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-1.)
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Aircraft weight 3,000 lb, bank angle 20 deg, level coordinated turn.

FORMULA
Load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle)
Structural load = weight x n

SOLVE
n = 1 / cos(20 deg) = 1 / 0.940 = 1.064 G (approx 1.06 G as read from the load factor graph)
Structural load = 3,000 lb x 1.06 = 3,180 lb

ANSWER
3,180 lb

Exam tip: the exact formula gives about 3,193 lb; this question wants the graph-read approximate value.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the load factor in a level 60° banked turn? (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-1.)
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Bank angle 60 deg, level coordinated turn.

FORMULA
Load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle)

SOLVE
n = 1 / cos(60 deg) = 1 / 0.5 = 2.0 G

ANSWER
2.0 G

principles-of-flight.q: What is the maximum bank angle for an aircraft limited to +2.5 G in a level turn? (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-1.)
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Load factor limit +2.5 G, level coordinated turn.

FORMULA
cos(bank angle) = 1 / load factor
bank angle = cos^-1(1 / load factor)

SOLVE
cos(bank angle) = 1 / 2.5 = 0.4
bank angle = cos^-1(0.4) = 66.4 deg, rounded to 66 deg

ANSWER
66°

principles-of-flight.q: What is the maximum bank angle for an aircraft limited to +3.8 G in a level turn? (Refer to Figure PPL PoF-1.)
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Load factor limit +3.8 G, level coordinated turn.

FORMULA
cos(bank angle) = 1 / load factor
bank angle = cos^-1(1 / load factor)

SOLVE
cos(bank angle) = 1 / 3.8 = 0.263
bank angle = cos^-1(0.263) = 74.7 deg, rounded to 75 deg

ANSWER
75°

principles-of-flight.q: True airspeed is the speed of the aircraft relative to what?
principles-of-flight.e: True airspeed is calibrated airspeed corrected for the effects of altitude and non-standard temperature on air density, since the airspeed indicator only measures a pressure difference, not speed directly. As altitude increases, air becomes thinner, so the aircraft must move faster through the surrounding air mass to generate the same dynamic pressure - meaning true airspeed pulls further ahead of indicated airspeed the higher you climb, which is exactly why true airspeed, not indicated airspeed, is what actually determines groundspeed and range.

principles-of-flight.q: During straight and level flight, where is the centre of gravity located relative to the centre of pressure?
principles-of-flight.a: At the same point as the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.b: On the aircraft datum line only
principles-of-flight.c: Forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.d: Aft of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: Forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: In straight and level flight, the centre of gravity normally sits forward of the centre of pressure (the point representing the wing's combined lift force). This forward CG creates a nose-down pitching tendency that the tailplane's small download continuously balances, which is exactly what gives the aircraft its natural, self-correcting pitch stability.

principles-of-flight.q: Newton’s second law refers to what concept?
principles-of-flight.e: Newton's second law states that when a net force acts on a mass, it produces acceleration in the direction of that force, proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass (F = ma). In aerodynamics, this is what links any imbalance among the four forces to a change in the aircraft's speed or flight path - excess thrust over drag accelerates the aircraft, for instance.

principles-of-flight.q: The elevator is a primary flight control used mainly to control what?
principles-of-flight.e: The elevator is hinged to the tailplane and, when deflected, changes the tail's lifting or downward force, which pitches the nose up or down. That pitching motion happens around the lateral axis - the imaginary line running wingtip to wingtip through the centre of gravity - which is exactly why controlling pitch means controlling rotation about that axis.

principles-of-flight.q: The primary and further effects of rudder are what?
principles-of-flight.a: Roll, then yaw, followed by spiral dive
principles-of-flight.b: Pitch, then speed change, followed by a dive
principles-of-flight.c: Yaw only with no further effect
principles-of-flight.d: Yaw, then roll, followed by spiral dive
principles-of-flight.ans: Yaw, then roll, followed by spiral dive
principles-of-flight.e: Rudder's primary effect is yaw, swinging the nose left or right about the vertical axis. But yawing the aircraft makes one wing momentarily travel faster through the air than the other, generating more lift on that side, which rolls the aircraft as a secondary effect - and if that roll and yaw combination is left uncorrected, it can develop into a steepening, accelerating spiral dive.

principles-of-flight.q: The equation of continuity states that if the area of a venturi is decreased, what happens to the velocity of the air?
principles-of-flight.b: Velocity increases only after separation occurs
principles-of-flight.d: Velocity remains constant and pressure decreases
principles-of-flight.e: For a steady flow, the same mass of air has to pass through every cross-section of the tube each second - none of it can pile up or vanish. Narrowing the venturi shrinks the cross-sectional area, so the air has to speed up through that section to keep pushing the same mass through in the same time, which is exactly what the equation of continuity describes.

principles-of-flight.q: If the centre of gravity is moved aft during flight, what happens to longitudinal stability?
principles-of-flight.e: Longitudinal stability depends heavily on where the centre of gravity sits relative to the centre of pressure - the further forward the CG, the longer the "moment arm" the tailplane has to work with in restoring the aircraft after a pitch disturbance. Moving the CG aft shortens that arm and weakens the restoring effect, which is exactly why an aft CG reduces pitch stability.

principles-of-flight.q: An aircraft with its CG too far aft would be what?
principles-of-flight.c: Easier to recover from a spin
principles-of-flight.e: A CG too far aft leaves the tailplane with very little leverage to restore the aircraft after any pitch disturbance, since the moment arm between CG and centre of pressure has shrunk. That weak restoring tendency makes pitch control edgy and over-sensitive, and it also degrades the nose-down authority needed to recover cleanly from a stall or spin.

principles-of-flight.q: The lift force produced by an aerofoil acts in what direction?
principles-of-flight.c: Perpendicular to the aircraft longitudinal axis
principles-of-flight.e: Lift is defined by convention as the aerodynamic force component acting perpendicular to the relative airflow - not straight up relative to the ground. In a climb, descent, or steep bank the aircraft's actual "up" and the direction lift acts can differ noticeably, since lift always follows the relative airflow's orientation, not gravity's.

principles-of-flight.q: As angle of attack is increased in normal level flight, the centre of pressure will normally move in which direction?
principles-of-flight.b: It remains fixed at the CG
principles-of-flight.e: As angle of attack increases, the airflow over the upper surface accelerates and its low-pressure region shifts toward the leading edge, pulling the centre of pressure - the effective point of the wing's combined lift - forward along the chord with it. This forward shift is part of why a wing's pitching behaviour changes as it approaches a stall, and why aft-CG aircraft can become progressively less stable at high angles of attack.

principles-of-flight.q: For elevator control effectiveness when loading an aeroplane, it is generally better to have what CG position?
principles-of-flight.a: Centre of gravity behind the tailplane
principles-of-flight.c: Aft centre of gravity behind the aft limit
principles-of-flight.d: Centre of gravity at the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: The elevator's job is to change the tailplane's angle of attack and, with it, the balancing force needed to hold the aircraft in trim against the pitching moment created by the CG-to-centre-of-pressure distance. A forward CG lengthens that distance, giving the tailplane a bigger job to do at any given elevator deflection - which is exactly why a forward CG position keeps the elevator working within its most effective range rather than running out of authority.

principles-of-flight.q: When an aeroplane is flying at zero degrees angle of attack, the pressure along the upper surface of the aerofoil will normally be what?
principles-of-flight.e: A cambered aerofoil is shaped so its upper surface is naturally longer and more convex than the lower one, which accelerates the airflow passing over it even at zero angle of attack. That faster flow brings lower pressure with it by Bernoulli's principle, so the upper surface sits below atmospheric pressure even before the chord line is angled into the wind at all.

principles-of-flight.q: A change in angle of attack will cause what?
principles-of-flight.a: A change in lift only, with no drag change
principles-of-flight.b: A change in drag only, with no lift change
principles-of-flight.c: No change until the critical angle is exceeded
principles-of-flight.d: A change in lift, drag and airspeed
principles-of-flight.ans: A change in lift, drag and airspeed
principles-of-flight.e: Changing the angle of attack directly changes both the lift and drag coefficients the wing produces, since it alters the pressure differential and downwash the wing generates. In level flight, that in turn changes how much airspeed is needed to generate the lift required to support the aircraft's weight - the three effects are linked, not independent.

principles-of-flight.q: A change in yaw causes an aircraft to rotate around which axis?
principles-of-flight.e: Yaw is rotation about the vertical (or normal) axis - the imaginary line running straight up and down through the centre of gravity, perpendicular to both the wingspan and the fuselage. It is this axis that the rudder acts around when it swings the nose left or right.

principles-of-flight.q: The straight line on an aerofoil joining the centre of curvature of the leading edge to the trailing edge is called what?
principles-of-flight.e: The chord line is the straight geometric reference running from the leading edge to the trailing edge of an aerofoil section - distinct from the curved mean camber line running through the middle of the wing's thickness. Angle of attack, angle of incidence and camber are all defined and measured relative to this one straight reference line.

principles-of-flight.q: The primary and further effects of aileron are what?
principles-of-flight.a: Yaw, then roll, followed by spiral dive
principles-of-flight.b: Roll, then yaw, followed by spiral dive
principles-of-flight.c: Pitch, then yaw, followed by spiral dive
principles-of-flight.d: Roll only with no secondary effect
principles-of-flight.ans: Roll, then yaw, followed by spiral dive
principles-of-flight.e: Ailerons primarily roll the aircraft about the longitudinal axis. But the down-going aileron's extra induced drag yaws the nose in the opposite direction to the roll as a secondary effect, and if that adverse yaw and the resulting sideslip are left uncorrected, the imbalance can develop into a spiral dive that steepens on its own.

principles-of-flight.q: Rotation about the longitudinal axis is called what and is controlled by which control?
principles-of-flight.e: Roll, or bank, is rotation about the longitudinal axis - the imaginary line running from nose to tail through the centre of gravity. Ailerons control this by deflecting in opposite directions on each wing, raising lift on one side and lowering it on the other to bank the aircraft.

principles-of-flight.q: In the lift formula, the main variables for an aeroplane in level flight are what?
principles-of-flight.b: Wing loading and ground speed only
principles-of-flight.e: In the lift equation L = ½ρV²SCL, wing area (S) and air density (ρ) are essentially fixed for a given aircraft in a given flight, leaving the lift coefficient (CL, set by angle of attack) and velocity squared (V²) as the two variables the pilot actually manipulates in level flight. Because velocity is squared, even a small change in speed has an outsized effect on lift compared with an equivalent change in CL.

principles-of-flight.q: The four forces are in equilibrium during what condition?
principles-of-flight.b: Straight and level cruise at constant speed
principles-of-flight.c: A climbing turn at constant speed
principles-of-flight.d: A steady glide with power off
principles-of-flight.ans: Straight and level cruise at constant speed
principles-of-flight.e: Lift, weight, thrust and drag are only truly in balance - equal and opposite pairs, with nothing left over to accelerate the aircraft - when the flight path, speed and attitude are all holding steady, as in level cruise at a constant speed. The instant any one force changes, the aircraft starts accelerating in some direction until a new equilibrium (or a new manoeuvre) is reached.

principles-of-flight.q: The rudder is a primary flight control used mainly to control what?
principles-of-flight.e: The rudder is hinged to the vertical stabiliser and, when deflected, pushes the tail sideways, swinging the nose left or right. That rotation happens around the vertical (or normal) axis, which is why the rudder's job is described as controlling yaw.

principles-of-flight.q: During level flight, where is the centre of pressure normally located relative to the centre of gravity?
principles-of-flight.a: Aft of the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.b: Directly on the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.d: Forward of the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.ans: Aft of the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.e: In level flight the centre of pressure, the point representing the wing's combined lift, normally sits aft of the centre of gravity. That arrangement is what gives the wing a nose-down pitching moment for the tailplane's download to balance against, producing the aircraft's stable pitch behaviour.

principles-of-flight.q: In normal level flight, a reduction in power causes the nose to drop mainly because of what?
principles-of-flight.a: The thrust line is always below the drag line
principles-of-flight.c: The centre of gravity is forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.d: The centre of pressure is forward of the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.ans: The centre of gravity is forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: Because the centre of gravity sits forward of the centre of pressure in normal flight, the wing is always trying to pitch the nose down, held in check by the tail's balancing download - and that download depends partly on airflow driven by power. Reduce power, and that balancing effect weakens relative to the CG-forward pitching moment, so the nose tends to drop.

principles-of-flight.q: A change in pitch causes an aircraft to rotate around which axis?
principles-of-flight.e: Pitch - the nose rising or falling - is rotation about the lateral axis, the imaginary line running wingtip to wingtip through the centre of gravity. The elevator controls this rotation by changing the tailplane's lifting or downward force.

principles-of-flight.q: The three axes of rotation of an aircraft intersect at what point?
principles-of-flight.e: The aircraft's three axes of rotation - longitudinal (roll), lateral (pitch), and vertical (yaw) - all pass through and intersect at a single common point: the centre of gravity. This is why the centre of gravity, not any arbitrary point on the airframe, is treated as the aircraft's true pivot for all rotational motion.

principles-of-flight.q: The layer of air in contact with the surface of an aerofoil during flight is called what?
principles-of-flight.e: Skin friction slows the very thinnest layer of air touching the aerofoil almost to a standstill, and this retarded layer - the boundary layer - grows thicker moving aft along the surface as more air is progressively dragged along with it. Its condition (laminar or turbulent) has a major effect on both skin-friction drag and how resistant the wing is to flow separation and stall.

principles-of-flight.q: Longitudinal stability in an aeroplane is achieved by what design feature?
principles-of-flight.e: Longitudinal stability is built in by mounting the tailplane at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane - longitudinal dihedral. This ensures that whenever the aircraft pitches nose-up, the tailplane's angle of attack (and downward-balancing force) changes in a way that generates a restoring, nose-down moment, and vice versa for a nose-down disturbance.

principles-of-flight.q: Which factor affects the longitudinal stability of an aeroplane?
principles-of-flight.b: Position of CG relative to centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: Position of CG relative to centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: Pitch stability comes down to where the centre of gravity sits relative to the centre of pressure, since this distance sets the moment arm the tailplane has to work with when restoring the aircraft after a disturbance. A forward CG gives a longer, more effective arm and greater stability; an aft CG shortens it and weakens the restoring tendency.

principles-of-flight.q: Newton’s third law refers to what concept?
principles-of-flight.e: Newton's third law states that every action force produces an equal and opposite reaction force. A propeller pushing a mass of air backward, for example, generates an equal and opposite reaction pushing the aircraft forward - the same principle behind the torque reaction that rolls the aircraft opposite to the propeller's direction of rotation.

principles-of-flight.q: An aircraft with its CG too far forward would be what?
principles-of-flight.a: Difficult to control in pitch due to reduced stability
principles-of-flight.b: More prone to a flat spin
principles-of-flight.e: A forward CG gives the tailplane a longer moment arm to work with, so it generates a strong, well-defined restoring force for any elevator input - the aircraft responds predictably and the elevator has plenty of authority in reserve. That strong, well-behaved pitch response is exactly what makes a forward-CG aircraft easy to control in pitch.

principles-of-flight.q: Which of the following is a primary flight control?
principles-of-flight.e: Ailerons are one of the three primary flight controls, alongside the elevator and rudder, because they directly and immediately control roll about the longitudinal axis - a fundamental axis of aircraft motion, distinct from secondary controls like flaps or trim, which adjust the aircraft's configuration rather than directly rotate it.

principles-of-flight.q: A change in bank causes an aircraft to rotate around which axis?
principles-of-flight.e: Bank, or roll, is rotation about the longitudinal axis - the imaginary line running from nose to tail through the centre of gravity. Ailerons control this rotation by raising lift on one wing and lowering it on the other, tilting the aircraft around that axis.

principles-of-flight.q: The symbol V in the lift formula refers to what airspeed?
principles-of-flight.e: The lift formula uses V for true airspeed - the aircraft's actual speed through the surrounding air mass, not groundspeed or indicated airspeed. This matters because lift is generated by air flowing over the wing, so it is the wing's motion relative to that air, not relative to the ground, that determines how much lift is produced.

principles-of-flight.q: Newton’s first law refers to what concept?
principles-of-flight.e: Newton's first law is the law of inertia: an object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion continues in a straight line at constant speed, unless acted on by an unbalanced force. This describes equilibrium - it is exactly the state an aircraft is in during steady, unaccelerated straight and level flight, where the four forces are perfectly balanced.

principles-of-flight.q: On an aerofoil or aircraft, the point through which total weight acts is called what?
principles-of-flight.e: The centre of gravity is the single point through which an aircraft's entire weight can be considered to act - if you could suspend the aircraft from a rope attached at exactly that point, it would balance perfectly level. Its position, controlled by how the aircraft is loaded, has a major effect on stability and performance, which is why weight and balance calculations are done before every flight.

principles-of-flight.q: What are the characteristics of a laminar-flow aerofoil?
principles-of-flight.b: High coefficient of lift and high profile drag
principles-of-flight.c: Low coefficient of lift and low coefficient of drag
principles-of-flight.d: High induced drag at all speeds
principles-of-flight.ans: Low coefficient of lift and low coefficient of drag
