principles-of-flight.e: A laminar-flow aerofoil is shaped to keep the boundary layer smooth and attached over more of the chord than a conventional section manages, which cuts skin-friction drag substantially - hence the low drag coefficient. That same thin, carefully-shaped profile, however, typically produces less camber-driven lift than a conventional aerofoil, giving it a correspondingly modest lift coefficient too.

principles-of-flight.q: Bernoulli’s principle states that if the velocity of air flowing through a venturi is increased, what must happen to pressure energy?
principles-of-flight.d: It changes to dynamic pressure only
principles-of-flight.e: Bernoulli's principle states that the pressure of a moving fluid falls at points where its speed rises. So as air accelerates through the narrowing throat of a venturi, its pressure energy has to decrease to compensate - the two trade off against each other so that the fluid's total energy stays constant.

principles-of-flight.q: If the centre of gravity is moved forward during flight, what is the effect on longitudinal stability?
principles-of-flight.e: Moving the CG forward lengthens the moment arm between the centre of gravity and the centre of pressure, giving the tailplane a stronger, more effective restoring moment for any given pitch disturbance. That longer arm is exactly why a forward CG shift increases longitudinal stability.

principles-of-flight.q: On an aerofoil, the point through which total lift acts is called what?
principles-of-flight.e: The centre of pressure is the single point along the chord through which the wing's entire resultant lift force can be considered to act, even though lift is really distributed as varying pressure across the whole surface. Its position isn't fixed - it moves as angle of attack, flap setting and airspeed change, which is exactly why it matters so much for pitch stability.

principles-of-flight.q: If altitude must be maintained while reducing power in level flight, what must be increased?
principles-of-flight.e: Lift depends on both airspeed and angle of attack working together to produce the same total force. If power is reduced and speed falls while altitude is held constant, the wing has less dynamic pressure to work with, so angle of attack has to increase to keep generating the lift needed to support the aircraft's weight.

principles-of-flight.q: Rotation about the vertical axis is called what and is controlled by which control?
principles-of-flight.e: Yaw is rotation about the vertical (or normal) axis, the line running straight up through the centre of gravity, and it is the rudder that controls it, by deflecting the tail sideways to swing the nose left or right.

principles-of-flight.q: If airspeed is doubled while angle of attack remains constant, what happens to lift?
principles-of-flight.e: Lift scales with the square of airspeed when angle of attack (and so lift coefficient) is held constant, since lift depends on dynamic pressure, q = ½ρV². Doubling speed means V² becomes four times larger, so lift increases fourfold, not just doubles.

principles-of-flight.q: In level flight, what is the relationship between the four forces?
principles-of-flight.a: Lift is less than weight and thrust equals drag
principles-of-flight.b: Lift equals weight and thrust is greater than drag
principles-of-flight.c: Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag
principles-of-flight.d: Lift equals drag and thrust equals weight
principles-of-flight.ans: Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag
principles-of-flight.e: Steady, unaccelerated level flight at constant speed is defined by two simultaneous balances: lift exactly equals weight (so altitude doesn't change), and thrust exactly equals drag (so speed doesn't change). Disturb either balance - more thrust than drag, or more lift than weight - and the aircraft starts accelerating or climbing rather than staying level.

principles-of-flight.q: Rotation about the lateral axis is called what and is controlled by which control?
principles-of-flight.e: Pitch is rotation about the lateral axis - the imaginary line from wingtip to wingtip through the centre of gravity - and the elevator controls it by changing the tailplane's lifting or downward force to raise or lower the nose.

principles-of-flight.q: According to Bernoulli’s theory, when air flows through the throat of a venturi tube, what happens?
principles-of-flight.e: Bernoulli's principle links speed and pressure inversely: wherever a fluid speeds up, its pressure drops. Through the narrowing throat of a venturi tube, continuity forces the air to accelerate, and that increase in velocity is accompanied by a corresponding decrease in static pressure.

principles-of-flight.q: If only aileron is applied during straight and level flight, what can occur?
principles-of-flight.a: Roll followed by yaw and spiral dive
principles-of-flight.c: Roll only with no further effect
principles-of-flight.ans: Roll followed by yaw and spiral dive
principles-of-flight.e: Applying aileron alone rolls the aircraft as its primary effect. But the down-going aileron's extra induced drag yaws the nose opposite to the roll as a secondary effect, and if neither is corrected with rudder, the combined roll, yaw and resulting sideslip can develop into a steepening, accelerating spiral dive.

principles-of-flight.q: The position that separates laminar airflow from turbulent airflow around an aerofoil is called what?
principles-of-flight.e: Near the leading edge, the boundary layer starts out smooth and orderly - laminar flow. Moving aft along the surface, it eventually becomes chaotic and mixing - turbulent flow - and the specific point where that changeover happens is called the transition point, whose location shifts with surface roughness, Reynolds number and the pressure gradient along the wing.

principles-of-flight.q: The angle of attack of an aeroplane is the angle between which two lines?
principles-of-flight.e: Angle of attack is measured between the chord line (the straight reference from leading to trailing edge) and the relative airflow (the direction air is actually meeting the wing) - not between the wing and the horizon, and not the same thing as pitch attitude. An aircraft can be at a low angle of attack while pitched steeply nose-up, or vice versa, depending on the direction of the relative airflow.

principles-of-flight.q: The angle between the chord line and the longitudinal axis is called what?
principles-of-flight.e: Angle of incidence is a fixed, built-in angle set by the manufacturer between the wing's chord line and the aircraft's longitudinal axis - unlike angle of attack, which changes constantly as the pilot manoeuvres and depends on the direction of the airflow, not the aircraft's structure.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, curve B on the graph indicates:
principles-of-flight.e: On a typical drag curve, curve B rises steadily with speed rather than falling at low speed - that upward-only shape belongs to parasite (or profile) drag, which grows because the aircraft is pushing more air aside and generating more skin friction the faster it flies. This is the opposite behaviour to induced drag, which is worst at low speed and improves as speed increases.

principles-of-flight.q: The primary and secondary effects of aileron are what?
principles-of-flight.a: Pitch then roll in the same direction
principles-of-flight.b: Roll only with no secondary yaw
principles-of-flight.c: Yaw then roll in the opposite direction
principles-of-flight.d: Roll then yaw in the same direction as the roll
principles-of-flight.ans: Roll then yaw in the same direction as the roll
principles-of-flight.e: Roll is the aileron's primary, intended effect. But lowering an aileron increases that wing's local camber and angle of attack, which raises lift and, along with it, induced drag on that side - more drag on the wing that's rising than on the wing with the raised aileron. That drag imbalance yaws the nose toward the rising wing, opposite to the direction of roll, which is why rudder is needed to keep the turn coordinated.

principles-of-flight.q: A dynamically stable aircraft, when disturbed from its flight path, will do what?
principles-of-flight.b: Diverge increasingly from the original flight path
principles-of-flight.c: Return towards the original flight path
principles-of-flight.d: Remain displaced with no tendency to return
principles-of-flight.ans: Return towards the original flight path
principles-of-flight.e: Positive dynamic stability means any oscillation set off by a disturbance progressively damps out over time, like a ball settling to rest at the bottom of a bowl rather than continuing to swing back and forth. Passenger aircraft are deliberately designed this way, so after turbulence disturbs the flight path, the aircraft naturally converges back toward it without the pilot having to actively correct every oscillation.

principles-of-flight.q: If the gross weight of an aircraft is increased, what drag effect can be expected?
principles-of-flight.a: Greater increase in induced drag than parasite drag
principles-of-flight.b: Greater increase in parasite drag than induced drag
principles-of-flight.d: Total drag decreases at the same speed
principles-of-flight.ans: Greater increase in induced drag than parasite drag
principles-of-flight.e: A heavier aircraft needs its wing to generate more total lift, which it does mainly by increasing angle of attack rather than by flying dramatically faster. Since induced drag is far more sensitive to angle of attack than parasite drag is to the small resulting change in speed, added weight drives up induced drag noticeably more than it drives up parasite drag.

principles-of-flight.q: The correct operation of an anti-balance tab on a stabilator is checked by observing that it moves in which direction?
principles-of-flight.c: Moves only with the trim wheel
principles-of-flight.e: An anti-balance (or anti-servo) tab is deliberately rigged to move the same way as the stabilator itself - when the stabilator goes up, the tab goes up with it. That opposing aerodynamic force makes the control feel heavier than it would otherwise, which is exactly the point: a stabilator is so aerodynamically light and sensitive that without this added resistance, a pilot could easily over-control it.

principles-of-flight.q: Induced drag increases with what?
principles-of-flight.e: At lower speeds the wing has less dynamic pressure to work with, so it must fly at a higher angle of attack to generate the lift needed to support the aircraft's weight. Since induced drag grows directly with angle of attack, this is exactly why induced drag rises sharply as speed decreases - it is the dominant drag source at the slow end of the speed range.

principles-of-flight.q: A balance tab operates in which direction relative to the primary control surface?
principles-of-flight.d: Same direction only at high speed
principles-of-flight.e: A balance tab moves opposite to the control surface it is attached to - when the elevator goes up, the tab goes down. That opposite deflection creates an aerodynamic force on the tab that actively helps swing the main surface further in the pilot's commanded direction, reducing the physical effort needed at the controls.

principles-of-flight.q: Dust on the surface of a wing before flight may still be there after flight because of what?
principles-of-flight.e: Skin friction slows the very thin layer of air in direct contact with the wing surface almost to a standstill, even while the air just above that layer is moving past at speed. Because that innermost layer barely moves at all, dust particles resting on the surface simply aren't swept away by the faster airflow further out, and can still be found there after landing.

principles-of-flight.q: The type of control balance most commonly used in light aeroplanes to counteract flutter is what?
principles-of-flight.e: Flutter is a rapid, self-sustaining oscillation that develops when a control surface's centre of mass sits aft of its hinge line, letting aerodynamic and inertial forces feed off each other. A mass balance corrects this by adding weight ahead of the hinge, shifting the surface's centre of mass forward enough to break that feedback loop - which is why it is the standard, low-cost flutter prevention method on light aircraft.

principles-of-flight.q: An increase in angle of attack will do what to pressure above the wing and drag?
principles-of-flight.a: Increase pressure below the wing and reduce drag
principles-of-flight.b: Have no effect before the stall
principles-of-flight.c: Increase pressure above the wing and reduce drag
principles-of-flight.d: Decrease pressure above the wing and increase drag
principles-of-flight.ans: Decrease pressure above the wing and increase drag
principles-of-flight.e: Increasing angle of attack forces the airflow to accelerate further over the wing's upper surface, and by Bernoulli's principle that faster flow comes with lower pressure - so pressure above the wing drops further. At the same time, both the widened pressure differential and the stronger downward deflection of the airstream (Newton's reaction) increase drag along with the extra lift.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, curve C on the graph indicates:
principles-of-flight.e: On a typical drag curve, curve C is the sum of the other two curves at every speed - it represents total drag, combining induced drag (dominant at low speed) and parasite drag (dominant at high speed) into a single curve that dips to a minimum at the best lift-to-drag speed, Vmd.

principles-of-flight.q: The initial effect of uncorrected adverse aileron yaw during a roll to the left is what?
principles-of-flight.e: Rolling left means the right aileron goes down and the left aileron goes up. The down-going right aileron increases that wing's lift and, with it, its induced drag, while the left wing produces comparatively less drag - so the extra drag on the right wing yaws the nose to the right, opposite to the roll, unless corrected with left rudder.

principles-of-flight.q: A mass balance ahead of the hinge line is attached to a control surface mainly to prevent what?
principles-of-flight.e: A control surface with its mass concentrated behind the hinge line is prone to flutter, a destructive oscillation driven by inertial and aerodynamic forces reinforcing each other as airspeed increases. Adding a weight ahead of the hinge line - a mass balance - shifts the surface's centre of mass forward, breaking that feedback loop before it can build into a dangerous vibration.

principles-of-flight.q: Longitudinal dihedral means what?
principles-of-flight.c: Mounting the tailplane at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane
principles-of-flight.d: Mounting the wings with upward slope from root to tip
principles-of-flight.ans: Mounting the tailplane at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane
principles-of-flight.e: Longitudinal dihedral means the tailplane is rigged at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane, so as the aircraft pitches, the tailplane's angle of attack - and the balancing force it generates - changes in a way that always pushes the aircraft back toward its trimmed attitude. This built-in geometric offset is the primary structural feature giving light aircraft their natural pitch stability.

principles-of-flight.q: A passenger-carrying aeroplane is usually designed to have what type of stability?
principles-of-flight.e: Positive dynamic stability means that oscillations set off by a disturbance progressively shrink over time rather than persisting or growing - the aircraft settles back toward its original flight condition on its own. This is essential for passenger comfort and safety, which is why passenger-carrying aircraft are specifically designed with this damping behaviour built in.

principles-of-flight.q: Dihedral is incorporated into aeroplane design to improve what stability?
principles-of-flight.e: Dihedral - the upward slant of the wings from root to tip - creates lateral stability through a simple mechanism: if one wing drops, the aircraft sideslips slightly, and that sideslip gives the lower, more exposed wing a greater effective angle of attack than the upper wing. The lower wing's extra lift produces a rolling moment that pushes the aircraft back toward wings-level flight.

principles-of-flight.q: When a wing has washout, what does it mean?
principles-of-flight.a: Angle of incidence increases towards the wingtip
principles-of-flight.d: Angle of incidence decreases towards the wingtip
principles-of-flight.ans: Angle of incidence decreases towards the wingtip
principles-of-flight.e: A washed-out wing is deliberately twisted so the angle of incidence is lower at the tip than at the root. This means the root reaches its critical angle of attack, and stalls, before the tip does, so the ailerons near the tip stay effective for roll control even as the inboard wing begins to stall - a valuable safety margin during a wing drop.

principles-of-flight.q: Adverse aileron yaw increases as what increases?
principles-of-flight.e: Induced drag grows with angle of attack, and the down-going aileron's extra lift - and the drag that comes with it - is really just a local spike in induced drag on that wing. At high angles of attack the whole wing is already closer to its drag-producing limit, so the same aileron deflection creates a proportionally bigger drag imbalance, making adverse yaw much more noticeable than it is at low angle of attack.

principles-of-flight.q: A high aspect ratio wing has what effect?
principles-of-flight.a: Increases induced drag at all speeds
principles-of-flight.e: Aspect ratio compares a wing's span to its average chord - a long, narrow wing has a high aspect ratio, while a short, wide wing has a low one. A higher aspect ratio spreads the same total lift over a longer span, weakening the wingtip vortices that roll up at each tip and feed the wing's induced drag, which is why high-aspect-ratio wings (like a glider's) are noticeably more efficient at generating lift for a given amount of drag.

principles-of-flight.q: Stability in the rolling plane is mainly a function of what?
principles-of-flight.e: Rolling-plane stability is lateral stability, and dihedral - the upward wing slant from root to tip - is the main design feature providing it. When a wing drops and the aircraft sideslips, dihedral gives the lower wing a greater effective angle of attack, and the resulting extra lift rolls the aircraft back toward level.

principles-of-flight.q: Stability in the yawing plane is mainly a function of what?
principles-of-flight.e: Yawing-plane stability is directional stability, and it comes mainly from the vertical fin mounted well aft of the centre of gravity. If the aircraft yaws out of alignment with the relative airflow, the fin experiences a sideways force from that airflow, acting like a weathervane to swing the tail back into line and restore the original heading.

principles-of-flight.q: During entry into a left turn from straight and level flight, why is rudder normally applied in the same direction as aileron?
principles-of-flight.b: To increase induced drag on the inner wing
principles-of-flight.c: To correct adverse aileron yaw from the lowered right aileron
principles-of-flight.d: To increase the rate of roll only
principles-of-flight.ans: To correct adverse aileron yaw from the lowered right aileron
principles-of-flight.e: Entering a left turn means the right aileron goes down, increasing that wing's lift and induced drag relative to the left wing. That extra drag on the right side yaws the nose away from the turn - to the right - so left rudder is applied together with the aileron input specifically to cancel that adverse yaw and keep the turn coordinated.

principles-of-flight.q: What common design feature is used to reduce adverse aileron yaw?
principles-of-flight.e: The core problem behind adverse yaw is that the down-going aileron produces noticeably more induced drag than the up-going aileron reduces on the opposite wing. Differential ailerons attack this directly by rigging the linkage so the up-going aileron travels through a larger angle than the down-going one, deliberately adding drag on the rising wing to better balance the drag from the falling wing's aileron.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, curve A on the graph indicates:
principles-of-flight.e: On a typical drag curve, curve A is high at low speed and falls as speed increases - that shape is the signature of induced drag, which is worst when the wing must fly at a high angle of attack to generate lift at low speed, and improves as increasing speed lets the wing fly at a lower, more efficient angle of attack.

principles-of-flight.q: The vertical fin improves stability in which plane?
principles-of-flight.e: Mounted aft of the centre of gravity, the vertical fin acts exactly like a weathervane: if the aircraft yaws out of alignment with the relative airflow, the fin catches a sideways force from that airflow that swings the tail back into line, restoring the aircraft's heading - the basis of directional (yawing-plane) stability.

principles-of-flight.q: Induced drag is created by what?
principles-of-flight.c: Pressure difference between the top and bottom surfaces of the aerofoil
principles-of-flight.d: Skin friction in the boundary layer only
principles-of-flight.ans: Pressure difference between the top and bottom surfaces of the aerofoil
principles-of-flight.e: Lift only exists because of a pressure difference between the wing's lower and upper surfaces, and that same pressure difference is what drives air to curl around the wingtips from the high-pressure underside to the low-pressure upper side, rolling up into wingtip vortices and downwash. Induced drag is the rearward-tilted component of the lift vector produced by that downwash, making it an unavoidable byproduct of generating lift at all.

principles-of-flight.q: During a sideslip, the effect of dihedral is to do what?
principles-of-flight.c: Create a rolling force which reduces the slip
principles-of-flight.ans: Create a rolling force which reduces the slip
principles-of-flight.e: A sideslip drops one wing relative to the airflow, and because of dihedral, that lower wing meets the air at a greater effective angle of attack than the upper wing, generating more lift on the lower side. That lift imbalance creates a rolling moment that lifts the low wing back up, directly counteracting the sideslip that caused it.

principles-of-flight.q: The use of horn balance on an aeroplane does what?
principles-of-flight.a: Improves aerodynamic balance of the controls
principles-of-flight.b: Increases induced drag on the control surface
principles-of-flight.ans: Improves aerodynamic balance of the controls
principles-of-flight.e: A horn balance extends part of the control surface forward of the hinge line, projecting into the airflow ahead of the hinge. The aerodynamic force on that forward section works to help swing the surface in the direction the pilot commands, reducing the physical stick or pedal force needed - improving the aerodynamic balance of the controls overall.

principles-of-flight.q: The airflow over an aerofoil that immediately contacts the surface is slowed by what effect?
principles-of-flight.e: The layer of air molecules touching the wing surface directly is slowed almost to a stop by skin friction - the viscous drag between the air and the surface - even while the air just above it continues moving at nearly full speed. This thin, slowed layer is the innermost part of the boundary layer that develops over every lifting surface.

principles-of-flight.q: Frise ailerons may be installed on some aeroplanes to reduce what?
principles-of-flight.e: Rather than balancing drag through unequal aileron travel, Frise ailerons use a hinge set back from the leading edge so that when an aileron goes up, part of its leading edge projects down into the airflow, deliberately adding drag on the up-going side. That extra drag on the wing that would otherwise produce less drag helps balance the induced drag spike on the down-going aileron's wing, reducing the net adverse yaw.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, position D on the total drag curve indicates:
principles-of-flight.b: The minimum drag speed (Vmd) / maximum lift-to-drag ratio
principles-of-flight.ans: The minimum drag speed (Vmd) / maximum lift-to-drag ratio
principles-of-flight.e: Position D marks the lowest point on the total drag curve - where induced drag (falling with speed) and parasite drag (rising with speed) add up to the smallest possible total. That same speed also gives the maximum lift-to-drag ratio, since the wing is generating the most lift for the least drag anywhere on the curve, making it the ideal speed for maximum range or glide performance.

principles-of-flight.q: Differential ailerons are used to reduce what?
principles-of-flight.b: Lift production at the wing root
principles-of-flight.e: Adverse yaw exists because the down-going aileron increases lift, and with it induced drag, more than the up-going aileron reduces it on the opposite wing. Differential ailerons correct this imbalance by making the up-going aileron deflect through a greater angle than the down-going one, adding extra drag on the rising wing to offset the drag spike on the falling wing.

principles-of-flight.q: Compared with a high aspect ratio wing, a low aspect ratio wing will create what?
principles-of-flight.c: Less parasite drag at all speeds
principles-of-flight.e: A low aspect ratio wing concentrates the same total lift over a shorter span, which strengthens the wingtip vortices relative to the wing's size and increases the induced drag penalty for producing that lift. This is the direct trade-off against a high aspect ratio wing, which spreads lift over a longer span and produces proportionally weaker tip vortices and less induced drag.

principles-of-flight.q: Aspect ratio of a wing refers to the ratio of what?
principles-of-flight.e: Aspect ratio is the ratio of a wing's span (tip to tip) to its mean aerodynamic chord (its average front-to-back width). A long, narrow wing has a high aspect ratio and produces relatively weak wingtip vortices and low induced drag for its lift; a short, wide wing has a low aspect ratio and the opposite trade-off.

principles-of-flight.q: Longitudinal dihedral improves stability in which plane?
principles-of-flight.e: Longitudinal dihedral - the tailplane set at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane - is specifically about restoring the aircraft after a nose-up or nose-down disturbance, which is pitch motion about the lateral axis. That is why it improves stability in the pitching plane, distinct from wing dihedral, which improves stability in the rolling plane.

principles-of-flight.q: Dihedral improves stability in which plane?
principles-of-flight.e: Dihedral works through sideslip: when a wing drops, the resulting slight sideslip gives the lower wing a greater effective angle of attack (and more lift) than the upper wing, and that lift imbalance rolls the aircraft back toward level. Since rolling motion happens about the longitudinal axis - the rolling plane - that is exactly the stability dihedral is designed to improve.

principles-of-flight.q: A design feature used to reduce induced drag and help control wingtip stall is what?
principles-of-flight.e: Washout deliberately reduces the wingtip's angle of incidence relative to the root, which lowers the tip's local angle of attack and, with it, the local induced drag and lift generated there. This both trims the vortex-driving lift concentrated at the tip and ensures the root stalls before the tip, keeping the ailerons effective into the early stages of a stall.

principles-of-flight.q: An adjustable trim tab attached to an elevator will, when the elevator is moved, do what?
principles-of-flight.a: Remain in the same position regardless of elevator deflection
principles-of-flight.c: Move in the same direction automatically
principles-of-flight.d: Move in the opposite direction automatically
principles-of-flight.ans: Remain in the same position regardless of elevator deflection
principles-of-flight.e: A trim tab remains set in its selected position. When the elevator moves, the trim tab does not automatically follow like a balance tab.

principles-of-flight.q: Adverse aileron yaw is more noticeable when?
principles-of-flight.e: Adverse yaw comes from the imbalance in induced drag between the down-going aileron's wing (extra lift, extra drag) and the up-going aileron's wing. Since induced drag itself grows with angle of attack, that same aileron deflection produces a much larger drag imbalance - and so a much more noticeable adverse yaw - when the wing is already working at a high angle of attack, such as during a slow, steep turn.

principles-of-flight.q: Application of trailing edge flaps will have what effect on lateral stability?
principles-of-flight.c: Have no effect on lateral stability
principles-of-flight.e: Extending trailing-edge flaps changes the lift distribution across the span and can locally alter how much extra lift a dropped wing generates in a sideslip compared with the clean configuration, weakening the dihedral effect that normally restores wings-level flight. This is one reason many aircraft feel a bit less crisp laterally with flaps extended than in the clean configuration.

principles-of-flight.q: Directional stability in an aeroplane is achieved mainly by what?
principles-of-flight.e: The vertical fin, mounted well aft of the centre of gravity, acts like a weathervane: any yaw that misaligns the aircraft with the relative airflow produces a sideways force on the fin that swings the tail back into line. This restoring effect around the vertical axis is exactly what defines directional stability.

principles-of-flight.q: Profile or parasite drag increases with what?
principles-of-flight.a: Increase in angle of attack only
principles-of-flight.e: Parasite (or profile) drag comes from the aircraft simply pushing through the air and from skin friction over its surfaces, and both of those effects intensify as speed rises - more air has to be displaced per second, and the friction force itself grows with the square of speed. This is why parasite drag climbs steadily across the speed range, in direct contrast to induced drag, which falls as speed increases.

principles-of-flight.q: The effect of dihedral is to provide lateral stability when turbulence creates what?
principles-of-flight.e: Turbulence that drops one wing produces a sideslip, and it is specifically that sideslip - the aircraft sliding sideways through the air toward the lowered wing - that dihedral responds to. The lower wing meets the resulting sideways airflow component at a greater effective angle of attack, generating extra lift that rolls the aircraft back toward level.

principles-of-flight.q: The main purpose of the vertical fin is to provide what?
principles-of-flight.e: Mounted aft of the centre of gravity, the vertical fin behaves like the feathers on an arrow: any yaw that misaligns the aircraft with the relative airflow produces a sideways force on the fin that swings the tail back into line. This weathervane-like restoring effect is the vertical fin's main purpose - providing directional stability about the vertical axis.

principles-of-flight.q: An increase in induced drag can be expected when what happens?
principles-of-flight.a: Airspeed is increased at zero lift
principles-of-flight.c: The aircraft is flown at very high TAS only
principles-of-flight.e: Increasing angle of attack raises the wing's lift coefficient, which strengthens both the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces and the downwash it produces behind the wing. Since induced drag is a direct byproduct of that downwash and pressure difference, a higher angle of attack drives induced drag up right along with the extra lift.

principles-of-flight.q: A method used to improve stability about the lateral axis is what?
principles-of-flight.e: Pitch happens about the lateral axis, and the design feature specifically built to resist pitch disturbances is longitudinal dihedral - the tailplane rigged at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane. This ensures that any pitch disturbance changes the tailplane's angle of attack in a way that generates a restoring moment back toward the trimmed attitude.

principles-of-flight.q: An increase in wing loading will have what effect on stalling speed?
principles-of-flight.a: Reduce the critical angle of attack to zero
principles-of-flight.e: A heavier aircraft, or one with the same weight concentrated on a smaller wing (higher wing loading), needs a greater angle of attack to generate the extra lift required to support that weight at any given speed. Since the critical angle of attack itself doesn't change, the wing simply reaches that same critical angle at a higher speed - so stalling speed rises with wing loading.

principles-of-flight.q: During a level coordinated turn, additional load imposed on the wings is mainly a function of what?
principles-of-flight.e: In a level turn, the wing has to tilt part of its lift sideways to provide the centripetal force that curves the flight path, while still producing enough vertical lift to hold altitude. The steeper the bank, the more the lift vector tilts and the more total lift the wing has to generate to keep both jobs covered - so load factor climbs directly with bank angle, roughly doubling at 60°.

principles-of-flight.q: The primary purpose of Fowler flaps is to do what?
principles-of-flight.a: Increase the surface area of the wing
principles-of-flight.b: Reduce lift and drag for descent
principles-of-flight.c: Move the centre of gravity forward
principles-of-flight.ans: Increase the surface area of the wing
principles-of-flight.e: Unlike a plain or split flap, which simply hinges downward, a Fowler flap slides backward on tracks before tilting down. That rearward travel is what actually increases the wing's surface area, on top of the camber increase every flap type provides - which is exactly why Fowler flaps can add substantial lift without the drag penalty of the other flap types.

principles-of-flight.q: Application of flaps during a glide has what effect on rate of descent?
principles-of-flight.a: Has no effect on rate of descent
principles-of-flight.d: Decreases rate of descent to zero
principles-of-flight.e: With the engine at idle, there is no thrust to offset the extra drag flaps add, so lowering flaps in a glide directly steepens the descent - the aircraft trades that added drag for a faster loss of altitude rather than more distance covered. This is exactly why flaps are used to steepen a glide approach without needing to add airspeed.

principles-of-flight.q: Application of flaps during a turn has what effect on stall speed?
principles-of-flight.a: Doubles stall speed in a turn
principles-of-flight.d: Has no effect on stall speed
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps increase the wing's maximum lift coefficient by adding camber, meaning the wing can now produce the lift needed to support the aircraft at a lower speed before reaching its critical angle of attack. That lower stall speed holds true in a turn just as much as in straight flight, which is exactly why flaps are used to keep the margin above stall speed comfortable during a slower, tighter pattern turn.

principles-of-flight.q: Load factor is the resultant of which forces during a turn?
principles-of-flight.e: In a turn, the wing's lift is tilted to curve the flight path, and the load the wing structure feels is the resultant of two things: the aircraft's gross weight pulling down, and the outward centrifugal tendency of the turning mass pulling the load factor up. That combined load is exactly what increases with steeper bank - reaching about 2G at 60° of bank.

principles-of-flight.q: If aircraft weight is increased, what happens to stalling speed and stalling angle of attack?
principles-of-flight.a: Stall speed decreases and stalling angle increases
principles-of-flight.b: Both stall speed and angle remain unchanged
principles-of-flight.c: Stall angle decreases as weight increases
principles-of-flight.d: Stall speed increases and stalling angle remains the same
principles-of-flight.ans: Stall speed increases and stalling angle remains the same
principles-of-flight.e: Extra weight means the wing has to generate more lift to support the aircraft, which it can only do by reaching a higher speed before hitting its critical angle of attack - so stalling speed increases. The critical angle of attack itself, however, is a fixed property of the wing's shape and doesn't change with weight; only the speed at which that same angle is reached does.

principles-of-flight.q: Wingtip stalling may be reduced by incorporating what?
principles-of-flight.e: A washed-out wing has its angle of incidence deliberately reduced toward the tip, so the wing root reaches its critical angle of attack - and stalls - before the tip does. That keeps the ailerons, mounted near the tip, still flying and effective even as the inboard wing begins to stall, reducing the risk of an uncommanded wing drop.

principles-of-flight.q: Application of trailing edge flaps will have what effect on L/D ratio?
principles-of-flight.e: Lift-to-drag ratio measures how far forward the aircraft travels for every unit of height lost, and flaps add proportionally more drag than useful lift at glide speeds. That worsened balance between lift and drag directly reduces the L/D ratio, which is exactly why extending flaps produces a shorter, steeper glide path.

principles-of-flight.q: During a turn, why does an aeroplane stall at a higher IAS than with wings level?
principles-of-flight.a: Critical angle of attack is reached at a higher IAS
principles-of-flight.b: Critical angle of attack decreases in the turn
principles-of-flight.c: Wing loading reduces in a turn
principles-of-flight.ans: Critical angle of attack is reached at a higher IAS
principles-of-flight.e: Turning increases the load factor on the wing, since it must now generate extra lift to both support the aircraft's weight and provide the centripetal force needed to curve the flight path. Producing that extra lift requires a higher angle of attack for any given speed, so the wing's fixed critical angle of attack is reached - and the stall occurs - at a higher indicated airspeed than in level flight.

principles-of-flight.q: When gliding into a headwind, what happens to the glide path over the ground and the rate of descent through the air mass?
principles-of-flight.a: The ground glide path becomes shallower and the rate of descent is unchanged
principles-of-flight.b: The rate of descent increases but the ground glide path is unchanged
principles-of-flight.c: Both the aerodynamic L/D ratio and the rate of descent improve
principles-of-flight.d: The ground glide path becomes steeper and the rate of descent is unchanged
principles-of-flight.ans: The ground glide path becomes steeper and the rate of descent is unchanged
principles-of-flight.e: The aircraft's rate of descent through the surrounding air mass depends on its aerodynamic configuration and airspeed, not on the wind - a headwind cannot change how fast the aircraft sinks relative to the air itself. What it does change is groundspeed: with less distance covered over the ground for the same height lost, the glide path measured by an observer on the ground appears steeper, purely because groundspeed is lower.

principles-of-flight.q: One design method used to prevent the wingtip from stalling before the rest of the wing is what?
principles-of-flight.c: Reduce angle of incidence toward the wingtip
principles-of-flight.d: Increase angle of incidence toward the wingtip
principles-of-flight.ans: Reduce angle of incidence toward the wingtip
principles-of-flight.e: Reducing the angle of incidence progressively toward the wingtip - a twist called washout - means the wing root reaches its critical angle of attack before the tip does as angle of attack increases. The root then stalls first, and the still-flying tip keeps the ailerons effective for roll control even as the inboard wing begins to lose lift.

principles-of-flight.q: During a glide, application of flap will do what to the best L/D ratio?
principles-of-flight.e: Best glide distance is achieved at the speed giving maximum lift-to-drag ratio, and flaps add drag that isn't matched by a proportional gain in useful lift at glide speeds - shifting the aircraft away from its cleanest, most efficient configuration. With a worse L/D ratio, the aircraft simply cannot travel as far forward for the same height lost, whatever speed it flies at with flaps out.

principles-of-flight.q: The stalling angle of attack of a particular aerofoil does what?
principles-of-flight.a: Remains constant regardless of airspeed, bank angle or weight
principles-of-flight.ans: Remains constant regardless of airspeed, bank angle or weight
principles-of-flight.e: For a given aerofoil shape and configuration, the critical (stalling) angle of attack is a fixed geometric property - it doesn't shift with airspeed, bank angle or weight. What changes under those conditions is only the speed at which the wing happens to reach that same fixed angle, which is why stall speed varies but stall angle does not.

principles-of-flight.q: During a full-flap approach to land, the nose position will be how compared with a flapless approach?
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps increase the wing's camber, so it can produce the same lift at a lower angle of attack for a given approach speed. In the conventional light-aircraft case, that lower angle of attack shows up in the cockpit as a lower nose attitude on a full-flap approach compared with the higher, flatter deck angle needed to generate the same lift without flaps.

principles-of-flight.q: Ailerons may be needed to prevent underbanking during what type of turn?
principles-of-flight.e: In a descending, power-reduced turn, reduced airflow over the wings weakens aileron effectiveness right when the aircraft's tendency is to shallow out rather than hold bank. Extra aileron toward the turn is often needed just to maintain the desired bank angle - the opposite problem to overbanking.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, the speed at point A represents:
principles-of-flight.b: The best rate of climb speed (Vy)
principles-of-flight.c: The best angle of climb speed (Vx)
principles-of-flight.ans: The best rate of climb speed (Vy)
principles-of-flight.e: Point A sits at the speed where the vertical gap between the power-available and power-required curves is greatest - the largest surplus of power left over after overcoming drag. That maximum excess power is exactly what determines best rate of climb, Vy: the speed that converts the most spare power into altitude gained per minute.

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane has a tendency to overbank during what type of turn?
principles-of-flight.e: In a banked climbing turn, engine slipstream effects and the combination of higher power and angle of attack can make the aircraft want to roll further into the bank on its own, steepening beyond what the pilot commanded. Opposite aileron pressure is often needed to hold the intended bank angle rather than let it increase.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, the speed at point A indicates:
principles-of-flight.a: The best rate of climb speed (Vy)
principles-of-flight.d: The best angle of climb speed (Vx)
principles-of-flight.ans: The best angle of climb speed (Vx)
principles-of-flight.e: Point A marks where the excess thrust - the gap between available and required thrust, not power - is at its maximum. Maximising excess thrust rather than excess power is what determines best angle of climb, Vx: the steepest possible climb path, gaining the most height over the shortest horizontal distance.

principles-of-flight.q: Application of flaps during a climb has what effect?
principles-of-flight.a: Has no effect on climb angle
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps add drag, and any extra drag eats directly into the excess power that would otherwise go toward climbing - the aircraft climbs because of power available over power required, not because of extra lift. With more of the available power now needed just to overcome the added drag, less is left over to convert into altitude gain, so rate of climb decreases.

principles-of-flight.q: In a steady climb with constant speed and power, what is true?
principles-of-flight.a: Lift and drag are both zero
principles-of-flight.b: Thrust is greater than drag and lift is less than weight
principles-of-flight.c: Thrust equals drag and lift equals weight
principles-of-flight.d: Thrust is less than drag and lift is greater than weight
principles-of-flight.ans: Thrust is greater than drag and lift is less than weight
principles-of-flight.e: In a steady climb, the aircraft's weight can be split into two components: one opposing lift, and one acting rearward along the flight path opposing thrust. Because part of the weight is now acting like extra drag, thrust must exceed the wing's own drag to keep climbing, while lift only needs to balance its own, smaller component of weight - so lift ends up less than total weight, with the difference made up by thrust.

principles-of-flight.q: When climbing to clear obstacles in the take-off path, which climb speed should be used?
principles-of-flight.e: Clearing an obstacle close beyond the runway is a distance problem, not a time problem - what matters is height gained per unit of ground covered, not per minute. That is exactly what best angle of climb speed, Vx, maximises, by climbing at the speed where excess thrust (not excess power) is greatest.

principles-of-flight.q: To gain maximum height in the shortest distance, an aeroplane should climb at what speed?
principles-of-flight.e: Gaining the most height for the least horizontal distance is a matter of excess thrust, not excess power, and that is precisely what best angle of climb speed, Vx, is defined to maximise - the steepest possible climb angle, ideal for clearing obstacles close ahead.

principles-of-flight.q: To initiate spin recovery, which control is applied before elevator?
principles-of-flight.e: A spin is a self-sustaining, autorotating descent in which one wing is stalled more deeply than the other, and applying rudder first is what stops that autorotation - only once the yawing rotation has been arrested does reducing angle of attack with forward elevator actually unstall the wings cleanly. Applying elevator first, while the aircraft is still rotating, can prolong or even worsen the spin rather than end it.

principles-of-flight.q: When lowering trailing edge flaps, what is the initial effect on the centre of pressure?
principles-of-flight.a: It moves to the leading edge
principles-of-flight.d: It remains fixed at the CG
principles-of-flight.e: Lowering trailing-edge flaps reshapes the pressure distribution over the wing, and on a conventional wing that shift typically moves the centre of pressure - the point representing the wing's combined lift - rearward. Because lift now acts further aft relative to the centre of gravity, this initially creates a nose-down pitching tendency, though the tailplane's response to the flap-altered downwash can modify the aircraft's final pitch behaviour.

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane stalls as a result of what?
principles-of-flight.a: Exceeding the critical angle of attack
principles-of-flight.b: Flying below the published stall speed only
principles-of-flight.c: Reducing power in level flight only
principles-of-flight.ans: Exceeding the critical angle of attack
principles-of-flight.e: A stall is purely a function of angle of attack: once the airflow can no longer follow the wing's upper surface smoothly past the critical angle, it separates and lift collapses. Because that critical angle can be reached at any airspeed, attitude or power setting - fast or slow, nose-up or nose-down - a stall is fundamentally an angle-of-attack event, not a speed event.

principles-of-flight.q: Trailing edge flaps increase what at a given angle of attack and airspeed?
principles-of-flight.a: Value of lift created by the wing
principles-of-flight.ans: Value of lift created by the wing
principles-of-flight.e: Trailing-edge flaps increase the wing's camber, and a more cambered aerofoil generates a higher lift coefficient at any given angle of attack and airspeed. That is the direct mechanism behind flaps' main purpose: producing more lift without needing to fly faster or pitch to a higher angle of attack.

principles-of-flight.q: If power is increased during a descent while speed is kept constant, what happens to rate of descent?
principles-of-flight.e: Once the aircraft is in a steady descent, adding power without changing airspeed effectively supplies part of the energy that would otherwise have to come from losing altitude. With more thrust helping to overcome drag at the same speed, less of the flight path needs to point downward to maintain that speed, so the rate of descent decreases.

principles-of-flight.q: To maintain altitude during a turn, what must be increased?
principles-of-flight.e: Tilting the lift vector to bank the aircraft reduces its vertical component, so unless something compensates, the aircraft will start to sink. Increasing angle of attack restores enough total lift for its vertical component to still equal weight, which is exactly what holding back pressure through a turn achieves.

principles-of-flight.q: During a level turn to the left, the ball deflected left of centre indicates what?
principles-of-flight.e: The inclinometer ball settles toward whichever side has the greater net sideways force. In a left turn, a ball deflected to the left - toward the inside of the turn - shows the aircraft is banked more steeply than the rate of turn calls for: a slipping turn, where the aircraft is sliding sideways down and into the turn.

principles-of-flight.q: Flaps are fitted to many light aeroplanes in order to do what?
principles-of-flight.b: Increase lift and decrease drag at all speeds
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps increase wing camber (and, on Fowler-type flaps, wing area too), which raises the maximum lift coefficient the wing can produce - but that added camber also increases drag. This dual effect is exactly why flaps are useful: the extra lift permits a slower approach speed, while the extra drag permits a steeper descent path without gaining speed.

principles-of-flight.q: During a balanced level turn, total lift produced by the wings must equal what?
principles-of-flight.a: Only the horizontal component of lift
principles-of-flight.d: The vertical component of lift and the centripetal force
principles-of-flight.ans: The vertical component of lift and the centripetal force
principles-of-flight.e: In a level turn the wing's single lift vector has to do two jobs at once: its vertical component must still balance the aircraft's weight to hold altitude, and its horizontal component has to supply the centripetal force that actually curves the flight path. Total lift is the resultant of those two required components, which is exactly why lift has to increase above the straight-and-level value as bank angle steepens.

principles-of-flight.q: The force required for an aeroplane to turn is called what?
principles-of-flight.e: Turning the flight path requires a continuous force pulling the aircraft toward the centre of the turn - centripetal force - and in a banked aircraft, that force comes from the horizontal component of the wing's tilted lift. Without banking (and so without a horizontal lift component), the aircraft has no way to curve its path at all, however hard the rudder is applied.

principles-of-flight.q: During a flapless approach to land, the nose position will be how compared with a normal full-flap approach?
principles-of-flight.e: Without flaps, the wing has less camber and needs a greater angle of attack to generate the lift required at approach speed. In the conventional light-aircraft case, that higher angle of attack translates directly into a higher, flatter-looking nose attitude compared with the lower nose position seen on a full-flap approach.

principles-of-flight.q: At the appropriate best-glide speed, what effect does an increase in aircraft weight have on glide angle and rate of descent?
principles-of-flight.a: Increases glide angle and decreases rate of descent
principles-of-flight.b: Decreases glide angle and decreases rate of descent
principles-of-flight.c: No effect on rate of descent or best glide speed
principles-of-flight.d: No effect on glide angle but increases rate of descent
principles-of-flight.ans: No effect on glide angle but increases rate of descent
principles-of-flight.e: Best glide speed is defined by the speed that gives the wing's maximum lift-to-drag ratio, and that ratio is essentially an aerodynamic property of the wing's shape - it barely changes with weight. A heavier aircraft simply has to fly a bit faster to reach the same L/D-optimal angle of attack, so its best glide angle in still air stays nearly the same, even though its higher speed means it sinks through the air faster, giving a higher rate of descent.

principles-of-flight.q: The stall warning device is adjusted to activate the cockpit warning when?
principles-of-flight.d: At the exact critical angle only
principles-of-flight.e: A stall warning device - whether a vane, pressure sensor or artificial horn - is calibrated to trigger a few degrees of angle of attack before the wing actually reaches its critical angle, giving the pilot a clear audible or tactile cue with enough margin to reduce angle of attack and prevent the stall from actually developing.

principles-of-flight.q: In a level turn, the slip indicator ball centred indicates what?
principles-of-flight.e: The inclinometer ball settles wherever the net sideways force pushes it. A centred ball means the aircraft's bank angle and rate of turn are perfectly matched for the airspeed - no sideways force acting on the aircraft at all - the definition of a balanced, coordinated turn.

principles-of-flight.q: The stalling angle of attack in a steady climb will do what with altitude?
principles-of-flight.a: Remain the same at all altitudes
principles-of-flight.ans: Remain the same at all altitudes
principles-of-flight.e: The stalling, or critical, angle of attack is a fixed property of a given wing shape and configuration - it does not change with altitude. What does change with altitude is the true airspeed needed to generate enough lift at that same angle, since thinner air at higher altitude requires more speed to produce the same lift; the angle itself stays constant throughout the climb.

principles-of-flight.q: During autorotation in a spin, what is the state of the wings?
principles-of-flight.a: Inner wing partially unstalled while outer wing is stalled
principles-of-flight.c: Both wings have equal angle of attack
principles-of-flight.d: Outer wing partially unstalled while inner wing is stalled
principles-of-flight.ans: Outer wing partially unstalled while inner wing is stalled
principles-of-flight.e: In a spin, the inner wing - the one on the side the aircraft is rotating toward - is travelling more slowly and at a higher angle of attack than the outer wing, so it is more deeply stalled while the outer wing, moving faster through the air, may be only partially stalled or still producing some lift. This asymmetry between the two wings is exactly what keeps the autorotation going.

principles-of-flight.q: In a straight and level power-off stall, flap application will do what to the speed at which the stall occurs?
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps increase the wing's maximum lift coefficient by adding camber, so the wing can generate the lift needed to support the aircraft's weight at a lower speed before its fixed critical angle of attack is reached. That is exactly why extending flaps lowers the stalling speed in a straight, level, power-off stall.

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane with a high lift-to-drag ratio will have what type of gliding angle?
principles-of-flight.d: High rate of descent at all speeds
principles-of-flight.e: Lift-to-drag ratio is a direct measure of how far the aircraft glides forward for every unit of height it gives up - a high L/D means a lot of forward distance per foot lost. That efficient trade is exactly what produces a shallow gliding angle, the signature of a low-drag airframe like a glider.

principles-of-flight.q: At 60 degrees angle of bank in a balanced level turn, the load factor is approximately what?
principles-of-flight.e: Load factor rises directly with bank angle since more of the wing's lift has to tilt sideways to provide centripetal force while still holding altitude. At 60° of bank specifically, the load factor works out to 1 ÷ cos(60°) = 2, meaning the wings are supporting twice the aircraft's gross weight.

principles-of-flight.q: Application of flap will allow an aeroplane to glide at what angle?
principles-of-flight.b: Same angle at a higher speed
principles-of-flight.c: No change in drag or glide path
principles-of-flight.e: Extending flaps adds drag that isn't matched by a proportional gain in useful glide-speed lift, worsening the aircraft's lift-to-drag ratio. With less forward distance covered for the same height lost, the glide path steepens - which is exactly why flaps are the standard tool for steepening an approach without adding speed.

principles-of-flight.q: In an aircraft spinning to the left, applying ailerons to the right may have what effect?
principles-of-flight.a: Reduce angle of attack on both wings instantly
principles-of-flight.e: In a left spin, the left wing is the inner, more deeply stalled wing, and applying right aileron deflects that wing's aileron downward - increasing its angle of attack even further into the stall rather than reducing it. That can deepen the stall on the already-critical wing and work against the recovery you're trying to achieve, which is why ailerons are normally kept neutral during spin recovery.

principles-of-flight.q: If power is reduced during a descent while speed is kept constant, what happens to rate of descent?
principles-of-flight.e: At a fixed airspeed, thrust and drag must still balance somehow, and reducing power removes part of that balancing force. To keep the same speed with less thrust available, the aircraft has to trade more altitude for energy, steepening the descent path - so the rate of descent increases.

principles-of-flight.q: To gain maximum height in the shortest time, an aeroplane should climb at what speed?
principles-of-flight.e: Gaining the most altitude in the least time is about converting the largest possible surplus of power - not thrust - into climb. Best rate of climb speed, Vy, is precisely the speed where that excess power (available power minus power required to overcome drag) is at its maximum.

principles-of-flight.q: The centripetal force required to turn an aeroplane is created by what?
principles-of-flight.e: A turn requires a continuous sideways pull toward the centre of the curve - centripetal force - and an aircraft has only one source of sideways aerodynamic force available: the wings. Banking tilts the lift vector so part of it points horizontally, and that horizontal component of wing lift is what actually curves the flight path.

principles-of-flight.q: In level flight, an increase in thrust will normally cause what pitch effect?
principles-of-flight.e: Because the centre of gravity sits forward of the centre of pressure, the propeller and tailplane airflow that comes with added thrust changes the balance of pitching moments acting on the aircraft. In this syllabus that shift is treated as producing a nose-up tendency when thrust is increased in level flight, distinct from the separate nose-down tendency seen when power is reduced.

principles-of-flight.q: Apart from stall warning devices, what aerodynamic indication warns of an approaching stall?
principles-of-flight.e: As the wing approaches its critical angle of attack, the smooth airflow over the upper surface starts to separate and become turbulent near the trailing edge. That separated, buffeting airflow often reaches the tailplane before the wing itself fully stalls, producing a noticeable shake or buffet through the airframe and controls that warns the pilot even without an electronic stall warning device.

principles-of-flight.q: Maintaining engine power at the stall has what effect on stalling speed?
principles-of-flight.c: Has no effect on stall speed
principles-of-flight.e: Adding power near the stall does two things at once: the propeller slipstream washes extra airflow over the wing root and inboard sections, keeping that airflow attached longer, and the propeller's thrust line develops a small upward component that directly helps support part of the aircraft's weight. Both effects mean less lift has to come from the wing's angle of attack alone, so the wing can be flown to a slower speed before it actually stalls.

principles-of-flight.q: The potential for a normal spin to develop into a flat spin increases with what CG position?
principles-of-flight.e: Recovering from any spin depends on the nose dropping enough, once rudder and elevator are applied, to reduce the stalled wing's angle of attack. An aft centre of gravity reduces that natural nose-down tendency, making it easier for the spin to flatten out - rotating with the nose closer to the horizon - where recovery becomes significantly harder or, in some aircraft, may not be possible at all.

principles-of-flight.q: During a level turn to the left, the ball deflected right of centre indicates what?
principles-of-flight.e: The inclinometer ball moves toward whichever side feels the greater net sideways force. In a left turn, a ball deflected to the right - toward the outside of the turn - shows the aircraft isn't banked steeply enough for its rate of turn: a skidding turn, where the aircraft slides outward away from the turn centre.

principles-of-flight.q: Ailerons may be needed to prevent overbanking during what type of turn?
principles-of-flight.e: A banked climbing turn combines higher power, higher angle of attack and slipstream effects in a way that can make the aircraft want to keep rolling deeper into the bank on its own. Opposite aileron pressure is often needed to hold the intended bank angle rather than let it steepen further than commanded.

principles-of-flight.q: During a steady climb, what is the relationship between thrust and drag?
principles-of-flight.e: In a steady climb the aircraft's weight splits into two components along different directions: one opposing lift, and one acting rearward along the flight path like additional drag. To keep climbing steadily, thrust has to overcome both the wing's normal drag and this rearward weight component, so thrust ends up greater than the wing's drag alone.

principles-of-flight.q: With angle of attack, airspeed and air density unchanged, what is the effect of increasing wing surface area?
principles-of-flight.e: Both lift and drag equations include wing surface area as a direct multiplying factor, alongside angle of attack, airspeed and air density. With those other factors held constant, a larger wing simply interacts with more air passing over it each second, so both the lift it generates and the drag it produces increase together.

principles-of-flight.q: When gliding with a tailwind, what happens to the glide path over the ground and the rate of descent through the air mass?
principles-of-flight.a: Only the rate of descent changes
principles-of-flight.c: The ground glide path becomes shallower and the rate of descent is unchanged
principles-of-flight.d: The ground glide path becomes steeper and the rate of descent is unchanged
principles-of-flight.ans: The ground glide path becomes shallower and the rate of descent is unchanged
principles-of-flight.e: The aircraft's rate of descent through the air mass depends on its configuration and airspeed, not on the wind itself - the glide angle relative to the surrounding air is unchanged by a tailwind. What does change is groundspeed: covering more distance over the ground for the same height lost makes the glide path measured from the ground appear shallower, purely because groundspeed is higher.

principles-of-flight.q: During the approach to a power-off stall in level flight, what happens to control effectiveness?
principles-of-flight.a: It disappears instantly at high speed
principles-of-flight.d: It remains unchanged until the stall break
principles-of-flight.e: As the aircraft slows toward a power-off stall, the airflow reaching the control surfaces weakens right along with the falling airspeed, since control effectiveness depends directly on how fast air is moving over them. This produces the classic sluggish, increasingly mushy control feel that builds steadily as the approach to the stall continues, well before the stall itself occurs.

principles-of-flight.q: During a straight climb at constant speed, lift is how compared with weight?
principles-of-flight.e: Climbing steadily splits the aircraft's weight into two components: one opposing lift, one acting rearward along the flight path. Since lift now only has to balance the smaller, lift-opposing component of weight rather than the aircraft's full weight, lift ends up less than total weight during a constant-speed climb - the difference is carried by the extra thrust pulling the aircraft up the flight path.

principles-of-flight.q: During the autorotation stage of a spin to the left, which wing has the greater angle of attack?
principles-of-flight.b: Both wings have equal angle of attack
principles-of-flight.e: In a spin to the left, the left wing is the inner wing - travelling slower through its smaller radius of rotation - and it is this slower speed that pushes it to a higher angle of attack and deeper into the stall than the outer, faster-moving right wing. That asymmetry in angle of attack between the two wings is what sustains the autorotation.

principles-of-flight.q: In the International Standard Atmosphere, sea-level air density is what?
principles-of-flight.a: 760 grams per cubic metre and remains constant
principles-of-flight.b: 15 grams per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
principles-of-flight.c: 1225 grams per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
principles-of-flight.d: 1013 grams per cubic metre and increases with altitude
principles-of-flight.ans: 1225 grams per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
principles-of-flight.e: The International Standard Atmosphere fixes sea-level dry-air density at 1.225 kg/m³, or 1225 g/m³, alongside its other reference values of 15°C and 1013.25 hPa. Density then falls with altitude because there is progressively less air above pressing down, reducing pressure and packing fewer molecules into each cubic metre at height.

principles-of-flight.q: Va is used to indicate what?
principles-of-flight.e: Design manoeuvring speed (Va) is the fastest speed at which the wing is guaranteed to stall before a full, abrupt control deflection can overstress the airframe - a rule-of-thumb approximation is about 1.7 times the unaccelerated stall speed. At or below Va, any single full control input or gust should stall the wing first rather than build up a damaging load, which is exactly why Va is the speed to slow to in severe turbulence.

principles-of-flight.q: Vy is used to indicate what?
principles-of-flight.e: Vy, best rate of climb speed, is the airspeed that converts the most excess power into altitude gain per minute - it maximises height gained over time, which is what you want when climbing to cruise altitude efficiently rather than clearing a specific nearby obstacle.

principles-of-flight.q: In the ISA, the temperature lapse rate is approximately what?
principles-of-flight.e: The ISA fixes the tropospheric temperature decrease at 1.98°C per 1000 ft, starting from a sea-level reference of +15°C, and this rate holds up to the standard tropopause near 36,090 ft. It is the single reference lapse rate every density-altitude and performance correction is measured against.

principles-of-flight.q: The maximum speed at which the undercarriage may be operated is referred to as what?
principles-of-flight.e: Vlo, landing gear operating speed, is the maximum speed at which retractable gear may be extended or retracted. Operating the gear faster than this risks damaging the gear doors and mechanism, which are only built to handle the aerodynamic loads up to that specific limit.

principles-of-flight.q: TAS may also be described as CAS/RAS corrected for what?
principles-of-flight.e: Calibrated (or rectified) airspeed reads correctly at sea level under standard conditions, but as altitude increases the air thins and the aircraft must fly physically faster to push the same mass of air past the pitot tube. True airspeed accounts for this by correcting calibrated airspeed for the combined effects of temperature and altitude on air density.

principles-of-flight.q: Vne is what speed?
principles-of-flight.a: Speed that may not be exceeded in any operation
principles-of-flight.ans: Speed that may not be exceeded in any operation
principles-of-flight.e: Vne, marked by the red line on the airspeed indicator, is the never-exceed speed: the maximum speed the aircraft may be flown at in smooth air, under any circumstances. It should never be intentionally exceeded, since beyond it the airframe risks flutter or structural failure that the aircraft was never certified to withstand.

principles-of-flight.q: Vx is used to indicate what?
principles-of-flight.e: Vx, best angle of climb speed, trades rate of climb for the steepest possible climb path - it gains the most altitude over the shortest horizontal distance, which is exactly what's needed to clear an obstacle close beyond a short runway, even though it climbs fewer feet per minute than Vy.

principles-of-flight.q: What effect does increased humidity have on aircraft lift performance?
principles-of-flight.a: It has no effect on density
principles-of-flight.e: Humid air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure, because the water-vapour molecules mixed into it are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they displace. Since lift, thrust and propeller efficiency all depend on air density, that reduction in density translates directly into reduced aircraft performance on a humid day, even with temperature and pressure unchanged.

principles-of-flight.q: To protect structural integrity from gusts or manoeuvring, an aircraft should not normally be flown above which speed?
principles-of-flight.e: Vno, the upper limit of the green arc, is the maximum structural cruising speed - the fastest the aircraft should normally be flown except in smooth air. Beyond it, gusts or abrupt control inputs can impose loads the airframe wasn't designed for in anything but calm conditions, which is why the yellow caution arc above Vno exists specifically for smooth-air-only operation.

principles-of-flight.q: If pressure is kept constant and temperature is increased, what happens to density?
principles-of-flight.e: At constant pressure, heating air makes it expand - the same mass of molecules now spreads out to fill a larger volume. Since density is simply mass divided by volume, that expansion is what causes density to fall as temperature rises, with nothing added or removed from the air itself.

principles-of-flight.q: Regarding humidity and air density, humid air is what?
principles-of-flight.b: The same density as dry air
principles-of-flight.e: Humid air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure, because water-vapour molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they replace in the mixture. This lower density is exactly why humid conditions degrade an aircraft's takeoff and climb performance compared to a dry day with identical temperature and pressure.

principles-of-flight.q: Vfe is used to indicate what?
principles-of-flight.e: Vfe, the top of the white arc, is the maximum speed at which flaps may be extended without risking severe strain or structural failure of the flap system. Flying faster than Vfe with flaps out subjects the flap structure and its attachment points to aerodynamic loads well beyond what they're built for.

principles-of-flight.q: ISA assumptions include which of the following?
principles-of-flight.b: MSL temperature 15°C and lapse rate 1.98°C/1000 ft up to about 36 090 ft
principles-of-flight.c: MSL temperature 0°C and no lapse rate
principles-of-flight.ans: MSL temperature 15°C and lapse rate 1.98°C/1000 ft up to about 36 090 ft
principles-of-flight.e: The ISA fixes a specific set of sea-level reference conditions so aircraft performance figures mean the same thing everywhere: +15°C, 1013.25 hPa, and a standard tropospheric lapse rate of about 1.98°C per 1000 ft up to the tropopause near 36,090 ft. Every density-altitude and performance calculation is measured as a deviation from this fixed baseline.

principles-of-flight.q: True airspeed is calibrated or rectified airspeed corrected for what?
principles-of-flight.e: True airspeed starts from calibrated (or rectified) airspeed - already corrected for instrument and position error - and adds a further correction for temperature and density, since a pitot-static system measures dynamic pressure, not speed directly. In thinner, colder, or warmer-than-standard air, the same true airspeed produces a different dynamic pressure, so this final correction is what recovers the aircraft's actual speed through the air.

principles-of-flight.q: If the temperature of a dry parcel of air is kept constant, what happens to density when pressure increases?
principles-of-flight.e: At constant temperature, raising the pressure on a parcel of dry air compresses it, forcing the same mass of air molecules into a smaller volume. Since density is mass per unit volume, packing the same mass into less space is, by definition, an increase in density.

principles-of-flight.q: In the ISA, mean sea-level temperature is what?
principles-of-flight.e: The ISA fixes +15°C as the standard mean sea-level temperature, alongside 1013.25 hPa pressure and 1.225 kg/m³ density. This is the fixed baseline every ISA-deviation, density-altitude and performance calculation is measured from.

principles-of-flight.q: Rectified airspeed or calibrated airspeed is IAS corrected for what?
principles-of-flight.e: Indicated airspeed comes straight off the gauge with no corrections applied at all. Calibrated (rectified) airspeed removes the errors introduced by imperfect pitot-static installation and the instrument mechanism itself - errors that are usually largest at low speeds and with flaps extended, and shrink to nearly nothing in the cruise.

principles-of-flight.q: An increase in induced drag can be expected:-
principles-of-flight.a: when the angle of attack is increased
principles-of-flight.b: when the angle of attack is decreased
principles-of-flight.c: when speed is increased in level flight
principles-of-flight.ans: when the angle of attack is increased
principles-of-flight.e: Raising the angle of attack increases the wing's lift coefficient, which in turn strengthens both the pressure difference driving lift and the downwash trailing behind the wing. Induced drag is a direct consequence of that downwash, so it rises whenever angle of attack does - exactly why induced drag dominates at low speed, when a high angle of attack is needed to stay aloft.

principles-of-flight.q: The correct operation of anti-balance tab can be checked before flight by moving the stabilator and observing that:-
principles-of-flight.a: the tab moves opposite to the stabilator
principles-of-flight.b: the anti-balance tab moves in the same direction as the elevator
principles-of-flight.c: the tab moves only after full control deflection
principles-of-flight.d: the tab remains fixed while the stabilator moves
principles-of-flight.ans: the anti-balance tab moves in the same direction as the elevator
principles-of-flight.e: Unlike a balance tab, an adjustable trim tab is set by the pilot to a chosen angle relative to the control surface and stays at that fixed setting - it does not move in response to the elevator being deflected. Its whole purpose is to hold a constant aerodynamic force that balances the aircraft's pitching moment for hands-off flight at the trimmed speed, which only works if it stays put while the elevator itself moves freely.

principles-of-flight.q: The total lift produced by the wings during a balanced level turn, must equal:-
principles-of-flight.b: the vertical component of lift and the centripetal force.
principles-of-flight.d: the vertical component of lift only
principles-of-flight.ans: the vertical component of lift and the centripetal force.
principles-of-flight.e: In a level turn the wing's single tilted lift vector must simultaneously do two jobs: its vertical component balances the aircraft's weight to hold altitude, and its horizontal component supplies the centripetal force that curves the flight path. Total lift is the resultant needed to satisfy both requirements at once, which is exactly why it must exceed the straight-and-level value as bank steepens.

principles-of-flight.q: A mass balance, extending ahead of the hinge line, is attached to the leading edge of a control surface in order to:-
principles-of-flight.c: reduce induced drag in the climb
principles-of-flight.d: increase elevator authority at the stall
principles-of-flight.e: A control surface with its mass sitting behind the hinge line is vulnerable to flutter - a rapid, self-reinforcing oscillation driven by inertial and aerodynamic forces feeding off each other as speed builds. Adding weight ahead of the hinge line, a mass balance, shifts the centre of mass forward enough to break that feedback loop, making it the standard, simple flutter-prevention fitted to most light aircraft control surfaces.

principles-of-flight.q: During normal level flight a reduction in power will cause the nose of an aeroplane to drop because:-
principles-of-flight.a: the thrust line moves above the drag line
principles-of-flight.b: the centre of pressure is ahead of the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.c: the centre of gravity is located forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.d: the tailplane stops producing any force
principles-of-flight.ans: the centre of gravity is located forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: Because the centre of gravity sits forward of the centre of pressure in normal flight, the wing is always producing a nose-down pitching tendency that the tailplane's balancing download continuously counteracts - and that download partly depends on airflow driven by power. Reducing power weakens that balancing effect relative to the CG-forward pitching moment, so the nose tends to drop.

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane which has a high lift/drag ratio:-
principles-of-flight.a: will have a shallow gliding angle
principles-of-flight.b: will have a high stalling speed only
principles-of-flight.c: will descend vertically at idle power
principles-of-flight.d: will have a steep gliding angle
