principles-of-flight.ans: will have a shallow gliding angle
principles-of-flight.e: A high lift-to-drag ratio means the aircraft covers a lot of forward distance for every unit of altitude it gives up - the defining trait of an efficient glide. That favourable trade-off between lift and drag is exactly what translates into a shallow gliding angle, the flattest possible descent for a given height loss.

principles-of-flight.q: A design feature which is used to reduce induced drag is:-
principles-of-flight.e: Washout reduces the wingtip's angle of incidence relative to the root, lowering the local angle of attack - and with it the local lift and induced drag - at the tip specifically. Trimming lift generation at the tip, where the vortex-driving pressure differential is strongest, is exactly what reduces the wing's overall induced drag while also protecting against tip stall.

principles-of-flight.q: The position which separates the laminar air flow from the turbulent air flow around an aerofoil is called:-
principles-of-flight.e: Moving aft along an aerofoil surface, the boundary layer starts out smooth and orderly (laminar flow near the leading edge) before becoming chaotic and mixing (turbulent flow further aft). The exact point where that changeover happens is called the transition point, and its position shifts with surface finish, Reynolds number and the pressure gradient along the chord.

principles-of-flight.q: A change in yaw will cause an aircraft to rotate around its:-
principles-of-flight.a: lateral axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.b: longitudinal axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.c: vertical axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.d: chord line and centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: vertical axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.e: Yaw is rotation about the vertical axis, an imaginary line running through the centre of gravity - the single point through which all three of the aircraft's rotational axes intersect. It is this axis, controlled by the rudder, that governs the nose swinging left or right.

principles-of-flight.q: If the centre of gravity is moved forward during flight, the effect will:-
principles-of-flight.e: Moving the CG forward lengthens the moment arm between the centre of gravity and the centre of pressure, giving the tailplane more leverage to restore the aircraft after any pitch disturbance - increasing longitudinal stability. The trade-off is that this same longer arm demands more elevator force to overcome during rotation on takeoff and the flare on landing.

principles-of-flight.q: On an aerofoil, the point through which the total lift force acts is known as:-
principles-of-flight.e: Although lift is generated as varying pressure spread across the entire wing surface, it is convenient to represent that whole distributed force as if it acted through one single point along the chord - the centre of pressure. That point is not fixed in place; it shifts forward or aft as angle of attack, flap setting and airspeed change, which is exactly why it matters so much to an aircraft's pitch stability.

principles-of-flight.q: If, during level flight, altitude must be maintained whilst reducing speed the:-
principles-of-flight.b: angle of attack must be increased
principles-of-flight.c: angle of attack must be decreased
principles-of-flight.d: centre of gravity must move aft
principles-of-flight.ans: angle of attack must be increased
principles-of-flight.e: Lift depends on both airspeed and angle of attack working together to produce the same total force needed to support the aircraft's weight. Slowing down in level flight reduces the dynamic pressure available, so angle of attack has to increase to make up the difference and keep generating the lift needed to hold altitude.

principles-of-flight.q: The forces acting on an aeroplane in a climb are so arranged that:-
principles-of-flight.c: the value of lift is less than that of weight
principles-of-flight.ans: the value of lift is less than that of weight
principles-of-flight.e: During a steady climb, gravity's effect on the aircraft splits into two components relative to the flight path: one opposing lift, and one acting rearward like extra drag. Because lift then only has to balance its own, reduced share of the aircraft's weight, lift is less than the aircraft's actual total weight throughout the climb.

principles-of-flight.q: Stability in the rolling plane of an aeroplane is a function of:-
principles-of-flight.e: Stability in the rolling plane is lateral stability, and the wing's dihedral - its upward slant from root to tip - is the main design feature responsible. When a wing drops, the resulting sideslip gives the lower wing a greater effective angle of attack, and the extra lift it produces rolls the aircraft back toward level.

principles-of-flight.q: Adverse aileron yaw, (aileron drag), will be most noticeable:-
principles-of-flight.a: at a high angle of attack
principles-of-flight.b: only when flaps are fully retracted
principles-of-flight.c: at low angle of attack and high speed
principles-of-flight.ans: at a high angle of attack
principles-of-flight.e: Because induced drag rises with angle of attack, the drag spike created by a down-going aileron (extra lift, extra drag on that wing) grows disproportionately large at high angles of attack - exactly when the wing is already closest to its performance limits, such as in a slow, steeply banked turn. That is why adverse aileron yaw becomes far more pronounced at high angle of attack than it is in normal cruise flight.

principles-of-flight.q: A change in pitch will cause an aircraft to rotate around its:-
principles-of-flight.a: relative airflow and centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.b: vertical axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.c: longitudinal axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.d: lateral axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.ans: lateral axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.e: Pitch is rotation about the lateral axis, running wingtip to wingtip through the centre of gravity - the common point every one of the aircraft's three rotational axes passes through. The elevator controls rotation about this specific axis.

principles-of-flight.q: As the angle of attack of an aerofoil in normal level flight is increased, the centre of pressure will:-
principles-of-flight.c: remain fixed at the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.e: Raising angle of attack accelerates the airflow further over the upper surface, and that faster flow's low-pressure region shifts toward the leading edge as it does. This pulls the centre of pressure - the effective point of the wing's combined lift - forward along the chord as angle of attack increases in normal flight.

principles-of-flight.q: Whilst maintaining level flight, a decrease in speed will result in an increase in:-
principles-of-flight.e: Slowing down in level flight forces the wing to fly at a higher angle of attack to keep generating enough lift to support the aircraft's weight. Since induced drag grows directly with angle of attack, it rises sharply as speed falls - the dominant drag penalty of flying slower.

principles-of-flight.q: The relationship between the four forces in level flight is that:-
principles-of-flight.a: lift is less than weight and thrust is greater than drag
principles-of-flight.b: lift is equal to drag and thrust is equal to weight
principles-of-flight.c: lift is greater than weight and thrust is equal to drag
principles-of-flight.d: lift is equal to weight and thrust is equal to drag
principles-of-flight.ans: lift is equal to weight and thrust is equal to drag
principles-of-flight.e: Steady, unaccelerated level flight at constant speed requires two separate balances at once: the vertical forces (lift and weight) must be equal so altitude holds steady, and the horizontal forces (thrust and drag) must be equal so speed holds steady. Break either balance and the aircraft either climbs/descends or speeds up/slows down.

principles-of-flight.q: When a wing has been given washout, it means that the wing will:-
principles-of-flight.a: have no geometric twist at all
principles-of-flight.b: have an increase in angle of incidence towards the wingtip
principles-of-flight.c: have a decrease in the angle of incidence towards the wingtip
principles-of-flight.d: have equal angle of incidence from root to tip
principles-of-flight.ans: have a decrease in the angle of incidence towards the wingtip
principles-of-flight.e: A washed-out wing has its angle of incidence deliberately reduced from root to tip, so the wingtip is set at a shallower angle than the root. Because the root then reaches its critical angle of attack before the tip does, the wing tends to stall from the root outward, leaving the ailerons near the tip still effective for roll control during the early stages of a stall.

principles-of-flight.q: Induced drag caused by pressure differences around a lifting wing is mainly due to:-
principles-of-flight.a: the pressure difference between the top and bottom surfaces
principles-of-flight.b: skin friction in the boundary layer
principles-of-flight.ans: the pressure difference between the top and bottom surfaces
principles-of-flight.e: Lift itself only exists because of a pressure difference between a wing's lower and upper surfaces, and that same pressure difference drives air to curl around the wingtips from high pressure below to low pressure above, rolling up into vortices. Induced drag is the direct aerodynamic penalty of that pressure difference, which is why it scales with however much lift the wing is producing.

principles-of-flight.q: Induced drag is produced as a result of:-
principles-of-flight.a: the lift produced by the wings.
principles-of-flight.c: static pressure increasing below sea level
principles-of-flight.ans: the lift produced by the wings.
principles-of-flight.e: Induced drag exists purely as an unavoidable byproduct of generating lift - the wingtip vortices and downwash caused by the pressure difference between the wing's surfaces tilt part of the lift vector rearward into drag. No lift means no induced drag at all, which is why it scales directly with however much lift the wing is asked to produce.

principles-of-flight.q: During a straight climb at a constant speed:-
principles-of-flight.a: lift is equal to weight and thrust is less than drag
principles-of-flight.e: Climbing at constant speed splits the aircraft's weight into a lift-opposing component and a rearward, drag-like component along the flight path. Lift only has to balance the smaller of these two components, so it ends up being less than the aircraft's full weight - with thrust making up the rest by overcoming both the wing's drag and that rearward weight component.

principles-of-flight.q: Balance tabs are normally adjusted to move:-
principles-of-flight.a: only when the aircraft is on the ground
principles-of-flight.b: in the same direction as the primary control surface
principles-of-flight.c: opposite direction to the primary control surface
principles-of-flight.d: only upward regardless of control movement
principles-of-flight.ans: opposite direction to the primary control surface
principles-of-flight.e: Balance tabs are rigged to move opposite to the main control surface - when the surface deflects one way, the tab deflects the other. That opposite deflection generates an aerodynamic force that actively helps drive the main surface further, reducing the physical effort the pilot needs to apply.

principles-of-flight.q: The angle between an aerofoil's chord line and the relative airflow is referred to as:-
principles-of-flight.e: The angle of attack is specifically defined as the angle between the aerofoil's chord line (the straight reference from leading to trailing edge) and the relative airflow meeting the wing - not the aircraft's pitch attitude relative to the horizon, and not the angle of incidence, which is a fixed structural angle rather than one that changes with flight condition.

principles-of-flight.q: On an aerofoil, the point through which the total lift acts is called the:-
principles-of-flight.e: Although the wing's lift is really distributed as varying pressure across the entire surface, it is represented for practical purposes as though it all acted through a single point on the chord - the centre of pressure. That point shifts position as angle of attack, flaps and airspeed change, which is exactly why its behaviour matters so much to pitch stability.

principles-of-flight.q: During straight and level flight the centre of gravity is normally located:-
principles-of-flight.a: forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.c: aft of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.d: at the same point as the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: In straight and level flight, the centre of gravity normally sits forward of the centre of pressure, creating a nose-down pitching tendency that the tailplane continuously balances with a small download - the standard, stable pitch arrangement built into most light aircraft.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the lift formula. If an aeroplane's speed is doubled whilst the angle of attack remains constant, the parasite drag will:-
principles-of-flight.e: Lift and parasite drag both scale with dynamic pressure, which depends on the square of speed (q = ½ρV²). Doubling speed quadruples dynamic pressure, so with angle of attack held constant, parasite drag becomes four times greater - not simply double.

principles-of-flight.q: In order to counteract the effect of control flutter, the type of control balance most commonly used in a light aeroplane is:-
principles-of-flight.e: Concentrating a control surface's mass aft of its hinge line makes it prone to flutter, a rapidly self-reinforcing oscillation as inertial and aerodynamic forces feed off each other with increasing airspeed. A mass balance - added weight ahead of the hinge - shifts that centre of mass forward enough to prevent the feedback loop from developing, making it the standard, lightweight flutter countermeasure on light aircraft.

principles-of-flight.q: An adjustable trim tab, when attached to an elevator, will, when the elevator is moved:-
principles-of-flight.a: remain at the same position irrespective of the deflection of the control surface
principles-of-flight.b: move opposite to the elevator automatically
principles-of-flight.c: lock the elevator in its trimmed position
principles-of-flight.d: move in the same direction as the elevator
principles-of-flight.ans: remain at the same position irrespective of the deflection of the control surface
principles-of-flight.e: Unlike a balance tab, which is rigged to move opposite to the control surface it's attached to, an adjustable trim tab is simply set to a chosen fixed angle and stays there regardless of how much the elevator itself is deflected. Holding that constant angle is exactly what lets it produce a steady aerodynamic force that balances the aircraft's pitching moment for hands-off flight.

principles-of-flight.q: In accordance with Bernoulli's theory when air flows through the throat of a venturi tube:-
principles-of-flight.c: the velocity decreases and the pressure increases
principles-of-flight.d: the velocity increases and the pressure decreases
principles-of-flight.ans: the velocity increases and the pressure decreases
principles-of-flight.e: Bernoulli's principle links speed and pressure inversely - wherever a fluid speeds up, its pressure falls. Continuity forces air to accelerate through the narrowing throat of a venturi tube, and that acceleration comes with a corresponding drop in static pressure.

principles-of-flight.q: In order to maintain elevator control effectiveness, when loading an aeroplane it would be better to:-
principles-of-flight.a: load all baggage behind the rear seats
principles-of-flight.b: load the CG beyond the aft limit
principles-of-flight.c: have a forward centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.d: place the CG behind the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: have a forward centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.e: The elevator has to overcome the pitching moment created by the distance between the centre of gravity and the centre of pressure, and a forward CG lengthens that moment arm, giving the tailplane - and so the elevator - more leverage to work with at any given deflection. That extra leverage is what keeps elevator control comfortably effective across the flight envelope, including during the landing flare.

principles-of-flight.q: A change in bank will cause an aircraft to rotate around its:-
principles-of-flight.a: lateral axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.b: vertical axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.c: longitudinal axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.d: chord line and centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: longitudinal axis and centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.e: Bank is rotation about the longitudinal axis, running nose to tail through the centre of gravity - the common point every one of the aircraft's three rotational axes passes through. Ailerons control rotation about this specific axis.

principles-of-flight.q: An anti-balance or anti-servo tab which is incorporated in a stabilator will:-
principles-of-flight.b: move in the same direction as the control surface
principles-of-flight.d: move opposite to the control surface
principles-of-flight.ans: move in the same direction as the control surface
principles-of-flight.e: An anti-balance (or anti-servo) tab is deliberately rigged to move in the same direction as the stabilator, not opposite it. That same-direction deflection creates an opposing aerodynamic force that adds resistance to the control, deliberately making it heavier - exactly what's needed to stop a highly sensitive stabilator from being over-controlled.

principles-of-flight.q: An aircraft which has its CG too far aft would:-
principles-of-flight.a: require less elevator control near the stall
principles-of-flight.c: be difficult to control in pitch
principles-of-flight.ans: be difficult to control in pitch
principles-of-flight.e: With the CG too far aft, the moment arm between the CG and the centre of pressure shrinks, leaving the tailplane with very little leverage to restore the aircraft after any pitch disturbance. The result is an overly sensitive, edgy pitch response, along with degraded nose-down authority for stall and spin recovery.

principles-of-flight.q: Balance tabs are adjusted in order to:-
principles-of-flight.c: remove aerodynamic forces from the controls
principles-of-flight.d: increase the stalling angle of attack
principles-of-flight.ans: remove aerodynamic forces from the controls
principles-of-flight.e: Balance tabs deflect opposite to the main control surface specifically to generate an aerodynamic force that assists the surface's movement rather than resisting it. By taking on part of the aerodynamic load that would otherwise be felt entirely at the stick or pedals, they reduce the physical effort the pilot needs to move the controls.

principles-of-flight.q: If the gross weight of an aircraft is increased:-
principles-of-flight.a: parasite drag will decrease more than induced drag
principles-of-flight.b: there will be a greater increase in induced drag than in parasite drag
principles-of-flight.c: total drag will remain unchanged at the same speed
principles-of-flight.d: induced drag will reduce because wing loading is higher
principles-of-flight.ans: there will be a greater increase in induced drag than in parasite drag
principles-of-flight.e: A heavier aircraft needs its wing to produce more total lift, which it primarily achieves by flying at a higher angle of attack rather than through the small speed change involved. Because induced drag responds far more strongly to angle of attack than parasite drag does to the resulting minor speed change, extra weight drives up induced drag noticeably more than parasite drag.

principles-of-flight.q: Bernoulli's principle states that if the velocity of air flowing through a venturi is increased, then the:-
principles-of-flight.b: density must remain constant and pressure must increase
principles-of-flight.e: Bernoulli's principle states that the pressure energy of a moving fluid decreases wherever its speed increases, since the fluid's total energy has to remain constant. Through a venturi's narrowing throat, continuity forces the air to speed up, and that rise in velocity comes at the direct expense of its pressure energy.

principles-of-flight.q: In respect of an aeroplane's wing, the term "aspect ratio" refers to the ratio of:-
principles-of-flight.a: the wingspan to the mean aerodynamic chord.
principles-of-flight.b: lift to drag at best glide
principles-of-flight.c: the root chord to the tip chord
principles-of-flight.ans: the wingspan to the mean aerodynamic chord.
principles-of-flight.e: Aspect ratio describes the relationship between a wing's span and its mean aerodynamic chord: a long, slender wing (like a glider's) has a high aspect ratio, while a short, stubby wing has a low one. This shape ratio directly affects how strong the wingtip vortices are relative to the wing's overall lift, and therefore how much induced drag the wing produces for a given amount of lift.

principles-of-flight.q: An increase in the angle of attack of an aerofoil will:-
principles-of-flight.a: have no effect until the aircraft stalls
principles-of-flight.b: decrease pressure below the wing and decrease drag
principles-of-flight.c: increase the pressure below the wing and increase drag.
principles-of-flight.d: increase pressure above the wing and reduce drag
principles-of-flight.ans: increase the pressure below the wing and increase drag.
principles-of-flight.e: Increasing angle of attack tilts the wing further into the airflow, raising pressure on the lower surface as the airstream is deflected downward more strongly. That stronger downward deflection (Newton's reaction) and the widened pressure differential across the wing both increase lift together with drag, particularly the induced drag component.

principles-of-flight.q: The lift force produced by an aerofoil always acts:-
principles-of-flight.e: Lift is defined by convention as the aerodynamic force acting perpendicular to the relative airflow, not straight up relative to the ground or the horizon. Because the relative airflow's direction changes with the aircraft's flight path - climbing, descending, or turning - the actual direction lift points relative to the earth changes right along with it.

principles-of-flight.q: The use of horn balance in an aeroplane:-
principles-of-flight.b: improves the aerodynamic balance of the controls
principles-of-flight.ans: improves the aerodynamic balance of the controls
principles-of-flight.e: A horn balance projects part of the control surface forward of its hinge line, out into the airflow. The aerodynamic force acting on that forward section works in the same direction as the pilot's intended deflection, offsetting some of the force the pilot would otherwise have to supply - which is exactly what "improving aerodynamic balance" means.

principles-of-flight.q: Whilst maintaining straight and level flight:-
principles-of-flight.a: the centre of pressure and centre of gravity are always the same point
principles-of-flight.b: the centre of gravity is located behind the tailplane
principles-of-flight.c: the centre of pressure is located ahead of the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.d: the centre of pressure is located behind the centre of gravity.
principles-of-flight.ans: the centre of pressure is located behind the centre of gravity.
principles-of-flight.e: In straight and level flight, the wing's centre of pressure - the effective point where its combined lift force acts - normally sits behind the centre of gravity, creating a nose-down pitching moment that the tailplane's small download continuously balances. This forward-CG, aft-CP arrangement is the standard, stable pitch geometry built into most light aircraft.

principles-of-flight.q: A factor which will affect the longitudinal stability of an aeroplane is:-
principles-of-flight.c: the position of the centre of gravity relative to the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: the position of the centre of gravity relative to the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: Pitch stability is set by the moment arm between the centre of gravity and the centre of pressure - the further apart these two points sit, the more leverage the tailplane has to restore the aircraft after any pitch disturbance. Because that CG-to-CP distance is exactly what the loading process controls, CG position relative to the centre of pressure is the primary factor determining longitudinal stability.

principles-of-flight.q: If the centre of gravity is moved aft during flight, the effect will be:-
principles-of-flight.d: to move the centre of pressure forward permanently
principles-of-flight.e: Moving the CG aft shortens the moment arm between the centre of gravity and the centre of pressure, leaving the tailplane with less leverage to generate a restoring moment after any pitch disturbance. That weakened restoring effect is exactly what reduces longitudinal stability as the CG moves aft.

principles-of-flight.q: The angle of attack of an aeroplane is defined as the angle:-
principles-of-flight.a: between the relative airflow and the horizon
principles-of-flight.b: between the chord line and the relative airflow
principles-of-flight.c: between the fuselage centreline and the ground
principles-of-flight.d: between the chord line and the longitudinal axis
principles-of-flight.ans: between the chord line and the relative airflow
principles-of-flight.e: Angle of attack is measured strictly between the aerofoil's chord line and the relative airflow meeting the wing, not between the aircraft's fuselage or wing and the horizon. This distinction matters because an aircraft's pitch attitude and its angle of attack can be quite different numbers depending on the direction of the relative airflow at that moment.

principles-of-flight.q: In comparison to a high aspect ratio wing, a low aspect ratio wing will:-
principles-of-flight.b: produce less parasite drag at all speeds
principles-of-flight.e: A low aspect ratio wing concentrates the same total lift over a shorter span, which strengthens the wingtip vortices relative to the wing's overall size and increases induced drag for a given amount of lift. A high aspect ratio wing spreads that same lift over a longer span, producing proportionally weaker vortices and less induced drag - the trade-off behind why gliders favour long, slender wings.

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane will stall as a result of:-
principles-of-flight.a: increasing bank angle below 30 degrees only
principles-of-flight.b: flying below the published stall speed only
principles-of-flight.c: exceeding the critical angle of attack
principles-of-flight.d: reducing power in level flight only
principles-of-flight.ans: exceeding the critical angle of attack
principles-of-flight.e: A stall happens purely because the critical angle of attack has been exceeded - the airflow separates from the wing's upper surface and lift collapses. Since that critical angle can be reached at any airspeed, attitude or power setting, a stall is fundamentally about angle of attack, not about flying too slowly in absolute terms.

principles-of-flight.q: The stalling angle of attack of a particular aerofoil:-
principles-of-flight.b: will remain constant irrespective of airspeed bank angle or weight
principles-of-flight.ans: will remain constant irrespective of airspeed bank angle or weight
principles-of-flight.e: For a given wing shape and configuration, the stalling angle of attack is a fixed geometric property that doesn't shift with airspeed, bank angle or weight. Those factors only change the speed at which the wing happens to reach that same fixed critical angle - which is why stall speed varies with conditions while stall angle does not.

principles-of-flight.q: Longitudinal dihedral is a design feature used as a method of improving stability:-
principles-of-flight.e: Longitudinal dihedral - the tailplane set at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane - is designed to restore the aircraft after a nose-up or nose-down disturbance, motion that happens by rotating about the lateral axis. That axis-specific restoring effect is exactly why it is described as improving stability about the lateral axis, distinct from wing dihedral's role in roll stability.

principles-of-flight.q: During the approach to a power off stall in level flight:-
principles-of-flight.a: control effectiveness remains unchanged until the stall break
principles-of-flight.b: rudder effectiveness increases but elevator effectiveness does not change
principles-of-flight.d: control effectiveness decreases at a steady rate.
principles-of-flight.ans: control effectiveness decreases at a steady rate.
principles-of-flight.e: As airspeed bleeds off approaching a power-off stall, the flow of air over the control surfaces weakens in direct proportion, since control effectiveness depends on airflow speed. That produces the classic steady loss of crispness in the controls - increasingly sluggish and mushy - well before the wing actually stalls.

principles-of-flight.q: The primary and further effects of rudder are:-
principles-of-flight.a: yaw only with no secondary effect
principles-of-flight.b: roll then yaw followed by a spiral dive
principles-of-flight.c: pitch then speed change followed by a dive
principles-of-flight.d: yaw then roll followed by a spiral dive
principles-of-flight.ans: yaw then roll followed by a spiral dive
principles-of-flight.e: Rudder's primary effect is yaw. But yawing the nose makes one wing briefly travel faster than the other, generating extra lift on that side and rolling the aircraft as a secondary effect - and if left uncorrected, that combined roll and yaw can develop into a spiral dive that steepens and accelerates on its own.

principles-of-flight.q: The force required by an aeroplane to make it turn is:-
principles-of-flight.a: called centrifugal force and is produced by the tailplane
principles-of-flight.b: called centripetal force and is created by the wings
principles-of-flight.c: called parasite force and is created by drag
principles-of-flight.d: called thrust force and is created by the propeller
principles-of-flight.ans: called centripetal force and is created by the wings
principles-of-flight.e: Turning the flight path requires a continuous pull toward the centre of the curve - centripetal force - and the only source of sideways aerodynamic force an aircraft has is its wings. Banking tilts the lift vector so part of it points horizontally, and that horizontal component of lift is what actually curves the aircraft's path, which is why it is called centripetal force.

principles-of-flight.q: The stalling angle of attack of an aeroplane:-
principles-of-flight.b: remains constant regardless of airspeed or weight
principles-of-flight.ans: remains constant regardless of airspeed or weight
principles-of-flight.e: The stalling angle of attack is a fixed property of a given wing's shape and configuration - it stays essentially the same no matter how fast the aircraft is flying or how much it weighs. What varies with airspeed and weight is only the specific speed at which the wing happens to reach that same fixed critical angle.

principles-of-flight.q: The application of trailing edge flaps will:-
principles-of-flight.a: increase the stalling angle of attack
principles-of-flight.b: reduce drag and increase glide range
principles-of-flight.c: increase the lift/drag ratio and flatten the glide angle
principles-of-flight.d: decrease the lift/drag ratio and increase the glide angle.
principles-of-flight.ans: decrease the lift/drag ratio and increase the glide angle.
principles-of-flight.e: Trailing-edge flaps add more drag than useful lift-to-drag benefit at glide speeds, pulling the aircraft away from its cleanest, most efficient configuration and reducing the L/D ratio. With less forward distance covered for the same height lost, the glide angle - measured as the angle below the horizontal - becomes larger, meaning a steeper, shorter glide.

principles-of-flight.q: A passenger carrying aeroplane is usually designed to have:-
principles-of-flight.e: A well-behaved passenger aircraft needs more than just an initial tendency to recover from a disturbance - it needs any resulting oscillation to actually die away over time rather than persist or grow. That damping behaviour is positive dynamic stability, and it is a deliberate, essential design goal for any aircraft carrying passengers.

principles-of-flight.q: Application of trailing edge flaps will:-
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps do increase the wing's lift coefficient, but the accompanying rise in drag outweighs that benefit at typical glide speeds, since the extra drag isn't matched by a proportional gain in useful lift-to-drag performance. The net effect moves the aircraft away from its cleanest, most efficient configuration, reducing the overall lift-to-drag ratio.

principles-of-flight.q: Trailing edge flaps are provided on an aeroplane in order to:-
principles-of-flight.a: increase the stalling angle of attack only
principles-of-flight.c: move the centre of gravity aft
principles-of-flight.d: increase the value of lift created by the wing at a particular angle of attack and airspeed
principles-of-flight.ans: increase the value of lift created by the wing at a particular angle of attack and airspeed
principles-of-flight.e: Trailing-edge flaps increase a wing's camber, and a more cambered aerofoil produces a higher lift coefficient - more lift - at any given angle of attack and airspeed. That single mechanism is the core reason flaps exist at all: it lets the wing generate enough lift to fly safely at a slower speed than it could manage in the clean configuration.

principles-of-flight.q: During a turn an aeroplane stalls at a higher IAS than it does with the wings level:-
principles-of-flight.a: because the critical angle of attack changes with bank angle
principles-of-flight.b: because the wing loading is reduced in the turn
principles-of-flight.c: because parasite drag is lower in the turn
principles-of-flight.d: because the critical angle of attack is reached at a higher IAS.
principles-of-flight.ans: because the critical angle of attack is reached at a higher IAS.
principles-of-flight.e: Turning increases the load factor on the wing, since it now has to produce extra lift to both support the aircraft and curve the flight path. That extra lift demand means the wing needs a higher angle of attack at any given speed, so its fixed critical angle of attack - and the stall - is reached at a higher indicated airspeed than it would be with the wings level.

principles-of-flight.q: Flaps are provided on many light aeroplanes in order to:-
principles-of-flight.b: reduce lift and drag during landing
principles-of-flight.c: increase both the lift and the drag
principles-of-flight.d: increase lift but reduce drag at all speeds
principles-of-flight.ans: increase both the lift and the drag
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps increase the wing's maximum lift coefficient, allowing slower, safer take-off and landing speeds, but that added camber comes with more drag as an unavoidable side effect. Rather than being a downside, this extra drag is put to use during approach - it permits a steeper descent path without the speed increasing, giving pilots better control over the approach profile.

principles-of-flight.q: In order to initiate spin recovery the controls should be used in the following manner:-
principles-of-flight.e: Spin recovery begins with rudder, applied opposite to the direction of rotation, to stop the autorotation first. Only once the yaw has been arrested does applying forward elevator to reduce angle of attack actually unstall the wings cleanly - using elevator before the rotation has stopped can prolong the spin instead of ending it.

principles-of-flight.q: Longitudinal dihedral is a design feature which may be used to improve stability:-
principles-of-flight.e: Pitch is rotation about the lateral axis, and longitudinal dihedral - the tailplane rigged at a lower angle of incidence than the mainplane - is the specific design feature that generates a restoring moment whenever the aircraft pitches away from its trimmed attitude. That is exactly why it improves stability in the pitching plane rather than the rolling or yawing planes.

principles-of-flight.q: The effect of maintaining engine power at the stall will be:-
principles-of-flight.a: to have no effect on stalling speed
principles-of-flight.b: to increase the critical angle of attack permanently
principles-of-flight.c: to cause an increase in stalling speed
principles-of-flight.d: to cause a reduction in the stalling speed
principles-of-flight.ans: to cause a reduction in the stalling speed
principles-of-flight.e: Keeping power on at the stall lets propeller slipstream wash extra airflow over the wing root, delaying separation there, while the propeller's thrust also develops a small upward component that helps carry part of the aircraft's weight directly. With less lift needing to come purely from angle of attack, the wing can be flown slower before it actually reaches its critical angle - reducing the stalling speed compared with a power-off stall.

principles-of-flight.q: The potential of a normal spin to develop into a flat spin increases with:-
principles-of-flight.e: Recovering from a spin relies on the nose dropping enough to reduce the stalled wing's angle of attack once rudder and elevator are applied. With an aft centre of gravity, that natural nose-down tendency is weaker, making it easier for the spin to flatten - rotating with the nose closer to the horizon - a configuration that is significantly harder to recover from, and in some aircraft may not be recoverable at all.

principles-of-flight.q: A design feature used in some aeroplanes to improve lateral stability:-
principles-of-flight.e: Dihedral - the upward slant of the wings from root to tip - is the classic design feature for improving lateral stability. When a wing drops, the resulting sideslip gives the lower wing a greater effective angle of attack and more lift than the upper wing, and that lift imbalance rolls the aircraft back toward wings-level flight.

principles-of-flight.q: Directional stability in an aeroplane is achieved:-
principles-of-flight.e: Directional stability comes from the vertical fin, mounted well aft of the centre of gravity, which acts like a weathervane: any yaw that misaligns the aircraft with the relative airflow produces a sideways aerodynamic force on the fin that swings the tail back into alignment, restoring the original heading.

principles-of-flight.q: During a flapless approach to land the nose position of the aeroplane will, in relation to a normal approach with full flap, be:-
principles-of-flight.e: Without flaps, the wing has less camber and must be flown at a higher angle of attack to produce the lift needed at approach speed. In the conventional light-aircraft case, that translates into a visibly higher nose attitude than the lower, flap-assisted nose position seen on a normal full-flap approach.

principles-of-flight.q: If the temperature of a dry parcel of air is kept constant:-
principles-of-flight.a: density will only change if humidity changes
principles-of-flight.b: an increase in pressure will result in an increase in density
principles-of-flight.c: an increase in pressure will reduce density
principles-of-flight.d: density will remain constant regardless of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: an increase in pressure will result in an increase in density
principles-of-flight.e: At constant temperature, increasing pressure on a parcel of dry air compresses it, forcing the same mass of molecules into a smaller volume. Since density is mass divided by volume, squeezing the same mass into less space directly increases density.

principles-of-flight.q: Dust which is on the surface of a wing before flight will often still be there at the end of the flight because of:-
principles-of-flight.e: Skin friction slows the thin layer of air in immediate contact with the wing surface almost to a standstill, while the faster-moving air further out streams past above it. Because that innermost stationary-feeling layer never gets swept away, dust resting directly on the surface can still be found there after the flight has ended.

principles-of-flight.q: With regard to humidity and air density:-
principles-of-flight.b: humidity has no effect on density
principles-of-flight.c: humid air has the same density as dry air at all temperatures
principles-of-flight.e: Humid air is less dense than dry air at the same temperature and pressure, because the water-vapour molecules mixed into it are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen they displace. That lower density is why a humid day measurably degrades an aircraft's lift, thrust and overall performance compared with a dry day at the same temperature and pressure.

principles-of-flight.q: When lowering trailing edge flaps, the initial effect is that:-
principles-of-flight.a: the centre of pressure generally moves aft
principles-of-flight.c: the centre of pressure generally moves forward
principles-of-flight.d: the centre of gravity moves aft
principles-of-flight.ans: the centre of pressure generally moves aft
principles-of-flight.e: Lowering trailing-edge flaps changes the pressure distribution along the wing chord, and on a conventional wing that shift moves the centre of pressure - the effective point of the wing's combined lift - rearward. With lift now acting further aft, the initial tendency is a nose-down pitching moment, though the tailplane's response to the flap-modified downwash can influence the aircraft's overall final pitch behaviour.

principles-of-flight.q: Wingtip stalling may be reduced by the incorporation of:-
principles-of-flight.e: A washed-out wing has its angle of incidence deliberately reduced toward the tip, so the wing root reaches its critical angle of attack, and stalls, before the tip section does. Keeping the tip - and its ailerons - flying longer preserves roll control right through the early stages of a stall, which is exactly why washout is built into most wing designs.

principles-of-flight.q: During the autorotation stage of a spin to the left:-
principles-of-flight.a: the right wing will have a greater angle of attack than the left wing
principles-of-flight.b: both wings have exactly the same angle of attack
principles-of-flight.c: the left wing will have a greater angle of attack than the right wing.
principles-of-flight.ans: the left wing will have a greater angle of attack than the right wing.
principles-of-flight.e: In a spin to the left, the left wing is the inner wing, moving more slowly through a tighter radius of rotation than the outer right wing. That slower speed pushes the left wing to a higher angle of attack, deepening its stall relative to the right wing - the asymmetry that keeps the autorotation going.

principles-of-flight.q: The layer of air in contact with the surface of an aerofoil during flight is referred to as:-
principles-of-flight.e: The thinnest layer of air in direct contact with the aerofoil surface is slowed almost to a standstill by skin friction, and this retarded layer - the boundary layer - grows progressively thicker moving aft along the wing as more air is dragged along with it. Whether it stays smooth (laminar) or becomes chaotic (turbulent) has a major effect on both skin-friction drag and the wing's resistance to flow separation.

principles-of-flight.q: If the pressure of a parcel of air is kept constant and the:-
principles-of-flight.a: temperature is decreased the density will decrease
principles-of-flight.c: temperature is increased the density will increase
principles-of-flight.d: temperature is increased the density will decrease
principles-of-flight.ans: temperature is increased the density will decrease
principles-of-flight.e: At constant pressure, warming air makes it expand - the molecules spread out and the same mass now fills a larger volume. Since density is mass divided by volume, that expansion, not any change in the amount of air present, is what causes density to fall as temperature rises.

principles-of-flight.q: During a steady climb the arrangement of the four forces is such that:-
principles-of-flight.e: In a steady climb the aircraft's weight resolves into two parts: one opposing lift, and one acting rearward along the flight path in the same sense as drag. To sustain that climb, thrust has to overcome both the wing's own drag and this extra rearward weight component, so thrust must be greater than drag alone.

principles-of-flight.q: During level flight, the centre of gravity is normally:-
principles-of-flight.a: located aft of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.b: located at the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.c: located forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.d: located below the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: located forward of the centre of pressure
principles-of-flight.e: In level flight, the centre of gravity is normally positioned forward of the centre of pressure, creating a small, continuous nose-down pitching tendency that the tailplane's balancing download counteracts. This forward-CG arrangement is what gives the aircraft its predictable, stable pitch characteristics.

principles-of-flight.q: The correct operation of anti-balance tab can be checked before flight by moving the stabilator and observing that the:-
principles-of-flight.a: anti-balance tab moves in the same direction as the elevator
principles-of-flight.b: anti-balance tab moves only when trimmed
principles-of-flight.c: anti-balance tab moves opposite to the elevator
principles-of-flight.ans: anti-balance tab moves in the same direction as the elevator
principles-of-flight.e: An anti-balance (or anti-servo) tab is deliberately rigged to deflect the same way as the stabilator itself, generating an opposing aerodynamic force that adds resistance to the control. Checking that it moves the same direction as the elevator confirms it will make the control appropriately heavier, protecting against over-controlling a stabilator that would otherwise be very sensitive.

principles-of-flight.q: The portion of the air flow over an aerofoil, in flight, which comes into immediate contact with the surface is slowed down due to the effect of:-
principles-of-flight.e: The layer of air touching the aerofoil surface is slowed nearly to zero relative velocity by skin friction - the viscous drag between the moving air and the fixed surface. This slowed layer forms the base of the boundary layer, the thin region of retarded flow that develops over every surface an airflow passes across.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, Position B on the total drag curve indicated represents:-
principles-of-flight.e: Position B on the total drag curve marks its lowest point - where the falling induced drag curve and the rising parasite drag curve add up to the smallest possible total. This is the minimum drag speed, also the point of maximum lift-to-drag ratio.

principles-of-flight.q: With reference to the figure below, Curve B on the graph indicated represents:-
principles-of-flight.e: On a typical drag curve, curve B rises steadily with speed rather than peaking at low speed - that shape belongs to parasite drag, which grows because the aircraft is pushing more air aside and generating more skin friction the faster it flies, the opposite behaviour to induced drag.

principles-of-flight.q: The primary purpose of Fowler flaps is to:-
principles-of-flight.b: move the centre of gravity aft
principles-of-flight.c: increase the camber only without changing area
principles-of-flight.d: increase the surface area of a wing
principles-of-flight.ans: increase the surface area of a wing
principles-of-flight.e: What distinguishes a Fowler flap from a plain or split flap is that it slides backward on tracks before deflecting downward, genuinely increasing the wing's surface area rather than just its camber and angle of attack. That extra area is exactly why Fowler flaps can add substantial lift without the large drag penalty that comes with the other flap designs.

principles-of-flight.q: At high angles of attack:-
principles-of-flight.b: the effect of aileron drag will be less noticeable
principles-of-flight.c: the effect of aileron drag will be more noticeable
principles-of-flight.ans: the effect of aileron drag will be more noticeable
principles-of-flight.e: Induced drag grows with angle of attack, and aileron drag is essentially a local, one-sided spike in that same induced drag on the down-going aileron's wing. At high angle of attack the baseline drag is already elevated, so the same aileron input produces a proportionally larger imbalance between the two wings - making the resulting adverse yaw much more noticeable than at low angle of attack.

principles-of-flight.q: In order to maintain altitude during a turn:-
principles-of-flight.a: the angle of attack must be decreased
principles-of-flight.c: the angle of attack must be increased
principles-of-flight.d: the bank angle must be reduced to zero
principles-of-flight.ans: the angle of attack must be increased
principles-of-flight.e: Banking the aircraft tilts the lift vector, reducing its vertical component below what's needed to balance weight - so without compensation the aircraft would start to descend. Increasing angle of attack restores enough total lift for its vertical component to again equal weight, which is exactly what holding gentle back pressure through a turn accomplishes.

principles-of-flight.q: The correct operation of a balance tab can be checked before flight by moving the elevator and observing that the:-
principles-of-flight.b: balance tab moves in the opposite direction to the elevator.
principles-of-flight.c: balance tab moves only after trimming
principles-of-flight.d: balance tab moves in the same direction as the elevator
principles-of-flight.ans: balance tab moves in the opposite direction to the elevator.
principles-of-flight.e: A balance tab is rigged to move opposite to the elevator so that its aerodynamic force actively assists the elevator's deflection rather than opposing it. Confirming it moves the opposite direction on a pre-flight check verifies it will genuinely reduce control loads in flight rather than add to them.

principles-of-flight.q: During the aerodynamic stage of a spin known as autorotation:-
principles-of-flight.a: the outer wing is partially unstalled whilst the inner wing is stalled
principles-of-flight.d: the inner wing is partially unstalled whilst the outer wing is stalled
principles-of-flight.ans: the outer wing is partially unstalled whilst the inner wing is stalled
principles-of-flight.e: During autorotation, the inner wing - travelling slower through a tighter radius - sits at a higher angle of attack and remains more deeply stalled, while the outer wing, moving faster, is only partially stalled and still producing some usable lift and drag. It is this asymmetry between the two wings, not a fully stalled aircraft overall, that keeps the rotation self-sustaining.

principles-of-flight.q: During a balanced, level turn at 60° angle of bank in an aeroplane, the load factor is:-
principles-of-flight.e: Load factor is set by the bank angle through 1 ÷ cos(bank angle), and at 60° of bank that works out to 1 ÷ cos(60°) = 2 - meaning the wings must support twice the aircraft's gross weight to maintain both altitude and the turn.

principles-of-flight.q: At the appropriate best-glide speed, an increase in aircraft weight will:
principles-of-flight.c: have no effect on the glide angle
principles-of-flight.d: make the best glide speed lower
principles-of-flight.ans: have no effect on the glide angle
principles-of-flight.e: Best glide angle depends on the wing's maximum lift-to-drag ratio, which is essentially a fixed aerodynamic property of the aircraft's shape and barely shifts with weight. A heavier aircraft simply needs to fly a bit faster to reach that same L/D-optimal angle of attack, so it descends faster (higher rate of descent) but glides at essentially the same angle in still air.

principles-of-flight.q: Newton's First Law refers to:-
principles-of-flight.e: Newton's first law is the law of inertia: an object at rest remains at rest, and one moving at constant speed in a straight line continues doing so, unless an unbalanced force acts on it. That is precisely what equilibrium means - the condition an aircraft is in during steady, unaccelerated flight, when the four forces are all in balance.

principles-of-flight.q: Newton's Second Law refers to:-
principles-of-flight.e: Newton's second law connects force directly to acceleration: a net (unbalanced) force acting on a mass produces acceleration in that force's direction, proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass. It is this law that explains why any imbalance among the four aerodynamic forces - say, thrust exceeding drag - causes the aircraft to speed up or change its flight path.

principles-of-flight.q: In terms of the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), the sea level density of the air is:-
principles-of-flight.a: 15 grammes per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
principles-of-flight.b: 1013 grammes per cubic metre and increases with altitude
principles-of-flight.c: 1225 grammes per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
principles-of-flight.d: 760 grammes per cubic metre and remains constant
principles-of-flight.ans: 1225 grammes per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
principles-of-flight.e: The International Standard Atmosphere fixes sea-level dry-air density at 1225 grams per cubic metre, alongside its 15°C and 1013.25 hPa reference conditions. Density falls with altitude because there is progressively less air above pressing down at height, reducing pressure and leaving fewer molecules packed into each cubic metre.

principles-of-flight.q: During a glide:-
principles-of-flight.a: application of flap will increase the best L/D ratio
principles-of-flight.b: application of flap will reduce the best L/D ratio.
principles-of-flight.c: flap has no effect on glide angle
principles-of-flight.d: flap will reduce drag at all speeds
principles-of-flight.ans: application of flap will reduce the best L/D ratio.
principles-of-flight.e: Flying with flaps out in a glide adds drag that isn't matched by a proportional gain in useful lift-to-drag performance, pulling the aircraft away from its cleanest configuration. Since best L/D directly determines how far the aircraft can travel forward per unit of height lost, the added drag from flaps reduces that ratio and shortens the achievable glide distance.

principles-of-flight.q: In order to prevent the effects of gusts or manouevring on the structural integrity of an aircraft, it should not be flown under normal operating conditions above:-
principles-of-flight.e: Vno marks the top of the green arc - the maximum structural cruising speed the aircraft should be flown at under normal conditions, since above it gusts or abrupt manoeuvres can impose loads the airframe isn't rated to handle outside smooth air. The yellow caution arc between Vno and Vne exists precisely for the rare occasions faster flight is needed, but only when turbulence is not a factor.

principles-of-flight.q: In an aircraft which is spinning to the left the application of ailerons to the right:-
principles-of-flight.b: has no aerodynamic effect in a spin
principles-of-flight.c: will always stop the spin immediately
principles-of-flight.d: will reduce the angle of attack of the inner wing
principles-of-flight.e: In a spin to the left, the left wing is the inner, more deeply stalled wing, and right aileron deflects its aileron downward - increasing its angle of attack further into the stall rather than reducing it. That can work directly against recovery, which is why ailerons are normally held neutral throughout spin recovery and rudder is used instead to control the yaw.

principles-of-flight.q: When climbing the maximum height gained in the shortest distance will be achieved:-
principles-of-flight.a: by climbing at minimum sink speed
principles-of-flight.b: by climbing at the best rate of climb speed
principles-of-flight.d: by climbing at the best angle of climb speed
principles-of-flight.ans: by climbing at the best angle of climb speed
principles-of-flight.e: The steepest possible climb path - the most height gained over the least horizontal distance - comes from flying at the speed where excess thrust (available thrust minus thrust required) is at its greatest, which is exactly the definition of best angle of climb speed, Vx. That makes it the correct choice whenever the goal is clearing an obstacle close ahead, rather than climbing quickly in terms of time.

principles-of-flight.q: The symbol V in the lift formula refers to:-
principles-of-flight.e: The lift formula uses V for true airspeed, the aircraft's speed relative to the air it is actually flying through. Lift depends on how fast air is moving over the wing, which has nothing to do with how fast the aircraft is moving over the ground below it.

principles-of-flight.q: When gliding into a headwind, what happens to the glide path over the ground?
principles-of-flight.a: It becomes shallower because the rate of descent decreases
principles-of-flight.b: It becomes steeper because groundspeed decreases
principles-of-flight.c: It is unchanged because lift-to-drag ratio increases
principles-of-flight.d: It becomes shallower because groundspeed increases
principles-of-flight.ans: It becomes steeper because groundspeed decreases
principles-of-flight.e: The aircraft's actual glide angle through the surrounding air mass is set by its aerodynamic configuration and airspeed alone - the wind has no effect on that relationship. What a headwind changes is groundspeed: covering less distance over the ground for the same rate of descent through the air makes the glide path measured from the ground appear steeper, purely as a groundspeed effect.

principles-of-flight.q: If power is reduced during a descent but the speed is kept constant:-
principles-of-flight.a: the rate of descent will increase
principles-of-flight.c: the rate of descent will decrease
principles-of-flight.ans: the rate of descent will increase
principles-of-flight.e: Holding airspeed constant while power is reduced means the aircraft has less thrust available to balance drag, so it must convert more altitude into the energy needed to maintain that speed. The result is a steeper descent path and therefore a higher rate of descent.

principles-of-flight.q: Load factor is the term given to:-
principles-of-flight.a: the force acting through the centre of pressure only
principles-of-flight.b: the ratio of thrust to drag in level flight
principles-of-flight.c: the resultant of centrifugal force and gross weight during a turn
principles-of-flight.d: the ratio of lift to parasite drag
principles-of-flight.ans: the resultant of centrifugal force and gross weight during a turn
principles-of-flight.e: During a turn, the wing's load isn't simply the aircraft's weight - it is the resultant of that weight combined with the outward, centrifugal tendency of the turning mass, both acting on the wing structure at once. That combined resultant load, expressed as a multiple of gross weight, is exactly what load factor measures.

principles-of-flight.q: True airspeed (TAS) is:-
principles-of-flight.b: CAS/RAS corrected for temperature and altitude.
principles-of-flight.ans: CAS/RAS corrected for temperature and altitude.
principles-of-flight.e: True airspeed is built up in stages: calibrated (or rectified) airspeed already has instrument and installation errors removed, and true airspeed then adds a correction for temperature and altitude's effect on air density. Since thinner air at altitude produces less dynamic pressure for a given true speed, the aircraft has to fly measurably faster through the air than its calibrated airspeed reading suggests.

principles-of-flight.q: When climbing to clear obstacles in the take-off path an aeroplane should climb:-
principles-of-flight.b: at the best angle of climb speed
principles-of-flight.d: at the best rate of climb speed
principles-of-flight.ans: at the best angle of climb speed
principles-of-flight.e: Clearing an obstacle in the takeoff path is about height gained per unit of horizontal distance covered, which is maximised by flying at the speed where excess thrust is greatest - best angle of climb speed, Vx. Climbing at Vy instead, the best rate speed, would gain altitude faster in time but cover more ground doing it, risking the obstacle.

principles-of-flight.q: The force required to turn an aeroplane in flight is called the:-
principles-of-flight.e: A turn needs a continuous sideways pull toward the centre of the curve, and the wings are the only source of that sideways aerodynamic force an aircraft has. Banking tilts the lift vector so part of it points horizontally, and that horizontal component of lift is the centripetal force that actually curves the flight path.

principles-of-flight.q: With a propeller rotating clockwise as viewed from the cockpit, increasing engine power tends to make the aircraft:
principles-of-flight.a: Roll to the right because of propeller torque
principles-of-flight.b: Yaw right with no rolling tendency
principles-of-flight.d: Roll to the left because of torque reaction
principles-of-flight.ans: Roll to the left because of torque reaction
principles-of-flight.e: Newton's third law - every action produces an equal and opposite reaction - applies directly to a spinning propeller: as the propeller exerts a rotational force on the surrounding air, the air exerts an equal and opposite reactive torque back on the engine and airframe. With a clockwise-turning propeller as viewed from the cockpit, that reaction torque rolls the whole aircraft to the left, an effect most pronounced when power is added abruptly.

principles-of-flight.q: A wing produces lift primarily because the pressure distribution around it results in:
principles-of-flight.a: Low pressure below the wing and high pressure above it
principles-of-flight.b: Equal pressure above and below the wing
principles-of-flight.c: High pressure below the wing and low pressure above it
principles-of-flight.d: High pressure above and below the wing
principles-of-flight.ans: High pressure below the wing and low pressure above it
principles-of-flight.e: A wing produces lift mainly because the pressure distribution around it works out to higher pressure beneath the wing and lower pressure above it - that pressure imbalance is the net upward force we call lift. The same airflow pattern also deflects air downward as it passes the wing, a Newtonian reaction that contributes to lift as well, working alongside the Bernoulli pressure-difference effect.

principles-of-flight.q: In a conventional light aircraft, which control input is normally required to counteract asymmetric blade effect at high power and high angle of attack?
principles-of-flight.e: At high power and high angle of attack, the descending propeller blade (on the side sweeping down through the arc) bites into the air at a higher effective angle of attack than the ascending blade, so it produces more thrust. With a standard clockwise-turning propeller, that asymmetric thrust yaws the nose to the left, so right rudder is needed to counteract it and keep the aircraft tracking straight - most noticeable during a full-power, high-angle-of-attack climb after takeoff.

principles-of-flight.q: Why are full flaps generally unsuitable for a normal take-off in a light aircraft?
principles-of-flight.a: They remove all wing camber and reduce lift
principles-of-flight.b: They prevent the aircraft from reaching the critical angle of attack
principles-of-flight.c: The additional drag can seriously reduce acceleration and climb performance
principles-of-flight.d: They increase the best angle-of-climb speed above VNE
principles-of-flight.ans: The additional drag can seriously reduce acceleration and climb performance
principles-of-flight.e: Full flap generates a large amount of lift, but it comes paired with a large amount of drag - drag that has nowhere useful to go during a takeoff, where the priority is accelerating and climbing away, not gliding efficiently. That extra drag can seriously blunt acceleration and climb performance even though the aircraft may lift off at a lower speed, which is exactly why manufacturers specify a smaller, carefully chosen takeoff flap setting rather than full flap.

principles-of-flight.q: What are the approximate proportions of the four most abundant gases in dry air?
principles-of-flight.e: Dry air is made up almost entirely of nitrogen (about 78%) and oxygen (about 21%), with argon making up just under 1% and carbon dioxide only a tiny trace beyond that. These proportions stay essentially constant with altitude, even though the total amount of air - and so its density - falls the higher you go.

principles-of-flight.q: A piston engine aircraft flies in that layer of the atmosphere called?
principles-of-flight.e: Nearly all piston-aircraft flying happens in the troposphere, the lowest atmospheric layer, since this is where sufficient air density for normal engine and wing performance exists and where the weather that most affects light aircraft occurs. The layers above it - stratosphere and beyond - are the domain of high-altitude jets, not typical piston singles and twins.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the ambient air pressure acting on an object immersed in the atmosphere called?
principles-of-flight.a: Is also known as Total Pressure
principles-of-flight.b: Is also known as Static Pressure
principles-of-flight.c: Is greater at altitude than at sea level
principles-of-flight.d: Is also known as Dynamic Pressure
principles-of-flight.ans: Is also known as Static Pressure
principles-of-flight.e: Static pressure is the ambient air pressure surrounding an object, acting equally in every direction regardless of any motion - it is what a barometer measures sitting still. Dynamic pressure, by contrast, exists only because of airflow velocity, which is why an airspeed indicator has to compare the two (impact pressure versus static pressure) rather than reading static pressure alone.

principles-of-flight.q: Which symbol is normally used for dynamic pressure?
principles-of-flight.e: Dynamic pressure - the pressure rise produced purely by an airflow's velocity - is conventionally written with the symbol q (sometimes capitalised as Q) in aerodynamic formulae, appearing directly in the lift equation and in how an airspeed indicator derives speed from the pitot-static pressure difference.

principles-of-flight.q: Why does increasing airspeed increase lift when angle of attack and the other lift factors remain unchanged?
principles-of-flight.a: The increased speed of the air passing over an aerofoil's upper surface decreases the static pressure above the wing, thus creating a greater pressure differential across the upper and lower surface
principles-of-flight.b: Lift is directly proportional to velocity
principles-of-flight.d: The increased velocity of the relative wind overcomes the increased drag
principles-of-flight.ans: The increased speed of the air passing over an aerofoil's upper surface decreases the static pressure above the wing, thus creating a greater pressure differential across the upper and lower surface
principles-of-flight.e: Lift comes from the pressure difference between a wing's upper and lower surfaces, and that pressure difference scales with dynamic pressure, which itself grows with the square of airspeed (q = ½ρV²). So even with angle of attack and every other factor unchanged, simply flying faster accelerates the air over the upper surface more, drops its static pressure further, and widens the pressure differential - producing more lift.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the SI unit of force?
principles-of-flight.e: The SI unit of force is the newton (N), named for the physicist whose laws describe how force, mass and acceleration relate. A newton-metre is a different, related unit - used for moment or torque - and a joule (also a newton-metre dimensionally) measures energy rather than force itself.

principles-of-flight.q: Which expression gives dynamic pressure in terms of air density and true airspeed?
principles-of-flight.a: Half the true airspeed multiplied by air density squared
principles-of-flight.b: Half the air density multiplied by indicated airspeed squared
principles-of-flight.c: Air density multiplied by airspeed squared
principles-of-flight.d: Half the air density multiplied by true airspeed squared
principles-of-flight.ans: Half the air density multiplied by true airspeed squared
principles-of-flight.e: Dynamic pressure is calculated as q = ½ρV², half the air density multiplied by the square of true airspeed. Because velocity is squared in this formula, dynamic pressure - and with it, lift and drag - grows much faster than speed itself: doubling airspeed quadruples dynamic pressure.

principles-of-flight.q: Which statement about air pressure is correct?
principles-of-flight.c: Is measured in Pascals per square inch
principles-of-flight.e: Air pressure is not a one-directional push downward the way weight is - in a fluid at rest, pressure at any point acts equally in every direction at once. This is exactly why a static port mounted flush anywhere on the fuselage still reads a valid ambient pressure, regardless of which way it happens to face.

principles-of-flight.q: On a day when the outside air temperature at 4,000 ft is 23°C, approximately how much warmer than ISA is it?
principles-of-flight.e: ISA temperature falls at roughly 1.98°C per 1000 ft (commonly rounded to 2°C/1000 ft) from the sea-level reference of 15°C, so at 4,000 ft the standard value works out to about 15 - (2 x 4) = 7°C. An actual outside air temperature of 23°C is therefore about 23 - 7 = 16°C warmer than the ISA value for that altitude.

principles-of-flight.q: Which atmospheric properties have the greatest direct influence on aircraft performance?
principles-of-flight.a: Its nitrogen content, oxygen content, temperature and pressure
principles-of-flight.b: Its oxygen content pressure, and water vapour content
principles-of-flight.c: Its water vapour content, temperature, pressure and density
principles-of-flight.ans: Its water vapour content, temperature, pressure and density
principles-of-flight.e: Aircraft performance depends on air density above all, since it governs lift, propeller and engine efficiency - and density itself is set by the combination of pressure, temperature and water-vapour content. That is why performance calculations always work back to these four linked atmospheric properties rather than treating any one of them in isolation.

principles-of-flight.q: Relative airflow is?
principles-of-flight.a: Perpendicular and opposite to the aircraft's direction of movement
principles-of-flight.b: Parallel and opposite to the aircraft's direction of movement
principles-of-flight.c: Parallel and in the same direction as the aircraft's movement
principles-of-flight.d: Perpendicular and in the same direction as the aircraft's movement
principles-of-flight.ans: Parallel and opposite to the aircraft's direction of movement
principles-of-flight.e: Relative airflow describes the air's motion as experienced by the aircraft - it runs parallel to the flight path but in the opposite direction to the aircraft's own movement through that air. This is the airflow angle of attack is actually measured against, not the horizon or the ground.

principles-of-flight.q: About which point are an aircraft's pitch, roll and yaw rotations considered to occur?
principles-of-flight.e: An aircraft's three axes of rotation - longitudinal, lateral and vertical - all intersect at a single common point, and pitch, roll and yaw are all considered to happen about that point: the centre of gravity. This is why CG position has such a direct effect on how the aircraft responds to control inputs.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the name for smooth airflow in which each particle follows the path of the particle ahead?
principles-of-flight.e: Laminar flow is smooth, orderly airflow in which each particle of air follows essentially the same path as the particle ahead of it, with minimal mixing between adjacent layers. It produces very little skin-friction drag compared with the more chaotic, mixing flow of turbulent air, which is why maintaining laminar flow over as much of a wing as possible is a key goal of efficient aerofoil design.

principles-of-flight.q: A boundary layer may consist of?
principles-of-flight.b: Turbulent flow at low speeds only
principles-of-flight.e: The thin layer of air clinging to a surface - the boundary layer - typically starts out smooth and orderly (laminar) near the leading edge, then transitions to a more chaotic, mixing state (turbulent) further aft as it travels over the surface. Where exactly that transition happens depends on factors like surface roughness, the pressure gradient, and the airflow's Reynolds number.

principles-of-flight.q: What happens when the cross-sectional area of a steady subsonic airflow is reduced?
principles-of-flight.a: The mass flow remains constant and the velocity of the airflow increases
principles-of-flight.b: The velocity of the airflow remains constant and the kinetic energy increases
principles-of-flight.c: The velocity of the airflow remains constant and the mass flow increases
principles-of-flight.d: The mass flow remains constant and the static pressure increases
principles-of-flight.ans: The mass flow remains constant and the velocity of the airflow increases
principles-of-flight.e: In steady subsonic flow, the same mass of air must pass through every cross-section of a duct or venturi each second - continuity doesn't allow air to pile up or vanish partway through. Shrinking the cross-sectional area therefore forces the air to speed up to keep pushing that same constant mass flow through the narrower opening.

principles-of-flight.q: An object placed in a moving airstream is subjected to?
principles-of-flight.e: Any object sitting in moving air experiences the surrounding ambient static pressure, exactly as it would in still air, plus an additional pressure caused specifically by the air's motion relative to it - dynamic pressure. Together, these two combine to determine the total force the airflow exerts on the object.

principles-of-flight.q: How is dynamic pressure obtained from total pressure and static pressure?
principles-of-flight.d: Total pressure divided by static pressure
principles-of-flight.e: Total pressure is simply the sum of static pressure and dynamic pressure combined - the pressure you'd measure if you brought the moving air to a complete stop. Rearranging that relationship gives dynamic pressure as total pressure minus static pressure, which is exactly the subtraction an airspeed indicator performs using the pitot (total) and static pressure lines.

principles-of-flight.q:
Consider these statements about air:
1. Air has mass.
2. Air is incompressible.
3. Air can flow or change shape under small pressure differences.
4. Air has very high viscosity.
5. Moving air has kinetic energy.

Which combination contains all the true statements?
principles-of-flight.e: Air genuinely has mass (which is why it has weight and density), it flows and changes shape readily under even small pressure differences (unlike a rigid solid), and moving air carries real kinetic energy (the basis of dynamic pressure and wind force). Air is not incompressible - it compresses noticeably at high speed and altitude - and its viscosity is actually quite low compared to liquids like water or oil.

principles-of-flight.q: As indicated airspeed is reduced in level flight, what must the pilot do to maintain altitude?
principles-of-flight.a: Decrease the angle of attack to reduce the drag
principles-of-flight.b: Deploy the speed brakes to increase drag
principles-of-flight.d: Increase the angle of attack to maintain the correct lift force
principles-of-flight.ans: Increase the angle of attack to maintain the correct lift force
principles-of-flight.e: Reducing IAS lowers the dynamic pressure the wing has available to work with, and dynamic pressure is what drives lift for any given lift coefficient. To keep generating the same total lift needed to hold altitude, the pilot has to raise the angle of attack, which increases the lift coefficient enough to offset the lower dynamic pressure - right up until the critical angle of attack, beyond which no further increase is possible.

principles-of-flight.q: Which statement correctly defines dynamic pressure?
principles-of-flight.a: The pressure change caused by heating when a moving airflow is brought completely to rest
principles-of-flight.b: The pressure due to the mass of air pressing down on the air beneath
principles-of-flight.c: The amount by which the pressure rises at a point where a moving airflow is brought completely to rest
principles-of-flight.d: The total pressure at a point where a moving airflow is brought completely to rest
principles-of-flight.ans: The amount by which the pressure rises at a point where a moving airflow is brought completely to rest
principles-of-flight.e: Total pressure is what you'd measure by bringing a moving airflow to a complete stop at a stagnation point - like the very tip of a pitot tube - and it equals the sum of the ambient static pressure plus the dynamic pressure created by the air's motion. Dynamic pressure, by definition, is exactly that rise above static pressure caused purely by stopping the moving air.

principles-of-flight.q: An aircraft has a nose-down pitching moment from the lift-weight couple and a nose-up pitching moment from the thrust-drag couple. What tendency follows an increase in power?
principles-of-flight.b: The couples both decrease in magnitude but remain balanced
principles-of-flight.c: The couples both increase in magnitude but remain balanced
principles-of-flight.e: With this particular force arrangement, the lift-weight couple and thrust-drag couple are pulling the nose in opposite pitching directions, and increasing power strengthens the thrust-drag couple specifically. Since that couple is the one producing the nose-up moment here, adding power tips the balance further toward nose-up pitch.

principles-of-flight.q: As subsonic air passes through a venturi, how do mass flow, velocity and static pressure change?
principles-of-flight.a: Mass flow decreases then increases; velocity and static pressure both increase then decrease
principles-of-flight.b: Mass flow decreases then increases; velocity remains constant; static pressure increases then decreases
principles-of-flight.c: Mass flow remains constant; velocity increases then decreases; static pressure also increases then decreases
principles-of-flight.d: Mass flow remains constant; velocity increases then decreases; static pressure decreases then increases
