principles-of-flight.ans: Mass flow remains constant; velocity increases then decreases; static pressure decreases then increases
principles-of-flight.e: Continuity keeps mass flow constant throughout a venturi, so as the passage narrows toward the throat, velocity has to rise to keep pushing the same mass through - and by Bernoulli's principle, that rising velocity is accompanied by falling static pressure. Past the throat, as the passage widens back out, the reverse happens: velocity falls back down and static pressure recovers toward its original value.

principles-of-flight.q: Which definition of lift is correct?
principles-of-flight.a: The aerodynamic force which acts at 90° to the relative airflow
principles-of-flight.b: The aerodynamic force that results from the pressure differentials about an aerofoil
principles-of-flight.c: The aerodynamic force which acts perpendicular to the chord line of the aerofoil
principles-of-flight.d: The aerodynamic force which acts perpendicular to the upper surface of the aerofoil
principles-of-flight.ans: The aerodynamic force which acts at 90° to the relative airflow
principles-of-flight.e: Lift is formally defined as the aerodynamic force component that acts at exactly 90° to the relative airflow, distinguishing it from drag (which acts parallel to, and opposite, the relative airflow) and from the aircraft's total aerodynamic force, of which lift and drag are simply the two perpendicular components.

principles-of-flight.q: A positively cambered aerofoil normally begins producing positive lift at approximately what angle of attack?
principles-of-flight.e: A positively cambered aerofoil is shaped so that even with the chord line pointed slightly below the oncoming airflow, the curved upper surface still accelerates air enough to generate a net upward pressure difference. This is why a typical cambered wing section keeps producing lift down to roughly -4° angle of attack, rather than needing a positive angle just to start generating any lift at all - unlike a symmetrical aerofoil, which produces zero lift at zero angle of attack.

principles-of-flight.q: With all other factors constant, lift is directly proportional to?
principles-of-flight.a: The dynamic pressure minus the static pressure
principles-of-flight.c: The square root of the velocity of the air flowing over it
principles-of-flight.e: The lift equation, L = ½ρV²SCL, shows air density (ρ) appearing as a direct multiplying factor alongside speed squared, wing area and lift coefficient. Hold speed, area and lift coefficient constant, and lift scales in direct proportion to density - which is exactly why thinner air at altitude or on a hot day costs an aircraft measurable lift for the same speed and angle of attack.

principles-of-flight.q: If indicated airspeed increases from 50 kt to 100 kt, approximately how does parasite drag change?
principles-of-flight.e: Parasite drag depends on dynamic pressure, which scales with the square of airspeed (q = ½ρV²). Going from 50 kt to 100 kt doubles the speed, and doubling speed quadruples dynamic pressure - so parasite drag becomes roughly four times greater, not simply double.

principles-of-flight.q: For a typical light-aircraft aerofoil, CLmax is reached at approximately what angle of attack?
principles-of-flight.e: CLmax - the highest lift coefficient a wing can produce - occurs right at the critical (stalling) angle of attack, the point where the airflow can no longer follow the wing's upper-surface curvature. For a typical light-aircraft aerofoil that critical angle sits around 15° to 18°, commonly cited near 16°, beyond which the airflow separates and lift collapses rather than continuing to increase.

principles-of-flight.q: Where is the maximum coefficient of lift, CLmax, found?
principles-of-flight.d: At the stalling angle of attack
principles-of-flight.ans: At the stalling angle of attack
principles-of-flight.e: As angle of attack increases, lift coefficient rises right along with it - until the airflow can no longer follow the wing's upper-surface curvature and separates. That separation point is the critical (stalling) angle of attack, and it is exactly where the lift coefficient reaches its maximum value, CLmax, before collapsing as the wing stalls.

principles-of-flight.q: Skin-friction resistance caused by air viscosity over a wing surface is a form of?
principles-of-flight.e: Skin-friction drag comes from the viscous shear between the air and the wing surface within the boundary layer - a resistance that exists regardless of whether the wing is producing lift. It is therefore grouped under parasite drag, alongside form drag and interference drag, all of which are present even at zero lift, unlike induced drag which only exists because lift is being generated.

principles-of-flight.q: In level flight below the speed for maximum lift-to-drag ratio, why does total drag increase?
principles-of-flight.a: Drag decreases because of lower induced drag
principles-of-flight.b: Drag decreases because of lower parasite drag
principles-of-flight.c: Drag increases because of increased induced drag
principles-of-flight.d: Drag increases because of increased parasite drag
principles-of-flight.ans: Drag increases because of increased induced drag
principles-of-flight.e: Below the speed for maximum lift-to-drag ratio, the wing needs a progressively higher angle of attack to keep generating enough lift as speed falls further. Since induced drag grows directly with angle of attack, that rising angle of attack drives induced drag - and with it total drag - back up, which is exactly why the drag curve turns upward again on the slow side of Vmd.

principles-of-flight.q: At constant angle of attack, what happens to lift and drag when airspeed decreases?
principles-of-flight.a: A decrease in lift and drag
principles-of-flight.b: An increase in lift and a decrease in drag
principles-of-flight.c: Possible increases or decreases in lift or drag, depending on the actual speed
principles-of-flight.d: An increase in drag and a decrease in lift
principles-of-flight.ans: A decrease in lift and drag
principles-of-flight.e: Both lift and aerodynamic drag depend on dynamic pressure, which scales with the square of airspeed (q = ½ρV²). Holding angle of attack (and so the lift and drag coefficients) fixed, a decrease in airspeed reduces dynamic pressure and therefore reduces both lift and drag together, not just one of them.

principles-of-flight.q: Lift acts perpendicular to, and drag acts parallel to, which reference direction?
principles-of-flight.e: The relative airflow lines up directly with the aircraft's flight path, since it is simply the air moving past the aircraft in the opposite direction to its actual motion through it. Lift, by definition, acts perpendicular to that relative airflow, while drag acts parallel to it, along the flight path direction - which is why both forces are always defined relative to the flight path, not the horizon or the fuselage.

principles-of-flight.q: As airspeed increases, what happens to induced drag, parasite drag and total drag?
principles-of-flight.a: Induced drag increases; parasite drag decreases; total drag increases then decreases
principles-of-flight.b: Induced drag increases; parasite drag increases; total drag increases
principles-of-flight.c: Induced drag decreases; parasite drag decreases; total drag decreases
principles-of-flight.d: Induced drag decreases; parasite drag increases; total drag decreases then increases
principles-of-flight.ans: Induced drag decreases; parasite drag increases; total drag decreases then increases
principles-of-flight.e: As airspeed increases from low speed, the wing needs a progressively smaller angle of attack to produce the required lift, so induced drag falls; meanwhile parasite drag climbs because it scales with the square of speed. Total drag, their sum, therefore starts high (induced-drag dominated), decreases to a minimum where the two curves cross most favourably, and then rises again as parasite drag takes over - the classic U-shaped total drag curve.

principles-of-flight.q: Flaps are lowered while airspeed and altitude remain constant. What must happen to angle of attack?
principles-of-flight.a: Must be kept constant and power required will be constant
principles-of-flight.b: Must be kept constant but power must be increased
principles-of-flight.e: Lowering flaps raises the wing's lift coefficient at any given angle of attack. If airspeed, altitude and weight all stay fixed, the wing is now generating more lift than it needs to at its current angle of attack - so the angle of attack has to be reduced to bring lift back down to exactly what's needed to maintain level flight, with extra power sometimes required to overcome the added flap drag.

principles-of-flight.q: Which description best defines aeroelastic flutter?
principles-of-flight.a: Oscillatory motion of part or parts of the aircraft relative to the remainder of the structure
principles-of-flight.b: Reversal of the ailerons caused by wing torsional flexibility
principles-of-flight.c: Rapid oscillatory motion involving only rotation of the control surfaces, associated with the shock waves produced around the control surfaces
principles-of-flight.d: Rapid movement of the airframe caused by vibration from the engines
principles-of-flight.ans: Oscillatory motion of part or parts of the aircraft relative to the remainder of the structure
principles-of-flight.e: Flutter is a self-sustaining vibration in which part of the airframe - typically a control surface - oscillates relative to the rest of the structure, driven by aerodynamic and inertial forces reinforcing each other rather than damping out. Left unchecked it can build in amplitude extremely quickly, which is why mass balancing and other flutter-prevention measures are a critical part of control-surface design.

principles-of-flight.q: What motion characterises Dutch-roll instability after a lateral disturbance?
principles-of-flight.a: Develop simultaneous oscillations in roll and yaw
principles-of-flight.ans: Develop simultaneous oscillations in roll and yaw
principles-of-flight.e: Dutch roll is a coupled lateral-directional oscillation: a lateral disturbance sets off roll and yaw motions that feed into each other, with the aircraft rolling one way while simultaneously yawing, then reversing, in a repeating wallowing pattern rather than settling directly back to wings-level flight. It happens on aircraft where directional (yaw) stability is comparatively weaker relative to their roll (dihedral) stability.

principles-of-flight.q: Compared with a low-wing aircraft having no dihedral, a high-wing aircraft with no dihedral normally has?
principles-of-flight.c: The same degree of longitudinal stability as any other configuration because dihedral gives longitudinal stability
principles-of-flight.e: On a high-wing aircraft, the fuselage hangs below the wing, so the weight tends to swing like a pendulum back under the wing whenever the aircraft rolls - a stabilising effect on top of any geometric dihedral. A low-wing aircraft lacks this pendulum benefit and typically needs more actual dihedral angle built into the wings to achieve comparable lateral stability, which is why a high-wing design with zero dihedral still tends to be laterally more stable than an equivalent low-wing design with zero dihedral.

principles-of-flight.q: After a roll disturbance creates a sideslip, how does wing dihedral help restore the aircraft?
principles-of-flight.a: The fin will cause a yawing moment which reduces the sideslip
principles-of-flight.b: Wing dihedral will cause a nose up pitching moment
principles-of-flight.c: Wing dihedral will cause a rolling moment which tends to correct the sideslip
principles-of-flight.d: Wing dihedral will cause a yawing moment which tends to correct the sideslip
principles-of-flight.ans: Wing dihedral will cause a rolling moment which tends to correct the sideslip
principles-of-flight.e: A roll disturbance tips the lift vector sideways, and the aircraft begins to sideslip toward the lowered wing. Dihedral means that lower wing now meets the sideways-shifted airflow at a greater effective angle of attack than the raised wing, generating more lift on that side - and that lift imbalance produces a rolling moment that lifts the low wing back up, correcting the original disturbance.

principles-of-flight.q: During a sideslip, wing dihedral creates a restoring rolling moment by increasing lift on:
principles-of-flight.a: On the lower wing whenever the aircraft is in a banked attitude
principles-of-flight.b: On the up-going wing when the aircraft rolls
principles-of-flight.c: On the up-going wing when the aircraft is sideslipping
principles-of-flight.d: On the lower wing when the aircraft is sideslipping
principles-of-flight.ans: On the lower wing when the aircraft is sideslipping
principles-of-flight.e: When the aircraft sideslips, the geometry of dihedral means the lower wing - now more directly exposed to the sideways component of the relative airflow - experiences a greater effective angle of attack than the upper wing. That increased angle of attack generates more lift specifically on the lower wing, producing the rolling moment that restores the aircraft to wings level.

principles-of-flight.q: An aircraft glides at its best lift-to-drag ratio in the clean configuration. What happens to maximum gliding distance when flaps are extended?
principles-of-flight.a: The maximum gliding distance will increase
principles-of-flight.b: The maximum gliding distance will be unaffected
principles-of-flight.c: The maximum gliding distance will be less
principles-of-flight.d: The lift-to-drag ratio will be unchanged but achieved at a lower airspeed
principles-of-flight.ans: The maximum gliding distance will be less
principles-of-flight.e: The clean configuration typically gives the best achievable lift-to-drag ratio, and extending flaps adds drag that isn't offset by a matching gain in useful lift at glide speed - pulling the aircraft away from that optimal efficiency. With a worse L/D ratio, the aircraft covers less forward distance for the same height lost, so maximum gliding distance shrinks compared with the clean glide.

principles-of-flight.q: Compared with a flap-assisted landing, a no-flap landing normally requires:
principles-of-flight.c: The same landing speed but a steeper approach
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps raise the wing's maximum lift coefficient, which is exactly what lowers stalling speed - and by extension, the minimum safe approach and landing speed. Without that flap-boosted lift capability, a no-flap landing has to be flown and touched down faster to maintain the same margin above the (now higher) unflapped stall speed.

principles-of-flight.q: At a given indicated airspeed and angle of attack, what effect does an increase in air density have on lift and drag?
principles-of-flight.b: Lift will increase but drag will decrease
principles-of-flight.d: Lift and drag will remain the same
principles-of-flight.ans: Lift and drag will remain the same
principles-of-flight.e: Indicated airspeed is itself a direct readout of dynamic pressure, the pitot-static pressure difference the airspeed indicator measures. So at a fixed IAS and angle of attack, the wing is experiencing essentially the same dynamic pressure and lift coefficient regardless of what the actual air density happens to be - any density change is already absorbed into how fast the aircraft has to move through that thinner or denser air to register the same IAS, leaving lift and drag themselves effectively unchanged.

principles-of-flight.q: If the centre of gravity is within limits for take-off, what additional check is still required?
principles-of-flight.a: The flight crew will always be certain of being able to adjust the C of G during flight in order to keep it within acceptable limits for landing
principles-of-flight.b: The C of G will not change during the flight
principles-of-flight.c: The C of G limits for landing must be checked, allowing for planned fuel consumption
principles-of-flight.d: The C of G will always be within limits for landing
principles-of-flight.ans: The C of G limits for landing must be checked, allowing for planned fuel consumption
principles-of-flight.e: Fuel burn during the flight shifts the aircraft's weight distribution, which can move the CG outside limits even if it started well within them at takeoff. A loading condition that is acceptable for the heavier, full-fuel takeoff configuration must therefore also be verified against the lighter, reduced-fuel landing configuration, since the CG can end up in a different, potentially out-of-limits position by the time the aircraft lands.

principles-of-flight.q: What normally happens to the wing's critical angle of attack and CLmax when trailing-edge flaps are lowered?
principles-of-flight.a: The critical angle remains unchanged and CLmax increases
principles-of-flight.b: The critical angle decreases and CLmax remains unchanged
principles-of-flight.c: The critical angle increases and CLmax increases
principles-of-flight.d: The critical angle decreases and CLmax increases
principles-of-flight.ans: The critical angle decreases and CLmax increases
principles-of-flight.e: Lowering trailing-edge flaps increases wing camber, which raises the maximum lift coefficient (CLmax) the wing can produce - the basis for a lower stall speed. That same added camber, though, means the wing's upper-surface airflow separates at a smaller geometric angle relative to the chord, so the critical angle of attack itself is reached sooner, at a lower angle than in the clean configuration.

principles-of-flight.q: After a small bank disturbance, an aircraft returns to wings level without further control input. How is it described?
principles-of-flight.e: Returning all the way to wings level without any further control input demonstrates two things at once: an initial restoring tendency right after the disturbance (positive static stability), and that restoring tendency actually carrying the aircraft all the way back rather than just partway or into a persistent oscillation (positive dynamic stability). Both properties are present here, which is why the aircraft is described as both statically and dynamically stable.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the stability effect if the wing aerodynamic centre is ahead of the centre of gravity?
principles-of-flight.a: Changes in lift produce a wing pitching moment which acts to increase the change of lift
principles-of-flight.b: Changes in lift produce a wing pitching moment which acts to reduce the change of lift
principles-of-flight.c: Changes in lift give no change in wing pitching moment
principles-of-flight.d: When the aircraft sideslips, the C of G causes the nose to turn into the sideslip thus applying a restoring moment
principles-of-flight.ans: Changes in lift produce a wing pitching moment which acts to increase the change of lift
principles-of-flight.e: If the wing's aerodynamic centre sits ahead of the centre of gravity, any change in lift acts through a point forward of the CG, creating a pitching moment that pushes the nose further in the same direction the disturbance already started - reinforcing rather than opposing the change. That self-amplifying feedback is the definition of longitudinal instability, which is exactly why a stable design needs the aerodynamic centre positioned aft of the CG instead.

principles-of-flight.q: Which description correctly defines the lateral axis?
principles-of-flight.a: Passes through the centre of gravity, parallel to a line through the wing tips
principles-of-flight.b: Passes through the centre of pressure, at right angles to the direction of the airflow
principles-of-flight.d: Passes through the quarter-chord point of the wing root at right angles to the longitudinal axis
principles-of-flight.ans: Passes through the centre of gravity, parallel to a line through the wing tips
principles-of-flight.e: The lateral axis is the imaginary line running parallel to the wingtips, passing through the centre of gravity - the pivot point shared by all three of the aircraft's rotational axes. Rotation about this specific axis is pitch, controlled by the elevator.

principles-of-flight.q: How do leading-edge slots allow a wing to operate at a higher angle of attack?
principles-of-flight.a: Changing the shape and hence the lift characteristics of the wing
principles-of-flight.b: Decreasing lift and hence induced drag
principles-of-flight.c: Providing an extra lifting surface and hence increase the lift available
principles-of-flight.d: Re-energising the airflow over the top of the wing, delaying separation
principles-of-flight.ans: Re-energising the airflow over the top of the wing, delaying separation
principles-of-flight.e: A leading-edge slot channels a stream of relatively high-energy air from beneath the wing over the upper surface near the leading edge. That injected energy re-energises the boundary layer right where it would otherwise be slowing down and separating, letting the airflow stay attached to a higher angle of attack than it could manage on a plain wing before finally stalling.

principles-of-flight.q: After a pitch disturbance, an aircraft initially tends to return but oscillates with increasing amplitude. How is its stability described?
principles-of-flight.e: An initial tendency to move back toward the original attitude right after a disturbance is positive static stability - the aircraft is not moving further away. But if the oscillations that follow grow larger with each swing instead of shrinking, that persistent divergence is dynamic instability, showing that having a correct initial reaction is not the same as the motion actually settling down over time.

principles-of-flight.q: A longitudinally stable aircraft is disturbed nose-down. What tailplane force provides a restoring nose-up moment?
principles-of-flight.a: The tailplane will generate an upward force
principles-of-flight.b: The aircraft will maintain its nose-down attitude
principles-of-flight.c: The tailplane will generate a downward force
principles-of-flight.d: Neither an upward nor a downward force will be generated by the tailplane, as the aircraft will already be in equilibrium
principles-of-flight.ans: The tailplane will generate a downward force
principles-of-flight.e: A nose-down disturbance needs an opposing, nose-up restoring moment to correct it, and the tailplane sits well aft of the centre of gravity - so a force pushing the tail down generates exactly that nose-up moment through leverage. A downward force from the tailplane is what produces this restoring effect, pushing the tail down and the nose back up toward the trimmed attitude.

principles-of-flight.q: Which pressure distribution around an aerofoil produces lift?
principles-of-flight.a: Higher air pressure below the surface and lower air pressure above the surface
principles-of-flight.b: Vacuum below the surface and greater air pressure above the surface
principles-of-flight.c: Negative air pressure below and a vacuum above the surface
principles-of-flight.d: Higher air pressure at the leading edge than at the trailing edge
principles-of-flight.ans: Higher air pressure below the surface and lower air pressure above the surface
principles-of-flight.e: Lift results directly from the pressure pattern that develops around a wing in motion: air accelerated over the more curved upper surface drops in pressure by Bernoulli's principle, while the lower surface retains relatively higher pressure. That imbalance - higher pressure pushing up from below, lower pressure "pulling" from above - is what produces the net upward force we call lift.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the usual effect of using the manufacturer's recommended take-off flap setting compared with a no-flap take-off?
principles-of-flight.a: A decrease in the length of the take-off run compared to a non-flap take-off
principles-of-flight.b: Easier avoidance of obstacles at the end of a runway
principles-of-flight.d: An increase in the length of the take-off run compared to a non-flap take-off
principles-of-flight.ans: A decrease in the length of the take-off run compared to a non-flap take-off
principles-of-flight.e: The manufacturer's recommended takeoff flap setting raises the wing's maximum lift coefficient just enough to let the aircraft accelerate to flying speed and lift off sooner, without the drag penalty of full flap seriously hurting acceleration. The usual result is a shorter ground roll than a no-flap takeoff, though the effect on subsequent climb and obstacle clearance varies by aircraft, which is why the approved performance charts should always be consulted rather than assumed.

principles-of-flight.q: A wing that slopes downward from root to tip is said to have what?
principles-of-flight.e: Anhedral is the opposite of the more common dihedral: instead of angling upward from root to tip, the wings droop downward when viewed from the front. Because dihedral is one of the main design features that gives an aircraft natural roll stability (a sideslip generates more lift on the lower, more exposed wing, rolling the aircraft back level), anhedral works against that effect and reduces lateral stability - sometimes used deliberately on high-winged or already very stable designs to tone down an otherwise excessive natural stability.

principles-of-flight.q: After a disturbance from its trimmed attitude, an aircraft has neutral static stability if it?
principles-of-flight.b: Oscillates about its original attitude before settling back to that original attitude
principles-of-flight.d: Continues to move in the disturbed direction until the displacement is resisted by opposing control forces
principles-of-flight.e: Neutral static stability means the initial disturbing force produces no restoring tendency at all, but also no tendency to diverge further - the aircraft simply settles into whatever new attitude the disturbance left it in and stays there, neither correcting back toward trim nor continuing to move away from it.

principles-of-flight.q: Which change increases directional stability about the normal axis?
principles-of-flight.b: Increasing the keel surface behind the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.ans: Increasing the keel surface behind the centre of gravity
principles-of-flight.e: The vertical fin and the fuselage's side area behind the centre of gravity both act as "keel surface" - area that catches the relative airflow and generates a weathervane-like restoring force when the aircraft yaws. Increasing that keel surface specifically behind the CG strengthens the leverage of this weathervane effect, directly improving directional (yaw) stability about the vertical axis.

principles-of-flight.q: At approximately what angle of attack does a conventional light-aircraft wing normally begin to stall?
principles-of-flight.e: A typical light-aircraft wing reaches its critical angle of attack somewhere between about 10° and 18°, commonly closer to 15-16° depending on the specific aerofoil section. Beyond that angle, the airflow can no longer follow the upper surface's curvature and separates, causing the sudden loss of lift that defines a stall.

principles-of-flight.q: When the control column is moved right, how should a balance tab on the left aileron move?
principles-of-flight.b: Move down relative to the aileron
principles-of-flight.c: Not move unless the aileron trim wheel is turned
principles-of-flight.d: Move up relative to the aileron
principles-of-flight.ans: Move up relative to the aileron
principles-of-flight.e: Moving the control column right lowers the left aileron to initiate the roll. A balance tab is rigged to move opposite to the surface it's attached to, so with the left aileron going down, its balance tab moves up relative to the aileron - generating an aerodynamic force that helps drive that aileron down with less effort from the pilot.

principles-of-flight.q: At the stall, an aft movement of centre of pressure tends to make the nose _____, while the loss of lift makes the aircraft _____.
principles-of-flight.e: As the wing approaches the stall, the point representing its combined lift force - the centre of pressure - shifts rearward, and that rearward shift changes the balance of pitching moments enough to drop the nose. At the same moment, the wing's sudden loss of lift means it can no longer fully support the aircraft's weight, so the aircraft also loses height - the nose-drop and the sink happening together, not as separate events.

principles-of-flight.q: At design manoeuvring speed VA, what is a full abrupt elevator input in one axis intended to do?
principles-of-flight.a: Allow the aircraft to exceed its limit load during any high-g manoeuvre
principles-of-flight.b: Prevent structural damage from every possible gust or combined control input
principles-of-flight.c: Require immediate deceleration whenever light turbulence is encountered
principles-of-flight.d: Cause the wing to stall before the positive limit load is exceeded
principles-of-flight.ans: Cause the wing to stall before the positive limit load is exceeded
principles-of-flight.e: At or below design manoeuvring speed, a full, abrupt elevator deflection is intended to stall the wing before the resulting aerodynamic load can exceed the aircraft's positive limit load factor - the wing simply runs out of lift to keep loading the structure further. This protection is specific to a single control input in one axis; it does not guarantee safety against gusts combined with control inputs, or against combined multi-axis manoeuvres, which is why Va is not a blanket structural guarantee.

principles-of-flight.q: When a conventional control surface with a simple trim tab moves, the trim tab remains at the selected angle relative to what?
principles-of-flight.e: A simple trim tab is set to a fixed angle relative to the control surface it's attached to, and it stays at that same relative angle as the surface itself moves through its full range of travel. Holding that constant relative angle is exactly what lets it apply a steady balancing force at the trimmed condition, regardless of how the pilot is otherwise deflecting the main surface.

principles-of-flight.q: When the control column is pushed forward, how does an elevator balance tab move?
principles-of-flight.b: Will only move if the trim wheel is operated
principles-of-flight.c: Will move down relative to the control surface
principles-of-flight.d: Will move up relative to the control surface
principles-of-flight.ans: Will move up relative to the control surface
principles-of-flight.e: Pushing the control column forward lowers the elevator to pitch the nose down. A balance tab moves opposite to the surface it's mounted on, so as the elevator moves down, its tab moves up relative to the elevator - producing an aerodynamic force that helps drive the elevator down and reduces the forward stick force needed.

principles-of-flight.q: What aerodynamic quantity determines an aeroplane's maximum angle of climb?
principles-of-flight.e: Climb angle is fundamentally about the balance of forces along the flight path, and the force that matters there is thrust versus drag - excess thrust is what is left over to accelerate the aircraft up a steeper path once drag is overcome. Excess power, by contrast, governs how fast that climbing can happen (rate of climb, Vy), which is a different quantity from the angle itself.

principles-of-flight.q: An aircraft flies right-wing-low hands off and is trimmed using a tab on the left aileron. How should the tab and ailerons move?
principles-of-flight.a: Move up causing the left wing to move down, ailerons remain neutral
principles-of-flight.b: Move down causing the left aileron to move up, and right aileron to move down
principles-of-flight.c: Move down, causing the left aileron to move up, right aileron remains neutral
principles-of-flight.d: Move up, causing the left aileron to move up and right aileron to move down
principles-of-flight.ans: Move down causing the left aileron to move up, and right aileron to move down
principles-of-flight.e: Flying right-wing-low hands off means the left wing is producing too much lift relative to the right, so the fix is to hold the left aileron up and the right aileron down to reduce lift on the left side. Since a trim tab drives its aileron in the opposite direction to its own deflection, moving the left aileron's trim tab down generates the aerodynamic force needed to hold that left aileron up, correcting the wing-low tendency hands-off.

principles-of-flight.q: An aircraft stalls at 60 kt IAS in straight-and-level flight. What is its approximate stall speed in a level 60° banked turn?
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Level straight-and-level stall speed 60 kt IAS, bank angle 60 deg in a level turn.

FORMULA
Load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle)
Stall speed in turn = level stall speed x sqrt(n)

SOLVE
n = 1 / cos(60 deg) = 1 / 0.5 = 2
Stall speed in turn = 60 x sqrt(2) = 60 x 1.414 = 84.9 kt, rounded to 85 kt

ANSWER
85 kt

principles-of-flight.q: When ailerons are displaced from neutral, which statement is correct?
principles-of-flight.a: The up-going aileron causes an increase in induced drag
principles-of-flight.b: The down-going aileron causes an increase in induced drag
principles-of-flight.c: Both cause an increase in induced drag
principles-of-flight.d: Induced drag remains the same; the up-going aileron causes a smaller increase in profile drag than the down-going aileron
principles-of-flight.ans: The down-going aileron causes an increase in induced drag
principles-of-flight.e: Deflecting an aileron downward increases the local camber of that section of wing, which raises both its angle of attack and its lift - and induced drag rises right along with lift. That extra induced drag on the down-going side, unmatched by an equal reduction on the up-going side, is exactly what produces adverse yaw and makes coordinated rudder necessary during roll.

principles-of-flight.q: For constant weight and configuration, stall speed is proportional to which load-factor relationship?
principles-of-flight.a: Square root of the load factor
principles-of-flight.ans: Square root of the load factor
principles-of-flight.e: For a given weight and configuration, stall speed changes with the square root of load factor: VS,new = VS,1g × √n.

principles-of-flight.q: How can an aileron be aerodynamically balanced?
principles-of-flight.a: Having springs in the control circuit to assist movement
principles-of-flight.b: Attaching a weight to the control surface forward of the hinge
principles-of-flight.c: Having the control hinge set back behind the control surface leading edge
principles-of-flight.d: Making the up aileron move through a larger angle than the down aileron
principles-of-flight.ans: Having the control hinge set back behind the control surface leading edge
principles-of-flight.e: Setting the hinge line back from the control surface's leading edge leaves a small portion of the surface projecting forward of the hinge, into the airflow. Air pressure on that forward section pushes in the same direction the surface is being deflected, aerodynamically assisting the pilot's input and reducing the control force needed - the same underlying principle as a horn balance, just built into the hinge geometry itself.

principles-of-flight.q: Why is VFE lower than normal cruising speed?
principles-of-flight.b: Flaps are used only when preparing to land
principles-of-flight.c: Flaps will stall if they are deployed at too high an airspeed
principles-of-flight.d: At speeds higher than VFE the aerodynamic forces would overload the flap and wing structures
principles-of-flight.ans: At speeds higher than VFE the aerodynamic forces would overload the flap and wing structures
principles-of-flight.e: Flaps and their supporting wing structure are built to handle the aerodynamic loads expected at flap-extension speeds, which are inherently lower-speed regimes. Flying faster than Vfe with flaps out drives loads on the flap surfaces and their attachment structure well past what they were designed for, risking severe strain or outright structural failure - which is exactly why Vfe sits well below normal cruising speed.

principles-of-flight.q: An aeroplane stalls at 80 kt in level 1 g flight. What is its approximate stall speed in a level 45° banked turn?
principles-of-flight.e:
WORKING

• Load factor at 45° bank: n = 1 ÷ cos 45° = 1.414
• VS(turn) = 80 × √1.414
• VS(turn) = 80 × 1.189 = 95.1 kt

FINAL ANSWER
Approximately 95 kt.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the significance of VNO?
principles-of-flight.a: It is the speed beyond which structural failure of the airframe will occur
principles-of-flight.b: It is the maximum speed at which abrupt movements of the controls will result in a stall, before the aircraft's positive load limit is exceeded
principles-of-flight.c: It signifies the airspeed which must never be exceeded
principles-of-flight.d: It signifies the upper limit of the normal operating speed range
principles-of-flight.ans: It signifies the upper limit of the normal operating speed range
principles-of-flight.e: Vno marks the top of the green arc: the maximum structural cruising speed for routine operation, and the boundary between the normal operating range and the yellow caution range that leads up to Vne. Flying above Vno is only advisable in smooth air, since it removes the margin the aircraft normally has against gust and manoeuvring loads.

principles-of-flight.q: After trimming for level flight with the centre of gravity near the forward limit, what happens to nose-up pitch authority?
principles-of-flight.a: Nose-up pitch authority will be reduced
principles-of-flight.c: Nose-down pitch authority will be reduced
principles-of-flight.ans: Nose-up pitch authority will be reduced
principles-of-flight.e: A centre of gravity near the forward limit means the tailplane already has to produce a larger download just to keep the aircraft in trim for level flight, using up more of the elevator's available nose-up travel before the pilot even asks for a manoeuvre. With less elevator travel left in reserve, there is less additional nose-up authority available for flaring, climbing, or recovering from an unusual attitude.

principles-of-flight.q: A rudder has a balance tab. When right rudder is applied, which movement is correct?
principles-of-flight.e: Applying right rudder swings the rudder to the right to yaw the nose that way. A balance tab is rigged to move opposite to the surface it's attached to, so as the rudder moves right, its balance tab moves left - generating an aerodynamic force that assists the rudder's own movement and reduces the pedal force the pilot has to apply.

principles-of-flight.q: During a spin, which instrument most reliably indicates the direction of rotation?
principles-of-flight.e: During a spin the aircraft is rotating rapidly around the yaw axis while descending steeply, conditions under which the attitude indicator and heading indicator can tumble or become unreliable. The turn needle, however, is specifically designed to indicate rate and direction of yaw regardless of attitude, making it the one instrument a pilot can trust to confirm which way the aircraft is actually rotating.

principles-of-flight.q: What is the purpose of a spring-bias trim system?
principles-of-flight.a: To increase the feel in the control system
principles-of-flight.b: To compensate for temperature changes in cable tension
principles-of-flight.c: To maintain a constant tension in the trim tab system
principles-of-flight.d: To reduce to zero the effort required by the pilot to counter stick force, after making a control movement
principles-of-flight.ans: To reduce to zero the effort required by the pilot to counter stick force, after making a control movement
principles-of-flight.e: After the pilot makes a control input and releases back-pressure at a new attitude, a conventional control would want to spring back toward its original position, forcing the pilot to hold a sustained force to stay there. A spring-bias trim system instead adjusts the preload on that spring so the control naturally rests at the newly selected position, letting the pilot let go of the controls entirely without the aircraft drifting back.

principles-of-flight.q: How are fixed aileron trim tabs normally used?
principles-of-flight.b: Can be adjusted on the ground after a test flight to make wings-level flight easier
principles-of-flight.d: Can be adjusted on the ground after a test flight to make turning easier
principles-of-flight.ans: Can be adjusted on the ground after a test flight to make wings-level flight easier
principles-of-flight.e: A fixed aileron trim tab has no cockpit control at all - it is a small metal tab bent by hand on the ground. After a test flight reveals the aircraft flying one wing low hands-off, a mechanic bends the tab slightly and the pilot re-checks the result on the next flight, repeating this trial-and-error process until the aircraft holds wings-level flight hands-off.

principles-of-flight.q: What control-surface movements result when the control column is moved forward and left?
principles-of-flight.a: The left aileron moves down, right aileron moves up, elevator moves down
principles-of-flight.b: The left aileron moves down, right aileron moves up, elevator moves up
principles-of-flight.c: The left aileron moves up, right aileron moves down, elevator moves up
principles-of-flight.d: The left aileron moves up, right aileron moves down, elevator moves down
principles-of-flight.ans: The left aileron moves up, right aileron moves down, elevator moves down
principles-of-flight.e: Moving the control column left raises the left aileron and lowers the right one, banking the aircraft to the left; pushing the column forward at the same time lowers the elevator, pitching the nose down. Together, a forward-and-left column movement produces a combined nose-down, left-rolling control input - exactly what's needed to enter a descending left turn.

principles-of-flight.q: With wing area unchanged, approximately how much does minimum speed increase if aircraft mass increases by 20%?
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Wing area unchanged, aircraft mass increases by 20%.

FORMULA
Wing loading increase = mass increase (wing area constant)
New minimum-speed factor = sqrt(1 + wing loading increase)

SOLVE
Wing loading increases by 20%, so new speed factor = sqrt(1.20) = 1.095
Minimum speed increase = 1.095 - 1 = 0.095, i.e. about 9.5%, rounded to 10%

ANSWER
10%

principles-of-flight.q: Approximately how much does stall speed increase if wing loading increases by 15%?
principles-of-flight.e:
GIVEN
Wing loading increases by 15%.

FORMULA
Stall speed varies with the square root of wing loading.
New stall-speed factor = sqrt(1 + wing loading increase)

SOLVE
New speed factor = sqrt(1.15) = 1.072
Stall speed increase = 1.072 - 1 = 0.072, i.e. about 7.2%, rounded to 7%

ANSWER
7%

principles-of-flight.q: If airspeed is doubled while density, reference area and drag coefficient remain constant, what happens to drag force?
principles-of-flight.e: Drag force depends on the square of airspeed when density, reference area and drag coefficient are held constant (D = ½ρV²SCd). Doubling airspeed means V² becomes four times larger, so the drag force itself increases fourfold.

principles-of-flight.q: Which of these wing planforms generally produces the greatest induced drag?
principles-of-flight.e: An elliptical lift distribution spreads the load most evenly along the span, producing the weakest possible wingtip vortices and therefore the least induced drag for a given amount of lift - the elliptical wing is the most efficient shape in this respect, though it has worse natural stall characteristics than a rectangular wing. A rectangular wing, with more area concentrated near the tip than the ideal elliptical distribution, departs furthest from that efficient loading and produces the greatest induced drag of common wing planforms.

human-performance.q: Why are humans more easily affected by carbon monoxide poisoning as altitude increases?
human-performance.a: The lower oxygen partial pressure at altitude leaves less oxygen available to the body
human-performance.b: Cabin pressure always increases with altitude
human-performance.c: The percentage of carbon monoxide in clean air automatically rises
human-performance.d: Carbon monoxide becomes heavier at altitude
human-performance.ans: The lower oxygen partial pressure at altitude leaves less oxygen available to the body
human-performance.e: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does, so even a small amount in the blood significantly reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. Because the partial pressure of oxygen already falls with altitude, leaving less oxygen available to begin with, any additional reduction in the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity from carbon monoxide has a proportionally bigger impact, making its effects far more severe at altitude than at sea level.

human-performance.q: What is the best treatment for a pilot suffering from acute stress?
human-performance.b: Increasing the workload to keep the mind active
human-performance.d: Using sleeping tablets to force deep sleep
human-performance.ans: Restful, uninterrupted natural sleep
human-performance.e: Acute stress is the body's short-term, immediate response to a demanding event, and once that event has passed, genuine natural sleep is what actually lets the body and mind recover - restoring alertness properly rather than just masking tiredness. Alcohol or sedating medication might induce sleep of a sort, but they disrupt normal sleep architecture and leave a pilot far from truly recovered.

human-performance.q: What is a motor programme?
human-performance.a: A new problem that requires full conscious analysis
human-performance.b: A written rule stored only in short-term memory
human-performance.c: A skill learned through practice that can later be performed with little conscious thought
human-performance.d: A decision based entirely on outside pressure
human-performance.ans: A skill learned through practice that can later be performed with little conscious thought
human-performance.e: A motor programme is an organised, co-ordinated pattern of activity - physical, social, linguistic or intellectual - that has been learned through practice and repetition until it can be carried out with little conscious thought, freeing the brain's single-channel decision-making capacity for other tasks. Walking is a simple example: once learned, it needs almost no conscious attention, which is exactly why an experienced pilot can fly the aircraft and hold a radio conversation at the same time.

human-performance.q: Cyanosis is most closely associated with which condition?
human-performance.ans: Hypoxia
human-performance.e: Cyanosis - a bluish discolouration of the lips and fingertips - occurs when the blood is carrying an inadequate supply of oxygen, making it one of the visible outward signs of hypoxia.

human-performance.q: In human performance, what is a defence mechanism?
human-performance.a: The most effective method of removing every stressor
human-performance.b: A method that prevents all stress from developing
human-performance.c: An unhealthy or incorrect way of coping with stress rather than dealing with its cause
human-performance.ans: An unhealthy or incorrect way of coping with stress rather than dealing with its cause
human-performance.e: A defence mechanism is a way of making the discomfort of stress feel smaller - denying it, avoiding it, or shifting blame elsewhere - without ever actually addressing what caused the stress in the first place. Because the underlying problem is left untouched, the stress tends to resurface, unlike genuine coping strategies that confront the actual source of the demand.

human-performance.q: A pilot makes the correct decision but performs the wrong physical action. What type of error is this?
human-performance.ans: An action slip
human-performance.e: An action slip is an error in which the intended action was correctly decided upon but the wrong physical action was actually carried out - the intent was right, but its execution went astray. This is distinct from an error in judgement or decision-making, where the intention itself was flawed from the start.

human-performance.q: Which gas makes up the largest proportion of the atmosphere?
human-performance.ans: Nitrogen
human-performance.e: By volume, dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and roughly 1% other gases such as argon and carbon dioxide, making nitrogen the atmosphere's largest single constituent, even though it plays no direct role in the body's own use of oxygen.

human-performance.q: What is the main protective function of white blood cells?
human-performance.a: They help fight infection and disease
human-performance.b: They form the main structure of blood clots
human-performance.c: They transport most of the oxygen in the blood
human-performance.d: They pump blood around the body
human-performance.ans: They help fight infection and disease
human-performance.e: White blood cells are the body's immune defence, patrolling the bloodstream to attack invading bacteria, viruses and other harmful micro-organisms. This distinguishes them from red blood cells, which carry oxygen, and platelets, which handle clotting - each blood component has its own dedicated job.

human-performance.q: In decompression sickness, what is the itching or crawling sensation caused by nitrogen bubbles in the skin called?
human-performance.ans: The creeps
human-performance.e: Nitrogen bubbles forming under the skin as ambient pressure drops rapidly produce an itching, tingling, or crawling sensation - as though something were moving just beneath the surface - known as the creeps. This is one of four named decompression-sickness patterns depending on where the bubbles form: the bends in the joints, the chokes in the lungs, and the staggers affecting the brain and nervous system.

human-performance.q: What visual condition may result from a sudden increase in negative G?
human-performance.ans: Red-out
human-performance.e: Negative G pushes blood upward toward the head rather than pooling it in the lower body, and that extra blood volume raises pressure in the delicate vessels of the eyes. Many pilots find even mild negative G distinctly unpleasant, and enough of it produces the reddish tint across the visual field known as red-out.

human-performance.q: How long can full dark adaptation of the eyes take?
human-performance.ans: About 30 minutes
human-performance.e: Full dark adaptation takes time because the two types of light receptor in the retina adapt at different rates: the cones (used for colour and detail) settle in about 7 minutes, but the rods, which give low-light and peripheral vision, take much longer - around 30 minutes - to reach maximum sensitivity. This is why pilots should allow a proper adjustment period before flying at night rather than stepping straight from a lit room into darkness.

human-performance.q: According to Boyle’s law, what happens to the volume of a gas when pressure decreases and temperature remains constant?
human-performance.d: Both pressure and volume increase together
human-performance.ans: The gas volume increases
human-performance.e: Boyle's Law describes an inverse relationship between pressure and volume at constant temperature: as one falls, the other must rise to compensate. As an aircraft climbs and the surrounding pressure drops, any trapped gas inside the body - in the sinuses, middle ear, or digestive tract - expands to fill the extra volume that lower pressure now allows.

human-performance.q: Which part of the eye controls how much light enters?
human-performance.ans: The iris
human-performance.e: The iris is the coloured, muscular ring at the front of the eye that acts like a camera's diaphragm, opening or closing the pupil at its centre to control how much light reaches the lens and retina. Its size can change rapidly to cope with sudden changes in light level, from a dim cockpit to bright sunlight reflected off cloud.

human-performance.q: Which is an early symptom of hypoxia?
human-performance.a: A large and reliable increase in alertness
human-performance.d: An immediate ability to recognise the problem
human-performance.ans: Reduced mental performance and judgement
human-performance.e: One of the earliest and most dangerous effects of hypoxia is a decline in mental performance and judgement, often preceded by a feeling of euphoria or well-being that can mask the danger. Because this impairs the very faculties a pilot needs to recognise something is wrong, hypoxia can progress a long way before it is noticed without deliberate self-monitoring or an oxygen system.

human-performance.q: Blood pressure that is persistently higher than normal is called:
human-performance.ans: Hypertension
human-performance.e: Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure - the "hyper" prefix meaning excessive, just as "hypo" means deficient (as in hypotension, or hypoglycaemia for low blood sugar). It is a genuinely serious aviation medical concern: high blood pressure can weaken and eventually rupture blood vessels, particularly in the brain, potentially causing a stroke - JAA regulations specifically ground a pilot with a blood pressure reading of 160/95.

human-performance.q: Knowledge-based behaviour mainly relies on:
human-performance.b: Information held only for a few seconds in sensory memory
human-performance.c: Conscious reasoning using knowledge and experience stored in long-term memory
human-performance.ans: Conscious reasoning using knowledge and experience stored in long-term memory
human-performance.e: Knowledge-based behaviour is the mode used when a situation is unfamiliar and there is no ready-made rule or practised skill to draw on, so the pilot has to consciously reason it through using general knowledge and experience held in long-term memory. It is the slowest and most effortful of the three behaviour types, precisely because it demands full conscious attention rather than running on a trained routine.

human-performance.q: Compared with eastward travel, how is the body clock usually affected by westward travel across several time zones?
human-performance.a: It is usually affected less because delaying sleep is easier than advancing it
human-performance.c: It is affected only when travelling north or south
human-performance.ans: It is usually affected less because delaying sleep is easier than advancing it
human-performance.e: Travelling west effectively lengthens the day, since local time falls further behind, and most people find it far easier to stay awake a few extra hours than to force themselves to sleep earlier than usual. Eastward travel does the opposite - it shortens the day and demands falling asleep ahead of the body's normal schedule - which is consistently the harder adjustment for the circadian rhythm to make.

human-performance.q: How is hypoxia best prevented in a non-pressurised aircraft?
human-performance.d: Remain at an altitude that provides adequate oxygen partial pressure or use approved supplemental oxygen
human-performance.ans: Remain at an altitude that provides adequate oxygen partial pressure or use approved supplemental oxygen
human-performance.e: Since hypoxia results from an inadequate partial pressure of oxygen reaching the body's tissues, it is prevented either by staying at an altitude where the partial pressure of oxygen is still sufficient - normally below about 10,000 feet - or, above that, by breathing supplementary oxygen delivered at a rate that restores an adequate partial pressure in the lungs.

human-performance.q: Which gas can the body store in larger quantities than oxygen?
human-performance.ans: Carbon dioxide
human-performance.e: The body has almost no reserve of oxygen - cells depend on a continuous supply - whereas carbon dioxide is far more soluble and can be buffered and stored in larger quantities in the blood and tissues before it needs to be exhaled. This is also why the blood's carbon dioxide level, not its oxygen level, is the primary trigger the body uses to regulate breathing.

human-performance.q: Which type of lens corrects long-sightedness (hypermetropia)?
human-performance.a: A cylindrical lens in every case
human-performance.ans: A convex lens
human-performance.e: In hypermetropia (long-sightedness) the eyeball is shorter than normal, so images form behind the retina rather than on it, and the eye's own accommodation often is not enough to bring close objects into focus. A convex lens corrects this by bending incoming light inwards before it reaches the cornea, bringing the focal point forward onto the retina.

human-performance.q: What normally happens when the carbon dioxide level in the blood rises?
human-performance.a: A tingling sensation in the fingertips
human-performance.b: The oxygen percentage in the atmosphere rises
human-performance.ans: The breathing rate increases
human-performance.e: The respiratory centre in the brain is especially sensitive to the level of carbon dioxide in the blood, and when that level rises, the automatic response is to increase the rate and depth of breathing to expel more carbon dioxide and bring the level back down.

human-performance.q: As altitude increases, what happens to the percentage composition of the main gases in clean air?
human-performance.d: The amount of oxygen in each breath remains constant at any altitude
human-performance.ans: It remains approximately constant
human-performance.e: The relative proportions of the atmosphere's constituent gases - about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases - remain essentially constant with altitude, up to around 70,000 feet; what changes with altitude is the total air pressure, and with it the partial pressure of each gas, not the percentage mixture itself.

human-performance.q: When blood pressure is measured, what is the lower reading called?
human-performance.ans: Diastolic pressure
human-performance.e: Diastolic pressure is the lower of the two blood pressure readings, measured while the heart muscle relaxes between beats and the arteries briefly experience their lowest pressure. Systolic pressure, the higher reading, is captured the moment the ventricles contract and push blood forcefully into the arteries.

human-performance.q: What is the purpose of the Eustachian tube?
human-performance.a: To amplify sound at the eardrum
human-performance.c: To convert sound into electrical signals
human-performance.d: To equalise pressure between the middle ear and the outside atmosphere
human-performance.ans: To equalise pressure between the middle ear and the outside atmosphere
human-performance.e: The Eustachian tube runs from the middle ear to the back of the mouth and nose, letting air pressure in the middle ear vent and equalise with the changing ambient pressure outside as an aircraft climbs or descends. On the climb, the higher pressure in the middle ear escapes easily down the tube; on descent a small flap makes equalising harder, which is why ear discomfort is more common then. A blocked tube (from a cold, catarrh or sinus infection) can trap a pressure difference across the eardrum severe enough to cause pain or even rupture it (otic barotrauma) - swallowing, yawning, or the Valsalva manoeuvre usually clears it.

human-performance.q: What does Dalton’s law state?
human-performance.a: Gas volume increases directly with pressure
human-performance.c: The total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of its gases
human-performance.d: Gas pressure is unrelated to its components
human-performance.ans: The total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures of its gases
human-performance.e: The air we breathe is a mixture of gases, and Dalton's Law states that each gas in that mixture contributes its own share of the total pressure - its partial pressure - independent of the others. Adding all those individual partial pressures together gives the total pressure of the mixture, which is why oxygen's partial pressure specifically (not total air pressure alone) is what determines how much oxygen actually reaches the blood at altitude.

human-performance.q: Acute insomnia is commonly caused by:
human-performance.c: Permanent damage to the body clock
human-performance.ans: Anticipating a stressful event
human-performance.e: Acute insomnia is a short-term, temporary sleeplessness, commonly triggered by an active, anxious mind ahead of a stressful event - an important flight, an exam, bad news expected the next day - or by a short-term disruption to the body clock, such as travel across time zones. It resolves once the triggering event passes or the body clock re-adjusts, distinguishing it from chronic insomnia, which persists over a long period and is usually tied to ongoing stress or an unresolved health issue.

human-performance.q: Anxiety during a stressful situation can directly cause:
human-performance.d: Too little carbon dioxide in the blood
human-performance.ans: Hyperventilation
human-performance.e: Anxiety often makes a person breathe faster and deeper than their body actually needs, and that excess breathing blows off more carbon dioxide than normal - hyperventilation. The resulting drop in blood CO2 produces the classic symptoms of tingling in the extremities, dizziness and light-headedness, which can then feed back into the anxiety itself, sometimes as an alarming self-reinforcing spiral.

human-performance.q: Which visible sign is typical of cyanosis?
human-performance.a: Blue or bluish lips and fingernails
human-performance.ans: Blue or bluish lips and fingernails
human-performance.e: Cyanosis shows up as a visible blue or bluish discolouration of the lips and fingernails, caused by blood that is inadequately saturated with oxygen.

human-performance.q: A pilot with blocked sinuses is most likely to experience severe sinus pain during:
human-performance.c: A climb in a non-pressurised aircraft
human-performance.ans: Descent
human-performance.e: During descent, outside pressure is rising, and air trapped in a blocked sinus cavity or behind a congested Eustachian tube can't easily equalise against that increasing external pressure - creating a painful pressure differential across the tissue. Climbing is usually far less troublesome, since trapped gas at higher internal pressure can typically force its own way out through a partially blocked passage more easily than outside air can force its way back in.

human-performance.q: After a prolonged unnoticed turn, a pilot may feel straight and level, then sense a turn in the opposite direction when the aircraft is levelled. What is this illusion called?
human-performance.ans: The leans
human-performance.e: The leans occur when a very gentle roll into a turn is too slow to move the fluid in the semicircular canals enough to bend the sensory hair cells, so the pilot feels level even though the aircraft has actually banked. If the roll back to wings-level is then made briskly, that sharper fluid movement is detected, and the ear reports a turn that is not happening, in the opposite direction. The same illusion works in reverse after a prolonged steady turn: the fluid settles during the turn, so rolling out to level flight feels like rolling into a turn the other way.

human-performance.q: Damage to the cochlea is most likely to cause:
human-performance.a: An inability to detect linear acceleration only
human-performance.c: An inability to equalise middle-ear pressure
human-performance.ans: Permanent hearing loss
human-performance.e: The cochlea contains the fine hair cells that detect vibration in its fluid and convert it into the nerve signals the auditory nerve carries to the brain; once these delicate cells are destroyed, they do not regenerate. This is why loud noise exposure above roughly 90 dB damages the cochlea's membrane and finer hair cells and produces permanent hearing loss, unlike damage further out in the ear (wax build-up, a punctured eardrum, or damaged ossicles), which is often temporary or treatable.

human-performance.q: Which type of lens corrects short-sightedness (myopia)?
human-performance.ans: A concave lens
human-performance.e: In myopia (short-sightedness) the eyeball is longer than normal, so images from distant objects focus in front of the retina rather than on it, leaving distant objects blurred. A concave lens corrects this by bending the light outward before it reaches the cornea, pushing the focal point back onto the retina.

human-performance.q: What approach error can be caused by a very wide unfamiliar runway?
human-performance.a: The pilot will always land short
human-performance.b: The runway slope becomes impossible to judge
human-performance.c: The pilot may fly a lower-than-normal approach
human-performance.d: The pilot may fly a higher-than-normal approach
human-performance.ans: The pilot may fly a higher-than-normal approach
human-performance.e: A runway that is wider than a pilot is used to fills more of the visual field than expected at a normal approach angle, creating the impression of being lower than the aircraft actually is. Instinctively correcting for that false impression, to match the familiar picture, tends to make the pilot fly and round out higher than intended.

human-performance.q: Which chambers of the heart pump blood out of the heart?
human-performance.a: The right atrium and right ventricle only
human-performance.b: The left atrium and left ventricle only
human-performance.ans: The left and right ventricles
human-performance.e: The heart has four chambers: two upper atria that receive incoming blood, and two lower, more muscular ventricles that do the actual pumping work, propelling blood onward through the lungs (right ventricle) and the rest of the body (left ventricle). It is specifically the ventricles' contraction that generates the pressure wave felt as a pulse and forces blood out of the heart.

human-performance.q: Which structures transmit vibration from the eardrum to the inner ear?
human-performance.ans: The ossicles
human-performance.e: The ossicles are the three tiny linked bones of the middle ear - the malleus, incus and stapes - that pick up the eardrum's vibrations and transmit them across the air-filled middle ear to the inner ear. The stapes seats against the oval window of the cochlea, where it sets the cochlear fluid moving so its hair cells can generate the nerve signals interpreted as sound.

human-performance.q: Chronic insomnia is commonly associated with:
human-performance.ans: Long-term stress
human-performance.e: Where acute stress flares up and settles once the immediate demand passes, chronic insomnia is different: it persists over a long period, and is usually a symptom of ongoing, unresolved stress, poor sleep habits built up over time, or a continuing underlying health issue. Because the cause is long-running, fixing chronic insomnia means addressing that underlying cause, not just having one good night's sleep.

human-performance.q: Which type of sleep is mainly associated with mental or brain rejuvenation?
human-performance.ans: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep
human-performance.e:
REM sleep is strongly associated with dreaming, memory processing and mental restoration. Slow-wave sleep is more closely associated with physical restoration.

Exam tip: REM = mental; slow-wave = physical.

human-performance.q: Short-term stress is classified as:
human-performance.a: A condition that develops quickly but requires a very long recovery period
human-performance.ans: Acute stress
human-performance.e: Stress that develops quickly in direct response to an immediate demand or threat, and that settles back down once the situation has passed, is classified as acute stress - distinct from chronic stress, which persists over a long period without fully resolving. Recognising which type is in play matters because the appropriate response differs: acute stress needs rest and recovery time, while chronic stress needs its underlying cause addressed.

human-performance.q: What is the immediate physiological cause of fainting?
human-performance.a: A temporary reduction of blood flow to the brain
human-performance.d: High blood pressure in every case
human-performance.ans: A temporary reduction of blood flow to the brain
human-performance.e: Fainting happens when blood flow to the brain briefly drops too low to sustain normal function - often triggered by standing up suddenly, emotional shock, or prolonged standing - starving brain tissue of oxygen for a short period. Consciousness typically returns quickly once the person is horizontal and blood flow to the brain is restored.

human-performance.q: What does selective attention involve?
human-performance.a: Ignoring all information during high workload
human-performance.c: Sorting incoming information and concentrating on what is most important
human-performance.d: Concentrating equally on every task at the same time
human-performance.ans: Sorting incoming information and concentrating on what is most important
human-performance.e: Selective attention is the continuous process of sampling incoming information and deciding what deserves conscious attention, so that the limited, single-channel capacity of the brain's decision-making process is directed at what matters most. It is why a pilot can pick their own call-sign out of a stream of radio chatter almost instantly, even while apparently focused on something else.

human-performance.q: What is the most common underlying cause of motion sickness?
human-performance.a: Low blood sugar as the only cause
human-performance.b: Conflicting or excessive stimulation of the balance system in the inner ear
human-performance.d: Eating a heavy meal in every case
human-performance.ans: Conflicting or excessive stimulation of the balance system in the inner ear
human-performance.e: Motion sickness is fundamentally a sensory conflict: the vestibular system in the inner ear senses the aircraft's actual motion, while the eyes - especially if fixed on something inside the cabin, like a chart or phone - report a relatively still visual scene. That mismatch between what the inner ear feels and what the eyes see is what the brain interprets as a warning sign, triggering the nausea and other symptoms of motion sickness.

human-performance.q: Which statement best describes chronic fatigue?
human-performance.a: It can only be treated with medication
human-performance.b: It is always permanent and incurable
human-performance.c: It is cured immediately by one short nap
human-performance.d: It develops over a long period and requires prolonged recovery and correction of its causes
human-performance.ans: It develops over a long period and requires prolonged recovery and correction of its causes
human-performance.e: Chronic fatigue builds up gradually from repeated sleep loss, ongoing stress, illness, or sustained excessive workload accumulating faster than the body can recover from it - a single good night's sleep is nowhere near enough to reverse it. Genuine recovery requires both a prolonged period of proper rest and actually removing or reducing whatever has been driving the fatigue in the first place.

human-performance.q: A person with persistently low blood pressure may experience:
human-performance.c: Improved blood flow to the brain
human-performance.ans: Dizziness or fainting
human-performance.e: Persistently low blood pressure struggles to maintain adequate perfusion to the brain, especially during postural changes like standing up quickly, when gravity briefly pulls blood away from the head before circulatory reflexes compensate. That temporary shortfall in brain blood flow is what produces the light-headedness, dizziness or fainting associated with hypotension.

human-performance.q: What causes anaemic hypoxia?
human-performance.a: Too little functioning haemoglobin in the circulating blood
human-performance.b: Poor circulation to the tissues only
human-performance.c: Excess nitrogen bubbles in the joints
human-performance.d: Low atmospheric oxygen partial pressure only
human-performance.ans: Too little functioning haemoglobin in the circulating blood
human-performance.e: Anaemic hypoxia occurs when the blood itself cannot carry enough oxygen, because there is too little functioning haemoglobin available to bind it - whether from anaemia, blood loss, or a substance like carbon monoxide occupying haemoglobin that oxygen would otherwise use. This is distinct from hypoxic hypoxia, where the problem is a low partial pressure of oxygen in the air being breathed rather than a defect in the blood's carrying capacity.

human-performance.q: What is the function of the alveoli?
human-performance.a: They are tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it
human-performance.c: They pump blood through the lungs
human-performance.d: They transport oxygen around the body
human-performance.ans: They are tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it
human-performance.e: The alveoli are the tiny, thin-walled air sacs at the very end of the airways in the lungs, where oxygen from inhaled air diffuses into the surrounding blood and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way, out of the blood and into the air to be exhaled. This gas exchange, called external respiration, is where the entire respiratory system's job is actually accomplished.

human-performance.q: Judgement based mainly on learned skills and previous experience is called:
human-performance.ans: Perceptual judgement
human-performance.e: Perceptual judgement is the fast, largely automatic recognition of a familiar situation or pattern, built up through repeated experience rather than deliberate step-by-step reasoning - the kind of instant read an experienced pilot gets from the sight picture on final approach. It contrasts with cognitive judgement, which involves consciously working through a problem from first principles.

human-performance.q: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere is oxygen?
human-performance.e: Oxygen makes up almost 21% of the atmosphere by volume, and this proportion stays essentially constant with altitude - it is the total air pressure, and hence the partial pressure of that 21% share, which falls as altitude increases.

human-performance.q: Which blood component is mainly responsible for clot formation?
human-performance.ans: Platelets
human-performance.e: Platelets are the smallest blood cells, and their specific role is gathering at the site of any vessel damage to begin the clotting process, sealing the wound and limiting blood loss. This is distinct from red cells (oxygen transport) and white cells (fighting infection) - each blood component performs one specialised job.

human-performance.q: Which type of memory stores personal events and experiences?
human-performance.ans: Episodic memory
human-performance.e: Episodic memory stores the record of specific events and experiences in a person's life - a particular flight, a conversation, an incident - as opposed to general facts or practised skills. It is notably less reliable than other forms of long-term memory, since episodic recollections tend to drift over time toward how we would have liked events to unfold rather than how they actually happened.

human-performance.q: A strong forward acceleration may create a false sensation of:
human-performance.a: The body rotating when no rotation is occurring
human-performance.ans: Tumbling or pitching backwards
human-performance.e: A strong linear acceleration deflects the sensory hairs in the otolith organs backwards, the same way they would move if the head were tilting back, so the brain wrongly interprets the acceleration as the nose pitching up - a somatogravic illusion. This is why carrier-borne pilots keep their hands off the controls during a catapult launch: believing the sensation could lead a pilot to push forward into an unintended dive.

human-performance.q: A passenger has mild chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness and a pale complexion. What is the most likely condition?
human-performance.ans: An angina attack
human-performance.e: Angina is the pain that results when narrowed coronary arteries can't deliver enough oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle, especially under the extra demand of exertion or stress - and mild chest pain paired with breathlessness, dizziness and pallor fits that pattern closely. Unlike ordinary airsickness, chest pain is never a symptom to dismiss - it needs to be taken seriously and appropriate medical assistance sought.

human-performance.q: What is empty-field myopia?
human-performance.a: Permanent inability to focus the lens
human-performance.b: Long-sightedness corrected by a convex lens
human-performance.c: Loss of colour vision in daylight
human-performance.d: The eyes focus at a short resting distance when there is no clear object to look at
human-performance.ans: The eyes focus at a short resting distance when there is no clear object to look at
human-performance.e: Empty field myopia is the eye's natural tendency, when there is nothing to focus on, to settle at a resting focus of only one to two metres rather than at infinity, as long assumed. This matters for a pilot scanning for distant traffic in a featureless sky, cloudless high-altitude conditions, or total darkness, since the eye simply will not adjust to bring a distant, faint contact into focus - and the problem worsens when a nearer distraction, such as raindrops or dirt specks on the windscreen, competes for the eye's attention.

human-performance.q: Which group of symptoms is typical of motion sickness?
human-performance.d: Tingling fingers caused only by hyperventilation
human-performance.ans: Pale skin, nausea and sweating
human-performance.e: Motion sickness produces a fairly consistent symptom pattern - pale skin, nausea and cold sweating - as the body reacts to the underlying conflict between what the vestibular system feels and what the eyes see. These symptoms build together as the sensory mismatch continues, sometimes progressing to hyperventilation or vomiting if not addressed.

human-performance.q: How does physical activity affect the time of useful consciousness at altitude?
human-performance.b: It makes oxygen partial pressure rise
human-performance.ans: It decreases it
human-performance.e: Physical activity raises the body's demand for oxygen at the exact moment altitude is reducing its supply, so any exertion during oxygen deprivation uses up the available reserve faster and shortens the time of useful consciousness.

human-performance.q: What does “chunking” mean in human memory?
human-performance.c: Turning every new action into a motor programme immediately
human-performance.d: Grouping separate items into meaningful units so working memory can handle them more easily
human-performance.ans: Grouping separate items into meaningful units so working memory can handle them more easily
human-performance.e: Chunking is grouping several separate items of information into fewer, more meaningful units, which lets the limited capacity of working memory - normally only about seven unrelated items at once - handle far more effective information.
