A long string of digits like a phone number becomes much easier to hold in mind once it is broken into a few chunks rather than remembered digit by digit.

human-performance.q: A pilot acts immediately simply because “something must be done,” without properly assessing the situation. Which hazardous attitude is this?
human-performance.ans: Impulsivity
human-performance.e: Impulsivity, as a hazardous attitude, is the tendency to act immediately just because something needs doing, without pausing to properly assess the situation or consider the best course of action first. It is dangerous precisely because it skips the evaluation step that sound decision-making depends on.

human-performance.q: What is the best treatment for acute fatigue?
human-performance.ans: Restful, uninterrupted natural sleep
human-performance.e: Acute fatigue typically follows a demanding stretch of work or a short bout of lost sleep, and the body's genuine recovery mechanism for it is straightforward: proper, natural, uninterrupted sleep. Stimulants like caffeine can temporarily mask the feeling of tiredness, but they don't actually restore the underlying physiological deficit - the fatigue is still there underneath, just less noticeable for a while.

human-performance.q: What does pulse rate measure?
human-performance.a: The amount of oxygen in the blood
human-performance.b: The difference between systolic and diastolic pressure
human-performance.d: The number of heartbeats per minute
human-performance.ans: The number of heartbeats per minute
human-performance.e: Every heartbeat sends a pressure wave through the arteries that can be felt at points close to the skin - the pulse - and counting how many of these waves occur in a minute gives the pulse rate. This is a frequency measurement (beats per minute), distinct from blood pressure, which measures the force of the blood against artery walls rather than how often the heart beats.

human-performance.q: What is the time of useful consciousness (TUC)?
human-performance.a: The time available to recognise hypoxia and take effective action before performance becomes seriously impaired
human-performance.b: The period a pilot can function without oxygen before losing consciousness
human-performance.c: A constant period at every altitude
human-performance.d: The time required for full night adaptation
human-performance.ans: The time available to recognise hypoxia and take effective action before performance becomes seriously impaired
human-performance.e: Time of useful consciousness is the period, following exposure to inadequate oxygen at altitude, during which a person remains capable enough to recognise what is happening and take effective corrective action - such as donning an oxygen mask or descending - before impairment becomes too severe to act. It shortens dramatically at higher altitudes and following rapid decompression rather than a gradual pressure loss.

human-performance.q: What is the function of the auditory nerve?
human-performance.b: To carry electrical hearing signals from the cochlea to the brain
human-performance.c: To carry sound waves from the eardrum to the cochlea
human-performance.d: To equalise pressure across the eardrum
human-performance.ans: To carry electrical hearing signals from the cochlea to the brain
human-performance.e: The auditory nerve is the pathway that carries the electrical signals generated by the cochlea's hair cells - produced as sound vibrations move fluid within the cochlea - onward to the auditory centre of the brain, where they are perceived as sound.

human-performance.q: Rule-based behaviour, such as following a memorised checklist, mainly uses:
human-performance.a: Rules and procedures stored in long-term memory
human-performance.ans: Rules and procedures stored in long-term memory
human-performance.e: Rule-based behaviour applies a known rule or memorised procedure - such as a checklist - to a recognised situation, drawing on procedures stored in long-term memory rather than working the problem out from scratch. It is faster than reasoning through a novel problem but still requires consciously recognising which rule applies and following it correctly.

human-performance.q: What causes hypoxic hypoxia?
human-performance.a: Insufficient oxygen partial pressure in the air reaching the lungs
human-performance.d: Excessive carbon dioxide in the body tissues
human-performance.ans: Insufficient oxygen partial pressure in the air reaching the lungs
human-performance.e: Hypoxic hypoxia is a lack of oxygen caused simply by an insufficient partial pressure of oxygen in the air reaching the lungs - the situation a pilot faces at altitude without supplementary oxygen, when there is nothing wrong with the blood or the body's tissues themselves, only with the oxygen supply available to breathe.

human-performance.q: Under South African general operating rules, how long must a flight crew member wait after donating blood before acting as crew?
human-performance.ans: At least 72 hours
human-performance.e: Donating blood temporarily reduces both circulating blood volume and the number of oxygen-carrying red cells, increasing the risk of weakness, dizziness or fainting - exactly the kind of impairment that has no place in the cockpit. South African operating rules build in a 72-hour recovery window before a flight crew member may resume duties after donating blood.

human-performance.q: Why can a faint object at night disappear when you look directly at it?
human-performance.a: Night vision depends mainly on cones
human-performance.b: Its image falls on the cone-rich fovea, which performs poorly in dim light
human-performance.c: The cornea stops transmitting light at night
human-performance.ans: Its image falls on the cone-rich fovea, which performs poorly in dim light
human-performance.e: The fovea, the small central area of the retina responsible for sharpest detail, contains only cones and no rods, and cones perform poorly in dim light. Looking straight at a faint object at night puts its image on this cone-only area, so it can seem to vanish - looking slightly to one side shifts the image onto the rod-rich surrounding retina, which is far more sensitive in low light.

human-performance.q: When blood pressure is measured, what is the higher reading called?
human-performance.ans: Systolic pressure
human-performance.e: Systolic pressure is captured at the exact moment the ventricles contract and forcefully push blood into the arteries - the peak pressure of each heartbeat cycle, and so the higher of the two blood pressure readings. It is always written first in a blood pressure reading, over the lower diastolic value measured when the heart relaxes between beats.

human-performance.q: In which direction is body-clock adjustment generally easier when crossing time zones?
human-performance.ans: From east to west
human-performance.e: Because the natural, unforced human circadian rhythm runs slightly longer than 24 hours, delaying sleep (as westward travel requires) works with that natural tendency, while advancing sleep earlier (as eastward travel requires) fights against it. This is why body-clock adjustment is generally easier travelling from east to west than the reverse.

human-performance.q: The natural free-running human circadian rhythm is approximately:
human-performance.ans: 25 hours
human-performance.e: Removed from all external time cues - daylight, clocks, routine - the human body clock doesn't settle on exactly 24 hours; it drifts to a naturally longer cycle, conventionally taken as about 25 hours in aviation human-performance material. This built-in tendency to run long is exactly why the body finds it easier to stay up later (delaying sleep, as westward travel requires) than to fall asleep earlier than usual.

human-performance.q: In decompression sickness, what is joint pain caused by nitrogen bubbles called?
human-performance.ans: The bends
human-performance.e: Nitrogen bubbles forming in or around the joints - most commonly the shoulders, wrists, knees and ankles in aviation cases - produce a deep, rheumatic-like pain known as the bends. Movement or rubbing the affected joint typically makes the pain worse, while descending back to a higher ambient pressure usually resolves it by redissolving the bubbles.

human-performance.q: What approach error can an unfamiliar upsloping runway cause?
human-performance.a: The pilot may fly a higher-than-normal approach
human-performance.b: The pilot may fly a lower-than-normal approach
human-performance.c: The pilot must land beyond the midpoint
human-performance.ans: The pilot may fly a lower-than-normal approach
human-performance.e: An upward-sloping runway appears longer than it is when viewed from the correct approach path, giving the pilot the false impression of being too high. Acting on that impression by flattening the approach leads to flying lower than intended, with the risk of getting dangerously low.

human-performance.q: What does presbycusis mean?
human-performance.a: An inability to equalise ear pressure
human-performance.c: Loss of balance after a turn
human-performance.d: The gradual loss of hearing associated with ageing
human-performance.ans: The gradual loss of hearing associated with ageing
human-performance.e: Presbycusis is the gradual, permanent loss of hearing that comes with advancing age, and like noise-induced hearing loss it affects the higher-frequency range first. Because reduced hearing can lead to misreading radiotelephony transmissions, it is a genuine flight-safety consideration and can ultimately affect a pilot's medical fitness to hold a licence.

human-performance.q: What can cause grey-out followed by black-out?
human-performance.ans: Sustained positive G
human-performance.e: Sustained positive G pulls blood away from the head and pools it in the lower body, starving the eyes of blood pressure before the brain itself is affected - the eyes are more sensitive to reduced blood pressure than almost anything else. That progressive starvation shows up first as narrowing peripheral vision, then grey-out as central vision dims, and finally black-out, with full G-induced loss of consciousness (G-LOC) possible if the loading continues.

human-performance.q: What are common early symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning?
human-performance.c: Severe joint pain from nitrogen bubbles
human-performance.ans: Headache and nausea
human-performance.e: Carbon monoxide poisoning typically starts subtly, with headache, dizziness and nausea - symptoms easy to mistake for simple fatigue or airsickness. Left unaddressed, it progresses to impaired vision, judgement and memory, and can eventually produce the telltale flushed cheeks and cherry-red lips characteristic of more severe poisoning - any of these symptoms appearing alongside cabin heat use should raise immediate suspicion.

human-performance.q: Which are typical environmental or physical stressors in an aircraft?
human-performance.b: Noise, vibration and changes in temperature and humidity
human-performance.ans: Noise, vibration and changes in temperature and humidity
human-performance.e: Physical stress isn't only about workload or emotional demands - the aircraft cabin itself is a source of ongoing physical stressors: continuous engine and airflow noise, vibration through the airframe, and swings in temperature and humidity as the aircraft climbs and descends. These physical loads add to a pilot's total fatigue over a flight even when none of them feels dramatic in the moment.

human-performance.q: Why is carbon monoxide especially dangerous in an aircraft?
human-performance.a: It always has a strong warning smell
human-performance.b: It affects only people above 20,000 ft
human-performance.c: It is colourless and odourless and binds strongly to haemoglobin
human-performance.d: It increases the blood’s oxygen-carrying ability
human-performance.ans: It is colourless and odourless and binds strongly to haemoglobin
human-performance.e: Carbon monoxide is both colourless and odourless, so a pilot has no sensory warning at all that it is present - unlike smoke or fumes with an obvious smell. Worse, it binds to haemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does, effectively hijacking the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity, and its effects accumulate over repeated exposures - even flying the same aircraft again after lunch can add to carbon monoxide already absorbed that morning.

human-performance.q: Which inner-ear structures sense angular acceleration?
human-performance.ans: The semicircular canals
human-performance.e: The three semicircular canals are set at right angles to one another so they can detect angular acceleration around each of the aircraft's axes - pitch, roll and yaw. Fluid inside each canal lags behind during an angular acceleration, bending sensory hairs that generate the nerve signal; once the rotation becomes steady, the fluid catches up and stops moving, so the sensation of turning fades even though the turn continues.

human-performance.q: What is an important function of the rods in the eye?
human-performance.a: Changing the curvature of the lens
human-performance.c: Fine colour vision in bright light
human-performance.ans: Peripheral and low-light vision
human-performance.e: Rods are the retina's low-light receptors: they cannot distinguish colour but are far more sensitive than cones at low light levels, and because they are distributed across the retina rather than concentrated at the fovea, they are also responsible for peripheral vision. As light fades, the visual task shifts from the cones to the rods, which is why colour and fine detail disappear first at dusk.

human-performance.q: What does visual acuity mean?
human-performance.a: The ability to change lens curvature
human-performance.b: The ability to detect angular acceleration
human-performance.c: The ability to equalise ear pressure
human-performance.d: The ability to see clearly and distinguish fine detail
human-performance.ans: The ability to see clearly and distinguish fine detail
human-performance.e: Visual acuity is the eye's ability to resolve fine detail clearly at a given distance - a person with normal, 20/20 (or 6/6) vision can read at 20 feet what a person with impaired acuity would need to be closer to read. It is sharpest when an image falls precisely on the fovea and drops off quickly even a few degrees away from it.

human-performance.q: What happens to oxygen partial pressure as altitude increases?
human-performance.b: It becomes greater than nitrogen pressure
human-performance.ans: It decreases
human-performance.e: As total atmospheric pressure falls with increasing altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen - the share of that total pressure contributed by oxygen - falls at the same proportional rate, even though oxygen's 21% share of the air by volume stays constant.

human-performance.q: What should a pilot do immediately when experiencing spatial disorientation without reliable external references?
human-performance.a: Make abrupt control movements to test the sensation
human-performance.b: Look at and trust the flight instruments
human-performance.c: Close the eyes and trust the inner ear
human-performance.ans: Look at and trust the flight instruments
human-performance.e: Because the vestibular apparatus can only sense changes in acceleration and not a constant attitude, speed or turn, it is unreliable as a source of spatial orientation whenever outside visual references are unavailable. The rule is therefore to look at the horizon when visual references exist, and to believe the flight instruments over any bodily sensation when they do not.

human-performance.q: A control process that continually compares the result with the desired outcome and sends feedback to the decision maker is called:
human-performance.ans: A closed-loop system
human-performance.e: A closed-loop control process continually feeds the actual outcome of an action back to the decision maker, who compares it with the intended result and adjusts accordingly - exactly how a pilot rolling into a bank uses the visual picture of the horizon as feedback, easing off control pressure once the desired angle is reached. Without that feedback loop, the pilot would have no way of knowing whether the correction was too much, too little, or just right.

human-performance.q: Which type of sleep is mainly associated with physical rejuvenation?
human-performance.ans: Slow-wave sleep
human-performance.e: Slow-wave sleep is the deep, non-REM stage most closely linked to physical repair and restoration - tissue repair, immune function and physical recovery from the day's exertion happen predominantly here. REM sleep, by contrast, is where dreaming and mental processing concentrate, making the two sleep stages complementary rather than interchangeable.

human-performance.q: What is the main purpose of haemoglobin?
human-performance.a: To protect the body from infection
human-performance.d: To transport oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues
human-performance.ans: To transport oxygen from the lungs to the body tissues
human-performance.e: Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein packed inside red blood cells, and its job is a two-step handoff: it binds oxygen tightly while passing through the lungs, then releases that oxygen wherever the body's tissues need it most. Too little haemoglobin - anaemia - directly limits how much oxygen the blood can deliver, regardless of how much oxygen is actually available to breathe.

human-performance.q: What colour may poorly oxygenated blood give to the lips and nail beds?
human-performance.ans: A bluish tinge
human-performance.e: Haemoglobin carrying plenty of oxygen gives blood its familiar bright red colour, but poorly oxygenated blood loses that vivid red tint and takes on a bluish tinge visible through thin-skinned areas like the lips and nail beds. This visible sign of inadequate oxygenation is called cyanosis, and it is a clear warning sign of hypoxia.

human-performance.q: What is hyperventilation?
human-performance.a: Breathing more rapidly or deeply than the body requires, removing carbon dioxide too quickly
human-performance.b: A reduction in atmospheric oxygen percentage
human-performance.c: A blockage of the Eustachian tube
human-performance.d: Breathing too slowly to remove carbon dioxide
human-performance.ans: Breathing more rapidly or deeply than the body requires, removing carbon dioxide too quickly
human-performance.e: Hyperventilation is breathing more rapidly or deeply than the body actually needs, which expels carbon dioxide from the blood faster than it is being produced. Because it is the level of carbon dioxide, not oxygen, that normally regulates breathing, this overrides the body's automatic breathing control and produces its own set of symptoms, separate from hypoxia.

human-performance.q: What happens to the blood carbon dioxide level during hyperventilation?
human-performance.ans: It becomes abnormally low
human-performance.e: Because hyperventilation is by definition breathing out more carbon dioxide than the body is producing, its direct physiological effect is an abnormally low level of carbon dioxide in the blood, which in turn disturbs the nervous system's normal control of breathing.

human-performance.q: What is a common consequence of circadian dysrhythmia (jet lag)?
human-performance.b: Poor mental performance and reduced alertness
human-performance.ans: Poor mental performance and reduced alertness
human-performance.e: When the internal body clock is out of step with local time - circadian dysrhythmia, or jet lag - the mismatch doesn't just make a pilot feel tired. Sleep quality, concentration, reaction time and judgement can all measurably suffer, making jet lag a genuine performance and safety issue for flight crew, not simply an uncomfortable travel symptom.

human-performance.q: What dangerous gas can enter the cabin through a leaking piston-engine exhaust or heater system?
human-performance.ans: Carbon monoxide
human-performance.e: A cracked exhaust manifold or heat exchanger in a piston aircraft's heating system can let exhaust gas, including carbon monoxide, leak straight into the cabin air supply. Because the gas is colourless and odourless, the first warning is often physical - headache, nausea or weakness - rather than anything a pilot can see or smell, which is exactly why many light aircraft carry a carbon monoxide detector that visibly discolours if the gas is present.

human-performance.q: What does tinnitus mean?
human-performance.b: Ringing, buzzing or a similar sound heard in the ears without an outside source
human-performance.ans: Ringing, buzzing or a similar sound heard in the ears without an outside source
human-performance.e: Tinnitus is the perception of ringing, buzzing or a similar sound in the ear when there is no actual external sound source producing it, and it can be a symptom of damage anywhere along the hearing pathway, from noise exposure to age-related changes in the ear.

human-performance.q: Why can negative G cause red-out?
human-performance.b: Blood is forced towards the head and eyes
human-performance.c: Blood is forced away from the brain
human-performance.ans: Blood is forced towards the head and eyes
human-performance.e: Negative G reverses the usual direction blood is pulled, forcing it up toward the head and eyes instead of down toward the feet. The resulting rise in pressure within the eyes' blood vessels is what produces the reddish visual field known as red-out - a sensation most pilots find unpleasant even at fairly mild levels of negative G.

human-performance.q: What is accommodation of the eye?
human-performance.a: Moving the image away from the retina
human-performance.c: Changing the curvature of the lens to focus at different distances
human-performance.d: Changing pupil size to control light
human-performance.ans: Changing the curvature of the lens to focus at different distances
human-performance.e: Accommodation is the change in the lens's curvature, produced by the surrounding ciliary muscles, that lets the eye bring objects at different distances into sharp focus on the retina. This ability weakens with age and with fatigue, which is one reason tired pilots can find their near vision blurring when reading instruments or charts.

human-performance.q: What is the main function of the cochlea?
human-performance.b: To convert sound vibrations into electrical nerve signals
human-performance.ans: To convert sound vibrations into electrical nerve signals
human-performance.e: The cochlea is the fluid-filled, coiled structure of the inner ear where vibrations delivered by the ossicles set the fluid moving; fine hair cells lining the cochlea detect this movement and convert it into the electrical nerve impulses that the auditory nerve carries to the brain to be perceived as sound.

human-performance.q: Which source of information is most important for maintaining spatial orientation in flight?
human-performance.ans: Vision
human-performance.e: Spatial orientation in flight draws on three sources - vision, the ear's vestibular apparatus, and the somatosensory ('seat of the pants') system - but vision is the dominant and most reliable of the three, since the balance organs can only detect changes in acceleration and the somatosensory system is easily deceived. This is why the rule for a disoriented pilot is to look at the visual horizon, or trust the flight instruments if no outside references are available.

human-performance.q: What is autokinesis?
human-performance.a: The illusion that a stationary light is moving when viewed against a dark, featureless background
human-performance.b: A false tumbling sensation during acceleration
human-performance.c: Mistaking an upsloping runway for a longer runway
human-performance.d: Focusing only one or two metres ahead
human-performance.ans: The illusion that a stationary light is moving when viewed against a dark, featureless background
human-performance.e: Autokinesis is caused by tiny, involuntary movements of the eye that go unnoticed by the brain when there is nothing else in the visual field to provide a fixed reference; the brain instead attributes the movement to the object being stared at. Staring at an isolated light at night, a single star for example, can therefore create the illusion that it is moving, and has led pilots to mistake a star for another aircraft. Regular visual scanning, rather than fixed staring, prevents it.

human-performance.q: During a familiar repetitive task, a pilot omits the final check even though the action feels complete. What type of error is this?
human-performance.ans: Environmental capture
human-performance.e: Environmental capture is an error caused by habit: on a familiar, well-practised task, the routine sequence of actions can run to what feels like its natural completion and be interrupted or curtailed before the final step, because the situation itself has effectively taken over from conscious step-by-step attention. A pilot who habitually skips a check because the task felt complete, even though the actual sequence was not finished, is falling victim to this kind of error.

human-performance.q: What does the iris do in dim light?
human-performance.b: It changes the curvature of the lens
human-performance.c: It enlarges the pupil so that more light enters the eye
human-performance.ans: It enlarges the pupil so that more light enters the eye
human-performance.e: In dim light the iris relaxes and widens the pupil at its centre, letting more of the available light reach the lens and retina; in bright light it does the opposite, constricting the pupil to limit how much light gets in. This adjustment happens quickly, though genuine dark adaptation of the retina's rods still takes much longer.

human-performance.q: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere is nitrogen?
human-performance.e: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere by volume, making it by far the largest constituent gas, ahead of oxygen's roughly 21% and the remaining 1% of argon, carbon dioxide and trace gases.

human-performance.q: What does the term blood pressure describe?
human-performance.a: The number of heartbeats per minute
human-performance.b: The amount of oxygen carried by haemoglobin
human-performance.c: The amount of blood in the lungs
human-performance.d: The force of blood against the walls of the arteries
human-performance.ans: The force of blood against the walls of the arteries
human-performance.e: Blood pressure is defined as the force exerted by circulating blood against the walls of the arteries as the heart pumps - a pressure that peaks with each contraction (systolic) and drops during each relaxation phase (diastolic), which is why it is always recorded as one value over the other. It is a distinct measurement from pulse, which counts how often the heart beats rather than how forcefully.

human-performance.q: As altitude increases in an unpressurised aircraft, what happens to the amount of oxygen available in each breath?
human-performance.a: It increases because the air is colder
human-performance.ans: It decreases
human-performance.e: As altitude increases, air density falls, so a given breath - a fixed volume of air - simply contains fewer oxygen molecules than the same breath would at sea level, even though oxygen's percentage share of that air is unchanged.

human-performance.q: What happens to oxygen transfer from the lungs into the blood when oxygen partial pressure decreases?
human-performance.ans: It decreases
human-performance.e: Oxygen moves from the alveoli into the blood because its partial pressure there is higher than in the blood arriving at the lungs; when the partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli falls, as it does with altitude, that pressure difference driving diffusion shrinks, so less oxygen transfers into the blood for a given breath.

human-performance.q: What colour is well-oxygenated arterial blood?
human-performance.b: It is found in the right ventricle
human-performance.ans: Bright red
human-performance.e: Blood that is well-loaded with oxygen has a bright red colour, a property of oxygenated haemoglobin - this is the colour of blood leaving the lungs through the pulmonary vein, the one vein in the body carrying oxygen-rich blood. Poorly oxygenated blood loses that vivid red tone and shifts toward a bluish tinge, producing the visible sign known as cyanosis when it shows through the lips and nail beds.

human-performance.q: A reduction in the amount of haemoglobin in the blood is called:
human-performance.ans: Anaemia
human-performance.e: Haemoglobin is what actually carries oxygen in the blood, so when the body has too little of it, the condition is called anaemia - and even with plenty of oxygen available to breathe, there simply isn't enough haemoglobin present to carry it all to the tissues that need it. This shortfall in oxygen-carrying capacity is exactly why anaemia contributes to what's classified as anaemic hypoxia.

human-performance.q: A passenger suddenly develops severe chest pain and collapses. What should be suspected?
human-performance.a: An angina attack that has already passed
human-performance.ans: A heart attack
human-performance.e: Severe, sudden chest pain followed by collapse goes well beyond the milder, effort-related discomfort of angina - it points toward a heart attack, where heart muscle tissue itself is being damaged by an interrupted blood supply. This must be treated as a genuine medical emergency: seek medical assistance immediately and follow the aircraft's emergency procedures.

human-performance.q: In an otherwise healthy person, hypoglycaemia can be caused by:
human-performance.c: Looking directly at a faint light
human-performance.d: Missing meals or not eating regularly
human-performance.ans: Missing meals or not eating regularly
human-performance.e: Hypoglycaemia simply means blood glucose has dropped too low to properly fuel the brain and muscles, and in an otherwise healthy person the most common everyday cause is skipping or delaying meals - the body running out of readily available fuel between eating periods. The resulting weakness, shaking, sweating and poor concentration are the brain and body signalling that they need more glucose, which regular, timely meals prevent.

human-performance.q: A conscious person has symptoms of low blood glucose, such as shaking and dizziness. What is the most appropriate immediate response?
human-performance.a: Give a fast-acting source of carbohydrate and monitor the person
human-performance.c: Give only water and delay food
human-performance.ans: Give a fast-acting source of carbohydrate and monitor the person
human-performance.e: A conscious person showing signs of low blood glucose - shaking, dizziness, sweating - needs a fast-acting source of sugar or carbohydrate to quickly raise their glucose level, followed by continued observation to confirm the symptoms actually improve. Food or drink should never be given to someone who is unconscious, since that risks choking - an unconscious hypoglycaemic episode is a medical emergency requiring immediate professional help instead.

human-performance.q: Which description best matches angina?
human-performance.a: Severe chest pain followed by collapse
human-performance.b: Chest discomfort that is often brought on by effort and may ease with rest
human-performance.d: A loss of vision caused by negative G
human-performance.ans: Chest discomfort that is often brought on by effort and may ease with rest
human-performance.e: Angina happens when the heart muscle temporarily receives less oxygen than it needs, typically because narrowed coronary arteries can't keep up with the extra demand of physical effort or stress - and because the shortfall is temporary, the discomfort often eases once the exertion stops and the heart's demand for oxygen drops back down. Pain that is severe, prolonged, or accompanied by collapse is a different, more serious picture and should be treated as a possible heart attack instead.

human-performance.q: Following rapid decompression at approximately 25,000 ft, the time of useful consciousness is roughly:
human-performance.ans: 2 to 3 minutes
human-performance.e: Following a rapid decompression at 25,000 feet, the time of useful consciousness falls to roughly 2 to 3 minutes - far shorter than the time available after a slow, progressive pressure loss at the same altitude, because rapid decompression also forces air out of the lungs, compounding the drop in available oxygen.

human-performance.q: Which factors can make a pilot more susceptible to hypoxia?
human-performance.ans: Alcohol, some drugs and smoking
human-performance.e: Alcohol, certain drugs, and smoking all increase susceptibility to hypoxia. Smoking is a well-documented example: it reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of haemoglobin in the blood, so a regular smoker can begin to show hypoxia symptoms some 4,000 to 5,000 feet lower than a non-smoker would under the same conditions.

human-performance.q: Which symptom is commonly associated with hyperventilation?
human-performance.a: Tingling in the fingers, toes or around the lips
human-performance.b: A permanent increase in visual acuity
human-performance.c: Bright red vision from negative G
human-performance.d: Pain caused by nitrogen bubbles in the joints
human-performance.ans: Tingling in the fingers, toes or around the lips
human-performance.e: Hyperventilation lowers blood carbon dioxide, and one of its characteristic symptoms is a tingling sensation in the fingers, toes and around the lips, alongside dizziness, visual disturbance and a feeling of unreality.

human-performance.q: What is the appropriate response to suspected hyperventilation in flight?
human-performance.b: Consciously slow and control the breathing rate while using oxygen if hypoxia cannot be ruled out
human-performance.d: Breathe into a paper bag while flying the aircraft
human-performance.ans: Consciously slow and control the breathing rate while using oxygen if hypoxia cannot be ruled out
human-performance.e: Because hyperventilation and hypoxia can produce very similar symptoms and are hard to tell apart in flight, if hypoxia cannot be confidently ruled out - such as at higher altitude - the safer response is to use oxygen and treat it as hypoxia. Once hypoxia is ruled out, hyperventilation is treated by consciously slowing and deepening the breathing rate to let carbon dioxide levels normalise.

human-performance.q: Which additional symptom may occur with carbon monoxide poisoning?
human-performance.c: Weakness or loss of muscle power
human-performance.d: A lower pulse rate in every case
human-performance.ans: Weakness or loss of muscle power
human-performance.e: As carbon monoxide progressively displaces oxygen from haemoglobin, the brain and muscles receive less and less oxygen, and weakness or loss of muscle power is a common symptom alongside headache, nausea, dizziness and impaired judgement. If any of these appear during flight with the cabin heater in use, the standard response is to turn off the heat, open fresh-air ventilation, use supplemental oxygen if available, and land as soon as practicable.

human-performance.q: Noise-induced hearing loss is usually associated with damage to:
human-performance.a: The inner ear and is often permanent
human-performance.b: The Eustachian tube only and is always temporary
human-performance.d: The blood vessels in the legs
human-performance.ans: The inner ear and is often permanent
human-performance.e: Noise-induced hearing loss comes from damage to the sensitive membrane and fine hair cells within the cochlea in the inner ear, and once those cells are destroyed by prolonged exposure to noise above roughly 90 dB, the loss is permanent. High-pitched notes, detected by the finest of these cells, are usually the first to go.

human-performance.q: Conductive hearing loss usually involves:
human-performance.a: It is associated with the inner ear and is always temporary
human-performance.b: The outer or middle ear and may be temporary or treatable
human-performance.d: A lack of oxygen in the blood
human-performance.ans: The outer or middle ear and may be temporary or treatable
human-performance.e: Conductive deafness results from a problem in the outer or middle ear - a build-up of wax, or damage to the eardrum or ossicles - rather than damage to the cochlea's sensory cells themselves. Because the sound-detecting mechanism of the inner ear is unaffected, conductive hearing loss is often temporary and can frequently be treated.

human-performance.q: Damage to the ossicles would most directly cause which type of hearing problem?
human-performance.b: Sensorineural hearing loss from retinal damage
human-performance.ans: Conductive hearing loss
human-performance.e: The ossicles - the malleus, incus and stapes - form the mechanical link carrying vibration from the eardrum to the cochlea, so damage to them (for example from a blow to the ear or barotrauma) disrupts that transmission path rather than the cochlea's own sensory cells. This places it firmly in the conductive category of hearing loss, which is often treatable, rather than the permanent, sensorineural loss caused by cochlear damage.

human-performance.q: Which inner-ear organs mainly sense linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity?
human-performance.ans: The otolith organs
human-performance.e: The otolith organs sit between the semicircular canals and the cochlea and contain sensory hairs ending in tiny weighted granules; when the head accelerates in a straight line or tilts relative to gravity, these hairs are deflected and generate a nerve signal, making the otoliths the sensors for linear acceleration and head position.

human-performance.q: What is vertigo?
human-performance.a: A false sensation that you or your surroundings are rotating
human-performance.b: A gradual loss of hearing with age
human-performance.c: The normal widening of the pupil
human-performance.ans: A false sensation that you or your surroundings are rotating
human-performance.e: Vertigo is a false sensation that either you or your surroundings are rotating, typically arising when the balance signals from the vestibular apparatus conflict with, or substitute for, the visual information a pilot would normally rely on.

human-performance.q: Which action can help a passenger who is developing motion sickness?
human-performance.a: Read a book while looking down
human-performance.b: Look at the natural horizon and recline or support the head
human-performance.c: Move the head rapidly from side to side
human-performance.ans: Look at the natural horizon and recline or support the head
human-performance.e: Fixing the eyes on a stable outside reference - the natural horizon - gives the visual system information that matches what the vestibular system is sensing, directly reducing the sensory conflict that causes motion sickness. Keeping the head still and supported (or reclined) minimises additional vestibular stimulation, while avoiding rapid head movements and unnecessary G loading prevents making the underlying mismatch worse.

human-performance.q: How should a pilot view a faint object at night to see it more effectively?
human-performance.a: Look directly at it with the fovea
human-performance.c: Look slightly to one side of it
human-performance.ans: Look slightly to one side of it
human-performance.e: Because the fovea, the area of sharpest vision, contains no rods, and rods are what detect faint light, looking straight at a dim object at night puts its image on the least sensitive part of the retina. Looking slightly off to one side shifts the image onto the surrounding, rod-rich retina, where it is far more likely to be detected - worth practising deliberately, for example when scanning for faint stars or lights on a clear night.

human-performance.q: Tunnel vision during high positive G is mainly caused by:
human-performance.a: Excess carbon dioxide in the cabin
human-performance.b: Expansion of gas in the middle ear
human-performance.c: A sudden increase in blood glucose
human-performance.d: Reduced blood flow to the retina
human-performance.ans: Reduced blood flow to the retina
human-performance.e: Under sustained positive G, blood is forced away from the head and pools lower in the body, reducing blood flow and oxygen supply to the retina. The peripheral retina is affected before the central, foveal area, so vision narrows progressively from the edges inward - tunnel vision - before further blood-flow loss can cause a complete blackout.

human-performance.q: What approach error can a very narrow unfamiliar runway cause?
human-performance.a: The pilot may fly a lower-than-normal approach
human-performance.b: The pilot will always fly a perfect approach
human-performance.c: The pilot may confuse north and south
human-performance.ans: The pilot may fly a lower-than-normal approach
human-performance.e: A runway that is narrower than a pilot is used to fills less of the visual field than expected at a normal approach angle, creating the impression of being higher than the aircraft actually is. Compensating for that false impression by descending more steeply than necessary leads to flying a lower-than-normal approach, risking a late round-out or an undershoot.

human-performance.q: What approach error can an unfamiliar downsloping runway cause?
human-performance.a: The pilot may fly a lower-than-normal approach
human-performance.b: The pilot may fly a higher-than-normal approach
human-performance.c: The pilot will automatically increase L/D ratio
human-performance.d: The pilot will experience the leans
human-performance.ans: The pilot may fly a higher-than-normal approach
human-performance.e: A downward-sloping runway appears shorter than it is when viewed from the normal approach path, giving the pilot the false impression of being too low. Correcting for that impression by steepening the approach leads to flying higher than intended.

human-performance.q: What is the purpose of the Valsalva manoeuvre?
human-performance.a: To increase oxygen percentage in the atmosphere
human-performance.b: To prevent all forms of decompression sickness
human-performance.ans: To help equalise middle-ear pressure
human-performance.e: The Valsalva manoeuvre - gently pinching the nose and blowing against closed lips - raises air pressure in the back of the throat enough to force air up through the Eustachian tubes and into the middle ear, equalising pressure across the eardrum. It is most often needed during descent, when rising outside pressure would otherwise press the eardrum inward, and should always be performed gently - persistent pain or an inability to equalise is a signal to stop descending and seek an alternative approach.

human-performance.q: In decompression sickness, nitrogen bubbles affecting the lungs may cause a condition called:
human-performance.ans: The chokes
human-performance.e: Nitrogen bubbles that lodge in the fine capillaries of the lungs can partially block pulmonary blood flow, producing serious shortness of breath along with a burning, gnawing, or sometimes piercing chest pain - a pattern known as the chokes. It is one of four named decompression-sickness patterns, distinguished from the joint pain of the bends, the skin sensation of the creeps, and the neurological effects of the staggers by its specifically respiratory symptoms.

human-performance.q: Why can sustained positive G lead to grey-out or black-out?
human-performance.a: Blood is forced away from the head, reducing blood flow to the eyes and brain
human-performance.b: Blood is forced towards the head and eyes
human-performance.c: The percentage of oxygen in air becomes zero
human-performance.ans: Blood is forced away from the head, reducing blood flow to the eyes and brain
human-performance.e: Sustained positive G pulls blood down and away from the head, and because the eyes are more sensitive to falling blood pressure than the brain itself, vision symptoms appear first: narrowing peripheral vision, then grey-out, then full black-out. Loss of consciousness (G-LOC) follows only after blackout, once the brain itself is starved of adequate blood flow - easing back pressure on the controls, or tensing the thigh and stomach muscles beforehand, are the standard ways to relieve or delay the effect.

human-performance.q: Long-term stress is classified as:
human-performance.ans: Chronic stress
human-performance.e: Stress that persists over a long period, without fully resolving between episodes, is classified as chronic stress - distinct from the short-lived spikes of acute stress tied to a single immediate demand. Left unaddressed, chronic stress can progressively erode sleep quality, concentration and general health, which is exactly why it needs its underlying, ongoing cause identified and dealt with rather than just waited out.

human-performance.q: What is the best way to maintain normal sleep and avoid building sleep debt?
human-performance.c: Maintain a regular period of adequate natural sleep
human-performance.d: Use sleeping tablets before every flight
human-performance.ans: Maintain a regular period of adequate natural sleep
human-performance.e: A regular routine of adequate natural sleep is the only genuinely reliable way to keep the body and brain fully restored night after night - short naps and caffeine can patch over alertness temporarily, but neither actually substitutes for real sleep. Building sleep debt by consistently under-sleeping, even with those temporary fixes in place, steadily erodes performance and is exactly the pattern a pilot's personal fitness-for-flight discipline needs to guard against.

human-performance.q: Cognitive judgement is based mainly on:
human-performance.ans: A complex, conscious thought process
human-performance.e: Cognitive judgement is a deliberate, conscious thought process - working through the available information, weighing options and reasoning to a conclusion - rather than an instinctive read based on prior experience. It is slower and more effortful than perceptual judgement, but it is what a pilot has to rely on when facing a genuinely novel situation with no close precedent to draw on.

human-performance.q: What is confirmation bias?
human-performance.a: Forgetting all information held in long-term memory
human-performance.b: Favouring information that supports an existing belief while ignoring conflicting evidence
human-performance.c: Performing a movement without any previous intention
human-performance.d: A deliberate decision to break a rule
human-performance.ans: Favouring information that supports an existing belief while ignoring conflicting evidence
human-performance.e: Confirmation bias is the natural tendency, once a decision has been made, to stick with it - seizing on any small piece of supporting information to confirm that the chosen course of action is correct, while discounting or ignoring more compelling evidence that it might be flawed. It is a significant hazard in the cockpit because it can keep a pilot committed to a bad plan well past the point where the evidence should have prompted a change of mind.

human-performance.q: Which statement best describes skill-based behaviour?
human-performance.a: It requires constant conscious involvement of the brain
human-performance.b: It can only occur during emergencies
human-performance.c: A well-practised action can be performed with little conscious attention
human-performance.d: It depends entirely on short-term memory
human-performance.ans: A well-practised action can be performed with little conscious attention
human-performance.e: Skill-based behaviour is a well-practised, largely automatic action that runs with little conscious attention once it has been learned - the final, automatic phase a motor skill reaches after passing through an initial conscious, then an integrated, stage of learning. It is fast and low-effort precisely because it no longer occupies the brain's single-channel decision-making capacity the way a novel task does.

human-performance.q: What does semantic memory mainly store?
human-performance.a: Only personal events linked to a time and place
human-performance.c: Unprocessed visual images for less than one second
human-performance.d: General knowledge such as words, facts, language and numbers
human-performance.ans: General knowledge such as words, facts, language and numbers
human-performance.e: Semantic memory stores general knowledge about the world - facts, language, numbers, concepts - independent of when or how it was learned, and unlike episodic memory it is believed to be essentially permanent once stored, though sometimes hard to retrieve. Struggling to recall a word is usually a retrieval problem, not evidence that the information has actually been lost from the store.

human-performance.q: In the traditional aviation human-factors model, short-term or working memory can handle approximately how many unrelated items at once?
human-performance.ans: About seven items
human-performance.e: Working (short-term) memory can normally hold only about seven, plus or minus two, unrelated items at once; beyond that limit, items start to be lost or transposed. This is exactly why complex air traffic control clearances often cannot simply be memorised and need to be written down, and why chunking related information together helps stretch that limited capacity.

human-performance.q: A pilot who repeatedly ignores rules and procedures because they believe the rules do not apply to them is showing which hazardous attitude?
human-performance.ans: Anti-authority
human-performance.e: Anti-authority, as a hazardous attitude, is the belief that rules and procedures are for other people and do not really apply to oneself, leading a pilot to disregard them even when there is no good reason to. It is dangerous because most rules and procedures in aviation exist precisely because ignoring them has previously led to accidents.

human-performance.q: What minimum waiting time is recommended before flying above 8,000 ft after any scuba dive?
human-performance.ans: 24 hours
human-performance.e: Diving to a depth of 30 feet exposes the body to about two atmospheres of pressure - one from the air above the water and one from the water itself - which drives extra nitrogen into solution in body tissues. A minimum of 24 hours is needed for that excess nitrogen to clear before flying above 8,000 ft, since climbing into lower pressure before it does risks nitrogen bubbles forming and triggering decompression sickness, potentially at altitudes as low as 6,000 ft if the rule is ignored.

human-performance.q: An abrupt upward vertical acceleration may create the false sensation that the aircraft is:
human-performance.ans: Climbing
human-performance.e: An abrupt vertical acceleration deflects the otolith organs' sensory hairs in much the same way a forward linear acceleration does, so the brain can misread it as a change in pitch rather than a change in vertical speed - an abrupt upward acceleration is typically felt as the aircraft climbing, a somatogravic-type illusion. As with all such illusions, the flight instruments or the external horizon should be trusted over the bodily sensation.

human-performance.q: What mainly determines the normal breathing rate?
human-performance.a: The level of carbon dioxide in the blood
human-performance.b: The amount of oxygen required by the body
human-performance.c: The percentage of nitrogen in the atmosphere
human-performance.ans: The level of carbon dioxide in the blood
human-performance.e: Normal breathing is an automatic process governed mainly by the level of carbon dioxide in the blood; the respiratory centre monitors this level and adjusts the rate and depth of breathing to keep it constant, rather than responding directly to the level of oxygen.

human-performance.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood around the body?
human-performance.ans: The left ventricle
human-performance.e: The left ventricle is the heart's most muscular chamber, built specifically to generate enough pressure to drive freshly oxygenated blood - arriving from the lungs via the pulmonary vein - out through the aorta and around the entire body's systemic circulation. The right side of the heart handles the opposite, lower-pressure job: sending oxygen-depleted blood to the lungs to be reoxygenated.

human-performance.q: Which structures make up the vestibular apparatus responsible for balance and motion sensing?
human-performance.b: The semicircular canals and Eustachian tube
human-performance.c: The semicircular canals and otolith organs
human-performance.ans: The semicircular canals and otolith organs
human-performance.e: The vestibular apparatus is the combination of the semicircular canals, which detect angular acceleration in pitch, roll and yaw, and the otolith organs, which detect linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity. Together they give the brain data to maintain a model of spatial orientation, though - unlike vision - that data only reflects changes in acceleration, not a steady state.

human-performance.q: Which statement best describes a closed-loop control process?
human-performance.a: It works independently of the central decision maker
human-performance.b: It performs a memorised action without checking the result
human-performance.c: It cannot be changed once the action has started
human-performance.d: It uses feedback so the decision maker can compare the result with the desired outcome
human-performance.ans: It uses feedback so the decision maker can compare the result with the desired outcome
human-performance.e: A closed-loop control process is one where the outcome of an action is continually fed back to the decision maker so it can be compared with the intended result and the action adjusted accordingly - for example, a pilot rolling into a bank angle uses the visual picture of the horizon as feedback, easing control pressure once the desired bank is reached. Without this feedback loop, there would be no way to know whether an action had achieved, overshot, or fallen short of its intended effect.

human-performance.q: What mainly drives oxygen from the alveoli into the blood?
human-performance.a: The difference in oxygen partial pressure between the alveoli and the blood
human-performance.b: The low oxygen level in the blood regardless of any pressure difference
human-performance.c: The pumping action of the heart inside the alveoli
human-performance.d: The percentage of nitrogen in the lungs
human-performance.ans: The difference in oxygen partial pressure between the alveoli and the blood
human-performance.e: Gas movement across the alveolar walls happens by diffusion, driven purely by the difference in partial pressure of oxygen between the air in the alveoli and the blood arriving at the lungs - oxygen moves from the higher-pressure side, the alveoli, to the lower-pressure side, the blood, until the difference is reduced.

human-performance.q: As the oxygen partial pressure in the alveoli increases, what normally happens to oxygen transfer into the blood?
human-performance.a: The body's demand for oxygen automatically increases
human-performance.b: Oxygen transfer into the blood increases
human-performance.d: The oxygen percentage changes into nitrogen
human-performance.ans: Oxygen transfer into the blood increases
human-performance.e: A higher partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli increases the pressure difference driving diffusion into the blood, so more oxygen transfers per breath - which is exactly why breathing supplementary oxygen at altitude, which raises the oxygen partial pressure in the alveoli well above what the thin outside air alone would provide, restores adequate oxygen transfer into the blood.

human-performance.q: Perceptual judgement is based mainly on:
human-performance.a: A complex conscious thought process used for a completely unfamiliar problem
human-performance.b: A written rule that must always be followed step by step
human-performance.c: Experience and learned recognition of familiar patterns
human-performance.d: An automatic action performed without any judgement
human-performance.ans: Experience and learned recognition of familiar patterns
human-performance.e: Perceptual judgement is based mainly on prior experience and the learned recognition of familiar patterns, letting a pilot make a fast, largely automatic assessment of a situation - such as recognising the correct sight picture on approach - without consciously reasoning it out step by step. It contrasts with cognitive judgement, which is the slower, deliberate process needed for genuinely unfamiliar situations.

human-performance.q: Under Visual Flight Rules, who is responsible for the safety of the aircraft and its occupants?
human-performance.a: The occupants of the cockpit collectively
human-performance.b: The flying instructor in all cases
human-performance.ans: The pilot-in-command
human-performance.e: Even under VFR, where a pilot relies heavily on their own eyes and judgement rather than instrument guidance, the legal and practical responsibility for the safety of the aircraft and everyone aboard rests squarely with the pilot-in-command. ATC instructions, an instructor's guidance, or a passenger's input can all inform that judgement, but none of them shift the PIC's ultimate responsibility.

human-performance.q: Which quality is essential in a competent pilot?
human-performance.b: A highly developed sense of responsibility
human-performance.d: A willingness to ignore personal limitations
human-performance.ans: A highly developed sense of responsibility
human-performance.e: Competence in the air is about more than stick-and-rudder skill - it depends just as heavily on a highly developed sense of responsibility: recognising personal limits, following procedures even under pressure, and consistently prioritising the safety of everyone aboard over confidence or convenience. A skilled pilot who lacks this sense of responsibility is exactly the profile behind many preventable accidents.

human-performance.q: At approximately what altitude is atmospheric pressure half its sea-level value?
human-performance.e: Atmospheric pressure falls steadily with altitude near sea level: at 8,000 feet it is about three-quarters of the sea-level value, and by 18,000 feet it has dropped to about half.

human-performance.q: Up to approximately what altitude can a healthy person normally operate for a considerable period without hypoxia in an unpressurised aircraft?
human-performance.e: A healthy person can normally operate for a considerable period without suffering the effects of hypoxia up to about 10,000 feet; above that altitude, the partial pressure of oxygen in the lungs falls below the level needed to keep the body properly supplied, and supplementary oxygen becomes necessary.

human-performance.q: Which option gives the approximate composition of dry atmospheric air?
human-performance.b: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% other gases
human-performance.ans: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% other gases
human-performance.e: Dry atmospheric air is, by volume, about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, with the remaining roughly 1% made up mostly of argon plus a small amount of carbon dioxide and traces of other gases.

human-performance.q: At approximately 36,000 ft, atmospheric pressure is about what fraction of its sea-level value?
human-performance.ans: One-quarter
human-performance.e: Atmospheric pressure falls steeply with altitude: it is about three-quarters of the sea-level value at 8,000 feet, about half at 18,000 feet, and by around 36,000 feet it has dropped to roughly one-quarter of what it is at sea level.

human-performance.q: Compared with a non-smoker, a smoker is likely to experience symptoms of hypoxia at:
human-performance.ans: A lower altitude
human-performance.e: Smoking reduces the amount of haemoglobin available in the blood to carry oxygen, so a smoker's blood is already operating with a handicap before altitude adds its own reduction in oxygen availability. As a result, a smoker typically starts to show hypoxia symptoms some 4,000 to 5,000 feet lower than a non-smoker experiencing the same conditions.

human-performance.q: Approximately how long does the body take to eliminate one standard unit of alcohol?
human-performance.ans: About one hour
human-performance.e: The body eliminates alcohol slowly and steadily through the liver, at roughly one standard unit per hour regardless of what else is done - coffee, exercise or a cold shower cannot speed the process up. As a practical example, 1½ pints of beer or three single whiskies raises blood alcohol to roughly 45-50 mg per 100 ml, taking a full 3-4 hours to clear back to zero.

human-performance.q: What is the system that maintains the circulation of blood around the body called?
human-performance.ans: The circulatory system
human-performance.e: The circulatory system - the heart and its network of blood vessels - is the transport mechanism that keeps blood constantly moving throughout the body, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues while carrying away carbon dioxide and other waste products. It works hand in hand with, but is distinct from, the respiratory system, which is specifically responsible for the gas exchange itself in the lungs.

human-performance.q: What is the main function of red blood cells?
human-performance.b: To carry oxygen to the body tissues
human-performance.ans: To carry oxygen to the body tissues
human-performance.e: Red blood cells are packed with haemoglobin, the protein that binds oxygen in the lungs and carries it to every tissue in the body that needs it - their single, defining function. White blood cells handle immune defence and platelets handle clotting, so each of the three main blood cell types has one specialised job.

human-performance.q: Which statement best defines hypoxia?
human-performance.a: Insufficient oxygen to meet the body’s needs
human-performance.b: Too much carbon dioxide in the cabin
human-performance.c: Nitrogen bubbles forming in the joints
human-performance.d: Breathing faster than the body requires
human-performance.ans: Insufficient oxygen to meet the body’s needs
human-performance.e: Hypoxia is the general term for the condition in which the body's tissues are not receiving enough oxygen to meet their needs, whatever the underlying cause - at altitude, this is most often hypoxic hypoxia, brought on simply by the fall in oxygen partial pressure as you climb.

human-performance.q: How does a fast aircraft approaching head-on usually appear to a pilot?
human-performance.a: Large immediately and then almost unchanged
human-performance.b: Small and constant in size until impact
human-performance.c: Large at first and becoming progressively smaller
human-performance.d: Small at first, growing slowly before increasing rapidly just before impact
human-performance.ans: Small at first, growing slowly before increasing rapidly just before impact
human-performance.e: An aircraft closing head-on presents an almost constant angular size for most of the approach, since its image only grows appreciably once the remaining distance becomes a large fraction of the closing distance already covered; the image therefore stays small and grows only slowly for most of the time available, then expands very rapidly in the last moments before impact. This is exactly why early detection and prompt avoiding action matter so much in a head-on collision risk - by the time the size change is obvious, very little time is left.

human-performance.q: Why can very bright light at altitude be harmful to the eyes?
human-performance.b: It stops the cornea from focusing
human-performance.c: It contains a greater proportion of damaging blue and ultraviolet radiation
human-performance.ans: It contains a greater proportion of damaging blue and ultraviolet radiation
human-performance.e: At altitude there is less atmosphere to scatter and filter sunlight, and reflection off cloud tops adds further intensity, so the light reaching a pilot's eyes contains a greater share of high-energy blue and ultraviolet wavelengths than at sea level. Cumulative exposure to this blue light can damage the retina over time, while ultraviolet wavelengths mainly threaten the lens - one reason good-quality sunglasses are worth wearing at altitude.

human-performance.q: Which description correctly identifies myopia and its correction?
human-performance.a: A short eyeball corrected by a concave lens
human-performance.b: A long eyeball corrected by a convex lens
human-performance.c: A long eyeball corrected by a concave lens
human-performance.d: A misshapen cornea corrected only by a convex lens
human-performance.ans: A long eyeball corrected by a concave lens
human-performance.e: Myopia (short-sightedness) results from an eyeball that is longer than normal, which brings the focal point of distant objects to a point in front of the retina rather than on it. A concave lens corrects this by diverging the incoming light before it enters the eye, moving the focal point back onto the retina.

human-performance.q: Which part of the retina provides the greatest visual acuity?
human-performance.ans: The fovea
human-performance.e: The fovea is the small central pit of the retina that contains only cones and no rods, and any object needing detailed examination is automatically brought to focus there. It is the point of sharpest vision on the whole retina - visual acuity drops rapidly even a few degrees away from it.

human-performance.q: Astigmatism is most commonly caused by:
human-performance.a: An eyeball that is too long
human-performance.ans: A misshapen cornea
human-performance.e: A healthy cornea is evenly curved in a near-hemispherical shape, focusing light consistently in every direction. Astigmatism occurs when the cornea is irregularly or unevenly shaped, so light is focused differently along different axes, blurring or distorting the image; it can usually be corrected with cylindrical lenses or corrected surgically.

human-performance.q: Two aircraft are closing head-on at 180 kt with a visibility of 3 km. Approximately how much time is available from first sighting to impact?
human-performance.ans: 34 seconds
human-performance.e: Closing speed is the sum of both aircraft's speeds, and time to impact is the sighting distance divided by that closing speed, once both are converted to matching units. Working through a 180-knot closing speed against a 3 km sighting distance gives a time to impact of about 34 seconds - a striking illustration of just how little time is available to spot traffic and react on a head-on collision course.

human-performance.q: What is the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye that contains rods and cones?
human-performance.ans: The retina
human-performance.e: The retina is the light-sensitive membrane lining the back of the eyeball, containing the rod and cone cells that convert incoming light into the electrical nerve signals carried to the brain by the optic nerve. The image formed on it is inverted, though the brain automatically interprets it the right way up.

human-performance.q: What are the three main anatomical sections of the ear?
human-performance.b: Eardrum, Eustachian tube and auditory nerve
human-performance.ans: Outer, middle and inner ear
human-performance.e: The ear is divided into three anatomical sections: the outer ear (the pinna and ear canal, which collect sound and conduct it to the eardrum), the middle ear (the air-filled cavity containing the ossicles), and the inner ear (the fluid-filled cochlea and vestibular apparatus).

human-performance.q: What is the approximate audible frequency range of a healthy young person?
human-performance.e: A fit young person can typically hear frequencies between about 20 and 20,000 Hertz, though the loudness of a sound, measured in decibels, also affects whether a given frequency is actually detectable. This range narrows with age (presbycusis) and with noise-induced damage, both of which affect the higher frequencies first.

human-performance.q: Continuous exposure to noise above approximately what level can cause permanent hearing damage?
human-performance.ans: 90 dB
human-performance.e: Continuous exposure to noise above roughly 90 decibels can damage the fine hair cells on the cochlea's sensitive membrane, and with repeated exposure this damage becomes permanent hearing loss. Because high-frequency noise is particularly damaging, good ear protection - a quality headset can cut noise by around 40 dB, earplugs by around 20 dB - is worth using whenever noise levels are high, such as near a running engine.

human-performance.q: How is body mass index (BMI) calculated?
human-performance.a: Weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared
human-performance.b: Weight in kilograms multiplied by height in metres
human-performance.c: Height in metres divided by weight in kilograms squared
human-performance.d: Weight in pounds divided by height in metres
human-performance.ans: Weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared
human-performance.e: Body Mass Index is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared (BMI = kg ÷ m²), expressed as a plain number with no units. A normal range is roughly 20-25 for men and 19-24 for women, and while it is a useful screening tool, it is only one indicator of overall fitness, not a complete health assessment on its own.

human-performance.q: Why is iron an important part of a pilot’s diet?
human-performance.b: It prevents all forms of decompression sickness
human-performance.c: It is required for the manufacture of haemoglobin
human-performance.d: It controls the size of the pupil
human-performance.ans: It is required for the manufacture of haemoglobin
human-performance.e: Iron is one of the body's three principal minerals, alongside calcium and phosphorus, and its specific job is enabling the manufacture of haemoglobin - the molecule in red blood cells that actually carries oxygen. Too little dietary iron limits haemoglobin production, contributing to anaemia and reducing the blood's overall oxygen-carrying capacity - a serious concern for a pilot who already needs every advantage against hypoxia at altitude.

human-performance.q: A pilot suffering from gastroenteritis should be considered:
human-performance.a: Fit to fly if the flight is short
human-performance.c: Fit to fly after taking any medicine
human-performance.d: Fit to fly if no vomiting occurred in the previous hour
human-performance.ans: Unfit to fly
human-performance.e: Gastroenteritis brings nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea that can cause rapid fluid loss - any one of which could suddenly incapacitate a pilot mid-flight, let alone in combination. Even if medication is managing the symptoms reasonably well on the ground, a pilot suffering from gastroenteritis is considered unfit to fly, since the risk of sudden incapacitation in the air remains real.

human-performance.q: A fit or seizure is normally associated with:
human-performance.a: A temporary blockage of the Eustachian tube
human-performance.b: A reduction in oxygen percentage in the atmosphere
human-performance.c: An inability of platelets to clot
human-performance.d: An electrical disturbance in the brain
human-performance.ans: An electrical disturbance in the brain
human-performance.e: A fit or seizure - commonly associated with epilepsy - results from a disturbance in the brain's normal electrical activity, ranging from a brief period of "absence" or loss of attention in a minor fit to full convulsions and loss of control in a major one. Because either form can strike without warning and remove a pilot's ability to control the aircraft, it represents a serious aviation safety risk regardless of severity.

human-performance.q: A pilot suffering from a significant cold or influenza should normally be considered:
human-performance.a: Fit if the ears can be cleared once
human-performance.d: Fit if the flight remains below 5,000 ft
human-performance.ans: Unfit to fly
human-performance.e: A significant cold or flu does more than just make flying uncomfortable: it can reduce concentration and reaction time, and critically, it commonly blocks the sinuses and Eustachian tubes - the very passages that need to equalise pressure smoothly during climb and descent. Combined with the drowsiness many cold and flu medications cause, this makes a pilot with a significant cold or influenza unfit to fly.

human-performance.q: A pilot is 2.0 m tall and weighs 90 kg. What is the BMI?
human-performance.e:
GIVEN
Height = 2.0 m, weight = 90 kg.

FORMULA
BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)^2

SOLVE
BMI = 90 / (2.0)^2 = 90 / 4.0 = 22.5

ANSWER
22.5

human-performance.q: In a balanced level turn, approximately what bank angle produces a load factor of 2 G?
human-performance.e:
GIVEN
Level balanced turn, target load factor 2 G.

FORMULA
Load factor n = 1 / cos(bank angle)
bank angle = cos^-1(1 / n)

SOLVE
cos(bank angle) = 1 / 2 = 0.5
bank angle = cos^-1(0.5) = 60 deg

ANSWER
60°

human-performance.q: What is the best way to reassure a nervous passenger before flight?
human-performance.a: Show the passenger the pilot licence only
human-performance.b: Give a clear and thorough pre-flight safety briefing
human-performance.c: Avoid discussing anything that could cause concern
human-performance.ans: Give a clear and thorough pre-flight safety briefing
human-performance.e: Nervous passengers are usually anxious because of uncertainty - not knowing what to expect, how the restraints work, or what will happen if something goes wrong. A clear, thorough pre-flight safety briefing directly addresses that uncertainty by explaining exactly what to expect and how to use the safety equipment, which is why it remains the most effective way to reassure a nervous passenger before departure.

human-performance.q: Which group contains health risks commonly associated with severe obesity?
human-performance.b: Colour blindness, vertigo and decompression only
human-performance.d: Heart attack, circulatory problems and hypertension
human-performance.ans: Heart attack, circulatory problems and hypertension
human-performance.e: Carrying significant excess weight places extra ongoing strain on the heart and circulatory system, contributing directly to conditions like hypertension, heart attack risk, and general circulatory problems - the same cardiovascular system that already has to work harder under G loading and heat stress in flight. On top of the long-term health impact, severe obesity can also physically restrict movement and reach in a cramped cockpit, directly affecting a pilot's ability to operate the controls.

human-performance.q: Unconditioned reflexes are:
human-performance.d: Actions that always require conscious thought
human-performance.ans: Instinctive responses present without training
human-performance.e: Unconditioned reflexes are instinctive responses, present from birth without any training or learning required, such as blinking when something moves toward the eye or pulling a hand away from a hot surface. Because they bypass conscious processing in the brain almost entirely, they have the shortest reaction time of any type of response.

human-performance.q: Why is perception an essential part of information processing?
human-performance.a: It physically moves the aircraft controls
human-performance.b: It turns sensory input into a meaningful mental picture
human-performance.d: It removes the need for attention
human-performance.ans: It turns sensory input into a meaningful mental picture
human-performance.e: Perception is what turns raw sensory input - patterns of light, sound and pressure - into a meaningful mental picture the brain can actually use, rather than leaving the senses to deliver nothing more than unprocessed noise. Without this interpretive step, detecting a stimulus would provide no usable information on which to base a decision.

human-performance.q: Which three forms are commonly recognised within long-term memory?
human-performance.ans: Semantic, episodic and procedural
human-performance.e: Long-term memory is generally divided into three forms: semantic memory (general knowledge and facts), episodic memory (personal events and experiences), and procedural memory (motor programmes or learned skills). Some models of memory only distinguish semantic and episodic, treating procedural memory as a separate skill system, but many models include all three under the long-term memory umbrella.

human-performance.q: What is an illusion?
human-performance.a: A deliberate lie told to the pilot
human-performance.b: A perception that does not match physical reality
human-performance.c: A complete loss of all sensory information
human-performance.ans: A perception that does not match physical reality
human-performance.e: An illusion is simply a mismatch between what someone perceives and what is physically true - the mental model the brain builds from incomplete or misleading information falling out of step with reality. In flying, illusions are particularly hazardous because pilots normally, and rightly, treat their visual sense as the most trustworthy source of information.

human-performance.q: A pilot flying above a sloping cloud layer may incorrectly:
human-performance.a: Use the sloping cloud top as a false horizon and bank the aircraft
human-performance.b: Believe the airspeed indicator is over-reading
human-performance.ans: Use the sloping cloud top as a false horizon and bank the aircraft
human-performance.e: A widespread layer of sloping cloud can be mistaken for the true horizon if a pilot levels the aircraft's wings against it rather than against the actual horizon or the artificial horizon instrument. Because the cloud top is tilted, levelling against it means the aircraft ends up flying with bank applied and out of balance, even though it feels wings-level to the pilot. Regular scanning of the attitude and instruments, not just the view outside, guards against this.

human-performance.q: In hazy conditions, objects commonly appear:
human-performance.c: Farther away than they really are
human-performance.ans: Farther away than they really are
human-performance.e: Haze scatters light and reduces the contrast of distant objects, so they appear duller and less distinct than they would in clear air - a cue the eye and brain interpret as greater distance, even when the object is actually closer than it looks.

human-performance.q: During a night approach over dark, featureless terrain with only runway lights visible, a pilot may tend to:
human-performance.a: Fly a higher-than-normal approach and risk overshooting
human-performance.c: Fly a lower-than-normal approach and risk undershooting
human-performance.d: Mistake a stationary light for a moving aircraft
human-performance.ans: Fly a lower-than-normal approach and risk undershooting
human-performance.e: With no terrain lighting to give the eye any reference except the runway lights themselves, a pilot loses the usual visual cues used to judge height and can perceive an apparent black hole with the airfield sitting at its centre - the black hole effect. This absence of surrounding cues creates the impression of being too high, so a pilot tends to fly a shallower, lower approach than intended, risking touching down short of the runway.

human-performance.q: Compared with a familiar runway, an unusually small runway may appear:
