human-performance.c: Farther away than it really is
human-performance.ans: Farther away than it really is
human-performance.e: A runway shorter than the ones a pilot is used to occupies less of the visual field at a given distance than expected, which the eye interprets as the runway being farther away than it actually is.

human-performance.q: Compared with a familiar runway, an unusually large runway may appear:
human-performance.a: Farther away than it really is
human-performance.c: Upsloping regardless of its actual slope
human-performance.ans: Nearer than it really is
human-performance.e: A runway longer than the ones a pilot is used to occupies more of the visual field at a given distance than expected, which the eye interprets as the runway being nearer than it actually is.

human-performance.q: Which behaviour is not a good leadership quality for a pilot-in-command?
human-performance.ans: Aggressive assertiveness
human-performance.e: Good leadership for a pilot-in-command combines thorough planning, self-awareness of one's own capabilities and limitations, sound situational awareness, and a willingness to ask for help early when things start going wrong - not forceful, aggressive assertiveness, which tends to suppress input from other crew members rather than draw on it.

human-performance.q: A pilot planned a passenger flight, but the weather is marginal and the runway has a strong crosswind. What is the safest decision?
human-performance.a: Continue because the plan should not be changed
human-performance.b: Let the passengers decide whether it is safe
human-performance.c: Use the flight as an opportunity to practise difficult conditions
human-performance.ans: Reschedule the flight
human-performance.e: Faced with marginal weather and a strong crosswind for a planned passenger flight, the safest decision is simply to reschedule - recognising and accepting the real risk of the situation rather than pressing on because the flight was planned or passengers are expecting it. Good decision-making means weighing the probability and consequences of things going wrong, not just the inconvenience of changing the plan.

human-performance.q: What is the usual effect of mental overload on performance?
human-performance.ans: It degrades performance
human-performance.e: Mental overload degrades performance: as demands on the brain's limited, single-channel decision-making capacity exceed what it can handle, attention narrows or funnels, correct procedures can be forgotten in favour of older habits (regression), and in severe cases a person can become unable to consider alternative solutions at all. Recognising the early symptoms of overload and deliberately shedding or prioritising tasks is the way to prevent it escalating.

human-performance.q: If another pilot, even one with much more experience, begins an action you believe is dangerous, you should:
human-performance.a: Question the action immediately and clearly
human-performance.c: Remain silent because the other pilot is more experienced
human-performance.ans: Question the action immediately and clearly
human-performance.e: Even when the other pilot has far more experience, if you believe they are doing something dangerous, you must question the action immediately and clearly. Accident investigations have repeatedly found cases where a less experienced crew member recognised a developing problem but stayed silent out of deference to a more senior colleague, with fatal results.

human-performance.q: What is the usual effect of a moderate level of arousal?
human-performance.a: It always causes a breakdown in health
human-performance.b: It supports interest, alertness and effective task performance
human-performance.c: It prevents the processing of sensory information
human-performance.d: It creates severe tunnel vision in every person
human-performance.ans: It supports interest, alertness and effective task performance
human-performance.e: Arousal - a person's readiness, fitness and ability to respond effectively to a stressor - has a sweet spot: too little leaves a pilot under-stimulated, bored and slow to react (a real risk during long, routine, low-workload flying), while too much narrows attention and can overload decision-making (a real risk in deteriorating weather or an emergency). A moderate level in between is where interest, alertness and task performance are all at their best.

human-performance.q: After successfully coping with a stressful task, how is a person likely to react when facing a similar task again?
human-performance.c: Stress may be lower because confidence and familiarity have increased
human-performance.d: The person will be unable to recognise the task
human-performance.ans: Stress may be lower because confidence and familiarity have increased
human-performance.e: Arousal is essentially a measure of readiness and ability to cope with a given stressor, and that readiness improves directly with successful past experience - confidence built from having handled a similar situation well before, plus a tested response plan already in memory. Facing the same or a similar challenge again, a pilot typically perceives it as less demanding relative to their now-greater coping ability, which is exactly why training and repeated practice reduce perceived stress over time.

human-performance.q: What important characteristic of stressors should a pilot remember?
human-performance.d: Only one stressor can act at a time
human-performance.ans: Their effects can accumulate
human-performance.e: Individually minor stressors - background noise, cabin heat, time pressure, a poor night's sleep - don't simply disappear because none of them alone feels overwhelming; their effects add up. A pilot who could easily handle any single one of these in isolation can still find their combined total load becoming genuinely significant, which is why assessing overall stress load matters more than fixating on whichever single stressor seems biggest.

human-performance.q: How do very low and very high arousal levels generally affect performance?
human-performance.ans: Both can degrade performance
human-performance.e: Arousal has a well-recognised inverted-U relationship with performance: too little produces boredom, inattentiveness and sluggish reactions - the risk during routine, low-workload flying - while too much produces fixation, rushed decisions and a narrowed field of attention that misses the wider picture, the risk during a genuine emergency or deteriorating conditions. Performance peaks somewhere in the middle, at a moderate level of arousal, which is why both extremes need to be actively managed.

human-performance.q: Which statement about individual reactions to stress is correct?
human-performance.a: Everyone reacts in exactly the same way
human-performance.d: People can react differently to the same stressor
human-performance.ans: People can react differently to the same stressor
human-performance.e: How much stress a given event or circumstance actually produces depends heavily on the individual experiencing it - their prior experience, current health, fatigue level, personality, and how well-prepared they are for that specific demand. The same stressor, whether it's a rough approach or an unexpected radio call, can therefore provoke a strong reaction in one pilot and barely register with another, since arousal is fundamentally a personal, subjective response.

human-performance.q: The amount of stress felt by a person depends mainly on:
human-performance.c: Perceived demand compared with the person’s perceived ability to cope
human-performance.d: The number of people in the aircraft
human-performance.ans: Perceived demand compared with the person’s perceived ability to cope
human-performance.e: Stress rises specifically from the gap between how demanding a person perceives a situation to be and how capable they believe they are of coping with it - not from the objective difficulty of the situation alone. This is exactly why thorough training and careful preparation reduce felt stress: they don't necessarily make the task itself easier, but they genuinely increase a pilot's real and perceived ability to cope with it.

human-performance.q: While completing pre-take-off checks, ATC issues a take-off clearance before the checks are finished. What should the pilot do?
human-performance.a: Ask ATC to stand by, complete the checks and recheck the last items
human-performance.b: Skip the remaining items and take off
human-performance.c: Rush through the checks while accepting the clearance
human-performance.ans: Ask ATC to stand by, complete the checks and recheck the last items
human-performance.e: An ATC clearance is permission to proceed, not an instruction to cut a safety check short - the pilot's responsibility to complete the checklist properly doesn't disappear just because the tower is ready sooner. The right response is to ask ATC to stand by, finish the checklist, and deliberately re-verify the last few items, since an interruption always leaves genuine doubt about exactly where the sequence was left off.

human-performance.q: What is a stressor?
human-performance.b: A method of eliminating all workload
human-performance.d: An event or condition that places a demand on the person and can provoke a stress response
human-performance.ans: An event or condition that places a demand on the person and can provoke a stress response
human-performance.e: A stressor is simply the event or condition placing a demand on a person - noise, time pressure, uncertainty, conflict, physical heat or cold - and stress is the body's response to that demand, not the demand itself. Keeping this distinction clear matters because managing stress effectively means addressing either the stressor itself or a pilot's capacity to cope with it, and confusing the two can lead to treating the wrong side of the equation.

human-performance.q: What can happen if a pilot sits below the correct eye-reference position?
human-performance.a: Part of the undershoot area may be hidden during the approach
human-performance.b: The instruments become easier to read
human-performance.c: The pilot always sees more of the runway
human-performance.d: The upward view improves without any disadvantage
human-performance.ans: Part of the undershoot area may be hidden during the approach
human-performance.e: Cockpits are designed around a specific reference eye position that balances the view over the nose with a clear line of sight to the instrument panel. Sitting too low shifts that balance, hiding the near approach area - the undershoot - behind the instrument panel or the nose itself, exactly when that visual reference matters most on final approach.

human-performance.q: After being interrupted during a checklist, where should the pilot normally restart?
human-performance.a: At least one item before the point of interruption
human-performance.b: At the item after the interruption
human-performance.d: From memory without using the checklist
human-performance.ans: At least one item before the point of interruption
human-performance.e: An interruption during a checklist creates genuine uncertainty about exactly which item was last completed properly - memory alone can't be trusted to fill that gap reliably. Restarting at least one item before the point of interruption builds in deliberate overlap, so nothing gets silently skipped because of a false assumption about where the sequence actually stopped.

human-performance.q: Which is not a sound principle for the design and arrangement of aircraft controls?
human-performance.a: Important controls should be easy to reach
human-performance.b: Controls need only be standardised by shape and material
human-performance.c: Controls with different functions should feel or look different
human-performance.d: Control direction and location should be standardised where possible
human-performance.ans: Controls need only be standardised by shape and material
human-performance.e: Well-designed controls reduce selection errors through several combined cues at once - standardised location, direction of movement, and distinct shape you can identify by touch alone, without looking. Matching controls only by material or general appearance ignores the tactile and positional cues that actually prevent a pilot from grabbing the wrong control under pressure or in the dark.

human-performance.q: A pilot cannot find the correct checklist before a training flight. What should the pilot do?
human-performance.b: Take time to find the correct checklist
human-performance.c: Use a checklist from another aircraft type
human-performance.d: Rely on the instructor to notice omissions
human-performance.ans: Take time to find the correct checklist
human-performance.e: A checklist is built for a specific aircraft type and operation - substituting memory, a generic list, or the wrong aircraft's checklist defeats the entire purpose of having one. Schedule pressure before a training flight is never a good enough reason to skip finding the correct checklist; taking the time to locate it is the only acceptable option.

human-performance.q:
Which effects can result from sitting too high in the cockpit?

(i) Improved downward outside view
(ii) Poorer view of some instruments
(iii) Restricted upward outside view
human-performance.ans: (i), (ii) and (iii)
human-performance.e: Sitting too high shifts every sightline at once: the view down over the nose does improve, but the instrument panel is now viewed from an awkward angle that makes some gauges harder to read accurately, and the cockpit roof or canopy frame can start cutting into the upward view outside. This is exactly why the manufacturer's designed reference eye position, not simply "as high as the seat goes," is the correct seating target.

human-performance.q: An analogue display is generally better than a digital display for showing:
human-performance.a: Qualitative information such as trend and rate of change
human-performance.ans: Qualitative information such as trend and rate of change
human-performance.e: An analogue pointer's position and, crucially, its motion give an instant sense of trend and rate of change - is the value rising fast or slowly, and in which direction - all visible at a glance without reading a single number. A digital readout is precise but static; it tells you the exact value right now but hides how quickly that value is changing, which is exactly why analogue displays remain preferred for parameters where trend matters as much as the number itself.

human-performance.q: In the standard flight-instrument “T” layout, which instrument is not one of the four main instruments forming the T?
human-performance.ans: Magnetic compass
human-performance.e: The standard basic "T" arrangement places the attitude indicator centrally, airspeed to its left, altimeter to its right, and the direction indicator below - four instruments chosen specifically to support a fast, organised scan pattern. The magnetic compass, while still essential for navigation, sits outside this core T and is not one of the four instruments the layout is built around.

human-performance.q: Which checklist behaviour is not a pilot error?
human-performance.a: Responding automatically without verifying the item
human-performance.c: Completing each check diligently and efficiently
human-performance.d: Working so slowly that attention and timing are lost
human-performance.ans: Completing each check diligently and efficiently
human-performance.e: A checklist only works if each item is genuinely verified, not merely recited from memory - rote "read and respond without checking" behaviour, skipped items, and dragging the process out so slowly it becomes a distraction are all recognised checklist errors. Completing each check diligently and at an appropriate operational pace is exactly the behaviour the checklist is designed to produce, not an error at all.

human-performance.q: Studies of human error during a simple, repetitive task suggest an error can normally be expected to occur about how often?
human-performance.ans: Once in about 100 actions
human-performance.e: Studies of simple, repetitive tasks have found that a person can normally be expected to make an error about once in every 100 actions - a rate built into the way humans process information, and one that rises further under stress, fatigue or low morale. Practice and training can improve on this baseline considerably, but the underlying error rate never disappears completely, which is exactly why checklists and cross-checks exist.

human-performance.q: What is 'error chain'?
human-performance.a: A single isolated mistake with no further consequences
human-performance.b: A checklist used to prevent errors
human-performance.c: A sequence in which one error leads to a second, which leads to a third, and so on
human-performance.d: The list of errors recorded after an accident investigation
human-performance.ans: A sequence in which one error leads to a second, which leads to a third, and so on
human-performance.e: An error chain is a sequence in which one error is allowed to lead to a second, which leads to a third, and so on, each one compounding the last rather than being caught and corrected. Because isolated errors are common but usually harmless on their own, breaking the chain early - catching and correcting the first error - is what prevents it from escalating into something serious.

human-performance.q: A student pilot follows through on the controls while an instructor demonstrates an approach, then flies the approach himself shortly afterwards. Which type of learning does this illustrate?
human-performance.ans: Observation and imitation
human-performance.e: Observation and imitation is a type of learning in which a skill is acquired by watching someone else perform it and then replicating the action - exactly what happens when a student pilot follows through on the controls while an instructor flies an approach, then flies the approach themselves shortly after.

human-performance.q: What is 'over-learning'?
human-performance.a: Learning too many unrelated subjects at once
human-performance.b: Learning beyond the degree required to perform a task to the minimum acceptable level
human-performance.c: A failure to retain information after training
human-performance.d: Learning that relies only on mnemonics
human-performance.ans: Learning beyond the degree required to perform a task to the minimum acceptable level
human-performance.e: Over-learning is practising a skill well beyond the point needed to perform it to just an acceptable standard. It is worth the extra effort because it both improves the chances of recalling the skill later and makes performing it far more resistant to the effects of stress, which is exactly when a pilot most needs a practised skill to hold up.

human-performance.q: In the simplest case, such as pushing a button when a single light illuminates, what is a typical human reaction time?
human-performance.ans: About 0.2 seconds
human-performance.e: In the simplest possible case - a single light triggering a single button press - typical human reaction time is about 0.2 seconds. Adding more choices, such as a second light and a second button, increases this time because the brain's central decision-making process has more information to sort through before selecting a response.

human-performance.q: How does a high level of arousal generally affect a pilot's response to a stimulus?
human-performance.a: It leads to a slower but more accurate response
human-performance.b: It leads to a faster but less accurate response
human-performance.c: It has no effect on the speed or accuracy of response
human-performance.d: It only affects visual responses, not auditory ones
human-performance.ans: It leads to a faster but less accurate response
human-performance.e: A high level of arousal tends to produce a faster but less accurate response, since the brain is primed to react quickly but has less capacity available to fully process and verify the correct response before acting. This is why performance follows an inverted-U with arousal: too little produces sluggish, inattentive responses, but too much can produce fast responses that are also more error-prone.

human-performance.q: Compared with visual stimuli, auditory stimuli (such as a warning tone) are:
human-performance.a: Less likely to attract attention but more accurately responded to
human-performance.b: Always ignored in a high workload cockpit
human-performance.c: More likely to attract a pilot's attention, but also more likely to be responded to in error
human-performance.d: Processed at exactly the same speed and accuracy as visual stimuli
human-performance.ans: More likely to attract a pilot's attention, but also more likely to be responded to in error
human-performance.e: Auditory stimuli, such as a warning tone, are more effective than visual ones at grabbing a pilot's attention in the first place - but that same immediacy also makes them more likely to trigger a hasty, incorrect response, since there is less opportunity to properly process the stimulus before reacting to it.

human-performance.q: A pilot, anticipating that rising engine temperature will require an engine shutdown, shuts the engine down in response to an unrelated and unexpected rpm fluctuation. What is this type of error called?
human-performance.ans: An error of commission
human-performance.e: This is an error of commission: because the pilot had already mentally prepared and rehearsed a specific response in anticipation of a particular problem, an unrelated but similarly-flavoured stimulus was enough to trigger that prepared response even though it was not actually the right one. Preparing for an anticipated emergency is sound practice, but it can make a pilot too quick to apply that prepared response to the wrong trigger.

human-performance.q: In assessing the risk of a proposed course of action, a pilot should weigh up:
human-performance.a: Only the probability of the event occurring
human-performance.b: Only the impact if the event occurred
human-performance.c: The probability of the event occurring and the impact if it did occur
human-performance.d: The cost of insurance against the event
human-performance.ans: The probability of the event occurring and the impact if it did occur
human-performance.e: Sound risk assessment weighs two things together: how likely the event is to actually happen, and how serious the consequences would be if it did. A low-probability event with severe consequences, or a high-probability event with only minor consequences, can both warrant real caution - risk is not just about how likely something is.

human-performance.q: What is the first step in a structured decision-making process?
human-performance.d: Diagnose the problem and define the objective
human-performance.ans: Diagnose the problem and define the objective
human-performance.e: The first step in a structured decision-making process is to diagnose the problem and define the objective - identifying what the real, most urgent issue actually is, specifying what you are trying to achieve, and assessing how much time is available - before moving on to gathering information, assessing risk, and developing and comparing options.

human-performance.q: A pilot recognises that a decision he has just made was wrong. What should he do?
human-performance.a: Continue with the original decision to avoid appearing indecisive
human-performance.b: Wait until landing before making any change
human-performance.c: Modify his action accordingly rather than persist with the flawed decision
human-performance.d: Hand control to another crew member immediately, regardless of their experience
human-performance.ans: Modify his action accordingly rather than persist with the flawed decision
human-performance.e: Recognising that a decision was wrong is only useful if it is acted on: the pilot should modify the action accordingly rather than persisting with a flawed decision simply because it was already made. To err is human, but persisting in the error once it is recognised is far more dangerous than the original mistake.

human-performance.q: How is 'airmanship' best described?
human-performance.a: Strict compliance with checklists and nothing more
human-performance.b: A keen awareness of the aircraft and flying environment, sound decision-making, and a highly developed sense of self-discipline, combined with a determination to advance piloting skill
human-performance.c: Natural talent that cannot be developed through training
human-performance.d: The ability to fly aerobatic manoeuvres safely
human-performance.ans: A keen awareness of the aircraft and flying environment, sound decision-making, and a highly developed sense of self-discipline, combined with a determination to advance piloting skill
human-performance.e: Airmanship is deliberately defined as more than raw flying skill - it combines a keen, ongoing awareness of the aircraft and the flying environment, sound decision-making under pressure, and a highly developed sense of self-discipline, all driven by a genuine determination to keep improving. It is a rounded professional attitude built through consistent self-discipline and continuous learning, not something a pilot simply has or lacks from day one.

human-performance.q: Which of the following is recognised as a barrier to good verbal communication in the cockpit?
human-performance.ans: Excessively authoritarian behaviour
human-performance.e: Cockpit communication research has identified a consistent set of attitudes that shut down good crew communication: excessive authoritarianism, impulsiveness, aggressiveness, arrogance, resignation and irresponsibility all make it harder for information to flow clearly between crew members. An overly authoritarian pilot in particular discourages others from speaking up, which is exactly the kind of barrier that has contributed to real accidents where a crew member noticed a problem but didn't feel able to raise it.

human-performance.q: Which of the following is a criterion for a good pre-flight briefing?
human-performance.a: It should include as much information as possible to avoid a follow-up briefing
human-performance.b: It should be delivered only after the flight, not before it
human-performance.c: It should avoid any interaction with the student or passenger
human-performance.d: It should conclude with a question and answer session to check understanding
human-performance.ans: It should conclude with a question and answer session to check understanding
human-performance.e: A good pre-flight briefing needs to be kept short and directly relevant to the specific sortie ahead - overloading it with excessive detail defeats its purpose just as much as leaving out something important. Ending with a genuine question-and-answer exchange is what actually confirms the listener understood the briefing, rather than simply assuming the information landed because it was said out loud.

human-performance.q: When supervising aircraft refuelling, which of the following must a Pilot-In-Command specifically check?
human-performance.a: Only that the fuel tanks are full
human-performance.c: The weather forecast for the destination airfield
human-performance.d: The correct grade and amount of fuel, fire safety precautions, and that filler caps are correctly replaced
human-performance.ans: The correct grade and amount of fuel, fire safety precautions, and that filler caps are correctly replaced
human-performance.e: Supervising refuelling is a multi-part responsibility for the pilot-in-command, not a single check: confirming the correct fuel grade and quantity (including checking for water contamination), observing fire safety precautions throughout, and afterward verifying that every filler cap has been correctly replaced and secured. Missing any one of these - wrong fuel grade, a fire hazard during fuelling, or a loose cap that lets fuel siphon out in flight - has been the direct cause of real accidents.

human-performance.q: Approximately what percentage of all aircraft accidents are attributed to human error?
human-performance.e: Human error, not mechanical failure, is now the dominant cause of aircraft accidents, accounting for roughly 70-75% of the total (commonly cited as 73%) - a figure that has held steady even as aircraft engines, instrumentation and air traffic control have all become dramatically more reliable. This is exactly why human-performance training exists: the weakest link in modern aviation safety is overwhelmingly the human one, not the machine.

human-performance.q: What is the most common single form of aircraft accident resulting from human error?
human-performance.ans: Controlled flight into terrain
human-performance.e: Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) - flying a perfectly airworthy aircraft into the ground, water or an obstacle while the pilot is still in control - is the single most common form of accident caused by human error. It happens not because anything failed mechanically, but because the pilot lost situational awareness of where the aircraft actually was relative to terrain, which is exactly the kind of failure human-factors training is designed to prevent.

human-performance.q: What is the most common specific cause of pilot-induced accidents?
human-performance.ans: Loss of directional control
human-performance.e: Among the specific pilot-induced causes of accidents, loss of directional control tops the list - ahead of poor judgement, failure to maintain airspeed, poor pre-flight planning, and failure to maintain ground clearance, in that order of frequency. These five recur together across accident investigations, with directional control consistently the most common single failure.

human-performance.q: Which phase of flight is statistically most prone to accidents?
human-performance.ans: Intermediate and final approach
human-performance.e: Accidents cluster heavily around the phases of flight demanding the highest workload and precision at the lowest altitude: intermediate and final approach is the single most accident-prone phase, followed by landing, then take-off, then descent. The relatively low-workload cruise, by contrast, accounts for comparatively few accidents - it is the demanding, close-to-the-ground phases where errors most often turn into accidents.

human-performance.q: What is 'patter', in the context of flying instruction?
human-performance.a: The pre-flight checklist read aloud before engine start
human-performance.b: Informal conversation unrelated to the flight
human-performance.c: The standard instructional phraseology an instructor uses to communicate clearly with a student in the air
human-performance.d: The formal radio phraseology used with Air Traffic Control
human-performance.ans: The standard instructional phraseology an instructor uses to communicate clearly with a student in the air
human-performance.e: Patter is the structured, standardised phraseology a flying instructor develops specifically to communicate clearly and consistently with a student during in-flight instruction - distinct from the radiotelephony phraseology used to talk to ATC. Building good patter, so instructions land clearly even over engine noise and radio static, is a specific, deliberately trained skill for instructors.

human-performance.q: A pilot who has mostly flown in relatively polluted or hazy air moves to a region with very clear air. How is he likely to misjudge distant objects?
human-performance.a: He may judge them to be farther away than they actually are
human-performance.b: He may judge them to be closer than they actually are, because of their unusual clarity
human-performance.c: He will judge distance with the same accuracy as usual
human-performance.d: He will be unable to see them at all
human-performance.ans: He may judge them to be closer than they actually are, because of their unusual clarity
human-performance.e: A pilot who has learned to judge distance mainly in relatively polluted or hazy air has effectively calibrated their sense of range to reduced clarity and contrast. Moving to very clear air, where distant objects look unusually crisp and well-defined, throws that calibration off and tends to make those objects seem closer than they really are - a documented cause of accidents in clear polar and mountain conditions where pilots misjudged the distance to high ground or a landing site.

human-performance.q: What is the 'Black Hole Effect' (Kraft Illusion)?
human-performance.a: An illusion caused by staring at a single stationary light
human-performance.b: An illusion, caused by approaching an airfield at night with only the runway lights visible and no surrounding terrain lighting, that makes the aircraft seem too high
human-performance.c: An illusion that makes a runway appear shorter than it is
human-performance.d: A loss of night vision caused by bright cockpit lighting
human-performance.ans: An illusion, caused by approaching an airfield at night with only the runway lights visible and no surrounding terrain lighting, that makes the aircraft seem too high
human-performance.e: The Black Hole Effect, or Kraft Illusion, occurs when approaching an airfield at night with only the runway and airfield lighting visible and no surrounding town or terrain lighting for reference. The lack of visual cues around the runway creates the impression that the aircraft is too high, tempting the pilot into a shallow, low approach that risks touching down short of the runway.

human-performance.q: What is 'white out'?
human-performance.a: A temporary loss of vision caused by very bright sunlight reflecting off cloud
human-performance.b: The bleaching of colour vision that occurs above 10,000 feet
human-performance.c: A condition, caused by snow coverage, in which the absence of terrain features makes it difficult to judge height, depth and slope
human-performance.d: A visual illusion caused only by fog, unrelated to snow
human-performance.ans: A condition, caused by snow coverage, in which the absence of terrain features makes it difficult to judge height, depth and slope
human-performance.e: White out is the loss of visual reference caused by extensive snow cover, where the absence of any terrain features makes it impossible to distinguish where the ground ends and the sky begins. It leaves a pilot with essentially no cues to judge height, depth or slope, since the landscape appears as a single flat, featureless white plane.

human-performance.q: A pilot used to a standard runway width of approximately 150 feet (46 m) lands at an unfamiliar airfield with a narrower runway. What is the likely effect on his approach?
human-performance.a: He is likely to judge himself too low and fly a higher than normal approach
human-performance.b: He is likely to judge himself too high and fly a lower than normal approach
human-performance.c: He will judge the approach with no error, since runway width has no effect on height perception
human-performance.d: He will round out too high and stall onto the runway
human-performance.ans: He is likely to judge himself too high and fly a lower than normal approach
human-performance.e: Pilots calibrate their sense of approach angle partly on the expected width of a runway, typically around 150 feet (46 m). A narrower-than-expected runway therefore looks farther away for a given apparent size, creating the impression of being too high; correcting for that false impression leads to flying a lower approach and rounding out too late, risking a heavy or short landing.

human-performance.q: Why is it difficult for a pilot to judge the relative altitude of another aircraft approaching at a distance?
human-performance.a: It is only difficult at night
human-performance.b: Vertical separation is easier to judge than horizontal separation
human-performance.c: Modern aircraft lighting makes this judgement automatic and reliable
human-performance.d: Vertical separation between aircraft is inherently difficult to judge visually, and an aircraft that appears higher may in fact pass below the observer
human-performance.ans: Vertical separation between aircraft is inherently difficult to judge visually, and an aircraft that appears higher may in fact pass below the observer
human-performance.e: At a distance, the visual cues that let a pilot judge another aircraft's relative altitude are weak, since apparent vertical displacement does not scale reliably with actual separation the way horizontal cues can. An aircraft that appears to be at a higher level may, in reality, pass beneath the observer - which is why any perceived collision risk should prompt avoiding action rather than being dismissed on the assumption of safe vertical separation.

human-performance.q: Why is judging height difficult when flying low over a smooth water surface?
human-performance.b: The pilot's eyes automatically focus at infinity over water
human-performance.c: There is a lack of visual cues from surface features to help judge height
human-performance.d: Water always appears closer than it really is
human-performance.ans: There is a lack of visual cues from surface features to help judge height
human-performance.e: A smooth water surface offers almost none of the visual texture - waves, ripples, shoreline features, shadows - that a pilot normally relies on to judge height above the ground. Without those cues, especially in hazy conditions where the horizon line between sky and water can also disappear, pilots have flown into the water under full control simply because they could not perceive how low they actually were.

human-performance.q: To what altitude does the Troposphere, the atmospheric layer in which almost all light aircraft flying takes place, extend?
human-performance.ans: About 11 km (36,000 feet)
human-performance.e: The Troposphere, the lowest layer of the atmosphere and the one in which almost all light aircraft flying takes place, extends from the surface up to roughly 11 km (about 36,000 feet); above it lies the Stratosphere, which reaches to over 32 km (100,000 feet). Despite being the lowest layer, the Troposphere contains about three-quarters of the atmosphere's total mass and virtually all of its weather.

human-performance.q: Angina is caused by:
human-performance.a: Death of part of the heart muscle
human-performance.b: A blockage of pulmonary blood vessels
human-performance.c: Insufficient blood reaching the heart muscle
human-performance.d: A blocked blood vessel in the brain
human-performance.ans: Insufficient blood reaching the heart muscle
human-performance.e: Angina's underlying cause is a mismatch between the heart muscle's oxygen demand and its oxygen supply - typically because narrowed coronary arteries can't deliver enough blood, especially when the heart is working harder under exertion or stress. This distinguishes angina from a heart attack, where heart tissue actually dies from a blocked supply, and from a stroke, where the blocked vessel serves the brain rather than the heart.

human-performance.q: The main function of the vestibular apparatus is to:
human-performance.b: Mechanically transmit sound to the cochlea
human-performance.c: Prevent excessive sounds from damaging the ear drum
human-performance.d: Prevent excessive sounds from damaging the otoliths
human-performance.ans: Detect angular and linear accelerations
human-performance.e: The vestibular apparatus's job is to detect both angular acceleration, sensed by the three semicircular canals, and linear acceleration, sensed by the otolith organs, and to pass that information to the brain as one input, alongside vision and the somatosensory system, for maintaining spatial orientation. Because it only responds to changes in acceleration and not to a constant attitude or speed, it cannot be relied on alone to tell a pilot whether the aircraft is level, climbing, or in a steady turn.

human-performance.q: Motion sickness arises when there is:
human-performance.a: Vertical displacement from the horizontal axis
human-performance.b: Disorientation caused by loss of visual references
human-performance.c: A mismatch between visual and vestibular signals
human-performance.d: Vertical displacement from the longitudinal axis
human-performance.ans: A mismatch between visual and vestibular signals
human-performance.e: Motion sickness arises specifically from a mismatch between the visual system and the vestibular (inner-ear) balance system - not from motion or disorientation on their own. A passenger looking down at a map or phone while the aircraft manoeuvres is a classic trigger: the inner ear feels the aircraft's actual motion, but the eyes, fixed on something inside the cabin, report a relatively still scene.

human-performance.q: Which of the following conditions are symptomatic of motion sickness? (i) Nausea (ii) Hypoxia (iii) Hyperventilation (iv) Pallor (v) Stomach cramp (vi) Cold sweating
human-performance.ans: i, iii, iv and vi
human-performance.e: The recognised symptoms of motion sickness are nausea, hyperventilation, pallor (pale skin) and cold sweating - a consistent pattern produced by the body's reaction to conflicting visual and vestibular signals. Hypoxia and stomach cramp are not part of this pattern and belong to entirely different conditions, which is exactly the kind of distinction "which combination" exam questions are testing.

human-performance.q: A body mass index of 23 for a male or female pilot indicates he/she is:
human-performance.ans: Normal
human-performance.e: BMI is classified into bands, and a value of 23 falls squarely within the normal healthy range - roughly 18.5 to 25 for most adults, regardless of sex. Values below that range indicate underweight, and values above it indicate overweight or, at higher levels, obese.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Nose wheel shimmy is controlled by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The brakes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A shimmy damper
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The oleo's metering pin
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Worn torque links
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A shimmy damper
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Shimmy is a rapid side-to-side oscillation of the nose wheel, most likely at speed during the take-off or landing run. A shimmy damper - a small hydraulic piston and cylinder, or a friction unit, between the strut and the steering fork - resists these fast movements while still allowing normal steering. Worn torque links cause shimmy rather than control it, and the brakes and the oleo's metering pin play no part.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The blade angle of a propeller is the angle:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Between the chord line and the plane of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Between the chord line and the relative airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Between the relative airflow and the plane of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Between the chord line and the aircraft's longitudinal axis
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Between the chord line and the plane of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Blade angle is the angle between a blade section's chord line and the plane of rotation. It is a fixed geometric setting (unless the pitch is variable), and it decreases from root to tip because of the helical twist. The angle between the chord and the relative airflow is the blade's angle of attack, and the angle between the relative airflow and the plane of rotation is the helix angle: blade angle = angle of attack + helix angle.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the tyre size "28 x 12.00-10", the figure "12.00" represents:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The outside diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The ply rating
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The bead diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The tyre width
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The tyre width
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An aircraft tyre size such as 28 x 12.00-10 reads outside diameter x section width - bead (rim) diameter, all in inches. So 28 is the overall diameter, 12.00 is the width across the tyre's section and 10 is the diameter of the wheel rim the tyre fits. The ply rating, which indicates strength, is marked separately on the sidewall (for example PR6).

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A fuselage which is constructed to allow the skin to take some of the load is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A monocoque structure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A truss structure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A semi-monocoque structure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A geodetic structure
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A semi-monocoque structure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The key word is 'some'. In a semi-monocoque fuselage, formers and stringers give the fuselage its shape and stiffness while the stressed skin carries part of the load, so the load is shared. In a pure monocoque the skin carries all of the load with no framework to help, a truss (girder) fuselage carries everything through a framework of longerons and bracing under a non-load-bearing covering, and a geodetic structure is a lattice of diagonal members.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The torque created by a rotating propeller has the effect on the propeller of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Bending the blade forward, towards the direction of flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Twisting the blade towards a finer pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Bending the blade in the opposite direction to the rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Pulling the blade outwards from the hub
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Bending the blade in the opposite direction to the rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The engine drives the propeller round while the air resists its rotation, so each blade is loaded like a beam: this torque loading bends the blades backwards, opposite to the direction of rotation. The other propeller forces act differently: thrust bends the tips forward, centrifugal force pulls the blades outward from the hub, and the centrifugal twisting moment tries to turn the blades to a finer pitch.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The blade angle of a propeller varies from hub to tip in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Reduce the noise produced by the blade tips at high RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Ensure that the thrust produced is constant along the propeller blade
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Allow the blade to be feathered after an engine failure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Make the blade stronger at the tip, where the loads are highest
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Ensure that the thrust produced is constant along the propeller blade
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Each section of the blade travels in a circle, and a section near the tip moves much faster than one near the hub. With the same blade angle everywhere, the fast outer sections would meet the air at a much higher angle of attack and produce most of the thrust. Reducing the blade angle progressively towards the tip (helical twist) keeps the angle of attack, and so the thrust, nearly even along the blade, making the propeller more efficient.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Torsion is the term used to describe the load on an airframe:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Caused by stretching
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Caused by squashing
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Caused by a sliding action
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Caused by twisting
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Caused by twisting
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An airframe has to cope with five basic stresses: tension (stretching), compression (squashing), shear (one layer sliding over another), bending (a combination of tension and compression) and torsion, which is twisting. A wing is twisted when the ailerons are deflected or the centre of pressure moves, and the spars and stressed skin together form a torsion box that resists it without permanent deformation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Identify the flap type shown in Figure 2:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Plain flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Split flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Fowler flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Slotted flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Split flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A split flap is a plate hinged from the underside of the trailing edge: only the lower surface deflects, while the upper surface stays where it is. It gives a moderate increase in lift but a large increase in drag, which steepens the approach. A plain flap hinges the whole trailing edge, a slotted flap opens a gap for air to flow through, and a Fowler flap slides rearward before it deflects.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: To reduce the aerodynamic loads the pilot feels on the controls, balance tabs are designed:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: To move in the same direction as the primary control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: To be moved directly by the pilot's controls
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: To stay at a fixed angle whatever the control surface deflection
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: To operate in the opposite direction to the primary control surface to which they are attached
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: To operate in the opposite direction to the primary control surface to which they are attached
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A balance tab is linked to fixed structure, so whenever the control surface moves the tab automatically moves the opposite way. The air load on the tab then helps push the surface in the direction the pilot wants, reducing the stick force. A tab that moves the same way as the surface is an anti-balance tab (it increases the force), a tab moved directly by the pilot is a servo tab, and one that stays where it is set is a trim tab.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An adjustable trim tab when attached to an elevator will, when the elevator is moved:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Move in the opposite direction to the elevator, reducing the stick force
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Remains in the same position irrespective of the deflection of the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Move in the same direction as the elevator, increasing the stick force
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Return automatically to neutral whenever the elevator is moved
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Remains in the same position irrespective of the deflection of the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An adjustable trim tab is positioned by the pilot using the trim wheel and holds that angle relative to the elevator. Moving the elevator with the control column does not re-position the tab; it simply moves with the elevator as a fixed part of it, and only a new trim setting changes it. Tabs that move automatically, opposite to or with the surface, are balance and anti-balance tabs.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A semi-cantilever monoplane is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: One where bracing struts mounted at the base of the fuselage are attached to the wings to provide additional support
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: One where the wing is supported entirely by internal spars, with no external bracing
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: One with two wings, one above the other, joined by struts and wires
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: One where the wing is mounted halfway up the fuselage
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: One where bracing struts mounted at the base of the fuselage are attached to the wings to provide additional support
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A cantilever wing is supported only at the root, with every load carried internally by the spars. A semi-cantilever wing is also braced by external struts running from the lower fuselage to the wing, as on many high-wing trainers such as the Cessna 172. The struts share the load, so the spar can be lighter, at the cost of some extra drag.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The main longitudinal member in a Truss type of fuselage construction would be:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Formers
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Longeron
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Stringers
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Longeron
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A truss (girder) fuselage is a framework, usually of welded steel tube, in which the main lengthwise members are the longerons. Vertical, horizontal and diagonal bracing members join them into rigid triangles that carry the loads, and the fabric or light covering carries none. Formers and stringers belong to monocoque and semi-monocoque construction, and the main spar is part of the wing.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The part of the wing to which the ailerons and flaps are usually attached is the:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Rear or auxiliary spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The wing root fitting
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The leading edge
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Rear or auxiliary spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The rear (auxiliary) spar runs along the back of the wing and provides the hinge points for the trailing-edge surfaces, so the ailerons and flaps are normally attached to it. The main spar, near the thickest part of the wing, carries most of the bending load, and the leading edge is where slats or de-icing boots would be fitted rather than the trailing-edge controls.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An under-inflated tyre may result in:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Excessive tread wear in the centre of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Excessive tread wear on one side of the tyre only
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Excessive tread wear on the outer edges of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Reduced rolling resistance during taxiing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Excessive tread wear on the outer edges of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An under-inflated tyre sags under load, so the centre of the tread lifts slightly and the shoulders carry the weight and wear quickly. The extra flexing also overheats the sidewalls, increases rolling resistance and makes creep - and a torn-out inflation valve - more likely. Over-inflation wears the centre of the tread instead, and wear on one side only points to wheel alignment rather than pressure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the centre of gravity is moved aft during flight the effect will be:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: To increase longitudinal stability
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: To increase the stalling speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: To reduce longitudinal stability
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: To make the controls heavier in pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: To reduce longitudinal stability
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Longitudinal stability depends on the CG being ahead of the aerodynamic centre, so the tailplane has a long moment arm with which to correct any disturbance in pitch. Moving the CG aft shortens that arm, so the restoring moment is weaker: the aircraft becomes less stable and lighter on the elevator. An aft CG actually lowers the stall speed slightly, because less tail download is needed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Newton's second law refers to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Conservation of momentum
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Action and reaction
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Equilibrium
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Acceleration and deceleration
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Acceleration and deceleration
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Newton's second law says a net (unbalanced) force produces an acceleration proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass: F = m × a. Acceleration means any change in velocity - speeding up, slowing down or changing direction - so opening the throttle, braking on the runway and turning are all second-law effects. Equilibrium is the first law and action and reaction is the third.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The effect of slats is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Allow the aeroplane to fly at a higher angle of attack and higher airspeed
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Allow the aeroplane to fly at a lower angle of attack and lower airspeed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Allow the aeroplane to fly at a higher angle of attack and lower airspeed
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase the maximum speed of the aeroplane
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Allow the aeroplane to fly at a higher angle of attack and lower airspeed
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A slat is a small aerofoil on the leading edge. When deployed it opens a slot that feeds high-energy air from beneath the wing over the upper surface, re-energising the boundary layer and delaying separation. The wing can therefore reach a higher angle of attack before it stalls, which lets the aeroplane fly at a lower airspeed. Slats do little at cruise angles of attack and do nothing for top speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The reduction in the blade angle of a propeller towards the tip ensures that the thrust is constant along the blade and is referred to as:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Blade angle
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Helical twist
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Helix angle
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Helical twist
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Because the blade sections travel faster the further they are from the hub, the blade angle is reduced progressively from root to tip so that every section meets the air at about the same angle of attack and produces an even share of thrust. This progressive twist is called helical twist. The helix angle is the angle between the relative airflow and the plane of rotation, and the blade angle is that between the chord line and the plane of rotation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The stall warning device, which is usually mounted on the leading edge of a wing, is adjusted to activate the cockpit warning:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Just after the stall
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Just before the stall
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: At the moment the wing stalls
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Only when the flaps are extended
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Just before the stall
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: As the angle of attack increases, the stagnation point moves down and back under the leading edge, and the airflow lifts the stall-warning vane (or draws air through the reed). It is set to sound a few knots, typically 5 to 10 kt, before the stall, giving the pilot time to lower the nose. A warning at or after the stall would be too late to help, and the system works in every configuration, not only with flap.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Tyre creep may cause:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The inflation valve to break away from the inner tube
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The tyre pressure to rise above normal
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Excessive tread wear on the outer edges of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Excessive tread wear in the centre of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The inflation valve to break away from the inner tube
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Tyre creep is the tyre slowly turning around the wheel rim, caused mainly by heavy braking and landing loads, especially when the tyre is under-inflated. In a tubed tyre the inner tube moves with the tyre, dragging the inflation valve sideways until it tears out; the tyre then deflates, possibly bursting on landing. Creep does not raise the pressure, and uneven tread wear comes from incorrect inflation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Tyre creep is most likely to occur as a result of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Taxiing slowly on smooth surfaces
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Long periods parked in the sun
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: High nitrogen pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Heavy braking on landing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Heavy braking on landing
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Tyre creep is the tyre rotating slightly on its wheel rim. It is caused by large forces between the tyre and the rim - above all heavy braking on landing, and also the wheel spinning up at touchdown - and it is more likely when the tyre is under-inflated, because the beads grip the rim less firmly. Creep marks painted across the tyre and rim show how far it has moved; high pressure makes creep less likely, not more.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: As the angle of attack of an aerofoil in normal flight is increased, the centre of pressure will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Move forward
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Move rearward
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Remain in the same position
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Move towards the wing tip
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Move forward
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: On a conventional cambered aerofoil, increasing the angle of attack up to the stall moves the centre of pressure forward, and reducing it moves the centre of pressure back. Beyond the stall the pressure distribution collapses and the centre of pressure moves rearward again, which is one reason the nose drops at the stall. Because the centre of pressure moves this way, a wing on its own is unstable in pitch and needs a tailplane.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The most important structural component of a wing is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The rear spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The ribs
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Longerons
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The main spar is the wing's primary beam: it runs from root to tip and carries most of the bending and shear loads produced by lift, weight and landing. Ribs give the wing its shape and pass the air loads to the spars, and the rear spar carries the trailing-edge controls, but damage to the main spar is by far the most serious. Longerons are fuselage members, not wing members.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Torque links may be incorporated on the nose shock struts of some undercarriage systems in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Absorb the vertical landing loads instead of the oleo
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Centre the nose wheel automatically before it is retracted
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Maintain the correct air pressure inside the shock strut
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent the shock-strut piston and nose wheel from rotating within the cylinder
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Prevent the shock-strut piston and nose wheel from rotating within the cylinder
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a nose oleo the inner piston slides inside the outer cylinder, and nothing in the strut itself stops it turning. Torque (scissor) links join the two parts so the strut can still compress and extend vertically, but the piston and nose wheel cannot rotate within the cylinder; the wheel stays aligned and steering inputs are passed to it. The oleo absorbs the landing loads, and a centring cam straightens the wheel for retraction.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The figure "10" indicated in the tyre size number "28 x 12.00-10" represents:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The bead diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The tyre width
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The outside diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The ply rating
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The bead diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the size 28 x 12.00-10 the last figure, 10, is the bead diameter: the diameter in inches of the wheel rim that the tyre's beads seat on. The first figure (28) is the outside diameter and the middle figure (12.00) is the section width. A useful way to remember it: the size reads from the outside in - overall diameter, width, then rim. The ply rating is marked separately.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Identify the flap type shown in Figure 4:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Fowler flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Split flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Plain flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Slotted flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Slotted flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A slotted flap moves down and slightly back, opening a slot between the wing and the flap. High-energy air from under the wing flows through the slot and over the flap's upper surface, keeping the airflow attached at large deflections, so it gives more lift than a plain or split flap. A Fowler flap also opens a slot but first slides well rearward to increase the wing area.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A shimmy in the nose wheel whilst taxying indicates that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The torque links are worn or have failed
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The brakes are binding
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The oleo is over-extended
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The main wheels are out of balance
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The torque links are worn or have failed
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Worn or failed torque links let the nose wheel twist back and forth on the strut, and at taxi speeds that play quickly develops into shimmy, a rapid side-to-side oscillation. A defective shimmy damper, worn wheel bearings or uneven tyre pressures can have the same effect, so all should be checked. Binding brakes pull the aircraft to one side, and an over-extended oleo or unbalanced main wheels do not make the nose wheel oscillate.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The most likely cause of under-extension of an oleo undercarriage leg is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: High air pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Over-inflated tyres
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Low air pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Worn torque links
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Low air pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An oleo leg is held extended by the compressed air or nitrogen in its upper chamber, which acts as the spring. If that gas pressure is too low the leg cannot support the aircraft at its normal extension and sits too low (under-extended), leaving less travel to absorb a landing. Too much gas pressure causes over-extension instead, while tyre pressure and torque links do not set the strut's extension.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Identify the flap type shown in Figure 1:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Fowler flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Slotted flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Plain flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Split flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Fowler flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A Fowler flap runs rearward on tracks before it deflects downward. The rearward movement increases the wing area and the downward movement increases the camber, and most Fowler flaps also open a slot, so it gives the largest lift increase of the common flap types. Plain, split and slotted flaps hinge close to the wing and do not add any significant area.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Newton's third law refers to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Action and reaction
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Conservation of energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Equilibrium
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Acceleration and deceleration
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Action and reaction
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. A propeller accelerates a mass of air rearward and the reaction pushes the aircraft forward; a wing deflects air downward and the reaction contributes to lift. Equilibrium is Newton's first law, and acceleration and deceleration is the second.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The operation of an oleo leg is based on:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Shock struts comprising a lower chamber containing hydraulic fluid and an upper chamber containing compressed air or nitrogen
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A coil spring inside the strut that absorbs the landing loads without any damping
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Rubber discs compressed between metal plates to absorb and damp the landing loads
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A solid spring-steel leg that flexes to absorb the landing loads
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Shock struts comprising a lower chamber containing hydraulic fluid and an upper chamber containing compressed air or nitrogen
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An oleo-pneumatic strut uses two media. Compressed air or nitrogen in the upper chamber acts as the spring, while hydraulic fluid is forced through a small orifice (often with a metering pin) to damp the movement: the gas absorbs the landing energy and the oil stops the aircraft bouncing back up. Coil springs, rubber discs and flexible spring-steel legs are other types of undercarriage suspension.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An aircraft which has its CG too far aft would:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Be more stable in pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Have a higher stalling speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Have heavier elevator control forces
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Be difficult to control in pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Be difficult to control in pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: With the CG behind its aft limit the tailplane's moment arm is short, so the aircraft has little natural tendency to return to trimmed flight: it becomes unstable in pitch, the elevator feels light and it is easy to over-control. Stall recovery can be difficult because there may not be enough nose-down elevator authority, and spin recovery may be impossible. An aft CG reduces stability, stall speed and stick forces rather than increasing them.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A rotating propeller will produce a force which acts in the opposite direction of rotation. This force is called:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Centrifugal force
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Torque
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: P-factor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Gyroscopic precession
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Torque
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When the engine turns the propeller one way, Newton's third law gives an equal and opposite reaction on the engine and airframe: this torque reaction tries to roll the aircraft opposite to the propeller's rotation, and on the ground it puts more weight on one main wheel, causing a swing. Centrifugal force acts outward along the blades, P-factor is uneven blade thrust at high angles of attack, and gyroscopic precession matters mainly when a tail-dragger's tail is raised.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Identify the flap type shown in Figure 3:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Split flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Fowler flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Plain flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Slotted flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Plain flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A plain flap is simply the rear part of the wing hinged so it can be lowered. Lowering it increases the camber, raising both lift and drag, but with no slot and no rearward movement it is the least effective type. A split flap hinges only the lower surface, a slotted flap opens a gap for air to flow through, and a Fowler flap slides rearward before it deflects.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Ignoring crosswind, an aeroplane with a tricycle undercarriage and a clockwise-rotating propeller, as viewed from the cockpit, will tend to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Yaw to the right
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Remain straight without any rudder input
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Roll to the right
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Yaw to the left
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Yaw to the left
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: With a propeller turning clockwise as seen from the cockpit, the spiralling slipstream strikes the left side of the fin, torque reaction presses the left wheel harder onto the runway, and at high power the down-going right-hand blade produces more thrust (asymmetric blade effect). All of these yaw the aeroplane to the left on the take-off run, so right rudder is needed to keep straight. A tricycle aeroplane has little gyroscopic effect because its tail is not raised.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The most likely cause of over-extension of an oleo undercarriage leg is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Low air pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: High air pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Worn torque links
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Under-inflated tyres
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: High air pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The gas charge in an oleo's upper chamber is the spring that holds the leg extended. With too much air or nitrogen pressure the spring is too stiff, so the leg stands too high (over-extended) and gives a harder ride and landing. Low gas pressure causes under-extension instead, and tyre pressure and torque links do not control the strut's extension.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In a Truss or Girder-type fuselage, the main structural component is a:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Longeron
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Former
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Stringer
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Longeron
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a truss or girder fuselage the main loads are carried by the longerons: the principal lengthwise members, usually four, braced by struts and diagonal members into a rigid framework of triangles. The covering carries no load. Formers and stringers are the shaping members of monocoque and semi-monocoque fuselages, and the main spar belongs to the wing.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the creep marks on the tyres have moved too far out of alignment:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The tyre should simply be re-inflated to a higher pressure before the next flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A blow-out may occur on landing because tyre movement may cause the inflation valve to be broken off from the tube
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: No action is needed, because creep marks only show normal tread wear
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The brakes must be adjusted, because the marks show that they are binding
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A blow-out may occur on landing because tyre movement may cause the inflation valve to be broken off from the tube
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Creep marks are painted across the tyre and the wheel rim. If they have moved too far apart, the tyre has rotated on the rim, and in a tubed tyre the inner tube will have moved with it, dragging the inflation valve sideways. The valve can then be torn out on the next landing, deflating the tyre suddenly or causing a blow-out, so it must be dealt with by an engineer before flight. Re-inflating it or adjusting the brakes does not fix it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A semi-monocoque fuselage design is one in which:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The loads are carried by a framework of longerons and bracing, with a non-load-bearing covering
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The fuselage is a lattice of diagonal members woven in a basket pattern
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: All flight loads are carried by the outer skin
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The shape and rigidity of the fuselage is provided by formers and stringers whilst the stressed skin carries part of the load
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The shape and rigidity of the fuselage is provided by formers and stringers whilst the stressed skin carries part of the load
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Semi-monocoque construction sits between a pure monocoque and a truss: formers (frames) and stringers give the fuselage its shape and stiffness, while the stressed skin carries part of the load. Because the load is shared, the skin can be thinner than in a pure monocoque, which saves weight and makes the structure more tolerant of minor damage. It is the most common construction in modern light aircraft.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A monocoque airframe structure is one where:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Formers and stringers give the shape while the skin carries part of the load
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: All flight loads are carried by the outer skin
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A framework of longerons and bracing carries all the loads
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: External struts carry the flight loads into the fuselage
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: All flight loads are carried by the outer skin
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Monocoque means 'single shell': the outer skin carries all the flight loads, with only light formers inside to hold its shape. With no load-bearing framework it can be light and roomy, but the skin must be strong and any dent weakens the whole structure, which is why most aircraft use semi-monocoque construction instead. A framework of longerons and bracing describes a truss fuselage.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The primary load carrying component of an aluminium stressed skin wing is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The rear spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Stringers
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Longerons
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Even in a stressed-skin wing, where the skin shares the load, the main spar is still the primary load-carrying member: it takes most of the bending caused by lift and weight. The skin and spars together form a box that resists twisting, stringers stiffen the skin against buckling, and longerons are fuselage members rather than wing members.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The figure "28" indicated in the tyre size number "28 x 12.00-10" represents:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The tyre width
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The bead diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The outside diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The ply rating
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The outside diameter
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The size 28 x 12.00-10 reads outside diameter x section width - bead diameter, in inches. The first figure, 28, is therefore the tyre's overall outside diameter; 12.00 is the section width and 10 is the rim (bead) diameter. The ply rating, which indicates the tyre's strength, is marked separately on the sidewall.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An over-inflated tyre may result in:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Excessive tread wear on the outer edges of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Excessive tread wear in the centre of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Excessive tread wear on one side of the tyre only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increased flexing and heating of the sidewalls
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Excessive tread wear in the centre of the tyre
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An over-inflated tyre bulges at the crown, so only the centre of the tread touches the ground and it wears quickly. The hard tyre also absorbs less of the landing shock and is more easily cut or bruised.
