Wear on the shoulders, with extra flexing and heating of the sidewalls, is the sign of under-inflation, and wear on one side only points to wheel alignment.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The components of a stressed skin wing which provide both strength and shape are called:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Stringers
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Longerons
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Ribs
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The main spar
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Ribs
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Ribs run chordwise from the leading edge to the trailing edge and are cut to the aerofoil section, so they give the wing its shape. They also support the skin against buckling and pass the air loads on the skin into the spars, providing strength as well. Stringers run spanwise to stiffen the skin, the main spar carries the bending loads, and longerons are found in the fuselage.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: With reference to tab balances:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A servo tab is connected directly to the pilot controls
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A balance tab moves in the same direction as the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: An anti-balance tab moves in the opposite direction to the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A trim tab moves automatically whenever the control surface moves
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A servo tab is connected directly to the pilot controls
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A servo tab is the only tab connected directly to the pilot's controls: the pilot moves the tab, and the air load on the tab then moves the free-floating main surface, so a large surface can be moved with little effort. A balance tab is linked to fixed structure and moves opposite to the surface, an anti-balance tab moves the same way as the surface, and a trim tab stays where the pilot sets it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An anti-balance, or anti-servo, tab which is incorporated in a stabilator will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Remain fixed while the stabilator moves
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Move in the opposite direction to the stabilator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Move in the same direction as the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Move only at high airspeeds
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Move in the same direction as the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A stabilator (all-moving tailplane) is very powerful and, because it pivots near its centre of pressure, can feel too light, making over-control easy. The anti-balance tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator, so its air load opposes the movement and the stick force builds progressively. A tab moving the opposite way would be a balance tab, which lightens the controls: the opposite of what is needed here.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The horizontal stabiliser on the tail:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Provides longitudinal stability by generating an upward or downward force as required
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Provides directional stability by generating sideways forces
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Always generates an upward lift force to hold the tail up
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Provides lateral stability by resisting roll
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Provides longitudinal stability by generating an upward or downward force as required
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The horizontal stabiliser (tailplane) provides longitudinal stability, returning the aircraft to balanced flight in pitch. It does this by generating an upward or a downward force as required, depending on the position of the centre of gravity and the flight condition. It does not always lift the tail, and directional stability comes from the fin, while lateral stability comes mainly from wing dihedral.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Newton's first law refers to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Action and reaction
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Conservation of energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Equilibrium
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Acceleration and deceleration
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Equilibrium
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Newton's first law, the law of inertia, says a body stays at rest or keeps moving at a constant velocity unless a net external force acts on it. When the forces balance - lift equals weight and thrust equals drag in steady straight and level flight - the aircraft is in equilibrium and its speed and direction do not change. Acceleration is the second law, and action and reaction the third.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The type of flap which, when extended, increases the surface area of the wing is called a:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Split flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Slotted flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Plain flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Fowler flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Fowler flap
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A Fowler flap runs rearward on tracks as it extends, so it first increases the wing area and then, as it moves down, the camber. This gives the greatest lift increase of the common flap types, and the early stages add relatively little drag, which makes partial Fowler flap useful for take-off. Plain, split and slotted flaps hinge close to the wing and do not add any significant area.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a normal level flight, the reduction in power will cause the nose of an aeroplane to drop because:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The centre of pressure is located forward of the centre of gravity
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The centre of gravity is located forward of centre of pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Drag increases when power is reduced
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The wing's angle of attack increases
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The centre of gravity is located forward of centre of pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In most light aircraft the CG is ahead of the centre of pressure, so lift and weight form a nose-down couple. In steady flight this is balanced by the tailplane download and the thrust-drag couple, both of which depend partly on power. Reduce the power and the nose-up contribution falls, so the nose drops: a deliberately safe design, because the aircraft lowers its nose to maintain airspeed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The control of fuel entering the carburettor is achieved by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The needle valve and the float chamber
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The accelerator pump and the discharge nozzle
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The throttle butterfly and the venturi
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The primer and the mixture control
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The needle valve and the float chamber
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Fuel entering the carburettor is controlled by the float and needle valve. As the float chamber fills, the float rises and pushes the needle valve onto its seat, shutting off the incoming fuel; as fuel is used the float drops and the valve opens again, so the level stays constant and the fuel is metered accurately. The throttle butterfly controls the mixture leaving the carburettor, and the accelerator pump and primer only add extra fuel.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of baffles in an aircraft's fuel tank is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Stop water entering the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Measure the quantity of fuel in the tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: To allow atmospheric pressure to be retained in the tank as the fuel is used
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent the fuel from surging about during the flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Prevent the fuel from surging about during the flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Baffles are internal walls with holes in them that divide a tank into compartments. They slow the fuel's movement when the aircraft accelerates, turns or manoeuvres, so it cannot surge from one end to the other: the outlet stays covered, the CG does not shift suddenly and the tank structure is not loaded by moving fuel. Vents keep the tank at atmospheric pressure, and the drain and sump deal with water.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When the mixture control lever is moved to the full rich position:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The amount of fuel entering the inlet manifold will be decreased
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The throttle butterfly will open further
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The amount of fuel entering the inlet manifold will be increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The ratio of fuel to air will be decreased
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The amount of fuel entering the inlet manifold will be increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The mixture control meters fuel only; the throttle controls the air. Moving it to full rich opens the mixture needle fully, so more fuel flows into the airflow and through the inlet manifold, and the fuel-to-air ratio rises. Full rich is normally used for take-off, climb and landing, when the extra fuel also helps cool the cylinders; it does not move the throttle butterfly.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During the operation of a reciprocating engine the piston is travelling up during:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The compression and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The induction and power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The power and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The induction and compression strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The compression and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a four-stroke engine the piston moves up twice and down twice in every two revolutions of the crankshaft. It travels up on the compression stroke, squeezing the fresh charge, and again on the exhaust stroke, pushing the burnt gases out. It travels down on induction, drawing the charge in, and on the power stroke, when the burning gases drive it. So 'up' means compression and exhaust.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Moving the mixture control to the lean position will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase the amount of fuel entering the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Reduce the amount of fuel entering the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Reduce the amount of air entering the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Close the throttle butterfly slightly
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Reduce the amount of fuel entering the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The mixture control works on the fuel side only: leaning moves the mixture needle to restrict the fuel flowing from the float chamber to the diffuser (discharge nozzle), so less fuel is mixed with the same amount of air. The airflow is set by the throttle butterfly and is not changed. Leaning corrects the mixture as the air becomes less dense with altitude, saving fuel and preventing rough running.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In a piston engine, the piston will have passed BDC and be moving towards TDC during:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The induction and power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The power and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The compression and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The induction and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The compression and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Moving from BDC towards TDC means the piston is travelling upwards, which happens on two of the four strokes: compression, when both valves are closed and the charge is squeezed, and exhaust, when the exhaust valve is open and the burnt gases are pushed out. The downward strokes, from TDC to BDC, are induction and power.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The term "valve lead" refers to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The inlet valve closes after the piston has passed bottom dead centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Lead fouling of the spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The short period when the inlet and exhaust valves are open together
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The inlet valve opening prior to the piston reaching TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The inlet valve opening prior to the piston reaching TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Valve lead means a valve opens early. The inlet valve opens before the piston reaches TDC at the end of the exhaust stroke, so it is already open as the piston starts down on induction, letting the charge begin to flow and making the most of the short time available. The inlet closing after BDC is valve lag, both valves open together is valve overlap, and the term has nothing to do with the lead in AVGAS.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During take-off in an aeroplane equipped with a Constant Speed Unit (CSU), it would be most beneficial to have:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A small blade angle
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The propeller lever set to minimum RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The propeller in the feathered position
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Coarse pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A small blade angle
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A constant-speed propeller works like a car's gearbox. For take-off the propeller lever is set fully forward (maximum RPM), which gives a small (fine) blade angle - first gear - so the engine can reach full RPM and develop maximum power while the aircraft is still slow. Coarse pitch is like top gear, efficient in the cruise but poor for acceleration, and a feathered propeller gives no thrust at all.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the four-stroke piston engine, the term "valve lag" is used to indicate that the:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The inlet valve closes after the piston has passed bottom dead centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The inlet valve closes before the piston has passed bottom dead centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The inlet valve opening prior to the piston reaching TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The short period that both inlet and exhaust valves are both open around TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The inlet valve closes after the piston has passed bottom dead centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Valve lag means a valve closes late. The inlet valve stays open after the piston has passed BDC and started the compression stroke, because the incoming charge has momentum and keeps flowing into the cylinder for a moment, improving volumetric efficiency. The inlet opening before TDC is valve lead, and the period when both valves are open around TDC is valve overlap.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of a needle mixture control in a carburettor is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Control the volume of fuel-air mixture entering the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Provide extra fuel when the throttle is opened rapidly
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Keep the fuel level in the float chamber constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Regulate the flow of fuel from the float chamber to the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Regulate the flow of fuel from the float chamber to the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The mixture control moves a needle in the passage between the float chamber and the diffuser (main jet), varying how much fuel can flow for a given airflow; this is how the pilot leans the mixture as air density falls. The throttle butterfly controls the volume of mixture entering the engine, the float and needle valve keep the float-chamber level constant, and the accelerator pump adds fuel when the throttle is opened quickly.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The application of carburettor heat:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Will also leanen the mixture because of the higher air temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Will also richen the mixture because of the higher air temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Will also richen the mixture because of the lower air temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Will increase the engine power available for take-off
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Will also richen the mixture because of the higher air temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Carburettor heat replaces the normal intake air with air heated around the exhaust. Warm air is less dense, so a smaller mass of air passes through the venturi while the carburettor meters much the same amount of fuel: the mixture becomes richer and the power falls, usually seen as a drop in RPM. Because the air is warmer, not cooler, it richens rather than leans the mixture.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When leaning the fuel/air mixture:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase fuel flow
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The ratio of fuel to air reduces
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The throttle butterfly closes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The ratio of fuel to air increases
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The ratio of fuel to air reduces
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Leaning reduces the fuel flow while the airflow stays the same, so the ratio of fuel to air goes down (the air-to-fuel ratio goes up). Pilots lean in the cruise, particularly at altitude where the air is less dense, to restore the correct mixture, save fuel and avoid fouling the plugs. Over-leaning leads to rough running, high cylinder temperatures and, at high power, detonation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Moving the mixture control to the rich position will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase the amount of fuel entering the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: decrease the amount of fuel entering the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increase the amount of air entering the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Have no effect on the fuel flow
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Increase the amount of fuel entering the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Moving the mixture control towards rich withdraws the mixture needle, opening the fuel passage so that more fuel flows from the float chamber to the diffuser for the same airflow. The fuel-to-air ratio rises, and the extra fuel helps cool the cylinders at high power. The amount of air entering the engine is controlled by the throttle, not by the mixture control.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: After about 20 minutes flight with full tanks the engine stops but restarts immediately after selection of another tank, a possible cause was:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Magneto failure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Carburettor icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: An over-rich mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A blocked fuel tank vent
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A blocked fuel tank vent
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: As fuel is used, air must enter the tank to replace it. If the vent is blocked, a partial vacuum builds up over time until fuel can no longer flow to the engine, which stops - here after about 20 minutes. Selecting another tank with a working vent restores the flow at once, which points to the blocked vent; carburettor icing, a magneto failure or a rich mixture would not be cured by changing tanks. Check the vents are clear on every pre-flight.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Prior to starting the engine of a carburettor equipped aircraft engine, the manual primer pump should be used, for easier starting, in order to supply additional fuel:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Into the float chamber to raise the fuel level
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Into the exhaust manifold to preheat it
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Discharge additional fuel into the venturi
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Into the induction system close to the inlet valves
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Into the induction system close to the inlet valves
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When a cold engine is cranked slowly, the carburettor produces very little suction and the fuel vaporises poorly. The primer is a small hand pump that squirts fuel directly into the induction system close to the inlet valves (or into the cylinders), bypassing the carburettor, so a combustible charge is ready to fire. Discharging extra fuel into the venturi is the accelerator pump's job when the throttle is opened quickly.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Fuel vents are provided in aircraft fuel tanks:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: To allow fuel to be added in flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: To release fuel vapour only when refuelling
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: To allow atmospheric pressure to be retained in the tank as the fuel is used
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent the fuel from surging about during the flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: To allow atmospheric pressure to be retained in the tank as the fuel is used
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Fuel tank vents let air into the tank as fuel is drawn out, keeping the pressure above the fuel at atmospheric. Without a vent a partial vacuum would form and eventually stop the fuel flowing to the engine, and in some tanks the vacuum could even collapse the tank. The vent also lets the tank breathe as the fuel expands and contracts with temperature. Baffles, not vents, stop the fuel surging.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The correct sequence for increasing power in an aeroplane with a Constant Speed Unit (CSU) is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Richen the mixture, increase RPM, then increase manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Richen the mixture, decrease RPM, then increase manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: leanen the mixture, increase RPM, then increase manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase manifold pressure, richen the mixture, then increase RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Richen the mixture, increase RPM, then increase manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: With a constant-speed propeller, high manifold pressure at low RPM overloads the engine, like accelerating hard in a high gear. So when increasing power the mixture goes rich first, then the propeller lever forward to increase RPM, and finally the throttle to increase manifold pressure. When reducing power the order is reversed. The memory aid is 'mixture, prop, throttle' going up and 'throttle, prop, mixture' coming down.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Applying carburettor heat allows:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Heated air from around the exhaust to enter the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Cold, filtered air to enter the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Heated fuel to be sprayed into the venturi
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The engine to run on a leaner mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Heated air from around the exhaust to enter the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Selecting carburettor heat moves a flap that shuts off the normal filtered cold-air inlet and draws air instead from a heater muff (shroud) around the exhaust. The warm air prevents or melts ice in the carburettor. This air bypasses the air filter, so carb heat should be used sparingly on the ground, and because warm air is less dense it richens the mixture rather than leaning it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Carburetor icing is most likely to occur:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: At the venturi butterfly valve or inlet manifold
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: At the exhaust manifold
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: At the fuel-tank vent
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: In the float chamber
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: At the venturi butterfly valve or inlet manifold
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Carburettor ice forms where the temperature drops most: in the venturi, where the air speeds up and its pressure and temperature fall, and around the throttle butterfly, where the fuel evaporates and absorbs heat. The combined cooling can be 20 to 30 °C, so ice can form with outside temperatures well above freezing, especially in humid air. The exhaust manifold is hot and the float chamber holds liquid fuel, so ice does not form there.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The function of the butterfly valve in a carburettor is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Regulate the flow of fuel from the float chamber to the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Keep the fuel level in the float chamber constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Provide extra fuel when the throttle is opened rapidly
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Control the volume of fuel-air mixture entering the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Control the volume of fuel-air mixture entering the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The butterfly is the throttle valve: a disc on a spindle just downstream of the venturi, linked to the pilot's throttle lever. Opening it lets more fuel-air mixture into the inlet manifold, so the engine produces more power; closing it restricts the flow. The mixture needle controls the fuel metering, the float valve the fuel level, and the accelerator pump the extra fuel when the throttle is opened quickly.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The fuel supply line from the fuel tank to the engine normally:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Draws fuel from a position higher than the sump to allow water or other impurities to settle at the bottom of the tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Draws fuel from the very lowest point of the tank, so that all the fuel can be used
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Draws fuel from the top of the tank, so that it stays well clear of any sediment
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Passes through a water trap in the cockpit before reaching the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Draws fuel from a position higher than the sump to allow water or other impurities to settle at the bottom of the tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The fuel outlet (pick-up) stands slightly above the bottom of the tank, so water and sediment, which are heavier than fuel, settle into the sump below it instead of flowing to the engine. The sump is drained through the drain valve at the lowest point during the pre-flight inspection. An outlet at the very bottom would feed water straight to the engine, and one at the top would leave most of the fuel unusable.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In a piston engine, the piston will have passed TDC and be moving towards BDC during:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The compression and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The induction and power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The induction and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The power and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The induction and power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: After TDC the piston travels down towards BDC, which happens on the induction stroke - the descending piston draws the fresh charge in through the open inlet valve - and on the power stroke, when the expanding gases drive it down and turn the crankshaft. Compression and exhaust are the two upward strokes, from BDC to TDC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When the mixture control lever is moved to the full lean position:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The amount of fuel entering the inlet manifold will be increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The throttle butterfly will close
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The ratio of fuel to air will be increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The amount of fuel entering the inlet manifold will be decreased
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The amount of fuel entering the inlet manifold will be decreased
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: At full lean, which is the idle cut-off position in most light aircraft, the mixture control shuts off the fuel from the carburettor, so the fuel entering the inlet manifold falls to almost nothing. That is why full lean is used to stop the engine: it runs the cylinders dry of fuel, leaving no unburnt charge that could fire if the propeller is moved. It does not move the throttle butterfly.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When attempting to start an engine which has been over-primed or flooded:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The mixture should be in the full lean position until the engine fires and then richened slowly to keep the engine running
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The engine should be primed again and cranked with the throttle closed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The mixture should be kept full rich and the throttle closed while cranking
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Carburettor heat should be selected fully hot to evaporate the excess fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The mixture should be in the full lean position until the engine fires and then richened slowly to keep the engine running
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A flooded engine has too much fuel in its cylinders to fire. With the mixture at full lean (idle cut-off) no more fuel is added, and with the throttle open plenty of air flows through as the engine is cranked, clearing the excess until the mixture will burn; as soon as the engine fires, the throttle is reduced and the mixture richened. Priming again or keeping the mixture rich only adds fuel. Always follow the POH procedure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The presence of carburettor icing would be indicated by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The engine starting to run rough and a increase in RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: An increase in oil pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The engine starting to run rough and a decrease in RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A rise in cylinder head temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The engine starting to run rough and a decrease in RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Ice in the carburettor restricts the airflow and upsets the mixture, so with a fixed-pitch propeller the first sign is a gradual drop in RPM, followed by rough running as the ice builds (with a constant-speed propeller the manifold pressure falls instead). When full carb heat is applied the engine may run rougher for a moment as the ice melts and passes through, and then the RPM recovers.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An accelerator pump is often incorporated in a carburettor in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Enrich the mixture at high altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Supply fuel for starting a cold engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Keep the fuel level in the float chamber constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Provide extra fuel when the throttle is opened rapidly
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Provide extra fuel when the throttle is opened rapidly
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When the throttle is opened quickly the airflow speeds up almost at once, but the heavier fuel lags behind, so the mixture goes momentarily lean and the engine can hesitate or even stop. The accelerator pump, linked to the throttle, squirts a small extra charge of fuel into the venturi as the throttle opens, covering the gap. Starting fuel comes from the primer, and the float and needle valve keep the fuel level constant.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: To eliminate the risk of fire when refuelling:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Keep the aircraft's master switch on so that the fuel gauges can be monitored
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Hold the nozzle clear of the filler neck so that metal does not touch metal
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Have an earth lead between ground, fuel truck, fuel nozzle and the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Pump the fuel as quickly as possible so that less vapour escapes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Have an earth lead between ground, fuel truck, fuel nozzle and the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Fuel flowing through hoses and into the tank generates static electricity, and a spark between the nozzle and the filler neck could ignite the fuel vapour. Bonding everything - ground, fuel truck, nozzle and aircraft - with earth leads keeps them at the same electrical potential, so no spark can jump. The nozzle should stay in contact with the filler neck, the master switch should be off, and fuel should not be pumped faster than normal.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In respect of piston engine operation, a rich mixture is one where:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The fuel-to-air ratio is increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The fuel-to-air ratio is decreased
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: There is more air than is needed to burn all the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The mixture burns hotter than a correctly balanced one
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The fuel-to-air ratio is increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A rich mixture has more fuel for a given mass of air than is needed for complete combustion, so its fuel-to-air ratio is increased (a chemically correct mixture is about 1:15 by weight). The surplus fuel absorbs heat as it evaporates, so a rich mixture runs cooler, which is why full rich is used for take-off; too rich wastes fuel, loses power and fouls the plugs. More air than needed describes a lean mixture.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The correct sequence of the four strokes of a piston engine is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Compression, induction, exhaust, power
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Power, exhaust, induction, compression
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Induction, compression, power, exhaust
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Induction, power, compression, exhaust
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Induction, compression, power, exhaust
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The four strokes follow in order over two crankshaft revolutions: induction (the piston moves down and draws in the fuel-air mixture), compression (up, squeezing it), power (down, driven by the burning gases) and exhaust (up, pushing the burnt gases out). The memory aid is 'suck, squeeze, bang, blow'. Each cylinder therefore fires once every two revolutions of the crankshaft.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: With reference to fixed pitch propeller:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A fine pitch propeller will produce a better cruise performance than a coarse pitch propeller
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A coarse pitch propeller will produce a better cruise performance than a fine pitch propeller
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A coarse pitch propeller will produce a better take-off performance than a fine pitch propeller
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pitch of a fixed pitch propeller has no effect on its take-off or cruise performance
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A coarse pitch propeller will produce a better cruise performance than a fine pitch propeller
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A fixed-pitch propeller is a compromise, like a car stuck in one gear. A coarse pitch (large blade angle) suits high forward speed, so it gives better cruise performance but less RPM and power for take-off and climb; a fine pitch lets the engine reach full RPM at low speed, so it gives better take-off and climb but over-speeds in the cruise. That trade-off is why fixed-pitch propellers are chosen as 'climb' or 'cruise' propellers.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During the operation of a reciprocating engine the piston is travelling down during:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The compression and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The compression and power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The induction and exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The induction and power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The induction and power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The piston travels down twice in each four-stroke cycle: on induction, when it increases the cylinder volume and draws in the fresh charge, and on the power stroke, when the burning mixture forces it down. It travels up on the compression and exhaust strokes. The memory aid 'suck, squeeze, bang, blow' gives the order: down, up, down, up.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: With regard to the engine handling:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The throttle should be opened as quickly as possible to stop the engine cooling
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The mixture should be leaned fully before any increase in power
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The throttle should be opened and closed smoothly to avoid overstressing the crankshaft
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Carburettor heat should be used continuously at full power
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The throttle should be opened and closed smoothly to avoid overstressing the crankshaft
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Opening or closing the throttle abruptly causes sudden changes in cylinder pressure and torque that stress the crankshaft, connecting rods and propeller, and a rapid opening can make the engine hesitate as the mixture goes momentarily lean. Smooth, progressive throttle movements are kinder to the engine and give predictable power. The mixture is set rich, not lean, before power is increased, and carb heat is not for continuous use at full power.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An engine which starts to run rough and then slowly loses power is probably suffering from:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Detonation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Carburetor icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A failed magneto
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Fuel starvation from an empty tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Carburetor icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Carburettor ice builds up gradually around the venturi and throttle butterfly, progressively restricting the airflow and upsetting the mixture, so the classic sign is rough running followed by a slow loss of power (falling RPM with a fixed-pitch propeller). A failed magneto causes an immediate drop and roughness, and fuel starvation makes the engine surge and stop rather than fade. Apply full carb heat at the first signs.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A manually operated primer pump should always be used to prime a cold engine for start because:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The primer heats the fuel so that it vaporises more easily
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The primer fills the float chamber before the engine is started
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The primer delivers fuel directly into the induction system near the inlet valves
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The primer raises the fuel pressure inside the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The primer delivers fuel directly into the induction system near the inlet valves
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: At cranking speed the airflow through the carburettor is too slow to draw much fuel, and cold fuel vaporises poorly, so a cold engine is hard to start. The primer is a simple hand pump that delivers a measured amount of fuel directly into the induction system near the inlet valves, where it forms a combustible charge without relying on the venturi. It does not heat the fuel, fill the float chamber or pressurise the carburettor.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A fuel pressure gauge is usually incorporated in aircraft fuel systems to measure the pressure of the fuel:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: In the fuel tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: At the fuel tank vent
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: After it leaves the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: As it enters the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: As it enters the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The fuel pressure gauge measures the pressure of the fuel being delivered to the carburettor inlet (or the injection system), so it shows whether the engine-driven and electric fuel pumps are supplying fuel at the pressure the metering system needs. A falling reading warns of a pump failure, a blockage or an empty tank before the engine stops. The pressure in the tank itself is atmospheric, and after the carburettor the fuel is already mixed with the air.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Application of "alternate air" in a fuel injection system:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Feeds cold air from outside the aircraft through a second filter
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Feeds air from within the engine cowling to the induction system
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increases power by ramming extra air into the intake
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Supplies extra fuel to the injectors to prevent icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Feeds air from within the engine cowling to the induction system
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Fuel-injected engines have no venturi and so do not suffer carburettor icing, but the air intake or filter can still be blocked by impact ice or debris. Selecting alternate air (or an automatic door opening) feeds air from inside the engine cowling to the induction system, bypassing the blocked intake. This air is warmer and usually unfiltered, so there is a small loss of power; it does not add fuel or ram extra air into the engine.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: 100 LL aviation fuel or AVGAS can be identified by its:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Red colour
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Blue colour
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Green colour
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Clear or colourless
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Blue colour
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: AVGAS 100LL (low lead) is dyed blue so its grade can be recognised in a fuel sample. AVGAS 100 is green, the older AVGAS 80 is red, and jet fuel (Jet A-1, or AVTUR) is clear or straw-coloured and must never be used in a piston engine. Colour is a cross-check: always confirm the grade from the fuel markings and the aircraft's documents.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Atmospheric pressure is maintained within the fuel tanks through the use of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: An engine-driven fuel pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A fuel vent in the fuel tank cap
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Fuel-tank baffles
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The fuel drain valve
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A fuel vent in the fuel tank cap
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A vent - often a small hole or tube in the filler cap, or a separate vent pipe - lets air into the tank as fuel is used, so the pressure above the fuel stays atmospheric and the fuel can flow freely to the engine. That is why the vent must be checked clear on the pre-flight inspection. Baffles stop the fuel surging, the drain valve removes water, and a fuel pump moves fuel but does not vent the tank.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The function of a diffuser in a carburettor is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Control airflow through the venturi
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Allow air to mix with the fuel before it is discharged into the venturi as the power is increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Maintain the float-chamber level
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent induction icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Allow air to mix with the fuel before it is discharged into the venturi as the power is increased
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the carburettor's main metering system the diffuser (emulsion tube) has small air-bleed holes that let air mix with the fuel before it leaves the discharge nozzle, forming a fine emulsion that atomises well in the venturi. As power is increased and the fuel flow rises, more bleed holes are uncovered, which stops the mixture becoming progressively richer. The throttle controls the airflow, the float maintains the fuel level and carb heat prevents icing.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The absorption of water into aviation fuel is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Unaffected by the temperature of the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: More likely with warm fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: More likely with cold fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Impossible, because water does not mix with fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: More likely with warm fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Warm fuel can hold more dissolved water than cold fuel, so absorption is more likely when the fuel is warm. As the fuel cools, overnight or at altitude, the dissolved water comes out of suspension as free droplets that settle in the sump or can freeze, which is why the tanks must be drained before flight. Water is always present in fuel in small amounts, so it is never impossible, and temperature matters.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: On an aeroplane equipped with a constant-speed unit, RPM has been selected. If power is then slowly increased, RPM will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Decrease
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Fluctuate continuously
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Remain the same
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Remain the same
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A constant-speed unit (governor) holds the RPM selected with the propeller lever. If power is increased, the propeller would tend to speed up, but the governor senses this and increases the blade angle (coarsens the pitch), so the extra power is absorbed as more thrust while the RPM stays the same. That is why, with this type of propeller, the manifold pressure gauge rather than the RPM shows the power being produced.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When leaning the air/fuel mixture:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The ratio of air to fuel decreases
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The throttle butterfly opens further
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The ratio of air to fuel increases
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase fuel flow
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The ratio of air to fuel increases
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Leaning reduces the fuel flow while the airflow is unchanged, so there is more air for each unit of fuel: the air-to-fuel ratio increases. Put the other way round, the fuel-to-air ratio decreases, so watch which way round a question asks. Leaning is done as air density falls with altitude, restoring the correct mixture, saving fuel and keeping the plugs clean.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: One of the advantages of refuelling an aeroplane with full fuel after flight is that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Full tanks will minimize the condensation forming overnight
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Full tanks keep the aircraft's CG further aft
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Full tanks allow the fuel to cool more quickly
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Full tanks prevent the fuel vents from icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Full tanks will minimize the condensation forming overnight
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A partly empty tank contains a large volume of air, and the moisture in it condenses on the cold tank walls overnight and runs into the fuel as water. Filling the tanks after the last flight of the day leaves very little air space, so very little water can form. Water is heavier than fuel and collects in the sump, so the tanks must still be drained and checked before the next flight.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When the throttle is opened from idle to full power rapidly, additional fuel is required to compensate for the increased volume of air. This is provided by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The primer pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The accelerator pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The mixture needle
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The butterfly valve
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The accelerator pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When the throttle is opened quickly the airflow increases almost immediately, but the much heavier fuel takes a moment to respond, so the mixture goes lean and the engine may hesitate or cut. The accelerator pump, linked to the throttle, squirts extra fuel into the venturi to bridge that gap. The butterfly valve is what lets the extra air in, the primer is for starting and the mixture needle sets the fuel metering.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The mixing of fuel and air in a carburettor is achieved:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: By the float chamber
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: By the throttle butterfly
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: By the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: By the accelerator pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: By the diffuser
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a float carburettor the fuel is metered by the main jet and then passes through the diffuser (emulsion tube and discharge nozzle), where air bleeds into it and it is sprayed as a fine mist into the low-pressure airflow in the venturi; that is where fuel and air are mixed. The float chamber only stores fuel at a constant level, the butterfly controls the amount of mixture, and the accelerator pump adds fuel when the throttle is opened quickly.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The helix angle of a propeller is the angle:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Between the chord line and the plane of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Between the chord line and the relative airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Between the propeller shaft and the relative airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Between the relative airflow and the plane of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Between the relative airflow and the plane of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The helix angle is the angle between the relative airflow meeting a blade section and the plane of rotation. It depends on the combination of forward speed and rotational speed: with the aircraft stationary it is zero, and it increases as the aircraft speeds up. The blade angle is from the chord line to the plane of rotation, and the difference between the two is the blade's angle of attack.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If A/C, with a fixed pitch propeller is placed in a shallow dive so that forward speed increases with no change in power setting, RPM will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: decrease
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Remain the same
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Fall to idle
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: With a fixed-pitch propeller, increasing the forward speed increases the helix angle, so each blade meets the air at a smaller angle of attack. The blades then absorb less torque, and with the throttle unchanged the engine speeds up: the RPM increases. In a steep dive the RPM can pass the red line, so the throttle must be reduced to prevent an overspeed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The pilot of an aircraft which is equipped with manifold pressure gauge would be able to identify the presence of carburettor icing by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A increase in manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: An increase in RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A rise in oil temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A decrease in manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A decrease in manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Ice in the carburettor narrows the passage through which the mixture flows to the inlet manifold, so the manifold pressure falls. With a constant-speed propeller the governor keeps the RPM constant, so a gradual, unexplained drop in manifold pressure, rather than any change in RPM, is the first sign of carburettor ice. Applying carb heat reduces the manifold pressure slightly further before it recovers as the ice melts.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When the throttle is opened quickly, the accelerator pump will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Discharge additional fuel into the venturi
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Close the mixture needle to prevent an over-rich mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Open the throttle butterfly further
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prime the cylinders directly for the next start
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Discharge additional fuel into the venturi
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Opening the throttle quickly lets air rush in faster than the fuel in the main metering system can follow, so the mixture momentarily goes lean. The accelerator pump, a small piston or diaphragm linked to the throttle, responds by discharging an additional squirt of fuel into the venturi, preventing hesitation or a flat spot. It does not move the throttle or the mixture needle, and priming is done by the separate primer.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The type of fuel supply system in which the fuel tank is constructed as an integral part of the wing structure is called:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A bladder tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A rigid removable tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A wet wing
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A tip tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A wet wing
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a wet-wing (integral tank) design, part of the wing structure itself - the spars, ribs and skin, sealed with sealant - forms the fuel tank, with no separate tank inside. It gives the most fuel capacity for the least weight. A bladder tank is a flexible rubber cell fitted inside the wing, a rigid tank is a separate metal container, and a tip tank is mounted on the wing tip.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: High oil temperature together with low oil pressure indicates:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A normal condition after a cold start
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A faulty oil temperature gauge only
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Are an indication of low oil supply
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Too much oil in the sump
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Are an indication of low oil supply
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Oil both lubricates and cools the engine. If the oil quantity is low, the smaller amount circulating has to carry away the same heat, so its temperature rises, and as it thins and the pump starts to draw air the pressure falls. Rising temperature with falling pressure is therefore a serious warning of oil starvation: land as soon as possible. A cold start gives high pressure and low temperature, and a single faulty gauge would not affect both readings.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The most appropriate method to deal with pre-ignition in a piston engine during flight is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: decrease engine cooling and enrich the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Increase engine cooling and enrich the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increase engine cooling and enlean the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase power and lean the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Increase engine cooling and enrich the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Pre-ignition is the charge being ignited before the spark by a hot spot, such as glowing carbon, an overheated spark-plug electrode or an exhaust valve. The cure is to remove the heat: enrich the mixture, because the extra fuel cools the charge as it evaporates, and increase the cooling, for example by opening the cowl flaps, reducing power and increasing airspeed. Leaning or reducing the cooling would make the hot spot hotter.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The lubricating system of a piston engine normally makes use of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Splash lubrication only
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A total-loss system, with the oil mixed into the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A gear type pump combined with splash lubrication
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Grease-packed bearings with no oil circulation
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A gear type pump combined with splash lubrication
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A light-aircraft piston engine uses a gear-type pressure pump to force oil through the galleries to the crankshaft main and big-end bearings, the camshaft and the accessory drives. Oil squeezed out of these bearings is flung around by the crankshaft as a fine mist, which splash-lubricates the cylinder walls, pistons, small-end bearings and gears. Oil mixed with the fuel is used only in some two-stroke engines.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The breather pipe on an engine is used to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Allow the oil to be topped up in flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Relieve excess sump pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Supply air to the carburettor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Cool the oil before it returns to the sump
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Relieve excess sump pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Some combustion gas always leaks past the piston rings (blow-by) into the crankcase, and the air inside expands as the engine warms up. The breather vents the crankcase to atmosphere so this pressure cannot build up and force oil out past the seals and gaskets. A breather blocked by ice or dirt can pressurise the crankcase and blow oil out, so it is checked on the pre-flight inspection.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The crankshaft of a piston engine is balanced by the addition of counter- weights in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase the power produced by each cylinder
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Reduce vibration caused by power impulses on the opposite crankpin
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Allow the engine to run at a higher compression ratio
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Help cool the oil in the crankcase
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Reduce vibration caused by power impulses on the opposite crankpin
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The crankpins, connecting rods and pistons are heavy offset masses, and every power impulse gives the crankshaft a jolt. Counterweights on the crank cheeks, opposite the crankpins, balance these masses and forces so the engine runs smoothly, reducing vibration that would otherwise fatigue the crankshaft, bearings and engine mounts. They add no power and have nothing to do with the compression ratio or cooling.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The colour of Phosphate Ester hydraulic fluid is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Purple
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Yellow
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Green
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Blue
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Purple
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Hydraulic fluids are dyed so they can be identified: vegetable-based fluid is blue, mineral-based fluid is red and phosphate-ester (synthetic, fire-resistant) fluid is purple - Purple and Phosphate both start with P. The three types are chemically incompatible and need different seal materials, so only the fluid specified for the aircraft may be used.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Unless approved for use, the use of motor car fuel (MOGAS) in aircraft engines:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: May be used freely, because it has a higher octane rating than AVGAS
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Should not be used because it may result in detonation, reduced power and lead fouling of the spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: May be used provided it is mixed half-and-half with AVGAS
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: May be used in any engine, provided the flight is a short one
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Should not be used because it may result in detonation, reduced power and lead fouling of the spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Car fuel (MOGAS) is made for car engines. It is much more volatile than AVGAS, so vapour lock and carburettor icing are more likely, and its anti-knock quality and additives are not controlled to aviation standards, so detonation, loss of power and plug deposits can follow. It may only be used in an aircraft and engine specifically approved for it, and never as an improvised mix with AVGAS.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Engine cylinders and barrels are usually fitted with the fins in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Reduce drag around the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Reduce the weight of the cylinder barrel
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Improve engine cooling
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase cooling airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Improve engine cooling
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An air-cooled engine gets rid of its heat directly to the air flowing over it. Fins on the cylinder barrels and heads greatly increase the surface area exposed to that air, so heat is carried away much faster and engine cooling is improved. The fins do not increase the airflow itself: the cowling, baffles and cowl flaps direct the air through the fins.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Blue smoke appearing from the exhaust pipes of a piston engine which is running is an indication that the engine:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Has too rich a mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Has water in the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Has too lean a mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Is burning oil
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Is burning oil
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Blue or blue-grey exhaust smoke means lubricating oil is getting into the combustion chambers and burning, typically past worn piston rings or valve guides, or because the engine has been over-filled with oil. Black smoke means the mixture is too rich, and white smoke or steam can indicate water. A little blue smoke just after start can be normal in some engines, but persistent blue smoke needs investigating.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Detonation may occur in a piston engine:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: When the mixture is set too rich
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: When fuel of too high an octane rating is used
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: When the engine is run at low power
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: When fuel of too low an octane rating is used
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: When fuel of too low an octane rating is used
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A fuel's octane rating is its anti-knock value: its resistance to detonation. If fuel of a lower octane rating than the engine requires is used, the unburnt charge ahead of the flame front can explode spontaneously instead of burning smoothly, which is detonation. A higher grade may always be used if the correct one is not available, while a rich mixture and low power make detonation less likely.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Normal operation of a piston engine would be indicated on the firing end of a spark plug by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Dry, black, powdery carbon
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A light grey coating
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Wet, black, oily deposits
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A white, blistered insulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A light grey coating
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A spark plug's firing end is a window into the combustion chamber. A light grey or light tan coating shows that the mixture and temperatures are about right. Dry, black, powdery carbon indicates an over-rich mixture, wet, black, oily deposits indicate oil being burnt, and a white or blistered insulator suggests the plug has been running too hot, for example from a lean mixture or detonation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An oil pressure gauge is usually located in the oil line of a wet sump system:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: after the oil enters the engine components
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Before the oil enters the engine components
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: At the inlet to the pressure pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: In the crankcase breather pipe
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Before the oil enters the engine components
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The oil pressure gauge is connected on the outlet side of the pressure pump, before the oil flows into the galleries and bearings. That is the pressure available to push oil through the engine, so it gives the pilot the most useful indication of whether the bearings are being lubricated. At the pump inlet or in the breather the gauge would show little more than atmospheric pressure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Dry sump piston engine lubrication systems make use of a scavenge pump to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Pump oil from the tank to the engine bearings
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Supply oil to the propeller governor
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Remove air from the oil tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Pump oil from the sump back to the oil tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Pump oil from the sump back to the oil tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a dry-sump system the oil is stored in a separate tank rather than in the engine. The pressure pump sends oil from the tank to the engine; after lubricating it, the oil drains to the bottom of the crankcase, where the scavenge pump picks it up and returns it to the tank, keeping the sump dry. The scavenge pump is larger than the pressure pump so it can always keep up with the frothy, aerated returning oil.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The oil in a wet sump lubrication system passes through the oil cooler:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: after being fed to the engine components
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Only when the oil is cold
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Before being fed to the engine components
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: On its way to the crankcase breather
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Before being fed to the engine components
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a wet-sump system the pressure pump draws oil from the sump and sends it through the oil cooler before it reaches the bearings and other components, so the oil arriving at the engine is at a suitable temperature and viscosity and can absorb more heat. When the oil is cold and thick, a bypass (anti-surge) valve lets it skip the cooler to protect the delicate cooler matrix, so it is not cooled 'only when cold'.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The component of hydraulic system which stores the hydraulic fluid under pressure is called:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The hydraulic pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The selector valve
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The reservoir
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The accumulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The accumulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An accumulator is a cylinder divided by a piston or diaphragm, with a gas charge (usually nitrogen) on one side. Fluid pumped in compresses the gas, so the accumulator holds a reserve of fluid under pressure. The reservoir stores fluid at or near atmospheric pressure, the pump creates the pressure, and the selector valve directs fluid to the chosen service.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The primary method of cooling oil in a wet sump system is by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Passing it through the fuel tanks
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Circulating it through the cabin heater
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Splashing it onto the cylinder walls
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Ram air through an oil cooler
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Ram air through an oil cooler
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The oil cooler is a small radiator: its matrix spreads the oil into thin films, and cold ram air from outside, ducted through the cowling, flows through the matrix and carries the heat away. Engines with a high power output may have shutters to control the airflow through the cooler. The oil is not cooled by the fuel or the cabin heater, and the cylinder walls add heat to the oil rather than removing it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The temperature of the oil in a wet sump lubrication system is usually measured:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: After leaving the oil cooler
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: before leaving the oil cooler
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: At the oil filler cap
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: In the crankcase breather
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: After leaving the oil cooler
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The oil temperature probe is placed after the oil cooler, where the oil is about to enter the engine. That shows the temperature of the oil actually being supplied to the bearings, which is what matters for its viscosity and lubricating ability. A reading taken before the cooler would show the hot oil leaving the engine rather than the oil the engine receives.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Ignition of fuel/air mixture in a four-stroke piston engine occurs during the:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Exhaust stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Compression stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Induction stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Power stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Compression stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The spark plug fires near the end of the compression stroke, typically 20 to 25 degrees before TDC. Burning takes a short time, so starting it early lets the pressure peak just after TDC, at the start of the power stroke, where it does the most useful work. A spark during the power stroke would waste much of the energy and overheat the engine, and there is nothing to ignite on the induction or exhaust strokes.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The most appropriate method to deal with detonation during flight is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Reduce power and enlean the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Increase power and enrich the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Reduce power and enrich the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase power and lean the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Reduce power and enrich the mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Detonation is the explosive burning of the end gas caused by excessive heat and pressure in the cylinder. Reducing power lowers the cylinder pressure and temperature, and enriching the mixture cools the charge because the extra fuel absorbs heat as it evaporates; opening the cowl flaps and increasing airspeed also help. Leaning or increasing power would push the cylinder further towards detonation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The colour of Vegetable Based hydraulic fluid is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Red
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Green
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Purple
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Blue
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Blue
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Vegetable-based hydraulic fluid is dyed blue, mineral-based fluid red and phosphate-ester fluid purple, so the colour of a sample shows which type is in the system. The colour code is a check, not a licence to mix: the types are incompatible, and the fluid to use is always the one specified in the aircraft's maintenance manual.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The colour of Mineral Based hydraulic fluid is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Blue
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Green
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Red
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Yellow
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Red
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Mineral-based hydraulic fluid is a petroleum product dyed red, and it is the fluid used in most light-aircraft brake and undercarriage systems. It must never be mixed with blue vegetable-based or purple phosphate-ester fluid, because each needs its own type of seal and incompatible fluids make the seals swell or deteriorate.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Valve overlap in the four-stroke piston engine will occur between the:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Compression and the power strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Exhaust and the induction strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Induction and the compression strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Power and the exhaust strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Exhaust and the induction strokes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Valve overlap happens around TDC, at the end of the exhaust stroke and the start of the induction stroke, when the inlet valve has already opened (valve lead) and the exhaust valve has not yet closed (valve lag). For those few degrees both valves are open, and the outgoing exhaust gases help draw the fresh charge in, improving the scavenging and filling of the cylinder.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An accumulator may be installed in a hydraulic system in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Store hydraulic fluid under pressure for peak demand or emergency use
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Allow the fluid level to expand and contract as fluid is used in the system
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Filter contaminants out of the fluid before it reaches the pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent a vacuum from forming by allowing air into the reservoir as the fluid is drawn off
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Store hydraulic fluid under pressure for peak demand or emergency use
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An accumulator stores fluid under pressure by compressing a gas charge behind a piston or diaphragm. It can meet peak demands that exceed the pump's output, damp out pressure surges and pump pulsations, and provide enough pressure to operate a service, such as the brakes, briefly after the pump has failed. Allowing for fluid expansion and venting the reservoir are jobs of the reservoir, and filters clean the fluid.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A non-pressurized hydraulic fluid reservoir is fitted with an air vent, often in the cap, in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Release excess system pressure to the atmosphere
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Allow the fluid level to expand and contract as fluid is used in the system
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Stop moisture entering the fluid
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Store hydraulic fluid under pressure for peak demand or emergency use
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Allow the fluid level to expand and contract as fluid is used in the system
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a non-pressurised reservoir the fluid level rises and falls as fluid returns from, or is drawn into, the system, and as it expands and contracts with temperature. The vent lets air in and out so the space above the fluid stays at atmospheric pressure; without it a vacuum would form and starve the pump. Excess system pressure is relieved by a pressure-relief valve, not the vent, and the vent does not keep moisture out.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The type of pump utilised in a piston engine to provide high pressure oil lubrication is a:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Gear type pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Centrifugal pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Diaphragm pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Plunger pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Gear type pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Engine oil pumps are gear pumps: two meshing spur gears in a close-fitting casing carry oil round from the inlet to the outlet in the spaces between their teeth. As positive-displacement pumps they deliver a definite volume every revolution and can build up the pressure needed to force oil through the bearings, with a relief valve limiting the maximum. Centrifugal, diaphragm and plunger pumps are not used for this job.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In a wet sump piston engine lubrication system:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Oil is supplied only by splash lubrication
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Oil is stored only in an external tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Oil is mixed directly with the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Oil is stored in the engine sump and distributed throughout the engine by a pressure pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Oil is stored in the engine sump and distributed throughout the engine by a pressure pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a wet-sump system, used in most light non-aerobatic aircraft, the oil is stored in the sump at the bottom of the engine. A gear-type pressure pump draws it from the sump and pushes it through the filter and galleries to the bearings, and the oil then drains back into the sump. An external tank is the dry-sump system, splash alone is not enough for the heavily loaded bearings, and oil mixed with the fuel is a two-stroke arrangement.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Balancing of the crankshaft of a piston engine is achieved by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A heavy flywheel on the propeller flange
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Lightening holes drilled in the connecting rods
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Adjusting the ignition timing
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Counter-weights attached to the crank cheeks
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Counter-weights attached to the crank cheeks
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The crankshaft is balanced by counterweights attached to the crank cheeks, on the opposite side from each crankpin. They offset the weight of the crankpins, connecting rods and pistons, so the crankshaft spins smoothly with less vibration and bearing load. In many aircraft engines some counterweights are pendulum-type dynamic dampers that also absorb torsional vibration from the power impulses.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Vegetable and mineral hydraulic fluids can be mixed in the same hydraulic system:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Only if topped up in small quantities
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Never
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Only in an emergency
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Provided they are the same colour
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Never
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Never. Vegetable- and mineral-based fluids are chemically incompatible and each needs its own type of seal: mixing them makes seals swell, soften or harden, and can form sludge that blocks valves and filters, leading to system failure. Even a small top-up with the wrong fluid contaminates the whole system, which must then be drained, flushed and resealed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A condition that may occur in only one cylinder as a result of an excessively lean mixture is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Pre-ignition
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Carburettor icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Vapour lock
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Fouled spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Pre-ignition
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Mixture distribution is never perfectly even, so when the engine is leaned too far one cylinder may run much leaner and hotter than the rest. A glowing carbon deposit, spark-plug electrode or exhaust valve in that cylinder can then ignite the charge before the spark: pre-ignition. Because it depends on a local hot spot, it often affects a single cylinder. Fouled plugs come from a rich mixture, and carb icing and vapour lock affect the whole engine.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: After starting an engine black smoke is seen coming from the exhaust. This indicates:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: That the mixture is too lean
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: That oil is being burnt
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: That the mixture is too rich
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: That there is water in the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: That the mixture is too rich
