aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Black smoke is unburnt carbon from fuel that has not burnt completely because there is too little air for it: the mixture is too rich. It is often seen just after start if the engine has been over-primed, and it should clear as the engine runs. Blue smoke indicates burning oil, and white smoke or steam can indicate water.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Counter-weights are attached to the crankshaft of an engine in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Prevent damage from vibrations
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Increase the engine's power output
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Raise the compression ratio
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Cool the crankshaft bearings
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Prevent damage from vibrations
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Counterweights on the crankshaft balance the heavy crankpins, connecting rods and pistons and help smooth out the power impulses, so the engine runs with much less vibration. Unchecked, that vibration would fatigue and damage the crankshaft, bearings, engine mounts and propeller. They add no power, do not change the compression ratio and play no part in cooling.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Lubrication of the main bearings and crankshaft of the engine is provided:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: By splash lubrication only
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: By high-pressure oil from the pressure pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: By oil mixed with the fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: By grease packed into the bearings during servicing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: By high-pressure oil from the pressure pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The main bearings and the big-end bearings on the crankshaft carry the heaviest loads, so they are fed with high-pressure oil: the pump forces oil through the oil galleries to the main bearings and on through drillings in the crankshaft to the big ends. The oil mist flung off the spinning crankshaft splash-lubricates the cylinder walls, pistons, small ends and gears, but splash alone could never give these bearings the positive supply they need. Grease and fuel-oil mixtures are not used.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Using fuel of a higher octane than recommended may result in:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Immediate failure of the fuel pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A permanent increase in engine power
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Lead fouling of the spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Detonation in every case
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Lead fouling of the spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: If the correct grade is not available a higher octane grade may be used, but never a lower one. Higher-grade AVGAS usually contains more tetraethyl lead, and in a low-compression engine designed for low-lead fuel that lead is not fully scavenged, so lead deposits build up and foul the spark plugs and valves. Higher octane adds no power to an engine not designed for it, and it makes detonation less likely, not more.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Loss of pressure in a hydraulic system is indicated to the pilot:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A warning light usually green
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A warning light usually red
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A change in the colour of the fluid
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A rise in the reservoir fluid level
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A warning light usually red
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A pressure switch in the system monitors hydraulic pressure and illuminates a warning light, usually red, when the pressure falls below a safe value. Red is reserved for warnings that need immediate attention, while green normally indicates a safe condition such as gear down and locked. The fluid's colour identifies its type, not its pressure, and a pressure loss usually means fluid is being lost, not gained.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of the pressure relief valve in a lubrication system is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Maintain a constant oil pressure over a range of engine power changes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Prevent the oil from overheating at high engine power
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Return oil from the sump to the oil tank in a dry-sump engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Stop the oil pump automatically when the engine is shut down
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Maintain a constant oil pressure over a range of engine power changes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A gear pump delivers more oil as RPM rises, so without control the pressure would climb with engine speed and could burst the oil cooler or filters. The spring-loaded relief valve, fitted across the pump's inlet and outlet, opens at a set pressure and returns surplus oil to the inlet side, keeping the oil pressure roughly constant over the working range. It does not cool the oil or scavenge the sump; those are the jobs of the cooler and the scavenge pump.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The primary purpose of a cowl-flap is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Reduce drag by streamlining the engine cowling at all airspeeds
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Direct the airflow over the engine cylinders for better cooling
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Control the flow of air over the engine cylinders in order to maintain the correct operating temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent carburettor icing by warming the air entering the intake
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Control the flow of air over the engine cylinders in order to maintain the correct operating temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Cowl flaps are adjustable flaps at the rear of the engine cowling that let the pilot control how much cooling air flows through the engine compartment, keeping the cylinder head and oil temperatures within limits. They are normally open on the ground and in the climb, when airspeed is low and power high, and closed in the cruise and descent to reduce drag and avoid over-cooling. Baffles are fixed plates that simply direct the air around the cylinders.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the RPM of an aircraft's piston engine is increased, the ignition timing will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Advance automatically
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Retard automatically
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Vary with the throttle setting
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Remain the same
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Remain the same
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Most light-aircraft piston engines have fixed ignition timing: once the engine is running and the impulse coupling has disengaged, each magneto fires at the same crank angle (typically 20 to 25 degrees before TDC) whatever the RPM. Higher RPM means the sparks come more often, not earlier. Unlike many car engines there is no automatic advance or retard; the only retard is the impulse coupling's, during starting.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of the vent on a hydraulic fluid reservoir is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Prevent a vacuum from forming by allowing air into the reservoir as the fluid is drawn off
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Store hydraulic fluid under pressure for peak demand or emergency use
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Filter the fluid as it returns to the reservoir
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Keep the fluid at a constant temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Prevent a vacuum from forming by allowing air into the reservoir as the fluid is drawn off
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: As the pump draws fluid from the reservoir, the space above the fluid would fall below atmospheric pressure if air could not get in. The vent admits air so the reservoir stays at atmospheric pressure, preventing a vacuum that would restrict the flow to the pump and cause cavitation; it also lets air out as fluid returns. The vent does not store pressure, filter the fluid or control its temperature.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The timing of the ignition of the fuel and air mixture in an internal combustion engine is arranged to occur:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Between 20 degrees and 25 degrees after TDC during the compression stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: At TDC at the end of the compression stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Between 20 degrees and 25 degrees before TDC during the compression stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Between 20 degrees and 25 degrees before TDC during the exhaust stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Between 20 degrees and 25 degrees before TDC during the compression stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Ignition is timed to occur before TDC on the compression stroke, typically 20 to 25 degrees, because the mixture takes a short time to burn. Firing early lets the pressure peak just after TDC, as the piston begins the power stroke, which gives the most useful work. A spark at or after TDC would leave the piston running away from the burning mixture, wasting power and overheating the engine, and there is nothing to ignite on the exhaust stroke.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Dry, black, powdery carbon on the firing end of a spark plug usually indicates:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A cracked spark-plug insulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: An excessively lean mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: An excessively rich mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Normal combustion
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: An excessively rich mixture
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Dry, black, powdery (sooty) carbon on the firing end means the mixture has been too rich, so the fuel has not burnt completely. It often comes from long periods of ground running or taxiing at full rich, which is why leaning on the ground is recommended. A lean mixture leaves light, often whitish deposits, normal combustion a light grey or tan coating, and wet, oily deposits point to oil being burnt.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The supply of electrical power to the engine starter motor is controlled by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The ignition switch contacts directly
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A circuit breaker in the starter cable
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A solenoid located near the starter motor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The alternator's voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A solenoid located near the starter motor
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A starter motor draws a very large current, often a few hundred amps - far more than a cockpit switch or thin wiring could carry. So the starter switch only energises a solenoid, a heavy-duty electromagnetic relay mounted near the starter, which closes the contacts in the short, thick cable from the battery to the motor. Switch contacts carrying that current would burn out, and the voltage regulator controls only the alternator's output.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A hydraulic system operates on the basic principle that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Fluid pressure decreases equally in all directions
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Pressure acts only in the direction of flow
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A confined fluid can be compressed easily
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: When pressure is increased on a confined volume of fluid the increased pressure will be transmitted by the fluid
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: When pressure is increased on a confined volume of fluid the increased pressure will be transmitted by the fluid
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Hydraulics work on Pascal's law: pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions. Because hydraulic fluid is practically incompressible, pushing a small master-cylinder piston produces the same pressure on a larger piston elsewhere, and since force = pressure × area the force is multiplied. A fluid that compressed easily would make the system spongy and useless.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The term "valve overlap" refers to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The short period that both inlet and exhaust valves are both open around TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The inlet valve closes after the piston has passed bottom dead centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The inlet valve opening prior to the piston reaching TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The inlet valve closing before the piston reaches BDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The short period that both inlet and exhaust valves are both open around TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Valve overlap is the short period around TDC, at the end of the exhaust stroke and the start of induction, when both valves are open together: the inlet has opened early (valve lead) and the exhaust has not yet closed (valve lag). The outgoing exhaust gases help draw in the fresh charge, improving scavenging and filling at normal operating RPM. Inlet opening before TDC is valve lead and inlet closing after BDC is valve lag.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The cylinder head temperature gauge usually obtains its reading from:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A cylinder which tests show runs the hottest
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The coolest-running cylinder
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The exhaust manifold
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The oil sump
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A cylinder which tests show runs the hottest
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The CHT probe, usually a thermocouple under a spark plug or in a threaded well, is fitted to the cylinder that flight tests show runs the hottest, often one with the least cooling airflow. If that cylinder is kept within limits, the cooler cylinders will be too. Engines with a multi-probe engine monitor show every cylinder, but a single CHT gauge reads only the hottest one - not the coolest, the exhaust or the oil.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Pre-ignition is likely to occur in a piston engine:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: When the mixture is set to full rich
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Only when the engine is cold
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: When fuel of a higher octane than required is used
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Where there are hot spots in one or more cylinders
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Where there are hot spots in one or more cylinders
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Pre-ignition happens when something in the combustion chamber is hot enough to ignite the fresh charge before the spark: a glowing carbon deposit, an overheated spark-plug electrode or a red-hot exhaust valve. It is therefore linked to overheating, lean mixtures and carbon build-up, not to cold engines or rich mixtures, which run cooler. It causes rough running and power loss, and can let the engine run on after the ignition is switched off.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The use of fuel with a lower octane rating than that recommended by the aircraft manufacturer may lead to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Detonation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Valve lead
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Valve lag
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Pre-ignition
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Detonation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The octane rating measures a fuel's resistance to detonation. With a lower grade than the engine needs, the end gas - the last of the charge ahead of the flame front - can explode spontaneously under the heat and pressure of combustion, which is detonation. It causes loss of power, overheating and, if prolonged, damage to pistons and valves. Pre-ignition is caused by hot spots rather than the fuel grade, and valve lead and lag are timing terms.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of baffles in the engine compartments is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Control the flow of air over the engine cylinders in order to maintain the correct operating temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Direct the airflow over the engine cylinders for better cooling
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Reduce the noise from the engine
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent oil leaking onto the exhaust
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Direct the airflow over the engine cylinders for better cooling
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Baffles are fixed metal plates and seals around the cylinders that force the incoming cooling air to flow closely over and between the cylinder fins, instead of taking the easy path around them, so every cylinder is cooled evenly. They work with the pressure difference created by the cowling. Controlling how much air flows to keep the right temperature is the job of the cowl flaps; baffles only direct it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A low-pressure filter is usually incorporated in a hydraulic system between:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The pump and the accumulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The selector valve and the actuator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The reservoir and the pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The accumulator and the selector valve
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The reservoir and the pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The low-pressure filter sits in the suction line between the reservoir and the pump, catching dirt before it can damage the pump. It is a low-pressure filter because this side of the system is at about reservoir (atmospheric) pressure. Every other location given is on the pressure side, downstream of the pump, where a high-pressure filter would be needed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In a simple airspeed indicator, pitot pressure is supplied to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Pitot pressure is fed to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The static vent directly
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The calibrated leak
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Pitot pressure is fed to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the ASI, pitot (total) pressure from the pitot tube is piped into the flexible capsule, while static pressure from the static vent fills the sealed instrument case around it. The capsule therefore expands in proportion to the difference - the dynamic pressure - which depends on airspeed. Feeding pitot pressure to the case would reverse the indication, and the calibrated leak belongs to the VSI.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A centre zero ammeter is incorporated in an electrical system to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Indicate electrical system voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Indicate the alternator's total output only
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Indicate the battery's state of charge in ampere-hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Indicate the flow of current into and out of battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Indicate the flow of current into and out of battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A centre-zero ammeter is fitted in the battery lead, so it shows current flowing into or out of the battery. A needle to the right (+) means the alternator is charging the battery; to the left (-) means the battery is discharging and supplying the load, which in flight warns of an alternator failure. Voltage is shown by a voltmeter, and a left-zero ammeter (loadmeter) shows the alternator's output only.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A reverse current cut-out relay, or circuit breaker, is used in a generator supplied electrical system to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Prevent the generator from being overloaded
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Prevent the flow of current from the battery to the generator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Regulate the generator's output voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Convert the generator's output to DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Prevent the flow of current from the battery to the generator
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When the engine is idling or stopped, the generator's voltage falls below the battery's. Without protection the battery would then drive current backwards through the generator, discharging itself and trying to run the generator as a motor. The reverse-current cut-out disconnects the generator whenever its output falls below battery voltage and reconnects it when it rises. The voltage regulator controls the output, and the commutator produces the DC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In order to generate electrical power, an aircraft magneto depends on:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Rotating magnet
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The distributor
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The alternator
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The commutator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Rotating magnet
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A magneto is a self-contained generator: a permanent magnet, driven by the engine, rotates between the poles of a soft-iron core carrying the coils. The constantly reversing magnetic flux induces current in the primary winding, and interrupting that current induces the high voltage for the plugs. Because it depends only on the rotating magnet, the ignition keeps working even if the battery and alternator fail. The distributor merely routes the high voltage to the plugs.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The electrical current produced by a magneto:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Is produced by the starter motor
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Is induced by the alternator stator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Is supplied by the aircraft battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Is created by the rotating magnet
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Is created by the rotating magnet
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The magneto makes its own electricity by electromagnetic induction: as the engine turns the permanent magnet, the flux through the coil keeps reversing, inducing a current in the primary winding. When the contact-breaker points open, the collapsing flux induces a very high voltage in the secondary winding for the spark plugs. It needs no battery, alternator or starter, which is why the engine keeps running after a total electrical failure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the event that a fuse in an electrical circuit has blown:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: It should be replaced with a fuse of a higher rating to stop it blowing again
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: It should be replaced only once with a fuse of same value
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: It may be replaced as many times as necessary until it holds
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: It should be bypassed with a piece of wire until after landing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: It should be replaced only once with a fuse of same value
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A fuse blows because the current in its circuit has exceeded its rating, which usually means there is a fault. It may be replaced once with a fuse of the same rating; if the new one also blows, the fault is still there and the circuit must be left off. A higher-rated fuse, repeated replacement or bypassing it with wire would let the wiring overheat and could start an electrical fire.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Control of the voltage output from a DC generator is achieved through a:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Reverse-current cut-out
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Rectifier
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Commutator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A generator's output voltage rises with its speed and falls with load. The voltage regulator keeps it within limits by varying the current through the generator's field winding: more field current strengthens the magnetic field and raises the output, less reduces it. The reverse-current cut-out stops the battery discharging through the generator, and the commutator converts the armature's AC into DC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Diodes are used in an AC alternator to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Regulate the output voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Convert the AC output to DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Store electrical energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Protect the circuit from overloads
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Convert the AC output to DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An alternator's stator windings produce alternating current, but the aircraft's system and battery need direct current. Diodes let current flow in one direction only, so a set of them (the rectifier) inside the alternator converts the AC output to DC; they also stop the battery discharging back through the alternator, so no reverse-current cut-out is needed. Voltage is controlled by the regulator, and overload protection by fuses and circuit breakers.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Modern aircraft electrical systems generally make use of circuit breakers:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: As a means of regulating the alternator's voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: As a means of measuring the current in each circuit
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: As a means of converting AC to DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: As a means of preventing the system from becoming overloaded
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: As a means of preventing the system from becoming overloaded
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A circuit breaker protects a circuit's wiring from overheating: if the current exceeds its rating, a bimetallic element heats up and trips the breaker, opening the circuit. Unlike a fuse it can be reset, but a tripped breaker should be reset only once, after a short cooling period, and never held in. It does not regulate voltage, measure current or convert AC to DC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The function of the distributor in a magneto is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Produce the high voltage in the secondary winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Open the primary circuit at the correct moment
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Retard the spark during engine start
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Route high voltage to each spark plug in the correct firing order
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Route high voltage to each spark plug in the correct firing order
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The magneto's secondary winding produces the high voltage, and the distributor sends it to the right place: a rotor turning at half engine speed passes each high-tension lead in turn, so each spark plug receives its spark in the engine's firing order. The contact-breaker points open the primary circuit to create the spark, and the impulse coupling provides the retarded spark for starting.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A breakage or disconnection of the magneto earth wire will have the effect of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Stopping the engine immediately
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Making the magneto produce no sparks at all
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Making it impossible to stop the engine by switching off the ignition
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Causing a large drop in RPM on the magneto check
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Making it impossible to stop the engine by switching off the ignition
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The magneto is switched off by earthing (grounding) its primary circuit through the P-lead, which stops it producing sparks. If the P-lead is broken or disconnected, turning the switch to OFF no longer earths the magneto, so it stays live and the engine keeps running. Worse, anyone moving the propeller of a parked aircraft could start it, so every propeller must be treated as live. The dead-cut check after start shows whether each magneto can be switched off.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A left-zero ammeter is incorporated in an electrical system to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Indicate electrical system voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Indicate current flowing into and out of the battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Indicate alternator or generator output current only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Indicate the battery's state of charge
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Indicate alternator or generator output current only
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A left-zero ammeter, or loadmeter, is connected in the alternator (or generator) output lead, so it reads from zero upwards and shows only how much current the alternator is producing to supply the loads and charge the battery; it cannot show a discharge. A centre-zero ammeter in the battery lead is the one that shows current flowing into and out of the battery, and voltage needs a voltmeter.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In a DC generator, The AC output is converted into DC through:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The field winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The condenser
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A commutator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A commutator
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The armature coils of a DC generator rotate in a magnetic field, so the voltage induced in them reverses every half-turn: it is alternating. The commutator, a ring of copper segments on the armature shaft with carbon brushes riding on it, reverses the connections to each coil at the right moment, so the output at the brushes is direct current. An alternator does the same job electronically, with diodes.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The indications of a centre-zero ammeter:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Are that positive indications are shown right of centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Are that positive indications are shown left of centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Are that zero is at the left-hand end of the scale
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Are that the scale is marked in volts
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Are that positive indications are shown right of centre
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A centre-zero ammeter has zero in the middle of its scale. A reading to the right, on the positive side, means current is flowing into the battery (it is being charged); a reading to the left, on the negative side, means the battery is discharging, and a steady discharge in flight usually means the alternator has failed. Zero at the left-hand end describes a loadmeter, and the scale is in amperes, not volts.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An operational advantage of the alternator is that it:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Needs no voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Produces direct current without the need for diodes
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Will still produce electrical power at low RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Can recharge a completely flat battery by itself
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Will still produce electrical power at low RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An alternator produces useful output even at low RPM, such as at idle or while taxiing, whereas an old-style DC generator produces little until the engine speed is fairly high; it is also lighter for the same output. It still needs a voltage regulator, relies on diodes to convert its AC to DC, and needs battery power to energise its field, so it cannot bring a completely flat battery back to life on its own.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The storage capacity of a battery is usually expressed in:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Volts
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Watts
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Ohms
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Ampere-hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Ampere-hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A battery's capacity is the amount of charge it can store, expressed in ampere-hours: current multiplied by time. A 24 Ah battery could in theory supply 24 A for one hour or 2 A for 12 hours, although in practice it delivers less at high currents and low temperatures. Volts measure its electrical pressure, watts power and ohms resistance, none of which describes its capacity.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of an ammeter is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Measure the system voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Measure electrical current flow
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Measure the resistance of a circuit
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Measure the electrical power being used
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Measure electrical current flow
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An ammeter measures electrical current - the rate of flow of charge - in amperes. In aircraft it is either a centre-zero type in the battery lead, showing charge and discharge, or a left-zero loadmeter showing the alternator's output. Voltage is measured by a voltmeter, resistance by an ohmmeter, and power in watts.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the earth wire from a magneto to the aircraft structure is broken:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The engine will stop immediately
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The engine will continue to run with the magneto switch in the off position
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The magneto will not produce any sparks
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The alternator will stop charging the battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The engine will continue to run with the magneto switch in the off position
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The magneto earth (P-) lead connects the magneto's primary circuit to the ignition switch. Selecting OFF earths the primary circuit so no sparks are produced; if the wire is broken the magneto cannot be earthed and remains live. The engine will keep running with the switch OFF, and a stationary engine can fire if the propeller is turned by hand, so always treat a propeller as live. A broken P-lead has no effect on the alternator.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Pitot pressure is taken from:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A port flush with the side of the fuselage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A tube mounted in the relative airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Inside the cockpit
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The engine's air intake
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A tube mounted in the relative airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Pitot (total) pressure is sensed by a forward-facing tube mounted where it meets the relative airflow head-on, usually under a wing or on the nose, clear of disturbed air. Air entering the open end is brought to rest, so the tube senses static plus dynamic pressure. A flush port on the fuselage side senses static pressure, and the cockpit is the usual alternate static source. The pitot cover must be removed before flight.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In an alternator, the stator:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Rotates inside the magnetic field
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Remains stationary
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Converts AC to DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Regulates the output voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Remains stationary
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In an alternator the stator is the fixed set of windings around the inside of the casing, while the rotor - an electromagnet fed through slip rings - spins inside it. The rotating magnetic field induces alternating current in the stationary stator windings, so the heavy output current does not have to pass through brushes. The diodes convert the AC to DC, and the voltage regulator controls the field current.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The correct level of electrolyte in a lead acid battery should be maintained by the addition of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Distilled water
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Sulphuric acid and water
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Tap water
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Sulphuric acid only
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Distilled water
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: During charging, some of the water in the electrolyte is split into hydrogen and oxygen and escapes, but the sulphuric acid stays in the battery. So only water needs to be replaced, and it must be distilled water, because the minerals in tap water would contaminate the plates; adding acid would make the electrolyte too strong. The hydrogen given off is explosive, so batteries must be kept well ventilated.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Electrical fuses are rated in:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Watts
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Volts
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Amperes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Ohms
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Amperes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A fuse is a thin wire or strip that melts when the current through it exceeds its rating, so it is rated in amperes: the current it can carry continuously without blowing. The rating is chosen to protect the wiring of that circuit, which is why a blown fuse must only be replaced with one of the same ampere rating. Volts, watts and ohms describe other electrical quantities.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The alternate static source draws air from:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A second pitot tube facing the airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The engine's induction manifold
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The vacuum pump outlet
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Within the cockpit
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Within the cockpit
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In most light aircraft the alternate static source is a valve under the instrument panel that, when opened, connects the static lines to the air inside the cockpit. It gives the altimeter, VSI and ASI a working static pressure if the external vent is blocked, for example by ice. Because cockpit pressure is usually slightly lower than outside static pressure, the altimeter and ASI read a little high and the VSI shows a brief climb when it is selected.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In comparison to the generator:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The power output of an alternator will be greater at a higher RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: An alternator cannot be used to charge a lead-acid battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: An alternator does not need a voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The power output of an alternator will be greater at a lower RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The power output of an alternator will be greater at a lower RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Compared with a DC generator, an alternator gives useful output at a much lower RPM - it will charge the battery even at idle or while taxiing - and it is lighter for the same output, which is why modern light aircraft use alternators. An alternator still needs a voltage regulator, and it charges the lead-acid battery normally through diodes that convert its AC output to DC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A capacitor is incorporated in an electrical circuit to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Limit the current in the circuit
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Store an electrical charge
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Convert AC to DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Measure the voltage of the circuit
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Store an electrical charge
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A capacitor (condenser) is two conducting plates separated by an insulator. When a voltage is applied, charge builds up on the plates and is stored there until the circuit lets it discharge. In a magneto the condenser absorbs the surge as the points open, preventing arcing and speeding the collapse of the magnetic field; elsewhere capacitors smooth voltage and suppress radio interference. Limiting current is a resistor's job, and diodes convert AC to DC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of a condenser or a capacitor in a magneto is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase magneto RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Distribute current to the cylinders
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Prevent arcing across the contact-breaker points
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Retard the ignition during cruise
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Prevent arcing across the contact-breaker points
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The condenser is connected across (in parallel with) the contact-breaker points. As the points open, the primary current tries to keep flowing and would jump the gap as an arc, burning the points and slowing the collapse of the magnetic field. The condenser absorbs that surge instead, so the points last longer and the field collapses quickly, giving a strong spark. The distributor sends the high voltage to the plugs, and the impulse coupling looks after starting.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During engine start, the low-tension booster coil:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Supplies the magneto's primary coil with a low voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Supplies high-voltage impulses to a trailing brush on the distributor rotor
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Uses a spring to briefly speed up the magneto's rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Stays switched on in flight to strengthen the spark
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Supplies the magneto's primary coil with a low voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: At cranking speed (about 120 rpm) a magneto cannot produce a strong enough spark, so the spark is augmented during the start. The battery-powered low-tension booster coil supplies the magneto's primary coil with a low voltage and is switched off once the engine is running. High-voltage impulses to a trailing brush come from a high-tension booster coil, and the spring mechanism is the impulse coupling.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Pitot pressure is used in:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Airspeed indicator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Vertical speed indicator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Attitude indicator
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The altimeter only
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Airspeed indicator
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Of the pressure instruments, only the airspeed indicator uses pitot pressure: it compares pitot (total) pressure with static pressure to measure the dynamic pressure. The altimeter and VSI use static pressure only, and the attitude indicator is a gyroscopic instrument. So a blocked pitot tube affects only the ASI, while a blocked static vent affects all three pressure instruments.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of a Voltage regulator is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Prevent current flowing from the battery into the generator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Control the voltage output from a DC generator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Route high voltage to each spark plug in the correct firing order
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Step up the low voltage to a high voltage before transmission to the spark plug
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Control the voltage output from a DC generator
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A generator's output voltage would otherwise rise with engine speed and fall with electrical load. The voltage regulator senses the system voltage and adjusts the current in the generator's field winding to keep the output within limits (about 14 V in a 12 V system, 28 V in a 24 V system), preventing both overcharging and undercharging of the battery. Stopping reverse current is the cut-out's job, routing the spark is the distributor's, and stepping up voltage is a transformer's.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of an impulse coupling in a magneto is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Disconnect the magneto during start
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Supply battery current to the spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increase spark advance at cruise RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Produce a strong, retarded spark at the low RPM of engine start
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Produce a strong, retarded spark at the low RPM of engine start
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: At cranking speed the magnet turns too slowly to produce a strong spark, and at the normal advanced timing the engine could kick back. The impulse coupling holds the magnet back while a spring winds up, then releases it to flick round quickly: this gives a strong spark, and because it fires later than normal it is retarded, near TDC, so the engine cannot kick back. Once the engine runs, centrifugal force holds the pawls clear and the coupling has no further effect.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A transformer is incorporated in a low-tension magneto system in order to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Step up the low voltage to a high voltage after transmission to the spark plug
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Step up the low voltage to a high voltage before transmission to the spark plug
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Convert the magneto's AC output into DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Reduce the voltage to protect the spark plugs
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Step up the low voltage to a high voltage before transmission to the spark plug
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a low-tension ignition system the magneto produces a low voltage, which is sent along the ignition leads to a small transformer (coil) mounted close to each spark plug. The transformer steps it up to the high voltage needed to jump the plug gap just before it reaches the plug. Keeping the long leads at low voltage greatly reduces flash-over and leakage, which get worse at altitude. The transformer raises the voltage; it does not reduce it or convert AC to DC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A rectifier in an Alternator is required to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Convert AC output into DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Control the alternator's output voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Store electrical charge
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Prevent arcing across the contact points
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Convert AC output into DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An alternator generates alternating current in its stator, but the aircraft's bus and battery need direct current. The rectifier - a set of diodes built into the alternator - lets current pass in one direction only and so converts the AC output to DC; the diodes also stop the battery discharging back into the alternator. The voltage regulator controls the output, a capacitor stores charge, and the magneto's condenser prevents arcing.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Position error of the static vent can be reduced:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: If two interconnected static vents are mounted one on either side of the fuselage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: By fitting a longer pitot tube so that it reaches clean air
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: By selecting the alternate static source inside the cockpit
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: By mounting the static vent on the nose, close to the propeller
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: If two interconnected static vents are mounted one on either side of the fuselage
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Position error arises because the static vent does not sense exactly the ambient pressure: the airflow around the fuselage changes with attitude, sideslip and flap setting. Two interconnected vents, one on each side of the fuselage, average the pressures, so in a sideslip an over-read on one side is largely cancelled by an under-read on the other. The cockpit alternate source adds error rather than removing it, and vents are placed well away from the propeller's disturbed air.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The operating principle of a DC generator is that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: It is self-excited and does not require battery power to come online
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: It produces alternating current at its output terminals
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: It requires battery excitation at all times
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: It cannot generate at low engine RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: It is self-excited and does not require battery power to come online
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A DC generator is self-exciting: its field poles keep a little residual magnetism, so as soon as the armature turns it produces a small voltage, which is fed back to the field winding to strengthen the field, and the output builds up until the regulator takes control. It therefore needs no battery power to start generating, unlike an alternator, whose field must be energised from the battery. Its commutator gives DC, not AC, at the terminals.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Reverse current flow from the battery to an alternator is prevented by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The alternator field switch
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A centre-zero ammeter
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The alternator rectifier diodes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The alternator rectifier diodes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An alternator's rectifier diodes let current flow only from the alternator to the bus. If the alternator's output falls below battery voltage - at low RPM, or when it fails - the diodes block any current trying to flow back from the battery, so no separate reverse-current cut-out is needed. The field switch turns the alternator on and off, the voltage regulator controls its output, and the ammeter only indicates the current.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Normal static pressure is taken from:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A forward-facing tube in the airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Inside the cockpit
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A port located in an area of undisturbed air
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Behind the propeller, in the slipstream
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A port located in an area of undisturbed air
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The static vent is a small flush hole, usually one on each side of the fuselage, placed where the airflow is undisturbed so it senses the true ambient atmospheric pressure without any effect from the aircraft's speed. A forward-facing tube would sense pitot pressure, the cockpit is only the alternate source, and the propeller slipstream would give false readings. The vents must be kept clean and unblocked, free of polish, tape or insects.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A battery rated at 40 ampere-hours can theoretically provide:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 10 amperes for 2 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 4 amperes for 5 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 4 amperes for 10 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 20 amperes for 1 hour
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 4 amperes for 10 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Battery capacity in ampere-hours is current multiplied by time. For 40 Ah, 4 A for 10 hours gives 40 Ah, so that is the answer; the others work out at only 20 Ah (10 A for 2 hours, 4 A for 5 hours and 20 A for 1 hour). In practice a battery delivers less than its rating, especially at high currents and low temperatures, so after an alternator failure the pilot should shed electrical load to make the battery last.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An airspeed indicator is constructed so that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: pitot pressure is fed to the instrument case and pitot pressure to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Static pressure is fed to the instrument case and static pressure to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Static pressure is fed to the instrument case and pitot pressure to the instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Static pressure is fed to the instrument case and pitot pressure to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Static pressure is fed to the instrument case and pitot pressure to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the ASI, static pressure fills the sealed instrument case and pitot (total) pressure is fed into the capsule. Pitot pressure is static plus dynamic pressure, so the static parts cancel and the capsule expands only by the dynamic pressure, which depends on airspeed; a linkage turns this into pointer movement. Any other arrangement would either cancel out completely or measure the wrong thing.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Resistors are used in electrical circuits to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Store electrical charge
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Convert AC to DC
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Vary the voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase the current in the circuit
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Vary the voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A resistor opposes the flow of current, and by Ohm's law (V = I × R) a voltage drop appears across it. Fixed resistors set the voltage or current in part of a circuit, and variable resistors (rheostats) let it be adjusted - for example to dim the panel lights. A resistor does not store charge (a capacitor does) or convert AC to DC (a rectifier does), and adding resistance reduces the current rather than increasing it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An aircraft's pitot tube is usually mounted:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Flush with the fuselage skin
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Inside the engine cowling
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Directly into the airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Facing rearwards to keep insects out
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Directly into the airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The pitot tube must face directly into the relative airflow so that the air entering it is brought to rest and its total (pitot) pressure is sensed. It is mounted clear of the fuselage and propeller, often under a wing, in undisturbed air, and pitot heat keeps it free of ice. A flush mounting suits a static vent, and a rearward-facing or enclosed tube could not sense the dynamic pressure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In a simple airspeed indicator, static pressure is supplied to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: pitot pressure is fed to the case
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Static pressure is fed to the case
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Static pressure is fed to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Static pressure is not used by the ASI
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Static pressure is fed to the case
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the ASI, static pressure from the static vent is fed into the sealed instrument case, surrounding the capsule, while pitot pressure goes inside the capsule. The static pressure acting on both sides cancels out, leaving the capsule to respond only to dynamic pressure - the part that depends on airspeed. If static pressure went into the capsule instead, the instrument could not measure airspeed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An inverter is used in an aircraft electrical system to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Convert direct current to direct current
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Convert alternating current to alternating current
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Convert direct current to alternating current
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Convert alternating current to direct current
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Convert direct current to alternating current
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An inverter changes direct current into alternating current. Light aircraft have DC electrical systems, but some instruments and avionics need AC, so an inverter provides it. The reverse process, AC to DC, is done by a rectifier such as the diodes in an alternator, and changing DC to DC or AC to AC at a different voltage is the job of converters and transformers.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the event that a circuit breaker in an electrical circuit has tripped:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: It should be pushed back in only once after allowing a cooling off period
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: It should be pushed back in only once before allowing a cooling off period
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: It should be held in by hand until the fault clears itself
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: It should be reset as many times as necessary until it stays in
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: It should be pushed back in only once after allowing a cooling off period
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A circuit breaker trips when the current in its circuit has been too high, which usually means there is a fault. The accepted practice is to wait a short time for it to cool and then reset it once, if the equipment is needed; if it trips again the fault is still there and it must be left out. Resetting it before it has cooled, holding it in or resetting it repeatedly can overheat the wiring and start a fire.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The electrolyte used in a lead acid battery is composed of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Potassium hydroxide and water
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Distilled water
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Nitric acid and water
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Sulphuric acid and pure water
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Sulphuric acid and pure water
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The electrolyte in a lead-acid battery is dilute sulphuric acid: sulphuric acid mixed with pure (distilled) water. As the battery discharges, the acid combines with the plates and the electrolyte becomes weaker, which is why its specific gravity shows the state of charge. Potassium hydroxide is the alkaline electrolyte of a nickel-cadmium battery, and the two battery types must never be serviced with each other's fluids or tools.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The AC output from an alternator is converted to DC by a:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Commutator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Voltage regulator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Inverter
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Rectifier
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Rectifier
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An alternator's stator produces AC, and a rectifier - a set of diodes, usually built into the alternator - converts it to DC for the bus and battery. A commutator does a similar job mechanically in a DC generator, the voltage regulator controls the output voltage, and an inverter does the opposite conversion, from DC to AC.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A voltmeter may be incorporated in an electrical system to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Indicate electrical system voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Measure electrical resistance
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Protect the circuit against overload
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Indicate current flow into and out of the battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Indicate electrical system voltage
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A voltmeter measures electrical potential - voltage - so in the aircraft it shows the bus or battery voltage. It lets the pilot check that the alternator is charging (about 14 V in a 12 V system, 28 V in a 24 V system) and spot a low voltage after an alternator failure or a high voltage from a faulty regulator. Current into and out of the battery is shown by a centre-zero ammeter, and overload protection comes from fuses and circuit breakers.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A twenty-four-volt lead acid battery would have:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: twelve cells
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: six cells
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: eight cells
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: twenty-four cells
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: twelve cells
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Each lead-acid cell produces about 2 volts, whatever its size, and the cells are connected in series so their voltages add. A 12 V battery therefore has six cells and a 24 V battery twelve. The size of the cells (their plate area) affects the capacity in ampere-hours, not the voltage.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A rating of 20 amps/hour means that a battery will provide:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 1 amp for 2 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 20 amps for 1 hour
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 2 amps for 20 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 20 amps for 20 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 20 amps for 1 hour
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A battery's capacity in ampere-hours is current multiplied by time, so a 20 Ah battery could in theory provide 20 amps for 1 hour, 10 amps for 2 hours or 1 amp for 20 hours. The other options work out at 2 Ah, 40 Ah and 400 Ah. In practice the usable capacity is lower, particularly at high discharge rates and in cold weather.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of an alternator is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Supply the aircraft electrical system and recharge the battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Convert the battery's DC into AC for the instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Provide the spark for the ignition system
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Turn the engine over for starting
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Supply the aircraft electrical system and recharge the battery
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The engine-driven alternator is the aircraft's main source of electrical power in flight: it supplies all the electrical loads and recharges the battery after the engine start. The battery then only has to provide power for starting and act as a reserve if the alternator fails. The ignition spark comes from the independent magnetos, the starter motor turns the engine, and converting DC to AC is an inverter's job.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The basic principle of an airspeed indicator is to measure the differential between:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Pitot pressure and cabin pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Static pressure and vacuum pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Dynamic pressure and cabin pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Static and pitot pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Static and pitot pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Pitot pressure is the total of static pressure and dynamic pressure. The ASI feeds pitot pressure to one side of its capsule and static pressure to the other, so the difference it measures is the dynamic pressure (½ρV²), which depends on airspeed and air density. Cabin pressure is used only when the alternate static source is selected, and vacuum drives the gyro instruments, not the ASI.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An operational problem of the conventional VSI which does not occur in the Instantaneous VSI is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Manoeuvre-induced error
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Time lag in the indication
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Position error at the static vent
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pointer returning to zero if the static vent is blocked
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Time lag in the indication
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A conventional VSI lags by a few seconds because the pressure difference across its metering unit takes time to build up or equalise. The IVSI adds an accelerometer (a vertical-acceleration pump) that changes the capsule pressure immediately, so it shows a climb or descent almost at once. Position error, manoeuvre-induced error and static blockages still affect both instruments.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The instruments which would be affected by a blockage in both pitot tube and static vent are:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The attitude indicator and turn coordinator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The altimeter, VSI and ASI
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The altimeter only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The altimeter and VSI only
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The altimeter, VSI and ASI
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The altimeter and VSI use static pressure, and the ASI uses both pitot and static pressure, so a blockage of both affects all three. The altimeter freezes at the altitude where the blockage happened, the VSI returns to zero, and the ASI's reading freezes because both of its pressures are trapped, whatever the actual speed. The gyro instruments are not affected.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a climb, the pressure in the capsule of a vertical speed indicator will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Remain the same
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Become equal to the case pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Decrease
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Decrease
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The VSI's capsule is connected directly to the static line, so its pressure follows the outside static pressure immediately, while the case is fed through a calibrated leak and lags behind. In a climb the outside pressure is falling, so the capsule pressure decreases and becomes lower than the case pressure; the capsule contracts and the pointer shows a rate of climb. In a descent the reverse happens.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The purpose of the engine driven vacuum pump used in an aircraft's gyroscopic instrument system is to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Reduce pressure inside the gyro capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Increase pressure inside the gyro instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Supply air pressure to the pitot-static instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Reduce pressure inside the gyro instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Reduce pressure inside the gyro instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Most light aircraft drive the attitude and direction indicators with air. The engine-driven vacuum pump sucks air out of the instrument cases, reducing the pressure inside them; filtered cabin air then rushes in through a jet and strikes buckets cut in the rotor, spinning it at high speed. The pump reduces the pressure in the case, not inside the rotor, and it plays no part in the pitot-static system.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the pitot tube became blocked in flight:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The ASI reading would remain the same in level flight, irrespective of power changes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The ASI would immediately read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The ASI would respond normally to changes in speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The altimeter would freeze at its present reading
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The ASI reading would remain the same in level flight, irrespective of power changes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: If the pitot tube and its drain hole are blocked, the pressure in the ASI capsule is trapped. In level flight the static pressure in the case does not change either, so the ASI keeps showing the same speed whatever the power - it behaves like an altimeter instead, over-reading in a climb and under-reading in a descent. It reads zero only if the pitot line also leaks, and the altimeter, which uses static pressure only, is unaffected.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If during a level flight, the ASI reading falls to zero:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The static tube becomes blocked and there is a leak in the pitot pressure system
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The static vent has become blocked
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The aircraft has flown into an area of lower pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pitot tube becomes blocked and there is a leak in the pitot pressure system
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The pitot tube becomes blocked and there is a leak in the pitot pressure system
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The ASI reads zero when there is no difference between the pressure in its capsule and that in its case. If the pitot tube is blocked and the pitot line also leaks, the capsule pressure leaks away until it equals the static pressure in the case, and the ASI drops to zero. A pitot blockage alone freezes the reading, a static blockage alone gives errors as altitude changes, and a change in atmospheric pressure does not remove the dynamic pressure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Rigidity is the term which describes:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The change in direction of a gyro's axis when a force is applied
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The drift of a gyro caused by the earth's rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The tendency of a gyro to slow down when its air supply fails
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The reluctance of a spinning gyro to turn away from its spinning axis
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The reluctance of a spinning gyro to turn away from its spinning axis
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Rigidity (or rigidity in space) is a spinning gyro's resistance to any change in the direction of its spin axis: left alone, the axis keeps pointing the same way in space, which is what makes the attitude and direction indicators work. It increases with the rotor's mass and speed. The change of direction when a force is applied is precession, and the drift caused by the earth's rotation is apparent wander.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The effect of a climb on an altimeter is that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The decrease in static pressure will allow the capsule to expand, registering a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The increase in static pressure will compress the capsule, registering a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The pitot pressure will expand the capsule, registering a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The static pressure inside the capsule will rise, registering a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The decrease in static pressure will allow the capsule to expand, registering a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The altimeter's capsule is sealed with a partial vacuum inside, and static pressure fills the case around it. As the aircraft climbs the static pressure falls, so there is less pressure squeezing the capsule and it expands; the linkage converts this expansion into a higher altitude reading. In a descent the rising pressure compresses the capsule. The altimeter uses no pitot pressure, and static pressure goes to the case, not into the capsule.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: As altitude is increased the capsule inside an altimeter will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Expand causing the instrument to show an decrease in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Expand causing the instrument to show an increase in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: contract causing the instrument to show an increase in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Contract causing the instrument to show a decrease in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Expand causing the instrument to show an increase in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: As altitude increases, the static pressure in the altimeter case falls. The sealed, partly evacuated capsule then has less pressure acting on it, so it expands, and the mechanism turns that expansion into a higher altitude on the dial. Descending does the opposite: rising pressure compresses the capsule and the reading falls. Expansion always means a higher reading, and contraction a lower one.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the static vent becomes blocked during a descent or climb, the altimeter will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Over-read in a climb and under-read in a descent
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Drop to zero and stay there
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Contract causing the instrument to shown a decrease in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Continue to indicate the altitude at which the blockage occurred
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Continue to indicate the altitude at which the blockage occurred
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: With the static vent blocked, the pressure in the altimeter case is trapped at the value it had when the blockage occurred, so the capsule stops moving and the altimeter keeps showing that altitude however much the aircraft climbs or descends. The VSI also returns to zero. Selecting the alternate static source (or, as a last resort, breaking the VSI glass) restores a static supply.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the alternate static vent, located in the aircraft's cockpit, is opened in flight in response to a blocked static vent, the altimeter will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Over-read because the cockpit pressure is usually lower than the outside pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Under-read because the cockpit pressure is usually higher than the outside pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Read correctly because the cockpit is at the same pressure as the outside air
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: An altitude lower than the aircraft's actual altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Over-read because the cockpit pressure is usually lower than the outside pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Air flowing over the fuselage creates a slight suction, so the pressure inside most unpressurised cockpits is a little lower than the true outside static pressure. With the cockpit alternate static source selected, the altimeter senses this lower pressure and interprets it as greater height, so it over-reads; the ASI also reads slightly high and the VSI shows a brief climb. The POH gives corrections for using the alternate source.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the pitot pressure line became blocked during level flight, the airspeed indicator (ASI) reading:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Will drop to zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Will remain constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Will increase in proportion to the power setting
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Will fluctuate rapidly
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Will remain constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: If the pitot line becomes blocked, the pressure in the ASI capsule is trapped. In level flight the static pressure in the case stays the same too, so the difference between them, and the reading, remains constant whatever the actual airspeed or power setting. If the aircraft then climbs, the falling static pressure makes the ASI over-read, and in a descent it under-reads. It drops to zero only if the trapped pressure leaks away.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An altimeter is constructed so that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The case is sealed at sea-level pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The capsule contains static pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The capsule contains pitot pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The capsule contains a partial vacuum and static pressure is fed to the instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The capsule contains a partial vacuum and static pressure is fed to the instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The altimeter's aneroid capsule (or stack of capsules) is sealed with a partial vacuum inside and held open by a spring, while static pressure from the static vent is fed into the airtight instrument case around it. As the static pressure changes with altitude, the capsule expands or contracts and a linkage drives the pointers. A capsule containing static or pitot pressure would not respond to altitude in this way.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The green arc on an airspeed indicator represents:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The flap operating range
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The never-exceed range
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The normal operating speed range
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The caution range
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The normal operating speed range
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The ASI's colour markings show the key speeds. The green arc is the normal operating range, from VS1 - the clean (flaps up) stalling speed at maximum weight - at its lower end, up to VNO, the maximum structural cruising speed, at its upper end. The white arc is the flap operating range, the yellow arc the caution range (smooth air only), and the red line VNE, the never-exceed speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The suction required to operate vacuum driven gyroscopes is usually between:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 5 to 7 inches of mercury
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 3 - 5 inches of mercury
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 1 to 2 inches of mercury
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 8 to 10 inches of mercury
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 3 - 5 inches of mercury
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Vacuum-driven gyro instruments normally need a suction of about 3 to 5 inches of mercury (inHg) below atmospheric pressure, shown on the suction gauge, although the POH gives the exact range. Below it the rotors spin too slowly, rigidity falls and the instruments become sluggish or erratic; above it the rotors can over-speed and wear. Always check the suction gauge during the run-up.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the only static vent becomes blocked, the vertical speed indicator during a subsequent climb or descent will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Indicate a climb continuously
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Indicate a descent continuously
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Respond normally but with a delay
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The VSI works by comparing the static pressure in its capsule with the delayed static pressure in its case. If the only static vent is blocked, neither can change any more: the small difference present at the time quickly leaks away through the calibrated leak, and the VSI settles at zero whatever the aircraft does. Together with a frozen altimeter, a VSI stuck at zero during a climb or descent is a strong clue to a static blockage.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Gyroscopic precession means that if a force is applied to a spinning gyroscope:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The effect of an applied force occurs 80 degrees later in the direction of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The effect of an applied force occurs 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The effect of an applied force occurs 110 degrees later in the direction of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The effect of an applied force occurs 100 degrees later in the direction of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The effect of an applied force occurs 90 degrees later in the direction of rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Precession is a gyro's reaction to an applied force: the rotor does not move in the direction it is pushed, but as though the force had been applied at a point 90 degrees further round in the direction of rotation. The turn indicator uses precession to measure the rate of turn, and the port vanes use it to keep the attitude gyro erect. A simple way to picture it is to carry the push 90 degrees round with the spin.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During the engine run-ups, prior to take off, a reading of 3 inches of mercury is indicated on the gyro suction gauge. This means that the gyro instruments:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Will over-speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Will not work at all
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Will function normally
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Will topple immediately
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Will function normally
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A suction of 3 inHg is at the lower end of the normal 3 to 5 inHg range, so the rotors will reach their proper speed and the gyro instruments will function normally, provided the reading is within the limits in the POH.
