The instruments become sluggish or erratic only below the normal range, and can over-speed above it; they do not topple or stop working at 3 inHg.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: True airspeed is calibrated airspeed corrected for:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Calibrated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Calibrated airspeed corrected for compressibility only
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Calibrated or rectified airspeed corrected for temperature and density
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Calibrated airspeed corrected for wind speed and direction
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Calibrated or rectified airspeed corrected for temperature and density
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Calibrated (rectified) airspeed is IAS corrected for instrument and position error. The ASI is calibrated for ISA sea-level air density, but at altitude or in warm air the air is less dense, so the ASI under-reads the aircraft's true speed through the air. Correcting CAS for density - using pressure altitude and temperature - gives TAS, roughly 2% more than CAS for every 1,000 ft. Wind affects groundspeed, not TAS.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A blockage of static vent during a descent would cause the ASI to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Remain constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Under-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When the static vent blocks, the ASI case keeps the lower static pressure from the higher altitude where the blockage occurred. As the aircraft descends, the real static pressure - and with it the pitot pressure fed to the capsule - increases, but the case pressure does not, so the capsule sees too large a pressure difference and the ASI over-reads. In a climb with a blocked static vent it under-reads, which could lead a pilot towards a stall.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Maneuver induced error is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: An error caused by the pitot tube being misaligned with the airflow
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: An error caused by temperature changes in the instrument mechanism
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Fluctuations of pressure at the static vent during rapid changes of altitude which can cause a false indication
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: An error caused by the delay in the VSI's calibrated leak
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Fluctuations of pressure at the static vent during rapid changes of altitude which can cause a false indication
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Manoeuvre-induced error is a temporary false reading caused by the changing airflow around the static vent during rapid changes of attitude or altitude. The disturbed airflow makes the pressure at the vent fluctuate, so the pressure instruments - particularly the VSI - briefly show a false climb or descent, which disappears once the manoeuvre is complete. A misaligned pitot tube is a position error, and the VSI's normal delay is time lag.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A vertical speed indicator (VSI) is constructed so that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Delayed static pressure is supplied to the instrument case and static pressure to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Static pressure is supplied only to the case
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Vacuum pressure is supplied to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Pitot pressure is supplied to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Delayed static pressure is supplied to the instrument case and static pressure to the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The VSI capsule is connected directly to the static line, so it always holds the current static pressure, while the case is fed through a calibrated leak (a fine restriction), so its pressure lags behind. In level flight both are equal and the pointer reads zero; in a climb or descent the capsule pressure changes first, and the difference between capsule and case, proportional to the rate of climb or descent, drives the pointer. No pitot pressure or vacuum is used.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the static vent becomes blocked during level flight at a constant airspeed, the ASI will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Under-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Remain constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Remain constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When the static vent blocks in level flight, the pressure trapped in the ASI case equals the actual static pressure at that altitude. As long as the aircraft stays at that level the ASI remains accurate, so at a constant airspeed its reading remains constant. The errors appear only when the altitude changes: it under-reads in a climb and over-reads in a descent.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The instantaneous vertical speed indicator (IVSI) utilizes an accelerometer to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase the static pressure of the capsule during the initiation of a descent
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: decrease the static pressure of the capsule during the initiation of a descent
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increase the pitot pressure of the capsule during the initiation of a descent
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase the static pressure of the instrument case during the initiation of a descent
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Increase the static pressure of the capsule during the initiation of a descent
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The IVSI adds an accelerometer: a small piston held by springs in a cylinder connected to the capsule line. When a descent begins, the downward acceleration makes the piston rise in its cylinder, immediately increasing the pressure in the capsule, so the pointer shows a descent at once instead of waiting for the static pressure difference to build up. In a climb the piston falls and decreases the capsule pressure. It does not act on pitot pressure or on the case.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The instruments that would be affected by a static vent blockage are:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The altimeter, airspeed indicator and vertical speed indicator
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The airspeed indicator only
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The altimeter only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The attitude indicator and heading indicator
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The altimeter, airspeed indicator and vertical speed indicator
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The altimeter and VSI work entirely on static pressure, and the ASI compares pitot pressure with static pressure, so a static blockage affects all three: the altimeter freezes, the VSI reads zero and the ASI gives wrong readings once the altitude changes (under-reading in a climb, over-reading in a descent). Selecting the alternate static source restores them. The gyro instruments, such as the attitude and heading indicators, are unaffected.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the only static vent becomes blocked in level flight and the aircraft does not climb or descend, the airspeed indicator will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Continue to show the correct indicated airspeed
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Fluctuate
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Continue to show the correct indicated airspeed
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: At the moment of blockage the static pressure trapped in the ASI case equals the real static pressure, and as long as the aircraft stays at the same level it continues to do so. The ASI therefore still shows the correct indicated airspeed and responds normally to changes in speed. Errors appear only when the altitude changes: it under-reads in a climb and over-reads in a descent.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a descent, the pressure inside the case of a vertical speed indicator (VSI) will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Remain constant while the capsule pressure increases
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: decrease at a slower rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increase at a higher rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase at a slower rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Increase at a slower rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a VSI the capsule receives static pressure directly, while the case is fed through a calibrated leak. In a descent the outside pressure rises, so the capsule pressure increases immediately and the case pressure follows more slowly. With the capsule pressure higher than the case pressure, the capsule expands and the pointer shows a descent, at a rate proportional to the pressure difference.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The effect of a climb on a vertical speed indicator (VSI) is that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The capsule pressure increases faster than the case pressure, so the capsule expands and the mechanism indicates a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The capsule pressure decreases faster than case pressure, so the capsule contracts and the mechanism indicates a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The case pressure decreases faster than the capsule pressure, so the capsule expands and the mechanism indicates a descent
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Both pressures remain equal, so the pointer stays at zero throughout the climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The capsule pressure decreases faster than case pressure, so the capsule contracts and the mechanism indicates a climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a climb the static pressure falls. The capsule, connected directly to the static line, loses pressure straight away, while the case, fed through the calibrated leak, loses pressure more slowly. With the capsule pressure now lower than the case pressure the capsule contracts, and the linkage moves the pointer to show a rate of climb; the faster the climb, the larger the difference.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During the initiation of a climb, the accelerometer in an Instantaneous Vertical Speed Indicator will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Cause a rapid increase in static pressure in the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Cause a rapid decrease in static pressure in the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Cause a rapid decrease in pitot pressure in the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Cause a rapid decrease in static pressure in the instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Cause a rapid decrease in static pressure in the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When a climb begins, the upward acceleration makes the IVSI's accelerometer piston fall in its cylinder, which immediately reduces the pressure in the capsule. The capsule contracts and the pointer shows a climb at once, without waiting for the normal static-pressure difference to develop. As the acceleration stops the piston slowly returns, by which time the normal VSI pressure difference has taken over. It acts on the capsule, not the case, and pitot pressure is not used.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When an aircraft levels out after a rapid descent the altimeter will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Under-read for a brief period
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Over-read for a brief period
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Read correctly at once
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Freeze at the altitude from which the descent began
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Over-read for a brief period
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An altimeter's mechanism has some friction and lag, so during a rapid descent it cannot quite keep up and shows an altitude slightly higher than the aircraft's actual altitude. When the aircraft levels off it takes a moment to catch up, so for a brief period it continues to over-read. This matters most when levelling off at a minimum altitude close to terrain, where the aircraft is actually a little lower than indicated.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The vacuum pump, which is engine-driven in most light aircraft:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Blows compressed air into the gyro instrument case to turn the rotor
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Is driven electrically by the alternator
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Sucks air from the gyro instrument case allowing the incoming air to turn the gyro rotor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Supplies air pressure to the pitot-static instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Sucks air from the gyro instrument case allowing the incoming air to turn the gyro rotor
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The engine-driven vacuum pump draws air out of the gyro instrument cases. Air at cabin pressure then flows in through a filter and is directed by a nozzle at buckets cut in the rotor's rim, so the incoming air spins the rotor, much like water turning a waterwheel, and the used air is drawn out to the pump. It does not blow compressed air into the instruments, it is driven by the engine, not the alternator, and it has nothing to do with the pitot-static system.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: On an airspeed indicator (ASI) the cautionary range is indicated by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A green arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A white arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A red radial line
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A yellow arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A yellow arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The yellow arc on the ASI is the caution range, from VNO (the maximum structural cruising speed) up to VNE, the red never-exceed line. Flight in the yellow arc is permitted only in smooth air and with care, because gusts could overstress the airframe. The green arc is the normal operating range and the white arc the flap operating range.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the pitot pressure line became blocked during level flight and the airspeed indicator (ASI) reading fell to zero:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: There is a leak in the static pressure line
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The static vent is also blocked
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: There is a leak in the pitot pressure line
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The alternate static source has been selected
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: There is a leak in the pitot pressure line
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A blocked pitot line normally traps the pressure in the ASI capsule, so the reading freezes rather than falling. If it falls to zero, the trapped pitot pressure must be escaping through a leak until it equals the static pressure in the case, leaving no pressure difference. A static blockage or the alternate static source would not make the ASI read zero in level flight.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: On an airspeed indicator (ASI) the full flap stalling speed is indicated by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The lower end of the white arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The higher end of the white arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The lower end of the green arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The red radial line
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The lower end of the white arc
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The white arc is the flap operating range. Its lower end is VSO, the stalling speed in the landing configuration (full flap and gear down) at maximum weight, and its upper end is VFE, the maximum speed with flaps extended. The lower end of the green arc is VS1, the clean stalling speed, and the red line is VNE.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a climb, the pressure inside the case of a vertical speed indicator will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Remain constant while the capsule pressure decreases
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: increase at a slower rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Decrease at a slower rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Decrease at a higher rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Decrease at a slower rate than that inside the capsule
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a climb the outside static pressure falls. The VSI capsule, connected directly to the static line, loses pressure immediately, while the case pressure falls more slowly because it can only change through the calibrated leak. So the case pressure decreases at a slower rate than the capsule pressure, the capsule ends up at a lower pressure than the case and contracts, and the pointer shows a climb.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An altimeter is indicating 5300ft with QNH 1023 is set, the pressure altitude:
aircraft-technical-and-general.e:
GIVEN
Altimeter indicates 5300 ft with QNH 1023 hPa set.

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = indicated altitude - (QNH - 1013) x 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
QNH - 1013 = 1023 - 1013 = 10 hPa
Correction = 10 x 30 = 300 ft
Pressure altitude = 5300 - 300 = 5000 ft

ANSWER
5000 ft

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The pressure altitude at an airfield is 2800ft and the airfield elevation above sea level is 2500ft. The QNH is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 1023 hpa
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 1003 hpa
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 1013 hpa
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 993 hpa
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 1003 hpa
aircraft-technical-and-general.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 2800 ft; airfield elevation 2500 ft.

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 - QNH) x 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
Pressure altitude - elevation = 2800 - 2500 = 300 ft
300 ft ÷ 30 ft per hPa = 10 hPa
Pressure altitude is above the elevation, so QNH is below 1013 hPa
QNH = 1013 - 10 = 1003 hPa

ANSWER
1003 hPa

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An altimeter in an aircraft on the ground at an airfield indicates a pressure altitude of 2200 ft. If the QNH is 1023 hPa, the airfield's elevation is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.e:
GIVEN
On the ground with QNH 1023 hPa set, altimeter reads pressure altitude 2200 ft.

FORMULA
Elevation (QNH altitude) = pressure altitude + (QNH - 1013) x 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
QNH - 1013 = 1023 - 1013 = 10 hPa
Correction = 10 x 30 = 300 ft
Elevation = 2200 + 300 = 2500 ft

ANSWER
2500 ft

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A blockage of pitot tube during a climb would cause the ASI to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Remain constant
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Under-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: With the pitot tube and its drain blocked, the capsule keeps the pitot pressure from the altitude where the blockage occurred. As the aircraft climbs, the static pressure in the case falls, so the difference between capsule and case grows and the ASI over-reads, showing an increasing speed even though the real speed may be falling. A pilot following it could raise the nose towards a stall. In a descent it would under-read.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a rapid climb, a simple pressure altimeter will tend to indicate:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: An altitude higher than the aircraft's actual altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The correct altitude at all times
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: An altitude lower than the aircraft's actual altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Zero until the aircraft levels off
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: An altitude lower than the aircraft's actual altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An altimeter's capsule and mechanism take a moment to respond, so in a rapid climb the indication lags behind and shows an altitude lower than the aircraft's actual altitude; in a rapid descent it shows a higher one. The lag is small in a normal climb and disappears once the aircraft levels off. The altimeter responds all the time: it is neither perfectly accurate at once nor stuck at zero.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The effect of having two static vents located one on either side of an aircraft's fuselage is that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Position error will be doubled
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Position error will be reduced
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The ASI will no longer need a pitot tube
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Instrument error will be removed
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Position error will be reduced
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a sideslip or yaw, the vent on the side facing the airflow senses a pressure that is too high and the one on the sheltered side a pressure that is too low. Connecting a vent on each side of the fuselage averages the two, so the errors largely cancel and position error is reduced. Instrument error is a separate, manufacturing error, and the ASI still needs its pitot tube.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Calibrated or Rectified airspeed is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Calibrated or rectified airspeed corrected for temperature and density
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Indicated airspeed corrected for temperature and density
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: True airspeed corrected for wind
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Indicated airspeed (IAS) is what the ASI shows. Correcting it for instrument error (manufacturing imperfections) and position error (the static vent not sensing the exact ambient pressure) gives calibrated, or rectified, airspeed (CAS or RAS); the POH lists these corrections. Correcting CAS for density - altitude and temperature - then gives true airspeed, and allowing for the wind gives groundspeed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a descent, the pressure in the capsule of a vertical speed indicator (VSI) will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: decrease
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Remain the same
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Become equal to the case pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The VSI capsule is connected directly to the static line. In a descent the outside pressure rises, so the capsule pressure increases immediately, while the case pressure rises more slowly through the calibrated leak. The capsule, now at a higher pressure than the case, expands and the pointer shows a rate of descent.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: True airspeed may be obtained from CAS/RAS by correcting for:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: CAS/RAS corrected for instrument and position error
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: CAS/RAS corrected for wind
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: CAS/RAS corrected for compressibility only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: CAS/RAS corrected for temperature and altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: CAS/RAS corrected for temperature and altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The ASI is calibrated for ISA sea-level density, but as altitude increases, or the temperature rises, the air becomes less dense and the ASI shows less than the true speed through the air. Correcting CAS (RAS) for altitude and temperature - that is, for density - gives true airspeed; a flight computer does this, or allow roughly 2% per 1,000 ft. Instrument and position error are corrected going from IAS to CAS, and the wind gives groundspeed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In many light aircraft, the alternate static source obtains pressure from:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The vacuum system
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: An external vent on the wingtip
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: From inside the cockpit
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pitot tube
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: From inside the cockpit
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In many light aircraft the alternate static source is simply a valve that opens the static system to the air inside the cockpit. The cockpit is protected from external icing, so it provides a usable static pressure if the external vents ice up or become blocked. The pressure inside is usually slightly lower than outside static pressure, so the altimeter and ASI read a little high. It does not use the pitot tube or the vacuum system.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the alternate static vent, located in the aircraft's cockpit, is opened in flight in response to a blocked static vent, the ASI will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Remain unaffected
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Read zero
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Under-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Over-read
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The cockpit pressure is usually a little lower than the true outside static pressure, because air flowing over the fuselage creates a slight suction. With the alternate source selected, that lower pressure is fed to the ASI case, so the difference between the pitot pressure in the capsule and the case is larger than it should be, and the ASI over-reads. The altimeter over-reads for the same reason.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The two properties associated with a spinning gyroscope are:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Torque and drift
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Mass and inertia
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Rigidity and precession
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Lift and drag
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Rigidity and precession
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A spinning gyroscope has two fundamental properties. Rigidity is its resistance to any change in the direction of its spin axis, used by the attitude and direction indicators as a stable reference; precession is its reaction to an applied force, which appears 90 degrees further round in the direction of rotation, used by the turn indicator. Torque, drift, mass and lift are not gyroscopic properties.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the mass and rate of rotation of a gyro is increased:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Rigidity will increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Rigidity will decrease
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Precession will increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Rigidity will be unaffected
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Rigidity will increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A gyro's rigidity depends on its angular momentum: the rotor's mass (its moment of inertia, greatest when the mass is concentrated at the rim) multiplied by its rotational speed. Increasing either makes the rotor more rigid, so it resists being displaced and precesses less for a given force. That is why gyro rotors are heavy rims spun at high RPM, and why low suction, which slows the rotor, reduces rigidity.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Over-speeding of vacuum driven gyro rotor is prevented by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A pressure relief valve which is located just before the vacuum pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A pressure relief valve which is located just after the vacuum pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A restrictor in the rotor's air jet
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The instrument's caging knob
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A pressure relief valve which is located just before the vacuum pump
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The vacuum pump can produce more suction than the instruments need, especially at high RPM, which would over-speed the gyro rotors and wear their bearings. A spring-loaded relief valve (vacuum regulator) in the line just before the pump opens to admit ambient air when the suction exceeds its setting, limiting the suction to the correct range. A valve after the pump would be on its outlet side and could not limit the suction.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: As altitude is decreased the capsule inside an altimeter will:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Contract causing the instrument to show an increase in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Expand causing the instrument to show a decrease in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Contract causing the instrument to show a decrease in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Expand causing the instrument to show an increase in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Contract causing the instrument to show a decrease in altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: As the aircraft descends, the static pressure in the altimeter case increases and squeezes the sealed, partly evacuated capsule, so it contracts. The mechanism converts the contraction into a lower altitude reading. Climbing does the opposite: the falling pressure lets the capsule expand and the reading rises. Contraction always means a lower reading and expansion a higher one.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The mandatory periodic inspection (MPl) should be carried out:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Either once a year or every 120 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Either once a year or every 150 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Either once a year or every 80 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Either once a year or every 100 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Either once a year or every 100 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A light aircraft on a standard maintenance programme must have a mandatory periodic inspection (MPI) at intervals of 12 months or 100 hours of flight time, whichever comes first. Once either limit is reached the aircraft may not fly until the inspection is done and a new certificate of release to service is issued. An approved maintenance or inspection programme may specify different intervals.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The gyro suction gauge will indicate to the pilot that the normal vacuum system pressure:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Is less than the atmospheric pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Is greater than the atmospheric pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Is equal to the atmospheric pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Varies only with the aircraft's altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Is less than the atmospheric pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A suction gauge measures how far the pressure in the vacuum system is below atmospheric pressure, in inches of mercury. A normal reading of about 3 to 5 inHg therefore means the system pressure is less than atmospheric, which is what draws air through the instruments to spin the rotors. A pressure equal to atmospheric would mean no suction at all, and the gyros would slow down and stop.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During the engine run-ups, prior to take off, a reading of 2 inches of mercury is indicated on the gyro suction gauge. This means that the gyro instruments:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Will function normally
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Will over-speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Will be unaffected, because they are electrically driven
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Will function erratically
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Will function erratically
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A suction of 2 inHg is below the normal 3 to 5 inHg range, so the rotors cannot reach their full speed. With reduced rigidity the attitude and direction indicators become sluggish, wander and give erratic readings, so the fault - a failing pump, a leak or a blocked filter - should be put right before flight in conditions where they are needed. In most light aircraft these gyros are vacuum-driven, not electric.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Apparent wander in a Direction Indicator is caused by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Friction in the gimbal bearings
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Turbulence
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The rotation of the earth
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: An unbalanced rotor
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The rotation of the earth
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A direction indicator's gyro stays fixed in space, but the earth rotates beneath it at 15 degrees per hour. To a pilot on the rotating earth the gyro's axis therefore appears to drift: apparent wander, which varies with latitude from zero at the equator to 15 degrees per hour at the poles. Friction in the bearings and gimbals, turbulence and an unbalanced rotor cause real wander, where the gyro actually moves in space.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When executing a turn from 210 degrees through south to 160 degrees, in the southern hemisphere, using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll out on would be:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 160deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 200deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 180deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 230deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 180deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the Southern Hemisphere the compass lags when turning onto southerly headings and leads onto northerly ones, so the rule is ONUS: Overshoot North, Undershoot South (the reverse of the Northern Hemisphere's UNOS). Turning left from 210 through south to 160, the compass lags behind the real heading, so roll out early - at about 180 on the compass, 20 degrees before the target - and it will settle on 160. The size of the correction depends on latitude and bank angle.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: With reference to the Attitude Indicator or Artificial Horizon, as an aircraft changes its pitch attitude or bank:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The gyro remains in the vertical relative to the earth
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The vertical axis gyro aligns itself with the vertical axis of the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The gyro precesses to follow the aircraft's new attitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The gyro tilts with the aircraft, so the display does not change
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The gyro remains in the vertical relative to the earth
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The attitude indicator's gyro is erected to the earth's vertical and, through rigidity, stays there as the aircraft manoeuvres. The instrument case and the aircraft pitch and roll around the gyro, so the horizon bar, attached to the gyro, stays level with the real horizon while the miniature aircraft moves with the aircraft. If the gyro moved with the aircraft there would be nothing to measure against.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the rotor speed of a turn indicator increases above normal:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The pointer/needle will show a higher rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The pointer/needle will show a lower rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The pointer/needle will be unaffected
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pointer/needle will show a turn in the opposite direction
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The pointer/needle will show a higher rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The turn indicator's rate gyro precesses when the aircraft turns, and a spring balances the precession, so the pointer deflection depends on the rotor's angular momentum as well as the rate of turn. A rotor spinning faster than normal precesses more strongly, so the pointer shows a higher rate of turn than the aircraft is actually achieving; a slow rotor under-reads. The direction of the indication does not change.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a level coordinated turn, the additional load imposed on the wings is a function of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The aircraft's airspeed only
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The angle of bank used
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The aircraft's weight only
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The angle of bank used
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a level turn the wing's lift must be tilted to provide the turning force while still supporting the weight, so total lift - and the load on the wings - must increase. The load factor depends only on the angle of bank: n = 1 / cos(bank), so 30 degrees gives about 1.15 g, 45 degrees 1.41 g and 60 degrees 2 g. For a given bank angle, airspeed and rate of turn change the radius of the turn, not the load factor.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Compass deviation in a particular aircraft:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Is the same on every heading
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Is caused by the earth's magnetic field
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Can be removed completely by a compass swing
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Varies with each heading
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Varies with each heading
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Deviation is caused by magnetic fields within the aircraft - its steel parts, engine, radios and electrical wiring. As the aircraft turns, the angle between these fields and the earth's field changes, so the deviation is different on each heading. It is measured during a compass swing, reduced with the compensating magnets, and the residual deviation for each heading is recorded on the deviation (correction) card. The earth's own field gives variation, not deviation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The needle or pointer of a Turn co-ordinator shows:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The angle of bank
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The rate of climb
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The balance (quality) of the turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The turn coordinator's miniature aircraft (or needle) shows the rate of turn, with a mark for a rate-one turn of 3 degrees per second (360 degrees in 2 minutes). Because its gyro is canted at about 30 degrees, it also responds to the rate of roll, giving an earlier indication of a turn. It does not show bank angle, and the balance ball (inclinometer) shows whether the turn is coordinated, slipping or skidding.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A Direction Indicator (DI) is so constructed that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The horizontal axis aligns itself with a fixed point in space
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The vertical axis aligns itself with the earth's vertical
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The gyro is kept aligned with magnetic north by a small magnet
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The gyro's spin axis stays aligned with the aircraft's longitudinal axis
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The horizontal axis aligns itself with a fixed point in space
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The direction indicator uses a horizontal-axis gyro: its spin axis is horizontal and, because of rigidity, stays aligned with a fixed direction in space while the aircraft turns around it. The card linked to the gyro therefore gives a steady heading reference, free of the magnetic compass's turning and acceleration errors. It has no magnet, so it must be set to the compass regularly because it drifts; the vertical-axis gyro is the attitude indicator's.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When executing a turn from 060deg through north to 300deg in the southern hemisphere, using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll out would be:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 280deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 330deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 300deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 260deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 280deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Turning from 060 through north to 300 in the Southern Hemisphere, the compass leads the real heading as the aircraft approaches north, so the ONUS rule (Overshoot North, Undershoot South) says overshoot: keep turning until the compass shows about 280, roughly 20 degrees past the target, and after the roll-out it will settle on 300. Rolling out when the compass first shows 300 would leave the aircraft short of the heading.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If the rotor speed of a turn indicator falls below normal:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The pointer/needle will show a higher rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The pointer/needle will show a lower rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The pointer/needle will be unaffected
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pointer/needle will show a turn in the opposite direction
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The pointer/needle will show a lower rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The turn indicator's pointer is deflected by precession of its rate gyro, balanced by a spring. If the rotor spins slower than normal - for example with low suction or a failing electrical supply - it has less angular momentum and precesses less for the same rate of turn, so the pointer shows a lower rate of turn than the actual one. A rotor that is too fast over-reads, but neither reverses the indication.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The indications on a turn indicator during a turn to the left whilst taxying is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Ball should move to the left and the needle should show a left turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Ball should move to the right and the needle should show a left turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Ball should move to the right and the needle should show a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Ball should move to the left and the needle should show a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Ball should move to the right and the needle should show a left turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Taxiing gives a quick check of the turn indicator and balance ball. In a turn to the left the gyro senses the yaw to the left and the needle (or miniature aircraft) shows a left turn, while the ball, like a passenger in a car, swings to the outside of the turn - to the right. If the needle moves the wrong way or not at all, or the ball does not move freely, the instrument is faulty.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The direction indicator should generally be realigned with the magnetic compass:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Every 30 minutes
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Every 10 to 15 minutes during the flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Every 5 minutes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Only before take-off
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Every 10 to 15 minutes during the flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The direction indicator has no magnetic reference, and real wander (bearing friction) plus apparent wander (the earth's rotation) make it drift away from the magnetic heading. It is therefore reset to the magnetic compass about every 10 to 15 minutes, in straight and level, unaccelerated flight when the compass is reading accurately. Resetting it in a turn or while accelerating would transfer the compass's errors to the DI.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the Southern Hemisphere, acceleration and deceleration error on east or west headings causes the compass to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Show no error on east or west headings
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Show a northerly turn when accelerating east
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Show an apparent turn toward South when accelerating and toward North when decelerating
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Show a southerly turn when decelerating east
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Show an apparent turn toward South when accelerating and toward North when decelerating
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Because of the way the compass magnets are balanced against magnetic dip, acceleration and deceleration on east or west headings swing the magnet assembly and produce a false turn. In the Southern Hemisphere, accelerating gives an apparent turn towards the South and decelerating an apparent turn towards the North - SAND: South Accelerate, North Decelerate (the Northern Hemisphere rule is the reverse, ANDS). There is no such error on north or south headings.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A magnetic compass is so constructed that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The magnets float freely in the liquid with no pivot
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Bar magnets suspended well below a high pivot point to reduce magnetic dip
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The bowl is filled with water to keep the magnets cool
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A single bar magnet is mounted well above the pivot point
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Bar magnets suspended well below a high pivot point to reduce magnetic dip
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The compass's bar magnets hang well below a high pivot point, so the assembly is pendulous: gravity holds the magnets nearly level and largely counters magnetic dip, which would otherwise tilt them towards the nearer magnetic pole. The bowl is filled with a clear liquid to damp oscillations and reduce pivot friction, not to cool it. Because the balance is not perfect, acceleration and turning errors remain.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The discrepancy between true bearings and magnetic bearings is a caused by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Magnetic dip
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Variation
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Acceleration error
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Deviation
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Variation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Variation is the angle between true north (the geographic pole) and magnetic north, where the compass points; it changes with position and slowly over the years, and is shown on charts by isogonals. In South Africa variation is westerly, about 18 to 26 degrees, so magnetic headings are larger than true ones: 'variation west, magnetic best'. Deviation is the aircraft's own error between magnetic and compass north, and dip is the vertical tilt of the earth's field.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The gyro rotor of an air driven artificial horizon is maintained in the vertical by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Springs attached to the gimbals
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The rotation of the earth
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The action of the port vanes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pilot's caging knob
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The action of the port vanes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The air leaving the attitude indicator's gyro housing escapes through four slots, each partly covered by a pendulous vane that hangs vertically under gravity. When the gyro is upright all four slots are half covered and the jets balance; if the gyro tilts, one slot opens wider and the opposite one closes, and the unbalanced jet reaction precesses the gyro back to the vertical. Springs, the earth's rotation and the caging knob do not keep it erect.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The type of gyroscope used in an attitude indicator or artificial horizon is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A horizontal-axis rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A vertical-axis earth gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A free directional gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A canted rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A vertical-axis earth gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The attitude indicator needs a stable reference for the earth's vertical, so it uses an earth gyro with its spin axis vertical. The rotor is mounted in gimbals that give it freedom in pitch and roll, and an erection system (the pendulous port vanes) keeps it aligned with the true vertical. The direction indicator uses a horizontal-axis gyro, and the turn indicator a rate gyro, canted in a turn coordinator.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The Direction Indicator is subject to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Magnetic deviation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Acceleration errors on east and west headings
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Northerly turning errors
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Apparent wander caused by the earth's rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Apparent wander caused by the earth's rotation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The direction indicator's gyro stays fixed in space while the earth rotates beneath it, so relative to the earth it appears to drift: this apparent wander (earth-rate drift) is one reason the DI must be realigned with the compass regularly, along with real wander from friction. Deviation, acceleration errors and northerly turning errors belong to the magnetic compass, which is exactly why the DI is used for accurate heading keeping in turns.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In an artificial horizon, the vertical-axis gyro:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The axis of the gyro tilts with the aircraft in pitch and roll
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The vertical axis gyro remains fixed in space and the aircraft pitches and rolls about the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The gyro is a horizontal-axis rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The vertical axis gyro aligns itself with the vertical axis of the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The vertical axis gyro remains fixed in space and the aircraft pitches and rolls about the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The attitude indicator's gyro is erected to the earth's vertical and, because of rigidity, stays fixed in space while the aircraft pitches and rolls around it. The horizon bar is connected to the gyro, so it stays level with the real horizon, while the miniature aircraft on the case moves with the aircraft. If the gyro aligned itself with the aircraft's own vertical axis, the instrument would show no change of attitude at all.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Control of the precession of the gyro in a turn indicator is achieved by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The speed of the air jet directed at the rotor by the vacuum system
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Pendulous vanes that open and close the air outlets of the gimbal
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The tension of a spring mounted between the gimbal and the case of the instrument
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A small magnet mounted between the gimbal and the instrument case
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The tension of a spring mounted between the gimbal and the case of the instrument
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The turn indicator's gyro is a rate gyro whose gimbal is restrained by a calibrated spring connecting it to the case. When the aircraft turns the gyro precesses, tilting its gimbal against the spring until the spring's force balances the precession, so the needle's deflection is proportional to the rate of turn. Without the spring the gimbal would simply topple to its stop. Pendulous vanes belong to the attitude indicator's erection system.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The turn coordinator uses:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A horizontal-axis earth gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A vertical-axis attitude gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A canted rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A free directional gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A canted rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A turn coordinator uses a rate gyro whose spin axis is canted (tilted) at about 30 degrees to the horizontal. Because of the tilt it senses rolling as well as yawing, so it starts to show a turn as soon as the wings begin to bank, before the aircraft actually yaws, and in a steady turn it shows the rate of turn. The older turn and slip indicator uses a horizontal-axis rate gyro, and the direction indicator a free gyro.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An aircraft is to maintain a constant heading of 180deg in the southern hemisphere, using a magnetic compass. If the airspeed is decreased from 110kts to 90kts, the compass would:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Show an apparent turn to the east
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Show an apparent turn to the west
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Continue to show the same reading
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Show an apparent turn to the north
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Continue to show the same reading
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Acceleration and deceleration errors occur only on easterly and westerly headings, and are greatest on east and west. On a north or south heading the forces act along the line of the magnet assembly's pivot and centre of gravity, so they cannot swing it sideways. Slowing from 110 to 90 kt on 180 degrees therefore leaves the compass showing the same reading.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Identify the turn condition shown in Figure 1:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A skidding turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Straight and level flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A coordinated turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Slipping turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Slipping turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The miniature aircraft shows a turn to the left, but the ball has moved to the inside of the turn, the low left side. That means the aircraft is slipping: there is too much bank for the rate of turn (or not enough rudder), so it is sliding sideways towards the inside. 'Step on the ball' - apply left rudder, or reduce the bank - to centre it. In a skid the ball goes to the outside, and in a coordinated turn it stays centred.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The Supplements section of the Aircraft Flight Manual contains information relevant to:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The normal operating procedures for the standard aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The operation of optional equipment which has not been installed in a standard aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The aircraft's weight and balance calculations
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The emergency procedures for the standard aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The operation of optional equipment which has not been installed in a standard aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A Pilot's Operating Handbook or Flight Manual follows a standard layout: general information, limitations, emergency procedures, normal procedures, performance, weight and balance, systems, handling and servicing, and finally supplements. The Supplements section covers optional equipment and modifications not fitted to the standard aircraft - such as a GPS, autopilot or long-range tanks - with their own limitations and procedures, which take precedence over the basic manual where they differ.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Identify the turn condition shown in Figure 2:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Skidding turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A slipping turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Straight and level flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A coordinated turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Skidding turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The miniature aircraft shows a turn to the left, and the ball has moved to the outside of the turn, to the right. That means the aircraft is skidding: the rate of turn is too great for the bank angle, usually from too much rudder into the turn, so the tail slides outwards. 'Step on the ball' - ease off the left rudder or increase the bank - to centre it. A skid close to the stall is dangerous because it can lead to a spin.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Details in respect of maintenance carried out on an aeroplane at its base of operation:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Shall be entered in its logbook(s) within 48 hours of completion of such maintenance
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Shall be entered in its logbook(s) within 58 hours of completion of such maintenance
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Shall be entered in its logbook(s) within 38 hours of completion of such maintenance
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Shall be entered in its logbook(s) within 68 hours of completion of such maintenance
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Shall be entered in its logbook(s) within 48 hours of completion of such maintenance
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Maintenance carried out at the aircraft's base must be entered in the relevant logbook(s) - airframe, engine or propeller - within 48 hours of the work being completed, so the records always show the aircraft's true maintenance state. For work done away from base, the 48 hours run from the aircraft's return to its base of operation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An Artificial Horizon (AH) is so constructed that:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The vertical axis gyro aligns itself with the vertical axis of the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The gyro's spin axis is horizontal
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The vertical axis gyro remains fixed in space and the aircraft pitches and rolls about the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The gyro is restrained by a spring so that it measures the rate of pitch
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The vertical axis gyro remains fixed in space and the aircraft pitches and rolls about the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The artificial horizon's rotor spins about a vertical axis in gimbals that let the aircraft move freely around it. Through rigidity the gyro stays fixed in space, aligned with the earth's vertical, while the aircraft and instrument case pitch and roll about it, so the horizon bar linked to the gyro stays level with the real horizon. A horizontal spin axis belongs to the direction indicator, and a spring-restrained gyro to the turn indicator.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The vertical axis of an air-driven artificial horizon is maintained by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The pilot resetting the caging knob in flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The axis of the gyro is maintained in the vertical by the port vanes
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A spring connected between the gimbal and the case
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The earth's magnetic field
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The axis of the gyro is maintained in the vertical by the port vanes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Rigidity holds the gyro's axis steady for a time, but friction and turbulence make it wander, so an erection system is needed to keep it vertical. In the air-driven artificial horizon this is done by the pendulous port vanes: the air leaving the gyro housing through four slots is controlled by vanes that hang under gravity, and any tilt produces an unbalanced jet that precesses the gyro back to the vertical. Springs, magnets and the caging knob do not do this.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A certificate of release to service:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Is issued on completion of an MPI and is valid for 12 months or 100 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Is issued by the pilot after each flight and is valid for 24 hours
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Is issued once, when the aircraft is first registered, and never expires
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Is issued on completion of an MPI and is valid for 6 months or 50 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Is issued on completion of an MPI and is valid for 12 months or 100 hours of flight time, whichever comes first
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A certificate of release to service (CRS) is signed by an appropriately licensed aircraft maintenance engineer or organisation to certify that maintenance, such as an MPI, has been completed correctly and the aircraft is fit to fly. After an MPI it remains valid for 12 months or 100 hours of flight time, whichever comes first, in step with the next MPI, and it must be carried on board. Pilots do not issue it after each flight.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Magnetic dip occurs:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Local magnetic fields in the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Friction in the compass pivot
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Aircraft acceleration
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Because of the stronger magnetic attraction close to the magnetic poles
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Because of the stronger magnetic attraction close to the magnetic poles
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The earth's magnetic field lines are parallel to the surface only near the magnetic equator; towards the magnetic poles they point increasingly down into the earth. A freely suspended magnet follows these lines and tilts, or dips, towards the nearer pole - by about 60 degrees over much of South Africa. The compass reduces dip by hanging its magnets below a high pivot, and what remains causes the turning and acceleration errors. The aircraft's own fields cause deviation, not dip.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During take-off the error which may be expected from an air-driven Artificial Horizon, or Attitude Indicator:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Is a temporary error in both pitch and roll
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: No error during acceleration
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A permanent pitch error only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A permanent roll error only
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Is a temporary error in both pitch and roll
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The pendulous vanes that erect the gyro hang under gravity, so during the take-off acceleration they swing back and cause the gyro to precess. The result is a temporary false indication, typically of a slight climbing turn, in both pitch and roll, which disappears once the acceleration stops. A similar error occurs on deceleration. It is neither permanent nor limited to one axis.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When checking a direction indicator while taxying, the correct indications are:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Headings increase in a left turn and increase in a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Headings decrease in a left turn and decrease in a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Headings decrease in a left turn and increase in a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Headings decrease in a left turn and increase in a left turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Headings decrease in a left turn and increase in a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A direction indicator reads like the compass card, with headings increasing clockwise. So when taxiing, a turn to the left should make the indicated heading decrease (for example from 090 towards 060) and a turn to the right should make it increase. If the heading does not change, or changes the wrong way, the DI is unserviceable. The check is made once the gyro is up to speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The deviation error found in a magnetic compass:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Is caused by the difference between true and magnetic north
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Is the same on all headings
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Is caused by local magnetic fields within the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Is caused by magnetic dip
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Is caused by local magnetic fields within the aircraft
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Deviation is caused by magnetic fields within the aircraft itself - steel components, the engine, radios, electrical wiring and even items placed near the compass. It deflects the compass away from magnetic north by an amount that changes with heading. It is minimised by swinging the compass and adjusting its compensating magnets, and the remaining error is shown on the deviation card. The difference between true and magnetic north is variation.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: According to the International Standard Atmosphere, sea-level air density is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The International Standard Atmosphere defines mean sea-level conditions as 1013.25 hPa, 15 °C and a density of 1.225 kg/m³. Density decreases with height, to roughly half its sea-level value at about 22,000 ft, and ISA sea-level density is the value the ASI is calibrated for. Real air is rarely exactly standard: warm, high or humid conditions reduce density and aircraft performance.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The Turn and Slip indicator make use of a:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A vertical-axis earth gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A horizontal-axis rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A free directional gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A canted attitude gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A horizontal-axis rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The turn and slip indicator uses a rate gyro with its spin axis horizontal (athwartships), mounted in a single gimbal restrained by a spring. When the aircraft yaws in a turn the gyro precesses, tilting against the spring by an amount proportional to the rate of turn, which the needle shows. The attitude indicator uses a vertical-axis earth gyro, the direction indicator a free horizontal gyro, and the turn coordinator a canted rate gyro.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The discrepancy between magnetic bearings and compass bearings is caused by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Deviation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Magnetic dip
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Variation
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Acceleration error
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Deviation
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The difference between magnetic north and compass north is deviation, caused by the aircraft's own magnetic fields; it changes with heading and is listed on the deviation card. The difference between true and magnetic north is variation. The full conversion runs True - Variation - Magnetic - Deviation - Compass ('True Virgins Make Dull Company'), adding westerly errors and subtracting easterly ones going from true towards compass.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Identify the turn condition shown in Figure 3:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Straight and level flight
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Coordinated turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A skidding turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A slipping turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Coordinated turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The miniature aircraft shows a turn to the left and the ball is centred, so the turn is coordinated: the bank angle and rate of turn are matched, and the resultant of weight and centrifugal force acts straight down through the seat, with no slip or skid. That is the aim in every turn, achieved by using rudder together with aileron so that the ball stays in the middle.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The effect of the magnetic dip in a compass is reduced by:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Suspending the magnets well below a high pivot point
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Filling the compass bowl with liquid
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Using a deviation correction card
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Mounting the magnets above the pivot point
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Suspending the magnets well below a high pivot point
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Magnetic dip would tilt the compass magnets towards the nearer magnetic pole. To reduce this, the magnet assembly is suspended from a high pivot point with the magnets well below it, so it hangs like a pendulum and gravity keeps it almost level. The liquid in the bowl damps swinging and the deviation card corrects for the aircraft's own fields; neither reduces dip, and magnets mounted above the pivot would make it worse.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: According to the International Standard Atmosphere, the standard sea-level temperature and lapse rate are:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 10 degrees C at sea level and 1.98 degrees C per 1,000 ft
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 15 degrees C at sea level and 1.98 degrees C per 1,000 ft up to 36,090 ft
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 15 degrees C at sea level and 3 degrees C per 1,000 ft
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 20 degrees C at sea level and 1 degree C per 1,000 ft
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 15 degrees C at sea level and 1.98 degrees C per 1,000 ft up to 36,090 ft
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the ISA the mean sea-level temperature is +15 °C, and it falls at about 1.98 °C per 1,000 ft (6.5 °C per km, usually rounded to 2 °C per 1,000 ft) up to the tropopause at 36,090 ft (11 km), above which it stays constant at -56.5 °C. The 3 °C per 1,000 ft figure is the dry adiabatic lapse rate, not the ISA value.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When executing a turn from 300deg through north to 060deg in the southern hemisphere, using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll out would be:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 100deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 70deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 90deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 080deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 080deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Turning right from 300 through north to 060 in the Southern Hemisphere, the compass leads as the aircraft turns onto northerly headings, so by ONUS (Overshoot North, Undershoot South) the pilot keeps turning past the target and rolls out when the compass shows about 080; it then settles back to 060. The size of this correction depends on latitude and bank, which is why the direction indicator is preferred for accurate turns.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Some aircrafts make use of electrically driven turn indicator because:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: It is more accurate than a vacuum-driven instrument, especially in turbulence
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: It removes the need for a balance ball, because the needle shows slip as well
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: It can be used to reset the direction indicator after it has drifted
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: It provides a valuable back-up instrument should the vacuum pump, or the artificial horizon fail
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: It provides a valuable back-up instrument should the vacuum pump, or the artificial horizon fail
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In most light aircraft the attitude and direction indicators are vacuum-driven. If the turn indicator (or turn coordinator) is electrically driven, a vacuum pump failure leaves the pilot with an independent gyro instrument showing the rate and direction of turn, which, with the ASI and altimeter, allows the aircraft to be kept under control. It is not more accurate, it does not replace the ball, and it cannot be used to reset the DI.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When checking a turn coordinator while taxying, the correct indications are:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The needle moves opposite the turn and the ball remains centred
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The needle remains centred and the ball moves into the turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The needle indicates the turn direction and the ball moves to the outside of the taxying turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Both needle and ball move into the turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The needle indicates the turn direction and the ball moves to the outside of the taxying turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When taxiing, turn gently each way to check the turn coordinator: the miniature aircraft (or needle) should show a turn in the same direction as the aircraft is turning, and the ball should swing to the outside of the turn, just as a passenger in a car is pushed outwards. If the needle stays still or moves the wrong way, or the ball moves into the turn, the instrument is faulty.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The gyroscope used in a Direction indicator or Heading indicator is a:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: A canted rate gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A vertical-axis earth gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A spring-restrained turn gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A horizontal-axis gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A horizontal-axis gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The direction (heading) indicator uses a gyro whose spin axis is horizontal. Through rigidity the axis keeps pointing in the same direction in space as the aircraft turns, so the card attached to it gives a stable heading reference, unaffected by the magnetic compass's turning and acceleration errors. A vertical-axis earth gyro is used in the attitude indicator, and canted or spring-restrained rate gyros in the turn instruments.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: With reference to the documents to be carried on an aeroplane engaged in a domestic flight in South Africa:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Only the certificate of registration need be carried, since the other documents are kept at the aircraft's base
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: No aircraft documents need be carried on a domestic flight, provided copies are kept at the operator's base
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The certificates of registration, airworthiness and release to service as well as a list of visual signals and procedures for use by intercepting aircraft must be carried
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Only the pilot's licence and medical certificate need be carried, as the aircraft documents stay with the owner
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The certificates of registration, airworthiness and release to service as well as a list of visual signals and procedures for use by intercepting aircraft must be carried
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: On a domestic flight in South Africa the aircraft must carry its certificate of registration, certificate of airworthiness and certificate of release to service, together with the visual signals and procedures for use by intercepting aircraft, as well as the other documents Part 91 requires. The pilot must also carry a licence and medical certificate, but these do not replace the aircraft documents, and keeping copies at base is not enough.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When executing a turn from 160 degrees through south to 210 degrees, in the southern hemisphere, using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll out on would be:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 240deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 190deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 210deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 170deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 190deg
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Turning right from 160 through south to 210 in the Southern Hemisphere, the compass lags on southerly headings, so the ONUS rule (Overshoot North, Undershoot South) calls for an undershoot: roll out when the compass shows about 190, some 20 degrees before the target, and it will settle on 210. Waiting until the compass shows 210 would carry the aircraft past the heading.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Wear in the bearings and the gimbals as well as air turbulence will have the effect of:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Causing a real wander of the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Causing an apparent wander of the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increasing the rigidity of the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Causing the gyro to topple instantly
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Causing a real wander of the gyro
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Real wander is any genuine movement of the gyro's spin axis in space. Friction and wear in the rotor bearings and gimbals, imbalance of the rotor and disturbances such as turbulence all apply small unwanted forces, and the gyro precesses in response, so its axis drifts. Apparent wander, by contrast, comes from the earth's rotation: the gyro stays fixed while the earth turns beneath it. Neither increases rigidity.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the southern hemisphere, an aircraft is to maintain a constant heading of 090 degrees (M) on a magnetic compass. If the aircraft speed is increased from 80 kts to 110 kts the compass would:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Show an apparent turn to the north
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Continue to show the same reading
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Show an apparent turn to the west
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Show an apparent turn to the south
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Show an apparent turn to the south
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: On an easterly heading in the Southern Hemisphere, acceleration gives a false turn towards the south - the SAND rule: South Accelerate, North Decelerate. So as the speed increases from 80 to 110 kt on 090, the compass swings towards the south, to a higher reading such as 110, even though the aircraft is holding its heading, and it settles back once the speed is steady. Hold the heading with the direction indicator meanwhile.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When the axis of the gyro rotor of an air of driven artificial horizon is in the vertical:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: One vane is fully open and the opposite vane fully closed
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: All four vanes are fully closed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The gyro topples against its stops
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: All four vanes are open by an equal amount
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: All four vanes are open by an equal amount
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Air leaves the artificial horizon's gyro housing through four slots, each partly covered by a pendulous vane. When the rotor's axis is vertical the vanes hang so that all four slots are open by an equal amount; the four jets of air balance and no correcting force is produced. If the gyro tilts, the vanes still hang vertically, so one slot opens wider and the opposite one closes, and the unbalanced jet precesses the gyro back to the vertical.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the southern hemisphere, an aircraft is to maintain a constant heading of 270 degrees (M) on a magnetic compass. If the aircraft speed is decreased from 110 kts to 80 kts the compass would:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Show an apparent turn to the north
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Show an apparent turn to the south
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Continue to show the same reading
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Show an apparent turn to the east
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Show an apparent turn to the north
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: On a westerly heading in the Southern Hemisphere, deceleration gives a false turn towards the north - SAND: South Accelerate, North Decelerate. So as the speed falls from 110 to 80 kt on 270, the compass swings towards the north, to a higher reading such as 290, even though the heading is unchanged, and settles once the speed is steady. The effect is greatest on east and west headings and absent on north and south.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Details in respect of maintenance carried out on an aeroplane while away from base shall be transferred to the appropriate logbook(s):
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Within 68 hours after the return of the aeroplane to its base of operation
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Within 58 hours after the return of the aeroplane to its base of operation
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Within 38 hours after the return of the aeroplane to its base of operation
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Within 48 hours after the return of the aeroplane to its base of operation
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Within 48 hours after the return of the aeroplane to its base of operation
