aircraft-technical-and-general.e: When maintenance is carried out away from the aircraft's base, the details are recorded on the spot and must be transferred to the appropriate logbook(s) within 48 hours after the aircraft returns to its base of operation. This keeps the permanent maintenance history complete, so the next engineer or pilot can see exactly what has been done. At base, the 48 hours run from completion of the work.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: The indications on a turn indicator during a turn to the right whilst taxying is:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Ball should move to the left and the needle should show a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Ball should move to the right and the needle should show a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Ball should move to the left and the needle should show a left turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Ball should move to the right and the needle should show a left turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Ball should move to the left and the needle should show a right turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a right turn while taxiing, the turn indicator's needle should show a turn to the right, and the ball should move to the outside of the turn - to the left - because of the centrifugal effect, just as a passenger is pushed outwards in a turning car. The needle shows the direction of the turn, and the ball shows the sideways force, not the direction.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During flight the gyro in a Direction Indicator aligns itself with:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Magnetic north
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A fixed point in space
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The aircraft's longitudinal axis
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: True north
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A fixed point in space
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A direction indicator's gyro has rigidity in space, so once set it keeps its axis pointing towards a fixed point in space while the aircraft turns around it. It has no magnetic sensing, so it does not align itself with magnetic or true north, and it does not follow the aircraft's longitudinal axis. Because the earth rotates beneath this fixed reference (apparent wander) and friction causes real wander, it must be reset to the compass every 10 to 15 minutes.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An aircraft is to maintain a constant heading of 360deg in the southern hemisphere, using a magnetic compass. If the airspeed is increased from 90kts to 110kts, the compass would:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Show an apparent turn to the east
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Continue to show the same reading
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Show an apparent turn to the west
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Show an apparent turn to the south
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Continue to show the same reading
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Acceleration errors are greatest on east and west headings and do not occur on north or south headings, where the accelerating force acts along the line of the magnet assembly's pivot and centre of gravity and cannot swing it sideways. So increasing speed from 90 to 110 kt on 360 degrees leaves the compass reading unchanged. On 090 or 270 in the Southern Hemisphere, the same acceleration would give an apparent turn towards the south.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which abbreviation denotes the maximum speed for normal operation?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: VNO
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: VNE
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: VFE
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: VA
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: VNO
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: VNO is the maximum structural cruising speed: the top of the green arc and the maximum speed for normal operations. Above it, in the yellow caution arc, the aircraft may be flown only in smooth air. VNE is the never-exceed speed (red line), VFE the maximum flap-extended speed, and VA the manoeuvring speed, above which full, abrupt control deflections could overstress the aircraft.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which type of field winding is commonly used in a DC starter motor?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Shunt winding only
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Series winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Separately excited winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Permanent-magnet alternator winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Series winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A starter motor has to turn a cold, stiff engine from rest, so it needs very high torque at low speed. In a series-wound DC motor the field winding carries the full armature current, so the torque is greatest at the start, when the current is highest - ideal for starting. Shunt-wound motors give a more constant speed but less starting torque, and an alternator winding is for generating, not driving.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which abbreviation denotes stall speed in the landing configuration?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: VSO
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: VS1
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: VNO
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: VFE
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: VSO
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: VSO is the stalling speed (or minimum steady flight speed) in the landing configuration - full flap and, if retractable, gear down - and it is shown by the lower end of the white arc. VS1 is the stalling speed in a specified configuration, normally clean, at the bottom of the green arc. VNO is the maximum structural cruising speed and VFE the maximum flap-extended speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What is the function of a constant-speed drive in an AC generating system?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: To vary engine RPM in response to electrical load
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: To vary generator frequency with electrical load
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: To drive the generator at approximately constant speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: To keep a fixed mechanical ratio without compensating for engine-speed changes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: To drive the generator at approximately constant speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An AC generator's frequency depends on its speed, and aircraft AC equipment needs a constant frequency (usually 400 Hz). Engine speed varies with the phase of flight, so a constant-speed drive (CSD) between the engine and the generator varies its drive ratio automatically so the generator always turns at almost the same speed. It does not change the engine RPM, and a fixed ratio would let the frequency drift with engine speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Under which atmospheric conditions can a normally aspirated piston engine produce the greatest power?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Warm, humid air at low pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Cold, humid air at high pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Cold, dry air at high pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Warm, dry air at high pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Cold, dry air at high pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Engine power depends on the mass of air, and so of oxygen, drawn into the cylinders on each stroke. Cold air is denser than warm air, high pressure means denser air, and dry air is denser than humid air because water vapour is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it displaces. So cold, dry, high-pressure air is the densest and gives the most power - worth remembering on hot, humid days at high-elevation airfields such as those on the Highveld.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which two effects are primarily responsible for magnetic-compass turning error?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Magnetic dip and acceleration forces during the turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Deviation and magnetic variation
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Instrument friction and pressure altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Magnetic variation and compass deviation
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Magnetic dip and acceleration forces during the turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Turning errors come from magnetic dip combined with the forces in a turn. Because the magnets are balanced against dip, their centre of gravity is offset from the pivot; when the aircraft banks and turns, the turning force on that offset mass, together with the tilted field, swings the assembly so the compass leads or lags, most of all on turns through north and south. Variation and deviation are fixed errors that do not change in a turn.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, an aeroplane decelerates on a magnetic heading of 270°. What temporary compass indication is expected?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Approximately 240°
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Approximately 090°
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Approximately 270° with no change
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Approximately 300°
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Approximately 240°
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the Northern Hemisphere the acceleration rule is ANDS: Accelerate North, Decelerate South. Decelerating on a westerly heading therefore gives an apparent turn towards the south, which from 270 means a lower reading - about 240 - even though the aircraft is holding 270; it returns once the speed is steady. In the Southern Hemisphere, as in South Africa, the rule reverses and deceleration gives an apparent turn towards the north.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What is a likely result of leaning the mixture excessively beyond the best-economy setting?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The engine runs rough, loses power and temperatures generally fall
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Engine RPM and power continue to increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Manifold pressure rises above its mechanical limit
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The mixture becomes progressively richer
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The engine runs rough, loses power and temperatures generally fall
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Beyond best economy there is too little fuel for the air: the mixture burns slowly and unevenly, so the engine runs rough and loses power, and if leaning continues it will eventually stop. Because less fuel is being burnt, the exhaust gas and cylinder head temperatures generally fall on this lean side of peak EGT. Excessive leaning never increases RPM or makes the mixture richer, and it does not raise the manifold pressure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which processes enclose the useful-work area on the ideal Otto-cycle pressure-volume diagram?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Two adiabatic, one constant-volume and one constant-pressure process
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Two adiabatic and one isothermal process
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Two adiabatic and two constant-pressure processes
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Two adiabatic and two constant-volume processes
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Two adiabatic and two constant-volume processes
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The ideal Otto cycle, on which the petrol engine is based, has four processes: adiabatic compression (the compression stroke), heat added at constant volume (combustion, assumed instantaneous at TDC), adiabatic expansion (the power stroke) and heat rejected at constant volume (the exhaust valve opening at BDC). The area enclosed by these two adiabatic and two constant-volume lines on the pressure-volume diagram is the useful work done per cycle.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a right turn, the slip-indicator ball is displaced to the right. Which correction can return it to the centre?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase bank and reduce the rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Reduce bank or increase the rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Reduce airspeed and increase bank
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Increase both bank and rate of turn by the same amount
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Reduce bank or increase the rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In a right turn a ball displaced to the right - the inside of the turn - means the aircraft is slipping: there is too much bank for the rate of turn, so the lift's sideways component pulls it towards the inside. To centre the ball, either reduce the bank or increase the rate of turn by applying right rudder ('step on the ball'). Increasing the bank or reducing the rate of turn would make the slip worse.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Gyroscopic rigidity is directly proportional to which quantities?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Angular speed only, and inversely proportional to rotor mass
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Rotor mass only, and inversely proportional to angular speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The rotor's moment of inertia and angular speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Applied force and gimbal friction
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The rotor's moment of inertia and angular speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Gyroscopic rigidity depends on the rotor's angular momentum: its moment of inertia (how much mass there is and how far it is from the axis) multiplied by its angular speed, so doubling either doubles the rigidity. That is why gyro rotors have heavy rims and spin at high RPM, and why low suction or a failing electrical supply, which slows the rotor, makes the instruments sluggish. Applied forces and friction cause precession and wander, not rigidity.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What does dynamic pressure depend on?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Static pressure and air temperature only
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Air density and lift coefficient
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Lift coefficient and drag coefficient
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Air density and the square of airflow speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Air density and the square of airflow speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Dynamic pressure is the pressure of the air due to its motion: q = ½ρV², where ρ is the air density and V the airspeed. Doubling the speed therefore quadruples the dynamic pressure, which is why lift, drag and control forces rise so quickly with speed, and it is what the ASI measures. Lift and drag coefficients describe the wing, not the air, and static pressure is a separate quantity.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which unit converts direct current into alternating current?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: An inverter
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: A transformer-rectifier unit
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A rectifier
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A thermistor
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: An inverter
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: An inverter converts DC into AC, and it is used in DC-powered aircraft to supply instruments and avionics that need AC. A rectifier does the opposite, converting AC to DC, and a transformer-rectifier unit changes the AC voltage and then rectifies it to DC. A thermistor is a temperature-sensitive resistor used in temperature probes.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: To which group of instruments does the artificial horizon belong?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Capsule instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Pitot-static instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Engine-monitoring instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Gyroscopic instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Gyroscopic instruments
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The artificial horizon (attitude indicator) is a gyroscopic instrument: it uses the rigidity of a vertical-axis gyro to provide a steady reference for the aircraft's pitch and bank attitude, and in light aircraft it is usually vacuum-driven. The pitot-static instruments - ASI, altimeter and VSI - use capsules that respond to air pressure, and the engine instruments show engine conditions.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which error can affect a conventional air-driven artificial horizon?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Altimeter hysteresis error
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Acceleration and deceleration error
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Pitot-tube blockage error
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Magnetic deviation error
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Acceleration and deceleration error
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The air-driven artificial horizon's pendulous vanes swing under acceleration and deceleration just as they would if the aircraft tilted, so the gyro is precessed away from the true vertical and the instrument shows a small, temporary false pitch and bank, most noticeable on take-off. Hysteresis is an altimeter error, a pitot blockage affects the ASI, and magnetic deviation affects the compass.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When increasing power on an engine with a constant-speed propeller, which sequence helps avoid excessive engine loading?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Increase manifold pressure before increasing RPM
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Increase RPM before increasing manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Reduce RPM before increasing manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Adjust mixture to idle cut-off before moving either control
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Increase RPM before increasing manifold pressure
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Increasing the manifold pressure while the RPM is low puts high cylinder pressures on a slowly turning engine - like accelerating hard in top gear - which can overstress it and encourage detonation. So when increasing power the propeller lever is moved forward to the higher RPM first, and the manifold pressure is increased afterwards; when reducing power the order is reversed. Selecting idle cut-off would simply stop the engine.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What occurs when current passes through a conductor positioned perpendicular to a magnetic field?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: No effect occurs unless the conductor is already moving
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The current necessarily increases
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A force is exerted on the conductor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The magnetic field disappears
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: A force is exerted on the conductor
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A current-carrying conductor has its own magnetic field. When it lies across an external magnetic field the two fields interact and push the conductor sideways: a force is exerted on it, in a direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule. This is the motor principle, used in the starter motor. The conductor does not need to be moving already - moving a conductor through a field to induce a current is the generator principle.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which colour marks the caution range on an airspeed indicator?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Green
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: White
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Yellow
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Red
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Yellow
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The yellow arc on the ASI marks the caution range, between VNO and VNE. The aircraft may be flown in it only in smooth air and with care, because a strong gust at that speed could overstress the structure. Green is the normal operating range, white the flap operating range, and the red radial line is VNE, the never-exceed speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which abbreviation denotes the maximum speed with flaps extended?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: VLE
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: VFE
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: VNO
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: VSO
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: VFE
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: VFE is the maximum speed at which the flaps may be extended or flown extended, shown by the upper end of the white arc; above it the air loads could damage the flaps and their mechanism. VLE is the maximum speed with the landing gear extended, VNO the maximum structural cruising speed and VSO the stalling speed in the landing configuration.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: During a descent at fully open throttle, what may happen if a turbocharger wastegate is stuck closed?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The turbine blades will immediately separate
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Engine power will necessarily fall to idle
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The turbine shaft will necessarily break
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Manifold pressure may exceed the maximum permitted value
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Manifold pressure may exceed the maximum permitted value
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The wastegate controls a turbocharger by letting some exhaust gas bypass the turbine. If it sticks closed, all the exhaust drives the turbine and the compressor keeps delivering maximum boost, so in a descent, where the air is denser, the manifold pressure can rise above its limit (an overboost), risking detonation and engine damage. The pilot must watch the manifold pressure and reduce the throttle as needed; the turbine does not necessarily fail and power does not fall to idle.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: How is the mechanical power output of a rotating piston engine determined?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Force multiplied by distance
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Torque multiplied by angular speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Work multiplied by time
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Pressure multiplied by lever arm
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Torque multiplied by angular speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Power is the rate of doing work. For a rotating shaft the work done in each revolution depends on the torque, so power equals torque multiplied by angular speed (P = T × ω), which is why engine power rises with RPM for the same torque. Force multiplied by distance is work, not power; power is work divided by time, not multiplied by it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What is the primary purpose of a trim tab?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: To increase the maximum control-surface deflection
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: To improve control effectiveness only at low airspeed
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: To reduce or cancel sustained pilot control forces
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: To reduce the aeroplane's manoeuvring speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: To reduce or cancel sustained pilot control forces
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A trim tab is a small adjustable surface on the trailing edge of a control surface. Its aerodynamic force holds the main surface at the deflection needed for the chosen attitude and airspeed, so the pilot no longer has to hold a steady pressure on the controls. It does not increase control-surface travel or change the aeroplane's limiting speeds: fly the attitude first, then trim out the remaining force.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Where is a fuel strainer fitted in relation to a carburettor needle valve?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Downstream of the discharge nozzle
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Between the main metering jet and discharge nozzle
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Between the needle valve and main metering jet
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Upstream of the needle valve
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Upstream of the needle valve
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Fuel entering the carburettor first passes through a fine strainer at the fuel inlet, upstream of the float needle valve. It catches dirt before it can stop the needle valve seating, which would flood the carburettor, or block the small metering jets further downstream. A strainer placed after the needle valve would be too late to protect it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which abbreviation denotes stall speed in a specified normal configuration?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: VSO
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: VS1
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: VNE
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: VX
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: VS1
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: VS1 is the stalling speed (or minimum steady flight speed) in a specified configuration, normally clean with the flaps up, and it is the lower end of the green arc on the ASI. VSO is the stalling speed in the landing configuration, at the bottom of the white arc. VNE is the never-exceed speed and VX the best angle-of-climb speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What does the ball in a slip indicator show?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The aeroplane's angle of bank
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The rate of turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The apparent vertical
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The pitch attitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The apparent vertical
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The ball in a slip indicator is free to roll in a curved, liquid-filled glass tube, so it settles where the resultant of gravity and any sideways (centrifugal) force acts: the apparent vertical. In a coordinated turn that resultant acts straight down through the seat and the ball stays centred; in a slip or skid it moves to one side. It does not show bank angle, rate of turn or pitch.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Why does an unadjusted fuel-air mixture become too rich as altitude increases?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Air density decreases while approximately the same fuel quantity is supplied
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Air density increases while less fuel is supplied
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Both air density and fuel flow decrease by exactly the same proportion
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Air density remains constant while fuel flow increases
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Air density decreases while approximately the same fuel quantity is supplied
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A carburettor meters fuel by the volume of air flowing through it, not its mass. As altitude increases the air becomes less dense, so each volume of air contains less oxygen, but the carburettor still delivers about the same amount of fuel. There is then too much fuel for the mass of air and the mixture becomes rich, which is why the pilot leans the mixture in the climb and at cruising altitude.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: An altimeter is set to QFE. What does it indicate in flight?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Pressure altitude above the 1013.25 hPa datum
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Altitude above mean sea level
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Height above the airfield pressure datum
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The airfield elevation above mean sea level
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Height above the airfield pressure datum
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: QFE is the atmospheric pressure at the airfield datum, usually the airfield elevation or runway threshold. With QFE set the altimeter reads zero on the ground there and shows height above the airfield in flight, which is useful in the circuit. QNH gives altitude above mean sea level, so the altimeter reads the airfield elevation on the ground, and 1013.25 hPa gives pressure altitude and flight levels.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If both magnetos are correctly grounded but a hot piston engine continues running after the ignition is switched OFF, what can cause this run-on?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Glowing carbon deposits in a combustion chamber
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: An open magneto condenser
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A fouled spark plug that cannot fire
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: A correctly grounded P-lead
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Glowing carbon deposits in a combustion chamber
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: With the magnetos properly earthed there is no spark when the ignition is switched off, so a hot engine that keeps running must be igniting its charge some other way: glowing carbon deposits or an overheated spark-plug electrode act as hot spots and fire the mixture, a form of pre-ignition. This is one reason engines are shut down with the mixture at idle cut-off, which starves them of fuel. An open condenser or a fouled plug reduces sparks rather than creating them.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What maintains atmospheric pressure in a vented fuel tank as fuel is consumed?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The tank vent system
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The tank drains
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The fuel dump system
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The fuel quantity transmitter
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The tank vent system
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: As fuel is drawn out, air must replace it or a partial vacuum will form and eventually stop the fuel flow. The tank vent system admits outside air to keep the tank at atmospheric pressure, and it also lets the tank breathe as the fuel expands and contracts with temperature. Drains remove water and sediment, a fuel dump system (on larger aircraft) jettisons fuel, and the quantity transmitter measures the contents.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: How does a conventional piston-engine magneto produce the high voltage required for ignition?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: It sends a brief low-voltage pulse directly from the battery to each spark plug
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Opening the primary circuit rapidly changes magnetic flux and induces a high voltage in the secondary winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: A capacitor stores battery current and supplies it directly to the distributor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: It produces a high-amperage, low-voltage current at the spark plug
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Opening the primary circuit rapidly changes magnetic flux and induces a high voltage in the secondary winding
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: As the magnet rotates, current builds up in the magneto's primary winding (a few turns of thick wire). At the moment of ignition the contact-breaker points open, the primary current stops and the magnetic flux collapses very rapidly. That rapid change induces a very high voltage in the secondary winding, which has thousands of turns of fine wire, and the distributor sends it to the plug. No battery is involved, and the spark needs high voltage, not high current.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Most light-aircraft piston engines use a relatively short piston stroke. What is an advantage of this arrangement?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: It eliminates the need for piston cooling
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: It permits a lighter, more compact construction
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: It eliminates the need for lubrication
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: It guarantees lower fuel consumption
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: It permits a lighter, more compact construction
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A short stroke means a shorter crank throw and less piston travel, so the cylinders, crankshaft and crankcase can be smaller and lighter, and the engine can run at the RPM a directly driven propeller needs without excessive piston speeds. It does not remove the need for piston cooling or lubrication, and it cannot guarantee lower fuel consumption.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, an aeroplane turns by the shortest route from 030° to 180°. At approximately which indicated magnetic heading should the turn be stopped?
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: In the Northern Hemisphere the compass leads when turning onto southerly headings and lags onto northerly ones, giving the rule UNOS: Undershoot North, Overshoot South. Turning right from 030 to 180, the compass reaches 180 before the aircraft does, so the pilot continues until it reads about 210 - roughly 30 degrees past - and it settles on 180 after the roll-out. In the Southern Hemisphere, as in South Africa, the rule reverses to ONUS.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When should a pilot adjust the pressure setting on an altimeter?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Before every flight and whenever an updated setting is required en route
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Only before the first flight of each day
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Only after maintenance
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Once per month
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Before every flight and whenever an updated setting is required en route
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The altimeter must be set before every flight and updated whenever a new setting is needed: when the QNH changes, when entering another altimeter-setting region, when passing the transition altitude or level, or when ATC passes a new setting. Pressure changes through the day, and an out-of-date setting can put the aircraft hundreds of feet lower than indicated - 'high to low, look out below'.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which components form the main crank assembly of a piston engine?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Propeller, crankshaft, pistons and connecting rods
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Crankshaft, camshaft, valves, springs and pushrods
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Crankcase, camshaft, valves and pistons
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Crankshaft, connecting rods and pistons
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Crankshaft, connecting rods and pistons
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The crank assembly is the group of parts that turns the pistons' up-and-down movement into rotation: the pistons, the connecting rods that link them to the crankpins, and the crankshaft itself. The camshaft, valves, springs and pushrods make up the separate valve-operating mechanism, the crankcase is the housing, and the propeller is driven by the crankshaft rather than being part of the assembly.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which piston-engine component converts reciprocating piston motion into rotary motion?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The crankshaft
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The camshaft
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The piston pin
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The reduction gear
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The crankshaft
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The pistons move up and down, and a connecting rod joins each piston to an offset crankpin on the crankshaft. As the piston pushes on the crankpin the crankshaft turns, converting reciprocating motion into rotary motion - much like a cyclist's legs turning the pedal cranks. The camshaft opens the valves, the piston (gudgeon) pin links piston and connecting rod, and a reduction gear, where fitted, lowers the propeller speed.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which statements about a tubeless aircraft tyre are correct? 1. The wheel rim must provide an airtight seal. 2. An inner tube is required to retain pressure. 3. Friction between an inner tube and the tyre is eliminated. 4. Damage to the rim sealing surface can cause leakage.
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: 1, 3 and 4 only
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: 1 and 2 only
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: 2 and 4 only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: 2, 3 and 4 only
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: 1, 3 and 4 only
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A tubeless tyre holds its air by sealing its beads directly against an airtight wheel rim, so statement 1 is true and statement 2 (an inner tube) is false. With no tube there is no friction between tube and tyre, and no valve to be torn out by creep (statement 3), but damage to the rim's sealing surface or the bead can let the tyre leak (statement 4). The correct combination is therefore 1, 3 and 4.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which abbreviation denotes the speed at which the pilot begins to raise the nose wheel during takeoff?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: V1
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: VR
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: VX
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: VY
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: VR
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: VR is the rotation speed: the speed at which the pilot raises the nose wheel and rotates the aeroplane to the take-off attitude. V1 is the take-off decision speed used on multi-engine and larger aircraft, VX the best angle-of-climb speed (the most height for distance, for clearing obstacles) and VY the best rate-of-climb speed (the most height for time).

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What is an advantage of mounting the horizontal stabilizer at the top of the vertical stabilizer?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: It deliberately creates a tail-heavy condition
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: It removes the need for tailplane anti-icing
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: It makes the tailplane effective only at high speed
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: It can place the tailplane outside the wing's normal wake and turbulence
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: It can place the tailplane outside the wing's normal wake and turbulence
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Mounting the horizontal stabiliser on top of the fin (a T-tail) usually keeps it above the wing's downwash and wake, and out of the propeller slipstream, in normal flight, so it works in cleaner, more consistent airflow; the tailplane also acts as an end plate that makes the fin more effective. The trade-off is that at very high angles of attack it can be immersed in the wake of the stalled wing, which can lead to a deep stall.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: When does ignition normally occur in each cylinder of a four-stroke engine?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Before TDC on every crankshaft revolution
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: After TDC on every second crankshaft revolution
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Before TDC on every second crankshaft revolution
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: After TDC on every crankshaft revolution
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Before TDC on every second crankshaft revolution
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A four-stroke cycle takes two crankshaft revolutions, and each cylinder fires only once per cycle, near the end of its compression stroke. The spark is timed before TDC so the mixture has time to burn and reach peak pressure just after TDC. So ignition in each cylinder occurs before TDC on every second revolution; firing on every revolution would put a spark into the exhaust stroke as well.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What is the compression ratio of a piston engine?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Bore diameter divided by piston stroke
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Cylinder volume with the piston at BDC divided by the volume with it at TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Mass of inducted air divided by its mass after compression
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Piston area divided by total cylinder volume
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Cylinder volume with the piston at BDC divided by the volume with it at TDC
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Compression ratio compares the total volume of the cylinder with the piston at BDC (swept volume plus clearance volume) with the volume left when the piston is at TDC (the clearance or combustion-chamber volume). A typical light-aircraft engine has a ratio of about 7:1 to 8.5:1; a higher ratio gives more power and efficiency but needs a higher-octane fuel to avoid detonation. Bore divided by stroke is the bore-stroke ratio, a different quantity.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Which design measure helps prevent control-surface flutter?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Using trim tabs to hold the control surface neutral
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Using balance tabs to reduce pilot effort
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Ensuring correct mass distribution within the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Making the wing structure more flexible
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Ensuring correct mass distribution within the control surface
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Flutter is a rapidly building oscillation in which the aerodynamic forces and the inertia of a control surface feed each other. It is prevented by mass balancing - weights ahead of the hinge line so the surface's centre of gravity is on or just ahead of the hinge - and by keeping hinges and cables free of play. Trim and balance tabs reduce pilot effort but do not prevent flutter, and a more flexible structure makes it more likely.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: If an aeroplane begins rolling left without rudder correction, what is the initial effect of adverse aileron yaw?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The nose initially yaws left, in the direction of roll
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The nose initially yaws right, opposite the direction of roll
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The nose pitches down without yawing
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The aeroplane initially yaws neither left nor right
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The nose initially yaws right, opposite the direction of roll
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: To roll left, the right aileron goes down and the left aileron goes up. The down-going aileron increases the right wing's lift and, with it, its induced drag, so the right wing is held back and the nose initially yaws right, away from the turn. This adverse yaw is why rudder is used with aileron, and why designers fit Frise or differential ailerons to reduce it.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: How does a Frise aileron help reduce adverse yaw?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The hinge is behind the leading edge, so the nose of the raised aileron projects below the wing and creates balancing drag
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Both ailerons move downward together to increase lift
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The lowered aileron moves farther than the raised aileron
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The ailerons are connected directly to the rudder and cannot move independently
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The hinge is behind the leading edge, so the nose of the raised aileron projects below the wing and creates balancing drag
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A Frise aileron is hinged behind its leading edge. When it is raised, its nose projects below the wing's lower surface into the airflow and creates drag on the down-going wing. That drag helps balance the extra induced drag of the lowered aileron on the other wing, reducing adverse yaw. Differential ailerons tackle the same problem by making the up-going aileron move further than the down-going one.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: How can the serviceability of a direction indicator be checked while taxiing?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: During a left turn the indicated heading should decrease, and during a right turn it should increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: During a left turn the indicated heading should increase, and during a right turn it should decrease
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The indicated heading should remain constant during every taxiing turn
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The direction indicator cannot be checked until the aeroplane is airborne
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: During a left turn the indicated heading should decrease, and during a right turn it should increase
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A direction indicator's card reads like a compass, with headings increasing clockwise. While taxiing, a left turn should make the indicated heading decrease and a right turn should make it increase, apart from the step between 360 and 001 when passing north. A DI that stays constant or moves the wrong way is unserviceable, and the check can and should be made on the ground.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What is the purpose of the torque links on a nose-wheel shock strut?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: To keep the nose wheel correctly aligned by preventing rotation between the inner and outer strut members
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: To absorb the vertical landing impact instead of the oleo
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: To maintain tyre pressure during retraction
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: To lock the nose wheel in the centred position throughout taxiing
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: To keep the nose wheel correctly aligned by preventing rotation between the inner and outer strut members
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Torque links, also called scissor links, connect the inner and outer members of the shock strut. They fold and unfold as the strut compresses, so vertical movement is unrestricted, but they stop the inner member rotating and keep the nose wheel pointing where the steering puts it. The oleo absorbs the landing impact, and the links do not lock the wheel or affect tyre pressure.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What does the term wet wing mean?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Fuel is carried in removable metal tanks mounted inside the wing
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Fuel is carried in flexible rubber cells installed inside the wing
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The sealed wing structure itself forms an integral, non-removable fuel tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The external wing skin is cooled continuously by circulating fuel
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The sealed wing structure itself forms an integral, non-removable fuel tank
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A wet wing means the fuel is carried directly inside a sealed section of the wing structure: the spars, ribs and skin form the walls of the tank, which cannot be removed. Rigid removable tanks and flexible rubber bladder cells are the alternatives, and fuel is not circulated to cool the wing skin. The integral tank saves weight and space but depends on the sealant, so fuel stains on the wing are a sign of a leak.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: On a turn-and-slip indicator, which component shows whether the aircraft is slipping or skidding?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: The inclinometer or balance ball
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The turn needle
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The gyro rotor
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The heading card
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: The inclinometer or balance ball
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: The turn-and-slip indicator has two parts. The needle, driven by the rate gyro, shows the rate and direction of turn; the inclinometer or balance ball shows the balance of the turn. With the ball centred the turn is coordinated; if it moves to the inside of the turn the aircraft is slipping, and if it moves to the outside it is skidding. The gyro rotor and heading card do not show slip or skid.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Under South African Part 43, when may a pilot carry out the maintenance prescribed in SA-CATS 43?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: When the pilot holds an appropriate type rating, is the aircraft's owner or operator, and the aircraft is used for non-commercial operations
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Whenever the pilot holds at least a private pilot licence, regardless of ownership or operation
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Only when the pilot holds a commercial pilot licence
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Whenever the pilot owns the aircraft, even without an appropriate type rating
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: When the pilot holds an appropriate type rating, is the aircraft's owner or operator, and the aircraft is used for non-commercial operations
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Part 43 allows a pilot to carry out limited maintenance - only the tasks listed in SA-CATS 43, such as simple servicing and minor replacements - and only when three conditions are all met: the pilot holds an appropriate type rating, the pilot is the aircraft's owner or operator, and the aircraft is used for non-commercial operations. The work must still be recorded in the logbook. A licence alone, ownership alone or a commercial licence is not enough.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: What is the main energy conversion performed by a piston aircraft engine?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Chemical energy to heat energy, then mechanical energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Mechanical energy to electrical energy, then chemical energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Heat energy to chemical energy, then electrical energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Pressure energy directly to electrical energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Chemical energy to heat energy, then mechanical energy
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Fuel stores chemical energy. Burning it in the cylinder releases that energy as heat, which raises the pressure of the gases; the expanding gases push the piston down, and the crankshaft turns that movement into mechanical energy that drives the propeller. So the engine converts chemical energy to heat and then to mechanical work. Electrical energy only appears if the engine drives an alternator.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: A simple airspeed indicator is calibrated using which reference condition?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Standard sea-level air density in the International Standard Atmosphere
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The actual air density at the aircraft's present altitude
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The local QNH setting only
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: The destination aerodrome's QFE setting
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Standard sea-level air density in the International Standard Atmosphere
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: A simple ASI measures dynamic pressure (½ρV²) and converts it to a speed assuming the air has the ISA sea-level density of 1.225 kg/m³. At that density IAS equals TAS; higher up, or in warmer air, the density is lower, so the ASI reads less than the true airspeed. That is why TAS must be worked out from CAS using altitude and temperature, while stalling speeds stay much the same in IAS.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: Black, oily deposits in the firing-end cavity of a spark plug most likely indicate:
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Engine oil is entering the combustion chamber and burning
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: The mixture is excessively rich but no oil is being burned
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: The mixture is excessively lean
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Normal combustion and correct mixture strength
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Engine oil is entering the combustion chamber and burning
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Wet, black, oily deposits in the firing end of a spark plug mean lubricating oil is reaching the combustion chamber and burning, typically past worn piston rings or valve guides, and they are most often found on the lower plugs. A rich mixture leaves dry, black, sooty carbon instead, while normal combustion leaves light grey or tan deposits.

aircraft-technical-and-general.q: After starting a cold piston engine, what should the pilot do if oil pressure does not rise within the time specified by the manufacturer?
aircraft-technical-and-general.a: Shut the engine down promptly and investigate the cause
aircraft-technical-and-general.b: Continue warming the engine until the aircraft is ready for take-off
aircraft-technical-and-general.c: Increase RPM sharply to force the pressure into the normal range
aircraft-technical-and-general.d: Begin taxiing and monitor only the oil temperature
aircraft-technical-and-general.ans: Shut the engine down promptly and investigate the cause
aircraft-technical-and-general.e: Oil pressure should appear within the time the manufacturer specifies, typically about 30 seconds and a little longer in very cold weather. If it does not, the engine may be running without lubrication and can be seriously damaged within a minute, so shut it down at once and find the cause (low oil, a failed pump or a faulty gauge). Raising the RPM would only increase the damage, and taxiing on or watching only the temperature risks the engine.

meteorology.q: In which atmospheric layer do most weather phenomena occur?
meteorology.e: If you imagine the Earth as an apple, the troposphere is only as thick as the apple's skin - yet nearly all of the atmosphere's water vapour is concentrated in this thin bottom layer, and air within it moves both vertically and horizontally. That combination of moisture and vertical mixing is exactly what generates cloud, precipitation and the weather systems pilots plan around, which is why virtually all weather occurs here rather than in the calmer layers above.

meteorology.q: What is the average height of the troposphere?
meteorology.e: The ISA fixes the average tropopause height at 36,090 ft, or 11 km, but the real figure varies a lot with latitude: roughly 26,000 ft (8 km) over the poles to about 60,000 ft (18 km) over the equator. The handy mnemonic is "HIGH TEMP - HIGH TROP, LOW TEMP - LOW TROP," since warmer surface temperatures expand the air column and push the tropopause higher.

meteorology.q: Where is the troposphere generally at its greatest height?
meteorology.e: The troposphere is deepest over the equator - up to about 60,000 ft (18 km) - because the strong solar heating there expands the air column and drives vigorous vertical convection that pushes the tropopause higher. Over the cold poles the troposphere shrinks to as little as 26,000 ft (8 km), which is the basis of the mnemonic "HIGH TEMP - HIGH TROP, LOW TEMP - LOW TROP."

meteorology.q: What is the boundary layer between the troposphere and stratosphere called?
meteorology.e: The tropopause is the boundary that separates the troposphere from the stratosphere above it, and it marks where the steady 1.98°C/1000 ft temperature decrease of the troposphere essentially stops. Above the tropopause, air movement also becomes almost entirely horizontal, since the vertical mixing characteristic of the troposphere no longer occurs.

meteorology.q: What is the primary importance of the ozone layer?
meteorology.e: Ozone is only a trace gas, but it plays an outsized role by absorbing a large share of the sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation before it can reach the surface. Without that shielding effect, the UV exposure at ground level would be far more damaging to life than it is.

meteorology.q: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere is oxygen?
meteorology.e: Dry air is a colourless mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and roughly 1% split between argon and trace gases such as carbon dioxide, water vapour and ozone. Oxygen's share stays essentially constant right through the atmosphere, though its partial pressure - and so its availability to breathe - falls as total pressure decreases with altitude.

meteorology.q: Approximately what percentage of the atmosphere is nitrogen?
meteorology.e: Nitrogen is by far the largest ingredient of dry air at about 78%, with oxygen making up roughly 21% and the remaining 1% shared between argon and the minor gases - carbon dioxide, water vapour and ozone - that, despite their small share, drive most of what we call weather.

meteorology.q: What happens to air density as humidity increases?
meteorology.e: At the same temperature and pressure, humid air is less dense than dry air, because the water-vapour molecules taking up space in the mixture are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they displace. So a given volume of humid air simply contains less mass than the same volume of dry air. This is why hot, humid days combine two separate density penalties for an aircraft: high temperature and high moisture content.

meteorology.q: If temperature remains constant increasing pressure will have what effect on density?
meteorology.e: With temperature held constant, squeezing the same air into a smaller space, or forcing more of it into the same space, raises its pressure - and packs more air molecules into every cubic metre. More mass in the same volume is exactly what density means, so density rises in step with pressure whenever temperature is unchanged.

meteorology.q: If pressure remains constant increasing temperature will:
meteorology.e: At constant pressure, heating air makes it expand: the molecules move faster and spread further apart, so the same mass of air now fills a larger volume. Because density is mass divided by volume, that expansion - not any change in the amount of air - is what drives density down as temperature rises.

meteorology.q: Which statement about humid air is correct?
meteorology.e: At the same temperature and pressure, humid air is less dense than dry air, because the water-vapour molecules mixed into it are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they displace. So even though humid air feels "heavier" or more oppressive, a given volume of it actually contains less mass - and, for a pilot, slightly worse performance - than the same volume of dry air.

meteorology.q: Relative humidity generally decreases when:
meteorology.e: A worked example shows air holding a fixed amount of water vapour cooling from 100% relative humidity at 10°C to 62% at 20°C and just 28% at 30°C. The absolute moisture content never changes in that example - only the temperature does - which is exactly why relative humidity falls as temperature rises: warmer air can hold more moisture, so the same vapour represents a shrinking fraction of what the air could now hold.

meteorology.q: What is density altitude?
meteorology.e: Pressure altitude is what the altimeter reads with 1013.25 hPa set. Density altitude takes that a step further by correcting for non-standard temperature: roughly 120 ft is added to pressure altitude for every 1°C the air is hotter than the ISA value for that level (and subtracted if colder), so a hot day can push density altitude thousands of feet above the field's actual elevation. Low pressure raises pressure altitude in the same direction, and high humidity lowers actual density a little further, all combining into the single number used to judge how the aircraft will actually perform.

meteorology.q: When QNE is set on an altimeter what pressure setting is used?
meteorology.e: QNE is the name for the ISA standard pressure setting: 1013.25 hPa, entered as 1013 on the subscale. Every aircraft above the transition altitude uses this same fixed reference so they are all flying relative to the same datum - reported as flight levels rather than altitudes - which is what gives air traffic control reliable vertical separation between aircraft regardless of the actual sea-level pressure below them.

meteorology.q: When QNH is set on an altimeter the instrument indicates:
meteorology.e: QNH is the local mean-sea-level pressure, and setting it makes the altimeter read altitude above mean sea level - which is why, on the ground at the aerodrome, a correctly set altimeter should read approximately the published field elevation. It is the setting used for take-off and landing precisely because it ties the reading to a fixed, known reference: sea level.

meteorology.q: When local QFE is set on an altimeter during flight what will the instrument indicate?
meteorology.e: QFE is the pressure at the aerodrome's own reference level rather than at sea level, so with local QFE set the altimeter reads height above that specific aerodrome instead of altitude above sea level. QFE isn't used in South Africa, though it remains common in the UK - worth knowing since you may hear it referenced even if you never fly with it set.

meteorology.q: When QFE is set on an altimeter while the aircraft is on the ground the instrument should indicate:
meteorology.e: QFE is defined as the pressure at the aerodrome reference level itself, so once set, the altimeter reads height above that level rather than altitude above sea level. Sitting on the ground at that same reference level, the aircraft's height above it is by definition zero - which is exactly what the altimeter should show.

meteorology.q: When QNH is set on an altimeter what does the instrument indicate?
meteorology.e: QNH is mean-sea-level pressure, so setting it makes the altimeter read altitude above mean sea level rather than height above any particular aerodrome. This is the setting used for take-off and landing, and it should read close to the published field elevation while the aircraft sits on the ground there.

meteorology.q: An aircraft lands with QNH correctly set and the next morning the altimeter reads higher than the airfield elevation. What happened overnight?
meteorology.e: With the previous day's QNH left unchanged, the altimeter only reflects the setting you dialled in - it has no way of knowing pressure has changed since. If actual pressure falls overnight, that old, now-too-high setting makes the instrument overread, showing more than the known field elevation (the same 30 ft-per-hPa relationship shown on Figures 4.15/4.16 is at work here).

meteorology.q: An aircraft lands with QNH correctly set and the next morning the altimeter reads lower than the airfield elevation. What happened overnight?
meteorology.e: The altimeter only knows the pressure setting you gave it - if actual pressure rises overnight while the old QNH stays dialled in, that setting is now too low relative to the real air, and the instrument underreads, showing less than the known field elevation. At roughly 30 ft per hPa, even a modest overnight pressure change can produce a noticeable difference on the ground.

meteorology.q: The term lapse rate refers to:
meteorology.e: A lapse rate is simply how fast temperature changes with height. The troposphere's normal state is temperature falling with altitude, at an ISA-standard average of about 1.98°C per 1000 ft, so "lapse" here means the usual downward trend - a rarer inversion is the opposite case where temperature rises with height instead.

meteorology.q: According to ISA what is the standard temperature lapse rate?
meteorology.e: The ISA sets the standard tropospheric temperature decrease at 1.98°C per 1000 ft, commonly rounded to 2°C/1000 ft for quick mental calculations, applying up to the standard tropopause at 36,090 ft. This single reference rate is what every ISA-deviation and density-altitude calculation is measured against.

meteorology.q: According to ISA what is the standard mean sea level temperature?
meteorology.e: The ISA fixes +15°C as the standard mean sea-level temperature, alongside 1013.25 hPa pressure and 1.225 kg/m³ air density. This is the fixed starting point from which the standard 1.98°C/1000 ft lapse rate is applied to predict temperature at any altitude.

meteorology.q: Which ISA assumptions are correct?
meteorology.d: Sea level temperature 15°C and lapse rate 1.98°C per 1000 ft
meteorology.ans: Sea level temperature 15°C and lapse rate 1.98°C per 1000 ft
meteorology.e: The ISA defines a specific set of sea-level reference conditions so aircraft performance figures mean the same thing everywhere: +15°C, 1013.25 hPa, and a tropospheric lapse rate of about 1.98°C per 1000 ft up to the tropopause at 36,090 ft, above which temperature is held constant at -56.5°C.

meteorology.q: According to ISA the density of air at sea level is approximately:
meteorology.e: The International Standard Atmosphere fixes sea-level dry-air density at 1.225 kg/m³, which is 1225 grams per cubic metre. This value goes hand in hand with the ISA's other sea-level reference conditions - 15°C and 1013.25 hPa - and is the baseline every density-altitude and performance calculation is measured against.

meteorology.q: What is the dry adiabatic lapse rate?
meteorology.e: An unsaturated parcel of air rising or sinking without exchanging heat with its surroundings cools or warms at the dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR) of about 3°C per 1000 ft, or 1°C per 100 m. This rate applies purely to expansion and compression - it has nothing to do with condensation, which only slows the cooling once the air becomes saturated.

meteorology.q: What does insolation mean?
meteorology.c: Heating of the Earth surface by the sun
meteorology.ans: Heating of the Earth surface by the sun
meteorology.e: Insolation is the incoming solar radiation Earth receives from the sun. The sun does not heat the air directly in any significant way - it heats the ground first, and the ground then warms the air sitting in contact with it, which is the entire basis of daytime surface heating and the local winds and instability it drives.

meteorology.q: At FL085 the temperature is ISA +7°C. What is the outside air temperature?
meteorology.e: Using the ISA rate of 1.98°C per 1000 ft, the standard temperature at FL085 (8500 ft) works out to about 15 - (8.5 x 1.98) ≈ -2°C. "ISA +7" means the actual air is 7°C warmer than that standard value, so the outside air temperature is approximately -2 + 7 = +5°C.

meteorology.q: The amount of water vapour air can hold depends mainly on:
meteorology.e: At any given temperature there is a limit to how much water vapour air can hold before it saturates, and that limit rises sharply with temperature: a parcel holding a fixed amount of vapour drops from 100% relative humidity at 10°C to just 28% at 30°C, purely because warmer air's capacity for moisture has grown. This is exactly why warm, moist tropical air can carry as much or more water vapour as saturated Arctic air, despite feeling completely different.

meteorology.q: Dew point temperature is defined as:
meteorology.a: The temperature at which pressure changes
meteorology.b: The temperature where air becomes saturated
meteorology.ans: The temperature where air becomes saturated
meteorology.e: Dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, with its moisture content and pressure held constant, for that air to become saturated. This is a genuine physical threshold: cool the air below its dew point and condensation must occur, because the air can no longer hold all the water vapour it contains.

meteorology.q: When temperature and dew point are close together and becoming closer what can be expected?
meteorology.e: A small and narrowing gap between temperature and dew point means the air is close to, and getting closer to, saturation - relative humidity is high and rising. Because only a little further cooling is then needed to reach the dew point and trigger condensation, low cloud or fog becomes increasingly likely as that spread shrinks.

meteorology.q: Adiabatic cooling refers to:
meteorology.a: Heating of air due to friction
meteorology.d: Cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.ans: Cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.e: Adiabatic cooling is a temperature drop caused purely by expansion, with no heat exchanged with the surrounding air. As a parcel rises it moves into lower pressure and expands, and that expansion alone - not any loss of heat to its surroundings - is what cools it at the dry adiabatic rate of about 3°C per 1000 ft.

meteorology.q: What occurs during a temperature inversion?
meteorology.e: A temperature inversion is exactly what its name says: the normal decrease of temperature with height is inverted, so temperature rises with altitude instead. There are two common causes - warm air subsiding and compressing over the sub-tropical highs above places like Johannesburg, and the permanent inversion above the tropopause where the stratosphere warms with height - and in both cases the layer is very stable and resists vertical mixing.

meteorology.q: Surface temperature inversions usually form because of:
meteorology.b: Terrestrial radiation on clear calm nights
meteorology.ans: Terrestrial radiation on clear calm nights
meteorology.e: On a clear, calm night the ground loses heat rapidly to space by terrestrial radiation, and with little or no wind to mix in warmer air from above, the air right at the surface cools faster than the air a little higher up. Johannesburg's Highveld is well known for exactly this kind of night-time winter surface inversion.

meteorology.q: Advection fog most commonly forms when:
meteorology.a: Cold dry air moves over warm water
meteorology.b: Strong winds mix warm and cold air
meteorology.c: Warm moist air moves over a colder surface
meteorology.ans: Warm moist air moves over a colder surface
meteorology.e: Advection fog needs horizontal air movement, not just cooling: warm, moist air is carried by wind across a surface colder than the air itself, and contact with that cold surface chills the air from below until it reaches its dew point. Unlike radiation fog, it can form under cloudy skies or in a moderate wind, and it is common along coasts - a classic example is South Africa's west coast, where Atlantic air crosses the cold Benguela Current.

meteorology.q: Radiation fog most commonly develops under which conditions?
meteorology.d: Clear skies light wind and high humidity
meteorology.ans: Clear skies light wind and high humidity
meteorology.e: Radiation fog needs a clear sky so the ground can radiate its heat away freely, a light wind to gently mix - but not disperse - the cooling air, and enough moisture that only a small temperature drop is needed to reach the dew point. Gauteng's Highveld winter nights are a classic local example of exactly these conditions coming together.

meteorology.q: A sea breeze usually develops:
meteorology.e: Land heats up faster than the sea once the sun is out, so by mid-morning the air over land is warmer and less dense than the air over the water. That warm air rises, and cooler, denser marine air flows in underneath it to replace it - which is why a sea breeze is a daytime phenomenon that dies away once the land stops heating in the late afternoon.

meteorology.q: A land breeze normally develops:
meteorology.e: After sunset, land loses its heat far faster than the sea, which stays close to its daytime temperature. Once the land becomes the cooler surface, the whole convective circulation reverses from the daytime pattern, and air now flows from the cooler land out toward the relatively warmer sea - a land breeze, the night-time mirror image of the sea breeze.

meteorology.q: An anabatic wind is:
meteorology.b: Wind rotating around a high pressure system
meteorology.c: Wind flowing uphill during the day
meteorology.ans: Wind flowing uphill during the day
meteorology.e: An anabatic wind is driven purely by daytime solar heating of a slope: the air in contact with the sun-warmed ground becomes buoyant and rises up the terrain, much like a sea breeze but on a hillside rather than a coastline. It is the daytime counterpart of the katabatic wind, which flows the opposite way down the same slope once the sun goes down.

meteorology.q: A katabatic wind is:
meteorology.a: Wind flowing uphill during the day
meteorology.d: Wind flowing downhill usually at night
meteorology.ans: Wind flowing downhill usually at night
meteorology.e: A katabatic wind flows downslope, typically at night when the ground - and the air resting on it - cools faster than the air at the same altitude over the adjacent valley or plain. That relatively cold, dense air simply flows downhill under gravity, and can reach speeds up to about 50 kt, with effects felt up to 100 miles from the slope in strong cases - the night-time reverse of the daytime anabatic wind.

meteorology.q: Air naturally moves:
meteorology.a: From high pressure to low pressure
meteorology.b: From low pressure to high pressure
meteorology.c: From warm air to cold air
meteorology.ans: From high pressure to low pressure
meteorology.e: Air is set in motion by the pressure-gradient force, which simply accelerates it from higher pressure toward lower pressure - nature's way of trying to even out an imbalance. Once moving, that flow is then bent by the Coriolis force and slowed by surface friction, but the fundamental driver is always the pressure difference itself.

meteorology.q: Flying from high pressure to low pressure without resetting the altimeter causes the altimeter to:
meteorology.e: An unchanged altimeter setting only reflects the pressure at your departure point, and flying from high to low pressure means the real air outside is thinner than the setting assumes at every level - so the instrument overreads, showing you higher than you actually are. The memory aid says it best: "high to low, look out below," since the real danger is being lower than indicated over rising or unknown terrain.

meteorology.q: Flying from low pressure to high pressure without resetting the altimeter causes the altimeter to:
meteorology.e: Flying from low pressure into high pressure without updating the altimeter setting means the real air is now denser than the old setting assumes, so the instrument underreads - the aircraft is actually higher than the indicated altitude. This is the safer direction error of the two (the opposite of "high to low, look out below"), since underreading errs on the side of extra terrain clearance rather than less.

meteorology.q: A trough is best described as:
meteorology.e: A trough is officially defined as "a wedge of low pressure extending out from the centre of a depression" - the low-pressure counterpart to a ridge. Even though it is only an extension rather than a full closed low, a trough still draws in converging air that is forced to rise, bringing the same cloud and precipitation a low pressure centre would.

meteorology.q: Which characteristic is associated with unstable air?
meteorology.e: Unstable air keeps parcels rising and mixing vertically, which stirs haze and smoke away from the surface instead of letting it accumulate in a shallow layer. That constant vertical mixing is what typically gives unstable air its good visibility between the cumuliform cloud, turbulence and showers it also produces.

meteorology.q: What combination is required for thunderstorm formation?
meteorology.b: Unstable moist air with lifting action
meteorology.ans: Unstable moist air with lifting action
meteorology.e: There are three essentials for a thunderstorm: enough moisture to build the cloud, an unstable atmosphere - a deep layer of instability over 10,000 ft - to sustain the updraught, and a trigger action to start the air rising, whether that is airmasses converging, a front, orographic lifting, or simple surface heating. Remove any one of the three and a cumulonimbus simply cannot develop.

meteorology.q: Which cloud type is commonly associated with thunderstorms?
meteorology.e: Cumulonimbus, or "Charlie Bravo" by its phonetic letters, is the thunderstorm cloud - the only cloud type that produces the lightning that gives a thunderstorm its name. Its enormous vertical depth, sometimes tens of thousands of feet, supports the powerful updraughts and downdraughts responsible for hail, icing, heavy precipitation and the severe turbulence that make it something to avoid entirely.

meteorology.q: Which condition is commonly associated with stable air?
meteorology.e: Stable air resists the vertical mixing that would otherwise clear haze, smoke and moisture away from low levels, so they stay trapped near the surface and reduce visibility. The lack of strong vertical currents also favours stratiform cloud spreading out sideways rather than building upward - the classic pairing of "stable air = poor visibility and layered cloud."

meteorology.q: Light drizzle is most commonly associated with which cloud type?
meteorology.e: Drizzle consists of very small droplets, and building large raindrops needs strong, sustained vertical currents to keep droplets aloft long enough to collide and grow - exactly what a shallow stratus or stratocumulus layer cannot provide. With only weak vertical motion available, droplet growth stalls out small, giving the fine, steady drizzle these cloud types are known for rather than the heavier rain of deeper cloud.

meteorology.q: Lenticular clouds usually indicate:
meteorology.e: Lenticular cloud forms at the crest of a standing mountain wave: air rising into the wave cools and condenses on the upwind edge, then descends and evaporates on the downwind edge, so the smooth, lens-shaped cloud appears to sit still even though air is streaming rapidly through it the whole time. Seeing one is a visual warning that mountain-wave conditions, and the turbulence that comes with them, are active.

meteorology.q: Rotor clouds on the lee side of mountains indicate:
meteorology.e: Rotor cloud marks a rolling, turbulent circulation that forms beneath a mountain wave, at roughly the height of the ridge crest on the lee side, produced by the very turbulent mixing of air in that zone. Its ragged, disorganised appearance - quite unlike the smooth lenticular cloud above it - is the visible sign of the severe turbulence trapped in that rotor.

meteorology.q: Nimbostratus cloud is commonly associated with:
meteorology.e: Nimbostratus is the thick, layered cloud built by the broad, gentle ascent typical of a warm front, where warm air glides up over cold air along a shallow slope of about 1:200 to 1:400. That widespread, sustained lifting - rather than the sharp, localised lift of a cold front - is exactly what produces nimbostratus's characteristic steady, prolonged rain.

meteorology.q: Which cloud sequence often indicates an approaching warm front?
meteorology.e: A warm front's shallow slope means the highest cloud arrives first, well ahead of the front itself: cirrus, thinning down from the leading edge of moisture aloft, followed by cirrostratus and then altostratus as the cloud base steadily thickens and lowers with the approaching frontal surface. Nimbostratus and widespread rain follow last, right at the front.

meteorology.q: Cirrus clouds are generally:
meteorology.e: Cirrus is a high, thin, wispy cloud made mainly of ice crystals rather than liquid droplets, since it forms well up in the cold upper troposphere. It is often the very first visible sign of an approaching warm front, appearing well before any of the thicker, lower cloud that follows.

meteorology.q: What is virga?
meteorology.c: Rain evaporating before reaching the ground
meteorology.ans: Rain evaporating before reaching the ground
meteorology.e: Virga is precipitation you can see falling out of a cloud base that evaporates, or sublimates, before it ever reaches the ground - visible rain or snow trails that simply never land. That evaporation cools the air beneath the cloud as it happens, which can strengthen the downdraughts feeding back into that cooled air and create turbulence at the surface even where no rain actually falls.

meteorology.q: A cold front forms when:
meteorology.a: Warm air rises slowly over cold air
meteorology.d: Cold air moves underneath warm air
meteorology.ans: Cold air moves underneath warm air
meteorology.e: A front is named for the air mass that is actively moving: when advancing cold air pushes underneath a slower or static warm air mass, forcing it upward, that boundary is a cold front. The slope where cold air undercuts warm air is steep - typically 1:50 to 1:100 - which is why cold fronts tend to produce abrupt, intense weather rather than the gentle, prolonged conditions of a warm front.

meteorology.q: When a cold front overtakes a warm front what forms?
meteorology.e: Because a cold front moves faster than a warm front, it can eventually catch up to and overtake one. When it does, the warm sector between them is lifted completely off the surface as the two cooler air masses close in beneath it, forming an occluded front - the final, most intense stage of a mid-latitude cyclone's life cycle.

meteorology.q: According to Buys Ballot's Law in the Southern Hemisphere standing with your back to the wind places low pressure on your:
meteorology.e: Buys Ballot's Law places low pressure on your right when you stand with your back to the wind in the Southern Hemisphere - the mirror image of the Northern Hemisphere relationship, where it falls on your left. It is a quick, practical way to estimate where the nearest low sits just from the wind direction you feel.

meteorology.q: The Coriolis force is caused by:
