meteorology.e: The Coriolis force is not a real push - it is the apparent deflection an observer on the rotating Earth sees in anything moving across it, in the same way a ball thrown across a spinning roundabout appears to curve to someone standing on the roundabout. It only changes the direction of air that is already moving; it never starts the motion in the first place, which is the job of the pressure-gradient force.

meteorology.q: In the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects wind:
meteorology.e: The Coriolis effect curves the path of a moving air parcel to the left in the Southern Hemisphere as the pressure-gradient force pushes it toward low pressure. The deflection reverses to the right north of the equator, which is why hemisphere matters so much in every wind-direction question.

meteorology.q: Carburettor icing is usually indicated by:
meteorology.a: Rough engine running and decreasing RPM
meteorology.ans: Rough engine running and decreasing RPM
meteorology.e: Carburettor ice narrows the venturi and disrupts the fuel/air ratio, so the engine loses power progressively rather than suddenly. On a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft this shows up first as rough running with a gradual, unexplained drop in RPM even though the throttle hasn't moved; on a constant-speed propeller aircraft, manifold pressure falls first since the governor holds RPM constant. Carb heat should be applied the moment this is noticed, before the constriction worsens into a full power loss.

meteorology.q: Carburettor icing may occur at outside-air temperatures as high as approximately:
meteorology.e: Carburettor icing is not just a cold-weather hazard. As air accelerates through the venturi its pressure drops, and with it the temperature - typically by 20 to 30°C below the outside air temperature - which is enough to freeze condensing moisture even on a warm day if humidity is high. Serious icing at descent power is possible with ambient temperatures above 30°C and relative humidity as low as 30%, and the light-icing zone extends to almost +40°C when the dewpoint is high, which is where the roughly +38°C figure comes from.

meteorology.q: At its cold oceanic source, polar maritime air is usually:
meteorology.e: At its source over cold, high-latitude ocean, polar maritime (mP) air is cold and picks up moisture from the long sea track, but the cold surface it sits over keeps it stable - cooling from below suppresses vertical currents rather than encouraging them. That stability only breaks down once the air mass moves on and crosses a surface warmer than itself.

meteorology.q: An air mass approaching South Africa from Antarctica is classified as:
meteorology.e: mP air arrives from the south across the Southern Ocean, the route any air mass originating near Antarctica would take to reach the country. Its polar source latitude makes it cold, and its long track over open ocean makes it moist, giving the combined classification polar maritime.

meteorology.q: A continental air mass is generally:
meteorology.a: Dry because it forms over land
meteorology.ans: Dry because it forms over land
meteorology.e: An air mass takes on the properties of whatever surface it sits over for long enough to become uniform, and land simply cannot supply moisture the way an ocean can. A continental air mass - labelled cT over the interior of Southern Africa - is therefore comparatively dry regardless of whether it is warm or cold; "continental" describes its low moisture content, not its temperature.

meteorology.q: A hot dry wind blowing from the South African interior toward the coast is called:
meteorology.e: South Africa's berg wind starts as moist air forced up the Drakensberg, cooling at the DALR and losing much of its moisture as rain on the eastern slopes. Having dried out, it warms at the same DALR through a greater height as it descends the other side, then swings anticlockwise around the interior high to reach the south and south-east coast as a genuinely hot, dry offshore wind - the same phenomenon known elsewhere as a föhn wind or, in the USA, a Chinook.

meteorology.q: Berg wind conditions are commonly associated with:
meteorology.e: A berg wind is driven by a strong high-pressure system over the interior plateau combined with lower pressure along the coast, which pushes air seaward and down off the escarpment. Compression during that descent warms the air at the dry adiabatic rate, so by the time it reaches the coast it arrives as the hot, dry offshore flow that defines berg-wind weather - conditions so extreme they produced South Africa's official record temperature of 51.5°C, recorded during a berg wind on the Eastern Cape coast.

meteorology.q: A warm dry wind descending a mountain slope is commonly called:
meteorology.e: A Föhn wind forms as moist air is forced to rise on the windward side of a mountain, cooling at the DALR until it saturates, then cooling more slowly at the SALR while shedding its moisture as precipitation. Having dried out near the summit, it descends the lee slope warming at the faster DALR the whole way down, arriving as a warm, dry wind - the effect South Africa knows specifically as the berg wind.

meteorology.q: The Cape Doctor refers to:
meteorology.e: The Cape Doctor is Cape Town's strong summer south-easter, driven by a well-developed high pressure system to the west of the Peninsula as the South Atlantic High ridges south and joins the South Indian High. It gets its name because it clears haze, pollutants and insects from the city, and famously produces the "tablecloth" cloud that spills over Table Mountain, with wind speeds ranging from about 10 kt up to 70 kt in its strongest gales.

meteorology.q: The Black South Easter occurs when:
meteorology.a: A weak pressure gradient and short land fetch
meteorology.b: A well-developed high west or south-west of Cape Town
meteorology.c: A stationary interior trough with no coastal flow
meteorology.d: A light sea breeze under clear skies
meteorology.ans: A well-developed high west or south-west of Cape Town
meteorology.e: The Black South Easter shares the Cape Doctor's south-easterly direction but is a very different animal: it forms when a deep low sits over the south-western Cape at the same time as an intense South Atlantic High builds to the south, creating a steep pressure gradient. Unlike the dry, clear-sky Cape Doctor, the low brings heavy rain with it - real examples include the 1981 Laingsburg floods and the 1994 Cape Town Easter floods, both showing just how severe this rain can get.

meteorology.q: During South African summer which condition commonly exists?
meteorology.e: During the South African summer, the South Indian High drives moist easterly to south-easterly trade-wind flow off the Indian Ocean onto the interior, while intense surface heating creates a thermal low that draws that moist air further inland. The combination of abundant moisture and strong daytime heating is exactly what fuels the frequent afternoon thunderstorms the interior experiences through summer.

meteorology.q: What does METAR represent?
meteorology.d: Actual weather report at an aerodrome
meteorology.ans: Actual weather report at an aerodrome
meteorology.e: METAR stands for Meteorological Aviation Routine report - sometimes simply called "an Actual" - a coded bulletin of the weather actually observed at a specific aerodrome at a stated time. It uses the same standard format worldwide (wind, visibility, present weather, cloud, temperature/dew point, QNH), which is exactly what makes it quick to decode once you know the code, and it is never a forecast of what's coming.

meteorology.q: What does TAF represent?
meteorology.e: TAF stands for Terminal Aerodrome Forecast: a detailed, coded prediction of the weather elements - wind, visibility, significant weather and cloud - expected at a specific aerodrome over a defined validity period of up to 30 hours. Where a METAR reports what conditions actually are right now, a TAF tells you what to expect, which is why flight planning leans on the TAF rather than the current METAR.

meteorology.q: Which set of conditions permits CAVOK to be reported?
meteorology.a: Visibility 5 km or more with no overcast below 3,000 ft
meteorology.b: Visibility at least 10 km, no significant weather, and no operationally significant cloud
meteorology.c: Any visibility provided the sky is clear directly overhead
meteorology.d: No cloud below 1,000 ft, even when thunderstorms are present
meteorology.ans: Visibility at least 10 km, no significant weather, and no operationally significant cloud
meteorology.e: CAVOK - pronounced "cav-oh-kay" - is a single code that replaces the visibility, weather and cloud groups whenever conditions are good enough on all three counts at once: visibility of 10 km or more, no cumulonimbus or towering cumulus, no cloud below 5000 ft (or the relevant minimum sector altitude, whichever is higher), and no weather significant to aviation. Missing any one of those conditions means CAVOK cannot be reported, however good the rest of the picture looks.

meteorology.q: The cloud symbol FEW indicates:
meteorology.e: The METAR/TAF cloud-amount code runs SKC (0 oktas), FEW (1-2 oktas), SCT (3-4), BKN (5-7), up to OVC (8, fully overcast). FEW sitting at the bottom of that scale means only 1 to 2 eighths of the sky is covered by that layer - noticeably cloudy, but a long way from constituting a ceiling.

meteorology.q: The cloud symbol SCT indicates:
meteorology.e: On the standard oktas scale used in every METAR and TAF (SKC 0, FEW 1-2, SCT 3-4, BKN 5-7, OVC 8), SCT sits in the middle: 3 to 4 eighths of the sky covered by that cloud layer. It represents noticeably more cloud than FEW, but - like FEW - is still not treated as a ceiling; only BKN or OVC layers count as one.

meteorology.q: The cloud symbol BKN indicates:
meteorology.e: BKN sits near the top of the oktas scale (SKC 0, FEW 1-2, SCT 3-4, BKN 5-7, OVC 8), covering 5 to 7 eighths of the sky. This matters operationally because the lowest BKN or OVC layer reported is what defines the ceiling - SCT and FEW layers, however low, never do.

meteorology.q: The cloud symbol OVC indicates:
meteorology.e: OVC is the top of the oktas scale (SKC 0, FEW 1-2, SCT 3-4, BKN 5-7, OVC 8): the cloud layer covers all 8 eighths of the sky, leaving no gaps. As with BKN, the height that follows OVC in the report gives the base in hundreds of feet above the aerodrome, and this layer defines the ceiling.

meteorology.q: Information normally provided by ATIS includes:
meteorology.c: Surface wind QNH visibility and runway in use
meteorology.ans: Surface wind QNH visibility and runway in use
meteorology.e: ATIS exists to relay the current operational picture without every aircraft needing its own individual transmission from ATC, and its core content includes runway in use, surface wind, visibility, significant weather, cloud and QNH. Broadcasting it continuously frees up the frequency for the traffic and clearance calls that genuinely need a live controller.

meteorology.q: The layer between the troposphere and the stratosphere is called:
meteorology.e: The tropopause is the transition layer that caps the troposphere and separates it from the stratosphere above. It marks the level where the normal decrease of temperature with height largely stops, which is why it's treated as the practical ceiling of "ordinary" weather.

meteorology.q: The weather experienced on the earth occurs in the:
meteorology.e: Nearly all of Earth's water vapour is concentrated low down in the troposphere, and this is also the only atmospheric layer where air mixes vertically as well as horizontally. That combination of available moisture and vertical motion is what builds the cloud and precipitation we experience as weather, which is why weather is essentially confined to the troposphere.

meteorology.q: On landing, an aircraft's altimeter indicates the airfield elevation of 4500 ft with QNH correctly set. During the pre-flight inspection the following morning the altimeter indicates 4200 ft. During the night:
meteorology.e: With the previous day's QNH still set, a change in the altimeter's reading on the ground reflects only a change in actual pressure, not any real change in elevation. Reading 4200 ft instead of the known 4500 ft field elevation means the old setting is now too low for the real air - which happens when pressure has risen overnight, causing the altimeter to underread by exactly the amount of that rise (roughly 30 ft per hPa, Figures 4.15/4.16).

meteorology.q: When QNE is set on the altimeter of an aircraft, the subscale will read:
meteorology.e: QNE is the name for the fixed ISA standard pressure setting, 1013.25 hPa, entered as 1013 on the subscale. Every aircraft flying above the transition altitude sets the same value, which is what turns the altimeter's reading into a common reference - reported as a flight level - shared by all traffic in that airspace regardless of the actual sea-level pressure below.

meteorology.q: Assuming that the pressure of a dry parcel of air remains constant:
meteorology.d: An increase in temperature will cause a decrease in density
meteorology.ans: An increase in temperature will cause a decrease in density
meteorology.e: With pressure held constant, warming a parcel of dry air makes it expand. The same mass of air then occupies a larger volume, and since density is mass per unit volume, that expansion means the density has decreased even though nothing was added or removed from the parcel.

meteorology.q: Relative humidity:
meteorology.a: Decreases with an increase in temperature
meteorology.ans: Decreases with an increase in temperature
meteorology.e: A parcel of air holding a constant amount of water vapour has its relative humidity fall from 100% at 10°C to 62% at 20°C and 28% at 30°C - purely because warming raises the air's capacity to hold moisture without adding any more of it. Relative humidity is the ratio of actual to maximum possible moisture at that temperature, so raising the temperature alone, with nothing else changing, must push that ratio down.

meteorology.q: The volume of nitrogen in the atmosphere is approximately:
meteorology.e: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of dry air by volume, by far the largest single component. Oxygen contributes roughly 21%, leaving only about 1% for argon and the trace gases - carbon dioxide, water vapour and ozone - that, despite being minor constituents, are the ones that actually shape day-to-day weather.

meteorology.q: The term “lapse rate” is used to describe:
meteorology.e: A lapse rate is simply the rate at which temperature falls with height. In the troposphere temperature normally decreases with altitude, and the steeper that decrease, the more likely a rising parcel is to stay warmer than its surroundings and keep climbing - which is why a steep lapse rate is linked to instability.

meteorology.q: When local QFE is set on the subscale of an altimeter of an aircraft in flight, the instrument will read:
meteorology.d: The aircraft’s height above an aerodrome
meteorology.ans: The aircraft’s height above an aerodrome
meteorology.e: QFE is defined as the pressure at the aerodrome's own reference level, so setting it in flight makes the altimeter read height above that specific aerodrome rather than altitude above sea level. This setting isn't used in South Africa, though it remains common in the UK.

meteorology.q: When QFE is set on an altimeter subscale of an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome, the instrument will indicate:
meteorology.e: QFE ties the altimeter to the aerodrome's own reference level rather than to sea level, so an aircraft sitting exactly at that reference level - on the ground - has, by definition, zero height above it. That is exactly what a correctly set QFE altimeter should show.

meteorology.q: In terms of the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), certain assumptions are made. These include:
meteorology.b: MSL temperature is 15°C and lapse rate is 1.98°C/1000 ft up to 36 090 ft
meteorology.ans: MSL temperature is 15°C and lapse rate is 1.98°C/1000 ft up to 36 090 ft
meteorology.e: The ISA fixes a specific set of sea-level reference conditions so aircraft performance can be compared on a common basis: a mean sea-level temperature of 15°C, a pressure of 1013.25 hPa, and a lapse rate of 1.98°C per 1000 ft (often rounded to 2°C/1000 ft) up to the standard tropopause at 36,090 ft, above which temperature is held constant at -56.5°C.

meteorology.q: The significance of the ozone layer in the atmosphere is that it:
meteorology.c: Acts as a shield against ultraviolet rays
meteorology.ans: Acts as a shield against ultraviolet rays
meteorology.e: Although ozone is only a trace gas, it absorbs a large proportion of the sun's ultraviolet radiation high in the atmosphere before it can reach the surface, acting as a shield for life below. This protective role is the ozone layer's main significance, despite it making up only a tiny fraction of the atmosphere's overall composition.

meteorology.q: Assuming that the temperature of a dry parcel of air remains constant:
meteorology.d: An increase in pressure will cause an increase in density
meteorology.ans: An increase in pressure will cause an increase in density
meteorology.e: With temperature held constant, raising the pressure on a parcel of dry air compresses it, forcing the same mass of air into a smaller volume. Packing the same mass into less space is, by definition, an increase in density.

meteorology.q: The volume of oxygen in the atmosphere is approximately:
meteorology.e: Oxygen makes up roughly 21% of dry atmospheric air, and that proportion stays almost constant with altitude. What changes with height is oxygen's partial pressure - as total atmospheric pressure falls, there is less oxygen available in each breath even though the percentage composition of the air hasn't changed, which is the physiological reason altitude affects breathing.

meteorology.q: When the standard pressure setting, 1013 hPa, is set on the subscale of the altimeter of an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome, the altimeter will indicate:
meteorology.e: Setting the ISA standard 1013 hPa makes the altimeter read pressure altitude - height above the standard 1013.25 hPa datum rather than above sea level or the aerodrome. On the ground this value only matches the published field elevation when local pressure happens to equal standard; otherwise it reads higher or lower by the difference, at roughly 30 ft per hPa.

meteorology.q: Air density will:
meteorology.c: Decrease with an increase in humidity
meteorology.ans: Decrease with an increase in humidity
meteorology.e: Air density decreases as humidity increases because water-vapour molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they replace in a given volume of air. At unchanged pressure and temperature, more moisture in the mix therefore means less total mass, which is why humid air gives an aircraft measurably worse take-off and climb performance than dry air on an otherwise identical day.

meteorology.q: When QNH is set on an altimeter subscale of an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome, the instrument will indicate:
meteorology.e: QNH ties the altimeter to mean sea level, so with it correctly set, the instrument reads altitude above sea level - which on the ground at a specific aerodrome should closely match that field's published elevation above sea level. That agreement is exactly what makes QNH the setting used for take-off and landing.

meteorology.q: Density altitude is:
meteorology.a: Pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature
meteorology.c: Indicated altitude corrected only for instrument error
meteorology.d: Height above the aerodrome with QFE set
meteorology.ans: Pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature
meteorology.e: Pressure altitude is what the altimeter reads with 1013.25 hPa set on the subscale. Density altitude takes that a step further by correcting for how far the actual temperature departs from the ISA standard for that level: roughly 120 ft is added to pressure altitude for every 1°C the air is hotter than ISA (and subtracted if colder), so a hot, high-elevation airfield can have a density altitude thousands of feet above its actual elevation. Because engine power, propeller efficiency and wing lift all fall as air density drops, the aircraft then performs as though it were taking off from that higher, thinner-air altitude - which is why density altitude, not field elevation, is the number used for performance planning.

meteorology.q: When QNH has been set on the subscale of an altimeter, the instrument will indicate:
meteorology.b: The aircraft’s altitude above sea level
meteorology.ans: The aircraft’s altitude above sea level
meteorology.e: QNH is mean-sea-level pressure, so once set, the altimeter reads the aircraft's altitude above mean sea level - distinct from QFE, which instead references height above the aerodrome, and from the 1013 hPa standard setting, which gives pressure altitude referenced to the ISA datum rather than to any real surface.

meteorology.q: The average height of the troposphere is:
meteorology.e: The ISA's average tropopause height is 11 km, or 36,090 ft, but this is only an average: the real height ranges from about 8 km (26,000 ft) over the cold poles to about 18 km (60,000 ft) over the warm equator, following the mnemonic "HIGH TEMP - HIGH TROP, LOW TEMP - LOW TROP."

meteorology.q: The average height of the troposphere:
meteorology.e: The troposphere reaches its greatest depth over the equator, roughly 18 km (60,000 ft), because intense solar heating there expands the air column and drives strong vertical convection that carries the tropopause higher. Over the cold poles it shrinks to as little as 8 km (26,000 ft) - the basis of the mnemonic "HIGH TEMP - HIGH TROP."

meteorology.q: In terms of the ISA, the mean sea level temperature is:
meteorology.e: The ISA fixes +15°C as the standard mean sea-level temperature - the reference point every other ISA calculation, including the 1.98°C/1000 ft lapse rate and density-altitude corrections, is built from.

meteorology.q: According to International Standard Atmosphere (ISA), the temperature lapse rate is:
meteorology.e: The ISA troposphere loses temperature at 1.98°C per 1000 ft (often rounded to 2°C/1000 ft) up to the tropopause at 36,090 ft, above which temperature is held constant at -56.5°C. This is the average environmental lapse rate baked into the standard atmosphere, and it is distinctly different from the dry adiabatic lapse rate of about 3°C/1000 ft that a rising air parcel itself follows.

meteorology.q: With regard to humidity and air density:
meteorology.e: Humid air is less dense than dry air at the same pressure and temperature. Water-vapour molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they displace, so as humidity rises the total mass packed into each cubic metre of air falls, even though the volume and pressure haven't changed.

meteorology.q: On landing, an aircraft’s altimeter indicates the airfield elevation of 1650 ft with QNH correctly set. During the pre-flight inspection on the following morning, the altimeter indicates 1800 ft. During the night:
meteorology.e: With the previous day's QNH still dialled in, any change in the ground reading reflects a real change in pressure overnight, not a change in elevation. A rise from 1650 ft to 1800 ft on that unchanged setting means actual pressure fell during the night, at roughly 30 ft per hPa, making the old, now-too-high setting cause the altimeter to overread.

meteorology.q: The dew point temperature is the temperature at which a particular air mass:
meteorology.e: The dew point of an air mass is the specific temperature at which its own moisture content is enough to saturate it, once cooled to that point at essentially constant pressure. Cooling below the dew point pushes the air past saturation, and condensation - as dew, fog, or cloud - is the result.

meteorology.q: Dew point temperature is the temperature at which:
meteorology.b: Air will become saturated at a constant pressure
meteorology.ans: Air will become saturated at a constant pressure
meteorology.e: Dew point is defined as the temperature to which air must be cooled, without changing its water-vapour content, for it to become saturated at that constant pressure. It is a fixed property of the air mass's actual moisture content - not the current temperature - which is why comparing temperature to dew point tells you how close the air already is to saturation.

meteorology.q: A sea breeze will be found at coastal areas:
meteorology.e: Land heats faster than the sea during the day, so by mid-morning the air over the coast has become warm and buoyant enough to rise, drawing in cooler, denser air from the water to replace it. This daytime onshore flow is the sea breeze, and it fades once the sun stops driving the temperature difference in the late afternoon.

meteorology.q: On a clear night, light winds and moist air blowing over the land will most probably create:
meteorology.e: A clear sky maximises overnight ground cooling by radiation, high humidity means only a small further temperature drop is needed to reach the dew point, and a light wind gently mixes that cooling through a shallow layer without dispersing it - together, exactly the recipe for radiation fog. Take away any one of the three (cloud cover, dry air, or too much wind) and the fog either fails to form or stays much thinner.

meteorology.q: The dry adiabatic lapse rate is:
meteorology.e: Unsaturated air rising or descending changes temperature at the dry adiabatic lapse rate (DALR) - approximately 3°C per 1000 ft, or 1°C per 100 m - purely because of expansion and compression as pressure changes with height, with no heat exchanged with the surrounding air.

meteorology.q: A surface temperature inversion is caused by:
meteorology.b: Terrestrial radiation with little or no wind on a clear night
meteorology.ans: Terrestrial radiation with little or no wind on a clear night
meteorology.e: A clear night lets the ground radiate heat away freely, and with little or no wind to stir in warmer air from above, the shallow layer right at the surface cools below the temperature of the air just above it. This is the mechanism behind the classic Highveld winter surface inversion at Johannesburg.

meteorology.q: Adiabatic process is the term used to describe:
meteorology.c: The cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.ans: The cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.e: An adiabatic process is a temperature change that happens purely because of expansion or compression, without any heat being added to or removed from the parcel of air. Rising air expands into the lower pressure aloft and cools; sinking air is compressed by the higher pressure below and warms - both without exchanging heat with the surrounding atmosphere.

meteorology.q: According to ISA, the sea level density of the air is:
meteorology.d: 1225 grammes per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
meteorology.ans: 1225 grammes per cubic metre and decreases with altitude
meteorology.e: The International Standard Atmosphere defines sea-level dry-air density as 1225 grams per cubic metre. Density then decreases with altitude because there is progressively less air above pressing down: pressure falls, and fewer air molecules are left packed into each cubic metre at height, which is the same mechanism that makes high-altitude airfields inherently harder for an aircraft to perform from.

meteorology.q: On flying overhead an aerodrome at which ground fog is present, the runway is clearly visible to the pilot when looking straight down. Assuming no change in conditions, from the final approach the visibility will appear to have:
meteorology.e: Looking straight down through shallow ground fog, the pilot's line of sight only has to cross the fog's actual depth - often just a few hundred feet - so the runway can be clearly visible. On final approach the same fog is viewed along a long, shallow slant path, which packs far more fog into the line of sight and makes the apparent visibility noticeably worse, even though the fog itself hasn't changed at all.

meteorology.q: The ideal conditions for the formation of radiation fog at night are:
meteorology.b: Clear sky, light wind and high relative humidity
meteorology.c: Clear sky with a strong, dry wind
meteorology.d: Warm, dry air moving over warm ground
meteorology.ans: Clear sky, light wind and high relative humidity
meteorology.e: Radiation fog's recipe is three conditions working together: a clear sky to maximise ground cooling by radiation, light wind to gently mix the cooling air without dispersing it, and high relative humidity so only a small temperature drop is needed to reach saturation. All three need to be present - strong wind mixes the cold layer away, cloud cover blocks the radiational cooling, and dry air needs too large a drop to ever reach its dew point.

meteorology.q: An anabatic wind:
meteorology.c: Flows up a slope during the day
meteorology.ans: Flows up a slope during the day
meteorology.e: Solar heating warms a slope and the thin layer of air touching it faster than it warms the free air at the same altitude away from the mountain. That heated air becomes buoyant and rises up the terrain as an anabatic wind, the same mechanism that drives a sea breeze but applied to a hillside instead of a coastline, and it only operates during daylight hours.

meteorology.q: The type of breeze which may be experienced at the coastal areas during the day is:
meteorology.e: Because land heats faster than the sea during the day, the warm air over the coast rises and cooler, denser marine air flows in beneath it - the sea breeze. Worth remembering for circuit flying: the return flow aloft moves in the opposite direction, so a coastal downwind leg in the afternoon can have a very different wind to the one on the ground.

meteorology.q: The temperature at FL085 is ISA+7°C. The outside air temperature is:
meteorology.e: The ISA-standard temperature at FL085 (8500 ft) is about 15 - (8.5 x 1.98) ≈ -2°C. An "ISA +7" condition means the actual air is 7°C above that standard value, giving an outside air temperature of roughly -2 + 7 = +5°C.

meteorology.q: In a temperature inversion:
meteorology.b: The temperature rises with increase in height
meteorology.ans: The temperature rises with increase in height
meteorology.e: An inversion reverses the troposphere's usual pattern: instead of falling with height, temperature rises as altitude increases. Because the warmer air sits above the cooler air, the layer is very stable and strongly resists the vertical mixing that would otherwise disperse haze, smoke or fog trapped beneath it.

meteorology.q: The type of wind which may be experienced at the coastal areas during night is:
meteorology.e: After sunset, land cools much faster than the sea, which holds onto its daytime warmth. Once the land is the cooler of the two, the whole daytime convective circulation reverses, and air flows offshore from the now-cooler land toward the relatively warmer water - the land breeze, felt overnight at coastal airfields.

meteorology.q: Advection fog is most likely to be found:
meteorology.c: Over deserts in strong dry winds
meteorology.e: Advection fog needs a temperature contrast between the air and the surface it is crossing, and coasts reliably provide exactly that: moist marine air is carried by wind over water or land colder than itself and cools from below to its dew point. A classic example is South Africa's west coast, where Atlantic air crossing the cold Benguela Current regularly produces advection fog.

meteorology.q: A land breeze will be found at coastal areas:
meteorology.e: Land loses heat to the night sky far faster than the sea does, so overnight the land becomes the colder surface while the sea stays relatively warm. That reversal drives air offshore, from the cooler land toward the warmer water, which is why a land breeze is specifically a night-time coastal wind.

meteorology.q: The amount of water vapour that can be held in the air is dependent upon:
meteorology.e: How much water vapour air can hold before saturating depends mainly on its temperature - warmer air has a much greater capacity. Relative humidity for a fixed vapour content falls from 100% at 10°C to just 28% at 30°C purely because of this temperature-driven change in holding capacity, with nothing added or removed from the air.

meteorology.q: An aircraft is flying at FL095, OAT +5°C. The temperature deviation from ISA is:
meteorology.e: At FL095 (9500 ft), the ISA-standard temperature is about 15 - (9.5 x 1.98) ≈ -4°C. An observed OAT of +5°C is roughly 9°C above that standard value, so the deviation from ISA is +9°C.

meteorology.q: The term “insolation” or “solar radiation” is used to define the:
meteorology.d: Heating of the earth's surface by the sun
meteorology.ans: Heating of the earth's surface by the sun
meteorology.e: Insolation (also called solar radiation) is the sun's incoming radiation reaching Earth. It heats the ground directly, and the ground in turn warms the air resting on it - the sun does not meaningfully heat the atmosphere on its own, which is why surface type and cover matter so much to daytime heating.

meteorology.q: Cooling of the earth’s surface during the night:
meteorology.a: Is greatest during clear skies over rocky or desert areas
meteorology.b: Is greatest during overcast skies over the ocean
meteorology.c: Is prevented by calm wind and clear sky
meteorology.ans: Is greatest during clear skies over rocky or desert areas
meteorology.e: Clear skies let the surface radiate heat away to space without any cloud to trap it, and dry rocky or desert ground has little moisture to moderate the temperature swing, so it cools fastest and furthest after sunset. This combination - clear sky plus a dry, low-heat-capacity surface - produces the strongest night-time surface cooling and is exactly the setup that builds a surface temperature inversion.

meteorology.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes mist from fog?
meteorology.a: Mist normally has visibility of 1 000 m or more
meteorology.b: Mist is reported only when visibility is below 1 000 m
meteorology.c: Fog normally has visibility greater than 5 km
meteorology.d: Fog can occur only above 1 500 ft AGL
meteorology.ans: Mist normally has visibility of 1 000 m or more
meteorology.e: Fog and mist are physically the same thing - dense suspensions of tiny droplets held in the air close to the ground - and the only difference the aviation definition draws is how far you can see through them. Once visibility climbs to 1,000 m or more, the obscuration is reported as mist rather than fog, even though nothing about the droplets themselves has changed.

meteorology.q: Fog is reported when suspended water droplets or ice crystals reduce visibility to:
meteorology.e: Fog and mist are the same phenomenon - suspended water droplets or ice crystals near the ground - distinguished purely by how much they reduce visibility. Below 1,000 m the report is fog; at 1,000 m or more, the same obscuration is called mist instead.

meteorology.q: The ideal conditions for the formation of advection fog are:
meteorology.a: Cold, dry air moving over warm water
meteorology.b: Dry air rising rapidly in a thunderstorm
meteorology.c: Clear, dry air over hot land
meteorology.d: Warm, moist air blowing over a cold surface
meteorology.ans: Warm, moist air blowing over a cold surface
meteorology.e: Advection fog specifically requires warm, moist air being carried horizontally over a surface colder than itself, so the air is chilled from below by contact rather than by losing its own heat to a clear night sky. That horizontal transport is the defining difference from radiation fog, which needs no wind at all - just the ground itself cooling under a clear sky.

meteorology.q: When the difference between the temperature and the dewpoint is small and reducing:
meteorology.a: Low cloud or fog may be expected
meteorology.ans: Low cloud or fog may be expected
meteorology.e: A small and shrinking spread between temperature and dew point means relative humidity is high and climbing toward saturation. Since the dew point marks the exact temperature at which the air's own moisture content saturates it, only a little more cooling is then required to reach that point and trigger condensation as low cloud or fog.

meteorology.q: According to Buys Ballots Law, an observer?
meteorology.b: standing with their back to the wind in the Southern Hemisphere will have low pressure on their right
meteorology.ans: standing with their back to the wind in the Southern Hemisphere will have low pressure on their right
meteorology.e: Picture exactly this scenario: with the geostrophic wind blowing westward across a north-south pressure gradient, an observer facing downwind, with the wind on their back, finds north - and the lower pressure - on their right. That is the Southern Hemisphere form of the law; north of the equator the relationship flips, with low pressure on the observer's left instead.

meteorology.q: A "trough" is?
meteorology.e: A trough is simply an elongated wedge or finger of relatively low pressure extending out from a larger low, visible on a chart as a kink in the isobars. Because it is still an area of lower pressure, a trough draws in converging air that is forced upward, so it commonly brings the same rising-air weather - cloud, showers and wind shifts - as a full low, just over a narrower band.

meteorology.q: Nimbostratus is most commonly associated with which frontal situation?
meteorology.a: An active cold front with isolated showers
meteorology.b: A warm front with widespread ascent
meteorology.ans: A warm front with widespread ascent
meteorology.e: Nimbostratus forms from broad, gentle lifting rather than sharp, forced ascent, and that is exactly the pattern of a warm front, where warm air glides up over cold air at a shallow slope of about 1:200 to 1:400. The widespread ascent builds a thick, featureless layer that produces steady rain over a large area, distinct from the short, heavy showers a cold front's steep lift produces.

meteorology.q: The Coriolis Force is created by?
meteorology.e: The cause is entirely a product of Earth's rotation, exactly like the apparent curve a thrown ball takes to someone standing on a spinning roundabout. Because the rotation's sense reverses between hemispheres, the deflection acts to the left south of the equator and to the right north of it.

meteorology.q: In a high pressure system in the southern hemisphere?
meteorology.a: clockwise with an inwards and upwards flow
meteorology.b: the wind rotates anticlockwise with an outwards and downwards flow
meteorology.c: anticlockwise with an inwards and upwards flow
meteorology.d: clockwise with an outwards and downwards flow
meteorology.ans: the wind rotates anticlockwise with an outwards and downwards flow
meteorology.e: Around a Southern Hemisphere high, air spirals anticlockwise while also diverging outward at the surface (the mirror image of the clockwise, converging flow around a low). As that outflowing air is replaced from above, it subsides and warms by compression, which is exactly why high-pressure systems are associated with settled, largely cloud-free weather.

meteorology.q: The type of wind which flows upslope during the day is called?
meteorology.e: The wind that flows upslope during the day, driven by solar heating of the terrain, is called anabatic - the daytime counterpart of the downslope katabatic wind that takes over once the sun sets and the slope starts cooling instead of warming.

meteorology.q: Cirrus type cloud refers to?
meteorology.e: Cirrus sits at the top of the cloud classification, made almost entirely of ice crystals because it forms so high in the cold upper troposphere. Its thin, fibrous, wispy look is what distinguishes it at a glance from the thicker, lower cloud families, and it is often the very first visible sign of an approaching frontal system, well before any lower cloud arrives.

meteorology.q: Air has a tendency to flow from?
meteorology.a: out of an area of high pressure and into an area of low pressure
meteorology.ans: out of an area of high pressure and into an area of low pressure
meteorology.e: Air is set in motion purely by the pressure-gradient force, which pushes it out of areas of high pressure toward areas of lower pressure - the atmosphere's way of trying to level out an imbalance. Coriolis force and surface friction then bend and slow that initial flow, but the pressure difference itself is what starts the air moving in the first place.

meteorology.q: In the Southern Hemisphere, the wind around a low pressure blows?
meteorology.a: straight across the isobars away from the centre
meteorology.b: clockwise with the area of lowest pressure in the centre
meteorology.c: clockwise with high pressure in the centre
meteorology.d: anticlockwise with the lowest pressure in the centre
meteorology.ans: clockwise with the area of lowest pressure in the centre
meteorology.e: Because the pressure patterns around a Southern Hemisphere low are roughly circular, the balance between the pressure-gradient force pulling air inward and the Coriolis force deflecting it left settles into a clockwise, inward spiral - surface friction is what lets the wind cross the isobars toward the centre rather than flowing purely parallel to them, as the pure geostrophic wind would.

meteorology.q: Instability in the atmosphere is associated with?
meteorology.c: a steep positive environmental lapse rate
meteorology.d: The cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.ans: a steep positive environmental lapse rate
meteorology.e: A steep positive environmental lapse rate means the surrounding air cools rapidly with height. A parcel lifted into that environment cools more slowly at its own adiabatic rate, so it stays warmer - and therefore less dense - than the air around it at every level, and keeps accelerating upward on its own buoyancy. That is the defining condition for instability.

meteorology.q: During Southern African summer, the ITCZ is generally displaced:
meteorology.a: South of the equator into the Southern Hemisphere
meteorology.d: Into the mid-latitude westerlies south of 40°S
meteorology.ans: South of the equator into the Southern Hemisphere
meteorology.e: The ITCZ follows the sun's seasonal heating, and during Southern Hemisphere summer it migrates south of the equator to around 17°S, bringing its convergence, moisture and characteristic thunderstorms within reach of South Africa's northern regions. In winter it retreats back north, well out of range, which is a major reason the interior has such a pronounced dry winter season.

meteorology.q: Which cloud is characteristically formed by convection?
meteorology.e: Cumulus is convection made visible: a buoyant parcel of air rises, expands and cools until it reaches its condensation level, where the resulting cloud takes on cumulus's signature flat base (marking that exact level) and puffy, cauliflower-like top as the rising currents keep pushing upward. Every cumulonimbus starts life as an ordinary cumulus cloud that simply kept growing.

meteorology.q: With reference to the METAR for Johannesburg (FAJS) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual?
meteorology.c: The wind varied between 070° and 350° through south
meteorology.d: The wind was variable with no mean direction
meteorology.e: The FAJS wind group includes 350V070. The letter V separates the two directional extremes, so the wind varied from 350° clockwise through north to 070° during the observation period.

meteorology.q: The characteristics of a stable air mass include?
meteorology.e: Stable air resists the vertical mixing that would otherwise stir smoke, haze and low-level moisture away from the surface, so these all stay trapped in a shallow layer near the ground. The result is the classic stable-air combination of layered cloud, smooth air, and reduced surface visibility.

meteorology.q: Ahead of a cold front approaching the south-western Cape, surface winds are commonly:
meteorology.e: A typical cold front approaching the south-western Cape is preceded by a warm sector with north-westerly surface flow, as air circulates around the approaching low-pressure system. Frontal passage then brings the classic cold-front signature: an abrupt wind shift, falling temperature, and a return to rising pressure behind the front.

meteorology.q: The term CAVOK is used in weather forecasts to indicate?
meteorology.a: Visibility at least 10 km, no significant weather, and no operationally significant cloud
meteorology.d: Thunderstorms in the vicinity with unrestricted visibility
meteorology.ans: Visibility at least 10 km, no significant weather, and no operationally significant cloud
meteorology.e: CAVOK - "cav-oh-kay" - is a single code that stands in for the visibility, weather and cloud groups whenever all three are good enough at once: visibility 10 km or more, no cumulonimbus or towering cumulus, no cloud below 5000 ft (or the relevant minimum sector altitude if higher), and nothing significant to aviation happening. It is an all-or-nothing report - if even one of those conditions isn't met, CAVOK cannot be used and the individual groups must be reported instead.

meteorology.q: The type of clouds which typically characterise a cold front are?
meteorology.e: At a cold front, the dense cold air undercuts the warmer air ahead of it and forces that warm air abruptly upward along a steep slope of about 1:50 to 1:100. That vigorous, forced lift is exactly what builds vertically developed cumulus and cumulonimbus along the front, producing its characteristic showers, thunderstorms and turbulence - quite different from the flat, layered nimbostratus a warm front's gentle overriding slope produces instead.

meteorology.q: The factor most likely to cause a decrease in the stability of an air mass is?
meteorology.c: warming of the air mass from below
meteorology.ans: warming of the air mass from below
meteorology.e: Heating an air mass from below - typically by daytime solar heating of the ground beneath it - makes the lowest layer more buoyant and steepens the lapse rate close to the surface. A parcel lifted even slightly then finds itself warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising on its own, which is precisely the loss of stability that produces convective cloud and showers.

meteorology.q: Which description best fits polar maritime air at its source?
meteorology.e: Polar maritime air is cold because of its high-latitude source and moist because of its long track over open ocean, and at that cold source it is usually stable - the cold surface below chills the lowest air and suppresses convection. Moving the same air mass over a warmer surface later in its journey removes that stabilising effect and can make it unstable.

meteorology.q: The symbol FEW is used to indicate?
meteorology.e: FEW sits at the bottom of the standard oktas scale (SKC 0, FEW 1-2, SCT 3-4, BKN 5-7, OVC 8), meaning only 1 to 2 eighths of the sky carries that cloud layer. It is the lightest cloud amount that still gets reported at all, distinct from SKC, which means no cloud whatsoever.

meteorology.q: A front caused by cold air cutting under warm air is referred to as?
meteorology.e: At a cold front, the dense advancing cold air cuts underneath the warmer air ahead of it and shoves it upward at a steep slope of roughly 1:50 to 1:100. That name - cold air cutting under warm air - is the defining mechanism of a cold front, and it is the more common of the two frontal types affecting Southern Africa.

meteorology.q: With reference to the TAF for Durban (FADN) on page 8 of the Meteorology Manual, an aircraft landing between 1800 and 2000 local time would expect the surface wind to be?
meteorology.e: South African local time is UTC+2. An arrival from 18:00 to 20:00 local corresponds to the FADN BECMG 1618 UTC period, whose wind group 14012KT means wind from 140° true at 12 kt.

meteorology.q: The symbol SCT is used to indicate?
meteorology.e: On the standard oktas scale used in every METAR and TAF (SKC 0, FEW 1-2, SCT 3-4, BKN 5-7, OVC 8), SCT sits in the middle: 3 to 4 eighths of the sky covered by that cloud layer. It represents noticeably more cloud than FEW, but - like FEW - is still not treated as a ceiling; only BKN or OVC layers count as one.

meteorology.q: In winter, an aeroplane which has been parked outside during a night with clear skies may expect to be covered with?
meteorology.c: Rime ice from flight in cloud
meteorology.e: On a clear winter night, an aircraft parked outside loses heat to the sky by radiation and its surfaces can cool below 0°C even while the surrounding air stays a little warmer. Water vapour then deposits directly onto those cold surfaces as ice crystals rather than first forming liquid dew - this direct vapour-to-ice deposit is hoar frost, and it has to be fully removed before flight since even a thin, sandpaper-like layer can cut lift significantly.

meteorology.q: Which cloud sequence most clearly indicates an approaching warm front?
meteorology.e: A warm front announces itself well before it arrives: the highest cloud, cirrus, appears first (often mistaken for the anvil of a distant storm), followed by cirrostratus and then altostratus as the cloud base steadily lowers and thickens with the approaching frontal slope. Nimbostratus and widespread rain follow last, right at the front itself.

meteorology.q: The characteristics of a moist, unstable air mass include?
meteorology.b: Stratiform cloud, smooth air and poor visibility
meteorology.e: In moist, unstable air, a lifted parcel stays warmer than its surroundings and keeps rising under its own buoyancy, building cumulus that can grow into cumulonimbus. The strong vertical currents inside these clouds produce turbulence and short, heavy showers, rather than the smooth air and steady drizzle typical of a stable air mass.

meteorology.q: Which cloud form is most typical of a stable air mass?
meteorology.e: Stable air actively resists vertical motion, so cloud that does form spreads out sideways instead of building upward - producing the flat, layered stratiform types (stratus, stratocumulus, altostratus, nimbostratus). Cumuliform cloud, by contrast, is the signature of an unstable air mass where rising parcels are free to keep climbing.

meteorology.q: Which circulation feature is characteristic of the South African summer?
meteorology.a: Moist easterly to south-easterly flow from the Indian Ocean
meteorology.b: Persistent dry polar outflow across the entire interior
meteorology.c: Continuous winter cold fronts over the plateau
meteorology.d: A permanent berg wind on every coast
meteorology.ans: Moist easterly to south-easterly flow from the Indian Ocean
meteorology.e: The defining feature of South African summer circulation is moist easterly to south-easterly trade-wind flow off the Indian Ocean, drawn inland toward the thermal low that intense surface heating creates over the interior. That steady supply of moisture, combined with strong daytime heating, is what makes deep convection and thunderstorms a daily feature of the summer interior.

meteorology.q: With reference to the METAR for George (FAGG) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual?
meteorology.a: Air will become saturated at a constant pressure
meteorology.e: In a METAR, the temperature/dew-point group reports temperature first and dew point second, separated by a slash - for FAGG's 16/15 group, that puts the temperature at 16°C and the dew point at 15°C. The narrow 1°C spread between them also signals air very close to saturation, consistent with high relative humidity at George.

meteorology.q: Cumulonimbus cloud is particularly associated with:
meteorology.e: Inside a mature cumulonimbus, the same cloud simultaneously contains powerful updraughts (up to about 30 m/s, or roughly 6,000 ft/min, in the growing stage) and equally powerful downdraughts once precipitation starts dragging air down with it. With those opposing currents packed closely together, the shear between them is what makes severe turbulence - strong enough to threaten structural failure - a defining hazard of cumulonimbus cloud.

meteorology.q: The presence of a coastal low, on the east coast of South Africa, may be characterised by?
meteorology.d: overcast conditions with light rain or drizzle
meteorology.ans: overcast conditions with light rain or drizzle
meteorology.e: On South Africa's east coast, a coastal low draws in cool, moist air from offshore once it passes through, replacing the hot, dry berg-wind flow that typically preceded it. That onshore, moisture-laden air commonly produces overcast skies with drizzle or light rain along the coastal belt, in marked contrast to the clear, dry conditions ahead of the low.

meteorology.q: With reference to the TAF for Port Elizabeth (FAPE) on page 8 of the Meteorology Manual, an aircraft that intends landing between 1300 and 1500 local time would expect?
meteorology.a: 3 to 4 oktas of cloud at 1,500 ft
meteorology.b: 5 to 7 oktas of cloud at 800 ft
meteorology.c: 1 to 2 oktas of cloud at 3,500 ft
meteorology.ans: 3 to 4 oktas of cloud at 1,500 ft
meteorology.e: The 13:00–15:00 South African local arrival corresponds to 11:00–13:00 UTC. In that FAPE BECMG 1113 period, SCT015 means 3–4 oktas with a base 1,500 ft above aerodrome level.

meteorology.q: The information which is provided by the ATIS includes?
meteorology.b: Surface wind, QNH, visibility and runway in use
meteorology.c: Upper-wind forecasts for the entire FIR
meteorology.ans: Surface wind, QNH, visibility and runway in use
meteorology.e: ATIS is designed to save controllers from repeating the same information to every aircraft, and its core content is the runway in use, surface wind, visibility, significant weather, cloud and QNH. A pilot listens to it before making first contact so the frequency stays free for calls that actually need a live response.

meteorology.q: In stable conditions, with a strong wind blowing over a mountain range or high ridge of hills?
meteorology.b: A steep positive environmental lapse rate
meteorology.c: mountain wave turbulence is to be expected
meteorology.d: The cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.ans: mountain wave turbulence is to be expected
meteorology.e: Strong wind blowing over a mountain range displaces a stable air layer upward on the windward side. Because stable air always tries to return to its original level, it overshoots downward on the lee side and oscillates, setting up standing mountain waves that can produce severe turbulence, strong downdraughts, and telltale lenticular, cap and rotor cloud.

meteorology.q: The greatest intensity of a thunderstorm occurs during?
meteorology.e: A thunderstorm reaches its mature stage once precipitation falling from the cloud reaches the ground, which typically happens about 30 minutes after the cumulus stage begins. This is when updraughts and downdraughts coexist side by side, and it is by far the most violent phase: heaviest rain, hail, lightning, and the most severe turbulence and outflow all peak during the mature stage before the storm moves into its dissipating phase.

meteorology.q: A TAF is?
meteorology.a: A weather forecast for an aerodrome
meteorology.b: A special observation of actual weather
meteorology.c: A routine observation of actual weather
meteorology.ans: A weather forecast for an aerodrome
meteorology.e: TAF stands for Terminal Aerodrome Forecast - a coded prediction, not an observation, of the wind, visibility, weather and cloud expected at a specific aerodrome over a defined validity period. It sits alongside METAR (what conditions actually are) and SPECI (a METAR issued for a significant change) as the three core coded reports pilots use for flight planning.

meteorology.q: A concave or almond-shaped cloud which appears to be stationary in the vicinity of mountains or hills is called referred to as?
meteorology.e: An almond or lens-shaped cloud that stays put near mountains or hills, while air visibly streams through it, is lenticular cloud - condensation forming on its upwind edge and evaporating on the downwind edge at the crest of a standing wave, which is why the cloud shape itself never moves even though the air inside it is moving rapidly.

meteorology.q: Whilst flying in the vicinity of a mountain range a pilot observes formations of static lenticular cloud. The pilot should expect?
meteorology.e: Static lenticular cloud is the visible signature of a standing mountain wave, and the pilot should expect considerable turbulence as a result - potentially severe rotor turbulence in particular, which tends to sit below the wave crest at about ridge height on the lee side, even though the lenticular cloud itself can look perfectly smooth.

meteorology.q: A METAR is?
meteorology.d: A routine report of actual weather at an aerodrome
meteorology.ans: A routine report of actual weather at an aerodrome
meteorology.e: A METAR is the routine coded report of weather actually observed at an aerodrome at a stated time, following the same standard format worldwide: identification and time, wind, visibility, present weather, cloud, temperature/dew point, and QNH. It differs from a SPECI only in that a SPECI is triggered by a specific significant change in conditions rather than issued on the routine schedule.

meteorology.q: The most hazardous type of thunderstorms to aircraft are?
meteorology.d: A cold front overtakes a warm front
meteorology.e: A thunderstorm embedded within widespread frontal cloud is hidden from view - a pilot flying on instruments through what looks like ordinary layered cloud can fly straight into a cumulonimbus cell with no visual warning at all, unlike an isolated storm that can usually be seen and avoided from a distance. Embedded thunderstorms are a particular hazard of unstable air forced up ahead of an occluded front, carrying the full set of thunderstorm dangers - severe turbulence, hail, lightning and icing - without any of the usual visual cues to steer around them.

meteorology.q: When flying from an area of high pressure to an area of low pressure?
meteorology.b: the altimeter will tend to over read
meteorology.ans: the altimeter will tend to over read
meteorology.e: An unchanged altimeter setting reflects only the pressure at the point you last updated it, and flying toward lower pressure means the real air outside is thinner than the setting assumes at every level - so the altimeter overreads, showing more altitude than the aircraft actually has. This is the situation behind the memory aid "high to low, look out below."

meteorology.q: The weather condition associated with a surface temperature inversion is?
meteorology.c: an increase in temperature with altitude
meteorology.ans: an increase in temperature with altitude
meteorology.e: The defining feature of any temperature inversion is that temperature rises with altitude instead of the normal decrease. A surface inversion of this kind, such as the Highveld's well-known winter night-time inversion, creates a very stable layer that commonly traps fog, haze, smoke or low cloud close to the ground until the sun burns it off the next day.

meteorology.q: Following the passage of a cold front, surface pressure will normally:
meteorology.a: Continue falling steadily for many hours
meteorology.b: Remain fixed at the frontal minimum
meteorology.e: Surface pressure falls steadily as a cold front approaches and bottoms out close to the moment of frontal passage. Once the front has gone through, colder, denser air and the ridge of higher pressure that follows it move in, so pressure begins to climb again behind the front.

meteorology.q: With reference to Station 2 of the Synoptic Station Models- 1 on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The barometric tendency during the past three hours was?
meteorology.e: Station 2's three-hour pressure-tendency trace slopes downward and then becomes horizontal. That shape means pressure was falling earlier in the period and then became steady.

meteorology.q: With reference to the Significant Weather Chart 3 on page 15 of the Meteorology Manual. An aircraft intending to fly from Port Elizabeth (PE) along the coast towards Cape Town (CT) would experience?
meteorology.b: initially drizzle from stratocumulus cloud becoming rain towards Cape Town
meteorology.ans: initially drizzle from stratocumulus cloud becoming rain towards Cape Town
meteorology.e: On the Significant Weather Chart shown, the coastal route from Port Elizabeth toward Cape Town first crosses an area of shallow stratocumulus with drizzle before entering deeper cloud and rain closer to Cape Town - the answer has to be read as a progression along the whole route rather than lifted from a single symbol at either end.

meteorology.q: With reference to Station 5 of the Synoptic Station Models- 1 on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The pressure change during the past three hours was?
meteorology.e: The pressure-change figure is encoded in tenths of a hectopascal. Station 5 shows 30 together with a falling tendency, so pressure fell by 3.0 hPa during the previous three hours.

meteorology.q: With reference to the Winds and Temperatures chart on page 16 of the Meteorology Manual. The wind direction on the Natal North Coast at 5000 ft is?
meteorology.e: On the page-16 upper-winds chart, the Natal North Coast entry at 5000 ft reads 115/5 with a temperature of +21°C. Wind directions on these charts are always given in degrees true, so the wind at that level is 115°T.

meteorology.q: With reference to Station 6 of the Synoptic Station Models- 1, on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The present weather is?
meteorology.e: Station 6 uses the present-weather symbol for moderate intermittent drizzle. Present weather is plotted to the left of the station circle; it must not be confused with the cloud-type and pressure-tendency symbols.

meteorology.q: The flow of air from a high to a low in the southern hemisphere is deflected by the coriolis force?
meteorology.e: Exactly this happens: as the pressure-gradient force starts air moving from high toward low pressure, the Coriolis force curves that path to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. The two forces settle into balance once the air is flowing parallel to the isobars as the geostrophic wind, but the deflection itself is what bends the flow away from a straight line in the first place.

meteorology.q: The term veering refers to?
meteorology.a: Out of an area of high pressure and into an area of low pressure
meteorology.b: Clockwise around a low in the Southern Hemisphere
meteorology.c: a wind that is changing in a clockwise direction
meteorology.d: Anticlockwise with an outwards and downwards flow
meteorology.ans: a wind that is changing in a clockwise direction
meteorology.e: Friction weakens the Coriolis force relative to the pressure-gradient force near the ground, so instead of flowing parallel to the isobars as the pure geostrophic wind would, the wind veers - turns clockwise - toward the low pressure. Veering describes any clockwise change in wind direction, whatever the cause, for example a shift from north through north-east toward east.

meteorology.q: The term backing refers to?
meteorology.a: Anticlockwise with an outwards and downwards flow
meteorology.b: Clockwise around a low in the Southern Hemisphere
meteorology.c: Out of an area of high pressure and into an area of low pressure
meteorology.d: a wind that is changing in an anticlockwise direction
meteorology.ans: a wind that is changing in an anticlockwise direction
meteorology.e: Backing is the mirror image of veering: an anticlockwise change in wind direction, for example from north through north-west toward west. Near the surface it is the opposite of the clockwise veer that surface friction produces, so a backing wind often signals a different mechanism at work, such as an approaching front.

meteorology.q: With reference to Station 4 of the Synoptic Station Models- 1 on page 5 of the Meteorology Manual. The medium cloud indicated is?
meteorology.e: The middle-cloud code below Station 4 identifies thick altostratus or nimbostratus. These are extensive layered clouds associated with broad ascent and possible continuous precipitation.

meteorology.q: Steady precipitation in the form of rain is most commonly expected from:
meteorology.e: Nimbostratus is the deep, layered cloud built from the broad, gentle uplift ahead of a warm front, and that widespread, sustained ascent is exactly what produces steady, relatively continuous rain over a large area. Cumulonimbus can also produce heavy rain, but its narrower, more violent convective cells make that rain intermittent and showery rather than the steady soaking nimbostratus delivers.

meteorology.q: In the southern hemisphere an aircraft which is being subjected to left drift is?
meteorology.c: flying towards an area of low pressure
meteorology.ans: flying towards an area of low pressure
meteorology.e: Left drift means the wind is pushing the aircraft from its right side, and applying Buys Ballot's Law in the Southern Hemisphere - back to the wind puts low pressure on your right - places that low pressure ahead and to the right of the aircraft's track. Since the wind is blowing from high toward that low, the aircraft experiencing left drift is, by the same logic, heading generally toward the area of lower pressure.

meteorology.q: With reference to Station 14 of the Synoptic Station Models- 2 on page 6 of the Meteorology Manual?
meteorology.e: At Station 14 the visibility code 02 represents 0.2 km, or 200 m, and the adjacent present-weather symbol denotes haze. Both plotted elements are needed to decode the condition.

meteorology.q: Virga is?
meteorology.a: Precipitation that evaporates before reaching the surface
meteorology.b: Freezing rain that coats an aircraft
meteorology.d: Ice crystals deposited directly on the ground
meteorology.ans: Precipitation that evaporates before reaching the surface
meteorology.e: Virga is precipitation that you can see falling from the base of a cloud but that evaporates, or sublimates, before it ever reaches the ground - visible rain or snow that simply never lands. As it evaporates it cools the air beneath the cloud, and that cooling can strengthen downdraughts enough to create turbulence or low-level wind shear well away from any rain actually reaching the surface.

meteorology.q: The weather conditions associated with a ridge of high pressure include?
meteorology.e: A ridge is officially defined as "a wedge of high pressure extending out from the centre of an anticyclone" - the high-pressure counterpart to a trough. Because it inherits the parent high's character, a ridge brings the same subsiding, warming, stabilising air that suppresses cloud development around a full anticyclone, just along a narrower, elongated band.

meteorology.q: Precipitation in the form of light drizzle can be expected from?
meteorology.e: Light drizzle is produced by shallow stratus or stratocumulus, where weak vertical currents can only carry very small droplets before they fall out - too weak to build the larger drops that fall as rain from deeper, more vigorously convective cloud. The result is fine, steady precipitation rather than the heavier, showery rain that comes from cumuliform cloud.

meteorology.q: In the southern hemisphere the wind is deflected to the left by the?
meteorology.e: This happens directly: as the pressure-gradient force starts air moving from high toward low pressure, Earth's rotation deflects that path to the left in the Southern Hemisphere - the same apparent curve a ball thrown across a spinning roundabout would show to someone standing on it.

meteorology.q: The type of cloud which can be expected to form as a result of a moist unstable air mass being forced upwards is?
meteorology.c: A shallow layer of stratus only
meteorology.d: No cloud because lifting stops condensation
meteorology.e: Forcing moist, unstable air upward removes any need for a trigger - once started, the air keeps rising on its own buoyancy. That continued ascent is what builds cloud with real vertical extent: cumulus growing into towering cumulus or cumulonimbus, with the accompanying turbulence and showers, rather than a thin layer that stops climbing as soon as the lifting force is removed.

meteorology.q: Where is frontal fog most commonly found?
meteorology.a: Well behind a dry cold front
meteorology.c: Only inside the warm sector aloft
meteorology.d: Beneath the centre of a stationary high only
meteorology.e: Frontal fog most commonly forms ahead of an approaching warm front, where rain falling from the warm overrunning air passes through the colder air mass still sitting at the surface. That rain evaporates into the cold layer, adding moisture until it saturates and condenses as fog - a direct consequence of the warm front's gentle overriding motion.

meteorology.q: With reference to the FAGM METAR on page 9, which decoding is correct?
meteorology.a: Temperature 16°C, dew point 15°C, observed on the 20th at 0730Z
meteorology.c: Temperature 15°C, dew point 16°C, observed on the 7th at 2000Z
meteorology.ans: Temperature 16°C, dew point 15°C, observed on the 20th at 0730Z
meteorology.e: The FAGM report is dated the 20th at 0730Z. Its 16/15 group gives an air temperature of 16°C and a dew point of 15°C; these are not maximum and minimum temperatures. In South Africa, 0730Z is 0930 SAST.

meteorology.q: With reference to the TAF for George (FAGG) on page 8 of the Meteorology Manual, the expected weather includes?
meteorology.d: Light rain, temporarily heavy rain between 1200 and 2000 local
meteorology.ans: Light rain, temporarily heavy rain between 1200 and 2000 local
meteorology.e: The FAGG forecast has prevailing -RA, meaning light rain, and TEMPO 1018 2000 +RA. Because South African local time is UTC+2, 10–18Z becomes 12:00–20:00 local, when heavy rain is temporarily expected.

meteorology.q: With reference to the Winds and Temperatures chart on page 16 of the Meteorology Manual. The wind direction and velocity (W/V) at 4000 ft at S25° E015° is?
meteorology.e: At 25°S 15°E, the chart gives roughly 246/10 at 3000 ft and 196/12 at 5000 ft. Interpolating halfway between those two rows for 4000 ft gives approximately 221° true at 11 kt, written 221/11.

meteorology.q: Coastal lows along the South African coast are commonly initiated by:
meteorology.a: Sea fog without any pressure change
meteorology.b: Strong offshore flow descending from the interior
meteorology.c: Upper westerlies alone with no surface response
meteorology.ans: Strong offshore flow descending from the interior
meteorology.e: A coastal low forms when strong offshore flow descending from the interior plateau - the same air that produces a berg wind - blows out to sea and leaves a relative vacuum at the surface near the coast. Air rises to fill that gap, and the resulting shallow low-pressure system then tracks around the coastline until it eventually fills in near the Mozambique border, where the elevated interior plateau runs out.

meteorology.q: Rime ice may be expected to form on an aircraft?
meteorology.a: When large drops spread before freezing
meteorology.b: When dry snow sticks to a warm surface
meteorology.c: When small supercooled droplets freeze rapidly on impact
meteorology.d: When water vapour deposits as frost
meteorology.ans: When small supercooled droplets freeze rapidly on impact
meteorology.e: Rime ice forms when small supercooled droplets strike the airframe and freeze almost instantly on impact, trapping air between the rapidly frozen particles. That trapped air is exactly why rime ice looks rough and opaque white rather than smooth and clear - the droplets have no time to spread before freezing, unlike the larger droplets that produce clear ice.

meteorology.q: With reference to the Winds and Temperatures chart on page 16 of the Meteorology Manual. The temperature at 5 000 ft at S30° E015° is?
meteorology.e: At 30°S 15°E, the chart's 5000-ft entry gives a temperature of +12°C. The ISA-standard temperature at 5000 ft is approximately +5°C (15 - 5 x 1.98 ≈ +5.1°C), so the observed value is about 7°C warmer than standard, expressed as ISA +7°C.

meteorology.q: In a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft, carburettor icing is commonly indicated by:
meteorology.a: Rough running and a gradual decrease in RPM
meteorology.d: An immediate increase in manifold pressure
meteorology.ans: Rough running and a gradual decrease in RPM
meteorology.e: As carburettor ice constricts the venturi and upsets the fuel/air ratio, a fixed-pitch propeller aircraft shows this first as rough engine running with a gradual, unexplained drop in RPM, since the propeller pitch cannot adjust to compensate the way a constant-speed unit can. Applying carburettor heat as soon as this is noticed, and following the aircraft's procedure, is the standard response before the constriction can worsen into a full power loss.

meteorology.q: With reference to the METAR for Upington (FAUP) on page 9 of the Meteorology Manual?
meteorology.b: No operationally significant cloud below 5,000 ft
meteorology.ans: No operationally significant cloud below 5,000 ft
meteorology.e: The FAUP METAR uses CAVOK. That includes the absence of operationally significant cloud below 5,000 ft or the relevant minimum sector altitude, as well as visibility of at least 10 km and no significant weather.

meteorology.q: Air at the surface which is forced to rise as a result of convergence?
meteorology.a: A steep positive environmental lapse rate
meteorology.d: The cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.e: Surface convergence happens where air masses move toward each other and have nowhere to go but up - the same mechanism that makes the equator a belt of low pressure. As that air is forced to rise it cools adiabatically, and rising, cooling air is inherently the unstable half of the atmosphere's vertical motion.

meteorology.q: Convergence is associated with?
meteorology.b: A steep positive environmental lapse rate
meteorology.c: The cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.d: rising air and a low pressure system with instability
meteorology.ans: rising air and a low pressure system with instability
meteorology.e: Convergence is air being drawn together at the surface with nowhere to go but up - the mechanism behind low-pressure systems. The forced ascent cools the air adiabatically, which favours instability, cloud development and precipitation, which is why converging surface winds are a classic signature of unsettled, low-pressure weather.

meteorology.q: As a polar maritime air mass passes over South Africa during summer it will?
meteorology.a: Absorb heat in the lower layers and become unstable
meteorology.b: Cool from below and become more stable
meteorology.c: Lose all moisture and remain neutral
meteorology.d: Warm uniformly from the top downward
meteorology.ans: Absorb heat in the lower layers and become unstable
meteorology.e: Polar maritime air arrives over South Africa cold from its Southern Ocean source, but a hot South African summer surface heats the lowest layers of the air mass from below. That warming steepens the lapse rate near the ground, makes the lower layers increasingly buoyant, and progressively destabilises the whole air mass the longer it sits over the warm land.

meteorology.q: An air mass approaching South Africa from the Antarctic across the Southern Ocean is classified as:
meteorology.e: Air originating near Antarctica is classified as polar because of its high-latitude source, and maritime because its route to South Africa crosses the open Southern Ocean, picking up moisture along the way. The combination gives the classification polar maritime - cold, moist, and typically stable at its cold source.

meteorology.q: Divergence is associated with?
meteorology.a: A steep positive environmental lapse rate
meteorology.c: Subsiding air and a high-pressure system with stable conditions
meteorology.d: The cooling of air as it rises and expands
meteorology.ans: Subsiding air and a high-pressure system with stable conditions
meteorology.e: Divergence is air spreading apart at the surface, as happens around 30°S where South Africa sits - the mechanism behind high-pressure systems. Air subsides to replace what has spread away, warming by compression as it descends, which increases stability and typically suppresses cloud rather than building it.

meteorology.q: A warm, dry wind blowing down a mountain during the day is a typical characteristic of?
meteorology.e: South Africa knows this phenomenon as the berg wind, but the underlying mechanism is the classic föhn effect: moist air is forced up the windward slope, cools and loses its moisture as precipitation, then descends the lee slope warming at the faster dry adiabatic rate through a greater height than it cooled on the way up - arriving at the base as noticeably warmer, and drier, than it started.

meteorology.q: Which statement best describes a continental air mass?
meteorology.a: It forms over land and remains comparatively dry
meteorology.b: It must always be tropical and humid
meteorology.c: It forms only over polar oceans
meteorology.d: It is defined by widespread stratiform cloud
meteorology.ans: It forms over land and remains comparatively dry
meteorology.e: A continental air mass forms over land, and land cannot supply the volume of moisture that an ocean surface can, so the air mass stays comparatively dry regardless of its temperature. This is exactly the pattern across Southern Africa: continental tropical (cT) air sits dry over the interior while maritime air masses (mT, mP) bring moisture in from the coasts.

meteorology.q: The type of wind which may be experienced at coastal areas during the day is?
meteorology.e: Because land heats faster than the ocean once the sun is up, the air over the coast becomes warm and buoyant and rises, drawing in cooler, denser air from the sea to take its place. This onshore flow - the sea breeze - is a purely daytime phenomenon that reverses into a land breeze once the sun sets and the temperature difference flips.

meteorology.q: The Black South Easter is a wind which occurs in South Africa when?
meteorology.a: a weak pressure gradient over Cape Town
meteorology.b: a coastal low moving east of Durban
meteorology.c: there is a well developed high pressure system to the west of Cape Town with strong pressure gradients and a long sea track
meteorology.d: a cold front over the interior only
meteorology.ans: there is a well developed high pressure system to the west of Cape Town with strong pressure gradients and a long sea track
meteorology.e: The Black South Easter needs two systems at once: a well-developed, intense high pressure system to the west or south-west of Cape Town, combined with a deep low over the south-western Cape, creating a steep pressure gradient over a long sea track. That long fetch loads the resulting south-easter with moisture, distinguishing it from the dry, clear Cape Doctor and producing the extensive low cloud and heavy rain the Black South Easter is known for - as in the Laingsburg 1981 and Cape Town Easter 1994 floods.

meteorology.q: In an occlusion, the air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front and undercuts both air masses. What type of occlusion forms?
