meteorology.e: When the air behind a cold front is colder than the air ahead of the slower warm front, it undercuts both the warm sector and the cooler pre-frontal air, lifting the entire warm sector off the ground - this is a cold occlusion, the type of occlusion actually experienced in Southern Africa. Its opposite, the warm occlusion, needs the coldest air to sit ahead of the system rather than behind it, which essentially never happens here.

meteorology.q: An occluded front occurs when?
meteorology.a: A cold front overtakes a warm front
meteorology.d: A stationary front loses all temperature contrast
meteorology.ans: A cold front overtakes a warm front
meteorology.e: An occlusion forms in the final stage of a mid-latitude cyclone's life cycle, once the faster-moving cold front has caught up to and overtaken the slower warm front ahead of it. As the occluded boundary passes, warm-front weather is felt first, immediately followed by cold-front weather, as the intervening warm sector is squeezed off the surface.

meteorology.q: The south westerly buster which affects the coast of KwaZulu-Natal (South Africa) is caused by?
meteorology.a: a tropical cyclone moving down the Mozambique Channel
meteorology.b: the anti-cyclonic flow of air from a high pressure system ridging in behind a coastal low
meteorology.c: a land breeze strengthened by nocturnal cooling
meteorology.d: a berg wind descending from the interior
meteorology.ans: the anti-cyclonic flow of air from a high pressure system ridging in behind a coastal low
meteorology.e: The KwaZulu-Natal south-westerly buster develops as a low-pressure system passes and a high ridges in behind it. Since surface wind circulates clockwise around a Southern Hemisphere low, the wind to the rear of the departing low - and ahead of the following high's anticyclonic flow - swings onshore, producing the buster's sudden, sharp deterioration: a near-180° wind change, a jump in wind speed, rain, and a drop in temperature, all within minutes.

meteorology.q: Following warm-front passage in a Southern Hemisphere depression, the surface wind will normally:
meteorology.e: In the Southern Hemisphere, wind direction changes anticlockwise (backs) as the warm sector of a depression arrives following warm-front passage, mirroring the reversed sense of rotation south of the equator. The exact directions depend on the storm's track, but the backing itself - the anticlockwise turn - is the consistent signature of a Southern Hemisphere warm-front passage.

meteorology.q: After the passage of a warm front in South Africa, what pressure tendency is normally expected?
meteorology.a: the pressure will continue to fall but at a slower rate and then start to rise
meteorology.b: the pressure will fall rapidly without rising
meteorology.c: the wind will back suddenly to the south
meteorology.ans: the pressure will continue to fall but at a slower rate and then start to rise
meteorology.e: Pressure keeps falling as a warm front approaches and passage brings the low's centre closer, so the fall typically continues after the front goes through, just at a slower rate as the pressure gradient eases within the warm sector. It is only once the following cold front approaches, and then passes, that pressure bottoms out and begins a sustained rise.

meteorology.q: The South African Berg Wind is generally caused by?
meteorology.a: a sea breeze circulation along the coast
meteorology.b: a strong high pressure system over southern Africa
meteorology.c: a low pressure system over the ocean only
meteorology.ans: a strong high pressure system over southern Africa
meteorology.e: A South African berg wind is set up by a strong high-pressure system sitting over the interior plateau, creating a pressure gradient that drives air seaward and down off the escarpment. As that air descends toward the coast it is compressed and warms adiabatically, arriving as the region's characteristic hot, dry wind - conditions extreme enough to have produced the country's official record temperature of 51.5°C on the Eastern Cape coast.

meteorology.q: When QFE is set on the subscale of the altimeter of an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome, the instrument will read?
meteorology.e: QFE ties the altimeter to the aerodrome's own reference level, so an aircraft sitting on the ground at that level has, by definition, zero height above it - which is exactly what a correctly set QFE altimeter reads, even though this setting is UK practice rather than something used in South Africa.

meteorology.q: A supercooled droplet is:
meteorology.a: An ice crystal above freezing temperature
meteorology.b: A water droplet at exactly 0°C only
meteorology.c: A droplet that cannot freeze on impact
meteorology.d: A liquid droplet below freezing temperature
meteorology.ans: A liquid droplet below freezing temperature
meteorology.e: Water droplets inside cloud can remain liquid at temperatures well below 0°C - a state called supercooled - because pure, undisturbed water doesn't automatically freeze just because it crosses the freezing point; it needs a disturbance or a nucleus to trigger ice formation. That disturbance is exactly what an aircraft surface provides, which is why supercooled liquid water is the principal ingredient of most airframe icing: the droplet freezes instantly on impact rather than before it.

meteorology.q: Steam fog is most likely when:
meteorology.a: Cold air moves over warm water
meteorology.b: Warm dry air moves over desert
meteorology.c: Moist air cools over land at night
meteorology.d: Strong wind mixes dry air over mountains
meteorology.ans: Cold air moves over warm water
meteorology.e: Steam fog forms when cold air moves over water noticeably warmer than itself - the opposite temperature pairing to ordinary advection fog. Rapid evaporation from the warm water adds moisture straight into the cold air above it, and that air saturates almost immediately, producing the visible rising wisps that give steam fog its name, often seen over lakes or the sea on a cold morning.

meteorology.q: Which front normally moves fastest?
meteorology.e: Cold fronts consistently outrun warm fronts because the dense cold air mass actively pushes its way forward and under the warm air, while a warm front can only creep ahead as fast as the warm air gently overrides the cold air in front of it. That speed gap is exactly what lets a cold front eventually catch a warm front from behind and occlude it.

meteorology.q: Radiation fog is most likely to form under which conditions?
meteorology.c: Light wind, clear sky and moist air
meteorology.ans: Light wind, clear sky and moist air
meteorology.e: Radiation fog's recipe combines light wind (to gently mix the cooling air without dispersing it), a clear sky (so the ground can radiate heat away freely), and moist air (so only a small temperature drop is needed to reach the dew point). Miss any one of those three and either the fog fails to form, or forms only thinly.

meteorology.q: Large hailstones are typically associated with:
meteorology.e: Hailstones grow inside a cumulonimbus through repeated cycles: strong updraughts carry droplets to altitude where they freeze, further condensation coats them on the way down, and a fresh updraught can carry them back up to repeat the process - sometimes many times - before they finally escape and fall as hail. Only a genuinely severe thunderstorm has updraughts powerful and sustained enough to keep recycling stones through enough of those cycles to grow them large.

meteorology.q: Precipitation in the form of showers occurs mainly from:
meteorology.e: Showers come from convective cloud - cumulus and cumulonimbus - because each cell is a distinct, self-contained pocket of rising air with a beginning, a peak, and an end, so the precipitation it produces starts and stops abruptly and can vary sharply in intensity within minutes. Layered stratiform cloud, by contrast, produces the steady, continuous rain of a warm front rather than showers.

meteorology.q: At a warm front, the warm air generally:
meteorology.e: Warm air is less dense than the cold air ahead of it, so at a warm front it cannot force the cold air out of the way - it can only glide gradually up and over it, at a shallow slope of about 1:200 to 1:400. That slow, widespread ascent builds the extensive layered stratiform cloud deck and steady, long-lasting precipitation typical of a warm front.

meteorology.q: A stationary front is best described as a front where:
meteorology.a: The cold air always moves fastest
meteorology.c: There is little or no horizontal motion perpendicular to the front
meteorology.d: The front has no wind change
meteorology.ans: There is little or no horizontal motion perpendicular to the front
meteorology.e: A stationary front sits where two air masses with opposing flow - warm air moving one way, cold air the other - are in balance, so neither one displaces the other and the boundary itself barely moves. Because the front stays over the same area, any cloud and precipitation it produces can persist there for an extended time until the balance is disturbed by a perturbation.

meteorology.q: In order to calculate QFE from QNH, what must be known?
meteorology.e: QNH is pressure reduced to mean sea level, while QFE is pressure at the aerodrome's own reference level - the two differ by exactly the height of that aerodrome above sea level, expressed in pressure terms at roughly 30 ft per hPa. Converting one to the other therefore requires knowing the airfield's elevation, the vertical distance the pressure correction has to account for.

meteorology.q: Freezing fog consists mainly of:
meteorology.e: Freezing fog is made up of supercooled water droplets - liquid, despite sitting at a temperature below 0°C, because pure water doesn't automatically freeze the instant it crosses the freezing point without something to trigger ice formation. An aircraft surface provides exactly that trigger, so the droplets freeze on contact rather than before, creating an icing hazard identical in mechanism to airborne supercooled cloud droplets.

meteorology.q: What is the dry adiabatic lapse rate per 100 metres?
meteorology.e: The dry adiabatic lapse rate of roughly 3°C per 1000 ft converts to 1°C per 100 m - the metric form of the same cooling rate an unsaturated parcel follows purely from expansion as it rises without exchanging heat with its surroundings.

meteorology.q: What is the technical term for an increase in temperature with altitude?
meteorology.e: The technical term for temperature rising with altitude, the reverse of the troposphere's normal decreasing pattern, is an inversion. It is a stable layer, and there are two common examples: a shallow surface inversion on a clear, calm night, and the permanent large-scale inversion above the tropopause, where the stratosphere warms with height.

meteorology.q: What is the boundary layer between the troposphere and the stratosphere called?
meteorology.e: The tropopause separates the troposphere from the stratosphere and marks the level where the troposphere's steady 1.98°C/1000 ft temperature decrease effectively stops. It is treated as the practical ceiling of ordinary weather, since above it vertical air motion becomes rare and the strong mixing that builds cloud largely disappears.

meteorology.q: A layer is conditionally unstable when the air is:
meteorology.a: Stable for unsaturated air and unstable for saturated air
meteorology.b: Unstable for dry air and stable for saturated air
meteorology.c: Stable for both dry and saturated air
meteorology.d: Unstable for both dry and saturated air
meteorology.ans: Stable for unsaturated air and unstable for saturated air
meteorology.e: Conditional instability sits between the two adiabatic rates: the environmental lapse rate is less steep than the dry adiabatic lapse rate (about 3°C/1000 ft) but steeper than the saturated adiabatic lapse rate (about 1.5°C/1000 ft). An unsaturated parcel following the faster DALR stays cooler than its surroundings and is stable, but once lifted enough to saturate, it switches to the slower SALR, can end up warmer than the environment, and becomes unstable - hence "conditional" on saturation being reached.

meteorology.q: What condition commonly causes a surface temperature inversion?
meteorology.b: Terrestrial radiation on a clear night with light wind
meteorology.ans: Terrestrial radiation on a clear night with light wind
meteorology.e: Terrestrial radiation on a clear night lets the ground lose heat rapidly, and light wind means there is little mixing to bring warmer air down from above, so the layer right at the surface cools below the air sitting just above it. This combination is the standard cause of a surface inversion, illustrated by the Highveld's well-known winter night-time inversions.

meteorology.q: Which clouds are classified as medium-level clouds in temperate regions?
meteorology.e: The "alto" prefix marks middle-level cloud: altostratus is the layered, featureless form, while altocumulus is broken into cellular patches or rolls. Both sit above the low cloud family (stratus, stratocumulus, cumulus) and below the high, ice-crystal cirrus family, with exact base heights varying somewhat by latitude and season.

meteorology.q: At a cold front, the cold air generally:
meteorology.a: Glides gradually over the warm air
meteorology.c: Mixes instantly with the warm air
meteorology.d: Pushes underneath the warm air mass
meteorology.ans: Pushes underneath the warm air mass
meteorology.e: At a cold front, the dense, advancing cold air pushes in underneath the warmer air ahead of it and forces that warm air upward at a steep slope of about 1:50 to 1:100. That abrupt, forced ascent is why cold fronts are associated with vertically developed cumulus and cumulonimbus, showers, and turbulence rather than the gentle stratiform weather of a warm front.

meteorology.q: What does dew point mean?
meteorology.a: The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated
meteorology.ans: The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated
meteorology.e: Dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, without changing its water-vapour content, for it to reach saturation. It is a direct measure of how much moisture the air actually contains - the higher the dew point, the more water vapour is present - which is why a small temperature-dew-point spread signals air that is already close to saturated.

meteorology.q: Which cloud may extend through more than one cloud level?
meteorology.e: Nimbostratus is thick enough that it commonly spans both the low and middle cloud levels at once, often with ragged, detached scud cloud drifting beneath its main base. That vertical extent, built by the broad, sustained ascent of a warm front, is exactly what lets it produce the widespread, continuous precipitation it is known for rather than the brief showers of a shallower layer.

meteorology.q: When a mass of air descends, its relative humidity generally:
meteorology.e: Descending air is compressed and warms adiabatically, and if its water-vapour content stays unchanged, that warming increases the air's capacity to hold moisture without adding any - exactly the mechanism that produces the same effect in warming air generally. The same vapour now represents a smaller fraction of what the warmer air could hold, so relative humidity decreases, which is why descending air (as in a föhn wind) typically becomes drier as well as warmer.

meteorology.q: The presence of altocumulus castellanus indicates:
meteorology.e: The turreted, cauliflower-like tops on altocumulus castellanus reveal small-scale convection breaking out inside an otherwise flat middle-level cloud layer, which is direct visual evidence of instability at that altitude. Because that instability can deepen through the day, castellanus is often treated as an early-warning sign that thunderstorms may develop later.

meteorology.q: Freezing rain is most likely when:
meteorology.a: Rain falls into a layer of air below 0°C
meteorology.b: Snow falls through dry warm air
meteorology.ans: Rain falls into a layer of air below 0°C
meteorology.e: Freezing rain typically starts as snow falling from a cold cloud, melts completely as it passes through a warm layer aloft, then re-enters a shallow layer of sub-zero air near the surface without having time to refreeze - leaving it as supercooled liquid. When those drops finally strike the cold ground or an aircraft, they freeze instantly on contact, producing the fast-building, dangerous clear-ice accretion freezing rain is known for.

meteorology.q: Which layer of the atmosphere contains most water vapour and most weather?
meteorology.e: The troposphere holds nearly all of the atmosphere's water vapour and is the only layer with significant vertical air movement, and that combination of moisture and vertical mixing is exactly what builds cloud, precipitation and the rest of what we call weather. Above the tropopause, air motion is mostly horizontal and there is very little moisture left to work with.

meteorology.q: Drizzle is most commonly associated with which cloud type?
meteorology.e: Drizzle is the signature precipitation of stratus: a shallow layer with only weak vertical currents, just enough to form many very small droplets but nowhere near enough to grow the larger drops that fall as rain. That weak, gentle lifting - rather than any deep convective process - is what caps drizzle droplets at such a small size.

meteorology.q: Which change of state releases latent heat?
meteorology.e: Condensation - water vapour turning to liquid, the gas-to-liquid change of state - releases latent heat energy into the surrounding air, producing a considerable heating effect that works against further adiabatic cooling as air rises. Evaporation is the reverse process and instead absorbs latent heat from its surroundings, which is why the two changes of state have opposite effects on a parcel's temperature.

meteorology.q: If unsaturated air is warmed while the water vapour content stays the same, relative humidity will:
meteorology.e: Warming raises the air's capacity to hold water vapour: a parcel holding a fixed amount of moisture drops from 100% relative humidity at 10°C to 62% at 20°C and just 28% at 30°C. Since the actual water-vapour content hasn't changed in that example, only the temperature has, relative humidity must decrease whenever unsaturated air is warmed with nothing added to it.

meteorology.q: Hill fog is most likely when:
meteorology.a: Dry unstable air sinks into a valley
meteorology.b: Humid stable air is forced up rising ground
meteorology.c: A cold front moves over flat desert
meteorology.d: Air warms rapidly on the lee side
meteorology.ans: Humid stable air is forced up rising ground
meteorology.e: Hill fog is simply low cloud that happens to intersect rising terrain: humid, stable air is forced up a slope, expanding and cooling until it reaches its dew point, and because the resulting cloud base sits right at hill level, anyone on the high ground finds themselves inside cloud with visibility dropping sharply. It needs stable air specifically - unstable air forced up the same slope would instead build cumulus rather than a smooth, ground-hugging layer.

meteorology.q: What are typical characteristics of cumuliform clouds?
meteorology.e: Cumuliform cloud only grows in unstable air, where a lifted parcel stays warmer than its surroundings and keeps accelerating upward on its own buoyancy. That same buoyant, uncontrolled vertical motion is what generates both the turbulence inside and around the cloud and the sudden, showery precipitation once droplets grow too heavy for the updraught to support - the full package of hazards that mark unstable, cumuliform weather.

meteorology.q: Which cloud types are evidence of unstable air?
meteorology.e: Cumulus and cumulonimbus are the visible signature of unstable air because they form only when a lifted parcel keeps rising under its own buoyancy rather than settling back to its original level. Stratiform types - stratus, altostratus, nimbostratus - form instead from the broad, gentle lifting typical of stable air, where cloud spreads sideways rather than building upward.

meteorology.q: What are common characteristics of a warm air mass moving over a cold surface?
meteorology.a: Stratiform cloud, smooth air and poor visibility
meteorology.ans: Stratiform cloud, smooth air and poor visibility
meteorology.e: When a warm air mass moves over a colder surface, it is cooled from below. That cooling increases stability in the lowest layers, suppressing the vertical mixing that would otherwise build cumuliform cloud - so the typical result is stratiform cloud, smooth flying conditions, and reduced visibility as moisture and haze stay trapped near the surface.

meteorology.q: Which weather condition can make true altitude lower than indicated altitude and therefore dangerous over high ground?
meteorology.e: Two separate effects stack up in cold, low-pressure conditions: lower-than-set pressure makes an unchanged altimeter overread on its own, and colder-than-standard air compresses the vertical spacing between pressure levels, further shrinking the real altitude packed into each hPa. Combined, these push true altitude well below what the altimeter shows - exactly the trap to watch for when flying over high ground in cold, low-pressure weather.

meteorology.q: Advection fog is most likely to form when:
meteorology.c: Warm moist air moves over a colder surface
meteorology.ans: Warm moist air moves over a colder surface
meteorology.e: Advection fog needs warm, moist air to be physically carried over a colder surface, cooling it from below by contact rather than by the air itself radiating heat away. Coastal areas commonly provide exactly this setup - a classic example is the South African west coast, where Atlantic air crossing the cold Benguela Current regularly produces advection fog.

meteorology.q: An air mass is best described as:
meteorology.a: A narrow line of thunderstorms only
meteorology.d: A large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and moisture properties
meteorology.ans: A large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and moisture properties
meteorology.e: An air mass is a large body of air, often covering more than 1000 nm, that has acquired fairly uniform temperature, stability and moisture characteristics by sitting over a broad, uniform source region while winds were light. It keeps those properties for some time after it starts moving, which is why classifying an air mass by its source tells you a great deal about the weather it will bring.

meteorology.q: Absolute instability exists when the environmental lapse rate:
meteorology.a: Exceeds the dry adiabatic lapse rate
meteorology.b: Is less than the saturated adiabatic lapse rate
meteorology.ans: Exceeds the dry adiabatic lapse rate
meteorology.e: Absolute instability exists when the environmental lapse rate is even steeper than the dry adiabatic lapse rate of about 3°C per 1000 ft. In that case even an unsaturated lifted parcel, cooling at the slower DALR, stays warmer than its rapidly-cooling surroundings at every level and keeps rising - no saturation or extra trigger is needed for the instability to take hold.

meteorology.q: Under what condition does pressure altitude have the same value as density altitude?
meteorology.d: When the aircraft is at sea level
meteorology.e: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for how far the actual temperature departs from the ISA standard value for that level. When the temperature happens to be exactly the ISA standard for that pressure altitude, there is nothing to correct for, so density altitude and pressure altitude come out equal - it is only non-standard temperature that ever pulls them apart.

meteorology.q: Fog is reported when visibility is reduced by water droplets or ice crystals to less than:
meteorology.e: Fog and mist describe the same physical thing - tiny suspended water droplets or ice crystals near the surface - with the aviation definition drawing the line purely by how much they cut visibility. Below 1,000 m the report is fog; at 1,000 m and above, the same obscuration is called mist instead.

meteorology.q: Which cloud type is least likely to produce precipitation?
meteorology.e: Cirrus sits so high and is so thin that any ice crystals falling from it almost always sublimate back into vapour long before reaching the ground - the same mechanism as virga, just at a much higher, colder altitude where the sublimation happens even more readily. Nimbostratus and cumulonimbus, by contrast, are deep enough and low enough to reliably deliver precipitation all the way to the surface.

meteorology.q: A parcel of air is saturated when its relative humidity is:
meteorology.e: Relative humidity is defined as the proportion of the actual water vapour in the air compared with the maximum the air could hold at that temperature, expressed as a percentage. Once that proportion reaches 100%, the air is holding all the moisture it possibly can at its current temperature - this is exactly what saturation, and the dew point, mean.

meteorology.q: What are fallstreaks or virga?
meteorology.b: Precipitation that evaporates before reaching the ground
meteorology.ans: Precipitation that evaporates before reaching the ground
meteorology.e: Fallstreaks and virga describe the same thing: precipitation that is clearly visible falling from a cloud base but that evaporates or sublimates completely before it reaches the ground. The cooling produced by that evaporation happens right where it falls, which can feed back into and strengthen the downdraughts beneath the cloud even though no rain ever actually lands.

meteorology.q: What are common characteristics of a cold air mass moving over a warm surface?
meteorology.a: Stratiform cloud, smooth air and poor visibility
meteorology.c: Cumuliform cloud, turbulence and good visibility
meteorology.d: Clear sky with no vertical motion
meteorology.ans: Cumuliform cloud, turbulence and good visibility
meteorology.e: When a cold air mass moves over a warmer surface, it is heated from below and becomes unstable, which is exactly what happens as cold air flows anticlockwise around the South Atlantic high and picks up warmth from the Indian Ocean along South Africa's east coast. The resulting convection produces cumuliform cloud and turbulence, but with good visibility in between the showers since there is no shallow trapped haze layer as there would be in stable air.

meteorology.q: Tropical revolving storms can occur in which area relevant to southern Africa?
meteorology.a: The South Atlantic west of Cape Town
meteorology.c: The cold Benguela Current south of Cape Point
meteorology.d: The Indian Ocean east of Madagascar
meteorology.ans: The Indian Ocean east of Madagascar
meteorology.e: Tropical revolving storms need warm ocean water to form, and the south-west Indian Ocean east of Madagascar and toward the Mozambique Channel is the only nearby body of water warm enough to sustain them - a real synoptic-chart example shows tropical storm "GAEL" sitting in exactly this area. The cold Benguela Current keeps the South Atlantic far too cool for tropical cyclones to develop.

meteorology.q: From which direction do the trade winds blow in the Southern Hemisphere?
meteorology.e: Trade winds blow toward the low-pressure equatorial trough (the ITCZ) that anchors the tropical zone, and in the Southern Hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects that equator-ward flow to the left, turning it into a south-easterly wind. This steady south-easterly trade-wind belt is exactly what feeds moisture onto South Africa's east coast during summer.

meteorology.q: Which instrument measures atmospheric humidity?
meteorology.e: A hygrometer measures atmospheric humidity - a psychrometer is simply one common type of hygrometer, using the difference between a wet-bulb and dry-bulb thermometer reading to work out moisture content. It sits alongside the anemometer (wind speed), barometer (pressure) and radiosonde (temperature/humidity aloft) as the standard instruments behind a weather observation.

meteorology.q: If heavy freezing rain is encountered and the aircraft cannot de-ice or land, the safest action is to:
meteorology.a: Continue straight ahead at the same altitude
meteorology.c: Turn back or leave the area immediately
meteorology.ans: Turn back or leave the area immediately
meteorology.e: Severe icing is a blunt reality: accumulation in a cumulonimbus's deep supercooled water can outpace even a properly functioning de-icing system, and most light aircraft have no icing protection at all. If heavy freezing rain cannot be shed and the aircraft cannot land immediately, the only real option is to leave the icing conditions entirely and as quickly as safely possible, since continuing to accumulate ice is not a survivable strategy.

meteorology.q: Which cloud type is most likely to produce moderate to severe airframe icing?
meteorology.e: Nimbostratus can hold a broad, deep layer of supercooled liquid water spanning both low and middle cloud levels at once, and its sheer horizontal and vertical extent means an aircraft may be exposed to that icing environment for a long, sustained period rather than a brief encounter. That combination of depth, extent and persistence is what lets nimbostratus build moderate to severe airframe ice, even though it lacks the violent convection of a cumulonimbus.

meteorology.q: Convective turbulence depends mainly on:
meteorology.e: Convective turbulence is caused by uneven solar heating of the surface, which creates thermals - warm parcels of rising air alongside pockets of sinking cooler air. It is therefore strongest on hot, sunny days with plenty of surface heating, and largely absent at night or under overcast skies where that heating disappears.

meteorology.q: Which cloud type may indicate severe turbulence near mountains?
meteorology.e: Standing mountain waves on the lee side of a ridge often produce altocumulus lenticularis - a smooth, lens-shaped cloud that forms at the wave crest as air is lifted and cools, then evaporates again as the air descends into the next trough. Its distinctive shape is a visible warning of strong wave activity and the potentially severe turbulence, especially rotor turbulence, that can accompany it near the mountain.

meteorology.q: Areas of sinking air are often cloudless because sinking air:
meteorology.e: Sinking air is compressed as it descends into higher pressure, and that compression warms it adiabatically without adding any moisture. Warmer air with the same water content has a lower relative humidity, which pushes any cloud droplets further from saturation - so they evaporate, which is exactly why broad areas of sinking air, as found under a high pressure system, tend to stay cloudless.

meteorology.q: What cloud sequence is typical when flying towards a warm front?
meteorology.a: Cumulonimbus, then cirrus, then clear sky
meteorology.d: Cirrus, then cirrostratus, altostratus and nimbostratus
meteorology.ans: Cirrus, then cirrostratus, altostratus and nimbostratus
meteorology.e: Flying toward a warm front, a pilot meets the cloud sequence in the same order it builds ahead of the frontal slope: cirrus first, as the leading edge of moisture arrives at high altitude, then cirrostratus, altostratus, and finally nimbostratus with its widespread precipitation right at the front. Cloud bases steadily lower and thicken throughout this sequence as the shallow 1:200-1:400 frontal slope is approached.

meteorology.q: When is a gust factor normally included in a METAR wind report?
meteorology.a: When gusts are at least 10 kt above the mean wind
meteorology.c: Only when visibility is below 1000 m
meteorology.ans: When gusts are at least 10 kt above the mean wind
meteorology.e: The METAR wind-code convention specifies that a maximum (gust) figure is only added when it exceeds the mean speed by 10 kt or more - so 22015G28KT means wind from 220°T at 15 kt with gusts to 28 kt, a 13 kt gap that clears the threshold. Below that 10 kt gap, the report simply states the mean speed with no gust group at all.

meteorology.q: A Foehn-type wind is best described as:
meteorology.e: A Föhn-type wind - called a berg wind in South Africa - is warm and dry because it has already shed its moisture as rain on the windward ascent, then descends the lee slope warming at the faster dry adiabatic rate through a greater vertical distance than it cooled going up. The result at the base of the mountain is air noticeably warmer and drier than when it started its journey.

meteorology.q: Subsidence means:
meteorology.e: Subsidence is broad, gentle downward motion of air, most often found spread across a high-pressure system as air slowly sinks to replace what diverges outward at the surface. As it descends into higher pressure it is compressed and warms adiabatically, which both increases stability and lowers relative humidity - the combination that gives high-pressure weather its characteristically settled, often cloudless nature.

meteorology.q: Frontal fog is most likely to occur:
meteorology.b: In the eye of a tropical cyclone
meteorology.e: Frontal fog is most likely just ahead of a warm front, where rain falling out of the warm, overrunning air passes down through the cold air mass still occupying the surface. As that rain evaporates it raises the humidity of the cold layer until it reaches saturation and condenses as fog - a direct side effect of the warm front's shallow overriding slope.

meteorology.q: A stationary high-pressure system over land in winter often causes:
meteorology.e: A high that parks itself over land through a winter night sets up the classic combination for fog: broad subsidence caps the atmosphere with a stable inversion, while the calm, clear conditions typical of a high let the ground radiate its heat away freely overnight. As the surface air cools under that inversion, any moisture present is brought to saturation and condenses as fog or low stratus, trapped beneath the inversion until the sun burns it off.

meteorology.q: Tropical revolving storms generally require sea-surface temperature of at least about:
meteorology.e: A tropical revolving storm draws its energy from a deep layer of warm ocean water, and the conventional threshold for enough heat and moisture to be available is about 26.5°C - so roughly +27°C is the closest match. Low vertical wind shear is also required, which is why the south-west Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, rather than the cold South Atlantic, is where these storms actually form near Southern Africa.

meteorology.q: A trough of low pressure on a surface chart is generally an area of:
meteorology.e: A trough is simply an elongated wedge of low pressure reaching out from a larger low, so it carries the same fundamental behaviour as a full low on a smaller scale: converging surface air with nowhere to go but up, favouring cloud and precipitation along the trough line.

meteorology.q: An active unstable cold front is most likely to produce:
meteorology.e: An active, unstable cold front lifts warm air abruptly along its steep 1:50 to 1:100 slope, and if that lifted air is itself unstable, the ascent runs away into deep convection. The result is the cold front's characteristic cumulonimbus development, with showers, thunderstorms, turbulence and sometimes hail rather than the steady rain of a stable lift.

meteorology.q: What is low-level wind shear?
meteorology.a: A sudden change in wind speed or direction over a small distance
meteorology.b: A constant wind at all heights
meteorology.d: A change in QNH over time
meteorology.ans: A sudden change in wind speed or direction over a small distance
meteorology.e: The turbulence chapter defines wind shear simply as a change in wind speed or direction (or both), and when that change happens rapidly over a short distance close to the ground, it is low-level wind shear. Because it can abruptly change an aircraft's airspeed and lift right at the moment of take-off or landing, it is one of the more dangerous low-altitude hazards a pilot can encounter.

meteorology.q: A squall line is most likely to be found:
meteorology.b: Ahead of an active cold front
meteorology.ans: Ahead of an active cold front
meteorology.e: A squall line is an organised band of thunderstorm cells, distinct from the parent front itself, and it typically forms in the warm, unstable air of the warm sector ahead of an active cold front - not on the front line but out ahead of it. Because it can bring severe turbulence, hail and abrupt wind shifts well before the actual frontal passage, it is an easy hazard to underestimate if a pilot is only watching for the front.

meteorology.q: What does BKN mean in a METAR or TAF?
meteorology.e: BKN is the second-highest step on the oktas cloud-amount scale (SKC 0, FEW 1-2, SCT 3-4, BKN 5-7, OVC 8), meaning 5 to 7 eighths of the sky is covered by that layer. Operationally this matters because the lowest BKN or OVC layer reported becomes the aerodrome's ceiling - FEW and SCT layers, however extensive, never count as one.

meteorology.q: A microburst is best described as:
meteorology.d: A concentrated downdraft with damaging surface outflow
meteorology.ans: A concentrated downdraft with damaging surface outflow
meteorology.e: A microburst is a small but intense downdraught that plunges out of a thunderstorm and, on striking the ground, spreads out rapidly in all directions as a violent horizontal outflow. Flying through one produces a rapid, dangerous sequence: an increasing headwind followed by a strong downdraught and then a tailwind, exactly the low-level wind-shear pattern that has caused numerous approach and departure accidents.

meteorology.q: A gust front is formed by:
meteorology.b: Warm air rising ahead of a warm front
meteorology.c: The centre of a high-pressure system
meteorology.e: A gust front is the leading edge of the cold, dense outflow air that a thunderstorm's downdraught spreads out across the surface once it strikes the ground - effectively a thunderstorm's own miniature cold front racing out ahead of the storm cell itself. Its passage can bring a sudden wind shift, a burst of gusty wind, turbulence and low-level wind shear well before the parent storm's rain or cloud ever arrives overhead.

meteorology.q: Clear ice forms mainly from:
meteorology.b: Large supercooled water droplets freezing slowly
meteorology.d: Dust freezing on the leading edge
meteorology.ans: Large supercooled water droplets freezing slowly
meteorology.e: Clear ice forms when relatively large supercooled droplets strike the airframe and only partially freeze on impact, leaving the rest of the water to spread across the surface before finally freezing solid. That spreading is exactly what makes clear ice so dangerous: it produces a smooth, dense, hard-to-see accretion that can extend well behind the leading edge and any de-icing boots protecting it, unlike the rougher rime ice built from smaller, instantly-freezing droplets.

meteorology.q: Which stage of a thunderstorm has both updraughts and downdraughts?
meteorology.e: A thunderstorm's mature stage is defined by updraughts and downdraughts existing side by side in the same cloud, which begins once precipitation falling through the cell finally reaches the ground - typically about 30 minutes after the cumulus stage starts. It is the most violent phase of the storm's life, combining the strongest turbulence, heaviest precipitation, hail and lightning all at once.

meteorology.q: What are the three main requirements for thunderstorm formation?
meteorology.e: The same three essentials apply every time: instability (a deep unstable layer, over 10,000 ft, that lets a rising parcel keep accelerating), moisture (especially at low level, to build the cloud and eventually the precipitation), and a trigger action to start the parcel rising in the first place - whether that is converging airmasses, a front, orographic lift, or simple surface heating. All three have to be present together for a cumulonimbus to develop.

meteorology.q: Hoar frost forms when:
meteorology.a: Water vapour changes directly into ice on a cold surface
meteorology.d: Ice pellets bounce off the aircraft
meteorology.ans: Water vapour changes directly into ice on a cold surface
meteorology.e: Hoar frost forms by deposition: water vapour in contact with a surface already below freezing turns directly into ice crystals without ever passing through a liquid stage, which is why it appears on an aircraft's cold skin on a clear winter morning even without any visible precipitation falling. Even a thin layer with the texture of sandpaper can cut lift by up to 30% and raise drag by 40%, so it must be fully cleared before flight.

meteorology.q: Rime ice forms mainly from:
meteorology.b: Small supercooled water droplets freezing rapidly
meteorology.c: Dry snow sticking to a warm wing
meteorology.d: Water vapour condensing as liquid only
meteorology.ans: Small supercooled water droplets freezing rapidly
meteorology.e: Rime ice builds when small supercooled droplets strike the airframe and freeze almost instantly, trapping air between the rapidly forming ice particles rather than letting the water spread first. That trapped air is what gives rime its rough, brittle, opaque-white appearance - visually and structurally quite different from the smooth, dense clear ice produced by larger, slower-freezing droplets.

meteorology.q: A stormscope is used to detect:
meteorology.e: A stormscope works by picking up the radio-frequency energy that a lightning discharge radiates outward, then plotting each detected strike on a cockpit display as a dot representing electrical activity. Unlike weather radar, which images precipitation directly, a stormscope only ever shows you where lightning - and by inference, convective activity - is occurring, not the shape or intensity of the rain or cloud itself.

meteorology.q: Where is the surface wind normally measured for official weather observations?
meteorology.d: On a mast about 8 to 10 m above the ground
meteorology.ans: On a mast about 8 to 10 m above the ground
meteorology.e: Official surface-wind sensors are exposed on a mast at approximately 10 m above the ground, a standard height chosen to keep the reading representative of the general surface wind while minimising the very local friction and turbulence effects that ground-level obstacles would otherwise introduce. This standardised height is exactly what makes wind reports from different aerodromes comparable to one another.

meteorology.q: Mechanical turbulence is caused by:
meteorology.a: Air flowing over the earth’s surface and obstacles
meteorology.c: Smooth airflow over the sea only
meteorology.ans: Air flowing over the earth’s surface and obstacles
meteorology.e: Wind breaks into swirling eddies as it flows over buildings, hangars and rough terrain - disruption to what would otherwise be smooth horizontal airflow. Its severity depends on the strength of the wind, the roughness of the terrain, and the size of the obstruction, and it is strongest just downwind of whatever is causing it.

meteorology.q: Which instrument measures wind speed?
meteorology.e: An anemometer measures wind speed, typically using a spinning cup or propeller whose rotation rate is proportional to the wind's velocity. Wind direction is measured separately, by a wind vane or the directional sensor built into a combined anemometer unit - the two readings together make up a full surface wind observation.

meteorology.q: Mountain waves should normally be expected:
meteorology.b: Directly under high cirrus clouds only
meteorology.c: On the downwind side of a mountain range
meteorology.ans: On the downwind side of a mountain range
meteorology.e: Mountain, or lee, waves form on the downwind side of a ridge when air forced up and over the mountain overshoots and oscillates as it descends the other side. The wave pattern can extend for tens of nautical miles downwind of the range, with severe turbulence and strong downdraughts possible beneath the wave crests, especially in rotor cloud near the height of the ridge.

meteorology.q: A thermal depression is most likely to form:
meteorology.e: A thermal depression, or heat low, forms where intense summer solar heating over land warms and expands the lower atmosphere enough to trigger sustained ascent, which lowers surface pressure beneath it. This is exactly the mechanism at work over the South African interior in summer, where daytime heating builds a shallow thermal low that helps draw moist air inland from the coast.

meteorology.q: What weather is common within the ITCZ?
meteorology.b: Clear sky and no vertical motion
meteorology.d: Smooth stratiform cloud with no showers
meteorology.e: The ITCZ is where the trade winds of both hemispheres converge, and that convergence forces the warm, humid tropical air upward with nowhere else to go. Deep, continuous convection is the result, making frequent cumulonimbus, heavy showers and thunderstorms - along with the turbulence and icing that come with them - the everyday weather inside the zone.

meteorology.q: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure?
meteorology.e: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure - a classic aneroid barometer has a sealed capsule that expands and contracts with changing pressure to move a needle across a dial marked in inches of mercury and hectopascals. Aerodrome pressure readings taken this way are then reduced or converted into the settings pilots actually use, such as QNH.

meteorology.q: Which type of icing is usually the most dangerous?
meteorology.e: Clear ice is the more dangerous of the two main icing types precisely because of how it forms: large supercooled droplets spread across the surface before fully freezing, building a dense, smooth, hard-to-see accretion that can extend well beyond the leading edge and past any ice protection equipment, unlike the rougher but more contained rime ice. Its weight and the way it distorts the aerofoil shape make it a particularly severe threat to lift and control.

meteorology.q: A strong low-level inversion can promote:
meteorology.a: No change in wind with height
meteorology.e: A strong low-level inversion is a very stable layer that resists the vertical mixing which would normally blend the wind above it with the wind below. Because the two layers stay essentially decoupled, they can end up moving at quite different speeds or in different directions, and the abrupt change across that shallow inversion boundary is exactly what produces significant wind shear.

meteorology.q: What is the approximate maximum diameter of a microburst damage area?
meteorology.e: By definition, a microburst's damaging surface outflow is confined to a small area - no more than about 4 km across - which is exactly what makes it so hazardous: an aircraft can pass through the entire event, headwind gust, downdraught and tailwind, in a matter of seconds during a critical low-altitude phase like final approach, with almost no time to react to conditions that change so abruptly over such a short distance.

meteorology.q: Which cloud is the most hazardous on a cross-country VFR flight?
meteorology.e: Cumulonimbus combines nearly every serious weather hazard a light aircraft can face into a single cloud: severe turbulence strong enough to threaten structural failure, hail, lightning, rapid airframe icing, heavy precipitation and low-level wind shear from its downdraughts - and the only sound strategy on a VFR cross-country is to avoid it by a wide margin, never to try to fly through or even close beneath it.

meteorology.q: The ITCZ is best described as:
meteorology.a: The boundary between stratus and cirrus cloud
meteorology.c: The zone where northern and southern trade winds converge
meteorology.ans: The zone where northern and southern trade winds converge
meteorology.e: The ITCZ is the belt, also called the Doldrums, where the Northern and Southern Hemisphere trade winds meet and converge. With that converging air having nowhere to go but up, the zone is marked by light surface winds but frequent heavy showers as the rising, moisture-laden air condenses; it also migrates seasonally, reaching as far south as about 17°S during South Africa's summer.

meteorology.q: Radiosondes are used to measure:
meteorology.b: Cloud amount at the surface only
meteorology.e: A radiosonde is a small instrument package carried aloft by a weather balloon, measuring pressure, temperature and humidity as it climbs through the atmosphere. Tracking the balloon's drift as it rises also lets forecasters derive the wind at each level, making a single radiosonde flight a rich vertical profile of the atmosphere's state.

air-law.q: Notification of an accident outside the Republic for a South African-registered aircraft must be made to whom?
air-law.a: The appropriate authority in the State where it occurred, and the SA Executive responsible for investigation
air-law.ans: The appropriate authority in the State where it occurred, and the SA Executive responsible for investigation
air-law.e: Notification goes to two parties because responsibility is split: the State where the accident happened has jurisdiction to launch the on-site response, while South Africa, as the State of Registry, retains an ongoing interest and obligation under ICAO Annex 13 principles. Exam tip: think 'who is on the ground' plus 'whose aircraft it is'.

air-law.q: For incidents, who must be notified within 24 hours?
air-law.b: Executive responsible for Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation
air-law.ans: Executive responsible for Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation
air-law.e: Incidents get a 24-hour reporting window rather than the 'as soon as possible' standard used for accidents, because no injury or major damage is involved and the information is less time-critical to collect. The Executive responsible for investigation still needs the data to spot trends before a similar event becomes an accident.

air-law.q: If an ATSU is notified of an accident outside the Republic, it must do what?
air-law.c: Pass the information to the appropriate authority and the SA Executive
air-law.d: Wait for confirmation from the PIC
air-law.ans: Pass the information to the appropriate authority and the SA Executive
air-law.e: An ATSU is often the first point of contact for a report, especially when the event happens abroad and the operator or crew reach out to the nearest air traffic facility. Its role is only to relay the information promptly to the correct authorities, not to investigate itself.

air-law.q: If there are no surviving flight crew members, responsibility to guard the accident aircraft falls to whom?
air-law.e: The regulation builds a chain of responsibility so someone is always accountable for guarding the aircraft: normally the PIC, then another crew member if the PIC cannot act, and finally the operator or owner if no crew member survives or is able to act.

air-law.q: Which of the following is not explicitly included in items to be protected from interference?
air-law.e: The listed protections (wreckage, items carried, and accident marks) cover the physical evidence investigators need intact to reconstruct what happened. ATC logs are administrative records retained separately by the ATSU, so they fall outside this specific scene-protection duty.

air-law.q: Information missing at the time of initial notification must be handled how?
air-law.b: Be sent in writing to the Executive as soon as available
air-law.ans: Be sent in writing to the Executive as soon as available
air-law.e: Notification must go out immediately with whatever facts are known, rather than being delayed until every detail is confirmed. Anything still outstanding is simply forwarded in writing once available, so the investigation can start quickly without losing accuracy.

air-law.q: A serious incident where no credible defences exist to prevent an accident is treated how?
air-law.e: Reportability depends on the risk an event exposed, not on whether an accident was narrowly avoided. Even where no specific safeguard failed, a serious incident stays reportable because the regulator needs visibility of every high-risk occurrence to manage systemic safety.

air-law.q: Fuel quantity emergencies requiring a declaration of emergency include what?
air-law.d: Fuel exhaustion, starvation, or inability to use all usable fuel
air-law.ans: Fuel exhaustion, starvation, or inability to use all usable fuel
air-law.e: These fuel emergencies are singled out because they are almost always preventable through planning and monitoring, so regulators want them declared and investigated to catch procedural failures before they cause an accident. Normal use of planned reserve fuel is not an emergency.

air-law.q: In the event of an accident within the Republic, the PIC must notify the relevant authority when?
air-law.a: As soon as possible but at least within 24 hours
air-law.c: Only at the next scheduled ATC contact
air-law.ans: As soon as possible but at least within 24 hours
air-law.e: The rule combines a general duty (notify as soon as possible) with a hard backstop (within 24 hours), so there is always a firm deadline even if the general standard is applied loosely. This protects time-critical evidence and injury/SAR information the authorities need.

air-law.q: Which of the following is not classified as a serious incident?
air-law.a: Fire or smoke in cockpit extinguished in flight
air-law.c: Wheels-up landing not classified as an accident
air-law.e: A serious incident is defined by a high probability that an accident could have occurred; a routine landing carries no such elevated risk, so it does not meet the threshold for reporting, however imperfect it might have looked.

air-law.q: When an accident occurs on an aerodrome and flight crew are incapacitated, who takes responsibility?
air-law.e: On an aerodrome, the aerodrome manager already has authority over the movement area and access, so when flight crew cannot act, responsibility naturally passes to that on-site authority rather than to an outside party.

air-law.q: If the PIC is incapacitated or killed, responsibility to guard the accident aircraft passes to whom?
air-law.e: The chain of responsibility for guarding wreckage mirrors the flight-deck chain of command: PIC first, then the next flight crew member if the PIC is incapacitated or killed, so the duty never falls to someone unfamiliar with the aircraft or situation.

air-law.q: An ATS incident witnessed by ATS personnel must be reported how?
air-law.a: To an ATSU as soon as possible
air-law.ans: To an ATSU as soon as possible
air-law.e: ATS personnel witnessing an incident have direct, first-hand knowledge, so they are required to report to an ATSU promptly rather than waiting for someone else to notice or for a formal review.

air-law.q: The identifying abbreviation for a serious incident is?
air-law.e: SINCID is the reporting abbreviation used for a serious incident. A serious incident involves circumstances showing that there was a high probability of an accident, even though an accident did not actually occur.

air-law.q: An ATSU notified of an incident must inform whom?
air-law.c: The Executive responsible for Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation, and the aerodrome manager if on an aerodrome
air-law.ans: The Executive responsible for Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation, and the aerodrome manager if on an aerodrome
air-law.e: Once informed, the ATSU passes the incident on to the body responsible for investigation, and to the aerodrome manager if it happened at an aerodrome, since local management may need to take immediate action such as a runway closure or hazard marking.

air-law.q: Which of the following is part of the required particulars in an accident or incident notification?
air-law.d: Number of fatalities or seriously injured persons on the ground
air-law.ans: Number of fatalities or seriously injured persons on the ground
air-law.e: Ground casualties are called out specifically because notification particulars must capture the full safety picture, not just harm to those on board; third parties on the ground are just as relevant to the investigation and any public safety response.

air-law.q: An intentional release of an external sling load is a serious incident under what condition?
air-law.a: If unintentional or as an emergency measure
air-law.ans: If unintentional or as an emergency measure
air-law.e: The distinction is between a controlled operational release (e.g. delivering a load) and one that happens unintentionally or as an emergency measure to save the aircraft — only the latter indicates a safety problem worth investigating as a serious incident.

air-law.q: In an accident within the Republic, who is first responsible for preventing interference with the wreck until police arrive?
air-law.b: The PIC, or next in line if incapacitated
air-law.ans: The PIC, or next in line if incapacitated
air-law.e: The PIC is on scene with first-hand knowledge of the accident and, until police arrive, is best placed to prevent interference that could destroy evidence; responsibility passes down the crew only if the PIC is unable to act.

air-law.q: Which of the following is not listed as a serious incident?
air-law.d: Fire or smoke in passenger cabin
air-law.e: A repositioning flight with no abnormal event carries no elevated accident risk, so it does not meet the definition of a serious incident, which requires circumstances showing a high probability of an accident.

air-law.q: A runway incursion classified as severity A is considered what?
air-law.e: Runway incursions are graded by severity, with A being the most serious — involving a high risk of collision or a very close call — which is why a severity A incursion is treated as a serious incident.

air-law.q: A serious incident includes which of the following?
air-law.e: A near collision needing an avoidance manoeuvre shows that safe separation was lost and only crew action prevented a collision — exactly the kind of high-risk, near-miss event the serious incident category exists to capture.

air-law.q: When an ATSU or police station is first notified of an accident, it must immediately inform whom?
air-law.b: The Director and the aerodrome manager if on an aerodrome
air-law.ans: The Director and the aerodrome manager if on an aerodrome
air-law.e: Whoever is first notified, whether an ATSU or police station, must pass the report up to the Director immediately, and to the aerodrome manager if relevant, so the formal investigation and any local safety response start without delay.

air-law.q: If there are no surviving or able flight crew after an accident, who must notify?
air-law.e: This rule ensures the notification duty never lapses just because the flight crew cannot fulfil it — responsibility shifts to the operator or owner, who has a continuing legal interest in and knowledge of the aircraft.

air-law.q: If the PIC is incapacitated or killed in an accident, who is next responsible for notification?
air-law.e: If the PIC cannot act, notification duty passes to another flight crew member rather than to a passenger or ground party, since flight crew are best placed to know what happened and the aircraft's history.

air-law.q: Which is not among the listed particulars for notification?
air-law.a: Exact maintenance history of the aircraft
air-law.ans: Exact maintenance history of the aircraft
air-law.e: Notification particulars cover only the immediate facts needed to trigger a response — what happened, where, injuries, and damage. The aircraft's maintenance history is a separate record examined later, during the investigation itself.

air-law.q: Which of the following is not mentioned as part of preventing interference at an accident scene?
air-law.e: As with wreckage and accident marks, the protection duty targets physical evidence relevant to reconstructing the accident. Personal items like crew uniforms are not part of that evidentiary scene and are not listed.

air-law.q: Removing wreckage to clear an obstruction is allowed if what condition applies?
air-law.c: It prevents danger or removes obstruction to other aircraft, transport, or public
air-law.ans: It prevents danger or removes obstruction to other aircraft, transport, or public
air-law.e: The rule balances two competing interests: preserving evidence versus preventing further danger or disruption. Where wreckage itself has become a hazard, such as blocking a runway or road, removing it to protect others is allowed.

air-law.q: The prohibition on interference with an accident aircraft applies to what aircraft?
air-law.d: Any aircraft involved in an accident within the Republic
air-law.ans: Any aircraft involved in an accident within the Republic
air-law.e: The protection duty applies uniformly to every accident aircraft within the Republic, regardless of size, operator type, or how much damage occurred, because the goal is to preserve evidence for every investigation, not just major ones.

air-law.q: Who must the responsible person arrange with for guarding an accident scene?
air-law.a: A member of the South African Police Service
air-law.ans: A member of the South African Police Service
air-law.e: Guarding is specifically assigned to the South African Police Service because they have the legal authority to control access and prevent interference, which a private party or the operator alone would not have.

air-law.q: Arrangements for police guard at an accident scene must be made when?
air-law.d: Before the aircraft is moved for recovery
air-law.e: 'Forthwith' means without delay, because an unguarded wreckage site can quickly be disturbed by onlookers, scavengers, or the elements, destroying the evidence the investigation depends on.

air-law.q: Which of the following is not prohibited without proper authorisation at an accident scene?
air-law.b: Removing items transported in the aircraft
air-law.e: Moving wreckage, removing transported items and interfering with marks are restricted without authorisation; taking photographs is not listed as prohibited.

air-law.q: Who may authorise interference with an accident aircraft before the investigation is complete?
air-law.e: Only the investigator-in-charge may authorise interference before the investigation is complete, so evidence is disturbed only once its condition and position have been properly recorded — this protects the chain of custody.

air-law.q: Before interfering with an aircraft that requires customs clearance, permission must also be obtained from whom?
air-law.a: A customs officer under the Customs and Excise Act
air-law.ans: A customs officer under the Customs and Excise Act
air-law.e: Where an aircraft has crossed a border or carries dutiable goods, customs law applies independently of the accident investigation, so a customs officer's permission is needed in addition to any accident-related authorisation.

air-law.q: What is one allowed reason to move wreckage before authorisation?
air-law.a: To inspect it for maintenance defects
air-law.c: To transport it to the operator’s hangar for storage
air-law.d: To speed up reopening the runway for normal operations without safety risk
air-law.e: Saving human or animal life always overrides the general duty to preserve wreckage undisturbed — rescue takes priority over evidence, even before formal authorisation is granted.

air-law.q: Moving an aircraft to a safe place before authorisation is permitted when?
air-law.c: It is in water or otherwise endangered
air-law.ans: It is in water or otherwise endangered
air-law.e: Where the aircraft itself is at further risk, for example sinking, drifting, or exposed to fire, moving it to safety is allowed immediately, since losing the wreckage entirely would be worse for the investigation than moving it under control.

air-law.q: Preventing interference before police arrival is important for what reason?
air-law.d: Preserve evidence that may assist in the investigation
air-law.ans: Preserve evidence that may assist in the investigation
air-law.e: The accident scene must be protected to preserve evidence for the investigation.

air-law.q: Preventing interference at an accident scene may include what action?
air-law.a: Protecting wreckage from destruction by fire or other causes
air-law.b: Painting over accident marks to prevent public alarm
air-law.d: Covering the aircraft for privacy from the public
air-law.ans: Protecting wreckage from destruction by fire or other causes
air-law.e: Physical protection duties include active steps like shielding wreckage from fire, not just passive access control, because fire or other damage after the accident can destroy evidence just as effectively as human interference.

air-law.q: The regulation on guarding the aircraft applies to what accidents?
air-law.c: Only if damage exceeds a certain value
air-law.e: The guarding duty is triggered by any accident, not just fatal or high-damage ones, since even a minor accident may hold safety lessons the investigation needs to capture.

air-law.q: Which of these is not listed as an exception for moving items before clearance?
air-law.e: Routine maintenance inspection is not urgent enough to justify disturbing an accident scene; only genuine emergencies — danger, rescue, or safeguarding valuables — qualify as exceptions to the general prohibition.

air-law.q: Which is a permitted exception for interference under accident scene regulations?
air-law.d: Safeguarding valuables like jewellery or precious metals
air-law.ans: Safeguarding valuables like jewellery or precious metals
air-law.e: Valuables like jewellery are excluded from the general prohibition mainly to prevent theft or loss at an unguarded site, while leaving the core evidence — wreckage, marks, and cargo relevant to the cause — untouched.

air-law.q: An applicant for a pilot licence under Part 61 must hold what medical certificate?
air-law.a: An appropriate valid medical certificate issued in terms of Part 67
air-law.b: Any medical certificate issued by a doctor
air-law.d: An ICAO Class 2 medical certificate from any ICAO state
air-law.ans: An appropriate valid medical certificate issued in terms of Part 67
air-law.e: A Part 61 pilot licence applicant must hold the appropriate, valid medical certificate issued under Part 67. Licensing and medical fitness are governed by separate Parts of the regulations, and licence privileges cannot legally be exercised without current medical certification behind them.

air-law.q: Which statement is true about language proficiency?
air-law.b: It must be valid for the pilot to use licence privileges
air-law.ans: It must be valid for the pilot to use licence privileges
air-law.e: Language proficiency is not a one-time box to tick — it must remain valid through periodic reassessment for as long as a pilot exercises licence privileges, because clear radio communication is safety-critical, especially in an emergency or unfamiliar airspace.

air-law.q: Which licence is exempt from the English proficiency requirement?
air-law.e: A Student Pilot Licence is exempt because a student trains under direct supervision within a controlled ATO environment, rather than independently exercising the communication-heavy privileges of a full licence where standardised English matters most.

air-law.q: Logbook entries for domestic Part 91 flights must be made within what period?
air-law.e: The 7-day window for domestic Part 91 entries balances accuracy (details still fresh) against practicality (not needing an entry after every single flight). It is distinct from the shorter 48-hour rule that applies specifically when a pilot has been away from their home base.

air-law.q: To be issued a pilot licence under Part 61, except SPL, a person must do what regarding English language ability?
air-law.a: Demonstrate or provide proof of English language ability per SA-CATS 61
air-law.b: Pass an ICAO Level 3 English test
air-law.ans: Demonstrate or provide proof of English language ability per SA-CATS 61
air-law.e: Every Part 61 licence holder other than an SPL must prove English ability under SA-CATS 61, because standardised aviation English is what keeps radio communication safe and unambiguous between pilots and ATC, including in an emergency.

air-law.q: How often must an electronic logbook be printed and filed?
air-law.d: Only when licence renewal is due
air-law.e: Printing and filing an electronic logbook every 90 days creates a permanent, tamper-resistant backup, protecting the flight record against data loss or a failed device — an electronic-only copy is not treated as a sufficiently durable record on its own.

air-law.q: A pilot may not exercise licence privileges without what language requirement?
air-law.e: Exercising licence privileges without a valid language proficiency rating is not permitted because reliable radio communication is treated as a safety-of-flight issue, not an administrative formality — the rating must stay current, much like a medical certificate.

air-law.q: Language proficiency requirements are set out in which document?
air-law.e: SA-CATS 61 is the technical standards document supporting Part 61 — it is where the detailed language proficiency levels and assessment methods actually live, rather than in the regulation itself.

air-law.q: When engaged in flight operations away from base, logbook entries must be made when?
air-law.a: Within 48 hours after return to base
air-law.d: At the end of the duty cycle
air-law.ans: Within 48 hours after return to base
air-law.e: The 48-hour window, shorter than the usual 7 days, applies specifically when a pilot returns from being away from their home base, since a backlog of entries builds up while access to the logbook is unavailable and needs to be cleared quickly once it resumes.

air-law.q: How long must pilots retain their logbooks after they no longer hold a valid licence?
air-law.e: The 60-month retention period after a licence lapses lets the CAA, an employer, or an investigation verify a pilot’s historical flight experience well after they have stopped flying under that licence, including for licence reinstatement.

air-law.q: For cross-country flights recorded as a single logbook entry, what details must be recorded?
air-law.b: Only departure and destination are recorded
air-law.c: The route and intermediate stops must be recorded
air-law.ans: The route and intermediate stops must be recorded
air-law.e: Recording the route and intermediate stops for a cross-country flight logged as a single entry preserves an accurate record of the navigation experience actually gained — this matters because cross-country time carries its own minimum requirements for licences and ratings.

air-law.q: Dual flight instruction time must include what in the logbook?
air-law.e: Noting the specific air exercises covered during dual instruction lets the instructor and later an examiner track syllabus progress, not just accumulated hours — it is evidence of what was actually taught, not only how long the flight lasted.

air-law.q: SPIC time may be credited as PIC time if what condition applies?
air-law.a: The instructor did not influence or control any part of the flight
air-law.b: The instructor provides constant verbal coaching
air-law.c: The instructor occupies the left seat
air-law.d: The flight is less than 1 hour
air-law.ans: The instructor did not influence or control any part of the flight
air-law.e: SPIC time can only be credited as PIC time when the instructor genuinely did not intervene, because logging it as PIC claims the student exercised full command authority and responsibility for the flight — not merely flew dual while an instructor quietly supervised.

air-law.q: PICUS time can be logged only under what condition?
air-law.a: There is constant intervention by the supervising PIC
air-law.b: There is no intervention by the supervising PIC and PICUS is noted and certified
air-law.c: The supervising PIC is not rated on type
air-law.d: The pilot is in training for a PPL
air-law.ans: There is no intervention by the supervising PIC and PICUS is noted and certified
air-law.e: PICUS may only be logged, and must be noted and certified as such, when the supervising PIC did not intervene. This keeps a clear line between PICUS — command experience gained under supervision, with someone else still legally responsible — and full PIC time, so hours are not inflated.

air-law.q: Instrument flight time must be logged when what condition applies?
air-law.c: Flying solely by reference to instruments with no external visual reference
air-law.ans: Flying solely by reference to instruments with no external visual reference
air-law.e: Instrument flight time is only loggable when there is genuinely no external visual reference, because the point of separating it out is to track real instrument-flying experience — time that counts specifically toward instrument and night rating requirements.

air-law.q: PIC time may be logged when what condition applies?
air-law.a: You are the senior pilot on board regardless of designation
air-law.b: You have more flight hours than the actual PIC
air-law.c: You sit in the left seat during the flight
air-law.d: You are the designated PIC of the aircraft
air-law.ans: You are the designated PIC of the aircraft
air-law.e: PIC time is tied strictly to who is designated pilot-in-command, not to seniority or hours, because the PIC carries legal responsibility for the flight — and it is PIC hours specifically that count toward licence and rating experience requirements.

air-law.q: A student solo flight is logged as PIC time if what applies?
air-law.a: The student is sole occupant and SOLO is entered in remarks
air-law.ans: The student is sole occupant and SOLO is entered in remarks
air-law.e: A student flying solo, with no instructor aboard, carries full responsibility for the flight and so meets the definition of PIC even while still training. The SOLO remark in the logbook distinguishes this from dual time or later licensed PIC time.

air-law.q: Multiple flights in a day can be recorded as a single logbook entry if what condition is met?
air-law.a: All flights are under 30 minutes each
air-law.b: The interval between flights does not exceed 180 minutes
air-law.c: They are all local training flights
air-law.ans: The interval between flights does not exceed 180 minutes
air-law.e: Grouping same-day flights into one entry when the gap is under 180 minutes cuts down on repetitive paperwork for back-to-back local flights such as circuits, while a longer gap still forces separate entries so each distinct flight is properly recorded.

air-law.q: In VMC, a PPL(A) holder may act in what capacity?
air-law.c: PIC or co-pilot in any aeroplane for which they hold the appropriate valid class or type rating
air-law.ans: PIC or co-pilot in any aeroplane for which they hold the appropriate valid class or type rating
air-law.e: A PPL(A) holder’s privileges in VMC are tied to holding the appropriate valid class or type rating, because the rating is what certifies competency on that specific aeroplane — the PPL itself does not automatically cover every aeroplane type.

air-law.q: The final theoretical knowledge exam for a PPL(A) must be passed within how long before the skills test?
air-law.e: The final theoretical exam’s 36-month validity before the skills test is a separate clock from the 18-month window to complete the whole exam series in the first place: pass all exams within 18 months of the first credit, then the skills test must follow within 36 months of that final pass.

air-law.q: A South African Air Force qualified pilot applying for a PPL(A) may receive what credit?
air-law.a: Be credited with theoretical knowledge and flight time in terms of Part 61
air-law.ans: Be credited with theoretical knowledge and flight time in terms of Part 61
air-law.e: SAAF-qualified pilots can be credited with equivalent theoretical knowledge and flight time under Part 61 so they are not forced to repeat training already demonstrated to a comparable military standard — though they must still meet any Part 61 requirements that training did not cover.

air-law.q: Out of the 45 hours total PPL(A) flight time, how many must be solo flight time?
air-law.e: The PPL(A) course requires at least 15 hours of solo flight within the minimum 45-hour total. Solo time proves that the student can operate safely without an instructor controlling the aircraft.

air-law.q: After receiving the PPL(A), the holder must do what?
air-law.a: Keep it unsigned until first renewal
air-law.b: Send a copy to the ATO
air-law.d: Only sign it before the first solo after issuance
air-law.e: Signing the PPL(A) in ink immediately on receipt is what makes it a valid, usable document — an unsigned licence is not legally exercisable and could more easily be misused by someone else.

air-law.q: Who issues the PPL(A) once all requirements are met?
air-law.e: Only the SACAA Director issues the licence, even though the ATO and instructor handle training and testing. This separation keeps training and certification independent, so the organisation that trains a candidate cannot also certify them.

air-law.q: Out of the 45 hours total PPL(A) flight time, how many must be dual instruction?
air-law.e: At least 25 of the minimum 45 PPL(A) hours must be dual instruction with a qualified instructor. The remaining required time includes solo flying and the specified navigation and instrument exercises.

air-law.q: The application for a PPL(A) must be submitted to the Director within how long of the skills test?
air-law.e: The 30-day deadline to submit the application after the skills test keeps the paperwork tied closely to the pass. Do not confuse it with the separate 30-day rule requiring the skills test itself to be completed within 30 days of the last dual instruction — the same number, but a different clock.

air-law.q: Who can conduct the skills test for a PPL(A)?
air-law.c: A CFI(Aeroplane) or Grade II or I instructor appointed by the CFI under SA-CATS 61
air-law.ans: A CFI(Aeroplane) or Grade II or I instructor appointed by the CFI under SA-CATS 61
air-law.e: Only a CFI(Aeroplane) or a Grade II or I instructor specifically appointed by the CFI may conduct the skills test. This ensures adequate seniority and avoids the conflict of interest of a candidate’s own primary instructor testing them without oversight.

air-law.q: What is the minimum age to apply for a PPL(A)?
air-law.e: A person must be at least 17 years old to be issued a PPL(A). Training may begin earlier, but the licence cannot be issued before the minimum age is reached.

air-law.q: Which of the following is not required in the application for a PPL(A)?
air-law.a: A copy of the examiner’s ID
air-law.c: Two passport-size photos unless already holding a Part 61 licence
air-law.ans: A copy of the examiner’s ID
air-law.e: A copy of the examiner’s ID is not listed as a PPL(A) application requirement.

air-law.q: The skills test for a PPL(A) must be done within how long of the last dual instruction?
air-law.e: The skills test must follow the last dual instruction within 30 days so the tested skills are still fresh. Do not confuse this with the separate 30-day window for submitting the application after the test itself.

air-law.q: The total minimum flight time required for a PPL(A) is how many hours?
