air-law.e: The minimum total flight experience for a PPL(A) is 45 hours. This total must also contain the required amounts of dual instruction, solo flying, cross-country work, and instrument training.

air-law.q: A PPL(A) holder may not exercise licence privileges unless what applies?
air-law.a: They have only a valid class rating
air-law.b: They have logged at least 10 hours in the last 6 months
air-law.c: They have a valid night rating
air-law.d: They have a valid Part 67 fitness certificate, have submitted it if needed, and comply with maintenance of competency
air-law.ans: They have a valid Part 67 fitness certificate, have submitted it if needed, and comply with maintenance of competency
air-law.e: A PPL(A) holder’s privileges depend on an unbroken chain: a valid Part 67 medical, submitting it when required, and maintaining competency. Losing any one of these suspends the ability to exercise licence privileges, even though the licence itself has not been revoked.

air-law.q: How many hours of dual instruction can be credited from an approved FSTD towards the PPL(A) 45 hours total?
air-law.e: FSTD time is capped at 5 of the 45 PPL(A) hours because a simulator cannot fully replicate real aircraft handling, motion cues and environmental factors — the bulk of training must still happen in an actual aeroplane.

air-law.q: The initial skills test and revalidation check must be conducted in an aircraft with a maximum certificated mass over what?
air-law.e: Requiring the test aircraft to exceed 450 kg MCM excludes microlights and very light aircraft, ensuring the skills test and revalidation check are flown in an aeroplane representative of typical PPL training and operations.

air-law.q: The theoretical knowledge exams for a PPL(A) must be completed within how long from obtaining the first credit?
air-law.e: The 18-month window to complete all theoretical knowledge exams, counted from the first credit, keeps ground-school knowledge current relative to when training culminates — let it lapse and earlier exam credits can expire, forcing a re-sit.

air-law.q: An applicant for a PPL(A) must hold at least what radiotelephony qualification?
air-law.c: An unrestricted certificate of proficiency in radiotelephony
air-law.d: A valid restricted certificate of proficiency in radiotelephony, aeronautical
air-law.ans: A valid restricted certificate of proficiency in radiotelephony, aeronautical
air-law.e: A restricted certificate of proficiency in radiotelephony is the minimum standard required before a PPL(A) is issued, because safe VFR flying depends on being able to communicate reliably with ATC and other traffic.

air-law.q: The required PPL(A) long navigation flight must include what?
air-law.a: At least 150 NM total distance, one point at least 50 NM from base, and two full-stop landings at different aerodromes away from base
air-law.b: At least 100 NM total distance and one full-stop landing
air-law.c: At least 200 NM total distance and two touch-and-go landings
air-law.d: At least 150 NM total distance and two landings at the same aerodrome
air-law.ans: At least 150 NM total distance, one point at least 50 NM from base, and two full-stop landings at different aerodromes away from base
air-law.e: The long navigation flight’s specific requirements — 150 NM total, a point at least 50 NM from base, and two full-stop landings away from base — are designed to genuinely test cross-country planning and diversion skills, not just repeat local circuit flying.

air-law.q: A PPL(A) holder who has not flown as PIC for at least 3 hours in the last 6 months before revalidation must do what?
air-law.b: Undergo sufficient ground and flight training at an approved ATO to meet standard and recency requirements
air-law.c: Complete a refresher skills test in an FSTD only
air-law.d: Apply for a waiver from the Director
air-law.ans: Undergo sufficient ground and flight training at an approved ATO to meet standard and recency requirements
air-law.e: If a PPL(A) holder has not met the 3-hour PIC recency, they must complete sufficient ground and flight training at an approved ATO.

air-law.q: The PPL(A) skills test must demonstrate the applicant’s ability to execute procedures and manoeuvres as prescribed where?
air-law.e: SA-CATS 61 sets the detailed manoeuvres and procedures for the skills test so every candidate is assessed against the same national standard, regardless of which ATO or examiner conducts it.

air-law.q: Under special VFR, a PPL(A) holder may fly in IMC within a control zone if what conditions are met?
air-law.b: They have at least 200 hours total time
air-law.c: They submit a special flight plan
air-law.d: They remain in sight of the surface, clear of cloud, fog and mist, and are authorised by ATC
air-law.ans: They remain in sight of the surface, clear of cloud, fog and mist, and are authorised by ATC
air-law.e: Special VFR in a control zone requires visual reference to the surface, remaining clear of cloud/fog/mist, and ATC authorisation.

air-law.q: Which certificate of fitness must an applicant for a PPL(A) hold?
air-law.a: Certificate issued in terms of Part 67
air-law.d: Aviation fitness certificate from the ATO
air-law.ans: Certificate issued in terms of Part 67
air-law.e: The Part 67 certificate of fitness is required because it is the medical standard confirming a pilot is fit to safely exercise licence privileges — a requirement separate from, but just as essential as, the flying skill tested for the licence itself.

air-law.q: Flight time for holders of Part 62 licences may be substituted how?
air-law.b: Up to the maximum specified in 61.01.9(9)
air-law.c: Only if they have over 100 hours
air-law.ans: Up to the maximum specified in 61.01.9(9)
air-law.e: Part 62 licence holders can substitute flight time up to the cap in 61.01.9(9) so their prior experience is recognised under the newer Part 61 framework, without being fully exempted from the current training standard.

air-law.q: The PIC must ensure what search and rescue information is available on board?
air-law.b: Only ATC frequencies for departure and arrival
air-law.c: All essential information on search and rescue services for the intended flight area
air-law.ans: All essential information on search and rescue services for the intended flight area
air-law.e: Carrying SAR information on board matters because, if things go wrong away from base, the crew may need to contact or coordinate with the SAR services covering that specific area directly, without relying on outside knowledge.

air-law.q: The owner or operator must have what available for immediate communication to rescue coordination centres?
air-law.a: List of all passengers and emergency contacts
air-law.d: List of emergency and survival equipment on board
air-law.ans: List of emergency and survival equipment on board
air-law.e: Rescue coordination centres plan a search around what a downed aircraft is carrying — food, water, signalling equipment, survival gear — so the operator must be able to supply that list immediately to guide the response.

air-law.q: Taxiing on the movement area requires knowledge of what?
air-law.a: Aerodrome layout, routes, signs, markings, lighting, ATC signals, phraseology, and procedures
air-law.c: Aircraft performance and weight and balance only
air-law.ans: Aerodrome layout, routes, signs, markings, lighting, ATC signals, phraseology, and procedures
air-law.e: Aerodromes are shared, often busy environments with multiple runways and taxiways, so a pilot unfamiliar with the layout, signage, lighting, or local phraseology is at real risk of a runway incursion or a wrong-turn conflict with other traffic.

air-law.q: If radio communication is mandatory, may an aeroplane enter the manoeuvring area without it?
air-law.e: Where radio contact is mandatory, ATC needs to be able to communicate directly with any aircraft entering the manoeuvring area to sequence it safely among other traffic; without that link, ATC cannot manage the area.

air-law.q: If radio apparatus is used during taxiing, the person must meet what condition?
air-law.b: Be in contact with the tower only
air-law.e: Requiring authorisation prevents an unqualified person from transmitting on frequency during taxi operations, where a garbled or incorrect radio call could cause confusion among other aircraft and ATC.

air-law.q: The minimum contents of the emergency or survival equipment list are prescribed in what document?
air-law.e: SA-CATS 91 sets the technical standard for what the list must contain, ensuring every operator's emergency equipment list is complete and consistent, so a rescue coordination centre always knows what to expect regardless of operator.

air-law.q: As a general rule, a passenger or crew member may operate a portable electronic device on an aircraft only with whose permission?
air-law.e: The PIC carries ultimate responsibility for the safety of the flight, including the risk that a PED might interfere with aircraft systems, so approval to use one rests with the PIC rather than being left to each passenger's own judgement.

air-law.q: A person may taxi an aeroplane at an aerodrome only if what condition is met?
air-law.a: They have at least 50 hours of flight experience
air-law.b: They hold a valid pilot licence, or have received taxi training from a qualified flight instructor and been declared competent
air-law.c: They hold a valid ATC certificate
air-law.d: They are the owner of the aircraft
air-law.ans: They hold a valid pilot licence, or have received taxi training from a qualified flight instructor and been declared competent
air-law.e: Even without flying, taxiing an aircraft carries collision and control risk around other aircraft, vehicles, and people, so the rule requires either a full pilot licence or specific taxi training and a competence check.

air-law.q: All persons on board an aircraft must follow what?
air-law.b: Commands only if an emergency is declared
air-law.c: All lawful commands of the PIC or crew for safety, security, good order, and discipline
air-law.d: Commands only in commercial air transport
air-law.ans: All lawful commands of the PIC or crew for safety, security, good order, and discipline
air-law.e: The PIC holds final legal authority and responsibility for the safety of the flight, so lawful commands issued for safety, security, or discipline must be obeyed by everyone on board, not just followed at each person's discretion.

air-law.q: Part 91 applies to which aircraft operations?
air-law.a: Only South African registered aircraft operating within the Republic
air-law.b: Only foreign aircraft operating in South Africa
air-law.d: Aircraft operated within the Republic regardless of registration, South African registered aircraft operated internationally, and certain crew or persons on board
air-law.ans: Aircraft operated within the Republic regardless of registration, South African registered aircraft operated internationally, and certain crew or persons on board
air-law.e: Part 91's reach follows the aircraft's registration and location: any aircraft flying within South Africa must comply regardless of where it is registered, and a South African-registered aircraft must comply even when operating abroad — the standard ICAO State-of-Registry principle.

air-law.q: Portable voice recorders, electric shavers, and other approved devices may be used at any time during flight. Is this true or false?
air-law.e: Even devices approved for general use can still be restricted during specific critical phases such as take-off and landing, when crew workload and distraction risk are highest, so 'approved' does not mean 'usable at any time'.

air-law.q: It is prohibited for a person, by act or omission, to do what?
air-law.a: Operate portable electronics without permission only
air-law.b: Endanger the safety of an aircraft or person therein, or allow an aircraft to endanger people or property
air-law.c: Fail to file a flight plan
air-law.ans: Endanger the safety of an aircraft or person therein, or allow an aircraft to endanger people or property
air-law.e: This is the broad catch-all safety duty behind many specific rules: it prohibits both directly endangering people through an act or omission, and knowingly permitting an aircraft to be operated in a way that endangers people or property on the ground.

air-law.q: Which portable electronic devices are exempt from the general prohibition in 91.01.9(1)?
air-law.e: These devices are exempt because they pose negligible interference risk — they are low-power, non-transmitting, or medically essential — unlike ordinary consumer electronics, which must first be shown not to interfere before use.

air-law.q: Alcohol or psychoactive substances may be consumed on board only under what condition?
air-law.d: It does not endanger, or is not likely to endanger, aircraft or occupant safety
air-law.ans: It does not endanger, or is not likely to endanger, aircraft or occupant safety
air-law.e: The rule is outcome-based rather than a blanket ban: consumption is judged by whether it endangers, or is likely to endanger, safety, which allows for controlled alcohol service on some commercial flights while still prohibiting anything that impairs safety.

air-law.q: Any behaviour likely to endanger the aircraft or its occupants is prohibited even if no actual harm occurs. Is this true or false?
air-law.d: Only after warning by the PIC
air-law.e: Aviation safety regulation is preventive: the offence is creating the risk of harm, not just causing actual harm, since waiting for an accident to occur before acting would defeat the purpose of the rule.

air-law.q: Who determines if another portable electronic device will not interfere with aircraft systems?
air-law.b: The operator for commercial air transport or the PIC for non-commercial operations
air-law.ans: The operator for commercial air transport or the PIC for non-commercial operations
air-law.e: Interference testing is a technical judgement, so the rule assigns it to whoever has the resources and operational picture to make that call — the operator for a fleet-wide commercial policy, or the PIC directly for a single non-commercial flight.

air-law.q: If an operator required to retain documents sells the aircraft before the retention period expires, what happens?
air-law.a: They may destroy the documents after transfer
air-law.b: Responsibility passes immediately to the new owner
air-law.c: They must still retain them for the full specified period
air-law.d: They must submit them to the CAA immediately
air-law.ans: They must still retain them for the full specified period
air-law.e: The retention duty attaches to the operator responsible for the aircraft during the period the records cover, not to current ownership, so selling the aircraft cannot be used to avoid the obligation to keep required records available for inspection.

air-law.q: No person may direct a beam of light or energy source at an aircraft or ATC tower in a way that could cause what?
air-law.d: Blindness or otherwise affect the ability to safely perform duties
air-law.ans: Blindness or otherwise affect the ability to safely perform duties
air-law.e: High-intensity beams such as lasers can cause temporary flash-blindness or glare, which is especially dangerous during critical phases like approach and landing, or when directed into an ATC tower where controllers are actively working traffic.

air-law.q: Life-sustaining portable equipment with electrical charge capability may be used under what condition?
air-law.a: If it is proven not to interfere with aircraft systems
air-law.c: At all times without PIC permission
air-law.d: Only when the PIC is not present in the cockpit
air-law.ans: If it is proven not to interfere with aircraft systems
air-law.e: The rule balances a genuine medical need against the risk of electrical interference: life-sustaining equipment is allowed once it has been shown not to affect aircraft systems, rather than being banned outright or allowed unconditionally.

air-law.q: A person may not board an aircraft if they are affected by alcohol or psychoactive substance to what extent?
air-law.a: Any alcohol within the last 24 hours
air-law.b: To the extent that safety is, or is likely to be, endangered
air-law.c: If they appear tired or drowsy
air-law.d: If they have taken any medication in the past week
air-law.ans: To the extent that safety is, or is likely to be, endangered
air-law.e: The standard is impairment-based rather than a fixed limit: a person may not board if their condition, from alcohol or any psychoactive substance, endangers or is likely to endanger the safety of the flight.

air-law.q: A maximum of how many hours of instrument time can be credited towards the 10-hour night rating requirement if the applicant already holds a night or instrument rating on another category?
air-law.e: A maximum of 5 hours may be credited in this situation. The credit reduces duplicated training, but the applicant must still complete the remaining night-rating experience and competency requirements.

air-law.q: The privileges of a night rating allow the holder to do what?
air-law.b: Fly IFR by night without restrictions
air-law.c: Operate only multi-pilot aircraft by night
air-law.d: Exercise the privileges of their licence by night
air-law.ans: Exercise the privileges of their licence by night
air-law.e: Night flying adds real risk — reduced visual references and a higher chance of spatial disorientation — which is why a separate night rating, on top of the base licence, is required before those privileges can be exercised.

air-law.q: The skills test for a night rating must be completed within how many days before the application?
air-law.e: Requiring the night rating skills test within 30 days of application keeps the demonstrated night-flying competency current relative to when the rating is actually granted.

air-law.q: For helicopters, the required dual cross-country flight by night must be at least what?
air-law.b: 75 NM with landings at two different aerodromes
air-law.ans: 75 NM with landings at two different aerodromes
air-law.e: A longer, more demanding cross-country than the training circuits — 75 NM with landings at two different aerodromes — makes sure a helicopter pilot has practised genuine night navigation and diversion decision-making, not just local circuit work.

air-law.q: For a night rating on aeroplanes, the applicant must complete at least what night circuit requirement?
air-law.c: 5 take-offs and 5 landings by night under dual instruction
air-law.ans: 5 take-offs and 5 landings by night under dual instruction
air-law.e: The 5 take-offs and 5 landings by night under dual instruction build the specific skill of judging height, depth and closure rate with reduced visual cues at night — the same requirement, scaled slightly differently, applies to helicopters.

air-law.q: The instrument component of the night rating skills test may be conducted when?
air-law.c: Must be conducted in a simulator
air-law.e: The instrument component can be flown by day because it tests the ability to fly solely by reference to instruments, using a hood or similar device — actual darkness outside is not what is being assessed, so it does not need to be conducted at night.

air-law.q: How many hours of instrument instruction are required for a night rating?
air-law.e: 10 hours of instrument instruction for the night rating builds the ability to control the aircraft purely by reference to instruments if visual references are lost after dark — a real risk given the reduced horizon and ground lighting cues at night.

air-law.q: How many hours of theoretical knowledge instruction are required for a night rating?
air-law.e: 5 hours of theoretical knowledge instruction covers hazards specific to night flying — visual illusions, lighting interpretation, and reduced situational awareness — that do not feature in day-only PPL training.

air-law.q: For a night rating on helicopters, the applicant must complete what?
air-law.a: 3 circuits by day and 3 by night
air-law.c: 5 circuits with 5 take-offs and 5 landings by night under dual instruction
air-law.ans: 5 circuits with 5 take-offs and 5 landings by night under dual instruction
air-law.e: Like the aeroplane requirement, the helicopter night rating’s 5 circuits with 5 take-offs and 5 landings under dual instruction build proficiency at judging height and closure rate using the reduced visual cues available at night.

air-law.q: Which of the following is not a requirement for obtaining a night rating?
air-law.b: Complete the prescribed training under an approved ATO
air-law.e: An instrument rating is not required before obtaining a night rating.

air-law.q: The skills test for a night rating must include at least what?
air-law.e: The skills test only requires 3 take-offs, 3 circuits and 3 landings by night — fewer than the 5 required during training — because the test confirms competency already built during training rather than repeating the full training volume.

air-law.q: The required dual cross-country flight by night for aeroplanes must be at least what distance?
air-law.e: The aeroplane night cross-country’s 150 NM and two full-stop landings are more demanding than the helicopter equivalent (75 NM, two aerodromes), reflecting the different speed and navigation profile of fixed-wing night flying.

air-law.q: A PPL Aeroplane requires at least which class of fitness certificate?
air-law.e: A PPL (Aeroplane) requires at least a Class 2 fitness certificate, the standard for private, non-commercial flying. Class 1, a higher medical standard, is reserved for commercial operations, where pilots carry fare-paying passengers and the consequences of incapacitation are greater.

air-law.q: A Class 2 fitness certificate for a pilot aged fifty-two is valid for how long?
air-law.e: A Class 2 certificate for a 52-year-old pilot is valid for 12 months. Validity periods shorten with age because the medical risk of an in-flight incapacitating event, such as a cardiac issue, rises with age, so older pilots are examined more frequently.

air-law.q: A Class 2 fitness certificate for a pilot aged thirty-five is valid for how long?
air-law.e: A Class 2 certificate for a 35-year-old pilot is valid for 60 months, the longest validity band, reflecting the lower medical risk in younger pilots. Validity shortens progressively as a pilot moves into older age brackets.

air-law.q: For helicopters, the 90-day recency requirement includes what?
air-law.e: For helicopters, the 90-day recency requirement is 3 circuits, including 3 take-offs and 3 landings. Helicopter landings are a perishable skill, so recent hands-on practice is required before carrying passengers or continuing to fly solo.

air-law.q: In a tail-wheel aeroplane, each required landing for recency must be what?
air-law.e: In a tail-wheel aeroplane, each recency landing must be a full-stop landing, not a touch-and-go. Tail-wheel types are less directionally stable on the ground, so the full landing roll-out, not just the touchdown, is what actually tests and maintains the relevant handling skill.

air-law.q: To carry passengers at night as PIC, what must the pilot meet within the last 90 days?
air-law.c: An instrument rating or 1 night take-off and landing as PF
air-law.e: To carry passengers at night as PIC, a pilot must hold an instrument rating or have completed at least one night take-off and landing as pilot flying within the preceding 90 days. Night flying removes most visual cues, so recent hands-on night experience, or instrument qualification, is required before passengers are exposed to that added risk.

air-law.q: If a single instrument is used by more than one pilot, how must it be installed?
air-law.a: Where both pilots can see and operate it
air-law.ans: Where both pilots can see and operate it
air-law.e: A shared instrument must be positioned where both pilots can see and operate it, since only one is fitted rather than duplicated at each station. This lets either pilot monitor and cross-check it in normal operations, and lets the pilot flying reach it even if the other crew member becomes incapacitated.

air-law.q: Aircraft must be equipped with means to indicate what about power supply?
air-law.b: Adequacy of power supply to required flight instruments
air-law.ans: Adequacy of power supply to required flight instruments
air-law.e: The aircraft must have a means of showing whether the power supply to required flight instruments is adequate, such as a voltmeter or warning light on the electrical bus. Many primary instruments (gyros, EFIS displays) depend on electrical power, so a pilot needs early warning of a failing supply before the instruments themselves become unreliable.

air-law.q: Operating limitations required by the type certificate must be shown by what means?
air-law.c: Placards or instrument markings visible from the cockpit
air-law.ans: Placards or instrument markings visible from the cockpit
air-law.e: Operating limitations set by the type certificate, such as never-exceed speed, weight limits or approved fuel grade, must be shown on placards or instrument markings visible from the cockpit. This lets the pilot see the limits at a glance in flight, without stopping to consult the flight manual.

air-law.q: A flight may not commence unless what applies to instruments and equipment?
air-law.c: The item is listed in the flight folio only
air-law.d: All are functioning and safe for the intended operation unless allowed by an MEL
air-law.ans: All are functioning and safe for the intended operation unless allowed by an MEL
air-law.e: A flight may not commence unless all required instruments and equipment are serviceable, or an unserviceable item is specifically permitted under an approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL). The MEL exists so operators don't have to ground an aircraft for every minor defect - it defines exactly which equipment may legally be missing for a given flight.

air-law.q: Glass-panel aircraft must have backup indications for at least which items?
air-law.c: Vertical speed, OAT and radio frequency
air-law.e: Glass-panel (EFIS) aircraft must retain backup indications for attitude, heading, airspeed and altitude - the core parameters needed to keep the aircraft under control. This protects the pilot if the primary electronic display fails or loses power, since that could take out several instruments at once rather than just one.

air-law.q: A VFR aircraft must have which basic flight instruments?
air-law.a: GPS, magnetic compass and radar altimeter
air-law.b: Magnetic compass, timepiece, sensitive altimeter and airspeed indicator
air-law.ans: Magnetic compass, timepiece, sensitive altimeter and airspeed indicator
air-law.e: The basic VFR flight instruments are a magnetic compass, a timepiece, a sensitive altimeter and an airspeed indicator. Each serves a distinct purpose: the compass gives heading reference, the timepiece supports elapsed-time and dead-reckoning navigation, the altimeter confirms terrain and airspace clearance, and the ASI keeps the aircraft within its safe speed range.

air-law.q: In aviation, an infant is a passenger who has not reached which age?
air-law.e: An infant is a passenger who has not yet reached their second birthday. This threshold matters mainly for seating and restraint rules: infants under two are generally held rather than given an individual seat, unlike children aged two and older.

air-law.q: Refuelling an aircraft with aviation gasoline may take place with passengers on board. Is this true or false?
air-law.e: Refuelling with aviation gasoline may not take place with passengers on board, because avgas is highly volatile and any spill or vapour build-up creates a fire and explosion risk that passengers, who may not know the evacuation routes, cannot be expected to react to quickly.

air-law.q: A hand-operated fire extinguisher must be carried on which aircraft?
air-law.e: A hand-operated fire extinguisher must be carried on all aircraft, since an in-flight fire (commonly electrical) has to be dealt with immediately by the crew - there is no fire brigade available in the air. It also covers a fire on the ground during start-up or refuelling.

air-law.q: “Day” is the period between what times?
air-law.b: 15 minutes before sunrise to 15 minutes after sunset
air-law.c: 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset
air-law.d: 15 minutes after sunrise to 15 minutes before sunset
air-law.ans: 15 minutes before sunrise to 15 minutes after sunset
air-law.e: Day runs from 15 minutes before sunrise to 15 minutes after sunset — the margin covers usable twilight visibility rather than the exact instant of sunrise or sunset. This boundary matters because it decides when a flight crosses into night flying for logging purposes, and it is the exact mirror of the “night” definition tested separately.

air-law.q: Flight time means which period?
air-law.a: From engine start until engine shutdown
air-law.b: From taxi start until parking brake set
air-law.c: From the moment the aircraft lifts off until it stops at the end of its landing roll
air-law.d: From take-off clearance until landing clearance cancelled
air-law.ans: From taxi start until parking brake set
air-law.e: This defines flight time as strictly airborne time — lift-off to the end of the landing roll — the period totalled toward logged flight-hour experience. Do not confuse it with block time (engine start to shutdown) or taxi time, which are tracked separately.

air-law.q: For an aircraft operated by night, is a serviceable rotating beacon or strobe light required?
air-law.e: By night, a serviceable rotating beacon or strobe light is required so the aircraft stays visible to other traffic against a dark sky, well beyond the range at which ordinary position lights alone would be seen. This anti-collision lighting is normally switched on before engine start and left on for the whole flight.

air-law.q: An aeroplane is an example of what type of rating?
air-law.e: Aeroplane is an aircraft category rating. Category identifies the broad type of aircraft, while class and type ratings describe more specific groups or individual aircraft types.

air-law.q: A single-engine piston aeroplane is an example of what type of rating?
air-law.e: A single-engine piston aeroplane sits under a class rating rather than a type rating because pilots can move between similar single-engine piston aircraft without a rating for each individual model — type ratings are reserved for more complex or high-performance aircraft.

air-law.q: A standard first-aid kit is required in which aircraft?
air-law.b: Only aircraft with more than 6 seats
air-law.d: Only aircraft flying outside an ATZ
air-law.e: A standard first-aid kit must be carried in all aircraft so that basic treatment is available for an injury or sudden illness in flight, when medical help is not immediately reachable. It must also be kept accessible and in serviceable condition, not just present on board.

air-law.q: A pilot may use a public road as a place of landing or take-off only in what case?
air-law.e: Roads are not designed, surveyed, or kept clear for aircraft operations, so using one is only justified when the alternative — not landing at all — poses a greater risk, i.e. a genuine emergency.

air-law.q: The manoeuvring area of an aerodrome includes what?
air-law.c: Runways, taxiways and apron parking bays
air-law.e: The manoeuvring area is the part of the aerodrome used for take-off, landing and taxiing, made up of the runways and taxiways. It excludes aprons, which are used for parking, loading and servicing aircraft. Together, the manoeuvring area and the aprons make up the wider movement area.

air-law.q: For an aircraft operated by day, is a serviceable rotating beacon or strobe light required?
air-law.e: By day, a rotating beacon or strobe light is not mandatory, since the aircraft is normally visible in daylight without extra anti-collision lighting. Many pilots still switch it on anyway, particularly before start-up and taxi, purely for extra conspicuity around other traffic.

air-law.q: A seat must be provided for each person of what age or older?
air-law.e: Each person aged two years or older must have an individual seat. This ensures that the occupant can be properly restrained during take-off, landing, turbulence, and an emergency.

air-law.q: Formation flights may only be conducted under what condition?
air-law.c: Only if all aircraft are from the same operator
air-law.d: By arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft in the formation
air-law.ans: By arrangement with the PIC of each aircraft in the formation
air-law.e: Formation flying deliberately reduces the normal separation between aircraft, so each PIC must agree to it in advance and take on responsibility for maintaining safe spacing, since ATC does not provide separation within the formation.

air-law.q: Where smoking is permitted in an aircraft, when is it still prohibited?
air-law.a: During take-off, approach to land, or when the aircraft is on the ground
air-law.ans: During take-off, approach to land, or when the aircraft is on the ground
air-law.e: Even where smoking is otherwise permitted on board, it is always prohibited during take-off, approach to land, and while the aircraft is on the ground. These are the phases with the highest fire risk, such as fuel vapours and proximity to fuel trucks, and the times a rapid evacuation might be needed, so no naked flame or ember is allowed.

air-law.q: Night operation equipment includes which item for each crew member?
air-law.e: Night operation requires an electrical torch for each crew member, mainly as a backup for checking the panel, instruments or circuit breakers if the aircraft's lighting or electrical system fails in flight. It also has an obvious use during any unscheduled stop or emergency after dark.

air-law.q: For a non-pressurised aircraft between 10 000 ft and 12 000 ft, oxygen must be available if the flight exceeds what duration?
air-law.e: Between 10 000 ft and 12 000 ft in a non-pressurised aircraft, the flight is limited to 120 minutes without supplemental oxygen. Reduced oxygen at these altitudes leads to hypoxia, and its effects - impaired judgement and slower reactions - build up with time, so exposure is time-limited rather than the altitude being banned outright.

air-law.q: Simulated emergencies affecting aircraft flight characteristics may be carried out when?
air-law.a: At any time with instructor approval
air-law.d: When passengers are not on board the aircraft
air-law.ans: When passengers are not on board the aircraft
air-law.e: Simulated emergencies that affect how the aircraft handles carry inherent risk, so they are restricted to training flights without passengers, protecting people who have not consented to that added risk.

air-law.q: Smoking on a licensed aerodrome is prohibited within what distance of an aircraft?
air-law.e: Smoking is prohibited within 15 metres of any aircraft on a licensed aerodrome. This distance is enforced because of the fire and explosion risk posed by fuel vapours near parked or operating aircraft.

air-law.q: “Night” is the period between what times?
air-law.b: 15 minutes after sunset to 15 minutes before sunrise
air-law.c: 30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise
air-law.d: 15 minutes before sunset to 15 minutes after sunrise
air-law.ans: 15 minutes after sunset to 15 minutes before sunrise
air-law.e: Night runs from 15 minutes after sunset to 15 minutes before sunrise — the mirror image of the “day” definition. Getting this boundary right matters because flights inside this window require night currency, and without a night rating a PPL(A) holder cannot legally fly in it.

air-law.q: A certificate of release to service, or a copy thereof if required, must be carried on which aircraft?
air-law.e: A certificate of release to service, or a permitted copy, must be carried on board every aircraft to prove it has been legally released as airworthy — this applies to all aircraft, not only commercial or training types.

air-law.q: If an intercepting aircraft rocks its wings in front and to the left of the intercepted aircraft, what does it mean?
air-law.b: Follow me away from a prohibited area
air-law.d: Follow me to a landing terrain
air-law.ans: Follow me to a landing terrain
air-law.e:
RULE
The First Series interception signal is: the intercepting aircraft rocks its wings while positioned in front and to the LEFT of the intercepted aircraft (flashing navigation and landing lights at night), followed by a slow level turn onto a specific course. Meaning: follow me away from a prohibited area and to a landing terrain. The intercepted aircraft acknowledges by rocking its wings (showing steady landing lights at night) and follows the interceptor.

ANSWER
Follow me to a landing terrain

air-law.q: A pilot may fly above a prohibited area if what condition is met?
air-law.a: The aircraft remains above the specified upper limit of the prohibited area
air-law.b: The flight is conducted by day only
air-law.c: The aircraft is below 1500 ft AGL
air-law.ans: The aircraft remains above the specified upper limit of the prohibited area
air-law.e: A pilot may fly above a prohibited area once above its specified upper limit, since the prohibited airspace itself only extends from the ground up to that height - for example FAP68 over the Modderfontein explosives factory extends from the ground to 1000 ft. Above that altitude, the aircraft is simply outside the prohibited airspace altogether.

air-law.q: A pilot may fly through a restricted area only if what has been obtained?
air-law.e: Entry into a restricted area requires permission from the appropriate authority, usually the military body responsible for it (per AIP ENR 5). These areas typically protect hazardous activity such as weapons testing or live firing, so unauthorised entry is a genuine safety risk, not just a paperwork formality.

air-law.q: The carriage of a flight folio is required in which aircraft?
air-law.e: A flight folio is a mandatory operational record required on every aircraft, not only commercial ones, used to log details such as flights flown and fuel and oil uplifts.

air-law.q: Unless two-way communication has already been established, what frequency is used by an intercepted and intercepting aircraft?
air-law.e: If two-way communication has not already been established, an intercepted aircraft should attempt to make contact on the international distress frequency 121.5 MHz (or another suitable frequency), while squawking 7700.

air-law.q: Information on the latest restricted areas affecting flights can be found where?
air-law.a: Latest AIP, AIP SUP, AICs and NOTAM
air-law.ans: Latest AIP, AIP SUP, AICs and NOTAM
air-law.e: Current information on restricted and other regulated areas is found in the latest AIP, AIP Supplements, AICs and NOTAMs. Boundaries, activation times and status can change, so a pilot relying only on an old chart could unknowingly plan a route through airspace that is now active or restricted differently.

air-law.q: In a right-hand circuit, an aircraft may overtake a slower aircraft by passing on which side?
air-law.e: Overtaking near an aerodrome has an exception to the general "always pass right" rule: in a right-hand circuit, the overtaking aircraft passes on the left — the outside of the circuit's turn. This keeps it clear of aircraft that are about to bank onto the next leg of a right-hand pattern. Outside the circuit, or in a left-hand circuit, the general rule (always alter heading/pass to the right) still applies.

air-law.q: When two aircraft approach head-on with danger of collision, each aircraft must alter heading in which direction?
air-law.e: Both aircraft turning right avoids the risk of pilots turning toward each other if the rule were ambiguous; this mirrors the road-traffic convention of keeping right and gives every pilot one predictable response to a head-on conflict.

air-law.q: A list of signals for use by intercepting aircraft must be carried when?
air-law.e: Although interception is very rare, pilots should carry a copy of the interception signals on all flights, to be prepared for any eventuality — the signals also form part of the R/T certificate syllabus.

air-law.q: Flight crew member licences or certified copies must be carried when?
air-law.e: Flight crew licences, or certified copies, must be carried on every flight so an inspector or authority can verify a crew member’s qualification and currency on the spot — not only on international flights. This is one of several documents, alongside the certificate of release to service and registration, required on board at all times.

air-law.q: An aircraft may not be operated unless a restraint device is provided for each passenger who is what age?
air-law.e: A restraint device must be provided for each passenger under two years of age. Below that age a child is generally too small for a standard seat harness, so a supplementary restraint, such as an infant strap held by an adult, is required instead of, or alongside, an individual seat.

air-law.q: A record of each fuel and oil uplift must be kept where?
air-law.e: Fuel and oil uplifts are recorded in the aircraft flight folio, not the pilot’s personal logbook, because the data belongs with the aircraft’s operational record — where it can be cross-checked against flight time and used to verify weight and balance or catch discrepancies.

air-law.q: A pilot may fly through a danger area under what condition?
air-law.b: Only with a special VFR clearance
air-law.d: At own risk while ensuring required broadcast communication has been established
air-law.ans: At own risk while ensuring required broadcast communication has been established
air-law.e: A pilot may fly through a danger area at their own risk, keeping the required broadcast or listening watch on the relevant frequency. Unlike a restricted area, entry is not barred - but danger areas often host military or general flying training activity, so situational awareness and traffic avoidance are entirely the pilot's own responsibility.

air-law.q: Original or certified copies of documents to be carried on a domestic flight include which of the following?
air-law.a: Certificate of release to service, certificate of registration and the pilot’s licence
air-law.ans: Certificate of release to service, certificate of registration and the pilot’s licence
air-law.e: These three documents together prove the aircraft is airworthy (release to service), correctly registered (certificate of registration), and being flown by a qualified pilot (licence) — the minimum paper trail an inspector needs to confirm a flight is legal. This applies to domestic flights too, not only international ones.

air-law.q: The mass and centre of gravity of an aircraft must be established at least how often?
air-law.e: The mass and centre of gravity of an aircraft must be established, by weighing, at least every 5 years. Repairs, repaints, modifications and equipment changes all shift an aircraft's true weight and balance over time, so periodic reweighing keeps the figures pilots rely on for loading calculations accurate.

air-law.q: At an unmanned aerodrome, the PIC is responsible for what circuit direction unless a right-hand circuit is in force?
air-law.d: Turns as directed by wind direction
air-law.e: At an unmanned aerodrome, the pilot-in-command is responsible for flying all turns in the traffic pattern to the left, unless a right-hand circuit has been established for that runway. Left-hand circuits are the default because, in most light aircraft, the pilot sits in the left seat and gets a clearer view of the runway during the turn onto base and final. A right-hand circuit is only flown where published or instructed, often to avoid noise-sensitive areas or terrain on the left.

air-law.q: When two heavier-than-air aircraft approach an aerodrome to land, which has right of way?
air-law.c: The aircraft closer to the runway centreline
air-law.d: The aircraft at the lower level
air-law.ans: The aircraft at the lower level
air-law.e: The lower aircraft is normally closer to committing to the approach and has a more restricted view of aircraft above it, so giving it right of way keeps the aircraft with the better vantage point — the higher one — responsible for keeping clear.

air-law.q: Outside an aerodrome circuit, an aircraft overtaking another at the same height and heading must pass on which side?
air-law.e: The overtaken aircraft keeps right of way and should not have to manoeuvre, so the overtaking aircraft, which has more room and information to act safely, is the one required to move — always to the right, for predictability.

air-law.q: An aircraft flight folio must be retained by the owner or operator for how long from the date of the last entry?
air-law.e: The flight folio’s 5-year retention period is far longer than the 12-month retention that applies to a certificate of release to service after a periodic inspection. The folio is the aircraft’s ongoing operational history, so it must be kept for longer to support maintenance and audit purposes.

air-law.q: The period of validity of a Class 2 fitness certificate for a private pilot over the age of 40 is what?
air-law.e: Correct answer: 12 months. For a private pilot over the age of 40, a Class 2 medical certificate is normally valid for 12 months, shorter than the validity given to younger pilots. A medical examiner may impose an even shorter period where closer monitoring of the pilot's fitness is required.

air-law.q: A vehicle towing an aircraft has right of way over what?
air-law.d: An aircraft taxiing across an apron
air-law.ans: An aircraft taxiing across an apron
air-law.e: A vehicle towing an aircraft has very limited manoeuvrability and cannot stop or divert quickly, so it is given right of way over a taxiing aircraft, which has full engine power and steering available to give way instead.

air-law.q: If an intercepting aircraft rocks its wings in front and to the left of the intercepted aircraft, what does it mean?
air-law.a: Follow me away from a prohibited area
air-law.ans: Follow me away from a prohibited area
air-law.e: This is the First Series interception signal: the intercepting aircraft rocks its wings (and, at night, flashes its navigation and landing lights) while positioned in front and to the left of the intercepted aircraft, followed by a slow level turn onto a specific course. It means follow me — away from a prohibited area and towards a landing aerodrome. The intercepted aircraft acknowledges by rocking its wings (showing steady landing lights at night) and follows the interceptor.

air-law.q: A licence holder must notify the Commissioner of a change in postal address within how long?
air-law.e: A pilot licence holder must notify the Commissioner of any change of postal address within 14 days, so that CAA records and correspondence remain accurate.

air-law.q: In an aircraft using fuses, how many spare fuses must be carried?
air-law.e: Where fuses, rather than circuit breakers, protect the electrical system, spares must equal at least 10% of each rating or three, whichever is greater. A blown fuse cannot be reset like a breaker, so without spares a failed circuit - such as instrument or avionics power - stays lost for the rest of the flight.

air-law.q: “Date of application” for issuing, renewing or reissuing a licence, certificate or rating means what?
air-law.a: The date the form is signed
air-law.b: The date the skills test is completed
air-law.d: The date the application is received in prescribed form by the Commissioner
air-law.ans: The date the application is received in prescribed form by the Commissioner
air-law.e: The "date of application" is not when the form is signed, the skills test is passed, or payment is made — it is the date the Commissioner actually receives the application in the prescribed form.

air-law.q: VFR navigation and associated equipment includes which of the following?
air-law.a: Airspeed indicator and a clock or watch showing hours, minutes and seconds
air-law.ans: Airspeed indicator and a clock or watch showing hours, minutes and seconds
air-law.e: VFR navigation equipment includes an airspeed indicator and a clock or watch showing hours, minutes and seconds. Accurate elapsed time is essential for dead-reckoning navigation, timing legs between waypoints, and for fuel planning on a cross-country flight.

air-law.q: A night rating is valid for how long?
air-law.b: As long as the holder’s pilot licence is valid
air-law.ans: As long as the holder’s pilot licence is valid
air-law.e: A night rating has no separate expiry or revalidation cycle of its own — it simply stays valid for as long as the underlying pilot licence does, unlike some other ratings that require periodic revalidation flights.

air-law.q: An Aerodrome Traffic Zone is an airspace of defined dimensions at an aerodrome that is what?
air-law.c: Controlled airspace where aerodrome control is in operation
air-law.d: A prohibited area around the aerodrome
air-law.ans: Controlled airspace where aerodrome control is in operation
air-law.e: An ATZ is airspace of defined dimensions established around an aerodrome to protect traffic taking off, landing and flying the circuit. Note the nuance here: an ATZ can be Class C, D or G — Class C/D ATZs are controlled airspace with aerodrome control in operation (this option), but a Class G ATZ is uncontrolled and only gets AFIS (advice, not control). Most ATZs at busier fields are C/D, which is why this is the expected answer, but don't assume every ATZ is controlled.

air-law.q: For VFR in uncontrolled airspace at or below 1000 ft AGL by day, what are the minima?
air-law.a: 1.5 km visibility and clear of cloud
air-law.b: 8 km visibility and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.c: 5 km visibility, 1.5 km horizontally and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.d: 5 km visibility, clear of cloud and with the surface in sight
air-law.ans: 5 km visibility, clear of cloud and with the surface in sight
air-law.e: For an aeroplane operating in Class F or G airspace in the lowest VFR altitude band, the current South African minima are 5 km flight visibility, clear of cloud, and with the surface in sight. The 1.5 km exception shown elsewhere applies to qualifying helicopter operations, not an ordinary PPL aeroplane question.

air-law.q: An ATS flight plan must be filed for which of the following?
air-law.b: A flight crossing an international boundary even if no landing will be made
air-law.c: A flight between two ATZs even if no controlled or advisory airspace is entered en route
air-law.d: A flight from a manned aerodrome to an ATZ in the stated circumstances
air-law.e: Correct answer: All of the above. An ATS flight plan is mandatory for a flight crossing an international boundary (even without landing), for flights between two airfields where an ATSU is operating (which covers two ATZs, even if no other controlled or advisory airspace is entered en route), and for the stated manned-aerodrome-to-ATZ case — these are all separate items on the list of flights for which a flight plan must be filed.

air-law.q: The PIC of a domestic VFR cross-country flight must not commence take-off unless what has been obtained?
air-law.b: A favourable meteorological forecast for the route
air-law.ans: A favourable meteorological forecast for the route
air-law.e: Before commencing a domestic VFR cross-country flight, the PIC must have obtained a favourable meteorological forecast for the route. VFR flight depends entirely on maintaining visual reference to the ground, so an unfavourable en-route forecast could put an unqualified pilot into cloud or poor visibility they cannot legally or safely handle.

air-law.q: In the case of radio failure, a flight with an activated flight plan may continue in controlled airspace if what procedures are complied with?
air-law.e: Correct answer: Communication failure procedures. If the radio fails after a flight plan has been activated, the pilot may continue in controlled airspace by following the published communication (radio) failure procedures, rather than being required to leave controlled airspace immediately.

air-law.q: Prior to undergoing the revalidation skills test, a private pilot must have flown at least how many hours as PIC in the preceding 6 months?
air-law.e: A PPL holder who has not flown at least 3 hours as pilot-in-command during the six months before a revalidation check must complete sufficient refresher training at an approved ATO before the check. The 3-hour figure is therefore the experience threshold used by the regulation.

air-law.q: The take-off visibility required for an aeroplane on a VFR flight departing from an ATZ is what?
air-law.e: Normal VFR operations within an aerodrome traffic zone require at least 5 km ground visibility. The aerodrome ceiling requirement is tested separately and is normally 1 500 ft for take-off, landing, or flight within the ATZ.

air-law.q: To change to another type of aeroplane not previously flown within one class rating, the pilot must undergo what?
air-law.d: No training if the class rating is valid
air-law.e: Differences or familiarisation training, rather than a full retest, is enough when moving to a new type within an already-held class rating, because the pilot is still operating broadly similar aircraft and only needs briefing on what differs in the new type’s systems and handling.

air-law.q: A pilot without a night rating may carry a passenger by day only if they have completed what recently?
air-law.a: One take-off and landing within 30 days
air-law.c: Three take-offs and landings within the preceding 90 days
air-law.ans: Three take-offs and landings within the preceding 90 days
air-law.e: A pilot without a night rating may carry a passenger by day only after completing at least three take-offs and three landings in the preceding 90 days, in the same class or type/variant. This recency rule ensures the pilot's hands-on take-off and landing skill is genuinely current, not just that the licence itself remains valid.

air-law.q: A VFR pilot crossing an airway at right angles in otherwise uncontrolled airspace may do so without filing a flight plan if what condition is met?
air-law.a: The aircraft remains below 1500 ft AGL
air-law.d: Clearance is obtained from the ATSU responsible for the airway
air-law.ans: Clearance is obtained from the ATSU responsible for the airway
air-law.e: Correct answer: Clearance is obtained from the ATSU responsible for the airway. A VFR pilot may cross a Class C airway at roughly right angles without filing a flight plan, but the airway is still controlled airspace, so the pilot must contact the responsible ATSU well in advance and get clearance to cross. If the ATSU cannot be reached, or clearance is not granted, the pilot must descend below the airway's lower limit before crossing.

air-law.q: An applicant for a private pilot licence must undergo the skills test within what period after passing the theoretical knowledge examinations?
air-law.e: The 6-month window ties the skills test to how recently theoretical knowledge was passed, ensuring the practical test is not conducted long after the ground-school knowledge was demonstrated — a different clock from the 30-day rule tied to the last dual instruction.

air-law.q: A cross-country flight may enter or leave an ATZ when ground visibility and ceiling are at least what?
air-law.e: Correct answer: 5 km visibility and 500 ft ceiling. This is the lower cross-country exception, not the standard ATZ minima: an aeroplane may take off and leave on a cross-country flight, or return and land, at an ATZ (Class C, D or G) once the ceiling is at least 500 ft and visibility at least 5 km, provided the pilot is in radio contact with the Tower or AFIS. This is lower than the 1 500 ft ceiling required for general operations, such as circuits, within the ATZ.

air-law.q: Cloud ceiling means the height above the surface of cloud bases below what altitude and covering more than half the sky?
air-law.e: Cloud ceiling is defined as the height above the surface of the base of the lowest cloud layer below 20 000 ft that covers more than half the sky. This matters because a thin, scattered layer covering less than half the sky does not count as a ceiling for VMC purposes, even if it sits lower than a true overcast layer above it.

air-law.q: Unless otherwise authorised by an ATSU, a flight plan for departure into controlled or advisory airspace must be filed at least when?
air-law.e: Unless the responsible ATSU has authorised otherwise, a flight plan for departure into controlled or advisory airspace must be filed at least 30 minutes before departure (60 minutes for an international flight). This lead time gives the ATSU enough time to process the plan and pass the details on to the units that will handle the flight.

air-law.q: For an aeroplane flying VFR below 10 000 ft AMSL but above 3 000 ft AMSL, or above 1 000 ft above terrain, whichever is higher, what minima apply?
air-law.a: 5 km visibility, 1.5 km horizontally and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.b: 1.5 km visibility, clear of cloud and with the surface in sight
air-law.c: 8 km visibility, 1.5 km horizontally and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.d: 5 km visibility, 600 m horizontally and 500 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.ans: 5 km visibility, 1.5 km horizontally and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.e: In this altitude band, the current South African VFR minima are 5 km flight visibility with at least 1.5 km horizontal and 1 000 ft vertical clearance from cloud. The older 2 000 ft horizontal and 500 ft vertical figures are no longer the values published in the current AIP table.

air-law.q: If a flight plan for controlled or advisory airspace is filed in flight, it must be filed at least when?
air-law.b: 10 minutes before entry into controlled or advisory airspace
air-law.ans: 10 minutes before entry into controlled or advisory airspace
air-law.e: If a flight plan for controlled or advisory airspace is filed in flight, only permitted in exceptional circumstances, it must reach ATS at least 10 minutes before entering that airspace, given on first contact. Even this shortened notice still gives controllers minimum lead time to fit the flight into their traffic picture before it arrives.

air-law.q: For a controlled flight deviating from its current flight plan, a revised ETA must be notified to ATC if the error exceeds what?
air-law.e: Correct answer: 2 minutes. Per CAR 91.03.4/ICAO, a controlled flight must notify ATC once its estimated time at the next reporting point or destination changes by more than 2 minutes from the flight-planned time. Older AIP ENR 1.10 and AIC D003/2022 text still quotes 3 minutes, but 2 minutes is the current, correct figure.

air-law.q: A pilot may apply an amendment to an ATC clearance only when?
air-law.e: A proposed amendment to an ATC clearance may not be applied until ATC has approved it. Since ATC is separating this aircraft from others under its control, an unapproved change could put it into conflict with traffic the pilot cannot see.

air-law.q: An aircraft for which an ATS flight plan has been filed may receive what advantage?
air-law.a: Priority over aircraft for which flight plans have not been filed
air-law.b: Automatic clearance into all controlled airspace
air-law.ans: Priority over aircraft for which flight plans have not been filed
air-law.e: A filed ATS flight plan can give an aircraft priority over aircraft without one, because it tells ATC the pilot's intentions in advance, letting controllers plan their sequencing around it. An aircraft with no flight plan is simply fitted in as capacity allows.

air-law.q: Before entering controlled airspace, the PIC must ensure what?
air-law.a: A flight plan has been closed
air-law.c: The aircraft is below 1500 ft AGL
air-law.e: Before entering controlled airspace, the PIC must ensure two-way radio communication has been established with the relevant ATC unit. Controlled airspace depends on ATC being able to sequence, separate and instruct all traffic within it - something that is impossible without a working communication link.

air-law.q: Every VFR flight must be conducted with visual reference to the surface and not above more than what cloud amount within 5 NM?
air-law.e: A VFR flight must stay clear enough of cloud to keep visual contact with the ground — specifically, not more than 3/8 cloud cover within a 5 NM radius. This exists because VFR flying depends entirely on the pilot seeing outside to navigate and avoid terrain/traffic; too much cloud within that radius risks losing that visual reference even if the immediate patch of sky is clear. Exam tip: this is one of three VFR conditions that must ALL be met together (visual contact with the ground/objects, this cloud-amount limit, and the ceiling/visibility/cloud-distance minima table) — failing any one of them means the flight cannot legally be conducted VFR.

air-law.q: A private pilot without an instrument rating may not act as flight crew if flight time exceeds or is likely to exceed what during the preceding 12 months?
air-law.e: The limit is 1000 hours in the preceding 12 months. It is an accumulated flight-time limit intended to prevent excessive workload and fatigue, not a target that a pilot should try to reach.

air-law.q: Unless authorised by the Commissioner, outside controlled airspace and below FL100 an aircraft may not exceed what indicated airspeed?
air-law.e: Outside controlled airspace and below FL100, an aircraft may not exceed 250 kt IAS unless authorised by the Commissioner. Keeping speeds down at lower levels reduces closure rates and gives pilots more time to see and avoid other traffic.

air-law.q: Except with prior written approval, no aircraft may circle or repeatedly fly over an open-air assembly of persons below what height?
air-law.e: The 3 000 ft minimum keeps aircraft well clear of a crowd on the ground, limiting the consequences of noise, debris, or — in the worst case — a forced landing directly over a large group of people.

air-law.q: VFR flights are not required to comply with the semi-circular rule when operating at what height?
air-law.e: Correct answer: Less than 1500 ft above ground. The semi-circular rule applies to aircraft cruising at or above 1500 ft AGL. Below that height, in uncontrolled airspace, VFR flights are not required to comply with it.

air-law.q: Special VFR operations may be conducted, subject to ATC approval, within which airspace?
air-law.e: Special VFR may be conducted, subject to ATC approval, only within a control zone (CTR), not in an ATZ. CTRs protect IFR traffic at busier aerodromes and can be formally declared IMC, which is exactly what creates the need for a special, ATC-authorised VFR clearance in the first place.

air-law.q: Unless authorised by an ATSU, a reciprocating-engine aircraft may not fly within a CTR or ATZ faster than what indicated airspeed?
air-law.e: Within a CTR or ATZ, a reciprocating-engine aircraft may not exceed 160 kt IAS unless the responsible ATSU authorises a higher speed. This keeps piston traffic compatible with circuit speeds and separation from other aerodrome traffic.

air-law.q: No person shall act as a flight crew member within what period following blood donation?
air-law.e: No flight crew duties may be performed within 72 hours of donating blood. Blood donation temporarily lowers red blood cell count and oxygen-carrying capacity, which combines badly with the reduced cabin oxygen levels experienced at altitude.

air-law.q: No person shall act as a flight crew member if the flight time exceeds or is likely to exceed what in the preceding 90 days?
air-law.e: Flight crew may not fly if flight time in the preceding 90 days exceeds, or would exceed, 400 hours - the planned flight itself must be included in that calculation. The limit exists to prevent cumulative fatigue building up over a rolling three-month period.

air-law.q: Unless instructed otherwise by an ATSU, an aircraft at or below 1500 ft AGL following a line feature must fly where?
air-law.a: To the left of the line feature
air-law.c: At least 5 NM away from the line feature
air-law.d: To the right of the line feature
air-law.ans: To the right of the line feature
air-law.e: Flying to the right of a line feature at low level keeps aircraft travelling in opposite directions along the same feature safely apart — the same logic as keeping to one side of a road.

air-law.q: Away from built-up areas or open-air assemblies, the minimum height for flight is what?
air-law.e: The 500 ft minimum away from people and buildings still leaves margin to select a forced-landing area if the engine fails, while permitting legitimate low-level work such as agricultural or survey flying.

air-law.q: Except by individual permission, aircraft may not be flown aerobatically within 5 NM of an aerodrome unless at least what height AGL?
air-law.e: Without individual permission from the Director, aerobatic flight within 5 NM of an aerodrome must be conducted at least 4 000 ft above ground level. The restriction protects circuit traffic and aircraft arriving at or departing from the aerodrome.

air-law.q: Unless otherwise directed by ATC, the semi-circular rule applies above what height?
air-law.e: Correct answer: 1500 ft AGL. Unless ATC directs otherwise, all aircraft cruising at or above 1500 ft AGL must comply with the semi-circular rule, choosing odd or even flight levels (plus 500 ft for VFR) according to their magnetic track.

air-law.q: Subject to ATC approval, special VFR operations may be conducted within a CTR with at least what cloud base and visibility?
air-law.a: 300 ft cloud base and 800 m visibility
air-law.b: 1000 ft cloud base and 5 km visibility
air-law.c: 1500 ft cloud base and 8 km visibility
air-law.d: 600 ft cloud base and 1500 m visibility
air-law.ans: 600 ft cloud base and 1500 m visibility
air-law.e: An aeroplane may operate Special VFR inside a control zone only with an ATC clearance, by day, with a cloud ceiling of at least 600 ft and visibility of at least 1.5 km. The flight must also meet the radio and traffic-delay conditions in the rule.

air-law.q: An aircraft maintains 344°T, drift 6° right, variation 20°W, high ground 4300 ft AMSL. What is the most appropriate VFR flight level?
air-law.e:
WORKING
- A heading of 344 degrees T with 6 degrees right drift gives a true track of approximately 350 degrees T.
- With 20 degrees west variation, the magnetic track is approximately 010 degrees M - the eastbound VFR sector (000-179), which uses odd-thousand flight levels plus 500 ft.
- High ground of 4 300 ft AMSL falls in the 3000-5000 ft band, which needs at least 1500 ft of terrain clearance, giving a minimum safe altitude of about 5 800 ft. FL055 (5 500 ft) falls short, so the next available odd VFR level, FL075 (7 500 ft), is used.

FINAL ANSWER
FL075

air-law.q: A VFR aircraft on magnetic track 359° and another VFR aircraft on magnetic track 180° could be at what relative flight levels?
air-law.d: Neither may use a flight level
air-law.e: Correct answer: The same flight level. Magnetic tracks of 359° and 180° both fall within the 180°-359° (westbound) sector, so both aircraft would select from the same set of even flight levels (plus 500 ft for VFR) — nothing in the semi-circular rule itself forces them onto different levels.

air-law.q: When approaching an unmanned aerodrome to land, the PIC should fly overhead at least at what height to establish runway in use?
air-law.e: When approaching an unmanned aerodrome to land, the pilot-in-command should first fly overhead the aerodrome at a height of at least 2 000 ft AGL. This overhead position allows the pilot to check the windsock, look out for other traffic, and establish which runway is in use before descending to join the circuit correctly.

air-law.q: In terms of the semi-circular rule, flight levels are selected based on what?
air-law.e: Correct answer: Magnetic track. The semi-circular rule allocates flight levels according to the aircraft's magnetic track: 000°-179° (roughly easterly) uses odd levels, and 180°-359° (roughly westerly) uses even levels.

air-law.q: No person shall act as a flight crew member within what period following scuba diving?
air-law.e: No flight crew duties may be performed within 24 hours of scuba diving. Diving leaves residual dissolved nitrogen in the blood, and flying, even in a pressurised cabin, exposes the body to lower ambient pressure, risking decompression sickness if too little time has passed.

air-law.q: An aircraft maintains track 160°T, drift 8° right, variation 20°W, high ground 3800 ft AMSL. What is the most appropriate VFR flight level?
air-law.e:
WORKING
- The stated true track is 160 degrees T.
- With 20 degrees west variation, the magnetic track is approximately 180 degrees M - the westbound VFR sector (180-359), which uses even-thousand flight levels plus 500 ft.
- High ground of 3 800 ft AMSL falls in the 3000-5000 ft band, which needs at least 1500 ft of terrain clearance, giving a minimum safe altitude of about 5 300 ft. FL045 (4 500 ft) falls short, so the next available even VFR level, FL065 (6 500 ft), is used.

FINAL ANSWER
FL065

air-law.q: No flight crew member may consume alcohol within how long before a flight?
air-law.e: A flight crew member may not consume alcohol during the 8 hours before acting as crew. The rule is only a minimum interval; a pilot must also be completely free from impairment or a hangover.

air-law.q: No person shall act as a flight crew member if the flight time exceeds or is likely to exceed what during the preceding 6 months?
air-law.e: Flight crew may not fly if flight time in the preceding 6 months exceeds, or would exceed, 700 hours, again counting the planned flight. Like the 90-day and 12-month limits, this rolling cap exists to prevent cumulative fatigue.

air-law.q: What is the minimum height for an aircraft to fly across an aerodrome without conforming to the traffic pattern?
air-law.e: An aircraft that needs to cross an aerodrome without joining or conforming to the local traffic pattern must remain at least 2 000 ft above the aerodrome. Staying at or above this height keeps the overflying aircraft well clear of circuit traffic operating below.

air-law.q: An aircraft following a railway line within 1 NM at or below 1500 ft AGL must normally fly where?
air-law.a: To the left of the railway line
air-law.b: To the right of the railway line
air-law.d: At least 2 NM away from the railway line
air-law.ans: To the right of the railway line
air-law.e: As with any line feature, flying to the right of a railway line at low level keeps opposite-direction traffic following the same feature safely separated — think of it as 'driving on the right' in the air.

air-law.q: A VFR aircraft on magnetic track 359° and another VFR aircraft on magnetic track 179° could be at what relative flight levels?
air-law.d: Both must use odd IFR levels
air-law.e: Correct answer: Different flight levels. A magnetic track of 359° falls in the 180°-359° (westbound, even levels) sector, while 179° falls in the 000°-179° (eastbound, odd levels) sector, so the two aircraft would be on different flight levels.

air-law.q: Except for take-off, landing or written approval, no aircraft may be flown over built-up areas below what height?
air-law.a: 500 ft above the highest obstacle within 1000 ft
air-law.d: 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2000 ft from the aircraft
air-law.ans: 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2000 ft from the aircraft
air-law.e: The 1 000 ft / 2 000 ft buffer over built-up areas gives a pilot enough height and lateral room to glide clear of the congested area and find open ground if the engine fails.

air-law.q: A landing T displayed in the signal area indicates what?
air-law.a: Take-off and landing must be in a direction parallel to the shaft of the T towards the cross arm
air-law.d: Aircraft must use runways and taxiways only
air-law.ans: Take-off and landing must be in a direction parallel to the shaft of the T towards the cross arm
air-law.e: A landing T displayed in the signal area indicates the direction for take-off and landing: aircraft must take off and land parallel to the shaft of the T, heading towards the cross-arm. It is one of several ground signals shown in the aerodrome signals area alongside the dumbbell, cross and letter symbols.

air-law.q: To an aircraft in flight at an aerodrome, a steady green light means what?
air-law.c: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
air-law.e: A steady green light shown to an aircraft in flight means the aircraft is cleared to land. (The same steady green light shown to an aircraft on the ground means cleared for take-off.)

air-law.q: A series of green flashes to an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome means what?
air-law.e: A series of green flashes shown to an aircraft on the ground means the aircraft is cleared to taxi. (The same series of green flashes shown to an aircraft in flight means return for landing — a landing clearance will follow.)

air-law.q: To an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome, a series of white flashes means what?
air-law.c: Taxi clear of landing area in use
air-law.d: Return to starting point on the aerodrome
air-law.ans: Return to starting point on the aerodrome
air-law.e: A series of white flashes shown to an aircraft on the ground means return to the starting point (starting area) on the aerodrome. (The same series of white flashes shown to an aircraft in flight means land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron.)

air-law.q: A letter A displayed in the signal area means what?
air-law.e: A large black letter A displayed in the aerodrome signal area means agricultural operations (crop spraying) are in progress. Pilots should expect low-flying aircraft working the surrounding fields and remain alert when overflying or approaching the aerodrome.

air-law.q: To an aircraft in the air at an aerodrome, a series of white flashes means what?
air-law.b: Land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron
air-law.d: Taxi clear of the landing area
air-law.ans: Land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron
air-law.e: A series of white flashes shown to an aircraft in flight means land at this aerodrome and proceed to the apron. (The same series of white flashes shown to an aircraft on the ground means return to the starting point on the aerodrome.)

air-law.q: A red square with yellow diagonal cross displayed in the signal area indicates what?
air-law.e: A red square with a yellow diagonal cross displayed in the signal area means landings are prohibited. (A related but different signal — a red square with only a single yellow diagonal stripe, not a full cross — warns pilots to exercise special precaution when landing, usually because of the poor state of the airfield.)

air-law.q: To an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome, a series of red flashes means what?
air-law.d: Taxi clear of the landing area in use
air-law.ans: Taxi clear of the landing area in use
air-law.e: A series of red flashes shown to an aircraft on the ground means taxi clear of the landing area in use. (The same series of red flashes shown to an aircraft in flight means the aerodrome is unsafe — do not land.)

air-law.q: A dumbbell symbol displayed in the signal area indicates what?
air-law.a: Aircraft are required to land, take off and taxi on runways and taxiways only
air-law.ans: Aircraft are required to land, take off and taxi on runways and taxiways only
air-law.e: A plain white dumbbell in the signal area restricts aircraft to runways and taxiways only, keeping them off the grass or other unpaved areas, which might be soft, waterlogged, or otherwise unsuitable. Compare this with a dumbbell with a black bar, which flips the restriction: take-off and landing on runways only, but taxiing is allowed anywhere, including the grass.

air-law.q: A white or yellow cross located at each end of a runway means what?
air-law.c: Landings are permitted only by day
air-law.d: Use caution because of poor surface condition
air-law.e: White or yellow crosses displayed at each end of a runway (or taxiway) mark an unserviceable or unsafe area — for example a waterlogged runway or ground undermined by moles. In effect, the runway is closed: aircraft may not land, take off or taxi in the area between the crosses. By night the unserviceable area is marked with red lights, and any runway/taxiway lighting between those red lights is switched off.

air-law.q: A double-cross signal displayed in the signal area means what?
air-law.e: A double white cross displayed in the signal area means glider operations are in progress at the aerodrome. Pilots should expect glider and tow-plane traffic in the circuit and remain especially vigilant when joining or overflying.

air-law.q: At transition altitude during climb, what should the pilot set on the altimeter?
air-law.e: At transition altitude, the pilot changes from altitude on QNH to flight levels on the standard setting.

air-law.q: A glider is best described as what?
air-law.a: A heavier-than-air aircraft whose free flight does not depend on an engine
air-law.b: A lighter-than-air aircraft supported by gas
air-law.c: A powered aircraft with restricted maximum mass
air-law.d: An aircraft that must always use an engine in free flight
air-law.ans: A heavier-than-air aircraft whose free flight does not depend on an engine
air-law.e: A glider is heavier-than-air and remains supported by aerodynamic reaction on fixed lifting surfaces without relying on an engine for free flight.

air-law.q: Which definition best describes an aeroplane?
air-law.a: A lighter-than-air aircraft supported by gas pressure
air-law.b: A power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft deriving lift mainly from aerodynamic reactions on fixed surfaces
air-law.c: An aircraft whose free flight does not depend on an engine
air-law.d: Any aircraft equipped with a rotor system
air-law.ans: A power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft deriving lift mainly from aerodynamic reactions on fixed surfaces
air-law.e: An aeroplane is defined by three features together: heavier-than-air, power-driven, and deriving lift mainly from fixed wings rather than a rotor. That last point is what distinguishes it from a helicopter (rotor-driven), while being power-driven distinguishes it from a glider.

air-law.q: Instrument time means what?
air-law.b: Only time spent in IMC in an aircraft
air-law.c: Instrument flight time or instrument ground time, as defined
air-law.d: Only time in a full-flight simulator
air-law.ans: Instrument flight time or instrument ground time, as defined
air-law.e: Instrument time covers both actual instrument flight time and approved instrument ground time, such as in an FSTD, because both build the skills counted toward instrument and night rating experience requirements — not only time spent airborne.

air-law.q: The empty mass of an aircraft includes which items?
air-law.a: Only the bare airframe with no fluids or fixed equipment
air-law.d: Engine coolant, unusable fuel, total oil, total hydraulic fluid, fixed ballast and fixed equipment
air-law.ans: Engine coolant, unusable fuel, total oil, total hydraulic fluid, fixed ballast and fixed equipment
air-law.e: Empty mass includes engine coolant, unusable fuel, total oil, total hydraulic fluid, fixed ballast and fixed equipment, but excludes payload such as usable fuel, crew, passengers and baggage.
