This baseline lets a pilot add fuel and payload for a specific flight without exceeding the aircraft's certificated maximum mass.

air-law.q: Who may have access to an accident scene?
air-law.a: Investigator, advisor and rescue team member
air-law.ans: Investigator, advisor and rescue team member
air-law.e: Only the accident investigator, an authorised advisor and rescue team personnel may enter the accident site. Unauthorised persons, including media and the general public, are excluded so evidence is preserved and rescue operations are not obstructed.

air-law.q: A certificate of airworthiness confirms what?
air-law.a: That the pilot is licensed to fly the aircraft
air-law.b: That the aircraft meets the required airworthiness standard or has an authority to fly where applicable
air-law.c: That the aircraft is registered in a flight school’s name
air-law.d: That the aircraft may operate without maintenance records
air-law.ans: That the aircraft meets the required airworthiness standard or has an authority to fly where applicable
air-law.e: The certificate of airworthiness relates to the aircraft’s airworthy status, not the pilot’s licence.

air-law.q: Information such as statements, ATC communications and recorder data may be publicly disclosed only when what condition is met?
air-law.b: Whenever the aircraft owner requests it
air-law.c: Only if a court determines that disclosure outweighs the adverse impact
air-law.ans: Only if a court determines that disclosure outweighs the adverse impact
air-law.e: Investigation records like witness statements and recorder data are protected from routine disclosure because people are more likely to give full, honest information if they know it will not automatically become public — this mirrors the ICAO Annex 13 principle that investigations are for safety, not blame. A court can still order disclosure if the public interest in doing so outweighs that protection.

air-law.q: What does “aerial work” mean in SACAA Air Law?
air-law.a: A private flight conducted for leisure only
air-law.c: Any flight conducted only under IFR
air-law.d: An aircraft operation used for specialised services such as patrol, survey, photography, fire spotting or banner towing
air-law.ans: An aircraft operation used for specialised services such as patrol, survey, photography, fire spotting or banner towing
air-law.e: Aerial work refers to specialised aircraft services, not normal private or airline transport operations.

air-law.q: Which details should an accident or incident notification include?
air-law.a: Aircraft details, date/time, location, persons injured or killed, and nature/extent of damage as known
air-law.b: Only aircraft registration and pilot name
air-law.d: Only the aerodrome and runway in use
air-law.ans: Aircraft details, date/time, location, persons injured or killed, and nature/extent of damage as known
air-law.e: These particulars give the authorities the minimum information needed to launch an appropriate response — search and rescue, investigation dispatch, or public safety action — without waiting for the full facts to be established.

air-law.q: An Aircraft Flight Manual is associated with which document?
air-law.e: The AFM is associated with the certificate of airworthiness and contains limitations and safe operating information.

air-law.q: For Air Law purposes, “flight” means the period between what events?
air-law.b: The aircraft becoming airborne and touching down
air-law.c: The aircraft commencing take-off and completing the next landing
air-law.d: The start and end of taxi only
air-law.ans: The aircraft commencing take-off and completing the next landing
air-law.e: The definition of flight is based on the take-off and landing sequence, not merely engine time.

air-law.q: An Electronic Flight Bag is best described as what?
air-law.a: Any cellphone carried by a passenger
air-law.b: A portable battery charger for cockpit devices
air-law.c: Only a fixed screen installed by the aircraft manufacturer
air-law.d: An electronic information management and display system used for functions traditionally done with paper references
air-law.ans: An electronic information management and display system used for functions traditionally done with paper references
air-law.e: An EFB replaces or supports paper cockpit references such as charts, manuals and performance material.

air-law.q: For licensing purposes, the “date of application” is which date?
air-law.a: The date the CAA receives the application in an acceptable form
air-law.b: The date written by the applicant on the form
air-law.c: The date the skills test was completed
air-law.ans: The date the CAA receives the application in an acceptable form
air-law.e: The date of application is fixed as the date the Commissioner actually receives the paperwork in prescribed form, not when it was signed or the test completed. This prevents an applicant from using an earlier signature date to argue a deadline was met when the CAA only received it later.

air-law.q: Approved training is training conducted under which part?
air-law.b: Part 141 under approved curricula and supervision
air-law.ans: Part 141 under approved curricula and supervision
air-law.e: Training under Part 141, with its approved curricula and supervision, is what qualifies as “approved training” — distinguishing it from ad hoc instruction and giving Part 141 graduates recognised credit, such as reduced minimum hours in some cases, that unsupervised training does not carry.

air-law.q: Cargo means property carried on an aircraft other than which items?
air-law.b: Fuel, oil and hydraulic fluid only
air-law.c: Mail, stores, unaccompanied or mishandled baggage
air-law.d: Aircraft equipment and spare parts only
air-law.ans: Mail, stores, unaccompanied or mishandled baggage
air-law.e: Cargo means property carried by aircraft, but the definition excludes mail, stores, and unaccompanied or mishandled baggage. Those items are recorded and handled under their own operational categories.

air-law.q: A designated aviation safety body may perform which functions?
air-law.a: Issue pilot licences and medical certificates
air-law.b: Control all air traffic services directly
air-law.c: Report only to the President on aviation safety
air-law.d: Promote aviation safety, reduce accident/incident risk and advise the Director on aviation safety matters
air-law.ans: Promote aviation safety, reduce accident/incident risk and advise the Director on aviation safety matters
air-law.e: The designated body supports aviation safety and advises the Director, but does not replace licensing or ATC functions.

air-law.q: What is the transition level?
air-law.a: The lowest available flight level above the established transition altitude
air-law.b: The highest available altitude below the transition altitude
air-law.d: The lowest circuit altitude at an aerodrome
air-law.ans: The lowest available flight level above the established transition altitude
air-law.e: The transition level is the lowest usable flight level above the transition altitude.

air-law.q: Part 12 applies to which aircraft?
air-law.b: All aircraft except aircraft designed to remain moored/towed on the surface and aircraft designed to fly without a person on board
air-law.c: Only piston aircraft and light sport aircraft
air-law.d: Only aircraft used for commercial operations
air-law.ans: All aircraft except aircraft designed to remain moored/towed on the surface and aircraft designed to fly without a person on board
air-law.e: The exclusions make operational sense: a permanently moored or towed object never flies under its own control, and an aircraft with no person on board cannot generate the crew-based reporting duties (such as PIC notification) that this Part assumes.

air-law.q: May a member of the public go directly to an accident scene after it happens?
air-law.a: Yes, if they arrive before the police
air-law.b: Yes, if they are an aviation student
air-law.d: Yes, if the aircraft is privately owned
air-law.e: The public may not simply enter an accident scene; access is controlled for safety and investigation integrity.

air-law.q: A crew member is a person assigned by whom to carry out duties on board during flight?
air-law.e: A crew member is a person assigned by the operator to carry out duties on board during flight. This distinguishes crew, who have specific safety and operating responsibilities, from ordinary passengers, who do not.

air-law.q: Flight time for an aeroplane means which period?
air-law.a: From first movement for take-off until finally coming to rest at the end of the flight
air-law.b: From engine start until engine shutdown
air-law.c: From take-off clearance until landing clearance is cancelled
air-law.d: Only the airborne time between lift-off and touchdown
air-law.ans: From first movement for take-off until finally coming to rest at the end of the flight
air-law.e: Aeroplane flight time is measured from first movement under its own power for take-off until it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight, which includes taxi time — unlike the airborne-only definition of “flight”. Keeping this distinction straight matters for correctly totalling logged hours.

air-law.q: A child passenger is generally between which ages?
air-law.e: In this question bank, a child passenger is treated as one between their second and twelfth birthday - the band between the infant category (under two) and being treated as an adult passenger for seating, fare and briefing purposes.

air-law.q: Notification of an accident or incident should be made in which order of priority?
air-law.e: This order ensures the regulator with authority to direct the investigation is engaged immediately, while the ATSU and police are also informed promptly so they can secure the wreckage, manage airspace, and preserve the scene.

air-law.q: Above FL100, what are the VFR flight visibility and cloud distance minima by day or night?
air-law.a: 5 km visibility, 2 000 ft horizontally and 500 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.b: 5 km visibility, 1.5 km horizontally and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.c: 1.5 km visibility and clear of cloud
air-law.d: 8 km visibility, 1.5 km horizontally and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.ans: 8 km visibility, 1.5 km horizontally and 1 000 ft vertically from cloud
air-law.e: Above FL100, the VFR minima are higher: 8 km visibility with 1.5 km horizontal and 1 000 ft vertical cloud clearance.

air-law.q: A marshaller raises an arm and hand horizontally in front of the body, fingers extended, then clenches the fist. What does this mean?
air-law.e:
A marshaller signals brakes with a raised open hand that closes into a fist. Open hand raised then closing into a fist means "set/apply brakes" - the aircraft must stop and hold position using its parking brake. The reverse motion (closed fist opening into an open hand) means "release brakes."

ANSWER
Apply parking brake

air-law.q: When refuelling is performed while passengers are boarding or disembarking, what must be maintained?
air-law.a: All aircraft doors closed and locked
air-law.b: Communication between ground personnel and qualified personnel on board
air-law.c: All flight crew on board at their stations
air-law.d: No communication until refuelling is complete
air-law.ans: Communication between ground personnel and qualified personnel on board
air-law.e: When refuelling takes place while passengers are boarding or disembarking, communication must be maintained between ground personnel and qualified personnel on board. This ensures refuelling can be stopped immediately, and passengers moved clear, if a spill, fumes or any other hazard develops near the aircraft.

air-law.q: A series of red flashes from the control tower to an aircraft taxiing means what?
air-law.c: Vacate the landing area in use
air-law.d: Continue taxiing to the take-off area
air-law.ans: Vacate the landing area in use
air-law.e: A series of red flashes from the control tower to an aircraft taxiing on the ground means taxi clear of (vacate) the landing area in use. An aircraft on the ground acknowledges light signals by moving the ailerons or rudder during the day, or by flashing the landing or navigation lights twice at night.

air-law.q: An aircraft operating over water beyond 30 minutes normal cruising speed or 50 NM, whichever is less, must be equipped with what?
air-law.c: Only a life jacket for the PIC
air-law.e: Beyond 30 minutes at normal cruising speed or 50 NM from shore, whichever is less, life rafts and survival equipment are required. That far offshore, a forced landing means ditching, and survivors may have to wait some time before search and rescue can reach them.

air-law.q: If a pilot taxiing at an uncontrolled aerodrome observes another aircraft converging from the right, what should the pilot do?
air-law.a: Slow down or stop and give way
air-law.b: Continue because taxiing aircraft have equal priority
air-law.d: Ignore the other aircraft if on an IFR flight plan
air-law.ans: Slow down or stop and give way
air-law.e: When taxiing at an uncontrolled aerodrome, if another aircraft is converging from the right, the pilot should slow down or stop and give way to it. This mirrors the right-of-way rule used in the air, where the aircraft approaching from the right has priority.

air-law.q: Portable electronic devices that may adversely affect aircraft systems are prohibited during flight, but which item is listed as an exception?
air-law.a: A cellular telephone without flight mode
air-law.c: Any notebook computer at any time
air-law.e: An electric shaver is a simple, non-transmitting device with negligible potential to interfere with aircraft systems, which is why it is specifically listed as an exception, unlike devices whose interference potential must first be assessed.

air-law.q: A white dumb-bell with a black perpendicular bar means what?
air-law.a: Glider flying is taking place outside the landing area
air-law.b: Taxiing need not be confined to taxiways
air-law.c: Landing, take-off and taxiing are allowed only on runways and/or taxiways
air-law.d: The aerodrome is using parallel runways
air-law.ans: Taxiing need not be confined to taxiways
air-law.e:
RULE
A white dumbbell with a black perpendicular bar means aircraft must take-off and land on runways only, but may taxi anywhere, including the grass - taxiing is not confined to taxiways. (A plain white dumbbell without the bar means the opposite restriction: aircraft may use runways AND taxiways only, not the grass.)

ANSWER
Taxiing need not be confined to taxiways

air-law.q: A series of green flashes to an aircraft in flight in the circuit means what?
air-law.b: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
air-law.d: Return for landing; landing clearance will be given in due time
air-law.ans: Return for landing; landing clearance will be given in due time
air-law.e: A series of green flashes shown to an aircraft in flight, including while in the circuit, means return for landing — a landing clearance will be given in due time. Acknowledge by rocking the wings during the day, or by flashing the landing or navigation lights twice at night.

air-law.q: A marshaller moves a hand across the throat with palm downward. What does this signal mean?
air-law.e:
A marshaller raises the left arm and draws the right arm from the left shoulder across the throat in a slicing motion. This signal means "cut engine(s)" - the pilot should shut down the engine(s) indicated by which arm is raised (or both, if not specific to one side).

ANSWER
Cut engine

air-law.q: When taxiing on the manoeuvring area, an aircraft shall give way to which traffic?
air-law.a: All vehicles on the apron only
air-law.b: Aircraft taking off or about to take off
air-law.ans: Aircraft taking off or about to take off
air-law.e: An aircraft already taking off, or committed to doing so, has the least ability to stop or give way, so taxiing traffic must yield to it rather than the other way around.

air-law.q: Unless otherwise authorised, an ATS flight plan for an international flight must be filed at least when?
air-law.e: Correct answer: 60 minutes before departure. An international flight plan requires more notice than a domestic one: unless otherwise authorised, it must be filed at least 60 minutes before departure, compared with 30 minutes for a domestic flight.

air-law.q: Subject to the rules, Special VFR operations may be conducted when?
air-law.e: Correct answer: By day only. Special VFR, for both aeroplanes and helicopters, may only be conducted by day - never at night - together with the other applicable ceiling, visibility and ATC-clearance conditions.

air-law.q: When approaching an unmanned aerodrome to land, what should the PIC do to establish the runway in use?
air-law.a: Fly overhead at least at 2 000 ft AGL
air-law.c: Land on the runway most convenient from the aircraft position
air-law.d: Remain outside the ATZ until another aircraft lands
air-law.ans: Fly overhead at least at 2 000 ft AGL
air-law.e: Before joining the circuit at an unmanned aerodrome, the pilot-in-command should fly overhead at a height of at least 2 000 ft AGL. This allows the pilot to check the windsock, look out for other traffic, and confirm the runway in use before descending to join the circuit at the correct position and height.

air-law.q: A flashing red light from the control tower during an approach to land means what?
air-law.e: A flashing red light, a series of red flashes, shown to an aircraft in flight, including during an approach to land, means the aerodrome is unsafe - do not land. It is used as a radio-failure backup: without it, a pilot with no radio would have no way of knowing about a hazard such as a runway obstruction or incursion ahead.

air-law.q: A series of green flashes from the tower to an aircraft taxiing means what?
air-law.b: Return to starting point on the aerodrome
air-law.e: A series of green flashes from the control tower to a taxiing aircraft means cleared to taxi. Light signals like this exist specifically as a backup for radio failure, letting the tower still control ground movement using colour and flash-pattern combinations instead of voice instructions.

air-law.q: A double white cross displayed horizontally in the signal area means what?
air-law.a: Special precautions are required due to bad taxiways
air-law.b: Aircraft must use only runways and taxiways
air-law.d: The aerodrome is being used by gliders and glider flights are being performed
air-law.ans: The aerodrome is being used by gliders and glider flights are being performed
air-law.e: A double white cross displayed horizontally in the signal area means the aerodrome is being used by gliders, and glider flights are in progress. Pilots should expect glider and tow-plane traffic in the circuit and stay especially alert when joining or overflying.

air-law.q: A marshaller moving arms down with palms toward the ground, then moving them up and down several times, means what?
air-law.e:
A marshaller lowers both arms with palms toward the ground, then moves them up and down several times. This is the standard "slow down" signal - reduce taxi speed. It is one of the most important marshalling signals for small aircraft, alongside stop, turn, brakes and engine-start/cut signals.

ANSWER
Slow down

air-law.q: If a passenger displays symptoms of a communicable disease, whom must the PIC notify immediately?
air-law.e: If a passenger shows symptoms of a communicable disease, the PIC must notify the Port Health Authority immediately, since an aircraft can carry an infectious illness across borders faster than almost any other means of transport, and health authorities need advance warning to manage the risk on arrival.

air-law.q: Who is responsible for signing the load and trim sheet?
air-law.e: The pilot-in-command is responsible for signing the load and trim sheet, because the PIC carries ultimate legal responsibility for ensuring the aircraft is loaded within its weight and centre of gravity limits before flight - incorrect loading can seriously affect controllability and performance.

air-law.q: No pilot may use a public road as a place of landing or take-off except in which case?
air-law.a: Only when no licensed aerodrome is available
air-law.d: In an emergency involving the safety of the aircraft or its occupants, or for saving lives / civil defence / law enforcement operations
air-law.ans: In an emergency involving the safety of the aircraft or its occupants, or for saving lives / civil defence / law enforcement operations
air-law.e: The permitted exceptions — genuine emergency, saving life, civil defence, or law enforcement — share a common thread: the risk of not landing outweighs the risk of using an unprepared surface.

air-law.q: A person may taxi an aircraft on the movement area only if they meet which requirement?
air-law.a: They hold a valid pilot licence or have been properly instructed and declared competent to taxi
air-law.b: They are at least a student pilot and have passenger approval
air-law.d: They have filed an ATS flight plan
air-law.ans: They hold a valid pilot licence or have been properly instructed and declared competent to taxi
air-law.e: A person may only taxi an aircraft on the movement area if they hold a valid pilot licence, or have been properly instructed in taxiing procedures and declared competent to do so. This requirement protects the safety of ground operations, since taxiing brings an aircraft close to other aircraft, vehicles and personnel.

air-law.q: Outside controlled airspace below 10 000 ft, the maximum indicated airspeed is normally what?
air-law.e: The 250 kt limit below 10 000 ft keeps closure rates manageable in airspace shared with slower traffic and pilots relying on see-and-avoid, where large speed differentials make collision avoidance much harder.

air-law.q: When two aircraft approach head-on with danger of collision, what must each aircraft do?
air-law.e: Both aircraft turning right avoids the risk of pilots turning toward each other if the rule were ambiguous; it mirrors the road-traffic convention of keeping right, giving every pilot one predictable response to a head-on conflict.

air-law.q: No person may fly in the airspace of a restricted area below the specified height unless what condition is met?
air-law.a: The flight is conducted by day
air-law.b: The aircraft remains below 1 500 ft AGL
air-law.c: A broadcast has been made on 124.8 MHz
air-law.d: Permission has been obtained from the relevant authority
air-law.ans: Permission has been obtained from the relevant authority
air-law.e: This describes a Restricted Area (FAR), not a Prohibited Area (FAP) — there is a sharp distinction between the two. A Restricted Area may only be entered with permission from the appropriate authority (usually military). A Prohibited Area is stricter: manned aircraft may never enter it under any circumstances — only commercial drones may enter, and only with permission.

air-law.q: A safety pilot must be rated on the type of aircraft and must also do what?
air-law.a: Occupy a control seat and be able to keep a good lookout
air-law.ans: Occupy a control seat and be able to keep a good lookout
air-law.e: A safety pilot must be rated on the aircraft type, occupy a control seat, and be able to maintain a good lookout. This role exists so that when the pilot flying has restricted vision, for example practising instrument flying under a hood, someone is still watching for other traffic and able to take control if needed.

air-law.q: If a pilot is away from the base where the logbook is normally kept, entries must be made within what time after return to base?
air-law.e: If a pilot has been away from the base where the logbook is normally kept, entries must be completed within 48 hours of returning to base, rather than the general 7-day window that applies to routine domestic Part 91 entries.

air-law.q: Except by individual permission, aircraft shall not be flown aerobatically unless which conditions are met?
air-law.a: Only outside 5 NM of an aerodrome, regardless of height
air-law.b: Only during daylight and below 1 500 ft AGL
air-law.c: The manoeuvre can be recovered by 2 000 ft, not within 5 NM of a licensed aerodrome unless at least 4 000 ft AGL, not near ATS routes and not over populous areas or public gatherings
air-law.d: Only if passengers agree in writing
air-law.ans: The manoeuvre can be recovered by 2 000 ft, not within 5 NM of a licensed aerodrome unless at least 4 000 ft AGL, not near ATS routes and not over populous areas or public gatherings
air-law.e: Aerobatic manoeuvres must be recoverable by 2 000 ft AGL, may not be flown within 5 NM of a licensed aerodrome unless at least 4 000 ft AGL, and must stay clear of ATS routes and populous areas or public gatherings. Exam tip: remember the two key heights — 2 000 ft recovery, 4 000 ft near an aerodrome.

air-law.q: An iPad or other EFB may only be used for flight purposes under what condition?
air-law.a: If it has any aviation app installed
air-law.b: Only if it is connected to the internet
air-law.d: If it meets SA-CATS 91 requirements and is approved for the purpose by the Director
air-law.ans: If it meets SA-CATS 91 requirements and is approved for the purpose by the Director
air-law.e: An EFB carries safety-critical information — charts, performance data, checklists — that pilots rely on operationally, so it cannot simply be a personal device loaded with an app. It must meet SA-CATS 91 standards and be approved by the Director before it can replace paper references in flight.

air-law.q: A release to service may pertain to what?
air-law.a: Both annual scheduled maintenance and specific line maintenance
air-law.ans: Both annual scheduled maintenance and specific line maintenance
air-law.e: A release to service is the maintenance sign-off confirming an aircraft or component is airworthy, and it can follow either a full scheduled inspection, such as an annual, or a specific piece of line maintenance, such as a single repair. Either way, it is what legally clears the aircraft to fly again.

air-law.q: The PIC of an aircraft may pick up an object only under what condition?
air-law.a: At the discretion of the PIC
air-law.b: With prior written approval from the Director
air-law.ans: With prior written approval from the Director
air-law.e: Picking up an object from the ground changes the aircraft's weight, balance, and handling characteristics in ways that need to be assessed beforehand, so it requires prior written approval from the Director rather than being left to pilot discretion.

air-law.q: A flight folio entry must be completed in what manner?
air-law.a: In pencil so that errors can be erased
air-law.b: Only electronically after the aircraft returns to base
air-law.c: In legible writing and permanent ink
air-law.ans: In legible writing and permanent ink
air-law.e: Flight folio entries must be legible and permanent to preserve the official operational record.

air-law.q: On any flight within South Africa, the certificate of release to service must be carried when?
air-law.a: Only on domestic flights over 50 NM
air-law.e: The certificate of release to service, or a permitted copy, must be carried on every flight within South Africa, regardless of distance flown or whether passengers are carried.

air-law.q: No pilot shall operate in formation flight except under what condition?
air-law.a: By arrangement between the pilot-in-command of each aircraft
air-law.d: Only during daylight at licensed aerodromes
air-law.ans: By arrangement between the pilot-in-command of each aircraft
air-law.e: Formation flying reduces normal aircraft separation by agreement rather than by ATC-provided spacing, so each PIC must consent in advance and accept responsibility for maintaining safe separation within the formation.

air-law.q: The minimum height above a proclaimed game reserve is what?
air-law.e: SA air law sets a minimum height of 500 m above a proclaimed game reserve, nature reserve or wildlife area, to reduce noise disturbance to animals and manage safety risk. Exam tip: this is a metres-based limit, unlike the feet-based minimum heights used elsewhere in Part 91 (e.g. 500 ft over open country) — do not confuse the units.

air-law.q: Which of the following are distress signals?
air-law.b: Only a white flare and landing light flash
air-law.c: Mayday spoken three times, red rocket shells fired one at a time, and a red parachute flare
air-law.d: Only a transponder code without any radio call
air-law.ans: Mayday spoken three times, red rocket shells fired one at a time, and a red parachute flare
air-law.e: Recognised distress signals include: SOS in Morse code; the spoken word MAYDAY, given three times; rockets or shells throwing red lights, fired one at a time at short intervals; and a parachute flare showing a red light. These signals may be used when an aircraft is in grave and imminent danger and needs immediate assistance.

air-law.q: Except with written permission, aircraft shall not circle over or within 1 km of an open-air assembly of persons below what height?
air-law.e: The 1 km lateral buffer, not just the 3 000 ft vertical one, matters because a large crowd can extend well beyond directly under the flight path, so both dimensions are needed to keep people clear of any debris or forced-landing risk.

air-law.q: An aeroplane must carry a flotation device or life jacket for each person on board when operating in which situation?
air-law.a: When flying over water and beyond gliding distance from land
air-law.b: When flying over land and beyond gliding distance from water
air-law.c: Only when more than 50 NM from land
air-law.d: Only when flying above FL100 over water
air-law.ans: When flying over water and beyond gliding distance from land
air-law.e: Life jackets or flotation devices must be carried for each occupant when flying over water beyond gliding distance from land. Within gliding distance, an engine failure still allows a landing on land; beyond it, ditching becomes the only option, so flotation equipment is required.

air-law.q: No aircraft shall be operated at night without which lighting equipment?
air-law.b: A rotating beacon, navigation/position lights and suitable landing lights
air-law.ans: A rotating beacon, navigation/position lights and suitable landing lights
air-law.e: Night flight requires a rotating beacon for anti-collision conspicuity, navigation/position lights to show other traffic the aircraft's orientation and right-of-way status, and landing lights suitable for the approach and landing phase. Together these replace the visual cues that daylight normally provides.

air-law.q: VFR flight is not permitted in which situation?
air-law.a: In Class G airspace below 1 500 ft
air-law.c: At supersonic speeds and in Class A airspace
air-law.ans: At supersonic speeds and in Class A airspace
air-law.e: VFR flight is not permitted at supersonic speeds or in Class A airspace. Class A is reserved for IFR traffic operating under full ATC separation at high density and speed, which VFR see-and-avoid cannot reliably support; supersonic flight is restricted mainly because of the sonic boom it generates.

air-law.q: When carrying passengers in a small aircraft, the PIC must ensure passengers are briefed on what?
air-law.b: How to operate the aircraft radio
air-law.c: How to calculate weight and balance
air-law.d: Smoking prohibition and portable electronic devices
air-law.ans: Smoking prohibition and portable electronic devices
air-law.e: When carrying passengers in a small aircraft, the PIC must brief them on the smoking prohibition and on portable electronic device restrictions. PEDs can interfere with radio and navigation equipment, and smoking near fuel systems or fumes is a fire hazard - both are safety issues the crew has to control from the outset.

air-law.q: Under normal VFR operations, an aircraft may not operate at or within an ATZ when ground visibility and ceiling are below what?
air-law.e: Correct answer: 5 km visibility and 1 500 ft ceiling. These are the standard VMC minima for operating at or within a CTR/ATZ, e.g. flying circuits: visibility at least 5 km and ceiling at least 1 500 ft. A lower 500 ft ceiling applies only to the separate cross-country exception, for an aeroplane transiting straight in or out on a cross-country flight.

air-law.q: A certificate of release to service issued after a mandatory periodic inspection is retained for how long?
air-law.e: A certificate of release to service issued after a mandatory periodic inspection must be retained for 12 months — a shorter period than the 5-year retention that applies to the aircraft flight folio.

air-law.q: Which statement best defines Special VFR?
air-law.b: A flight in IMC without an ATC clearance
air-law.c: A flight cleared by ATC to operate within a control zone in conditions below normal VMC
air-law.d: A procedure used only for IFR aircraft
air-law.ans: A flight cleared by ATC to operate within a control zone in conditions below normal VMC
air-law.e: Special VFR allows ATC-cleared VFR operation in a control zone when normal VMC minima are not met.

air-law.q: To conduct Special VFR, the minimum visibility required is what?
air-law.e: Special VFR requires a minimum visibility of 1 500 m, alongside the other SVFR conditions: by day only, a 600 ft ceiling, clear of cloud, and in radio contact with the tower. These are all lower than normal VMC minima, which is exactly why SVFR needs an individual ATC clearance rather than being available as of right.

air-law.q: If intercepted, and the intercepting aircraft’s instructions conflict with ATC instructions, what should the pilot do?
air-law.a: Follow the instructions of the intercepting aircraft
air-law.d: Ignore both until communication is restored
air-law.ans: Follow the instructions of the intercepting aircraft
air-law.e: If an intercepting aircraft's instructions conflict with ATC, the pilot must follow the intercepting aircraft. The interceptor has direct visual contact and full situational awareness of the encounter in real time, while ATC may not even be aware an interception is taking place.

air-law.q: A commander must ensure that usable fuel remaining in flight is sufficient to proceed to an aerodrome where a safe landing can be made with what remaining?
air-law.d: Fuel to fly 20 minutes at best range speed only
air-law.e: Correct answer: Final reserve fuel. The commander must ensure enough usable fuel remains to reach an aerodrome where a safe landing can be made while still keeping the planned final reserve fuel intact. If any further delay would eat into that reserve, the pilot must declare "minimum fuel"; if continuing would mean landing with less than final reserve fuel, "Mayday mayday mayday fuel" must be declared instead.

air-law.q: An aircraft must be equipped with means for indicating the adequacy of power supplied to what?
air-law.e: The aircraft must have a means of indicating whether required flight instruments are receiving adequate power, since several of them, particularly gyro and electronic displays, depend on an electrical supply. Without this indication, a failing bus could degrade the instruments before the pilot notices anything is wrong.

air-law.q: A regular requirement for completion of a flight folio is which item?
air-law.a: The number of passengers carried only
air-law.d: The duty assignment of flight crew members
air-law.ans: The duty assignment of flight crew members
air-law.e: Recording crew duty assignments in the flight folio supports compliance with flight and duty time limitations and establishes accountability for who performed which role — part of the folio’s wider function as the aircraft’s operational record, alongside fuel uplifts and release-to-service details.

air-law.q: Except in an emergency, no aircraft may take off or land by night unless what condition is met?
air-law.a: The aerodrome is equipped for night flying and the PIC has ensured night flying facilities are available
air-law.b: The pilot has a handheld torch only
air-law.c: Only the landing light is serviceable
air-law.d: The aircraft has filed a VFR flight plan
air-law.ans: The aerodrome is equipped for night flying and the PIC has ensured night flying facilities are available
air-law.e: Except in an emergency, an aircraft may not take off or land by night unless the aerodrome is equipped for night flying and the PIC has confirmed night flying facilities, such as runway and approach lighting, are actually available. Unlit runways and unfamiliar terrain at night significantly raise the risk of hitting an unseen obstacle.

air-law.q: In an aeroplane using fuses, the minimum spare fuses required are what?
air-law.a: 20% or 2 of each rating, whichever is greater
air-law.b: 10% or 3 of each rating, whichever is greater
air-law.c: 10% or 1 of each rating, whichever is greater
air-law.d: 5% or 1 of each rating, whichever is greater
air-law.ans: 10% or 3 of each rating, whichever is greater
air-law.e: Where fuses are used, spare fuses must equal at least 10% of each rating, or three, whichever is greater. Since a blown fuse cannot be reset in flight the way a breaker can, carrying spares is the only way to restore a lost circuit, such as instrument or avionics power, during the flight.

air-law.q: Which signal from an intercepting aircraft indicates that the intercepted aircraft is clear to proceed?
air-law.a: Rocking wings continuously in front of the aircraft
air-law.c: A breaking climbing turn to the left
air-law.ans: A breaking climbing turn to the left
air-law.e: This is the Second Series interception signal: the intercepting aircraft makes an abrupt breakaway manoeuvre — a climbing turn of 90 degrees or more, without crossing the flight path of the intercepted aircraft. It means you may proceed. The intercepted aircraft acknowledges by rocking its wings, showing steady landing lights, and continuing its flight.

air-law.q: A flight plan shall be submitted for which flights?
air-law.b: Only local flights within an ATZ
air-law.d: All flights for which search and rescue is required and international flights
air-law.ans: All flights for which search and rescue is required and international flights
air-law.e: Correct answer: All flights for which search and rescue is required and international flights. These are two of the specific categories for which an ATS flight plan is mandatory, regardless of the flight's duration or the type of aerodrome used. A local flight, or a short flight below 1500 ft AGL, does not by itself trigger the requirement.

air-law.q: If an ATC clearance is not suitable, what may the PIC do?
air-law.a: Request an amended clearance and obtain it if practicable
air-law.ans: Request an amended clearance and obtain it if practicable
air-law.e: The PIC may request a change to an unsuitable ATC clearance; ATC approval is still required before acting on the amendment.

air-law.q: Unless otherwise authorised by the responsible ATSU, a flight plan for controlled airspace must normally be filed when?
air-law.e: Correct answer: 30 minutes before departure. Unless otherwise authorised by the responsible ATSU, a flight plan for a flight into controlled airspace must normally be filed at least 30 minutes before departure.

air-law.q: What are the correct colours for an aircraft's left and right navigation (position) lights, and through what angle from dead ahead must each be visible?
air-law.a: Left red, right green, each visible through 110° from dead ahead
air-law.b: Left green, right red, each visible through 110° from dead ahead
air-law.c: Left red, right green, each visible through 140° from dead ahead
air-law.d: Both white, each visible through 110° from dead ahead
air-law.ans: Left red, right green, each visible through 110° from dead ahead
air-law.e: Left = red, right = green, each covering 110° from dead ahead round to the side — the same convention used on ships, so a pilot seeing a red light on their left knows another aircraft's left wingtip is facing them. A steady white light covering 140° (70° either side of dead astern) covers the tail. Exam tip: red and left both have 4 letters — an easy way to remember which side is which.

air-law.q: A right-hand arrow of conspicuous colour displayed in the signal area, or horizontally at the end of the runway or strip in use, indicates what?
air-law.a: Turns are to be made to the right before landing and after take-off
air-law.b: The runway in use is closed to right-hand circuits
air-law.c: Aircraft must give way to traffic approaching from the right
air-law.d: The wind is from the right of the runway heading
air-law.ans: Turns are to be made to the right before landing and after take-off
air-law.e: A right-hand arrow displayed in the signal area (or at the runway/strip in use) tells arriving and departing pilots the circuit is non-standard: turns before landing and after take-off must be made to the right instead of the usual left. This is the visual backup for when a right-hand circuit hasn't already been briefed or published for that runway.

air-law.q: A set of two digits displayed vertically at or near the aerodrome control tower indicates what to aircraft on the manoeuvring area?
air-law.a: The direction for take-off, expressed in units of 10 degrees to the nearest 10 degrees of the magnetic compass
air-law.b: The current QNH, expressed in tens of hectopascals
air-law.c: The active runway number only, with no directional meaning
air-law.d: The number of aircraft currently in the circuit
air-law.ans: The direction for take-off, expressed in units of 10 degrees to the nearest 10 degrees of the magnetic compass
air-law.e: Two digits displayed vertically at or near the control tower give the take-off direction to the nearest 10 degrees of the magnetic compass — so "09" means take off on a heading of approximately 090°. This lets a pilot confirm the active direction visually, as a backup to radio calls or when the tower frequency can't be raised.

navigation.q: An aircraft on a cross country flight is to maintain a heading of 290° (M). From the figures extracted from the compass correction card in the figure below, the compass heading to steer is: FOR °(M) STEER °(C) 270 270 315 311
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Compass correction card: 270°(M) → 270°(C); 315°(M) → 311°(C). Heading to steer for 290°(M).

FORMULA
Interpolate the deviation correction between the two card entries, then apply it to the required magnetic heading to get compass heading.

SOLVE
Correction at 270°M = 270° − 270° = 0°.
Correction at 315°M = 311° − 315° = −4°.
Change in correction over the 45° interval (270° to 315°) = −4°.
Fraction of the interval to 290°M = (290° − 270°) ÷ 45° = 20 ÷ 45 = 0.444.
Interpolated correction = −4° × 0.444 = −1.8°.
Compass heading = 290° + (−1.8°) = 288.2° ≈ 288°C.

ANSWER
288° (C)

navigation.q: When referring to direction on the earth the cardinal points are:
navigation.e: The four cardinal points are north, east, south and west. The intermediate directions are quadrantal or intercardinal points.

navigation.q: When referring to the direction on the earth the cardinal points are:
navigation.e: The cardinal directions are north 360°/000°, east 090°, south 180° and west 270°.

navigation.q: The quadrantal directions expressed as names are:
navigation.b: North east, south east, north west, south west
navigation.ans: North east, south east, north west, south west
navigation.e: The quadrantal points lie halfway between the cardinal points: north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west.

navigation.q: The quadrantal directions expressed in degrees are:
navigation.e: Each quadrantal point is 45° from the adjacent cardinal points: NE 045°, SE 135°, SW 225° and NW 315°.

navigation.q: The most correct statement is:
navigation.a: The earth rotates about the polar axis from east to west at the rate of 15deg per hour
navigation.b: The earth rotates about the polar axis from west to east at the rate of 10deg per hour
navigation.c: The earth rotates about the equatorial axis at the rate of 15deg per hour
navigation.d: The earth rotates about the polar axis from west to east at the rate of 15deg per hour
navigation.ans: The earth rotates about the polar axis from west to east at the rate of 15deg per hour
navigation.e: The Earth completes 360° in about 24 hours, so it rotates west to east at 360 ÷ 24 = 15° per hour.

navigation.q: The earth rotates about the polar axis:
navigation.a: From the west to east at a rate of 15deg per hour
navigation.b: From east to west at a rate of 15deg per hour
navigation.c: From west to east at a rate of 10deg per hour
navigation.d: From west to east at a rate of 20deg per hour
navigation.ans: From the west to east at a rate of 15deg per hour
navigation.e: The Earth rotates from west to east through 360° in roughly 24 hours, equivalent to 15° of longitude per hour.

navigation.q: The axis about which the earth rotates is between:
navigation.a: The magnetic north and magnetic south poles
navigation.c: The two points where the equator meets the prime meridian
navigation.e: The geographic rotation axis passes through the true North Pole and true South Pole. The equator lies perpendicular to this axis.

navigation.q: The reference for the measurement of longitude is:
navigation.e: Longitude is measured east or west from the prime meridian through Greenwich, designated 0° longitude.

navigation.q: The longitude of a position refers to its location:
navigation.a: North or south of the equator
navigation.b: Angular distance from the nearest pole
navigation.c: East or west of magnetic north
navigation.d: East or west of the prime meridian
navigation.ans: East or west of the prime meridian
navigation.e: Longitude is angular distance measured east or west from the Greenwich prime meridian, from 0° to 180°.

navigation.q: Meridians of longitude are half of a:
navigation.a: Great circle and are measured up to 180deg east and to the west of prime meridian
navigation.b: A great circle and are measured up to 175deg east and west of the prime meridian
navigation.c: A small circle and are measured up to 180deg east and west
navigation.d: A great circle and are measured up to 90deg east and west
navigation.ans: Great circle and are measured up to 180deg east and to the west of prime meridian
navigation.e: A single meridian runs from pole to pole and is half of a great circle. Longitude is measured from 0° to 180° east or west of Greenwich.

navigation.q: Which statement about a meridian of longitude is correct?
navigation.a: Every parallel of latitude is both a great circle and a rhumb line
navigation.b: The meridian of longitude is both a great circle and a rhumb line
navigation.c: A meridian is a small circle except at Greenwich
navigation.d: A meridian is a great circle but cannot be a rhumb line
navigation.ans: The meridian of longitude is both a great circle and a rhumb line
navigation.e: A complete meridian with its opposite meridian forms a great circle. Following a meridian also maintains a constant track of 000° or 180°, so it is a rhumb line.

navigation.q: The reference for the measurement of latitude is:
navigation.e: Latitude is angular distance north or south of the equator, measured from 0° at the equator to 90° at either pole.

navigation.q: Parallels of latitude are measured up to:
navigation.a: 85deg north or south of the equator
navigation.b: 95deg north or south of the equator
navigation.c: 180deg north or south of the equator
navigation.d: 90deg north or south of the equator
navigation.ans: 90deg north or south of the equator
navigation.e: Latitude is measured from 0° at the equator to a maximum of 90° north or 90° south at the geographic poles.

navigation.q: With regard to the following, the correct statement is:
navigation.a: The equator is both rhumb line and great circle
navigation.b: Every parallel is both a rhumb line and a great circle
navigation.c: The equator is a great circle but not a rhumb line
navigation.d: The equator is a rhumb line but not a great circle
navigation.ans: The equator is both rhumb line and great circle
navigation.e: The equator is a great circle because its plane passes through Earth’s centre, and it is also a rhumb line because it crosses every meridian at 90°.

navigation.q: Which statement about a parallel of latitude is correct?
navigation.a: Every parallel of latitude is a great circle
navigation.b: A parallel of latitude is a rhumb line
navigation.c: Every meridian is a small circle
navigation.d: A parallel requires a continuously changing track
navigation.ans: A parallel of latitude is a rhumb line
navigation.e: A parallel crosses each meridian at the same angle, so it is a rhumb line. Except for the equator, parallels are small circles rather than great circles.

navigation.q: One kilometre is defined as:
navigation.a: One thousandth of the distance from equator to pole
navigation.b: One hundred thousandth of the distance from equator to pole
navigation.c: One ten thousandth of the distance from the equator to either pole
navigation.d: The average length of one minute of latitude
navigation.ans: One ten thousandth of the distance from the equator to either pole
navigation.e: The historical definition of the metre made one kilometre one ten-thousandth of the meridional distance from the equator to a pole.

navigation.q: One nautical mile is defined as being the average length on the surface of the earth:
navigation.a: Of the arc of one degree of latitude
navigation.c: Of one minute of longitude at every latitude
navigation.d: Of the arc of one-minute latitude measured along a meridian of longitude
navigation.ans: Of the arc of one-minute latitude measured along a meridian of longitude
navigation.e: A nautical mile is based on the average length of one minute of latitude measured along a meridian; its internationally defined length is 1 852 metres.

navigation.q: The type of chart on which meridians of longitude and parallels of latitude are at 90° to each other is called:
navigation.e: An orthomorphic chart preserves angles locally, so meridians and parallels intersect at right angles and small shapes are represented correctly.

navigation.q: An aeronautical chart which portrays the earth’s feature with a little distortion, is known as:
navigation.e: An orthomorphic, or conformal, chart preserves local angles and shapes, allowing Earth features to be shown with limited shape distortion over the charted area.

navigation.q: When applied to an aeronautical chart, the term topographical chart means:
navigation.a: That only relief and elevation are shown
navigation.c: That the earth’s features are represented with a minimum distortion
navigation.d: That only aeronautical symbols are shown
navigation.ans: That the earth’s features are represented with a minimum distortion
navigation.e: A topographical chart aims to portray natural and constructed surface features in their correct relative positions while keeping distortion as small as practicable.

navigation.q: When the term Orthomorphic is applied to an aeronautical chart, it means that:
navigation.a: Parallels remain equally spaced at every latitude
navigation.b: Scale is correct at every point on the chart
navigation.c: Areas retain their exact true proportions
navigation.d: Meridians of longitude and parallels of latitude cut each other at 90°
navigation.ans: Meridians of longitude and parallels of latitude cut each other at 90°
navigation.e: Orthomorphic means conformal: angles are preserved locally. Consequently, meridians and parallels intersect at 90° on the chart.

navigation.q: Convergency is defined as being:
navigation.a: The angle between two adjacent meridians
navigation.b: The difference between true north and magnetic north
navigation.c: The angle between a rhumb line and a great circle
navigation.d: The longitude difference measured only at the equator
navigation.ans: The angle between two adjacent meridians
navigation.e: Convergency is the angle at which two meridians approach one another. For two selected meridians, it is their angular separation at the latitude concerned.

navigation.q: How does convergency between meridians change with latitude?
navigation.d: Is zero on every conformal chart
navigation.e: Meridians converge increasingly toward the poles. Convergency therefore varies with latitude and is smaller near the equator.

navigation.q: Compared with lower latitudes, convergency at higher latitudes is:
navigation.a: Is greater at low latitudes than at high latitudes
navigation.b: Is constant between any two meridians
navigation.c: Is greater at high latitudes than it is at lower latitudes
navigation.ans: Is greater at high latitudes than it is at lower latitudes
navigation.e: For a given longitude difference, meridians converge more strongly as latitude increases, so convergency is greater at high latitudes.

navigation.q: Convergency on the earth is:
navigation.a: Maximum at the equator and zero at the poles
navigation.d: Maximum at the poles and zero at the equator
navigation.ans: Maximum at the poles and zero at the equator
navigation.e: At the equator meridians are parallel locally, giving zero convergency. They meet at the poles, where convergency reaches its maximum.

navigation.q: The type of chart projection which is constructed by placing a cone around an imaginary earth, so that it cuts the earth at two different parallels of latitude is called a:
navigation.e: A Lambert conformal conic projection is produced by projecting onto a cone that intersects the Earth along two standard parallels.

navigation.q: On a chart constructed using the Lambert’s Conformal Conic projection:
navigation.a: Convergency is exact and constant everywhere on Earth
navigation.b: Convergency is constant throughout the chart but correct only at the parallel of origin
navigation.c: Convergency varies randomly across the chart
navigation.d: Convergency is zero throughout the chart
navigation.ans: Convergency is constant throughout the chart but correct only at the parallel of origin
navigation.e: On a Lambert chart, chart convergency is represented by a constant convergence factor. It corresponds exactly with Earth convergency at the parallel of origin.

navigation.q: On a Lambert’s Conformal Conic chart convergency is:
navigation.d: Equal to the longitude difference everywhere
navigation.e: On a Lambert conformal conic chart the meridians are straight lines that all meet at one point beyond the edge of the chart, and the angle between any two of them is fixed by how the chart is constructed. So the convergency between two meridians is the same wherever you measure it on the sheet: it is constant and does not change with latitude. It matches the true convergency of the Earth only at the parallel of origin and differs slightly elsewhere, which is why you measure a track against the meridian closest to its mid-point.

navigation.q: A practical method used to reduce the effects of convergency when measuring bearings on a Lambert’s Conformal Conic Chart is to:
navigation.a: Measure only at the departure meridian
navigation.b: Measure only at the destination meridian
navigation.c: Measure along the nearest standard parallel
navigation.d: Measure the bearing at the mid meridian
navigation.ans: Measure the bearing at the mid meridian
navigation.e: For a long Lambert-chart track, measuring direction at the mid-meridian gives a practical mean track and balances the change caused by meridian convergence.

navigation.q: On Lambert’s Conformal Conic Projection:
navigation.a: The scale is only correct at the standard parallels
navigation.c: The scale is correct only at the equator
navigation.d: The scale is correct only along the central meridian
navigation.ans: The scale is only correct at the standard parallels
navigation.e: The projecting cone intersects the Earth at the standard parallels, so the nominal chart scale is exact along those parallels.

navigation.q: The scale on a Lambert’s Conformal Conic Projection is correct:
navigation.e: Lambert scale is exact where the cone intersects the Earth: the two standard parallels. Between and beyond them, small scale errors occur.

navigation.q: On a chart constructed using Lambert’s Conformal conic projection:
navigation.a: Parallels are straight lines converging toward the pole
navigation.b: Meridians are curved and equally spaced
navigation.c: Meridian lines are straight lines that converge towards the nearer pole
navigation.ans: Meridian lines are straight lines that converge towards the nearer pole
navigation.e: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, meridians are straight radial lines that converge toward the apex of the cone, in the direction of the nearer pole.

navigation.q: The meridians shown on a Lambert’s conformal conic projection will appear as:
navigation.a: Parallel straight lines with equal spacing
navigation.b: Curved lines that converge toward the equator
navigation.d: Straight lines which converge towards the nearer pole
navigation.ans: Straight lines which converge towards the nearer pole
navigation.e: Lambert meridians are represented as straight lines radiating from the cone’s apex, so they converge toward the nearer pole.

navigation.q: The Lambert’s conformal conic projection is created by:
navigation.a: Using a paper cone which cuts the imaginary earth at two different parallels of latitude
navigation.b: Using a cone tangent at one parallel only
navigation.c: Using a cylinder tangent to the equator
navigation.d: Using a flat plane tangent at a pole
navigation.ans: Using a paper cone which cuts the imaginary earth at two different parallels of latitude
navigation.e: The secant Lambert construction uses a cone that intersects the Earth at two standard parallels, where chart scale is correct.

navigation.q: With reference to the Lambert’s Conformal Conic chart:
navigation.a: A rhumb line is always the shortest route
navigation.b: The shorter arc of a great circle track will be the shortest distance between two points
navigation.c: Scale is exact at every point
navigation.d: Every straight chart line is a rhumb line
navigation.ans: The shorter arc of a great circle track will be the shortest distance between two points
navigation.e: On a sphere, the shorter arc of a great circle is the shortest surface route between two positions. Lambert straight lines closely approximate great-circle tracks.

navigation.q: On a chart constructed using Lambert’s Conformal Conic projection, a rhumb line track:
navigation.a: Will always represent a great-circle route
navigation.b: Will always be the shortest route
navigation.c: Will always cut every meridian at the same angle
navigation.d: Will cross successive meridians at changing angles
navigation.ans: Will always cut every meridian at the same angle
navigation.e: A rhumb line is defined by a constant track angle, so it intersects every meridian at the same angle.

navigation.q: The significance of the two standard parallels on a Lambert’s Conformal Conic Projection is that:
navigation.a: They enclose an area with no chart distortion
navigation.b: They make convergency zero throughout the chart
navigation.c: They make every rhumb line appear straight
navigation.d: They are the points where the cone of the projection cuts through the imaginary earth’s surface and therefore the scale of the chart is correct only at these points.
navigation.ans: They are the points where the cone of the projection cuts through the imaginary earth’s surface and therefore the scale of the chart is correct only at these points.
navigation.e: The standard parallels are the two circles where the secant cone intersects the Earth. Along them, the chart’s representative scale is exact.

navigation.q: True Airspeed (TAS) is:
navigation.a: RAS corrected for temperature and altitude
navigation.b: IAS corrected for instrument and position error
navigation.c: IAS corrected for pressure error only
navigation.ans: RAS corrected for temperature and altitude
navigation.e:
TAS is the aircraft's actual speed through the air mass, regardless of whether that air mass is itself moving over the ground. A balloon or cloud has zero TAS because it is stationary relative to the surrounding air; an aircraft's TAS is its speed relative to that same air mass.

Reaching TAS from the airspeed indicator reading is a two-step correction:
1. IAS -> RAS/CAS: correct for instrument and position (pitot-static) errors specific to that aircraft.
2. RAS/CAS -> TAS: correct for density error - the ASI is calibrated to read accurately only at ISA MSL density (1225 g/m^3), so at any other density (almost always, since density falls with altitude and rises with temperature) CAS under-reads the true speed through the thinner air.

Wind velocity is only applied afterwards, to convert TAS into groundspeed.

navigation.q: Rectified Airspeed (RAS) or Calibrated Airspeed (CAS) is:
navigation.a: IAS corrected for pressure and temperature
navigation.b: IAS corrected for instrument and position error
navigation.ans: IAS corrected for instrument and position error
navigation.e:
RAS (rectified airspeed) - called CAS (calibrated airspeed) in most of the world outside the UK - is IAS corrected for the two small errors inherent in a particular aircraft's pitot-static system:
- Instrument error: imperfections in the manufacture of the airspeed indicator itself.
- Position error: the pitot tube and static vent position on the airframe disturbs the local airflow they sense, varying with angle of attack, flap setting, etc.

These corrections come from the aircraft's own calibration/POH data and are usually only a few knots, which is why IAS and RAS/CAS are often treated as equal at PPL level. RAS/CAS is what the ASI would read if the instrument and its plumbing were perfect - it is not yet corrected for air density, which is the further step needed to reach TAS.

navigation.q: The angular difference between true north and magnetic north is called:
navigation.e: Variation is the angular difference between true north and magnetic north at a particular place. Deviation is the separate error caused by magnetic fields within the aircraft.

navigation.q: A line joining places of equal variation is called:
navigation.e: An isogonal joins places having equal magnetic variation. An agonic line is the special isogonal on which variation is zero.

navigation.q: An agonic line is used to indicate:
navigation.e: An isogonal is a line on a chart joining all places that share the same magnetic variation. The agonic line is the special isogonal where that shared variation is zero — true north and magnetic north coincide there, so a compass on this line points at true north with no correction needed at all. Everywhere else, the compass points at magnetic north, offset from true north by that place's own variation value.

navigation.q: To convert a true heading to magnetic when variation is west:
navigation.a: The variation must be subtracted from true heading to obtain magnetic heading
navigation.b: The value of variation must be added to the true heading to obtain the magnetic heading
navigation.c: The variation must be added to compass heading to obtain magnetic heading
navigation.d: No correction is required between true and magnetic heading
navigation.ans: The value of variation must be added to the true heading to obtain the magnetic heading
navigation.e: When converting true to magnetic, westerly variation is added: magnetic = true + west variation. The correction changes direction when converting back to true.

navigation.q: When magnetic variation is given as East:
navigation.a: The variation must be subtracted from magnetic heading to obtain true heading
navigation.b: The variation must be added to true heading to obtain magnetic heading
navigation.c: The value of variation must be added to the magnetic heading to obtain the true heading.
navigation.d: The variation must be applied as compass deviation
navigation.ans: The value of variation must be added to the magnetic heading to obtain the true heading.
navigation.e: For easterly variation, true heading is obtained by adding the variation to magnetic heading. Equivalently, east variation is subtracted when converting true to magnetic.

navigation.q: To convert a magnetic heading to true when variation is west:
navigation.a: The variation must be added to magnetic heading to obtain true heading
navigation.b: The variation must be subtracted from compass heading as deviation
navigation.d: The value of variation must be subtracted from a magnetic heading to get the true heading
navigation.ans: The value of variation must be subtracted from a magnetic heading to get the true heading
navigation.e: With west variation, magnetic = true + variation. Rearranging gives true = magnetic − west variation.

navigation.q: When magnetic variation is indicated as East:
navigation.a: The value of variation must be subtracted from a true heading to obtain a magnetic heading
navigation.b: The variation must be added to true heading to obtain magnetic heading
navigation.c: The variation must be subtracted from compass heading as deviation
navigation.d: The variation must be added to compass heading only
navigation.ans: The value of variation must be subtracted from a true heading to obtain a magnetic heading
navigation.e: For east variation, magnetic heading is less than true heading by the value of variation, so subtract east variation from true heading.

navigation.q: Westerly variation must be added to a true bearing to create a magnetic bearing because:
navigation.a: Magnetic north is east of true north
navigation.b: Magnetic north is to the west of true north
navigation.c: Magnetic north and true north coincide
navigation.d: Compass north is west of magnetic north
navigation.ans: Magnetic north is to the west of true north
navigation.e: Westerly variation means the magnetic north reference lies west of true north. The clockwise angle measured from magnetic north therefore makes the magnetic bearing numerically greater.

navigation.q: When magnetic variation is indicated as "West", it means that:
navigation.a: Magnetic north is east of true north
navigation.b: Compass north is west of magnetic north
navigation.c: Magnetic north is located to the west of true north
navigation.ans: Magnetic north is located to the west of true north
navigation.e: The label west variation describes the position of magnetic north relative to true north: magnetic north lies to the west.

navigation.q: When magnetic variation is indicated as East, it means that:
navigation.a: Magnetic north is west of true north
navigation.b: Compass north is east of magnetic north
navigation.c: True north and magnetic north coincide
navigation.d: Magnetic north is located to the east of True north
navigation.ans: Magnetic north is located to the east of True north
navigation.e: Easterly variation means magnetic north lies east of true north. This is a geographic variation effect, not aircraft compass deviation.

navigation.q: Sunrise is defined as:
navigation.a: When the very first part of the sun appears above the horizon
navigation.b: When the centre of the sun reaches the horizon
navigation.c: When the entire solar disc is above the horizon
navigation.d: When the lower edge of the sun clears the horizon
navigation.ans: When the very first part of the sun appears above the horizon
navigation.e: Sunrise occurs when the first visible portion of the sun appears above the horizon. Official day begins 15 minutes before this event in the South African exam convention.

navigation.q: An aircraft in the southern hemisphere is to maintain a constant heading of 90deg (M) on a magnetic compass. If the aircraft’s speed is increased, the compass would:
navigation.a: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.b: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.ans: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Acceleration error is greatest on east–west headings.
• In the Northern Hemisphere, acceleration indicates an apparent turn north.
• The effect is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere.
• Therefore, accelerating while maintaining 090°M produces an apparent turn south.

FINAL ANSWER
Show an apparent turn to the south

navigation.q: Sunset is defined as:
navigation.a: At the start of official night
navigation.c: Being 15 minutes before the start of official night
navigation.ans: Being 15 minutes before the start of official night
navigation.e: Official night begins 15 minutes after sunset. Therefore sunset occurs 15 minutes before the start of official night.

navigation.q: An aircraft in the southern hemisphere is to maintain a constant heading of 180deg (M) using a magnetic compass. If the airspeed is increased the compass would:
navigation.a: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.b: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.d: Continue to show the same heading
navigation.ans: Continue to show the same heading
navigation.e:
WORKING

• The compass card's centre of gravity is displaced from its pivot to counter magnetic dip, and that displacement lies along the magnetic north–south line.
• On a southerly heading the pivot and the CG are in line with the aircraft's fore-and-aft axis. Increasing speed pushes the pivot forward and the CG lags straight behind it, so no turning couple acts on the card and it does not swing.
• Acceleration error is greatest on east/west headings, where the CG sits to one side of the line of acceleration. It grows as the heading gets closer to east or west.

FINAL ANSWER
Continue to show the same heading

navigation.q: If the time of sunset is given as 1845, official night begins at:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunset = 1845

FORMULA
Official night begins 15 minutes after sunset: official night = sunset + 15 min

SOLVE
1845 + 0015 = 1860 → minutes only run 00–59, so 60 min carries into the next hour
= 1900

ANSWER
1900

navigation.q: Compass deviation:
navigation.a: Has one constant value for every heading
navigation.b: Usually varies on all headings in the same aircraft
navigation.d: Is identical in all aircraft of the same type
navigation.ans: Usually varies on all headings in the same aircraft
navigation.e: Deviation is caused by the aircraft's own stray magnetic fields — its metal structure, engine, radios and wiring — acting on the compass magnet, not by the earth's field. As the aircraft turns onto different headings, these fixed internal fields present themselves to the compass magnet at different angles relative to the earth's magnetic field, so the size and direction of the deflection changes with heading: on some headings the unwanted field may line up fore-and-aft and cause little or no deviation, while on others it causes the largest error. This is why the deviation (compass correction) card lists a different correction for each heading rather than one constant value for the whole compass rose.

navigation.q: 140km equals:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 140 km

FORMULA
1 nm = 1.852 km, so nm = km ÷ 1.852
Why 1.852: the metre is one ten-millionth of the distance from equator to pole (10 000 km). That quarter-meridian spans 90° × 60′ = 5400′ of latitude = 5400 nm. 10 000 ÷ 5400 = 1.852 km per nm.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
140 ÷ 1.852 = 75.59 nm ≈ 76 nm
Trap: 87 is 140 ÷ 1.609, the answer in statute miles, not nautical miles.

ANSWER
76nm

navigation.q: If official night in South Africa starts at 1645 UTC, the local time of sunset is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Official night begins at 1645 UTC. South Africa is UTC+2.

FORMULA
Local time = UTC + 2 h
Sunset = official night start (local) − 15 min

SOLVE
1645 UTC + 2:00 = 1845 local
1845 − 0015 = 1830

ANSWER
1830 LMT

navigation.q: When compass deviation is indicated as "West", it means that:
navigation.a: Compass north is to the west of magnetic north.
navigation.b: Compass north is east of magnetic north.
navigation.c: True north is west of magnetic north.
navigation.d: Compass north and magnetic north coincide.
navigation.ans: Compass north is to the west of magnetic north.
navigation.e: Westerly deviation means the compass north reference lies west of magnetic north — geometrically the same relationship as westerly variation, but caused by the aircraft's own stray magnetic fields rather than the earth's field, and it is specific to that aircraft and to the heading being flown, taken from its compass correction card. The mnemonic 'deviation west, compass best' is the reminder: with west deviation the compass reading is numerically greater than the magnetic heading, so compass heading = magnetic heading + west deviation.

navigation.q: If official day starts at 0535, the time of sunrise is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Official day starts at 0535.

FORMULA
Sunrise = official day start + 15 min

SOLVE
0535 + 0015 = 0550

ANSWER
0550

navigation.q: If official day ends at 1910, the time of sunset is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Official day ends at 1910.

FORMULA
Sunset = official day end − 15 min

SOLVE
1910 − 0015: borrow one hour (60 min) → 1870 − 0015
= 1855 (minutes run 00–59, not 00–99)

ANSWER
1855

navigation.q: 40 US gallons equals:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Volume = 40 US gallons

FORMULA
1 US gal = 3.785 litres, so litres = US gal × 3.785
Quick-check values: 1 US gal ≈ 4 L ≈ 0.8 Imp gal; 1 Imp gal ≈ 1.2 US gal ≈ 4.5 L.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
40 × 3.785 = 151.4 litres ≈ 151 litres
Traps: 160 is the ×4 rough figure; 182 is 40 × 4.546, treating the fuel as imperial gallons. GA gauges read US gallons but fuel is ordered in litres — confusing the two is a real refuelling error.

ANSWER
151 litres

navigation.q: An aircraft in the southern hemisphere is to maintain a constant heading of 270deg (M) on a magnetic compass. If the aircraft’s airspeed is decreased, the compass would:
navigation.a: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.b: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.ans: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Acceleration error is greatest on east–west headings.
• On 270°M in the Southern Hemisphere, deceleration produces an apparent northerly swing.

FINAL ANSWER
Show an apparent turn to the north

navigation.q: When executing a turn from 210deg through south to 150deg, in the southern hemisphere, using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll out would be:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Turning error (caused by magnetic dip) is greatest when passing through a heading of North or South, and negligible on East/West headings.
• Why the rule reverses: the needle dips toward the nearer magnetic pole, so its centre of gravity is displaced to the equator side of the pivot to keep it roughly level. South of the equator the nearer pole is the south magnetic pole, so the CG sits on the north side of the pivot, the mirror image of a Northern Hemisphere compass. In a turn the pivot is pulled toward the centre of the turn while the CG tries to carry on at a tangent, so the card is dragged the opposite way to a Northern Hemisphere compass.
• In the Northern Hemisphere the rule is "Undershoot North, Overshoot South" (UNOS). In the Southern Hemisphere this is reversed: Overshoot North, Undershoot South.
• This turn passes through South (180°), so the Southern-Hemisphere "Undershoot South" rule applies: roll out before the compass reaches the desired heading, then let it settle onto the correct reading.
• Required heading 150°M, turning left through south, so roll out about 20° short of the target, at approximately 170°.

FINAL ANSWER
170deg

navigation.q: 120 litres equals:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Volume = 120 litres

FORMULA
1 US gal = 3.785 litres, so US gal = litres ÷ 3.785
Quick-check value: 1 US gal ≈ 4 L.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
120 ÷ 3.785 = 31.70 US gal ≈ 32 US gal

ANSWER
32USG

navigation.q: If official day in South Africa starts at 0325 UTC, the local time of sunrise is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Official day starts at 0325 UTC. South Africa is UTC+2.

FORMULA
Local time = UTC + 2 h
Sunrise = official day start (local) + 15 min

SOLVE
0325 UTC + 2:00 = 0525 local
0525 + 0015 = 0540

ANSWER
0540 LMT

navigation.q: If official night ends at 0500, the time of sunrise is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Official night ends at 0500.

FORMULA
Sunrise = official night end + 15 min

SOLVE
0500 + 0015 = 0515

ANSWER
0515

navigation.q: When executing a turn from 060deg through north to 340deg in the southern hemisphere, using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll out would be:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Turning error peaks when passing through North or South and is negligible on East/West headings.
• Why the rule reverses: the needle dips toward the nearer magnetic pole, so its centre of gravity is displaced to the equator side of the pivot to keep it roughly level. South of the equator the nearer pole is the south magnetic pole, so the CG sits on the north side of the pivot, the mirror image of a Northern Hemisphere compass. In a turn the pivot is pulled toward the centre of the turn while the CG tries to carry on at a tangent, so the card is dragged the opposite way to a Northern Hemisphere compass.
• Northern Hemisphere rule: Undershoot North, Overshoot South (UNOS). In the Southern Hemisphere this reverses: Overshoot North, Undershoot South.
• This turn passes through North, so the Southern-Hemisphere "Overshoot North" rule applies: continue turning past the point where the compass first reads the desired heading before rolling out.
• Required heading 340°M, turning left through north, so roll out about 20° beyond the target, at approximately 320°.

FINAL ANSWER
320deg

navigation.q: If the time of Sunset in South Africa is given as 1615 UTC, the official night begins at:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunset = 1615 UTC. South Africa is UTC+2.

FORMULA
Local time = UTC + 2 h
Official night start = sunset (local) + 15 min

SOLVE
1615 UTC + 2:00 = 1815 local
1815 + 0015 = 1830

ANSWER
1830 LMT

navigation.q: When executing a turn from 310deg through north to 050deg in the southern hemisphere, using only a magnetic compass, the most appropriate heading to roll would be:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Turning error peaks passing through North or South and is negligible on East/West headings.
• Southern Hemisphere rule (the reverse of the Northern Hemisphere's UNOS): Overshoot North, Undershoot South.
• This turn passes through North, so overshoot applies: continue turning past the point the compass first shows the desired heading before rolling out.
• Required heading 050°M, turning right through north, so roll out about 10° beyond the target, at approximately 060°.

FINAL ANSWER
060deg

navigation.q: An aircraft in the southern hemisphere is to maintain a constant heading of 360deg (M) using a magnetic compass. If the airspeed is decreased, the compass would:
navigation.a: Continue to show the same heading.
navigation.b: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.c: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.ans: Continue to show the same heading.
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Acceleration and deceleration errors are mainly experienced on east–west headings.
• On the exact northerly heading of 360°M, decreasing speed should not cause the same apparent turn.

FINAL ANSWER
Continue to show the same heading.

navigation.q: Compass turning errors occur in an aircraft:
navigation.a: On every heading by the same amount
navigation.b: Only when turning through northerly or southerly headings
navigation.c: Only when turning through easterly or westerly headings
navigation.ans: Only when turning through northerly or southerly headings
navigation.e: Turning error stems from magnetic dip. To keep the compass needle roughly level despite dip, the compass card's centre of gravity is deliberately offset from its pivot.
