During a turn, the aircraft (and the pivot) accelerates toward the centre of the turn, while the card's CG lags behind under its own inertia — this produces a false rotation of the card independent of the aircraft's actual heading change. That false rotation is largest while the aircraft is actually passing through a heading of magnetic north or south, and reduces to virtually nothing as the heading passes through east or west, which is why turning error is only significant near north/south headings.

navigation.q: Official day is defined as the period:
navigation.a: from sunrise exactly to sunset exactly
navigation.b: from 15 minutes after sunrise to 15 minutes before sunset
navigation.c: from 15 minutes before sunrise to 15 minutes after sunset
navigation.d: from 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset
navigation.ans: from 15 minutes before sunrise to 15 minutes after sunset
navigation.e: For South African PPL exam purposes, official day extends from 15 minutes before sunrise until 15 minutes after sunset.

navigation.q: Acceleration error occurs in an aircraft’s magnetic compass:
navigation.c: Only while the aircraft is turning
navigation.e: Acceleration error has the same root cause as turning error: the compass card's centre of gravity is offset from its pivot to counter magnetic dip. Any fore-and-aft acceleration or deceleration is transmitted to the pivot, but the CG's inertia makes it lag behind, producing a couple that rotates the card exactly as if the aircraft had turned — even though it is flying straight. On a north or south heading this dip-compensating offset lies along the aircraft's fore-and-aft axis, in line with the acceleration, so it produces no rotating couple and no error. On an easterly or westerly heading the offset lies across the direction of acceleration, giving the maximum false turn indication.

navigation.q: If the time of sunrise is given as 0505, the official night ends at:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunrise = 0505.

FORMULA
Official night ends = sunrise − 15 min

SOLVE
0505 − 0015: borrow one hour (60 min) → 0465 − 0015
= 0450 (minutes run 00–59, not as a decimal)

ANSWER
0450

navigation.q: When compass deviation is indicated as East, it means that:
navigation.a: Compass north is west of magnetic north
navigation.b: Compass north is to the east of magnetic north
navigation.c: True north is east of magnetic north
navigation.d: Compass north and magnetic north coincide
navigation.ans: Compass north is to the east of magnetic north
navigation.e: Easterly deviation means the compass north reference lies east of magnetic north, caused by the aircraft's own stray magnetic fields rather than the earth's field. It is aircraft- and heading-specific, taken from that aircraft's compass correction card. The mnemonic 'deviation east, compass least' is the reminder: with east deviation the compass reading is numerically less than the magnetic heading, so compass heading = magnetic heading − east deviation.

navigation.q: Compass deviation on a particular aircraft:
navigation.a: Is the same on every heading
navigation.b: Is published on the aeronautical chart
navigation.c: Must be applied to magnetic headings used on cross country flights
navigation.ans: Must be applied to magnetic headings used on cross country flights
navigation.e: Deviation is specific to both the aircraft and its heading. It is measured by an engineer 'swinging the compass' — turning the aircraft through a series of known headings and comparing the compass reading with the true magnetic direction — and the results are written on the deviation (compass correction) card mounted beside the instrument. Because deviation changes with heading, the pilot must read the correction for the heading actually being flown and apply it to the magnetic heading to obtain the compass heading to steer. The card is only valid for the magnetic influences present when it was swung, so loose metal or electronic items placed near the compass afterwards (calculators, headsets, portable radios) are not accounted for and can introduce large, unpredictable extra errors.

navigation.q: If the time of sunrise is given as 0535, official day begins at:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunrise = 0535.

FORMULA
Official day begins = sunrise − 15 min

SOLVE
0535 − 0015 = 0520

ANSWER
0520

navigation.q: An aircraft in the southern hemisphere is to maintain a constant heading of 90 deg (M) on a magnetic compass. If the aircraft’s airspeed is decreased, the compass would:
navigation.a: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.b: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.ans: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Deceleration error is greatest on east–west headings.
• In the Northern Hemisphere, deceleration indicates an apparent turn south.
• The effect is reversed in the Southern Hemisphere.
• Therefore, decelerating while maintaining 090°M produces an apparent turn north.

FINAL ANSWER
Show an apparent turn to the north

navigation.q: An aircraft in the southern hemisphere is to maintain a constant heading of 270deg (M) on a magnetic compass. If the aircraft’s speed is increased, the compass would:
navigation.a: Show an apparent turn to the north
navigation.b: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.ans: Show an apparent turn to the south
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Acceleration/deceleration (dip) error is greatest on East/West headings and negligible on North/South headings.
• In the Northern Hemisphere the rule is "Accelerate North, Decelerate South" (ANDS). In the Southern Hemisphere this is reversed: Accelerate South, Decelerate North.
• Maintaining 270°M (West) and increasing speed (accelerating) therefore produces an apparent turn toward South.

FINAL ANSWER
Show an apparent turn to the south

navigation.q: Heading 005°T, TAS 118 kt, drift 5° left and groundspeed 108 kt. The wind velocity is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 005°T, TAS 118 kt, drift 5° left, groundspeed 108 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 5° left means track = 005° − 5° = 000°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 000°T under the index and move the slide so GS 108 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector now ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 005°T lies 5° right of track. Follow the 5° drift line on the right of the centreline to where it crosses the 118 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The wind blows the aircraft from heading to track, so the W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot, then read wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index and wind speed as the distance down to the centre dot: W/V ≈ 047/14.

ANSWER
047/14

navigation.q: Track 115°T, heading 110°T, TAS 115 kt and groundspeed 105 kt. The wind velocity is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 115°T, heading 110°T, TAS 115 kt, groundspeed 105 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put track 115°T under the index and move the slide so GS 105 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector now ends at the centre dot.
Step 2: Heading 110°T lies 5° left of track. Follow the 5° drift line on the left of the centreline to where it crosses the 115 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 3: The wind blows the aircraft from heading to track, so the W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot, then read wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index and wind speed as the distance down to the centre dot: W/V ≈ 069/14.

ANSWER
069/14

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 3790ft, QNH 1006, temperature ISA +23deg C. The density altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 3790 ft, QNH 1006 hPa, OAT ISA +23°C

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa
Density altitude = pressure altitude + (120 × ISA deviation)

SOLVE
PA = 3790 + (1013 − 1006) × 30 = 3790 + (7 × 30) = 3790 + 210 = 4000 ft
DA = 4000 + (120 × 23) = 4000 + 2760 = 6760 ft

ANSWER
6760ft

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 4500ft, QNH 1013, temperature ISA+12deg C. The density altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 4500 ft, QNH 1013 hPa (standard), OAT ISA +12°C

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa
Density altitude = pressure altitude + (120 × ISA deviation)

SOLVE
QNH is standard (1013), so PA = elevation = 4500 ft
DA = 4500 + (120 × 12) = 4500 + 1440 = 5940 ft

ANSWER
5940ft

navigation.q: Heading 198deg (M), TAS 110, W/V 240/15, Variation 20deg W. Track and Groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 198°(M), TAS 110 kt, W/V 240/15, variation 20°W.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Convert heading to true: 198°M − 20°W = 178°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 240° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put heading 178°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 110 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector now ends at the centre dot, which is where the W/V vector begins.
Step 4: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 104 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 7° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
Track 171deg (T), GS 104

navigation.q: W/V 290/15, TAS 90kts, track 320° (T). The heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 290/15, TAS 90 kt, track 320°(T).

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 290° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 320°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 90 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins, so the wind-mark marks the end of HDG/TAS.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 5° left of track. Heading = track − WCA (nose into wind); drift is the same size on the opposite side (5° right). Read GS ≈ 77 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
315° (T)

navigation.q: Using the following information, W/V 220/10, Hdg 176deg (T), TAS 100kts:
navigation.a: The track is 172deg (T) and the groundspeed is 93kts
navigation.b: The track is 172deg (T) and the groundspeed is 107kts
navigation.c: The track is 180deg (T) and the groundspeed is 93kts
navigation.d: The track is 168deg (T) and the groundspeed is 100kts
navigation.ans: The track is 172deg (T) and the groundspeed is 93kts
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 220/10, heading 176°T, TAS 100 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 220° under the index and place the wind-mark 10 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 176°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 100 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector now ends at the centre dot, which is where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 93 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 4° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
The track is 172deg (T) and the groundspeed is 93kts

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 3380ft, QNH 1009, temperature +28deg C. The density altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 3380 ft, QNH 1009 hPa, OAT +28°C (actual)

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa
ISA temperature at PA = 15 − (2 × PA/1000)
Density altitude = PA + (120 × (OAT − ISA temp))

SOLVE
PA = 3380 + (1013 − 1009) × 30 = 3380 + 120 = 3500 ft
ISA temp at 3500 ft = 15 − (2 × 3.5) = 15 − 7 = 8°C
Deviation = 28 − 8 = ISA +20°C
DA = 3500 + (120 × 20) = 3500 + 2400 = 5900 ft

ANSWER
5900ft

navigation.q: Pressure altitude 5000ft, temperature ISA+23deg C. The density altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5000 ft, OAT ISA +23°C

FORMULA
Density altitude = pressure altitude + (120 × ISA deviation)

SOLVE
DA = 5000 + (120 × 23) = 5000 + 2760 = 7760 ft

ANSWER
7760ft

navigation.q: W/V 125/18, heading 092deg (T), TAS 90. The groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 125/18, heading 092°T, TAS 90 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 125° under the index and place the wind-mark 18 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 092°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 90 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector now ends at the centre dot, which is where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 76 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 8° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
76kts

navigation.q: TAS 90kts, W/V 355/20, Track 145° (T). The drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 90 kt, W/V 355/20, track 145°(T).

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 355° under the index and place the wind-mark 20 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 145°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 90 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins, so the wind-mark marks the end of HDG/TAS.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 6° left of track. Heading = track − WCA (nose into wind); drift is the same size on the opposite side (6° right). Read GS ≈ 107 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
6° right

navigation.q: An aircraft maintaining FL065, TAS 100kts, GS 95kts, Heading 230° (M), Track 200° (T), variation 23°W. The W/V is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
FL065, TAS 100 kt, groundspeed 95 kt, heading 230°(M), track 200°T, variation 23°W.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Convert heading to true: 230°M − 23°W = 207°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 200°T under the index and move the slide so GS 95 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector now ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 207°T lies 7° right of track. Follow the 7° drift line on the right of the centreline to where it crosses the 100 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The wind blows the aircraft from heading to track, so the W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot, then read wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index and wind speed as the distance down to the centre dot: W/V ≈ 271/13.

ANSWER
271/13

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 2800ft, QNH 1023. The pressure altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 2800 ft, QNH 1023 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
PA = 2800 + (1013 − 1023) × 30 = 2800 + (−10 × 30) = 2800 − 300 = 2500 ft

ANSWER
2500ft

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 4150ft, QNH 1018. The pressure altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 4150 ft, QNH 1018 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
PA = 4150 + (1013 − 1018) × 30 = 4150 + (−5 × 30) = 4150 − 150 = 4000 ft

ANSWER
4000ft

navigation.q: W/V 245/15 Hdg 195deg (T) groundspeed 91kts, headwind 9kts. Track is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 245/15, heading 195°T, groundspeed 91 kt, headwind component 9 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Recover TAS from the headwind component: TAS ≈ GS + headwind = 91 + 9 = 100 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 245° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put heading 195°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 100 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector now ends at the centre dot, which is where the W/V vector begins.
Step 4: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 91 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 7° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
188deg (T)

navigation.q: TAS 100kts, W/V 005/15 Track 345deg (T). The groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 100 kt, W/V 005/15, track 345°(T).

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 005° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 345°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 100 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins, so the wind-mark marks the end of HDG/TAS.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 3° right of track. Heading = track + WCA (nose into wind); drift is the same size on the opposite side (3° left). Read GS ≈ 86 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
86kts

navigation.q: F085 temperature -3deg C, RAS 90kts, headwind 8kts. The groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Flight level 085 (pressure altitude 8500 ft), OAT −3°C, RAS (CAS) 90 kt, headwind 8 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: On the airspeed correction window, align OAT −3°C with pressure altitude 8.5 (thousands of ft).
Step 2: Opposite RAS 90 kt on the inner scale, read TAS ≈ 102 kt on the outer scale.
Step 3: Subtract the headwind component from TAS: GS ≈ 102 − 8 = 94 kt.

ANSWER
94kts

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 1090ft QNH 1016, temperature +22deg C. The density altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 1090 ft, QNH 1016 hPa, OAT +22°C (actual)

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa
ISA temperature at PA = 15 − (2 × PA/1000)
Density altitude = PA + (120 × (OAT − ISA temp))

SOLVE
PA = 1090 + (1013 − 1016) × 30 = 1090 − 90 = 1000 ft
ISA temp at 1000 ft = 15 − (2 × 1) = 13°C
Deviation = 22 − 13 = ISA +9°C
DA = 1000 + (120 × 9) = 1000 + 1080 = 2080 ft

ANSWER
2080ft

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 1850ft, QNH 1008. The pressure altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 1850 ft, QNH 1008 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
PA = 1850 + (1013 − 1008) × 30 = 1850 + 150 = 2000 ft

ANSWER
2000ft

navigation.q: W/V 290/15, TAS 90kts, Track 320° (T). The drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 290/15, TAS 90 kt, track 320°(T).

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 290° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 320°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 90 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins, so the wind-mark marks the end of HDG/TAS.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 5° left of track. Heading = track − WCA (nose into wind); drift is the same size on the opposite side (5° right). Read GS ≈ 77 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
5° right

navigation.q: Heading 225deg (T), Drift 5deg right, TAS 115kts, tailwind 6kts. The W/V is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 225°T, drift 5° right, TAS 115 kt, tailwind 6 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 5° right means track = 225° + 5° = 230°T. A tailwind of 6 kt means GS = 115 + 6 = 121 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 230°T under the index and move the slide so GS 121 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector now ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 225°T lies 5° left of track. Follow the 5° drift line on the left of the centreline to where it crosses the 115 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The wind blows the aircraft from heading to track, so the W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot, then read wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index and wind speed as the distance down to the centre dot: W/V ≈ 107/12.

ANSWER
107/12

navigation.q: W/V 005/15, Hdg 340deg (T), TAS 95. The track is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 005/15, heading 340°T, TAS 95 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 005° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 340°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 95 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector now ends at the centre dot, which is where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 82 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 4° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
336deg (T)

navigation.q: Pressure altitude 3050ft, temperature 23deg C. The density altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3050 ft, OAT 23°C (actual)

FORMULA
ISA temperature at PA = 15 − (2 × PA/1000)
Density altitude = PA + (120 × (OAT − ISA temp))

SOLVE
ISA temp at 3050 ft = 15 − (2 × 3.05) = 15 − 6.1 = 8.9°C, taken as 9°C
Deviation = 23 − 9 = ISA +14°C
DA = 3050 + (120 × 14) = 3050 + 1680 = 4730 ft

ANSWER
4730ft

navigation.q: Heading 355deg (T), Drift 7deg right, GS 110kts, tailwind 5kts. The W/V is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 355°T, drift 7° right, groundspeed 110 kt, tailwind 5 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 7° right means track = 355° + 7° = 002°T. A tailwind of 5 kt means TAS = 110 − 5 = 105 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 002°T under the index and move the slide so GS 110 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector now ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 355°T lies 7° left of track. Follow the 7° drift line on the left of the centreline to where it crosses the 105 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The wind blows the aircraft from heading to track, so the W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot, then read wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index and wind speed as the distance down to the centre dot: W/V ≈ 248/14.

ANSWER
248/14

navigation.q: W/V 045/12, Track 101deg (T), drift 6deg right, TAS 95kts. Groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 045/12, track 101°T, drift 6° right, TAS 95 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 6° right means heading = 101° − 6° = 095°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 045° under the index and place the wind-mark 12 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put heading 095°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 95 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector now ends at the centre dot, which is where the W/V vector begins.
Step 4: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 88 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 6° right. Track = heading + drift.

ANSWER
88kts

navigation.q: Pressure altitude 3310ft, QNH 1020, the airfield elevation is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 3310 ft, QNH 1020 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa, so elevation = PA − (1013 − QNH) × 30

SOLVE
Elevation = 3310 − (1013 − 1020) × 30 = 3310 − (−7 × 30) = 3310 + 210 = 3520 ft

ANSWER
3520ft

navigation.q: W/V 290/15, TAS 90kts, Track 320° (T). The ground speed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
W/V 290/15, TAS 90 kt, track 320°(T).

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 290° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 320°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 90 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins, so the wind-mark marks the end of HDG/TAS.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 5° left of track. Heading = track − WCA (nose into wind); drift is the same size on the opposite side (5° right). Read GS ≈ 77 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
77kts

navigation.q: Pressure altitude 2250ft, QNH 1005. The airfield elevation is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 2250 ft, QNH 1005 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa, so elevation = PA − (1013 − QNH) × 30

SOLVE
Elevation = 2250 − (1013 − 1005) × 30 = 2250 − (8 × 30) = 2250 − 240 = 2010 ft

ANSWER
2010ft

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 3000ft, QNH 1003. Pressure altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 3000 ft, QNH 1003 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
PA = 3000 + (1013 − 1003) × 30 = 3000 + 300 = 3300 ft

ANSWER
3300ft

navigation.q: Track 183deg (T), Heading 209deg (M), TAS 110kts groundspeed 118kts. Variation 19deg W. The W/V is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 183°T, heading 209°(M), TAS 110 kt, groundspeed 118 kt, variation 19°W.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Convert heading to true: 209°M − 19°W = 190°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 183°T under the index and move the slide so GS 118 kt is under the centre dot — this is where the TR/GS vector ends.
Step 3: Heading 190°T is 7° right of track. Follow the 7° drift line right of the centreline to where it crosses the 110 kt TAS arc, and mark that point as the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot, then read wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index and wind speed as the distance from mark to centre dot. Read W/V ≈ 306/16.

ANSWER
306/16

navigation.q: An aircraft flies from A to B, distance 133nm in 1hr12mins. If there is a headwind of 12kts the TAS is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 133 nm
Flight time = 1 hr 12 min
Headwind component = 12 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 1 h 12 min = 1 + 12/60 = 1.2 h
GS = 133 ÷ 1.2 = 110.8 kt
TAS = 110.8 + 12 = 122.8 kt ≈ 123 kt

ANSWER
123kts

navigation.q: An aircraft is overhead airfield A (elevation sea level) at 1000ft and is required to be at 8500ft within 25nm. Mean climb TAS 100kts, mean climb headwind 6kts. The mean rate of climb required is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Start altitude = 1000 ft, target altitude = 8500 ft
Distance to climb = 25 nm
Climb TAS = 100 kt, headwind = 6 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height to gain = 8500 − 1000 = 7500 ft
Climb GS = 100 − 6 = 94 kt
Time = 25 ÷ 94 × 60 = 16.0 min (nearest minute)
ROC = 7500 ÷ 16 = 468.75 ≈ 469 fpm

ANSWER
469fpm

navigation.q: F065, OAT +15deg C, RAS 84kts. The TAS is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 6 500 ft (F065), OAT +15°C, RAS 84 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: In the airspeed window, set the OAT +15°C against pressure altitude 6.5 (thousands of feet).
Step 2: Opposite RAS 84 kt on the inner scale, read TAS ≈ 95 kt on the outer scale.

ANSWER
95kts

navigation.q: TAS 110kts, W/V 155/15, Track 085deg (T). The drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 110 kt, W/V 155/15, track 085°T.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 155° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 085°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 110 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark — this is where the HDG/TAS vector ends and the W/V vector begins.
Step 4: Read WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 7° right of track, so heading = track + WCA (nose into wind). Drift is the same size but opposite: 7° left. Read GS ≈ 104 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
7deg left

navigation.q: An aircraft is to fly from A to B, distance 235nm, TAS 90kts, tailwind 5kts, cruise fuel flow 8.5USG/hr, assume 3 USG is required to take off and climb to cruising altitude and the reserve fuel requirement is 9USG. The total fuel required is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 235 nm
TAS = 90 kt, tailwind = 5 kt
Cruise fuel flow = 8.5 USG/hr
Climb/take-off fuel = 3 USG
Reserve fuel = 9 USG

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
GS = 90 + 5 = 95 kt
Cruise time = 235 ÷ 95 = 2.474 h
Cruise fuel = 2.474 × 8.5 = 21.0 USG
Total fuel = 21.0 + 3 + 9 = 33.0 USG

ANSWER
33USG

navigation.q: The distance between A (S20deg E035deg) and B (S17deg E035deg) is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
A: S20° E035°  B: S17° E035° (same meridian)

FORMULA
Distance along a meridian = change in latitude (minutes) × 1 nm, since 1' of latitude = 1 nm

SOLVE
Latitude difference = 20° − 17° = 3° = 180'
Distance = 180 × 1 nm = 180 nm

ANSWER
180nm

navigation.q: An aircraft takes 33mins to cover a distance of 10cm on a chart, the scale of which is 1:1000000. The groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 10 cm
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000
Time = 33 min

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator
Groundspeed = distance ÷ time

SOLVE
Ground distance = 10 cm × 1 000 000 = 10 000 000 cm = 100 km
Convert to nautical miles: 100 km ÷ 1.852 = 54.0 NM
Time = 33 min ÷ 60 = 0.55 h
Groundspeed = 54.0 NM ÷ 0.55 h = 98.2 kt

ANSWER
98kts

navigation.q: Runway 16 in use, surface wind 270/12. The aircraft would have a:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Runway 16 in use (runway heading ≈ 160°), surface wind 270/12.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the centre dot on the zero point of the square grid. Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 270° under the index and mark the wind-mark 12 kt straight down from the centre dot.
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put the runway direction 160° under the index.
Step 3: Drop a vertical line to the wind-mark. Distance BELOW the centre-dot horizontal line is headwind; ABOVE is tailwind (consider the reciprocal runway). Sideways distance from the centreline is crosswind. Here the wind-mark sits about 4 kt above the horizontal line (tailwind component 4 kt) and about 11 kt to the side (crosswind component 11 kt).

ANSWER
4kt tailwind

navigation.q: Runway 03 in use, surface wind 090/20. The crosswind component is
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Runway 03 in use (runway heading ≈ 030°), surface wind 090/20.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the centre dot on the zero point of the square grid. Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 090° under the index and mark the wind-mark 20 kt straight down from the centre dot.
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put the runway direction 030° under the index.
Step 3: Drop a vertical line to the wind-mark. Distance BELOW the centre-dot horizontal line is headwind; ABOVE is tailwind (consider the reciprocal runway). Sideways distance from the centreline is crosswind. Here the wind-mark sits about 10 kt below the horizontal line (headwind component 10 kt) and about 17 kt to the side (crosswind component 17 kt).

ANSWER
17kts

navigation.q: An aircraft is flying from Alpha to Bravo, total distance 96nm. After flying for 40nm a fix is obtained which places the aircraft 3nm right of the track. The track error is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Total distance 96 nm, distance flown 40 nm, 3 nm right of track

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: track error (°) = (distance off track ÷ distance flown) × 60

SOLVE
Track error = (3 ÷ 40) × 60 = 180 ÷ 40 = 4.5°

ANSWER
4.5°

navigation.q: Distance 148nm, TAS 100kts, headwind 8kts, fuel flow 6.8USG/hr. The trip fuel is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 148 nm
TAS = 100 kt, headwind = 8 kt
Fuel flow = 6.8 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
GS = 100 − 8 = 92 kt
Time = 148 ÷ 92 = 1.609 h
Trip fuel = 1.609 × 6.8 = 10.94 USG ≈ 11 USG

ANSWER
11USG

navigation.q: The distance between A (S15deg E023deg) and B (S17deg E023deg) is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
A: S15° E023°  B: S17° E023° (same meridian)

FORMULA
Distance along a meridian = change in latitude (minutes) × 1 nm, since 1' of latitude = 1 nm

SOLVE
Latitude difference = 17° − 15° = 2° = 120'
Distance = 120 × 1 nm = 120 nm

ANSWER
120nm

navigation.q: An aircraft covers a distance of 88nm in 42mins, tailwind 5kts. The TAS is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 88 nm
Flight time = 42 min
Tailwind = 5 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 42 ÷ 60 = 0.70 h
GS = 88 ÷ 0.70 = 125.7 kt
TAS = 125.7 − 5 = 120.7 ≈ 121 kt

ANSWER
121kts

navigation.q: Runway 25 in use, surface wind 190/15. The crosswind component is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Runway 25 in use (runway heading ≈ 250°), surface wind 190/15.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the centre dot on the zero point of the square grid. Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 190° under the index and mark the wind-mark 15 kt straight down from the centre dot.
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put the runway direction 250° under the index.
Step 3: Drop a vertical line to the wind-mark. Distance BELOW the centre-dot horizontal line is headwind; ABOVE is tailwind (consider the reciprocal runway). Sideways distance from the centreline is crosswind. Here the wind-mark sits about 8 kt below the horizontal line (headwind component 8 kt) and about 13 kt to the side (crosswind component 13 kt).

ANSWER
13kts

navigation.q: An aircraft climbs from 2500ft to 9500ft at a constant rate of climb of 350fpm. If the mean climb groundspeed is 85kts the distance covered during the climb is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Climb from 2500 ft to 9500 ft
Rate of climb = 350 fpm
Mean climb groundspeed = 85 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height gained = 9500 − 2500 = 7000 ft
Climb time = 7000 ÷ 350 = 20 min
Distance = 85 × (20 ÷ 60) = 28.3 nm ≈ 28 nm

ANSWER
28nm

navigation.q: An aircraft is flying from Alpha to Bravo. After flying for 45nm, the aircraft is 4nm left of track. The track error is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance flown 45 nm, 4 nm left of track

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: track error (°) = (distance off track ÷ distance flown) × 60

SOLVE
Track error = (4 ÷ 45) × 60 = 240 ÷ 45 = 5.33°, rounds to 5.3°

ANSWER
5.3°

navigation.q: An aircraft with a TAS of 110kts flies from A to B, distance 148nm, in 1hr14mins. The TAS required to fly from B back to A in 1hr 20mins is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Outbound: distance 148 nm, TAS 110 kt, flight time 1 hr 14 min
Return: same 148 nm, required time 1 hr 20 min

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Outbound time = 1 h 14 min = 74 ÷ 60 = 1.233 h
Outbound GS = 148 ÷ 1.233 = 120 kt
Wind component = 120 − 110 = 10 kt tailwind outbound, so a 10 kt headwind on the return
Return time = 1 h 20 min = 80 ÷ 60 = 1.333 h
Required return GS = 148 ÷ 1.333 = 111 kt
Required TAS = 111 + 10 = 121 kt

ANSWER
121kts

navigation.q: The scale of a chart is expressed as 15cm to 25nm. As a representative fraction, this is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 15 cm
Ground distance = 25 NM

FORMULA
Scale (RF) = ground distance ÷ chart distance, both measured in the same units

SOLVE
Convert 25 NM to cm: 25 × 1853 m = 46 325 m = 4 632 500 cm
Scale denominator = 4 632 500 cm ÷ 15 cm = 308 833.3
Round to a whole number

ANSWER
1:308833

navigation.q: FL105, temperature ISA+1deg, RAS 85kts. The TAS will be:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 10 500 ft (FL105), temperature ISA +1°C, RAS 85 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 10 500 ft = 15 − (2 × 10.5) = −6°C, so ISA +1 gives OAT = −5°C.
Step 2: In the airspeed window, set the OAT −5°C against pressure altitude 10.5 (thousands of feet).
Step 3: Opposite RAS 85 kt on the inner scale, read TAS ≈ 100 kt on the outer scale.

ANSWER
100kts

navigation.q: Distance 185 nm, GS 95, fuel flow 6.8 USG/hr. The trip fuel is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 185 nm
Groundspeed = 95 kt
Fuel flow = 6.8 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 185 ÷ 95 = 1.947 h = 116.8 min ≈ 117 min = 1.95 h (nearest minute)
Trip fuel = 1.95 × 6.8 = 13.26 ≈ 13.3 USG

ANSWER
13.3 USG

navigation.q: The scale of a chart is 10cm to 40nm. The scale as a representative fraction is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 10 cm
Ground distance = 40 NM

FORMULA
Scale (RF) = ground distance ÷ chart distance, both measured in the same units

SOLVE
Convert 40 NM to cm: 40 × 1853 m = 74 120 m = 7 412 000 cm
Scale denominator = 7 412 000 cm ÷ 10 cm = 741 200

ANSWER
1:741200

navigation.q: An aircraft is flying from A 32°E in an easterly direction to B 38°E along the 18°S parallel. The aircraft:
navigation.a: Is following a great-circle track only
navigation.b: Is flying along a rhumb line track
navigation.c: Is following both a great circle and rhumb line
navigation.d: Must continuously alter track to remain on the parallel
navigation.ans: Is flying along a rhumb line track
navigation.e:
WORKING

• The aircraft remains on the 18°S parallel while longitude changes from 32°E to 38°E.
• A parallel of latitude cuts every meridian at the same angle.
• A route that maintains a constant direction is a rhumb line.

FINAL ANSWER
Is flying along a rhumb line track

navigation.q: Runway 29 in use, surface wind 040/15. The aircraft would have a:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Runway 29 in use (runway heading ≈ 290°), surface wind 040/15.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the centre dot on the zero point of the square grid. Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 040° under the index and mark the wind-mark 15 kt straight down from the centre dot.
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put the runway direction 290° under the index.
Step 3: Drop a vertical line to the wind-mark. Distance BELOW the centre-dot horizontal line is headwind; ABOVE is tailwind (consider the reciprocal runway). Sideways distance from the centreline is crosswind. Here the wind-mark sits about 5 kt above the horizontal line (tailwind component 5 kt) and about 14 kt to the side (crosswind component 14 kt).

ANSWER
5kt tailwind

navigation.q: Aircraft heading 008deg (T), variation 24deg W, deviation 4deg west. The aircraft’s compass heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
True heading 008°T, variation 24°W, deviation 4°W.

FORMULA
True → Magnetic: add west variation. Magnetic → Compass: add west deviation.

SOLVE
Magnetic heading = 008° + 24° = 032°M.
Compass heading = 032° + 4° = 036°C.

ANSWER
036deg (C)

navigation.q: Runway 17 in use, surface wind 240/15. The headwind component is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Runway 17 in use (runway heading ≈ 170°), surface wind 240/15.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Set the centre dot on the zero point of the square grid. Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 240° under the index and mark the wind-mark 15 kt straight down from the centre dot.
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put the runway direction 170° under the index.
Step 3: Drop a vertical line to the wind-mark. Distance BELOW the centre-dot horizontal line is headwind; ABOVE is tailwind (consider the reciprocal runway). Sideways distance from the centreline is crosswind. Here the wind-mark sits about 5 kt below the horizontal line (headwind component 5 kt) and about 14 kt to the side (crosswind component 14 kt).

ANSWER
5kts

navigation.q: During a descent from 6000ft to 1500ft an aircraft with mean descent groundspeed of 90kts covers a distance of 15nm. The rate of descent is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Descent from 6000 ft to 1500 ft
Mean descent groundspeed = 90 kt
Distance covered = 15 nm

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height lost = 6000 − 1500 = 4500 ft
Time = 15 ÷ 90 × 60 = 10 min
ROD = 4500 ÷ 10 = 450 fpm

ANSWER
450fpm

navigation.q: Distance flown 88nm, flight time 43mins, the groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance flown = 88 nm
Flight time = 43 min

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 43 ÷ 60 = 0.7167 h
GS = 88 ÷ 0.7167 = 122.8 ≈ 123 kt

ANSWER
123kts

navigation.q: An aircraft takes 45mins to cover a distance of 18cm on chart, the scale of which is 1:1000000. If the TAS is 120kts there is a:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 18 cm
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000
Time = 45 min
TAS = 120 kt

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator
Groundspeed = distance ÷ time
Wind component = groundspeed − TAS

SOLVE
Ground distance = 18 cm × 1 000 000 = 18 000 000 cm = 180 km
Convert to nautical miles: 180 km ÷ 1.852 = 97.2 NM
Time = 45 min ÷ 60 = 0.75 h
Groundspeed = 97.2 NM ÷ 0.75 h = 129.6 kt
Wind component = 129.6 − 120 = 9.6 kt; since groundspeed exceeds TAS, this is a tailwind

ANSWER
9kts tailwind

navigation.q: Flight time A to B = 1 hr 15 minutes, Fuel Flow 7.3USG/hr. The trip fuel is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Flight time A to B = 1 hr 15 min
Fuel flow = 7.3 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 1 h 15 min = 1.25 h
Trip fuel = 1.25 × 7.3 = 9.125 ≈ 9.1 USG

ANSWER
9.1 USG

navigation.q: An aircraft is flying from A (32deg E) in a Westerly direction to B (12deg W) along the equator. The aircraft:
navigation.b: Flying a great circle as well as rhumb line track
navigation.ans: Flying a great circle as well as rhumb line track
navigation.e: The equator is both a great circle and a rhumb line. A flight along it therefore follows the shortest great-circle route while maintaining a constant east–west track.

navigation.q: At 0830 an aircraft was overhead NELSPRUIT (S25° 30’ E030° 55’) on track for PILANESBURG (S25° 22’ E027° 12’). At 0924 the aircraft crosses radial 020 WIV (S25° 50’ E029° 12’). The groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot radial 020 from WIV and mark where it crosses the Nelspruit–Pilanesberg track.
• Chart distance from Nelspruit to the crossing is approximately 92 NM.
• Elapsed time = 0924 − 0830 = 54 min = 0.90 h.
• Groundspeed = 92 ÷ 0.90 ≈ 102 kt.

FINAL ANSWER
102 kts

navigation.q: Overhead HEIDELBERG VOR (HGV), (S26°42’ E028°18’), en route DURBAN INTERNATIONAL (S29°58’ E030°58’), TAS 120kts, W/V 100/15. The mean magnetic heading to steer is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Overhead Heidelberg HGV en route Durban International, TAS 120 kt, W/V 100/15.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Plot the route on the chart and measure the true track: about 144°T.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 100° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 144°T under the index and move the slide so the 120 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 5° left of track, so heading ≈ 139°T. Read GS ≈ 109 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Convert to magnetic with the chart variation (about 21°W): 139°T + 21° = 160°M.

ANSWER
160° (M)

navigation.q: Track 145° (T), W/V 220/20, TAS 125 kts, variation 22°W. The magnetic heading to steer is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Required track 145°T, W/V 220/20, TAS 125 kt, variation 22°W.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 220° under the index and place the wind-mark 20 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 145°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 125 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 9° right of track (the wind is from the right), so heading ≈ 145° + 9° = 154°T. GS ≈ 118 kt is under the centre dot.
Step 5: Convert to magnetic: 154°T + 22°W = 176°M.

ANSWER
176° (M)

navigation.q: Overhead BLOEMFONTEIN at 1018 UTC en route EAST LONDON. At 1108 UTC a GPS fix is obtained at S30deg 40’ E027deg 15’. The ETA for EAST LONDON is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot the 1108 GPS fix at S30°40′ E027°15′.
• Elapsed time from Bloemfontein = 1108 − 1018 = 50 min.
• Measure distance flown and calculate actual GS: GS = distance flown ÷ (50 ÷ 60).
• Measure the distance remaining from the fix to East London.
• Time remaining = distance remaining ÷ actual GS ≈ 1 h 07 min.
• Revised ETA = 1108 + 0107 = 1215 UTC.

FINAL ANSWER
1215 UTC

navigation.q: An aircraft maintaining a heading of 331deg (M) obtains a relative nearing of 257deg from an NDB. If the aircraft variation is 21deg W, the bearing to plot from the NDB is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Aircraft heading 331°M, relative bearing to NDB 257°, variation 21°W.

FORMULA
QDM (magnetic bearing to station) = heading + relative bearing. QDR (bearing from station) = QDM ± 180°. Convert magnetic to true by subtracting west variation.

SOLVE
QDM = 331° + 257° = 588°, − 360° = 228°M.
QDR (reciprocal, bearing from the NDB) = 228° − 180° = 048°M.
True bearing = 048° − 21° = 027°T.

ANSWER
027deg

navigation.q: The mean magnetic track and distance from BISHO (S32° 55’ E027° 16’) to BURGERSDORP (S30° 58’ E026° 20’) is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot Bisho and Burgersdorp on the chart.
• Measure the mean true track at the mid-meridian.
• Apply the mean variation to convert the track to magnetic.
• Measure the route distance using the chart scale.

FINAL ANSWER
001° (M) and 127 nm

navigation.q: An aircraft is flying from COOKHOUSE NDB (S32°45’ E025°49’) to GEORGE (S34°00’ E022°23’), drift 10°R. The relative bearing required from the COOKHOUSE NDB to maintain the track is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot the Cookhouse-to-George track and determine the magnetic track.
• A drift of 10° right means the track lies 10° right of the aircraft heading.
• Determine the bearing from the aircraft back to Cookhouse NDB.
• Relative bearing = magnetic bearing to the NDB − magnetic heading, reduced to 000°–359°.

FINAL ANSWER
192°

navigation.q: If the local mean time at airfield A, longitude E018deg 45’ is 0818 then, if both positions are in South Africa, the time UTC at airfield B, longitude E021deg 45’ will be:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
LMT at airfield A (018°45'E) = 0818

FORMULA
Longitude time = degrees × 4 min + minutes × 4 sec
UTC = LMT − longitude time (east of Greenwich)
UTC is the same everywhere, so it also gives the time at airfield B

SOLVE
Longitude time = 18° × 4 min + 45' × 4 sec = 72 min + 180 sec = 1 h 15 min
UTC = 0818 − 0115 = 0703

ANSWER
0703 UTC

navigation.q: If the local mean time at SISHEN, longitude 23deg E is 0748, then the local mean time at NEWCASTLE longitude 30deg E will be:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
LMT at Sishen (023°E) = 0748
Newcastle is at 030°E

FORMULA
Time difference = longitude difference × 4 min per degree
LMT increases eastward

SOLVE
Longitude difference = 30° − 23° = 7°
Time difference = 7 × 4 min = 28 min
Newcastle is east of Sishen: 0748 + 0028 = 0816

ANSWER
0816

navigation.q: Track 225deg (T), Drift 6deg left, Variation 21deg W. The magnetic heading to steer is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 225°T, drift 6° left, variation 21°W.

FORMULA
Drift left means heading is to the right of track: heading = track + drift. Then convert true to magnetic by adding west variation.

SOLVE
True heading = 225° + 6° = 231°T.
Magnetic heading = 231° + 21° = 252°M.

ANSWER
252deg (M)

navigation.q: South Africa uses a standard time factor of:
navigation.e: South African Standard Time is UTC +2 throughout the year; South Africa does not normally apply daylight-saving time.

navigation.q: VOR AAV, radial 163, aircraft variation 19deg W, station variation 21deg W. The true bearing to plot from AAV is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
VOR AAV radial 163°, station variation 21°W (aircraft variation of 19°W is a distractor — a radial is referenced to the station's own variation, not the aircraft's).

FORMULA
Convert the magnetic radial to true by subtracting the station's west variation.

SOLVE
True bearing = 163° − 21° = 142°T.

ANSWER
142deg

navigation.q: Aircraft heading 175deg (C) variation 18deg W, deviation 4deg W. The aircraft’s true heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Compass heading 175°C, variation 18°W, deviation 4°W.

FORMULA
Compass → Magnetic: subtract west deviation. Magnetic → True: subtract west variation.

SOLVE
Magnetic heading = 175° − 4° = 171°M.
True heading = 171° − 18° = 153°T.

ANSWER
153deg (T)

navigation.q: Track 184deg (T), drift 5deg left, variation 22deg W, deviation 4deg W. The compass heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 184°T, drift 5° left, variation 22°W, deviation 4°W.

FORMULA
Drift left means heading is to the right of track: heading = track + drift. Then True → Magnetic: add west variation. Magnetic → Compass: add west deviation.

SOLVE
True heading = 184° + 5° = 189°T.
Magnetic heading = 189° + 22° = 211°M.
Compass heading = 211° + 4° = 215°C.

ANSWER
215deg (C)

navigation.q: An aircraft inbound to DURBAN INTERNATIONAL DNV obtains a fix at 40 DME, radial 013 DNV and diverts to RICHARDS BAY. The true track required is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot Durban DNV's magnetic radial 013 outbound from the VOR/DME and mark the fix at the point where it crosses the 40 DME arc.
• From that fix, draw a straight line to Richards Bay.
• Measure the direction of that line against the nearest meridian using a protractor/plotter to obtain the true track — meridians converge toward true north, so always measure against the meridian nearest the line, not the departure point.
• Richards Bay lies to the north-east of the fix, giving a measured true track in the low 060s.

FINAL ANSWER
064° (T)

navigation.q: An aircraft, maintaining a heading of 295° (C), obtains a relative bearing of 345° from an NDB. If the aircraft’s variation is 20° W and deviation is 3° E, the bearing to plot from the NDB is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Compass heading 295°C, relative bearing to NDB 345°, variation 20°W, deviation 3°E.

FORMULA
Compass → Magnetic: add east deviation. QDM = magnetic heading + relative bearing. QDR = QDM ± 180°. Magnetic → True: subtract west variation.

SOLVE
Magnetic heading = 295° + 3° = 298°M.
QDM = 298° + 345° = 643°, − 360° = 283°M.
QDR (reciprocal) = 283° − 180° = 103°M.
True bearing = 103° − 20° = 083°T.

ANSWER
083°

navigation.q: Track 002deg (T), W/V 315/15, TAS 115kts, variation 18deg W, deviation 2deg W. The compass heading to fly is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 002°T, W/V 315/15, TAS 115 kt, variation 18°W, deviation 2°W.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 315° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 002°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 115 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 5.5° left of track (wind from the left), so heading ≈ 002° − 5.5° ≈ 357°T. GS ≈ 104 kt is under the centre dot.
Step 5: Magnetic: 357° + 18°W = 375° → 015°M. Compass: 015° + 2°W = 017°C.

ANSWER
017deg (C)

navigation.q: Overhead Welkom, at 0840 UTC en route to UPINGTON. At 0930 UTC a fix is obtained with radial 040KMV and radial 109UCV. The ETA for UPINGTON is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot radial 040 from KMV and radial 109 from UCV; their intersection is the 0930 fix.
• Elapsed time from Welkom = 0930 − 0840 = 50 min.
• Actual GS = chart distance flown ÷ (50 ÷ 60).
• Measure the distance remaining from the fix to Upington.
• Time remaining is approximately 1 h 44 min.
• ETA = 0930 + 0144 = 1114 UTC.

FINAL ANSWER
1114 UTC

navigation.q: An aircraft is en route from A to B, distance 130nm, track 278deg (T), mean variation 23deg W. After flying 92nm a fix places the aircraft 5nm right of track. The new magnetic track from fix to B is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance A to B = 130 nm, track 278°T, variation 23°W. After flying 92 nm, a fix places the aircraft 5 nm right of track.

FORMULA
Find the closing angle to regain track to B, subtract it from the original track (aircraft is right of track), then convert true to magnetic by adding west variation.

SOLVE
Distance remaining = 130 − 92 = 38 nm.
Closing angle = (5 × 60) ÷ 38 = 300 ÷ 38 = 7.9° ≈ 8°.
New true track = 278° − 8° = 270°T.
New magnetic track = 270° + 23° = 293°M.

ANSWER
293deg (M)

navigation.q: If the local mean time at an airfield A longitude E028 30 is 1428, then the local mean time at airfield B, longitude E021 30 will be:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
LMT at airfield A (028°30'E) = 1428
Airfield B is at 021°30'E

FORMULA
Time difference = longitude difference × 4 min per degree
LMT decreases westward

SOLVE
Longitude difference = 28°30' − 21°30' = 7°
Time difference = 7 × 4 min = 28 min
Airfield B is west of A: 1428 − 0028 = 1400

ANSWER
1400

navigation.q: At 1415 aircraft was overhead a VOR maintaining radial 215deg en route for B, heading 210deg (M). At 1430, the pilot decides to return to the VOR. The heading to steer is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Outbound from the VOR, the aircraft is tracking radial 215° (QDR 215°M) and flies heading 210°M to hold that radial — a 5° left correction for wind drift.

FORMULA
QDM (direct bearing to the station) is the reciprocal of the QDR: QDM = QDR ± 180°.
On the reverse track, the same wind requires the same size drift correction applied to the opposite side of the new track.

SOLVE
Reciprocal track to return direct to the VOR: QDM = 215° − 180° = 035°M.
Outbound drift correction was 5° left (215° track, 210° heading flown). On the return leg the correction applies to the opposite side: 5° right.
Heading to steer = 035° + 5° = 040°M.

ANSWER
040deg (M)

navigation.q: An aircraft was overhead PORT ALFRED at 1025 en route for UMTATA. At 1116 the aircraft obtains a fix at 35 DME, radial 006 ELV. The aircraft’s groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot the 006 radial from ELV and the 35-DME arc to obtain the 1116 fix.
• Measure the chart distance from Port Alfred to the fix: approximately 75 NM.
• Elapsed time = 1116 − 1025 = 51 min = 0.85 h.
• Groundspeed = 75 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 88 kt.

FINAL ANSWER
88kts

navigation.q: An aircraft flies from A (S26deg 45’ E021deg 10’) to B (S22deg 35’ E021deg 10’) at TAS 125kts. Headwind 8kts. The flying time is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Both positions are on longitude E021°10′.
• Latitude difference = 26°45′ − 22°35′ = 4°10′.
• Distance = 4 × 60 + 10 = 250 NM.
• Groundspeed = 125 − 8 = 117 kt.
• Time = 250 ÷ 117 = 2.137 h = 2 h 08 min.

FINAL ANSWER
2hrs 08mins

navigation.q: Overhead MAFIKENG at F085 en route to UPINGTON, RAS 110kts, Temperature ISA, forecast W/V 180/10, deviation 3deg east. The heading (C) to steer:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Overhead Mafikeng at FL085 en route Upington, RAS 110 kt, temperature ISA, W/V 180/10, deviation 3°E.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 8 500 ft = 15 − (2 × 8.5) = −2°C. In the airspeed window, set −2°C against pressure altitude 8.5 and read TAS ≈ 125 kt opposite RAS 110 kt.
Step 2: Measure the true track Mafikeng–Upington on the chart: about 236°T.
Step 3: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 180° under the index and place the wind-mark 10 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 4: Rotate the rose to put track 236°T under the index and move the slide so the 125 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 4° left of track, so heading ≈ 232°T. Read GS ≈ 119 kt under the centre dot.
Step 6: Apply the chart variation for the leg (about 17°W): 232°T + 17° = 249°M.
Step 7: Deviation east, compass least: 249°M − 3° = 246°C.

ANSWER
246deg (C)

navigation.q: From a visual fix at S26°20’ E021°15’ at 0925UTC an aircraft flied direct to KEETMANSHOOP (S26°32’ E018°17’) TAS 120, tailwind 12kts. The ETA for KEETMANSHOOP is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot the direct route from S26°20′ E021°15′ to Keetmanshoop.
• Measured distance is approximately 169 NM.
• Groundspeed = TAS + tailwind = 120 + 12 = 132 kt.
• Time = 169 ÷ 132 = 1.28 h ≈ 1 h 17 min.
• ETA = 0925 + 0117 = 1042 UTC.

FINAL ANSWER
1042UTC

navigation.q: An aircraft was overhead PORT ALFRED at 0752 on track VICTORIA WEST, heading 310deg (T). At 0840 the aircraft obtains a relative bearing of 083deg COOKHOUSE. The ground speed is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Convert the relative bearing to a true bearing using heading 310°T.
• Bearing to Cookhouse = 310° + 083° = 393° − 360° = 033°T.
• Plot the reciprocal 213° line from Cookhouse to intersect the Port Alfred–Victoria West track.
• Distance flown to the fix is approximately 72 NM.
• Elapsed time = 0840 − 0752 = 48 min = 0.80 h.
• GS = 72 ÷ 0.80 = 90 kt.

FINAL ANSWER
90kts

navigation.q: An aircraft is overhead HEIDELBERG en route to KIMBERLEY heading 230deg (T). At 1237 UTC a fix is obtained with a relative bearing of 230 KROONSTAD NDB and radial 014 WMV. From this fix the true track to KIMBERLEY is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Convert the 230° relative bearing to Kroonstad NDB (read against the 230°T heading being flown) into a magnetic/true bearing, and plot the corresponding line from Kroonstad NDB.
• Plot radial 014 outward from WMV VOR.
• The intersection of the NDB bearing line and the VOR radial gives the aircraft's fix at 1237 UTC.
• From the fix, draw a line to Kimberley and measure its direction against the nearest meridian to obtain the true track.

FINAL ANSWER
232deg (T)

navigation.q: Overhead PILANESBERG at 0730 UTC, en route MAPUTO, FL095, OAT -5deg C, RAS 103kts, W/V 240/10. The ETA for MAPUTO is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Overhead Pilanesberg at 0730 UTC en route Maputo, FL095, OAT −5°C, RAS 103 kt, W/V 240/10.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: In the airspeed window, set OAT −5°C against pressure altitude 9.5 and read TAS ≈ 119 kt opposite RAS 103 kt.
Step 2: Measure on the chart: track about 097°T, distance about 295 nm.
Step 3: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 240° under the index and place the wind-mark 10 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 4: Rotate the rose to put track 097°T under the index and move the slide so the 119 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 3° right of track, so heading ≈ 100°T. Read GS ≈ 126 kt under the centre dot.
Step 6: Time = 295 ÷ 126 = 2.34 h ≈ 2 h 20 min.
Step 7: ETA ≈ 0730 + 0220 = 0950 UTC. The closest option is 0948 UTC.

ANSWER
0948 UTC

navigation.q: An aircraft is flying from EAST LONDON, (S33° 03' E027° 50'), to COOKHOUSE NDB, (S32° 45' E025° 49'), drift 8°L. The relative bearing required from the COOKHOUSE NDB to maintain the track is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot the East London-to-Cookhouse track and convert it to magnetic.
• A drift of 8° left means the track lies 8° left of heading.
• Determine the magnetic bearing from the aircraft to Cookhouse NDB.
• Relative bearing = QDM − magnetic heading, reduced to 000°–359°.

FINAL ANSWER
352°

navigation.q: Aircraft heading 218deg (T), variation 22deg W, deviation 3deg E. The aircraft’s compass heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
True heading 218°T, variation 22°W, deviation 3°E.

FORMULA
True → Magnetic: add west variation. Magnetic → Compass: subtract east deviation.

SOLVE
Magnetic heading = 218° + 22° = 240°M.
Compass heading = 240° − 3° = 237°C.

ANSWER
237deg (C)

navigation.q: An aircraft is en route from GEORGE to EAST LONDON. At 0842 it obtains a fix at 45 DME radial 036 PEV. The aircraft’s position is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot radial 036 outward from PEV using the VOR station reference.
• Draw the 45-NM DME arc centred on PEV.
• The radial and DME arc intersect at the aircraft position.
• Read the latitude and longitude at the intersection.

FINAL ANSWER
S33deg 15’ E025deg 46’

navigation.q: The mean magnetic track and distance from DURBAN INTERNATIONAL to BLOEMFONTEIN is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Route from Durban International to Bloemfontein. Chart plot: mean true track ≈ 283°T, distance ≈ 247 nm, mean variation ≈ 21°W.

FORMULA
Magnetic Track = True Track + Westerly Variation.

SOLVE
Magnetic Track = 283° + 21° = 304°M.
Distance = 247 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
304° (M) and 247 nm

navigation.q: An aircraft is on track from PBV to MAFIKENG. When passing abeam PILANESBERG, the radial from PNV is:
navigation.e: At the abeam position, draw the line from the VOR to the aircraft and read its magnetic bearing from the station. That outward bearing is the radial, approximately 346°.

navigation.q: Overhead RICHARDS BAY, en route WELKOM, heading 308deg (M). At 0905 UTC a fix is obtained with a relative bearing of 328deg LADYSMITH NDB and a relative bearing of 043deg NEWCASTLE NDB. The aircraft’s position is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• LadySmith QDM = heading + relative bearing = 308° + 328° = 276°M.
• Reciprocal QDR from LadySmith = 276° − 180° = 096°M.
• Newcastle QDM = 308° + 043° = 351°M.
• Reciprocal QDR from Newcastle = 351° − 180° = 171°M.
• Plot the two QDR lines from the NDBs; their intersection gives the fix.

FINAL ANSWER
S28deg 27’ E030deg 24’

navigation.q: An aircraft departs SUTHERLAND maintaining a track of 050deg (T). After flying for 70nm, the aircraft’s position is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• From Sutherland, draw a true track of 050°.
• Measure 70 NM along that track using the chart scale.
• Read the latitude and longitude at the endpoint.

FINAL ANSWER
S31deg 42’ E021deg 42’

navigation.q: An aircraft was overhead A (S23deg 43’ E030deg 42’) at 1422. Tailwind 15kts. At 1540 the aircraft is overhead B (S26deg 33’ E030deg 42’). The TAS is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
A at S23°43′, B at S26°33′, same longitude (E030°42′)
Elapsed time 1422–1540
Tailwind = 15 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Latitude difference = 26°33′ − 23°43′ = 2°50′ = 170′ = 170 nm
Elapsed time = 1540 − 1422 = 1 h 18 min = 1.3 h
GS = 170 ÷ 1.3 = 130.8 kt
TAS = 130.8 − 15 = 115.8 ≈ 116 kt

ANSWER
116kts

navigation.q: Which transponder code is used for radio communication failure?
navigation.e: The standard transponder code for radio communication failure is 7600. This alerts ATC that the aircraft has lost radio contact.

navigation.q: A VOR/DME installation provides the pilot with:
navigation.d: Bearing information from the VOR and distance information from the DME
navigation.ans: Bearing information from the VOR and distance information from the DME
navigation.e: The VOR gives angular information such as radials or course guidance, while DME provides slant range to the station.

navigation.q: The term QDR means:
navigation.a: Magnetic bearing from the station to the aircraft
navigation.b: True bearing from the aircraft to the station
navigation.c: Magnetic bearing from the aircraft to the station
navigation.d: Compass bearing from the aircraft to the station
navigation.ans: Magnetic bearing from the station to the aircraft
navigation.e: QDR is the magnetic bearing from the station. It tells you on which magnetic bearing you are located from the station.

navigation.q: Mode C transponder altitude is based on:
navigation.e: Mode C transmits pressure altitude referenced to the standard pressure datum, not local QNH or GPS altitude.

navigation.q: NDBs used for aviation normally transmit in which frequency range?
navigation.e: Most NDBs operate in the low and medium frequency bands, which is why their signals are more affected by night effect and coastal refraction.

navigation.q: What aircraft equipment is required to use VDF direction-finding service?
navigation.e: VDF uses the aircraft's VHF radio transmission. The ground station determines the aircraft bearing from the received VHF signal.

navigation.q: LF/MF radio signals such as NDB transmissions can travel as:
navigation.b: Ground waves only at all times
navigation.e: NDB transmissions use LF/MF frequencies. They can propagate along the surface as ground waves and, particularly at night, return from the ionosphere as skywaves, which can introduce night-effect errors.

navigation.q: If a pilot receives QDM 090° from a VDF station, the aircraft is approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• QDM is the magnetic bearing from the aircraft to the station.
• QDM 090° means the station is due east of the aircraft.
• Therefore the aircraft is due west of the station.

FINAL ANSWER
West of the station

navigation.q: The key difference between primary and secondary radar is that:
navigation.a: Primary radar requires a transponder; secondary radar does not
navigation.b: Primary radar only works with GPS
navigation.c: Primary radar uses reflected signals; secondary radar uses aircraft transponder replies
navigation.d: Secondary radar measures wind direction directly
navigation.ans: Primary radar uses reflected signals; secondary radar uses aircraft transponder replies
navigation.e: Primary radar detects reflections from the aircraft surface. Secondary radar receives coded replies from the aircraft transponder.

navigation.q: Why can an NDB indication become less reliable at night?
navigation.a: Because VHF line-of-sight range is reduced
navigation.c: Because GPS satellites are below the horizon
navigation.d: Because skywave reflections can interfere with the ground wave
navigation.ans: Because skywave reflections can interfere with the ground wave
navigation.e: At night, LF/MF signals can reflect from the ionosphere. The reflected skywave may interfere with the direct ground wave and cause bearing errors.

navigation.q: The GPS system is made up of which broad segments?
navigation.e: GPS consists of satellites in space, ground/control monitoring stations, and user receivers in aircraft or other devices.

navigation.q: The term QTE means:
navigation.b: True bearing from the station to the aircraft
navigation.ans: True bearing from the station to the aircraft
navigation.e: QTE is a true bearing from the station to the aircraft. It is useful for plotting a position line on a chart.

navigation.q: DME calculates distance mainly by measuring:
navigation.a: The phase difference between two VOR signals
navigation.b: The magnetic bearing of the aircraft
navigation.c: The time taken for signal pulses to travel to and from the station
navigation.d: The pressure altitude transmitted by the aircraft
navigation.ans: The time taken for signal pulses to travel to and from the station
navigation.e: DME is based on timing. The aircraft interrogates the station and measures the time delay of the reply to determine slant range.

navigation.q: What happens to VOR indications when flying directly over the station?
navigation.d: The aircraft enters the cone of confusion
navigation.ans: The aircraft enters the cone of confusion
navigation.e: Overhead a VOR, the signal geometry can become unreliable for a short time. This area is called the cone of confusion.

navigation.q: If a VDF station gives QDR 225°, the aircraft is located approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• QDR is the magnetic bearing from the station to the aircraft.
• A bearing of 225° points south-west.

FINAL ANSWER
South-west of the station

navigation.q: When is DME slant-range error most noticeable?
navigation.a: When far from the station at low altitude
navigation.b: When close to the station and relatively high above it
navigation.ans: When close to the station and relatively high above it
navigation.e: Near the DME, the vertical separation forms a large part of the measured distance, so slant range can over-read the actual ground distance.

navigation.q: When a transmitter and receiver move towards each other, the received frequency tends to:
navigation.e: The Doppler effect compresses the received wavefronts when transmitter and receiver are closing, so the received frequency increases. When they move apart, the received frequency decreases.

navigation.q: On a VOR indicator, full-scale CDI deflection normally means the aircraft is at least approximately:
navigation.e: A VOR CDI is angular, not distance-based. Full deflection is normally about 10° or more from the selected course.

navigation.q: Coastal refraction errors on NDB bearings are usually greatest when the signal crosses the coastline:
navigation.a: At a shallow angle and at low altitude
navigation.b: At right angles and at high altitude
navigation.ans: At a shallow angle and at low altitude
navigation.e: NDB signals bend when crossing land/sea boundaries. The effect is worst when the signal crosses the coast at a shallow angle, especially at lower altitude.

navigation.q: Which aircraft instrument is used to receive and display bearing information from an NDB?
navigation.e: An NDB transmits a non-directional signal and the aircraft uses an ADF to indicate the relative bearing to the beacon.

navigation.q: The airborne equipment used by secondary surveillance radar is the:
navigation.e: Secondary surveillance radar interrogates the aircraft transponder, which replies with a code and, in Mode C, pressure altitude.

navigation.q: VHF radio navigation signals such as VOR normally travel mainly as:
navigation.a: Surface waves following the curvature of Earth
navigation.c: Ground waves guided by the terrain
navigation.e: VOR operates in the VHF band, where propagation is mainly line-of-sight. Reception range therefore increases with aircraft and station height and can be blocked by terrain.

navigation.q: The term QDM means:
navigation.a: Magnetic bearing from the aircraft to the station
navigation.b: True bearing from the station to the aircraft
navigation.c: Magnetic bearing from the station to the aircraft
navigation.d: Relative bearing from the aircraft nose
navigation.ans: Magnetic bearing from the aircraft to the station
navigation.e: QDM is the magnetic bearing to the station. It is the magnetic heading to fly in still air to reach the station.

navigation.q: An aircraft is heading 090°(M) and the ADF relative bearing is 030°. The magnetic bearing to the NDB is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Magnetic heading = 090°(M). ADF relative bearing to the NDB = 030°.

FORMULA
Magnetic bearing to the station (QDM) = Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing (subtract 360° if the result exceeds 360°).

SOLVE
QDM = 090° + 030° = 120°M.

ANSWER
120°

navigation.q: The term QUJ means:
navigation.a: Magnetic bearing from the station to the aircraft
navigation.c: True bearing from the aircraft to the station
navigation.d: Relative bearing from the aircraft nose
navigation.ans: True bearing from the aircraft to the station
navigation.e: QUJ is the true bearing to the station from the aircraft. It is the true equivalent of a bearing to the station.

navigation.q: Which transponder code is used for a general emergency?
navigation.e: Code 7700 is used for a general emergency. It makes the aircraft conspicuous to ATC radar systems.

navigation.q: For a full 3D GPS position and receiver clock correction, a receiver normally needs at least:
navigation.e: Four satellites allow the receiver to solve latitude, longitude, altitude and clock error. Fewer satellites reduce the quality or completeness of the fix.

navigation.q: A VOR radial is best described as:
navigation.a: A magnetic bearing to the station
navigation.b: A magnetic bearing from the station
navigation.c: A true bearing to the aircraft
navigation.d: A relative bearing from the nose
navigation.ans: A magnetic bearing from the station
navigation.e: A VOR radial is named by the magnetic bearing from the VOR station. The 270 radial means you are west of the station.

navigation.q: The range of a VOR is mainly limited by:
navigation.e: VOR operates in VHF and is largely line-of-sight. Higher aircraft altitude generally improves reception range.

navigation.q: A DME indication represents:
navigation.e: DME measures the straight-line distance between aircraft and station, known as slant range. Close to the station this can be noticeably greater than ground distance.

navigation.q: At a chart scale of 1:500 000, 4 cm measured on the chart represents approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 4 cm
Chart scale = 1:500 000

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator

SOLVE
Ground distance = 4 cm × 500 000 = 2 000 000 cm = 20 km

ANSWER
20 km

navigation.q: If magnetic variation is 12°W and the true track is 080°, the magnetic track is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
True track 080°T, variation 12°W.

FORMULA
True → Magnetic: add west variation.

SOLVE
Magnetic track = 080° + 12° = 092°M.

ANSWER
092°

navigation.q: TAS is 110 kt and the headwind component is 15 kt. The groundspeed is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS = 110 kt
Headwind component = 15 kt

FORMULA
Groundspeed = TAS − Headwind component

SOLVE
GS = 110 − 15 = 95 kt

ANSWER
95 kt

navigation.q: A trip takes 1 hour 30 minutes at a fuel flow of 8 USG/hr. Trip fuel required is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Flight time = 1 hr 30 min
Fuel flow = 8 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 1 h 30 min = 1.5 h
Fuel = 1.5 × 8 = 12 USG

ANSWER
12 USG

navigation.q: Using the rule of thumb, TAS is roughly how much higher than IAS per 1000 ft of altitude?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Standard PPL rule of thumb relating TAS to IAS/RAS with altitude

WORKING
Climbing at a constant IAS holds a constant dynamic pressure (½ × rho × V²). As altitude increases, air density (rho) falls, so TAS (V) must rise to keep that product constant for the same IAS. Standard PPL rule of thumb: TAS exceeds IAS/RAS by about 2% per 1000 ft of pressure altitude.

This matches worked figures for a climb at IAS 100 kt in ISA conditions: TAS is about 8% higher at 5000 ft, 17% higher at 10,000 ft, 26% higher at 15,000 ft, and 37% higher at 20,000 ft. The true relationship is slightly less than 2% per 1000 ft at lower levels, but 2%/1000 ft remains the standard quick rule.

ANSWER
2%

navigation.q: Variation is the angular difference between:
navigation.e: Variation is the difference between true north and magnetic north at a location. It changes with position and slowly over time.

navigation.q: Away from the equator, the distance represented by one degree of longitude:
navigation.d: Is always equal to one degree of latitude
navigation.e: Meridians converge toward the poles, so degrees of longitude represent shorter distances at higher latitudes.

navigation.q: Convergency between meridians is greatest at the:
navigation.e: Meridians meet at the poles and are farthest apart at the equator. Convergency is therefore maximum at the poles and zero at the equator.

navigation.q: If QNH is lower than 1013 hPa, pressure altitude will be:
navigation.e:
Pressure altitude is height above the standard 1013 hPa datum, as would be read with 1013 set in the altimeter subscale. If the actual sea-level pressure (QNH) is lower than 1013, the 1013 hPa level itself sits higher in the real atmosphere above the aerodrome than it would on a standard day, so the aircraft must be physically higher before an altimeter set to 1013 reads through that level.

Using the standard rate of 30 ft per hPa: pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30. With QNH below 1013, (1013 − QNH) is positive, so pressure altitude works out higher than the aerodrome elevation.

navigation.q: If magnetic variation is 8°E and the true track is 210°, the magnetic track is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
True track 210°T, variation 8°E.

FORMULA
True → Magnetic: subtract east variation.

SOLVE
Magnetic track = 210° − 8° = 202°M.

ANSWER
202°

navigation.q: An aircraft is 2 NM right of track after flying 30 NM, with 60 NM still to go. The approximate correction to regain track at destination is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
2 nm right of track after 30 nm flown, 60 nm still to run

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: opening angle = (off track ÷ distance flown) × 60
Closing angle = (off track ÷ distance remaining) × 60
Correction to regain track at destination = opening angle + closing angle, turned toward the track

SOLVE
Opening angle = (2 ÷ 30) × 60 = 4°
Closing angle = (2 ÷ 60) × 60 = 2°
Total correction = 4° + 2° = 6°
Aircraft is right of track, so correct left

ANSWER
6° left

navigation.q: On a direct Mercator chart, rhumb lines normally appear as:
navigation.e: Mercator charts are useful for rhumb-line navigation because constant-track lines are shown as straight lines.

navigation.q: A chart scale of 1:1 000 000 means that 1 cm on the chart represents:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000
Chart distance = 1 cm

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator

SOLVE
Ground distance = 1 cm × 1 000 000 = 1 000 000 cm = 10 000 m = 10 km

ANSWER
10 km on the ground

navigation.q: If sunrise is 0540 local time, official day begins at:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunrise = 0540 local.

FORMULA
Official day begins = sunrise − 15 min

SOLVE
0540 − 0015 = 0525

ANSWER
0525

navigation.q: If sunset is 1810 local time, official night begins at:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunset = 1810 local.

FORMULA
Official night begins = sunset + 15 min

SOLVE
1810 + 0015 = 1825

ANSWER
1825

navigation.q: On a Mercator chart, great circle tracks away from the equator are normally shown as:
navigation.e: On a Mercator chart, rhumb lines are straight, while great circles usually appear curved except along the equator or meridians.

navigation.q: An aircraft flies 40 NM in 20 minutes. Its groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 40 nm
Time = 20 min

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 20 ÷ 60 = 1/3 h
GS = 40 ÷ (1/3) = 120 kt

ANSWER
120 kt

navigation.q: On the equator, one degree of longitude is approximately:
navigation.e: At the equator, meridians are widest apart. One degree of longitude equals approximately 60 NM there.

navigation.q: Which line is both a great circle and a rhumb line?
navigation.e: The equator is a great circle because its plane passes through the centre of the Earth, and it is also a rhumb line because it cuts all meridians at 90°.

navigation.q: On a Lambert conformal conic chart, scale is most accurate at the:
navigation.e: The cone cuts the Earth at the standard parallels, so distortion is least and scale is correct along those parallels.

navigation.q: South African Standard Time is normally:
navigation.e: South Africa uses UTC+2 for standard time. This is important when converting exam times, sunrise/sunset and navigation logs.

navigation.q: One degree of latitude represents approximately what distance along a meridian?
navigation.e: One degree contains 60 minutes of latitude, and 1 minute of latitude ≈ 1 NM. Therefore 1° latitude = 60 × 1 = 60 NM.

navigation.q: A point is at S28°20'. If you move 180 NM north along the same meridian, the new latitude is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Position: S28°20'
Distance flown: 180 nm north, along the same meridian

FORMULA
1' of latitude = 1 nm, so change in latitude (degrees) = distance (nm) ÷ 60

SOLVE
Change in latitude = 180 ÷ 60 = 3°
Flying north reduces south latitude: S28°20' − 3°00' = S25°20'

ANSWER
S25°20'

navigation.q: The shortest path between two points on the Earth is normally along:
navigation.e: A great circle is formed by a plane through the centre of the Earth and represents the shortest surface distance between two points.

navigation.q: A rhumb line is a track that:
navigation.a: Cuts each meridian at a constant angle
navigation.b: Always gives the shortest distance between two points
navigation.d: Always follows a parallel of longitude
navigation.ans: Cuts each meridian at a constant angle
navigation.e: A rhumb line maintains a constant track angle. It is easy to steer but is not normally the shortest route except in special cases.

navigation.q: High temperature mainly causes density altitude to:
navigation.e:
Density altitude is the height in the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA) at which the actual air density would be found. Warm air holds fewer molecules per unit volume than cold air at the same pressure, so it is less dense.

Less dense air means fewer air molecules for the wings to generate lift from and for the engine/propeller to work with, so the aircraft and its engine perform as though they were at a higher altitude than the actual pressure altitude - hence density altitude rises with temperature. This is why hot, high (and humid) conditions are linked to longer take-off runs and reduced climb performance.

navigation.q: Compass deviation is the angular difference between:
navigation.e: Deviation is caused by magnetic influences in the aircraft and is the angle between compass north and magnetic north.
