navigation.q: Using the 1-in-60 rule, 3 NM off track after 60 NM flown equals a track error of approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
3 nm off track after 60 nm flown

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: track error (°) = (distance off track ÷ distance flown) × 60

SOLVE
Track error = (3 ÷ 60) × 60 = 3°

ANSWER
3°

navigation.q: If two places are on the same latitude, the place farther east will generally have local mean noon:
navigation.c: At the same local mean time
navigation.d: One hour later regardless of longitude difference
navigation.e: Earth rotates from west to east, so a position farther east reaches local meridian passage sooner. Its local mean noon therefore occurs earlier in UTC than at the western position.

navigation.q: The Earth rotates through 15° of longitude in approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
The Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours.

FORMULA
Rotation rate = 360° ÷ 24 h
Time for a given longitude change = degrees ÷ rate

SOLVE
Rotation rate = 360 ÷ 24 = 15° per hour
Time for 15° = 15 ÷ 15 = 1 hour

ANSWER
1 hour

navigation.q: In South African Air Law, official day normally starts:
navigation.e: For South African PPL exam purposes, official day begins 15 minutes before sunrise and ends 15 minutes after sunset.

navigation.q: Local mean time at 014°20'E is 15:36. What is the approximate LMT at 027°30'E?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
LMT at 014°20'E = 15:36
Second position: 027°30'E

FORMULA
Time difference = longitude difference × 4 min per degree (+ 4 sec per minute of arc)
LMT increases eastward

SOLVE
Longitude difference = 027°30' − 014°20' = 13°10'
Time difference = 13° × 4 min + 10' × 4 sec = 52 min + 40 sec = 52 min 40 sec
027°30'E is east of 014°20'E: 15:36:00 + 00:52:40 = 16:28:40 ≈ 16:29

ANSWER
16:29

navigation.q: On long tracks on a Lambert chart, measuring the course near the midpoint helps reduce error because:
navigation.a: The track direction changes slightly as meridians converge
navigation.b: Magnetic variation is zero at the midpoint
navigation.c: Scale is correct only at the destination
navigation.d: Latitude lines are not drawn accurately
navigation.ans: The track direction changes slightly as meridians converge
navigation.e: On a Lambert chart, meridian convergence can change the true direction along a long track, so using the midpoint gives a better mean course.

navigation.q: On a Lambert conformal chart, a straight line drawn between two positions is normally treated as:
navigation.e: On a Lambert conformal chart, straight lines closely represent great-circle tracks, which are normally the shortest practical tracks over longer distances.

navigation.q: If magnetic variation is east, the magnetic heading will be:
navigation.b: Always equal to the compass heading
navigation.e: For easterly variation, magnetic north lies east of true north, so measuring the same physical direction clockwise from magnetic north gives a smaller number than measuring it from true north — the mnemonic is 'variation east, magnetic least'. Magnetic direction is therefore obtained by subtracting the easterly variation from the true direction.

navigation.q: If you are left of track and your ETAs are increasing, the wind most likely has:
navigation.a: A tailwind component with crosswind from the left
navigation.b: A headwind component with crosswind from the left
navigation.d: A headwind component with crosswind from the right
navigation.ans: A headwind component with crosswind from the right
navigation.e: Being left of track suggests drift from right to left. Increasing ETAs indicate slower groundspeed, therefore a headwind component.

navigation.q: One degree of longitude on the Earth is equal to 60 NM only when measured:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Meridians are farthest apart at the equator.
• At the equator, 1° of longitude equals approximately 60 NM.
• Toward the poles, meridians converge and the distance per degree decreases.

FINAL ANSWER
Along the equator

navigation.q: A constant direction route which is not normally the shortest distance between two points is a:
navigation.e: A rhumb line maintains a constant track angle, but except in special cases it is longer than the great-circle route.

navigation.q: In aviation, the standard time reference used for flight planning and communication is:
navigation.e: UTC, also called Zulu time, gives aviation one common time reference across countries and time zones. The international basis for standard time changed from Greenwich Mean Time (GMT) to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) in 1985; UTC is kept by atomic clocks rather than the sun. Local times (e.g. SAST = UTC+2) are then derived from UTC, so a single time reference avoids confusion on flight plans, NOTAMs and weather reports.

navigation.q: A distance of 33 cm on a 1:1 000 000 chart represents approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 33 cm
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator

SOLVE
Ground distance = 33 cm × 1 000 000 = 33 000 000 cm = 330 km
Convert to nautical miles: 330 km ÷ 1.852 = 178.2 NM

ANSWER
178 NM

navigation.q: If you are right of track and your ETAs are decreasing, the wind most likely has:
navigation.a: A tailwind component with crosswind from the left
navigation.b: A headwind component with crosswind from the right
navigation.c: A tailwind component with crosswind from the right
navigation.ans: A tailwind component with crosswind from the left
navigation.e: Being right of track suggests drift from left to right. Decreasing ETAs indicate higher groundspeed, therefore a tailwind component.

navigation.q: The quadrantal directions are:
navigation.e: The quadrantal points are NE, SE, SW and NW, halfway between the cardinal directions.

navigation.q: If magnetic variation is west, the magnetic heading will be:
navigation.e: For westerly variation, magnetic north lies west of true north, so measuring the same physical direction clockwise from magnetic north gives a larger number than measuring it from true north — the mnemonic is 'variation west, magnetic best'. Magnetic direction is therefore obtained by adding the westerly variation to the true direction.

navigation.q: If official night starts at 18:06 local time, the sunset time is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Official night starts at 18:06 local.

FORMULA
Sunset = official night start − 15 min

SOLVE
18:06 − 00:15: borrow one hour (60 min) → 17:66 − 00:15
= 17:51 (minutes run 00–59 on the 24-hour clock)

ANSWER
17:51

navigation.q: What is the approximate scale if 15 cm on a chart represents 81 NM on the Earth?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 15 cm
Ground distance = 81 NM

FORMULA
Scale (RF) = ground distance ÷ chart distance, both measured in the same units

SOLVE
Convert 81 NM to km: 81 × 1.852 = 150.0 km
150.0 km = 15 000 000 cm
Scale denominator = 15 000 000 cm ÷ 15 cm = 1 000 000

ANSWER
1:1 000 000

navigation.q: The cardinal directions expressed in degrees are:
navigation.e: The cardinal points are north, east, south and west, corresponding to 360/000, 090, 180 and 270 degrees.

navigation.q: Deviation is the angular difference between:
navigation.e: Deviation is the angular difference between compass north (where the compass needle actually settles in that particular aircraft) and magnetic north (the true direction of the earth's magnetic field). It is caused by stray magnetic influences within the aircraft itself — airframe metal, engine, radios, wiring — and is therefore aircraft-specific and heading-specific, unlike variation, which depends only on geographic position and is common to every aircraft flying in the same area.

navigation.q: On a 1:1 000 000 chart, an Earth distance of 255 NM is represented by approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Ground distance = 255 NM
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000

FORMULA
Chart distance = ground distance ÷ scale denominator

SOLVE
Convert 255 NM to km: 255 × 1.852 = 472.3 km
Convert to cm: 472.3 km = 47 230 000 cm
Chart distance = 47 230 000 cm ÷ 1 000 000 = 47.23 cm

ANSWER
47 cm

navigation.q: You are 5 NM left of track after flying 20 NM, with 30 NM remaining. The correction needed to regain track is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
5 nm left of track after 20 nm flown, 30 nm still to run

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: opening angle = (off track ÷ distance flown) × 60
Closing angle = (off track ÷ distance remaining) × 60
Correction to regain track = opening angle + closing angle, turned toward the track

SOLVE
Opening angle = (5 ÷ 20) × 60 = 15°
Closing angle = (5 ÷ 30) × 60 = 10°
Total correction = 15° + 10° = 25°
Aircraft is left of track, so correct right

ANSWER
25° right

navigation.q: On a Lambert conformal chart in the Southern Hemisphere, meridians of longitude generally:
navigation.e: Lambert conformal meridians are straight lines that converge toward the nearer pole. In the Southern Hemisphere that is the South Pole.

navigation.q: A great circle passing through both the North Pole and South Pole is called a:
navigation.e: A meridian runs from the North Pole to the South Pole. Together with the opposite meridian it forms a complete great circle; parallels other than the equator are small circles.

navigation.q: Isogonal lines on an aeronautical chart are used to determine:
navigation.e: Isogonal lines join places of equal magnetic variation, so they help convert between true and magnetic directions.

navigation.q: The primary reference used for measuring direction in navigation is:
navigation.e: True direction is measured from true north, then corrected for variation and deviation when magnetic or compass headings are required.

navigation.q: On a 1:1 000 000 chart, 23 cm represents a flight distance covered in 45 minutes. The approximate groundspeed is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000
Chart distance = 23 cm
Flight time = 45 min

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Ground distance = 23 cm × 1 000 000 = 23 000 000 cm = 230 km
Convert to nm: 230 ÷ 1.852 = 124.2 ≈ 124 nm
Time = 45 ÷ 60 = 0.75 h
GS = 124 ÷ 0.75 = 165.3 ≈ 165 kt

ANSWER
165 kt

navigation.q: One degree of latitude is approximately equal to:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
1 degree of latitude = 60 minutes of arc

FORMULA
Along a meridian, 1 minute of latitude subtends approximately 1 nautical mile (the nm's definition).
This is why the latitude scale on any chart meridian doubles as a distance scale in nm.

SOLVE
1 degree = 60 minutes = 60 × 1 nm = 60 nm
Trap: 60 statute miles is wrong because the statute mile is shorter (1 nm ≈ 1.15 sm), so 60 nm ≈ 69 sm.

ANSWER
60 nautical miles

navigation.q: One minute of latitude is approximately equal to:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
The nautical mile is defined from the size of the Earth, measured along a meridian (line of longitude).

FORMULA
1 minute of latitude (1/60 of a degree, measured along a meridian) = 1 nautical mile, by definition (approximately 1852 m).
Comparison: 1 nm = 1.15 statute miles = 1.852 km = about 6076 ft.

SOLVE
Definitional equivalence, not a calculation: 1' of latitude = 1 nm.
Traps: 1 km is only about 0.54 nm. The statute mile (1609 m) is an arbitrary legal unit, not linked to latitude, so '1 statute mile exactly' is wrong.

ANSWER
1 nautical mile

navigation.q: Which chart features are best for checking groundspeed and ETA on a navigation leg?
navigation.a: Features that cross the track at right angles
navigation.b: Features that run parallel to the track
navigation.ans: Features that cross the track at right angles
navigation.e:
REASONING
Features that cross the track at right angles are crossed almost instantaneously, so the time of the fix is sharp and accurate, giving a reliable groundspeed and ETA recalculation.
Features running parallel to the track (roads, rivers, coastlines running alongside the route) stay in view for an extended period, so there is no single, precise crossing time — the fix time is vague.
High terrain or features with vertical development may be seen from a distance before or after the true crossing point, which also blurs the fix time and is not a general rule for all checkpoints.

ANSWER
Features that cross the track at right angles

navigation.q: When measuring a course on a 1:500 000 aeronautical chart, the protractor should normally be aligned with:
navigation.a: The edge of the paper only
navigation.e: True direction is measured relative to true north, which is represented on the chart by the meridians of longitude.

navigation.q: Sunset is reached when:
navigation.a: The lower edge of the sun first touches the horizon
navigation.b: The centre of the sun reaches the horizon
navigation.c: The upper edge of the sun disappears below the horizon
navigation.d: Fifteen minutes after the upper edge disappears
navigation.ans: The upper edge of the sun disappears below the horizon
navigation.e: Sunset is the instant the last visible part—the upper limb—disappears below the horizon. Official night begins later, under the applicable official-day definition.

navigation.q: In navigation, a line which maintains a constant bearing is called a:
navigation.e: A rhumb line cuts each meridian at the same angle, so it represents a constant bearing or constant direction track.

navigation.q: A flight distance is 235 NM, cruise GS 145 kt. The aircraft must descend from FL95 to 2500 ft at 450 ft/min with descent GS 105 kt. If departure is 09:15, approximate top of descent time is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Total distance = 235 nm, cruise GS = 145 kt
Descend from FL95 (9500 ft) to 2500 ft at 450 fpm, descent GS = 105 kt
Departure time = 0915

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height to lose = 9500 − 2500 = 7000 ft
Descent time = 7000 ÷ 450 = 15.6 min
Descent distance = 105 × (15.6 ÷ 60) = 27.2 nm
Cruise distance = 235 − 27.2 = 207.8 nm
Cruise time = 207.8 ÷ 145 × 60 = 86.0 min = 1 h 26 min
TOD time = 0915 + 0126 = 1041

ANSWER
10:41

navigation.q: Cruising at FL125, RAS 135 kt, track 235°T, wind 195/40, variation 23°W and deviation 4°E. The compass heading to steer is closest to:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cruising at FL125, RAS 135 kt, track 235°T, wind 195/40, variation 23°W, deviation 4°E.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: On the airspeed window, set the ISA temperature at 12 500 ft (about −10°C) against pressure altitude 12.5 and read TAS ≈ 163 kt opposite RAS 135 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 195° under the index and place the wind-mark 40 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 3: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 235°T under the index.
Step 4: Move the slide so the 163 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 9° left of track. Heading = track − WCA, nose into wind (drift is 9° right on the opposite side). Read GS ≈ 131 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
245°C

navigation.q: Track is 184°T, drift is 5° left, variation 22°W and deviation 4°W. The compass heading is closest to:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 184°T, drift 5° left, variation 22°W, deviation 4°W.

FORMULA
Drift left means heading is to the right of track: heading = track + drift. Then True → Magnetic: add west variation. Magnetic → Compass: add west deviation.

SOLVE
True heading = 184° + 5° = 189°T.
Magnetic heading = 189° + 22° = 211°M.
Compass heading = 211° + 4° = 215°C.

ANSWER
215°C

navigation.q: An aircraft with TAS 110 kt flies 148 NM in 1 hour 14 minutes. The TAS required for the return leg to take 1 hour 20 minutes is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Outbound: TAS 110 kt, distance 148 nm, flight time 1 hr 14 min
Return leg must take 1 hr 20 min over the same 148 nm

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Outbound time = 74 ÷ 60 = 1.233 h
Outbound GS = 148 ÷ 1.233 = 120 kt
Wind component = 120 − 110 = 10 kt tailwind outbound → 10 kt headwind on return
Return time = 80 ÷ 60 = 1.333 h
Required return GS = 148 ÷ 1.333 = 111 kt
Required TAS = 111 + 10 = 121 kt

ANSWER
121 kt

navigation.q: You are 4 NM left of track after flying 42 NM, with 25 NM remaining. If steering 135°M, the approximate heading to regain track is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
4 nm left of track after 42 nm flown, 25 nm still to run, steering 135°M

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: opening angle = (off track ÷ distance flown) × 60
Closing angle = (off track ÷ distance remaining) × 60
New heading = present heading ± (opening angle + closing angle), turned toward the track

SOLVE
Opening angle = (4 ÷ 42) × 60 = 5.7°
Closing angle = (4 ÷ 25) × 60 = 9.6°
Total correction = 5.7° + 9.6° = 15.3°, rounds to 15°
Aircraft is left of track, so turn right
New heading = 135° + 15° = 150°M

ANSWER
150°M

navigation.q: An aircraft cruising at FL95 must descend to 2500 ft at 400 ft/min with a descent groundspeed of 120 kt. Approximately how far from destination should descent start?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cruise at FL95 (9500 ft), descend to 2500 ft
Rate of descent = 400 fpm
Descent groundspeed = 120 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height to lose = 9500 − 2500 = 7000 ft
Descent time = 7000 ÷ 400 = 17.5 min
Distance = 120 × (17.5 ÷ 60) = 35.0 nm

ANSWER
35 NM

navigation.q: You are 7 NM left of track after flying 22 NM, with 15 NM remaining. If you were steering 119°M and want to parallel the planned track, the approximate parallel heading is:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• To fly parallel, use only the opening or track-error angle.
• Track error = 7 × 60 ÷ 22 = 19.1°.
• The aircraft is left of track, so correct right.
• New heading = 119° + 19° = 138°, rounded to the listed 139°M.

FINAL ANSWER
139°M

navigation.q: For a planned 235 NM flight at FL95, descent to 2500 ft is to start 35 NM from destination. If descent groundspeed is 105 kt, the approximate rate of descent required is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Total distance = 235 nm at FL95 (9500 ft), descend to 2500 ft
Descent starts 35 nm from destination
Descent groundspeed = 105 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height to lose = 9500 − 2500 = 7000 ft
Descent time = 35 ÷ 105 × 60 = 20 min
ROD = 7000 ÷ 20 = 350 fpm

ANSWER
350 ft/min

navigation.q: TAS is 140 kt, wind is 190/30 and heading is 120°T. The resulting track is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 140 kt, wind 190/30, heading 120°T.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 190° under the index and place the wind-mark 30 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 120°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 140 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector ends at the centre dot, where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 133 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 12° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
108°T

navigation.q: Cruising at FL65 with TAS 100 kt, GS 95 kt, heading 230°M, track 200°T and variation 23°W, the wind is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cruising at FL65 with TAS 100 kt, groundspeed 95 kt, heading 230°M, track 200°T, variation 23°W.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Convert heading to true: 230°M − 23°W = 207°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 200°T under the index and move the slide so GS 95 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 207°T lies 7° right of track. Follow the 7° drift line on the right of the centreline to where it crosses the 100 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 271/13.

ANSWER
271/13

navigation.q: An aircraft heading 008°T has variation 24°W and deviation 4°W. The compass heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
True heading 008°T, variation 24°W, deviation 4°W.

FORMULA
True → Magnetic: add west variation. Magnetic → Compass: add west deviation.

SOLVE
Magnetic heading = 008° + 24° = 032°M.
Compass heading = 032° + 4° = 036°C.

ANSWER
036°C

navigation.q: Distance en route is 325 NM, TAS is 120 mph, wind is 070/30 and track is 180°T. With fuel flow 7.3 USG/hr, the trip fuel is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance 325 nm, TAS 120 mph, W/V 070/30, track 180°T, fuel flow 7.3 USG/hr.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Convert TAS to knots: 120 mph ÷ 1.15 ≈ 104 kt. Distance and wind are already in nm and kt.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 070° under the index and place the wind-mark 30 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 180°T under the index and move the slide so the 104 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 16° left of track, so heading ≈ 164°T. Read GS ≈ 111 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Time = 325 ÷ 111 = 2.93 h ≈ 2 h 56 min (176 min).
Step 6: Fuel = 7.3 USG/hr × 2.93 h ≈ 21.4 USG.
Step 7: Litres = 21.4 × 3.785 ≈ 81 L. The closest option is 85 litres.

ANSWER
85 litres

navigation.q: Aircraft heading is 175°C, variation 18°W and deviation 4°W. The true heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Compass heading 175°C, variation 18°W, deviation 4°W.

FORMULA
Compass → Magnetic: subtract west deviation. Magnetic → True: subtract west variation.

SOLVE
Magnetic heading = 175° − 4° = 171°M.
True heading = 171° − 18° = 153°T.

ANSWER
153°T

navigation.q: You are 7 NM left of track after flying 22 NM, with 15 NM remaining. If you were steering 112°M, the approximate heading to regain the destination is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
7 nm left of track after 22 nm flown, 15 nm still to run, steering 112°M, want to regain the destination directly

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: opening angle = (off track ÷ distance flown) × 60
Closing angle = (off track ÷ distance remaining) × 60
New heading = present heading ± (opening angle + closing angle), turned toward the track

SOLVE
Opening angle = (7 ÷ 22) × 60 = 19.1°
Closing angle = (7 ÷ 15) × 60 = 28°
Total correction = 19.1° + 28° = 47.1°, rounds to 47°
Aircraft is left of track, so turn right
New heading = 112° + 47° = 159°M

ANSWER
159°M

navigation.q: At FL055, RAS is 100 mph and temperature is ISA +15°C. The approximate TAS is closest to:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5 500 ft (FL055), RAS 100 mph, temperature ISA +15°C.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 5 500 ft = 15 − (2 × 5.5) = +4°C, so ISA +15 gives OAT = +19°C.
Step 2: In the airspeed window, set OAT +19°C against pressure altitude 5.5 (thousands of feet).
Step 3: Opposite 100 on the inner scale, read TAS ≈ 111 mph on the outer scale.
Step 4: Convert to knots: 111 mph ÷ 1.15 ≈ 97 kt.

ANSWER
97 kt

navigation.q: An aircraft in the Southern Hemisphere is maintaining 090°M. If airspeed is increased, the magnetic compass will show:
navigation.a: An apparent turn to the south
navigation.d: An apparent turn to the north
navigation.ans: An apparent turn to the south
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Acceleration error occurs on easterly and westerly headings.
• In the Southern Hemisphere, the Northern-Hemisphere acceleration rule is reversed.
• Accelerating on an easterly heading therefore causes an apparent compass turn toward south.

FINAL ANSWER
An apparent turn to the south

navigation.q: To obtain true airspeed from indicated airspeed, the IAS must be corrected for:
navigation.a: Instrument, position, pressure and temperature effects
navigation.ans: Instrument, position, pressure and temperature effects
navigation.e:
Getting from IAS to TAS involves two distinct stages of correction:
1. Instrument and position error correction: IAS -> RAS/CAS, using the aircraft's own pitot-static calibration data. Instrument error comes from imperfections in the ASI itself; position error comes from the pitot tube/static vent location disturbing the airflow they sense.
2. Density error correction: RAS/CAS -> TAS. The ASI scale is calibrated assuming ISA MSL air density (1225 g/m^3). Actual density almost always differs from this - falling with pressure altitude and rising with outside air temperature - so this second correction accounts for both pressure altitude and temperature, the two factors that determine density.

Wind is not part of this chain: it is only applied afterwards, to convert TAS into groundspeed.

navigation.q: A flight will take 2 hours 54 minutes at a fuel flow of 15.5 USG/hr. The approximate fuel required is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Flight time = 2 hr 54 min
Fuel flow = 15.5 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 2 h 54 min = 2 + 54 ÷ 60 = 2.9 h
Fuel = 2.9 × 15.5 = 44.95 ≈ 45 USG

ANSWER
45 USG

navigation.q: Pressure altitude is 2500 ft and QNH is 1003 hPa. The approximate aerodrome elevation is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 2500 ft, QNH 1003 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa, so elevation = PA − (1013 − QNH) × 30

SOLVE
Elevation = 2500 − (1013 − 1003) × 30 = 2500 − (10 × 30) = 2500 − 300 = 2200 ft

ANSWER
2200 ft

navigation.q: Pressure altitude is 5000 ft and the temperature is ISA +10°C. The approximate density altitude is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 5000 ft, OAT ISA +10°C

FORMULA
Density altitude = pressure altitude + (120 × ISA deviation)

SOLVE
DA = 5000 + (120 × 10) = 5000 + 1200 = 6200 ft

ANSWER
6200 ft

navigation.q: Distance en route is 525 NM, TAS is 130 mph, wind is 050/30 and track is 180°T. If fuel flow is 6.6 USG/hr, the fuel required is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance 525 nm, TAS 130 mph, W/V 050/30, track 180°T, fuel flow 6.6 USG/hr.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Convert TAS to knots: 130 mph ÷ 1.15 ≈ 113 kt.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 050° under the index and place the wind-mark 30 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 180°T under the index and move the slide so the 113 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 12° left of track, so heading ≈ 168°T. Read GS ≈ 130 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Time = 525 ÷ 130 = 4.04 h ≈ 4 h 02 min (242 min).
Step 6: Fuel = 6.6 USG/hr × 4.04 h ≈ 26.7 USG.
Step 7: Litres = 26.7 × 3.785 ≈ 101 L, so about 100 litres.

ANSWER
100 litres

navigation.q: A flight time of 1 hour 15 minutes with a fuel flow of 7.3 USG/hr requires approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Flight time = 1 hr 15 min
Fuel flow = 7.3 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 1 h 15 min = 1.25 h
Fuel = 1.25 × 7.3 = 9.125 ≈ 9.1 USG

ANSWER
9.1 USG

navigation.q: The wind triangle of velocities contains wind direction and speed. The other two velocity pairs are:
navigation.e:
REASONING
Heading pairs with TAS because both describe the aircraft's motion relative to the air mass. Track pairs with groundspeed because both describe its motion over the earth. The wind blows the aircraft from its heading onto its track, so the W/V vector joins the end of HDG/TAS to the end of TR/GS.
Heading/groundspeed and track/TAS mix an air quantity with a ground quantity, so neither pair is a vector in the triangle. Heading/track and GS/TAS put two directions together and two speeds together. Variation is a chart correction between true and magnetic north, not a velocity.

ANSWER
Heading/TAS and track/groundspeed

navigation.q: You are at FL125 and must descend to 2000 ft above an airfield elevation of 1500 ft. If you are 32 NM out and descent GS is 110 kt, the approximate ROD required is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cruise at FL125 (12 500 ft)
Descend to 2000 ft above airfield elevation 1500 ft
32 nm from the airfield, descent GS = 110 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Target altitude = 1500 + 2000 = 3500 ft
Height to lose = 12 500 − 3500 = 9000 ft
Time available = 32 ÷ 110 × 60 = 17.5 min
Required ROD = 9000 ÷ 17.5 = 515.8 fpm, closest listed value 500 fpm

ANSWER
500 ft/min

navigation.q: Wind is 005/15, heading is 340°T and TAS is 95 kt. The resulting track is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Wind 005/15, heading 340°T, TAS 95 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 005° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 340°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 95 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector ends at the centre dot, where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 82 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 4° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
336°T

navigation.q: At FL140, CAS is 145 kt and temperature is ISA +15°C. The approximate TAS is closest to:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Pressure altitude 14 000 ft (FL140), CAS 145 kt, temperature ISA +15°C.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 14 000 ft = 15 − (2 × 14) = −13°C, so ISA +15 gives OAT = +2°C.
Step 2: In the airspeed window, set OAT +2°C against pressure altitude 14 (thousands of feet).
Step 3: Opposite CAS 145 kt on the inner scale, read TAS ≈ 185 kt on the outer scale.

ANSWER
185 kt

navigation.q: A FREDA check was completed at 1105Z. At 1247Z the fuel burn is 12.5 USG/hr. Approximately how much fuel has been consumed?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
FREDA check completed at 1105Z, now 1247Z
Fuel flow = 12.5 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Elapsed time = 1247 − 1105 = 1 h 42 min = 1.70 h
Fuel used = 1.70 × 12.5 = 21.25 ≈ 21.3 USG

ANSWER
21.3 USG

navigation.q: Compass deviation on a particular aircraft usually:
navigation.a: Is the same on every heading
navigation.c: Is zero in the Southern Hemisphere
navigation.e: Deviation varies with heading because it is produced by magnetic fields fixed within the airframe itself — structure, engine, avionics, wiring — rather than by the earth's field. As the aircraft's heading changes relative to those fixed internal fields, the strength and direction of their pull on the compass magnet changes too, so the correction card typically shows a different value — sometimes easterly, sometimes westerly, sometimes near zero — for each heading rather than one constant figure for the whole aircraft.

navigation.q: A FREDA check was completed at 1213Z. At 1247Z the fuel burn is 11.5 USG/hr. Approximately how much fuel has been consumed?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
FREDA check completed at 1213Z, now 1247Z
Fuel flow = 11.5 USG/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Elapsed time = 1247 − 1213 = 34 min = 0.5667 h
Fuel used = 0.5667 × 11.5 = 6.52 ≈ 6.5 USG

ANSWER
6.5 USG

navigation.q: TAS is 120 kt, track is 095°T, groundspeed is 125 kt and drift is 7° right. The wind is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 120 kt, track 095°T, groundspeed 125 kt, drift 7° right.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 7° right means heading = 095° − 7° = 088°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 095°T under the index and move the slide so GS 125 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 088°T lies 7° left of track. Follow the 7° drift line on the left of the centreline to where it crosses the 120 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 345/15.

ANSWER
345/15

navigation.q: Heading 120°T, TAS 175 kt, wind 045/35. The resulting track and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 120°T, TAS 175 kt, wind 045/35.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 045° under the index and place the wind-mark 35 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 120°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 175 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector ends at the centre dot, where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 169 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 12° right. Track = heading + drift.

ANSWER
132°T and 169 kt

navigation.q: En route from Heidelberg to Durban, the aircraft is abeam Vrede. The distance and magnetic bearing (QDM) to Vrede are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Abeam Vrede on the Heidelberg–Durban route. Chart plot gives the true bearing from the aircraft to Vrede as 053°T and the mean variation at that point as 21°W. Perpendicular distance measured off the chart is 14 nm.

FORMULA
QDM = True Bearing + Westerly Variation (west variation is added when converting true to magnetic).

SOLVE
QDM = 053° + 21° = 074°M.
Distance abeam = 14 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
074° QDM, 14 nm

navigation.q: TAS 186 kt, 4° left drift, track 312°T, groundspeed 174 kt. The wind velocity is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 186 kt, 4° left drift, track 312°T, groundspeed 174 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: A 4° left drift means heading = 312° + 4° = 316°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 312°T under the index and move the slide so GS 174 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 316°T lies 4° right of track. Follow the 4° drift line on the right of the centreline to where it crosses the 186 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 360/17.

ANSWER
360/17

navigation.q: RAS 138 kt, FL105, OAT -7°C, track 341°T, wind 135/15. The approximate heading and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
RAS 138 kt, FL105, OAT −7°C, track 341°T, wind 135/15.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: On the airspeed window, set OAT −7°C against pressure altitude 10.5 and read TAS ≈ 161 kt opposite RAS 138 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 135° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 3: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 341°T under the index.
Step 4: Move the slide so the 161 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 2° right of track. Heading = track + WCA, with the nose pointed into wind. Drift is the same size on the opposite side (2° left). Read GS ≈ 174 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
343°T and 174 kt

navigation.q: Heading 270°T, TAS 142 kt, wind 190/25. The resulting track and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 270°T, TAS 142 kt, wind 190/25.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 190° under the index and place the wind-mark 25 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 270°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 142 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector ends at the centre dot, where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 140 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 10° right. Track = heading + drift.

ANSWER
280°T and 140 kt

navigation.q: From Maseru MZV to Ermelo, the distance and magnetic bearing (QDM) to Secunda SU when abeam are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
On the Maseru MZV–Ermelo route, abeam Secunda SU. Chart plot gives the true bearing to Secunda as 307°T and the mean variation as 21°W. Chart distance is 43 nm.

FORMULA
QDM = True Bearing + Westerly Variation.

SOLVE
QDM = 307° + 21° = 328°M.
Distance = 43 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
328° QDM, 43 nm

navigation.q: The distance and magnetic bearing (QDR) from Cape Town CTV to Robben Island are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
From Cape Town CTV to Robben Island. Chart plot gives the true bearing from Cape Town to Robben Island as 312°T and the mean variation at Cape Town as 24°W. Chart distance is 16 nm.

FORMULA
QDR = True Bearing + Westerly Variation (QDR is the magnetic bearing measured outward from the station, so the same true-to-magnetic conversion applies).

SOLVE
QDR = 312° + 24° = 336°M.
Distance = 16 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
336° QDR, 16 nm

navigation.q: On a flight from Nieuwoudtville (S31°23' E019°04') to Kimberley (S28°50' E024°46'), the mean magnetic track and distance are:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot Nieuwoudtville and Kimberley on the chart.
• Measure the mean true track at the mid-meridian: approximately 063°T.
• Apply approximately 21°W mean variation: magnetic track = 063° + 21° = 084°M.
• Measure the route distance using the chart scale: approximately 335 NM.

FINAL ANSWER
084°(M), 335 nm

navigation.q: The magnetic track and distance from Cape Town CTV to Durban BDV are:
navigation.e: Measured true track ≈ 069°T and distance ≈ 675 NM. Apply 23°W mean variation: magnetic track = 069° + 23° = 092°M. Result: 092°M, 675 NM.

navigation.q: The magnetic track and distance from Skukuza SZ to Malelane MN are:
navigation.e: Measured true track ≈ 180°T and distance ≈ 30 NM. Apply 17°W variation: magnetic track = 180° + 17° = 197°M. Result: 197°M, 30 NM.

navigation.q: The magnetic track and distance from Maputo to Cape Agulhas are:
navigation.e: Measured mean true track ≈ 231°T and distance ≈ 840 NM. Apply 23°W mean variation: magnetic track = 231° + 23° = 254°M. Result: 254°M, 840 NM.

navigation.q: Halfway from George to Lanseria, the distance and magnetic bearing (QDR) from Kimberley are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Halfway between George and Lanseria. Chart plot gives the true bearing from Kimberley to that midpoint as 160°T and the mean variation at Kimberley as 20°W. Chart distance is 75 nm.

FORMULA
QDR = True Bearing + Westerly Variation.

SOLVE
QDR = 160° + 20° = 180°M.
Distance = 75 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
180° QDR, 75 nm

navigation.q: The mean magnetic track and distance from Rand (S26°15' E028°09') to JSV (S26°09' E028°14') are:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot Rand and JSV and measure the short true track: approximately 041°T.
• Apply approximately 17°W variation: 041° + 17° = 058°M.
• Measure the distance using the chart scale: approximately 8 NM.

FINAL ANSWER
058°(M), 8 nm

navigation.q: Heading 053°T, TAS 155 kt, 4° right drift, groundspeed 165 kt. The wind velocity is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 053°T, TAS 155 kt, 4° right drift, groundspeed 165 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 4° right means track = 053° + 4° = 057°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 057°T under the index and move the slide so GS 165 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 053°T lies 4° left of track. Follow the 4° drift line on the left of the centreline to where it crosses the 155 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 283/15.

ANSWER
283/15

navigation.q: From Alexander Bay to Cape St Lucia, the initial true track, mean true track and final true track are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Alexander Bay (about S28°38' E016°28') to Cape St Lucia (about S28°23' E032°25'). This is a long, roughly west-to-east route in the Southern Hemisphere.

METHOD (Chart and Protractor)
Step 1: Draw a straight line from Alexander Bay to Cape St Lucia.
Step 2: At the start, measure the angle between the line and the nearest meridian: initial track about 093°T.
Step 3: At the mid-point, measure against the meridian there: mean track about 090°T.
Step 4: At the end, measure against the meridian near Cape St Lucia: final track about 087°T.
Step 5: Sense check: flying west to east in the Southern Hemisphere, true track DECREASES along the route, because meridians further east lean towards the South Pole.

ANSWER
093°T, 090°T, 087°T

navigation.q: RAS 115 kt, FL085, OAT +3°C, track 213°T, wind 055/15. The approximate heading and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
RAS 115 kt, FL085, OAT +3°C, track 213°T, wind 055/15.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: On the airspeed window, set OAT +3°C against pressure altitude 8.5 and read TAS ≈ 132 kt opposite RAS 115 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 055° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 3: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 213°T under the index.
Step 4: Move the slide so the 132 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 2° left of track. Heading = track − WCA, with the nose pointed into wind. Drift is the same size on the opposite side (2° right). Read GS ≈ 146 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
211°T and 146 kt

navigation.q: The distance and magnetic bearing (QDM) from Umtata to Lusikisiki are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
From Umtata to Lusikisiki. Chart plot gives the true bearing as 072°T and the mean variation as 21°W. Chart distance is 45 nm.

FORMULA
QDM = True Bearing + Westerly Variation.

SOLVE
QDM = 072° + 21° = 093°M.
Distance = 45 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
093° QDM, 45 nm

navigation.q: Track 084°T, TAS 102 kt, wind 300/28. The heading and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 084°T, TAS 102 kt, wind 300/28.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 300° under the index and place the wind-mark 28 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 084°T under the index.
Step 3: Move the slide so the 102 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark. The HDG/TAS vector ends where the W/V vector begins.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 9° left of track. Heading = track − WCA, with the nose pointed into wind. Drift is the same size on the opposite side (9° right). Read GS ≈ 123 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
075°T and 123 kt

navigation.q: The magnetic track and distance from Johannesburg International (S26°09' E028°14') to Cape Town CTV (S33°58' E018°36') are:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot Johannesburg International to Cape Town CTV.
• Measure the mean true track at the mid-meridian: approximately 227°T.
• Apply approximately 21°W mean variation: 227° + 21° = 248°M.
• Measure the route distance on the chart: approximately 684 NM.

FINAL ANSWER
248°(M), 684 nm

navigation.q: TAS 200 kt, heading 095°T, wind 010/45. The resulting track and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 200 kt, heading 095°T, wind 010/45.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 010° under the index and place the wind-mark 45 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 095°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 200 kt is under the centre dot. The HDG/TAS vector ends at the centre dot, where the W/V vector begins.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 201 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 13° right. Track = heading + drift.

ANSWER
108°T and 201 kt

navigation.q: Heading 095°T, TAS 200 kt, track 079°T, groundspeed 148 kt. The wind velocity is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 095°T, TAS 200 kt, track 079°T, groundspeed 148 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put track 079°T under the index and move the slide so GS 148 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 2: Heading 095°T lies 16° right of track. Follow the 16° drift line on the right of the centreline to where it crosses the 200 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 3: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 130/71.

ANSWER
130/71

navigation.q: RAS 165 kt, FL130, ISA +15, track 108°T, wind 270/18. The approximate heading and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
RAS 165 kt, FL130, ISA +15, track 108°T, wind 270/18.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 13 000 ft ≈ 15 − (2 × 13) = −11°C, so ISA +15 gives OAT ≈ +4°C. On the airspeed window, set +4°C against pressure altitude 13 and read TAS ≈ 207 kt opposite RAS 165 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 270° under the index and place the wind-mark 18 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 3: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 108°T under the index.
Step 4: Move the slide so the 207 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 1.5° right of track, so heading ≈ 109.5°T. Read GS ≈ 223–224 kt under the centre dot; the closest option is 223 kt. Heading 109.5°T rounds to 110°T.

ANSWER
110°T and 223 kt

navigation.q: Heading 341°T, TAS 128 kt, track 336°T, distance 78 nm in 45 minutes. The wind velocity is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 341°T, TAS 128 kt, track 336°T, distance 78 nm covered in 45 minutes.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Groundspeed = 78 nm ÷ 45 min × 60 = 104 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 336°T under the index and move the slide so GS 104 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 341°T lies 5° right of track. Follow the 5° drift line on the right of the centreline to where it crosses the 128 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 360/26.

ANSWER
360/26

navigation.q: TAS 155 kt, 7° right drift, track 224°T, distance 102 nm in 38 minutes. The wind velocity is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
TAS 155 kt, 7° right drift, track 224°T, distance 102 nm covered in 38 minutes.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 7° right means heading = 224° − 7° = 217°T. Groundspeed = 102 nm ÷ 38 min × 60 ≈ 161 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 224°T under the index and move the slide so GS 161 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 217°T lies 7° left of track. Follow the 7° drift line on the left of the centreline to where it crosses the 155 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 113/20.

ANSWER
113/20

navigation.q: RAS 128 kt, FL115, ISA +8, track 242°T, wind 010/15. The approximate heading and groundspeed are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
RAS 128 kt, FL115, ISA +8, track 242°T, wind 010/15.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 11 500 ft ≈ 15 − (2 × 11.5) = −8°C, so ISA +8 gives OAT ≈ 0°C. On the airspeed window, set 0°C against pressure altitude 11.5 and read TAS ≈ 155 kt opposite RAS 128 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 010° under the index and place the wind-mark 15 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 3: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 242°T under the index.
Step 4: Move the slide so the 155 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 4° right of track (the wind is from the right), so heading ≈ 246°T. Read GS ≈ 163 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
246°T and 163 kt

navigation.q: The magnetic track and distance from Morija MR to Maseru MU are:
navigation.e: Measured true track ≈ 001°T and distance ≈ 19 NM. Apply 21°W variation: magnetic track = 001° + 21° = 022°M. Result: 022°M, 19 NM.

navigation.q: From Richards Bay to Cape Columbine, the initial true track, mean true track and final true track are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Richards Bay (about S28°48' E032°05') to Cape Columbine (about S32°49' E017°51'). This is a long west-south-westerly route in the Southern Hemisphere.

METHOD (Chart and Protractor)
Step 1: Draw a straight line from Richards Bay to Cape Columbine.
Step 2: At the start, measure the angle between the line and the nearest meridian: initial track about 248°T.
Step 3: At the mid-point, measure against the meridian there: mean track about 252°T.
Step 4: At the end, measure against the meridian near Cape Columbine: final track about 255°T.
Step 5: Sense check: flying east to west in the Southern Hemisphere, true track INCREASES along the route — the opposite of a west-to-east route.

ANSWER
248°T, 252°T, 255°T

navigation.q: The magnetic track and distance from Upington (S28°24' E021°16') to George (S34°00' E022°23') are:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot Upington to George and measure the mean true track: approximately 171°T.
• Apply approximately 22°W mean variation: 171° + 22° = 193°M.
• Measure the chart distance: approximately 340 NM.

FINAL ANSWER
193°(M), 340 nm

navigation.q: Heading 183°T, TAS 136 kt, 7° right drift, groundspeed 142 kt. The wind velocity is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 183°T, TAS 136 kt, 7° right drift, groundspeed 142 kt.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Drift 7° right means track = 183° + 7° = 190°T.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put track 190°T under the index and move the slide so GS 142 kt is under the centre dot. The TR/GS vector ends at the centre dot.
Step 3: Heading 183°T lies 7° left of track. Follow the 7° drift line on the left of the centreline to where it crosses the 136 kt TAS arc, and mark that point. This is the end of the HDG/TAS vector.
Step 4: The W/V vector runs from this mark to the centre dot. Rotate the compass rose until the mark sits on the centreline directly ABOVE the centre dot. Read the wind direction (the direction it blows FROM) under the index. The wind speed is the distance from the mark down to the centre dot. With the mark above the centre dot, read W/V ≈ 077/18.

ANSWER
077/18

navigation.q: From Burgersdorp to Humansdorp, halfway along track, the distance and magnetic bearing (QDM) to Cookhouse CH are:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Halfway on the Burgersdorp–Humansdorp route, bearing to Cookhouse CH. Chart plot gives the true bearing as 150°T and the mean variation as 21°W. Chart distance is 20 nm.

FORMULA
QDM = True Bearing + Westerly Variation.

SOLVE
QDM = 150° + 21° = 171°M.
Distance = 20 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
171° QDM, 20 nm

navigation.q: Cape Town to Sutherland is flown from 0932Z to 1010Z over 137 nm with a 15 kt tailwind component. The TAS is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cape Town to Sutherland, 0932Z–1010Z, distance 137 nm
Tailwind component = 15 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Elapsed time = 1010 − 0932 = 38 min = 0.6333 h
GS = 137 ÷ 0.6333 = 216.3 kt
TAS = 216.3 − 15 = 201.3 ≈ 201 kt

ANSWER
201 kt

navigation.q: Maseru MZV at 1615Z direct to Cape Town, TAS 180 kt, wind 300/50. The ETA abeam Victoria West is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Maseru MZV at 1615Z direct to Cape Town, TAS 180 kt, W/V 300/50.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Plot Maseru–Cape Town: track about 238°T. Mark the point abeam Victoria West and measure the distance to it: about 259 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 300° under the index and place the wind-mark 50 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 238°T under the index and move the slide so the 180 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 14° right of track, so heading ≈ 252°T. Read GS ≈ 151 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Time = 259 ÷ 151 = 1.72 h ≈ 1 h 43 min.
Step 6: ETA = 1615 + 0143 = 1758Z.

ANSWER
1758Z

navigation.q: An aircraft climbs from an airfield elevation of 3225 ft to 6870 ft within 13 nm at a climb GS of 90 kt. The required rate of climb is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Climb from airfield elevation 3225 ft to 6870 ft
Within 13 nm, climb groundspeed = 90 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height to gain = 6870 − 3225 = 3645 ft
Time = 13 ÷ 90 × 60 = 8.67 min
ROC = 3645 ÷ 8.67 = 420.6 ≈ 421 fpm

ANSWER
421 fpm

navigation.q: If heading is 046° and track is 038°, the drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 046°, track 038°.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Step 1: Track 038° is less than heading 046°, so the aircraft is blown LEFT of the nose.
Step 2: Drift = 046° − 038° = 8° left (port).

ANSWER
8° left

navigation.q: Alexander Bay at 1347Z direct to Upington. Abeam Karasburg at 1453Z. The ETA for Upington is approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Time from Alexander Bay to abeam Karasburg = 1453 − 1347 = 1 h 06 min.
• Measure the distance flown to the abeam point and calculate actual GS.
• GS = distance flown ÷ 1.10 h.
• Measure the distance remaining from abeam Karasburg to Upington.
• Remaining time is approximately 1 h 15 min.
• ETA = 1453 + 0115 = 1608Z.

FINAL ANSWER
1608Z

navigation.q: Overhead Pomfret at 0915Z direct to Phalaborwa, with a relative bearing fix from Gaborone at 0954Z. The ETA for Phalaborwa is approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Convert the Gaborone relative bearing into a plotted true bearing and obtain the 0954 fix.
• Elapsed time from Pomfret = 0954 − 0915 = 39 min.
• Actual GS = measured distance flown ÷ (39 ÷ 60).
• Measure the distance remaining to Phalaborwa.
• Time remaining is approximately 1 h 15 min.
• ETA = 0954 + 0115 = 1109Z.

FINAL ANSWER
1109Z

navigation.q: Heading 316°, drift 5° right. The track is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 316°, drift 5° right.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Step 1: Right (starboard) drift blows the aircraft clockwise of heading, so track is greater than heading.
Step 2: Track = heading + right drift = 316° + 5° = 321°.

ANSWER
321°

navigation.q: Plan a descent from FL115 to an airfield elevation of 1050 ft. ROD is 550 fpm and descent GS is 85 kt. The top of descent should be approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Descend from FL115 (11 500 ft) to airfield elevation 1050 ft
Rate of descent = 550 fpm, descent groundspeed = 85 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Height to lose = 11 500 − 1050 = 10 450 ft
Descent time = 10 450 ÷ 550 = 19.0 min
Distance = 85 × (19.0 ÷ 60) = 26.9 ≈ 27 nm

ANSWER
27 nm from the airfield

navigation.q: Cape Town CTV direct to Durban DNV, TAS 210 kt, wind 310/45. The mean magnetic heading, groundspeed and leg time are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cape Town CTV direct to Durban DNV, TAS 210 kt, W/V 310/45.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Measure on the chart: mean track about 069°T, distance about 675 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 310° under the index and place the wind-mark 45 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 069°T under the index and move the slide so the 210 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 11° left of track, so heading ≈ 058°T. Read GS ≈ 228 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Convert to magnetic with about 23°W variation: 058°T + 23° = 081°M.
Step 6: Time = 675 ÷ 228 = 2.96 h ≈ 2 h 57 min.

ANSWER
081°M, 228 kt, 2 hr 57 min

navigation.q: Overhead Upington at 1127Z direct to Bisho, with a relative bearing fix at Victoria West at 1235Z. The ETA at Bisho is approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Convert the Victoria West relative bearing to a plotted bearing and obtain the 1235 fix.
• Elapsed time from Upington = 1235 − 1127 = 1 h 08 min.
• Calculate actual GS from distance flown ÷ 1.133 h.
• Measure the distance remaining from the fix to Bisho.
• Remaining time is approximately 1 h 17 min.
• ETA = 1235 + 0117 = 1352Z.

FINAL ANSWER
1352Z

navigation.q: Overhead East London at 1652Z en route to Ladysmith, a relative bearing fix at 1736Z gives a revised ETA of approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Use the relative bearing to obtain the 1736 position fix.
• Elapsed time from East London = 1736 − 1652 = 44 min.
• Calculate actual GS from the chart distance flown.
• Apply that GS to the distance remaining to Ladysmith.
• Remaining time is approximately 29 min.
• ETA = 1736 + 0029 = 1805Z.

FINAL ANSWER
1805Z

navigation.q: RAS 144 kt, FL170, ISA +12, track 216°T, wind 090/35. The approximate drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
RAS 144 kt, FL170, ISA +12, track 216°T, wind 090/35.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 17 000 ft ≈ −19°C, so ISA +12 gives OAT ≈ −7°C. Set this against pressure altitude 17 in the airspeed window and read TAS ≈ 192 kt opposite RAS 144 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 090° under the index and place the wind-mark 35 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 3: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 216°T under the index.
Step 4: Move the slide so the 192 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 8° left of track. Heading = track − WCA. Drift is the same size on the opposite side (8° right). Read GS ≈ 210 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
8° right

navigation.q: If track is 002° and heading is 358°, the drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 002°, heading 358°.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Step 1: Track 002° lies just clockwise of heading 358° across north: 358° → 360° is 2°, then 360° → 002° is another 2°.
Step 2: Drift = 4° right (starboard).

ANSWER
4° right

navigation.q: From Pietermaritzburg to Bisho, overhead Kokstad at 1010Z. The Durban DNV fix and ETA for Bisho are approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Plot the Pietermaritzburg-to-Bisho route and mark Kokstad as the 1010Z position.
• From Durban DNV, measure the magnetic bearing from the station to Kokstad: approximately radial 268.
• Measure the distance from DNV to Kokstad: approximately 83 NM.
• Use actual progress to Kokstad to calculate groundspeed, then apply it to the distance remaining to Bisho.
• The revised ETA is approximately 1123Z.

FINAL ANSWER
DNV R268 / 83 DME, ETA 1123Z

navigation.q: The true bearing (QTE) and distance of Willowmore from George GGV are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
QTE and distance of Willowmore measured from George GGV. Chart plot gives the bearing as 051° and distance 81 nm.

FORMULA
QTE is by definition a true bearing (station to aircraft/point), so no variation correction applies.

SOLVE
QTE = 051°T (already true, no correction needed).
Distance = 81 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
051°T, 81 nm

navigation.q: The radial and DME of Cradock from Bisho BOV are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Radial and DME of Cradock measured from Bisho BOV. Chart plot gives the true bearing from Bisho to Cradock as 305°T and the mean variation at Bisho as 21°W. Chart distance is 96 nm.

FORMULA
Radial (QDR) = True Bearing + Westerly Variation.

SOLVE
Radial = 305° + 21° = 326°M.
DME distance = 96 nm (measured on chart).

ANSWER
326 radial, 96 DME

navigation.q: Victoria West to Willowmore is flown in 1 hr 10 min with an 18 kt headwind component. If the distance is 109 nm, the TAS is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Victoria West to Willowmore, distance = 109 nm, flight time = 1 hr 10 min
Headwind component = 18 kt

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Time = 1 h 10 min = 70 ÷ 60 = 1.1667 h
GS = 109 ÷ 1.1667 = 93.4 kt
TAS = 93.4 + 18 = 111.4 ≈ 111 kt

ANSWER
111 kt

navigation.q: Near Cradock, heading 057°M, relative bearing 077° to Bisho BOV. The true bearing (QTE) from Bisho is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Near Cradock, heading 057°M, ADF relative bearing to Bisho BOV = 077°. Mean variation at Bisho ≈ 24°W.

FORMULA
QDM = Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing.
QDR (reciprocal, from the station) = QDM ± 180°.
QTE = QDR − Westerly Variation (west variation is subtracted when converting magnetic to true).

SOLVE
QDM = 057° + 077° = 134°M.
QDR = 134° + 180° = 314°M.
QTE = 314° − 24° = 290°T.

ANSWER
290°T

navigation.q: Track 182°, drift 5° right. The heading is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 182°, drift 5° right.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Step 1: Right drift blows the aircraft clockwise of heading, so the nose must point 5° anticlockwise of track 182° (into wind).
Step 2: Heading = track − right drift = 182° − 5° = 177°.

ANSWER
177°

navigation.q: Durban DNV at 1321Z direct to Keetmanshoop, TAS 180 kt, wind 330/45. The initial magnetic heading, groundspeed and ETA are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Durban DNV at 1321Z direct to Keetmanshoop, TAS 180 kt, W/V 330/45.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Measure on the chart: initial track about 285°T, distance about 713 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 330° under the index and place the wind-mark 45 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 285°T under the index and move the slide so the 180 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 10° right of track, so heading ≈ 295°T. Read GS ≈ 145 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Convert to magnetic with about 23°W variation: 295°T + 23° = 318°M.
Step 6: Time = 713 ÷ 145 = 4.92 h ≈ 4 h 55 min.
Step 7: ETA = 1321 + 0455 = 1816Z.

ANSWER
318°M, 145 kt, 1816Z

navigation.q: Alexander Bay ABV direct to Ladysmith LYV, FL130, OAT -5°C, RAS 175 kt, wind 345/50, deviation 2°E. The mean compass heading and flight time are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Alexander Bay ABV direct to Ladysmith LYV, FL130, OAT −5°C, RAS 175 kt, W/V 345/50, deviation 2°E.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: In the airspeed window, set OAT −5°C against pressure altitude 13 and read TAS ≈ 216 kt opposite RAS 175 kt.
Step 2: Measure on the chart: mean track about 090°T, distance about 696 nm.
Step 3: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 345° under the index and place the wind-mark 50 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 4: Rotate the rose to put track 090°T under the index and move the slide so the 216 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 13° left of track, so heading ≈ 077°T. Read GS ≈ 223 kt under the centre dot.
Step 6: Convert with the mean variation (about 20°W): 077°T + 20° = 097°M. Deviation east, compass least: 097° − 2° = 095°C.
Step 7: Time = 696 ÷ 223 = 3.12 h ≈ 3 h 07–3 h 08 min.

ANSWER
095°C and 3 hr 08 min

navigation.q: Mafikeng MMV at 1330Z direct to Keetmanshoop, TAS 195 kt, wind 255/20. The ETA at the Windhoek FIR boundary on E020°00' is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Mafikeng MMV at 1330Z direct to Keetmanshoop, TAS 195 kt, W/V 255/20.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Plot the route: track about 264°T. Mark where it crosses the Windhoek FIR boundary on E020°00′ and measure the distance to it: about 300 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 255° under the index and place the wind-mark 20 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 264°T under the index and move the slide so the 195 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 1° left of track, so heading ≈ 263°T. Read GS ≈ 175 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Time = 300 ÷ 175 = 1.71 h ≈ 1 h 43 min.
Step 6: ETA = 1330 + 0143 = 1513Z.

ANSWER
1513Z

navigation.q: If track is 226° and heading is 222°, the drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Track 226°, heading 222°.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Step 1: Track 226° is greater than heading 222°, so the aircraft is blown to the right of heading.
Step 2: Drift = 226° − 222° = 4° right (starboard).

ANSWER
4° right

navigation.q: Overhead Hotazel at 1000Z direct to Ladysmith, overhead Welkom at 1057Z. The revised ETA for Ladysmith is approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Elapsed time from Hotazel to Welkom = 1057 − 1000 = 57 min.
• Measure the Hotazel–Welkom distance and calculate actual GS.
• GS = distance flown ÷ (57 ÷ 60).
• Measure the remaining distance from Welkom to Ladysmith.
• Remaining time is approximately 46 min.
• ETA = 1057 + 0046 = 1143Z.

FINAL ANSWER
1143Z

navigation.q: RAS 107 kt, FL085, OAT +6°C, track 043°T, wind 215/25. The approximate drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
RAS 107 kt, FL085, OAT +6°C, track 043°T, wind 215/25.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: On the airspeed window, set OAT +6°C against pressure altitude 8.5 and read TAS ≈ 123 kt opposite RAS 107 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 215° under the index and place the wind-mark 25 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot (grommet).
Step 3: Rotate the compass rose to put the required track 043°T under the index.
Step 4: Move the slide so the 123 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 5: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 2° right of track. Heading = track + WCA. Drift is the same size on the opposite side (2° left). Read GS ≈ 148 kt under the centre dot.

ANSWER
2° left

navigation.q: George GGV at 0730Z direct to Keetmanshoop, TAS 175 kt, wind 225/25. The ETA at the Windhoek FIR boundary is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
George GGV at 0730Z direct to Keetmanshoop, TAS 175 kt, W/V 225/25.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Plot the route: track about 334°T. Mark the Windhoek FIR boundary crossing and measure the distance to it: about 440 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 225° under the index and place the wind-mark 25 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 334°T under the index and move the slide so the 175 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 8° left of track, so heading ≈ 326°T. Read GS ≈ 182 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Time = 440 ÷ 182 = 2.42 h ≈ 2 h 25 min.
Step 6: ETA = 0730 + 0225 = 0955Z.

ANSWER
0955Z

navigation.q: If heading is 312° and track is 316°, the drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 312°, track 316°.

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Step 1: Track 316° is greater than heading 312°, so the aircraft is blown to the right of heading.
Step 2: Drift = 316° − 312° = 4° right (starboard).

ANSWER
4° right

navigation.q: At 1324Z overhead Alexander Bay ABV, direct to Lanseria, TAS 180 kt, wind 230/45. The heading, groundspeed and ETA are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
At 1324Z overhead Alexander Bay ABV direct to Lanseria, TAS 180 kt, W/V 230/45.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Measure on the chart: track about 076°T, distance about 628 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 230° under the index and place the wind-mark 45 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 076°T under the index and move the slide so the 180 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 6° right of track, so heading ≈ 082°T. Read GS ≈ 219 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Time = 628 ÷ 219 = 2.87 h ≈ 2 h 52 min.
Step 6: ETA = 1324 + 0252 = 1616Z.

ANSWER
082°T, 219 kt, 1616Z

navigation.q: Port Shepstone to Port Elizabeth, overhead Bisho at 1656Z. The revised ETA for Port Elizabeth is approximately:
navigation.e:
WORKING

• Use Bisho as the known position at 1656Z.
• Calculate actual groundspeed from the distance and elapsed time flown before Bisho.
• Measure the distance remaining from Bisho to Port Elizabeth.
• Time remaining = distance remaining ÷ actual GS ≈ 1 h 03 min.
• ETA = 1656 + 0103 = 1759Z.

FINAL ANSWER
1759Z

navigation.q: Cape Town CTV at 1700Z direct to Margate, TAS 220 kt, wind 300/55. The heading, groundspeed and ETA are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cape Town CTV at 1700Z direct to Margate, TAS 220 kt, W/V 300/55.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Measure on the chart: track about 073°T, distance about 627 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 300° under the index and place the wind-mark 55 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 073°T under the index and move the slide so the 220 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 10° left of track, so heading ≈ 063°T. Read GS ≈ 254 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Convert to magnetic with about 24°W variation: 063°T + 24° = 087°M.
Step 6: Time = 627 ÷ 254 = 2.47 h ≈ 2 h 28 min.
Step 7: ETA = 1700 + 0228 = 1928Z.

ANSWER
087°M, 254 kt, 1928Z

navigation.q: Cape Town direct to East London, departing 0807Z, TAS 175 kt, wind 300/35. The ETA at the Port Elizabeth FIR boundary 24°E is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Cape Town direct to East London, departing 0807Z, TAS 175 kt, W/V 300/35.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Plot the route: track about 083°T. Mark where it crosses the Port Elizabeth FIR boundary on 24°E and measure the distance to it: about 272 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 300° under the index and place the wind-mark 35 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 083°T under the index and move the slide so the 175 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 7° left of track, so heading ≈ 076°T. Read GS ≈ 202 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Time = 272 ÷ 202 = 1.35 h ≈ 1 h 21 min.
Step 6: ETA = 0807 + 0121 = 0928Z.

ANSWER
0928Z

navigation.q: Heading 004°T, TAS 121 kt, wind 085/25. The approximate drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Heading 004°T, TAS 121 kt, wind 085/25.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 085° under the index and place the wind-mark 25 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 2: Rotate the rose to put heading 004°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 121 kt is under the centre dot.
Step 3: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 120 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 12° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
12° left

navigation.q: Ladysmith LYV direct to Sutherland SLV, TAS 125 kt, wind 320/25, deviation 4°W. The compass heading, groundspeed and leg time are approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Ladysmith LYV direct to Sutherland SLV, TAS 125 kt, W/V 320/25, deviation 4°W.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: Measure on the chart: mean track about 244°T, distance about 522 nm.
Step 2: Wind side: rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 320° under the index and place the wind-mark 25 kt directly ABOVE the centre dot.
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put track 244°T under the index and move the slide so the 125 kt TAS arc lies under the wind-mark.
Step 4: Read the WCA from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 11° right of track, so heading ≈ 255°T. Read GS ≈ 117 kt under the centre dot.
Step 5: Convert with the mean variation (about 22°W): 255°T + 22° = 277°M. Deviation west, compass best: 277° + 4° = 281°C.
Step 6: Time = 522 ÷ 117 = 4.46 h ≈ 4 h 28 min.

ANSWER
281°C, 117 kt, 4 hr 28 min

navigation.q: RAS 121 kt, FL105, ISA +7, heading 323°T, wind 035/25. The approximate drift is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
RAS 121 kt, FL105, ISA +7, heading 323°T, wind 035/25.

METHOD (CRP-5 Flight Computer)
Step 1: ISA at 10 500 ft ≈ −6°C, so ISA +7 gives OAT ≈ +1°C. Set this against pressure altitude 10.5 in the airspeed window and read TAS ≈ 144 kt opposite RAS 121 kt.
Step 2: Rotate the compass rose to put the wind direction 035° under the index and place the wind-mark 25 kt directly BELOW the centre dot (the 'wind-mark-down' method).
Step 3: Rotate the rose to put heading 323°T under the index and move the slide so TAS 144 kt is under the centre dot.
Step 4: The wind-mark now sits at the end of the TR/GS vector. Read GS ≈ 138 kt from the speed arc under the wind-mark. Read drift from the drift line through the wind-mark: about 10° left. Track = heading − drift.

ANSWER
10° left

navigation.q: Flying from E to F, 88 nm apart. After 35 nm, you are 4 nm left of track. What heading change is required to fly parallel to track?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Total distance E to F 88 nm, after 35 nm flown, 4 nm left of track

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: track error (°) = (distance off track ÷ distance flown) × 60
To fly parallel to the original track, apply only the track-error angle, turned toward the track

SOLVE
Track error = (4 ÷ 35) × 60 = 6.86°, rounds to 7°
Aircraft is left of track, so correct right

ANSWER
7° right

navigation.q: A distance of 18 cm measured on a 1:1 000 000 chart is covered in 37 minutes. The groundspeed is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 18 cm
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000
Time = 37 min

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator
Groundspeed = distance ÷ time

SOLVE
Ground distance = 18 cm × 1 000 000 = 18 000 000 cm = 180 km
Convert to nautical miles: 180 km ÷ 1.852 = 97.2 NM
Time = 37 min ÷ 60 = 0.617 h
Groundspeed = 97.2 NM ÷ 0.617 h = 157.6 kt ≈ 158 kt
Convert to mph: 158 kt × 1.151 = 181.9 mph ≈ 181 mph
Convert to km/h: 180 km ÷ 0.617 h = 291.7 km/h ≈ 292 km/h

ANSWER
158 kt, 181 mph, 292 km/h

navigation.q: What is the approximate scale of a map on which 31 cm represents an earth distance of 93 nm?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 31 cm
Ground distance = 93 NM

FORMULA
Scale (RF) = ground distance ÷ chart distance, both measured in the same units

SOLVE
Convert 93 NM to cm using 1 NM = 1853.18 m: 93 × 1853.18 = 172 346 m = 17 234 600 cm
Scale denominator = 17 234 600 cm ÷ 31 cm = 555 955

ANSWER
1:555 955

navigation.q: Flying from A to B, 127 nm apart. After 44 nm, you are 3 nm left of track. If maintaining 312°C, what heading should you fly to parallel the planned track?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Total distance A to B 127 nm, after 44 nm flown, 3 nm left of track, maintaining 312°C

FORMULA
1-in-60 rule: track error (°) = (distance off track ÷ distance flown) × 60
To fly parallel to the original track, apply only the track-error angle, turned toward the track

SOLVE
Track error = (3 ÷ 44) × 60 = 4.09°, rounds to 4°
Aircraft is left of track, so turn right
New heading = 312° + 4° = 316°C

ANSWER
316°C

navigation.q: Airfield elevation 5345 ft, QNH 1003 hPa. The pressure altitude is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Elevation 5345 ft, QNH 1003 hPa

FORMULA
Pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − QNH) × 30 ft/hPa

SOLVE
PA = 5345 + (1013 − 1003) × 30 = 5345 + 300 = 5645 ft

ANSWER
5645 ft

navigation.q: A distance of 27 cm measured on a 1:500 000 chart is covered in 41 minutes. The groundspeed is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 27 cm
Chart scale = 1:500 000
Time = 41 min

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator
Groundspeed = distance ÷ time

SOLVE
Ground distance = 27 cm × 500 000 = 13 500 000 cm = 135 km
Convert to nautical miles: 135 km ÷ 1.852 = 72.9 NM
Time = 41 min ÷ 60 = 0.683 h
Groundspeed = 72.9 NM ÷ 0.683 h = 106.7 kt ≈ 107 kt
Convert to mph: 107 kt × 1.151 = 123.2 mph ≈ 123 mph
Convert to km/h: 135 km ÷ 0.683 h = 197.7 km/h ≈ 198 km/h

ANSWER
107 kt, 123 mph, 198 km/h

navigation.q: If sunset is 1823 LMT at Cape Town (S33°58' E018°35'), the official start of night in SAST is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunset = 1823 LMT at Cape Town, longitude 018°35'E.

FORMULA
Official night = sunset + 15 min (LMT)
Longitude time = degrees × 4 min + minutes × 4 sec
UTC = LMT − longitude time (east of Greenwich)
SAST = UTC + 2 h

SOLVE
Official night (LMT) = 1823 + 0015 = 1838
Longitude time = 18° × 4 min + 35' × 4 sec = 72 min + 140 sec = 1 h 14 min 20 sec
UTC = 1838:00 − 1:14:20 = 1723:40
SAST = 1723:40 + 2:00:00 = 1923:40 ≈ 1924

ANSWER
1924 SAST

navigation.q: The distance between two VORs is 32 cm on a 1:1 000 000 chart. At 117 kt groundspeed, the flight time is approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 32 cm
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000
Groundspeed = 117 kt

FORMULA
Ground distance = chart distance × scale denominator
Time = distance ÷ groundspeed

SOLVE
Ground distance = 32 cm × 1 000 000 = 32 000 000 cm = 320 km
Convert to nautical miles: 320 km ÷ 1.852 = 172.8 NM
Time = 172.8 NM ÷ 117 kt = 1.477 h
0.477 h × 60 = 28.6 min

ANSWER
1 hr 29 min

navigation.q: If sunrise is 0543 LMT at Upington (S28°25' E021°16'), the official end of night in SAST is:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Sunrise = 0543 LMT at Upington, longitude 021°16'E.

FORMULA
Official night ends = sunrise − 15 min (LMT)
Longitude time = degrees × 4 min + minutes × 4 sec
UTC = LMT − longitude time (east of Greenwich)
SAST = UTC + 2 h

SOLVE
Official night end (LMT) = 0543 − 0015 = 0528
Longitude time = 21° × 4 min + 16' × 4 sec = 84 min + 64 sec = 1 h 25 min 04 sec
UTC = 0528:00 − 1:25:04 = 0402:56
SAST = 0402:56 + 2:00:00 = 0602:56 ≈ 0603

ANSWER
0603 SAST

navigation.q: A flight covers 243 nm. Fuel used is 17.7 USG and fuel flow is 7.8 Imp gal/hr. The groundspeed was approximately:
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Distance = 243 nm
Fuel used = 17.7 USG
Fuel flow = 7.8 Imp gal/hr

METHOD (Simple Calculation)
Fuel used = 17.7 × 0.8327 = 14.74 Imp gal
Time = 14.74 ÷ 7.8 = 1.89 h
GS = 243 ÷ 1.89 = 128.6 ≈ 129 kt

ANSWER
129 kt

navigation.q: Flying straight and level in a westerly direction in the Southern Hemisphere, the aircraft is accelerated. The magnetic compass will indicate:
navigation.a: An apparent turn to the south
navigation.b: An apparent turn to the north
navigation.d: An immediate turn to the east
navigation.ans: An apparent turn to the south
navigation.e: In the Southern Hemisphere, acceleration errors occur on easterly/westerly headings. On a westerly heading, acceleration causes an apparent turn towards south.

navigation.q: How many centimetres on a 1:1 000 000 chart represent an earth distance of 214 nm?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Ground distance = 214 NM
Chart scale = 1:1 000 000

FORMULA
Chart distance = ground distance ÷ scale denominator

SOLVE
Convert 214 NM to km: 214 × 1.853 = 396.5 km
Convert to cm: 396.5 km = 39 650 000 cm
Chart distance = 39 650 000 cm ÷ 1 000 000 = 39.65 cm ≈ 39.66 cm

ANSWER
39.66 cm

navigation.q: What is the approximate scale of a map on which 47 cm represents an earth distance of 71 nm?
navigation.e:
GIVEN
Chart distance = 47 cm
Ground distance = 71 NM

FORMULA
Scale (RF) = ground distance ÷ chart distance, both measured in the same units

SOLVE
Convert 71 NM to cm using 1 NM = 1853.18 m: 71 × 1853.18 = 131 576 m = 13 157 600 cm
Scale denominator = 13 157 600 cm ÷ 47 cm = 279 949

ANSWER
1:279 949
